how_used: Given desired values gcd_p(a n_p+b,c n_p+d) for each p|ad-bc, pick one n with n=n_p mod a large power of p for all such p, so the single gcd(an+b,cn+d) equals the product of those independently chosen p-parts; combined with each p-part ranging over all p-power divisors of ad-bc, the full value set is all divisors of the largest factor of ad-bc coprime to gcd(a,c)

technique: Clear the denominator in a nested-iteration functional equation to express n^2 as a product of two specific iterate-values of the unknown function
how_used: The relation f^{f(n)}(n) = n^2 / f(f(n)) is rewritten as f^{f(n)}(n) · f^2(n) = n^2, turning the equation into a factorization of n^2 into two terms that are themselves values of iterates of f at n, setting up an extremal/factoring argument.

technique: Take the minimal element of a function's forward orbit so that any factors of a product equal to its square, being orbit terms no smaller than it, are each forced equal to it
how_used: For the smallest term m of the sequence n, f(n), f(f(n)), ..., both factors f^2(m) and f^{f(m)}(m) of m^2 = f^2(m)·f^{f(m)}(m) are iterates of m hence ≥ m, so each equals m; this gives f(f(m))=m, and (with injectivity to fold back any pre-periodic tail) every orbit is 2-periodic, so f∘f = identity everywhere.

technique: Reduce an iteration count to its value mod 2 once the function is known to be an involution, collapsing f^k(n) to n or f(n) by parity of k
how_used: With f∘f = id established, f^{f(n)}(n)=n must equal n, but f^{f(n)}(n) equals n when f(n) is even and f(n) when f(n) is odd; forcing the odd case to give f(n)=n shows f fixes all odd integers while acting as an involution on evens, so f(1000) can be any even integer.

technique: Find a residue class modulo a well-chosen prime that is closed under every allowed operation, making it a conserved invariant the target value escapes.
how_used: Pick an odd prime p dividing m+n; then q = m/n satisfies q ≡ 1/q ≡ -1 (mod p) since m ≡ -n. Because both numbers are units ≡ -1 mod p, the denominator x+y ≡ -2 is invertible, so the arithmetic mean (x+y)/2 ≡ -1 and the harmonic mean 2xy/(x+y) ≡ -1 both stay ≡ -1. Thus every board number is ≡ -1 (mod p) forever, but 1 ≢ -1, so an odd prime factor of m+n makes 1 unreachable — forcing m+n to be a power of 2.

technique: Realize a target value as a dyadic convex combination of two seed values via iterated arithmetic-mean bisection.
how_used: With m+n = 2^k, the identity (n/(m+n))·q + (m/(m+n))·(1/q) = 1 writes 1 as a convex combination of the seeds q and 1/q with power-of-two-denominator weights n/2^k and m/2^k. Since the arithmetic mean of two dyadic combinations of the seeds is again a dyadic combination with averaged weights, binary bisection reaches the weight n/2^k in k steps, producing 1 using the arithmetic mean alone (harmonic mean unneeded).

technique: Realize a system of multiplicative congruences with an unknown modulus by first solving the corresponding exact equations over the rationals, then reducing a chosen sufficiently large prime.
how_used: Instead of directly finding residues a_i mod p with a_i a_{i+1} a_{i+2} a_{i+3} ≡ i (mod p), first produce distinct positive rationals r_i = u_i/v_i (irreducible) with the exact identity r_i r_{i+1} r_{i+2} r_{i+3} = i for 1≤i≤k, then set a_i ≡ u_i v_i^{-1} (mod p); a prime p must avoid every v_i (so a_i is defined), every u_i (so a_i ≢ 0, i.e. a_i ∈ {1..p-1}), and every cross-difference v_j u_i − v_i u_j (so the a_i stay distinct), reducing the existence claim to a finite avoidance of bad primes.

technique: Divide two consecutive sliding-window product constraints to collapse the whole family into a single fixed-shift recurrence, with the window length as free seed parameters.
how_used: From r_i r_{i+1} r_{i+2} r_{i+3} = i and r_{i+1} r_{i+2} r_{i+3} r_{i+4} = i+1, taking the ratio gives r_{i+4} = ((i+1)/i) r_i; the first window is seeded by three distinct primes r_1=x, r_2=y, r_3=z greater than k and r_4 = 1/(r_1 r_2 r_3), and the step-4 recurrence then determines all remaining r_i as exact positive rationals satisfying every window constraint by telescoping.

technique: Prove all terms of a constructed sequence are distinct by attaching a distinct prime tag to each residue class through the prime that divides each term's numerator.
how_used: In the step-4 recurrence the numerator of r_i (as an irreducible fraction) is divisible by x when i≡1, by y when i≡2, by z when i≡3, and by none of x,y,z when i≡0 (mod 4) since the seed primes exceed all small integer factors; this separates the four classes, and within each class the relation r_i < r_{i+4} makes the subsequence strictly increasing, so no two r_i coincide and the cross-differences r_i − r_j are all nonzero.

technique: Orient each edge along a deterministic successor map so every vertex has out-degree at most 1, bounding the total edge count by the number of vertices that emit an arrow.
how_used: A bridge joins islands m,n iff n≡m²+1 or m≡n²+1 (mod p). Orient the bridge from m to n exactly when n≡m²+1, i.e. along the map f(m)=m²+1 mod p. Then at most one arrow leaves each island, so the number of bridges is at most the number of arrows ≤ p.

technique: Count the out-degree-zero vertices as roots of the orienting map's fixed-point equation, pairing them via a root involution to guarantee at least two, dropping the edge total below |V|−1 (whence disconnection follows routinely).
how_used: An island m emits no arrow precisely when f(m)=m, i.e. m²+1≡m, so m is a root of x²−x+1≡0 (mod p). When p divides some x²−x+1 there are two distinct such roots x and p+1−x (via the involution x↦1−x, since (1−x)²−(1−x)+1=x²−x+1, and they coincide only at x=(p+1)/2 where 4(x²−x+1)=p²+3 is not divisible by p). Hence bridges ≤ p−2 < p−1, and a p-vertex graph with fewer than p−1 edges is disconnected.

technique: Euclid-style construction for primes dividing polynomial values: evaluate the polynomial at the product of the known qualifying primes to get a value coprime to all of them, forcing a new prime divisor of the same form.
how_used: Given primes p₁,…,p_k each dividing some x²−x+1, the number (p₁···p_k)²−(p₁···p_k)+1 exceeds 1 and is ≡1 modulo every p_i, so it is divisible by none of them and contributes a fresh prime dividing a value of x²−x+1, giving infinitely many such primes.

technique: Recognize the difference of two equal-length prefix sums of an additive function as the value of that function on a binomial coefficient.
how_used: Since f is additive, sum_{j=1}^k f(n-j) = f((n-1)(n-2)...(n-k)) and sum_{j=1}^k f(j) = f(k!), so their difference is f of the quotient (n-1)!/[k!(n-1-k)!] = f(C(n-1,k)). The symmetry condition f(k)=f(n-k) makes the two sums equal, forcing f(C(n-1,k))=0 for all k; because f is additive and non-negative, this means the prime p with f(p)>0 divides no entry C(n-1,k) of row n-1 of Pascal's triangle, for every good n.

technique: Apply Lucas' theorem to convert 'an entire row of Pascal's triangle is coprime to p' into a base-p digit constraint on the row index.
how_used: From p not dividing any C(n-1,k) (k=1,...,n-2), Lucas' theorem (equivalently Kummer's carry criterion) forces n-1 to have all base-p digits maximal below its top digit, i.e. n = a*p^s with a0 would likewise force n = b*q^t with b

technique: To inflate one multiplicative function while holding another fixed, multiply n by extra primes p whose p-1 is smooth over the prime set already present in n: each such p multiplies d(n) but introduces no new prime into phi(n).
how_used: Adjoin to n all primes p in (N,2N], each to the first power. Their p-1 factors only over primes <= N (since p-1 = 2t with t < N), so phi(n) stays supported on those small primes (the prime support of d(phi(n)) is unaffected), while each new p contributes an extra factor 2 to d(n), producing the 2^s boost that becomes 2^{s-1} in phi(d(n)).

technique: Give every base prime of n the common exponent q-1 with q a huge prime, so the same large prime power q^k appears as the leading factor of both d(n) and (through it) d(phi(n)), forcing the q-dependence to cancel in the target ratio and leaving a fixed residual.
how_used: With all primes <= N raised to q-1, d(n)=q^k*2^s gives phi(d(n))=q^{k-1}(q-1)2^{s-1}, while phi(n)=prod p_i^{q-2+c_i} gives d(phi(n))=prod(q-1+c_i); the ratio = 2^{s-1}*(q-1)/q*prod q/(q-1+c_i) -> 2^{s-1} as q->infinity.

technique: Establish that the count of primes in (N,2N] is unbounded by arguing that a uniform cap of C primes per dyadic block [2^l,2^{l+1}) would make sum 1/p converge, contradicting its divergence.
how_used: Need s = #primes in (N,2N) arbitrarily large; if every block held <= C primes, sum_p 1/p <= sum_l C/2^l < infinity, contradicting the known divergence of the reciprocal-prime sum.

technique: Strengthen the inductive invariant to a symmetric sum-AND-difference divisibility ban, so the step's failure produces exactly the forbidden term.
how_used: Instead of only forbidding a_i | a_{i-1}+a_{i+1}, prove the stronger 'nice' property that a_i divides neither a_{i-1}+a_{i+1} nor a_{i-1}-a_{i+1}; the extra difference-clause is precisely what the final contradiction (b_k | b_{k-1} - ε1ε2 b_{k+1}) needs to contradict niceness of T.

technique: Pigeonhole the insertion slots against the elements that can block them: more gaps than possible blockers forces one element to block two adjacent gaps.
how_used: Inserting a=max S into the (n-1)-term nice ordering of T gives n candidate positions N_j; each failing N_j is blamed on a neighbor b_{j-1} or b_j (never on a, by Observation A). With n slots but only n-1 elements of T, some b_k is assigned to two indices, which must be k and k+1.

technique: Eliminate the freshly inserted element between two divisibility relations sharing the same modulus to recover a relation among the old elements.
how_used: From b_k | b_{k-1}+ε1 a and b_k | a+ε2 b_{k+1}, reduce mod b_k to get b_{k-1} ≡ -ε1 a ≡ ε1ε2 b_{k+1}, so b_k | b_{k-1} - ε1ε2 b_{k+1} — a sum-or-difference divisibility entirely within T, contradicting its niceness.

technique: When an operation can only multiply by 2, treat the power-of-two part of a denominator as free and reduce 'become an integer' to killing the odd primes of the denominator one at a time.
how_used: Since x_n = 2x_{n-1} (+ optional 1/n), extra doublings clear any power of two in the denominator; so it suffices to show that at any time t one can strip a single factor of an odd prime p from the odd part q=p^e of the denominator of x_t while introducing only new powers of two, then iterate over all odd prime factors and finally double to an integer.

technique: Schedule the optional additive operations only at indices that are powers of two times the current denominator, so each surviving contribution becomes a power-of-two numerator over that fixed denominator (hence a unit modulo the target odd prime).
how_used: With q=p^e the odd part of the denominator fixed, take the '+1/n' option only at indices n=2^{r+i}q (r large so all exceed t); running forward to N the add at 2^{r+i}q becomes c_i/q with c_i=2^{N-2^{r+i}q}/2^{r+1} a power of 2, a unit mod p, giving x_N = 2^{N-t}x_t + sum_i c_i ε_i/q with independent ε_i in {0,1} and no new odd prime introduced.

technique: Show that a subset-sum set built from nonzero residues covers all of Z/p by lower-bounding the iterated sumset with Cauchy-Davenport (or a pigeonhole count).
how_used: The free binary ε_i make the achievable numerator adjustment the sumset {0,c_1}+...+{0,c_m} mod p with each c_i a unit; Cauchy-Davenport gives |sumset| >= min(p, m+1), so m=p-1 forces it to equal Z/p (pigeonhole with m=O(p^2) also works), letting one choose ε_i with 2^{N-t}A + sum ε_i c_i ≡ 0 mod p, dropping v_p of the denominator by one.

technique: Parametrize a half-integer sequence term by the 2-adic decomposition of its integer part, writing it as (power-of-two)·(odd) plus the fixed fractional remainder, so that the appearance of an integer is reduced to the power-of-two exponent reaching zero
how_used: For odd m=2^p·n_0+1, write each term as a_k = 2^p·n_k + 3/2 with n_k odd; since a_{k+1}=a_k⌊a_k⌋ and a_k is a half-integer, the product is an integer exactly when ⌊a_k⌋ is even, i.e. when the exponent p has dropped to 0

technique: Use the exponent in the 2-adic decomposition as a strict monovariant, computing the recurrence's product directly to show the exponent drops by exactly one each step while the cofactor stays odd, forcing termination
how_used: Expanding a_{k+1}=(2^p n_k+3/2)(2^p n_k+1)=2^{p-1}(2^{p+1}n_k^2+5n_k)+3/2 with the bracket odd shows p decreases by 1 per iteration; after p steps the exponent is 0, the floor is even, and the next term is an integer

technique: Split the middle term of a three-term partial-fraction triple by adding and subtracting a copy of it, so the surviving terms close up into a complete consecutive-integer harmonic block minus a dilated every-third-term harmonic block.
how_used: Partial fractions give 2/((3k-1)(3k)(3k+1)) = 1/(3k-1) - 2/(3k) + 1/(3k+1); rewriting -2/(3k) = +1/(3k) - 3/(3k), the +1/(3k) fills the multiples-of-3 gaps so the running terms become the full block 1/2+1/3+...+1/(q+2), while -3*sum 1/(3k) = -(1+1/2+...+1/((q+1)/3)), turning 2S_q into a difference of two harmonic sums.

technique: Translate a harmonic block whose denominators exceed p down to start at 1 using the inverse-periodicity 1/(p+i) congruent to 1/i (mod p).
how_used: The tail block 1/(p+1)+1/(p+2)+...+1/(q+2) is reduced mod p to 1+1/2+...+1/(q-p+2), re-indexing it to begin at 1 so it can be matched against the subtracted dilated block.

technique: Exploit a problem-specific index coincidence to make two harmonic blocks identical so they cancel, leaving only the canonical H_{p-1}.
how_used: From q=(3p-5)/2 one derives q-p+2 = (q+1)/3, so the translated tail block 1+...+1/(q-p+2) equals the subtracted dilated block 1+...+1/((q+1)/3) and they cancel; the remainder is H_{p-1}=1+1/2+...+1/(p-1), which is congruent to 0 mod p by pairing i with p-i, yielding 2S_q - 1/p + 1 congruent to 0, i.e. 1/p - 2S_q congruent to 1, so p divides m-n.

technique: Translate "prime p divides 2^n - 1" into a divisibility condition on n by computing the multiplicative order of 2 modulo p
how_used: Computing ord_3(2)=2, ord_5(2)=4, ord_7(2)=3 turns the constraint into: 3 | 2^n-1 iff 2|n, 5 | 2^n-1 iff 4|n, 7 | 2^n-1 iff 3|n. This lets the solver restrict to which of 3,5,7 can occur for a given parity/divisibility of n, e.g. odd n forces 2^n-1 to avoid factors 3 and 5, partitioning the problem into a finite menu of pure/mixed prime-power equations indexed by n mod 12.

technique: Rule out a 2^n - 1 = (prime power) equation by reducing modulo a power of 2 where 2^n-1 sits in a forced residue but the prime power can only land in a restricted residue set
how_used: For odd n divisible by 3 the only chance is 2^n-1 = 7^c; for n>=4 this needs 7^c == -1 mod 16, but 7^2 = 49 == 1 mod 16 so 7^c is only ever 1 or 7 mod 16, a contradiction, leaving n=3.

technique: When a single prime power equals a product of two near-equal factors with small gcd, factor and force one factor to be at most the gcd to kill all large solutions
how_used: In each even case the equation collapses to a prime power equal to (x-1)(x+1) (e.g. 4^k = 5^{4d'}-1 = (25^{d'}-1)(25^{d'}+1), or 8^k = (3^{a'}-1)(3^{a'}+1)) where gcd of the two factors is 2; since the whole product is a power of a single prime, one factor must be <= 2, forcing the exponent to its minimal value and pinning n=2,4,6.

technique: To prove a digit subsequence sampled at moving indices is eventually periodic, track the sampling index modulo the period of the source's eventually-periodic digit string.
how_used: x rational has eventually period-d digits; the nth digit of y is the (2^n)th digit of x, so y's nth digit depends only on 2^n mod d. Showing the residue sequence 2^n mod d is eventually periodic with some period w forces y's digits to repeat with period w, hence y rational.

technique: To control 2^n modulo a composite m, factor out the 2-adic part m = 2^u·v (v odd): the power-of-two part has 2^n ≡ 0 (mod 2^u) once n ≥ u, and the odd part is handled by the multiplicative order of 2 mod v.
how_used: With d = 2^u·v, choose w (e.g. w = φ(v)) so 2^w ≡ 1 (mod v), giving 2^{n+w} ≡ 2^n (mod v); meanwhile 2^{n+w} ≡ 2^n ≡ 0 (mod 2^u) for n ≥ u. Combining the two coprime moduli yields 2^{n+w} ≡ 2^n (mod d) for all n ≥ u, the eventual periodicity needed.

technique: When integer iterates close into a cycle, use that each consecutive difference divides the next all the way around the loop, so a cyclic chain of divisibilities forces every difference to share one absolute value.
how_used: From u-v | P(u)-P(v), the orbit differences x_0-x_1, x_1-x_2, ..., x_{k-1}-x_k each divide the next, and since x_k-x_{k+1}=x_0-x_1 the chain closes, so all |x_i-x_{i+1}| are equal; taking the minimum x_m of the orbit forces x_{m-1}=x_{m+1}, making the orbit alternate between two values, i.e. every integer fixed point of Q is a fixed point of P(P(x)).

technique: Apply the difference-divisibility u-v | P(u)-P(v) to cross-pairs drawn from two DISTINCT 2-orbits, getting mutual divisibilities that collapse (after ruling out the all-plus case by subtraction) into a single linear relation between the orbits.
how_used: With one 2-orbit {a,b=P(a)} fixed and any other fixed point alpha of P∘P with beta=P(alpha), the four pairs (alpha,a),(beta,b),(alpha,b),(beta,a) give alpha-b=±(beta-a) and alpha-a=±(beta-b); both-plus yields a-b=b-a (contradiction since a≠b), so a minus sign forces alpha+beta=a+b.

technique: Bound the number of integer solutions by exhibiting that they all satisfy one fixed polynomial relation, then invoke that a degree-n polynomial has at most n roots.
how_used: Setting C=a+b, every integer fixed point alpha satisfies C-alpha-P(alpha)=0, so all of them are roots of F(x)=C-x-P(x); since deg P=n>1 forces deg F=n, there are at most n such fixed points.

technique: When a prime p satisfies both x^a ≡ 1 and x^{p-1} ≡ 1 with gcd(a, p-1)=1, use a Bézout combination of the two exponents to force x ≡ 1 (mod p)
how_used: For a prime p | (x^7-1)/(x-1), p divides x^7-1, and Fermat gives x^{p-1}≡1. Assuming 7∤(p-1) makes gcd(7,p-1)=1, so 7k+(p-1)m=1 yields x ≡ (x^7)^k(x^{p-1})^m ≡ 1 (mod p); then the cyclotomic value 1+x+...+x^6 ≡ 7 (mod p), forcing p=7. Hence every prime divisor is ≡1 mod 7 or equals 7, so every divisor d of N is ≡0 or 1 (mod 7).

technique: Push a derived divisor-residue restriction onto a polynomial factor of the right-hand side and check its forced residue for a contradiction
how_used: Since N = y^5-1 and both y-1 and 1+y+y^2+y^3+y^4 are positive divisors of N, each must be ≡0 or 1 (mod 7), forcing y≡1 or y≡2 (mod 7). Evaluating 1+y+y^2+y^3+y^4 gives 5 (mod 7) when y≡1 and 3 (mod 7) when y≡2 — neither is 0 or 1, contradicting that this factor is also a divisor of N. So no solutions exist.

technique: Parametrize every solution of a linear Diophantine equation by adding the kernel vector, turning a minimum-norm quantity into a minimization over a single integer shift.
how_used: All representations of c are written c = a(x-kb) + b(y+ka), so w(c) = min over integer k of |x-kb| + |y+ka|; this reframing of the weight as a one-parameter integer minimization is what makes the local-champion inequalities w(c) >= w(c +/- a), w(c +/- b) comparable across shifts.

technique: Pin the minimizer of a convex, integer-valued lattice function to the adjacent step: interpolate (Jensen) from a known distant value that is <= 0 down to the neighbor to get a strict <1 bound, which integrality rounds to <= 0.
how_used: With f(t)=|x+1-bt|+|y-at|-(x+y), known f(0)=1 and f(k)<=0 for the true optimal shift k>0, convexity gives f(1) <= (1-1/k)f(0)+(1/k)f(k) < 1; since f(1) is an integer, f(1)<=0, forcing the competing representation to use k=1 and yielding |x|<b, |y|<a and x+y = floor((a+b)/2).

technique: Decide whether two sign-symmetric arithmetic progressions coincide or are disjoint by comparing their residues modulo the common difference, splitting on the parity of the parameters.
how_used: Champions form C+ and C- = +/-(ax-by), each an AP of length b-1 with difference a+b; for a,b both odd the symmetry x<->b-x, y<->a-y makes C+=C- giving b-1 champions, while for opposite parities computing 2c1 = -2c2 = -a (mod a+b) and a+b odd & coprime to a shows C+, C- lie in distinct residue classes, hence disjoint, giving 2(b-1).

technique: Strengthen a bare existence/surjectivity claim mod n into a uniform induction hypothesis that hits EVERY residue mod n and can place its witnesses beyond any prescribed bound, so the hypothesis produces exactly the raw material the inductive step consumes.
how_used: Instead of proving only that some m has n | 2^m + m, prove by induction on d that for every bound N there exist b_0,...,b_{d-1} > N with 2^{b_i}+b_i ≡ i (mod d) for all i; taking m=b_0 (the i=0 witness) recovers the original claim, and the 'every residue' plus '>N' freedom is exactly what the inductive step needs to feed a smaller modulus.

technique: Bound the eventual period of a base's powers mod a strictly below a by noting its residue-cycle cannot contain all a residues (0 is either absent or isolated in the cycle), yielding a strictly smaller modulus via gcd for the descent.
how_used: Let k be the period of 2^i mod a (repeating from exponent M on); since the cycle of powers of 2 omits 0 or contains it alone, k<a, hence d=gcd(a,k) satisfies 0<d<a, so the induction hypothesis applies to the smaller modulus d to supply the base witnesses b_i with 2^{b_i}+b_i ≡ i (mod d).

technique: Increment the exponent by the period so the power term stays fixed mod a while the linear term sweeps an arithmetic progression, decoupling the two summands so that combining several such progressions realizes a complete residue system.
how_used: For each i form 2^{b_i+mk}+(b_i+mk), m=0..a'-1 (a'=a/d); since 2^{b_i+mk}≡2^{b_i} (mod a), these equal 2^{b_i}+(b_i+mk), so the additive part advances by k each step; the d progressions give a'd=a values, proven pairwise distinct mod a by reducing mod d (forcing i=j since d|k) then cancelling k via k'=k/d coprime to a' (forcing m=n), so they realize all residues mod a.

technique: Substitute n = 10^k - 1 so the input digit-sum S(n) = 9k scales linearly in the parameter k while the polynomial output P(n) keeps only O(k) decimal digits.
how_used: For deg P = d >= 2, plugging n = 10^k - 1 into S(P(n)) = P(S(n)) gives S(P(n)) = P(9k); since P(n) ~ n^d has O(dk) digits its digit sum S(P(n)) is O(k), but P(9k) grows like k^d, impossible for large k when d >= 2, eliminating all degrees >= 2.

technique: Apply digit-sum subadditivity S(m+n) <= S(m) + S(n) to the increment between two chosen evaluation points to bound a leading coefficient.
how_used: From S(an+b) = aS(n)+b, evaluating at n=2025 and n=2020 gives S(2025a+b) - S(2020a+b) = 5a; writing 2025a+b = (2020a+b)+5a and applying subadditivity yields 5a <= S(5a), which with a >= 1 forces a = 1.

technique: Choose the variable so that adding the constant offset produces an all-9's number, triggering a maximal carry cascade that makes the digit-sum drop by a large multiple of the digit count.
how_used: After reducing to S(n+b) = S(n)+b, pick n with n+1+b = 10^k so n+b is all 9's; then S(n+1+b)-S(n+b) = 1-9k, while the equality forces it to equal S(n+1)-S(n) >= 2-9k (as S(n) < 9k), a contradiction killing b > 0 (and symmetrically b < 0), leaving P(x) = x.

technique: Classify prime factors by their residue mod p, then convert a target residue condition on a divisor into a parity condition on how many of the (-1)-residue primes it uses.
how_used: A divisor of m is ≡1 mod 3 exactly when it contains no factor of 3, uses primes ≡1 mod 3 freely (they contribute 1), and uses an EVEN total number (with multiplicity) of primes ≡2 mod 3 (each contributing -1≡2). This isolates the q_j-primes (≡2 mod 3) as the only constrained part, reducing τ₁ to counting exponent tuples on the q's with even total exponent.

technique: Count exponent tuples whose total is even by splitting each factor's exponent range into even-count ⌈(b+1)/2⌉ vs odd-count ⌊(b+1)/2⌋ and convolving: if any single range has even size the split is exactly half, otherwise track even/odd subtotals inductively.
how_used: Number of q-exponent choices with even total exponent equals ⌈½∏(b_j+1)⌉, so τ₁(m)=∏(a_i+1)·⌈½∏(b_j+1)⌉; for 10n this becomes ∏(a_i+1)·⌈½(y+2)(z+2)∏(b_j+1)⌉, the ceiling being what distinguishes the c-even and c-odd cases.

technique: When a quantity equals 2(x+1)c/(c+1), use gcd(c,c+1)=1 to shift the integrality requirement onto the complementary factor c+1, forcing (c+1)∣2(x+1) and rewriting the value as k·c.
how_used: With c=(y+2)(z+2)∏(b_j+1) odd, the ratio is 2(x+1)c/(c+1); coprimality of c and c+1 forces c+1∣2(x+1), so writing 2(x+1)=k(c+1) gives ratio=kc=k(y+2)(z+2)∏(b_j+1). Since y,z odd ⇒ y+2,z+2≥3, every such value is composite; combined with ratio=2(x+1) (any even integer) when c is even, and the construction n=3^{(ab-1)/2}2^{a-2}5^{b-2} realizing each odd composite ab, the value set is exactly 2 plus all composites.

technique: Add the divisor itself to the dividend to absorb the lone +1/-1 constant and expose a multiple that factors out a power of the base
how_used: From n^k+mn^l+1 | n^{k+l}-1, add the divisor to the dividend so n^k+mn^l+1 | (n^{k+l}-1)+(n^k+mn^l+1)=n^{k+l}+n^k+mn^l, a positive multiple every term of which carries a positive power of n

technique: Cancel a coprime power of the base out of a divisibility because gcd(divisor, base)=1
how_used: Since (n^k+mn^l+1, n)=1, the divisor must divide n^{k+l}+n^k+mn^l with its common factor n^{min} stripped: dividing by n^k (case l>=k) gives n^k+mn^l+1 | n^l+mn^{l-k}+1, and dividing by n^l (case l<k) gives n^k+mn^l+1 | n^k+n^{k-l}+m

technique: Pin a divisibility to an equality by sandwiching the (positive) dividend strictly between the divisor and twice it
how_used: The reduced target n^l+mn^{l-k}+1 (resp. n^k+n^{k-l}+m) is positive and less than 2(n^k+mn^l+1), so it must equal the divisor; equating then forces m=1, l=2k in the first case and m=(n^{k-l}-1)/(n^l-1) with l|k in the second (l|k via the standard n^a-1 | n^b-1 iff a|b)

technique: With the parameter fixed, view the defining relation as a monic integer quadratic in one symmetric coordinate and use Vieta to read off the conjugate root as a second integer solution
how_used: Substituting u=x+y, v=x-y turns k=(x^2-a)/(x^2-y^2) into u^2-(4k-2)uv+(v^2-4a)=0; treating this as a quadratic in u with v,k fixed, one root known, Vieta gives the other root as an integer, yielding a new solution (x_1,y_1) of (1) -- equivalently x_1=-x+2k(x-y) is manifestly integral, with x_1+y_1=x-y preserved

technique: Bound the size of the Vieta-conjugate solution to show a single jump lands on the opposite side of a fixed threshold, then run the jump as a monovariant down to the minimal representative
how_used: For B subset A the conjugate satisfies x_1 >= 2a/(x+y) > sqrt(a) (since x,y<sqrt(a) gives x+y<2sqrt(a)), so a solution with x<sqrt(a) jumps to one with x>sqrt(a); for A subset B, choosing the solution of smallest x+y, the estimates y_1>4a/(x+y)>0 and 4a/(x+y)<x+y force x_1+y_1<x+y, so by minimality x_1 cannot exceed sqrt(a), and x_1=sqrt(a) is impossible as a is a nonsquare, giving 0<=x_1<sqrt(a)

technique: From a divisibility d | A, subtract a chosen integer multiple of d from the dividend A to replace it by a much smaller, controllable expression that d still divides.
how_used: Using f(m)+f(n)-mn | mf(m)+nf(n): with n=1 (and f(1)=1 from m=n=1) subtract p times the divisor f(p)-p+1 from pf(p)+1 to get f(p)-p+1 | p^2-p+1; with m=n=p subtract p times 2f(p)-p^2 from 2pf(p) to get 2f(p)-p^2 | p^3. These reduce the messy dividend to a fixed/prime-power target.

technique: Combine an explicit size bound on a divisor of a prime power with the fact that all its divisors are powers of the prime, then show the divisor is trapped in an open interval that contains no such power to force a contradiction.
how_used: The n=1 relation forces either f(p)=p^2 or (since p^2-p+1 is odd) p^2-p+1 >= 3(f(p)-p+1), giving f(p) <= (p^2+2p-2)/3. Plugging this into 2f(p)-p^2 | p^3 puts 2f(p)-p^2 strictly in (-p^2,-p) for p>=7, an interval containing no divisor (1,p,p^2,p^3) of p^3, so the alternative is impossible and f(p)=p^2.

technique: Specialize one variable to an arbitrarily large prime so a target divisor grows without bound while the remaining congruence difference is a fixed quantity; a fixed integer divisible by an unbounded modulus must be zero.
how_used: Setting m=p (large prime) with f(p)=p^2 and stripping the coprime factor p (p does not divide f(n) for large p) yields p^2-pn+f(n) | p^2-pn+n^2, hence p^2-pn+f(n) | n^2-f(n). Since n^2-f(n) is fixed but the modulus can be made arbitrarily large, n^2-f(n)=0, so f(n)=n^2 for all n.

technique: Reduce a cyclic-polygon divisibility problem to smaller cyclic polygons by cutting along a diagonal that still satisfies the hypothesis, isolating the hard case where no diagonal qualifies
how_used: After the k=3 Heron base case, for k>=4: if some diagonal has squared length divisible by n it splits P into two smaller cyclic polygons whose sides and that diagonal all have squares divisible by n, so induction on k applies; this lets the solver assume no diagonal's squared length is divisible by n=p^t, i.e. nu_p(diagonal^2) < t while nu_p(side^2) >= t

technique: Square Ptolemy's chord relation for a cyclic quadrilateral to clear the radical cross-term and obtain a polynomial identity among only the squared chord lengths
how_used: On cyclic quadrilateral A1 A_{m-1} A_m A_{m+1}, Ptolemy gives A1A_{m+1}*A_{m-1}A_m + A1A_{m-1}*A_mA_{m+1} = A1A_m*A_{m-1}A_{m+1}; isolating and squaring yields A1A_{m+1}^2*A_{m-1}A_m^2 = A1A_{m-1}^2*A_mA_{m+1}^2 + A1A_m^2*A_{m-1}A_{m+1}^2 - 2*A1A_{m-1}*A_mA_{m+1}*A1A_m*A_{m-1}A_{m+1}, an integer relation among squared distances from A1 to consecutive vertices

technique: In an additive identity among products, exploit that two terms of unequal p-adic valuation cannot cancel so a third term inherits the minimum valuation, propagating a strict valuation inequality to the next index until a bounded strictly-decreasing valuation chain gives a contradiction
how_used: In the squared-Ptolemy identity nu_p(A1A_{m-1}^2*A_mA_{m+1}^2) > nu_p(A1A_m^2*A_{m-1}A_{m+1}^2) and the 2-sqrt cross term has even larger valuation, forcing nu_p(A1A_{m+1}^2) < nu_p(A1A_m^2); this builds p^t > nu_p(A1A_3^2) > ... > nu_p(A1A_k^2), yet the side A1A_k has nu_p >= p^t, contradiction

technique: Pick a prime in an arithmetic progression so that gcd(p-1, d) = 1, making the d-th-power map a bijection mod p and upgrading a^d ≡ b^d to a ≡ b.
how_used: By Dirichlet's theorem (d odd) choose a large prime p ≡ 2 (mod d), so (p-1, d) = 1. After pigeonholing d+1 of the y_i into one residue class mod p, in the case p∤cQ(y_1) the congruence cQ(y_1) ≡ cQ(y_i) gives l^d ≡ m^d (mod p); injectivity of x↦x^d then forces l ≡ m (mod p), hence p | (m·y_i − l·y_1).

technique: To force two near-equal d-th powers to be literally equal, factor a^d − b^d = (a−b)·(cofactor) and show that a single gained prime factor (or a smallness bound on a side) makes the leading cofactor term dominate the bounded lower-degree remainder, so the linear factor a−b must vanish.
how_used: Writing Q(y_i)/Q(y_1) = l^d/m^d and expanding gives b_d(m^d y_i^d − l^d y_1^d) = −Σ_{j≤d-2} b_j(m^d y_i^j − l^d y_1^j). Factor the LHS as b_d(m·y_i − l·y_1)(Σ m^{d-1-k}y_i^{d-1-k} l^k y_1^k). In Case 1 (p | cQ(y_1)) cancellation forces m ≤ p^{-1/d}(2cB)^{1/d}y_1, shrinking the RHS bound; in Case 2 the factor p | (m·y_i − l·y_1) multiplies the LHS by p. Either way, against the bound (RHS ≤ 21(d−1)B(2cB)^{1/d}m^{d-1}y_i^{d-1}), large p makes m·y_i − l·y_1 ≠ 0 impossible, giving Q(y_i)/Q(y_1) = y_i^d/y_1^d.

technique: Convert pointwise value-ratios into a polynomial identity by exhibiting a polynomial of degree ≤ d that vanishes at d+1 distinct points, hence is identically zero.
how_used: From the Claim Q(y_i)/Q(y_1) = y_i^d/y_1^d, the polynomial Q(y_1)·y^d − y_1^d·Q(y) (degree ≤ d) vanishes at the d+1 distinct values y_1,...,y_{d+1}, so it is the zero polynomial, forcing Q(y) = b_d y^d. Reversing the Tschirnhaus substitution y = d·a_d·x + a_{d-1} and clearing denominators yields P(x) = a(rx+s)^d.

technique: Subtract two simultaneous perfect-square equations so the unknown squares combine into a single difference of squares equal to a known factored quantity.
how_used: From a^2=p-q and b^2=pq-q, subtracting gives b^2-a^2=p(q-1), i.e. (b-a)(b+a)=p(q-1), turning the prime p into a factor of a difference of squares.

technique: Bound each factor of a difference of squares strictly below the prime's range so the prime is forced to equal the sum-factor of the factorization.
how_used: Since 0

technique: Exploit that a sum and a difference of the same two integers always share parity to pin down a variable.
how_used: b+a=p and b-a=q-1 have equal parity, so p and q-1 share parity; with p an odd prime this forces q-1 odd, i.e. q=2 (then mod 3 gives p=3).

technique: Encode a permutation statistic as a q-generating polynomial so that proving two count-distributions coincide for every value collapses to a single polynomial identity.
how_used: Instead of matching, for each k, the number of permutations of the multiset M with exactly k A-inversions against the count for B, define F_A = sum over permutations of q^(number of A-inversions). The claim 'counts agree for all k, A, B' becomes F_A(q) = F_B(q); strengthen to F_A being independent of A entirely, which forces it to equal the ordinary-inversion generating function. Reading off coefficients of q^k then yields the equidistribution simultaneously for all k, A, B.

technique: Build a recurrence by deleting the first entry of the permutation and weighting it by q raised to the number of statistic-inversions that entry forms with the remaining entries.
how_used: Induct on n: condition on which distinct value theta_i heads the permutation (e_i labeled copies), with threshold index k defined by theta_k <= a_1 < theta_{k+1}. The three A-inversion rules make the head's inversion count depend on where a_1 sits: heading values below the threshold (i<=k) contribute exponent (e_1+...+e_{i-1})+(e_{k+1}+...+e_m); those above (i>k) contribute (e_{k+1}+...+e_{i-1}); each times e_i * F(e_1,...,e_i-1,...,e_m), with the tail F's A-independent by the induction hypothesis.

technique: Normalize each recurrence term by the total generating function so per-block factors collapse to a closed ratio, then telescope the resulting sum to erase the free parameter.
how_used: Using the closed form F = n!_q * prod_i e_i!/e_i!_q gives e_i*F(e_i-1)/F = (1-q^{e_i})/(1-q^n), turning the required identity into 1-q^n = q^{e_{k+1}+...+e_m} sum_{i<=k} q^{e_1+...+e_{i-1}}(1-q^{e_i}) + sum_{i>k} q^{e_{k+1}+...+e_{i-1}}(1-q^{e_i}); the two sums telescope to q^{e_{k+1}+...+e_m}-q^n and 1-q^{e_{k+1}+...+e_m}, so the threshold index k (hence A) drops out.

technique: Reduce an 'invariant under all orderings/permutations' claim to invariance under a single adjacent transposition, since adjacent transpositions generate the symmetric group
how_used: To prove the count of arcs R_i->B_i covering (1,0) is independent of the ordering of the red points, it suffices to show that interchanging the positions of two consecutive red points R_i and R_{i+1} (a geometric swap of their two locations on the circle, which permutes the induced greedy pairing) does not change the covered arcs; every permutation of the reds is a product of such adjacent swaps, so invariance under one swap gives invariance under all orderings.

technique: Verify a claimed local invariance by exhaustive casework on how many of the involved points fall inside a critical arc
how_used: After reducing to swapping the positions of adjacent reds R_i,R_{i+1}, split into the three cases according to whether 0, 1, or 2 of the two associated blue points B_i,B_{i+1} lie on the counterclockwise arc R_i->R_{i+1} (no other blue point lies inside the two arcs being compared, by the greedy nearest-blue rule); in each case one checks directly from the picture that the number of arcs covering any given point of the circle is unchanged, hence the covered region is preserved.

technique: Encode a matching-count invariant as an extremal (minimum) value of a running +/- 1 tally read once around the circle, then prove it by an induction that deletes an innermost matched pair
how_used: Traverse the circle counterclockwise from (1,0), keeping a counter that starts at 0, adds +1 at each red point and -1 at each blue point (ending at 0 since there are n of each); the number of inverted chords (arcs R_i->B_i covering (1,0)) equals -x, where x<=0 is the minimum value the counter ever attains — a quantity depending only on the coloring/positions, not on the chord choice. This is proved by induction on n by deleting the chord R_1B_1 (whose arc contains no blue point): a stable chord leaves x unchanged, while an inverted chord forces the last point before (1,0) to be red, so x<0, and deleting it raises x by exactly 1.

technique: Extract a sublattice that is a scaled similar copy of the original by a coloring, assign it the next label, and recurse on the leftover copy.
how_used: Checkerboard-color Z^2, label all black points 1; the white points form another copy of Z^2 scaled by sqrt(2). Repeat: at step i the surviving lattice is scaled by 2^{(i-1)/2}, so its minimum spacing beats c^i whenever c<sqrt(2). Stop at N with c^N < 2^{(N-1)/2} and label everything remaining N, giving finitely many labels.

technique: Prove a global impossibility by inducting on a geometrically doubling square, choosing the sharp inductive statement (a size-2^n square cannot avoid using some label above a linear-in-n threshold).
how_used: Claim: a 2^n x 2^n square cannot be filled using only labels <= 2n. Base n=1 clear; assume up to n-1. Under the hypothesis each 2^{n-1} sub-square must contain a label >= 2n-1, which is the contrapositive engine that drives the whole contradiction at c=sqrt(2), where label 2n forces pairwise distance (sqrt2)^{2n}=2^n. Finiteness of labels then contradicts the claim for n large.

technique: Slide a half-size box anchored to touch one forced label and bounded by a second forced label so that its interior can legally contain neither, producing the contradiction.
how_used: First a four-points-in-a-unit-square pigeonhole bounds the copies of the max label 2n to fewer than four, freeing (WLOG) the NW quadrant of 2n's. Place square A right of a NW-located 2n-1 forcing a 2n in the NE; then place square B either north of the 2n-1 bounded east by that 2n, or west of it bounded north, so B contains neither 2n-1 nor 2n, contradicting that every 2^{n-1} square needs a label >= 2n-1.

technique: For a 'smallest k that always works' lower bound, build the extremal instance from equal indivisible pieces sized just over the group capacity divided by the count, so no two fit in one group
how_used: Take d=2n-1 equal values a_i = n/(2n-1); the sum is n and each lies in [0,1], but any two sum to 2n/(2n-1)>1, forcing every value into its own group and giving k >= 2n-1

technique: Run an induction on the number of items where the inductive step deletes one item by fusing a pair that the pigeonhole guarantees can be safely combined
how_used: Induct on d for the upper bound (every instance fits in 2n-1 groups). Base d<=2n-1 is trivial (one value per group). For d>=2n, the n disjoint consecutive pairs (a_1+a_2)+...+(a_{2n-1}+a_{2n}) sum to <= n, so some pair has a_i+a_{i+1} <= 1; replace it by the single value a_i+a_{i+1} in [0,1] to get d-1 values still summing to n, partition those into 2n-1 groups by the hypothesis, then un-merge inside its group without changing that group's sum.

technique: Bound a partition count by a greedy fill that forces each closed part past a fixed capacity threshold, then charge the total against that per-part surplus
how_used: For the upper bound: give each a_i>1/2 its own group; among the rest (all <=1/2) greedily add values to a group and close it the instant its sum exceeds 1/2 (the pushing summand <=1/2 keeps the sum <=1), so every closed group has sum in (1/2,1]. If the last two groups together sum <=1, merge them; then in the resulting m groups the first m-2 each exceed 1/2 and the last two together exceed 1, so n > (m-2)/2 + 1, i.e. m <= 2n-1.

technique: For a smallest-k / minimal-count answer, exhibit an extremal instance of equal values tuned so no two can share a part, forcing the matching lower bound
how_used: To show k>=2n-1 (so the upper bound 2n-1 is optimal, not merely sufficient): take d=2n-1 with all values equal to n/(2n-1). This is admissible (sum = n, each value <=1 since n<=2n-1). Since 2n/(2n-1)>1, any two of them already exceed 1, so no group can hold two; the 2n-1 values need 2n-1 separate groups. Hence k cannot be smaller than 2n-1.

technique: To show a required part-count is not too large, repeatedly find a mergeable adjacent pair by pigeonhole on consecutive pair-sums (their total is bounded, so one pair is small), fuse it into a single element, and induct on the reduced count
how_used: For the upper bound (that 2n-1 groups always suffice): induct on d. Base d<=2n-1: each number is its own group, sum <=1. Step d>=2n: the n consecutive pair-sums (a1+a2)+(a3+a4)+...+(a_{2n-1}+a_{2n}) total at most the whole sum n, so by pigeonhole some pair a_i,a_{i+1} has a_i+a_{i+1}<=1. Merge them into one number b=a_i+a_{i+1} in [0,1], giving d-1 numbers with the same total n. By induction these fit in 2n-1 groups each of sum <=1; splitting b back into a_i,a_{i+1} inside its group leaves that group's sum unchanged, giving a valid 2n-1-group partition of the original d numbers.

technique: For the lower-bound half of a 'smallest k' packing problem, choose the extremal input of equal items tuned so any two together already exceed the capacity, forcing one item per group
how_used: Take d=2n-1 and a_i=n/(2n-1) for all i. Each lies in (0,1] and they sum to n, so the input is valid. Any two sum to 2n/(2n-1)>1, so no group of sum <=1 holds two of them; the 2n-1 numbers each need their own group, giving k>=2n-1. Matched with the sufficiency argument this pins k=2n-1.

technique: To shrink an instance for an induction on the number of items, use an averaging/pigeonhole bound on grouped consecutive pairs to guarantee some adjacent pair fits within one unit of capacity, then merge that pair into a single item
how_used: For the upper bound (2n-1 groups always suffice), induct on d. When d>=2n, group the first 2n terms into consecutive pairs; the total of the n pair-sums (a_1+a_2)+...+(a_{2n-1}+a_{2n}) is at most the whole sum n, so by averaging some pair a_i+a_{i+1}<=1. Merge those two into one number a_i+a_{i+1} (still in (0,1] with total still n, now over d-1 items). The induction hypothesis partitions the d-1 numbers into 2n-1 valid groups, which pulls back to a valid partition of the original d numbers.

technique: Build the lower-bound instance by placing the two colors in strictly alternating cyclic order on a circle so every arc between adjacent points is bichromatic and must be cut, then bound cuts per line by its intersections with the circle.
how_used: Put 2013 red and 2013 blue points alternately on a circle (plus one stray blue elsewhere), creating 4026 bichromatic arcs; each arc must meet a drawn line, and a line meets the circle in at most 2 points, so it resolves at most 2 arcs, giving k >= 4026/2 = 2013.

technique: Isolate two chosen same-color points from every other point at once by drawing two lines parallel to their connecting segment, placed just on either side so the thin strip contains only those two.
how_used: For each same-color pair A,B, two lines parallel to AB and close on both sides fence off exactly A and B (epsilon below the min distance from line AB to all other points); pairing the minority color's remaining 2012 points into 1006 such pairs uses 2 lines each = 2012 lines, with the entire other color left as one untouched monochromatic background.

technique: Cut off a single convex-hull vertex from all remaining points with one line, since all other points lie strictly on one side of a supporting line at that vertex.
how_used: To absorb the odd count of the minority color, separate one red convex-hull vertex with a single line so the total is 1 + 2*1006 = 2013; if the hull is all-blue, a line parallel to a hull edge isolates its two blue endpoints as the odd-handling move instead.

technique: Recast an unstructured reachability goal as lowering a graph invariant by one, and prove only the single-step reduction lemma.
how_used: The target "reach an edgeless graph" is reframed as "reach a 1-colorable graph"; the whole problem is reduced to a lemma that operations can turn an n-colorable graph into an (n-1)-colorable one, then iterated from the trivial n-coloring by vertices down to 1 color.

technique: Exhaustively apply the given degree-reducing operation until the graph is stuck in a uniform-parity state, using that it must terminate.
how_used: Operation (i) (delete a vertex of odd degree) is applied repeatedly until impossible; since vertex count strictly drops it terminates in a graph where every degree is even, which is the precondition that makes the later doubling flip every degree to odd.

technique: Color the duplicated copy of each vertex with the cyclically-next color so that one whole color class becomes an odd-degree independent set that can be peeled off.
how_used: After doubling an all-even-degree properly n-colored graph, copy I' of a color-k vertex is given color k+1 mod n (valid since n>1); every degree is now odd, and the color-n class has no internal edges, so its vertices are deleted one by one by operation (i) without disturbing each other's odd degrees, yielding an (n-1)-coloring.

technique: Convert a minimum-number-of-parts optimality hypothesis into a ban on two equal-sum sub-collections of different sizes, so exhibiting one such pair swaps to a strictly shorter representation.
how_used: On the optimal A-partition with distinct-part set S={b_1<...<b_s}, the sought contradiction is subsets X,Y of S with |X|<|Y| but equal sum: delete one copy of each element of Y from the partition and insert one copy of each element of X, giving an A-partition of n into fewer than k_min parts, contradicting optimality. This reduces 'at most cube-root(6n) distinct parts' to finding an equal-sum size-mismatched subset pair whenever s>cube-root(6n).

technique: Lower-bound the number of distinct subset sums of a fixed size by walking through equal-size subsets one element-shift-to-the-right at a time, each shift strictly increasing the sum, so the whole walk gives that many distinct values.
how_used: For each k<=s, start from the k smallest elements {b_1,...,b_k} and repeatedly move the rightmost movable chosen index up by one slot; each single shift changes the sum by b_new - b_old > 0, so the sums strictly increase along a chain of length k(s-k)+1 of k-element subsets, all lying in [1,n]. This produces k(s-k)+1 distinct integer sums for that size k.

technique: Add the per-parameter lower bounds on distinct values across all parameter choices and compare the total to the size of the ambient integer range to force a pigeonhole collision.
how_used: Summing k(s-k)+1 over k=1..s gives s(s^2+5)/6 > s^3/6 > n (using s>cube-root(6n)). All these sums lie in [1,n], only n values, so two coincide; because each size k contributes distinct sums, the collision must come from two different sizes k<k', yielding equal-sum subsets X,Y with |X|=k<k'=|Y|.

technique: From a local 'a value repeats within a bounded window ahead' hypothesis, build an infinite chain of equal-value indices with bounded gaps to force the value to appear in every later window of that length.
how_used: The lemma: given that each b_m equals some b_n with n in [m+1, m+r], iterate to get k=k_1<k_2<... with all b_{k_i} equal and gaps at most r; unboundedness makes this hit every segment [ell, ell+r-1], so b_k reappears arbitrarily far out.

technique: Bound the number of distinct values a windowed sequence takes by showing more than that many distinct values would all have to reappear inside a single fixed-length window, exceeding its capacity.
how_used: Assuming r+1 distinct b-values, the reappearance claim forces all r+1 to appear in one segment [s, s+r-1] of length r, a contradiction; applied with s=0 to a_i it caps the sequence at r distinct values, then the r-tuples A_i at r^r types.

technique: Upgrade an 'equal infinitely often' shift relation on state-tuples to 'holds for all indices' by a one-step downward induction, using an auxiliary windowed-sum sequence to transport the relation one index earlier.
how_used: With D={d: A_d=A_{d+p}} infinite hence unbounded, show d+1 in D implies d in D: apply the lemma to b_k=S(k,k+p) to get t in [d+1,d+r] with S(t,t+p)=S(d,d+p), combine with A_{d+1}=A_{d+p+1} to derive a_d=a_{d+p} and thus A_d=A_{d+p}.

technique: Take a minimum-size cover of the target set and read off a private element for each cover member from minimality
how_used: Cover D=S_4(x) by the distance-3 balls S_3(a) of neighbors a in A=S_1(x); fix a minimal 'substantial' subset A* of size m, so removing any y from A* leaves some d_y in D reachable at distance 4 only through y — a witness attached exclusively to y.

technique: Bound a covered total by (number of parts)x(share per part) and maximize that product over the free part-count to force a numeric contradiction
how_used: If every a in A* had |S_3(a)∩D| ≤ 101-m then |D| ≤ m(101-m) ≤ 50·51 = 2550 < 2551, so some a covers ≥ 102-m of D; since |S_3(a)| ≤ 100 this leaves at most m-2 cities of S_3(a) at distance ≤3 from x, i.e. |T| ≤ m-2.

technique: Use that distance to a fixed vertex changes by at most 1 along each edge of a path to land on an intermediate vertex at a prescribed exact distance
how_used: Along x-y-b_y-c_y-d_y the values d(a,·) satisfy d(a,y)≤2 and d(a,d_y)>3 with consecutive terms differing by ≤1, so some b_y or c_y is at distance exactly 3 from a, giving an element of T; the private-witness property makes these m-1 elements distinct, so m-1 ≤ |T| ≤ m-2, a contradiction.

technique: Embed the labels as points at fractional parts {k·alpha} of a circular rotation, so that an additive equal-sum relation among labels turns into a pair of parallel chords.
how_used: Points 0,1,...,n are marked at clockwise distance {k·alpha} on a unit-perimeter circle (arrangement A(alpha)). Any a+c=b+d gives a·alpha+c·alpha=b·alpha+d·alpha, so the a-c chord is parallel to the b-d chord; parallel chords never cross, so every A(alpha) is beautiful. This realizes the arrangements as a one-parameter family and is the whole engine for producing beautiful configurations.

technique: Count the distinct combinatorial orders produced by sweeping a real parameter as one more than the number of parameter values at which two marked points collide.
how_used: As alpha runs 0 to 1, the clockwise order of A(alpha) changes only when {p·alpha}={q·alpha}, i.e. alpha equals a reduced fraction of denominator at most n; there are exactly N such fractions (each pair (x,y), x+y<=n, gcd=1 gives x/(x+y)). So at most N+1 orders arise; distinctness is confirmed by decoding f_i=a_i/b_i back from the cluster pattern of A(f_i+eps), yielding exactly N+1 cyclic arrangements.

technique: Prove a construction is exhaustive by inducting on deletion of the largest label and showing the constraints force the reinserted label into its slot(s).
how_used: Given beautiful A on [0,n], delete n to get a cyclic A_{n-1}(alpha) by induction. Depending on whether a fraction i/n lies in the Farey interval containing alpha, non-crossing of the n-1-to-x and n-to-(x-1) chords forces n between its neighbors uniquely (Case 1) or into exactly one of two positions (Case 2), so A itself is cyclic; hence M=N+1.

technique: In a covering game, respond to each opponent move by painting the cell immediately beyond the current filled frontier rather than the gap at the frontier, so that no cell-size is ever painted twice ahead of the frontier.
how_used: When A supplies ink for length 1/2^m, B paints the next dyadic interval I_1 (just right of the leftmost still-uncolored dyadic cell I_0) whenever I_1 still has an uncolored point, and only fills I_0 otherwise; this look-ahead guarantees B never places two intervals of the same length 1/2^m to the right of the frontier x_r.

technique: Bound a family of dyadic-length pieces of pairwise distinct sizes by twice the largest, via the geometric sum of distinct negative powers of two.
how_used: Because at most one interval of each length lies right of the frontier, the pre-painted pieces swallowed when the frontier advances total less than 2/2^m, and the scattered pieces in [x_r,1] total at most 2(1-x_r); these give the '3x_r + 1/2^m' step and the final '2(1-x_r)' term.

technique: Maintain a linear potential bounding cumulative resource by a constant times progress, proved by amortized induction that charges each frontier advance against the pieces it absorbs.
how_used: B keeps invariant (i): ink spent on [0,x_r] is at most 3x_r; each advance x_{r+1}=x_r+alpha with alpha>1/2^m costs at most 2/2^m (scattered) + 1/2^m (the filled I_0), giving 3(x_r+1/2^m) < 3x_{r+1}, and combined with the tail bound yields total ink < 3 < 4, so the pot is never empty.

technique: Set up a counting recurrence by deleting the extremal element and showing the deletion always lands on a valid smaller configuration, so building up is inserting that element back.
how_used: Remove the radius-(n+1) disk from a valid (n+1)-stack: since the largest disk can never be hidden by anything, what remains is automatically a valid n-stack. Hence every valid (n+1)-stack arises by reinserting the radius-(n+1) disk into some valid n-stack, so a_{n+1} is a fixed multiplier times a_n with base a_1 = 2.

technique: Compute the recurrence multiplier by case-splitting the reinsertion slots according to how many of the choices the constraint still permits at each slot.
how_used: Of the n+1 slots to insert the radius-(n+1) disk into a fixed valid n-stack, only the very bottom slot permits both colors (2 ways, nothing below it to block), while each of the other n slots permits only the transparent copy (an opaque one would hide the smaller disks beneath). This gives multiplier 2 + n = n+2, so a_{n+1} = (n+2) a_n and a_n = (n+1)!.

technique: Recast a path-length parity goal as a same-color condition on the path's endpoints in the graph's proper 2-coloring
how_used: A longest path in a tree runs between two leaves, and a path has an even number of edges iff its two endpoints receive the same color in the unique 2-coloring of the tree; so the whole problem reduces to showing all k leaves get the same color.

technique: Bound the degree-sum over an independent set by counting each edge at most once, with equality exactly when the set is also a vertex cover
how_used: For an independent set S, sum of deg(v) over S equals the number of tree edges meeting S (independence means no edge is double-counted), which is at most the n-1 edges of the tree; equality holds iff every edge meets S (a vertex cover), and an independent vertex cover of a connected bipartite tree is precisely one of the two color classes.

technique: Match an upper bound with a minimum-degree lower bound on the same quantity to force the equality case (pincer)
how_used: The given size-(n+k-1)/2 independent set can contain at most the k leaves as degree-1 vertices, all its other vertices having degree at least 2, so its degree-sum is at least k + 2*((n-k-1)/2) = n-1, matching the n-1 ceiling; equality forces S to contain every leaf and to be a color class, hence all leaves share that class's color.

technique: When one branch of a peeled first step is entirely unavailable, attribute a dedicated obstacle that must block it and delete that obstacle from the resource budget of the surviving branch's inductive subproblem.
how_used: Inducting on n by splitting mine-avoiding paths at the first step into those through (1,0) and (0,1): in the case where no path starts at (0,1), some mine must sit at (0,k) to block the y-axis; that mine is irrelevant to paths through (1,0), so the induction runs with |M|-1, giving 2^{n-1-(|M|-1)}=2^{n-|M|} and recovering the lost factor of 2.

technique: Construct one alternative continuation per branch point of a given path so the continuations are pairwise disjoint away from that path, then pigeonhole: fewer obstacles than continuations forces at least one obstacle-free alternative.
how_used: For each prefix point P_i of an existing mine-avoiding path, form the hook path Q_i that leaves the path at step i and runs straight to the line x+y=n; the Q_i meet only on the original path, so with |M|<n mines each mine lies on at most one Q_i, and pigeonhole yields a Q_i avoiding all mines, i.e. a second mine-avoiding path.

technique: Repeatedly place a new obstacle on whichever of two competing options carries the larger share of a count, so each obstacle spent at most halves the surviving count, and compare total obstacles spent against a known threshold.
how_used: Walk from (0,0) and at the first vertex with two live directions add a mine on the direction through which more mine-avoiding paths pass, at-most-halving the path total while raising |M| by 1; iterate to a single path. Since the lemma forces at least n mines to reach one path, the halving step ran at least n-|M| times, so the original count was at least 2^{n-|M|}.

technique: Group a closed tour's hops into consecutive pairs and bound each pair's combined shorter-arc length by the circumference minus the direct shorter distance between the pair's two endpoints.
how_used: The 2n hops are split into n legs A_{2i-1}->A_{2i}->A_{2i+1}; each leg's length is bounded by 2n - d_i, where d_i is the shorter arc distance from A_{2i-1} to A_{2i+1} (casework: if the midpoint A_{2i} sits on the short arc between the endpoints then x+y=d_i<=2n-d_i, if on the long arc then each hop is at most its sub-arc so x+y<=2n-d_i). Summing over i gives total <= 2n^2 - (d_1+...+d_n), reducing the whole maximization to controlling the sum of the d_i.

technique: Lower-bound the total shorter-arc length of a closed cyclic route through a set of distinct points on a circle by observing it is minimized when the points sit in one contiguous block traversed out-and-back.
how_used: Applied to the n odd-labeled points A_1,A_3,...,A_{2n-1} taken in cyclic order: d_1+...+d_n is exactly the total shorter-arc length of the closed route A_1->A_3->...->A_{2n-1}->A_1, so it is at least 2(n-1)=2n-2 (attained by a contiguous block of span n-1 traversed out-and-back), yielding total <= 2n^2-(2n-2)=2n^2-2n+2.

technique: Recast the shorter-arc distance between two points as the number of chords from a fixed family (the diameters through the arc-midpoints) that separate them.
how_used: Draw the n diameters through the 2n arc-midpoints; each hop's shorter-arc length equals the number of these diameters it crosses. Then closed-tour parity forces each diameter to be crossed an even number of times (so <= 2n-2 unless crossed by all 2n), and at most one diameter can be crossed by all 2n hops, so the crossing total is at most n(2n-2)+2 = 2n^2-2n+2.

technique: Recast the extremal object as an iterated set-addition (Minkowski sum) of a Young diagram, then exploit conjugation (reflection across x=y) as a symmetry that fixes the whole construction while swapping a partition with its conjugate, so any bound proved for one side holds verbatim for the other.
how_used: g's Young diagram is the k-fold Minkowski sum of f's (the inf-convolution g(n)=min over compositions of sum f(n_i) equals set addition of diagrams). Reflection about x=y commutes with set addition and sends f,g to their conjugates f_*,g_*, so the (f,g) instance is identical to the (f_*,g_*) instance with the same total area A=sum g. This hands the free companion bound A <= k^2 * sum(f) - k(k-1)/2 * f_*(0), mirroring the Hermite bound with f(0) replaced by f_*(0). Here sum(f)=s(s+1)/2=300 (s=24), k=20.

technique: Upgrade a pointwise inf-convolution inequality into a summed bound by picking, for every argument, one canonical composition into k near-equal floor terms via Hermite's identity, then re-counting how many times each value is hit.
how_used: g(n) <= f(n_1)+...+f(n_k) for every composition; Hermite's identity n = sum_{i=0}^{k-1} floor((n+i)/k) supplies a canonical one, so A = sum g(n) <= sum_n sum_i f(floor((n+i)/k)). Counting multiplicities (each interior value hit k^2 times, endpoints k(k+1)/2) collapses this to k^2 * sum(f) - k(k-1)/2 * f(0). With sum(f)=s(s+1)/2 this is the first bound A <= k^2 s(s+1)/2 - k(k-1)/2 * f(0).

technique: Index the domain by a q*base+r rectangle and, in each cell, bound the inf-convolution value by an explicit spread-out composition that dumps mass onto a coordinate where the function vanishes, yielding a product-type bound that closes the residual case.
how_used: Using f(f_*(0))=0, write n = q*f_*(0)+r with 0<=q<k, 0<=r<f_*(0) and compose as q copies of f_*(0), one r, and (k-q-1) copies of 0: g(n) <= (k-q-1)f(0)+f(r). Summing over the rectangle gives the third bound A <= k(k-1)/2 * f_*(0)f(0) + k*sum(f), i.e. + k*s(s+1)/2. Then casework f(0)>=s, f_*(0)>=s, else f(0)f_*(0)<=s^2 makes each of the three bounds reach the target ks(ks+1)/2 = 115440.

technique: To prove a hidden global configuration can never be pinned down by finitely many queries, exhibit a family of valid configurations with a free parameter in every one of infinitely many disjoint regions, so any finite query set leaves an untouched region free to vary.
how_used: For gcd(m,n)=d>1, since d|m and d|n every m x n or n x m rectangle partitions each of its rows into whole 1 x d blocks; hence any labeling in which every horizontal 1 x d block sums to zero already satisfies all rectangle constraints. Rows are then mutually unconstrained, so any finite query set misses a whole row that can be perturbed within its 1 x d zero-sum freedom, forcing a query in every row -> infinitely many.

technique: Encode a doubly-periodic grid labeling as a bivariate polynomial mod (x^L-1, y^L-1) and translate each rectangle-sum constraint into that polynomial times a product of cyclotomic window-factors vanishing at all root-of-unity pairs.
how_used: On the mn x mn torus write f(x,y)=sum c_{a,b} x^a y^b. The n x m zero-sum constraint is convolution with the all-ones window, i.e. f * (x^m-1)/(x-1) * (y^n-1)/(y-1) = 0, and the m x n one is f * (x^n-1)/(x-1) * (y^m-1)/(y-1) = 0, both mod x^{mn}-1, y^{mn}-1. Plugging w=exp(2 pi i/mn): for every (a,b), f(w^a,w^b) times each cyclotomic product must be 0.

technique: Turn all-zero rectangle constraints into a deterministic recovery algorithm: from a coprime pair of window lengths, recover every term of a 1D sequence given all its length-m and length-n contiguous block sums, then propagate the known region cell-by-cell using zero-sum rectangles with one unknown cell.
how_used: Core 1D Lemma (gcd(m,n)=1, length s>=m+n-2): all m-block and n-block sums determine every entry, via Bezout am-bn=1 chaining overlapping-block differences to single-step differences. In 2D Freyja queries a fixed seed (the squares [1,m-1]^2 and [m,m+n-2] x [1,n-1]); then every new cell sits in an m x n or n x m rectangle whose sum is 0 and whose other cells are known, forcing it. She fills a strip, uses the Lemma to grow the region up/down and then left/right until it tiles the plane.

technique: Lower-bound the number of queries by the dimension of the space of valid configurations, and lower-bound that dimension by exhibiting two explicit valid subspaces whose only common member is zero, so their dimensions add.
how_used: For gcd(m,n)=1, the labelings in which every m x 1 and 1 x m rectangle sums to zero are all valid (an m x n rectangle is a union of such zero-sum strips) and form a space of dimension (m-1)^2 (a free (m-1) x (m-1) corner determines the rest); likewise the m<->n analogue has dimension (n-1)^2. A labeling in both is doubly periodic with period m and with period n, hence (coprime) period 1, hence constant, hence zero. So the sum space has dimension (m-1)^2+(n-1)^2, and Freyja needs at least that many questions.

technique: Show a constraint that holds for all rectangles of two consecutive heights forces exact periodicity: subtract the two to get the single-extra-row rectangle constant, collapsing an infinite grid to a finite torus.
how_used: Any valid labeling: for every N both an mn x N and an mn x (N+1) rectangle have zero sum (each is a union of the given m x n / n x m rectangles since m|mn, n|mn), so their difference shows every mn x 1 strip sums to zero, meaning cells at vertical displacement mn are equal; symmetrically horizontal. Thus every valid labeling is doubly periodic with period mn, so it is determined by an mn x mn block and lives on the torus (Z/mn)^2.

technique: Bound the number of nonvanishing transform modes by a divisibility case-split: determine exactly when each cyclotomic window-factor evaluates to zero at a root of unity, then intersect the two orientation constraints.
how_used: The factor (w^{am}-1)/(w^a-1) vanishes iff n|a and a>0 (its numerator is 0 while denominator isn't). For f(w^a,w^b) to be allowed nonzero, neither product may vanish: the first product being possibly zero needs (n|a,a>0) or (m|b,b>0); the second needs (m|a,a>0) or (n|b,b>0). If a 'first-type' condition held in both, then mn|a with 0<a<mn -- contradiction; so n|a forces n|b, and m|a forces m|b. Counting: n|a & n|b gives (m-1)^2 pairs, m|a & m|b gives (n-1)^2, so at most (m-1)^2+(n-1)^2 modes survive, capping the dimension.

technique: Show no finite query set suffices by exhibiting a family of valid configurations with an independent free parameter in each of infinitely many rows, so any finite query set leaves an unqueried row undetermined.
how_used: With d=gcd(m,n)>1, since d|m and d|n every m x n or n x m rectangle splits into horizontal 1 x d strips, so ANY labeling in which each 1 x d strip sums to zero is already valid. That condition couples only cells inside a single row and never across rows, leaving d-1>=1 free parameters per row, chosen independently per row. Given any finite query set, pick an unqueried row r; the all-zero labeling and the labeling that is zero except a nonzero d-periodic zero-sum pattern in row r are both valid and agree on every query, so Freyja cannot deduce row r. Hence no finite number of questions wins.

technique: Lower-bound the dimension of an unknown-recovery space by summing two independent constraint-satisfying families whose only common member is the trivial one, so their dimensions add.
how_used: For gcd(m,n)=1, labelings whose every m x 1 and 1 x m strip sums to zero form a vector space of dimension (m-1)^2 (freely set an (m-1) x (m-1) block, the rest is forced) and are valid; likewise the n x 1 / 1 x n family has dimension (n-1)^2. The first family is doubly periodic with period m, the second with period n, so a labeling in both is constant hence zero: the intersection is trivial. Their sum therefore has dimension (m-1)^2+(n-1)^2, all valid, so the point-evaluation functionals given by Freyja's queries must span a space of that dimension, giving the lower bound (m-1)^2+(n-1)^2.

technique: To upper-bound the dimension of a doubly-periodic solution space, encode labelings as a bivariate generating function mod the period and translate the linear constraints into vanishing of the DFT (evaluations at roots of unity), so the surviving Fourier modes bound the dimension.
how_used: For gcd(m,n)=1, first show any valid labeling is doubly periodic with period mn (mn x N and mn x (N+1) zero sums force mn x 1 zero sums, so cells at displacement mn are equal). Encode it as f(x,y)=sum c_{a,b} x^a y^b mod (x^{mn}-1, y^{mn}-1); the m x n and n x m zero-sum constraints become f(x,y) times the ramp factors (x^m-1)/(x-1)*(y^n-1)/(y-1) and (x^n-1)/(x-1)*(y^m-1)/(y-1) vanishing, i.e. with w=exp(2 pi i/mn), each product of two ramp factors is zero at (w^a,w^b). A mode (a,b) survives only if both ramp products fail to vanish; analyzing the divisibility conditions (n|a>0 or m|b>0 for one product, m|a>0 or n|b>0 for the other, with mn|a impossible for 0<a<mn) forces n|a => n|b and m|a => m|b, giving exactly (m-1)^2+(n-1)^2 surviving pairs. Since the (mn)^2 evaluation maps are the DFT and linearly independent, dim <= (m-1)^2+(n-1)^2, matching the lower bound.

technique: To prove an extremal bound is tight, replace each ideal single site with a tiny tight cluster of several nearly-coincident points, so any region that isolates just one point of a cluster is forced into a narrow slot around that site
how_used: Placed n four-point clusters (\frac{i}{n+1}\pm\epsilon, \frac12\pm\epsilon), one per evenly spaced x-site; any axis-parallel rectangle catching exactly one cluster point has width <\frac1{n+1}+\epsilon and height <\frac12+\epsilon, so its area is below \frac1{2n+2}, ruling out any larger \mu

technique: Reduce a 2D 'one-point axis-parallel rectangle of area \ge\mu_0' to a 1D isolation problem by fixing the horizontal side to a column's two-neighbor span w=x_{i+1}-x_{i-1} and demanding only a vertical isolating interval of the reciprocal length \mu_0/w, so the width cancels and the area is \ge\mu_0 automatically
how_used: For column \ell_i with m_i points, the rectangle (x_{i-1},x_{i+1})\times J contains exactly one point once J vertically isolates one of the m_i points; Lemma 1 guarantees a vertical isolating interval of length \ge 1/(\lfloor m_i/2\rfloor+1), which meets the required \mu_0/w whenever x_{i+1}-x_{i-1}>(\lfloor m_i/2\rfloor+1)\mu_0

technique: Rule out the 'no good index' case by summing the overlapping two-step spans (x_{i+1}-x_{i-1}) over all indices so each interior coordinate is counted twice, giving exactly twice the total length, then bound each span to reach a numeric contradiction
how_used: Assuming x_{i+1}-x_{i-1}\le(\lfloor m_i/2\rfloor+1)\mu_0 for all i, the double count 2=(x_1-x_0)+\sum_i(x_{i+1}-x_{i-1})+(x_{k+1}-x_k) (the two endpoint gaps added explicitly, which is exactly where Lemma 2's extra \lfloor m_1/2\rfloor,\lfloor m_k/2\rfloor terms come from); substituting the per-column bounds and Lemma 2's floor inequality forces 2<(|C|+4)\mu_0=2, a contradiction, so \mu_0=\frac2{|C|+4} always works

technique: Choose the free parameter set so a scale/rotation-invariant similarity test collapses into membership in one canonical region, turning the edge rule into an empty-region predicate.
how_used: Alice sets S to be all points outside the disk with diameter PQ; the unique spiral similarity A->P,B->Q sends C to R0 with angle(P R0 Q)=angle(ACB), so 'triangle PQR directly similar to ABC or BAC for some R in S' becomes 'angle(ACB) < 90', i.e. no city C lies inside the disk with diameter AB. Hence road AB exists iff that diametral disk is empty and the network is exactly the Gabriel graph.

technique: Upgrade a merely strict monovariant decrease into an additive drop of a fixed amount, so an infinite-descent argument still terminates for an infinite configuration.
how_used: Assuming disconnection, a non-edge across two components forces a point strictly inside its diametral disk that is again split from an endpoint; iterating nests these witnesses, and since every point lies inside the diametral disk (Thales, AC^2+BC^2<AB^2) yet distinct cities are at distance >1, each squared length obeys delta_i^2 <= delta_{i-1}^2 - 1. The additive -1 (not just delta_i < delta_{i-1}) forces delta_i^2 <= delta_1^2-(i-1)<0, contradiction, and is exactly what fails for the relative-neighbor graph.

technique: Rule out two segments crossing by using that any convex quadrilateral has an angle at least 90 degrees, so a vertex sits inside the diametral disk of the opposite diagonal (Thales converse).
how_used: If edges ac and bd crossed, abcd is a convex quadrilateral; the vertex carrying the >=90 angle (say angle bad at a) subtends the opposite diagonal bd, putting a inside the disk with diameter bd, contradicting that bd is a Gabriel edge with empty diametral disk. Hence the graph is planar.

technique: When a perfect matching may fail, iterate Hall-deficient-set deletion (remove a violating set and its neighborhood, repeat) until the survivors satisfy Hall, using a vertex adjacent to every candidate to force the terminal matching nonempty.
how_used: Fix one person Pip and her n arcs; build the bipartite graph joining each person to every Pip-arc worth >=1 to them. If no perfect matching exists, Hall gives a bad set B_1 of people with fewer than |B_1| neighboring arcs; delete B_1 and its neighbor arcs and repeat, peeling off successive bad sets, until the remaining graph has a matching M. Pip is adjacent to all her own arcs (a universal vertex on the arc side), so any set containing Pip has neighborhood = all n arcs and can never be deficient; hence Pip survives and the terminal M is nonempty. Commit each matched person to their arc; the unmatched people are handled by the deletion-induction of the next crux.

technique: To carry an induction through the deletion of a low-value region, argue the region is too small to contain any whole part of a person's valid partition, so removing it merges at most two adjacent parts into one whose value is bounded below by (part)+(part)-(region).
how_used: Every unmatched person Q is, by definition of M, adjacent to none of the committed arcs, so each committed arc A has Q-value < 1. Since A is worth < 1 to Q and each of Q's own n parts is worth >= 1, A cannot contain any whole Q-part, so A meets at most one of Q's cut endpoints; deleting A merges at most two adjacent Q-arcs into one of value >= (>=1)+(>=1)-(<=1) >= 1. This holds for every committed arc against every unmatched Q, so each unmatched person retains a valid partition of the shortened circle with fewer parts, preserving the induction hypothesis after the reduction.

technique: Certify a survival lower bound by tiling the board into small independent blocks and running a self-contained periodic orbit inside each block
how_used: Drop one row and one column to get a 2022x2022 subboard tiling into disjoint 2x2 blocks; put 4 beetles in each block cycling around the little square (each corner-to-corner step is a forced 90-degree turn), so 2022^2 beetles occupy distinct cells at every minute forever, showing 2022^2 beetles need not collide.

technique: When moves are forced to alternate between two move-types that each flip a different binary coordinate, color cells by the pair of parities so every trajectory becomes a fixed cyclic tour through the color classes
how_used: Color cell (r,c) by (r mod 2, c mod 2): A=(odd,odd), B=(odd,even), C=(even,even), D=(even,odd). A left/right move flips only column-parity, an up/down move flips only row-parity; the forced H/V alternation makes each beetle traverse a fixed 4-cycle A->B->C->D->A or A->D->C->B->A, so a beetle's color class at each minute is choice-independent. On the 2023x2023 board (1012 odd coordinates, 1011 even) the class sizes are A=1012^2, C=1011^2, B=D=1011*1012, so C is the unique smallest class.

technique: To force a collision in the smallest class, case-split the tokens by starting class and push each group forward along its fixed cycle to its next visit of the smallest class, where the deterministic schedule makes the count overflow that class's capacity
how_used: The smallest class is C with 1011^2 cells. With more than 2022^2 = 4*1011^2 beetles, at most 1011^2 start on C, so either more than 1011^2 start on A, or more than 2*1011^2 start on B and D together. Case A: after 2 minutes those A-beetles all sit on C -> more than 1011^2 on 1011^2 cells, collision. Case B/D: after 1 minute the B,D beetles all sit on A or C; if C already exceeds 1011^2 we are done, else more than 1011^2 sit on A, and after a further 2 minutes those overflow C. Either way two beetles coincide, so 2022^2+1 beetles force a collision (the upper bound on the guaranteeing number).

technique: To show one fewer token can dodge a forced coincidence forever, partition the board into small independent blocks and let each block's tokens cycle within their own block so no two ever share a cell
how_used: Answer is 2022^2+1, so we must exhibit 2022^2 beetles that never collide. Partition a 2022x2022 subboard into 1011^2 disjoint 2x2 blocks; fill each block with 4 beetles walking clockwise around it (right, down, left, up, repeating), which respects the H/V-alternation rule. Each 2x2 loop keeps its 4 beetles on 4 distinct cells confined to that block for all time, and distinct blocks never interact, so no two beetles ever coincide. This tightness construction matches the upper bound, giving answer >= 2022^2+1.

technique: To bound how many synchronized walkers can avoid ever coinciding under a forced turn rule, color cells by a joint parity that every walker's forced move permutes in lockstep, then cap the walkers by the size of the smallest color class each cohort is periodically flushed into
how_used: Upper bound (answer 2022^2+1). Color cell (r,c) by (row parity, col parity): A=(odd,odd), B=(odd,even), C=(even,even), D=(even,odd). On 2023x2023 there are 1012 odd and 1011 even coordinates, so |A|=1012^2, |C|=1011^2, |B|=|D|=1011*1012; C is the smallest class (capacity 1011^2). Each minute a beetle moves one step along ONE axis, so exactly one coordinate parity flips; the forced 90-degree alternation means that over ANY two consecutive minutes each beetle makes one horizontal and one vertical move, so both parities flip and the swaps A<->C, B<->D happen synchronously for ALL beetles every two minutes. Also r+c parity flips every minute for everyone, so at each instant all beetles occupy {A,C} or all occupy {B,D}. Split the beetles into the {A,C}-starters and the {B,D}-starters; the two cohorts occupy the A/C cells at disjoint times (even vs odd minutes), so C's capacity 1011^2 binds each cohort separately. Within a cohort, the synchronized 2-minute A<->C swap flushes its A-occupants entirely onto C two minutes later, while its C-occupants already sit on C now; since C holds only 1011^2, each cohort has at most 1011^2 (on C now) + 1011^2 (swapped onto C in two minutes) = 2*1011^2 beetles, else two share a C-cell. Two cohorts give at most 4*1011^2 = 2022^2 beetles that can avoid all collisions, so 2022^2+1 forces a collision. (Note: 2022^2 = 4*1011^2; the naive single-class C-overrun reading is too weak, the per-cohort 2*1011^2 cap is what gives 2022^2.)

technique: To show an extremal collision-free bound is tight, tile the achievable region with independent small cyclic gadgets and let a full orbit of walkers circulate around each
how_used: Lower bound (construction showing 2022^2 beetles can avoid all collisions forever). Partition a 2022x2022 subboard of the 2023x2023 board into 1011^2 disjoint 2x2 blocks. In each 2x2 block place 4 beetles, one per cell, and have them all rotate clockwise around the block (each beetle steps to the next cell of its block every minute: right, down, left, up, ...). This obeys the 90-degree alternation rule (the move directions around the square go H,V,H,V,...), keeps each beetle inside its own 2x2 block forever, and the four beetles of a block permute the block's four cells cyclically so they never coincide; beetles in different disjoint blocks never meet.
