This places 4*1011^2 = 2022^2 beetles with no collision ever, so 2022^2 is achievable and 2022^2+1 is at least necessary.

technique: When a forced local motion rule makes every token cyclically visit each class of a parity coloring, bound the collision-free population by the size of the SMALLEST color class the tokens are forced through
how_used: Upper bound (any 2022^2+1 beetles must collide). Color each cell by the parity pair (row parity, column parity): A=(odd,odd), B=(odd,even), C=(even,even), D=(even,odd). On the 2023x2023 board this gives |A|=1012^2, |C|=1011^2, |B|=|D|=1011*1012. The 90-degree alternation forces every beetle to step between opposite-parity-in-one-coordinate cells, so each beetle traces a 4-cycle through the colors A->B->C->D->A or A->D->C->B->A, hitting color C every other minute. Since only 1011^2 cells have color C, at most 1011^2 beetles can sit on C simultaneously without colliding. With more than 2022^2 = 2*1011^2 + (extra) beetles, count by starting color: at most 1011^2 can start on C, so more than 1011^2 start on A, or more than 2*1011^2 start on B and D together. If >1011^2 start on A, then two minutes later they all sit on C (>1011^2 in 1011^2 cells) -> collision. If >2*1011^2 start on B,D, then after one minute they occupy A and C; either C already overflows, or >1011^2 are on A, which two minutes later overflow C. Either way the scarce C class is overloaded, forcing a collision. Hence 2022^2+1 beetles always collide, and combined with the construction the exact threshold is 2022^2+1.

technique: Reduce a place-value divisibility target to only the residue-relevant columns by discarding places already divisible by the modulus
how_used: For divisibility by 4, since 4 | 2^k for every k>=2, columns 3..n contribute a multiple of 4 to any row value no matter who fills them, so a row is divisible by 4 iff its first two cells (weights 1 and 2) are both 0. The entire game collapses to: One wins iff One can force some row to begin with two 0s.

technique: Blocking-in-place pairing strategy: answer each opponent placement in a target zone by immediately neutralizing the same local slot so the forbidden pattern can never complete
how_used: In the two-leading-columns game, Zero delays placing in the left region; when forced, he puts his 0 in a row whose other leading cell already holds a 1 (turning (0,empty) into (0,1)), or else opens a fresh empty-leading row. The maintained invariant 'at most one row is in (0,empty) state' means One's next move either fills that row to (0,1) or opens a (1,empty) row Zero can answer, so Zero is never forced to create a (0,0) row; hence Zero wins all n>1 and One wins only the degenerate n=1.

technique: Reduce a place-value divisibility target to a signed count of chosen cells by weight class, using the modulus-period cycle of the place values
how_used: For divisibility by 3, the column powers of two cycle 1,2,1,2,... mod 3 since 2 == -1 mod 3, so each column carries weight class +1 (value-1 cell) or -1 (value-2 cell). A row's reverse-binary value is 0 mod 3 iff (#1s placed on value-1 columns) - (#1s placed on value-2 columns) == 0 mod 3, converting the divisibility goal into controlling, in some row, the difference of two occupancy counts. The per-row supply is ceil(n/2) value-1 cells and floor(n/2) value-2 cells, whose parities and the parity of the total board (n^2) fix who moves last and hence hinge everything on n mod 4, setting up the four cases n=4k, 4k+1, 4k+2, 4k+3.

technique: Same-weight mirroring paired with who-moves-last: copy the opponent's move onto a cell of matching weight in the same row, so the last mover controls the final count balance
how_used: Since div-by-3 reduces to balancing value-1 vs value-2 occupancy in a row, the controlling player mirrors: when the opponent places on a value-w cell of a row, respond by placing the wanted symbol on another value-w cell of that same row, preserving the count balance. Whoever has the LAST relevant move can complete the mirror. n=4k (2k value-1, 2k value-2, both even): One mirrors, ending k ones on each weight -> sum 3k == 0. n=4k+1 (2k+1 value-1, 2k value-2): One mirrors, else fills value-1 cells first then value-2, forcing some row to k on each weight -> 3k. n=4k+3 (2k+2 value-1, 2k+1 value-2): One seeds a value-2 cell in a special row Zero didn't open, then copies on it, using the odd leftover parity to end k+1 on each weight -> 3(k+1). n=4k+2 (both supplies odd, One moves last): Zero instead mirrors defensively from its second move, forcing every row to residue k+2(k+1) == 2 or k+1+2k == 1, never 0. Hence One wins iff n is NOT 2 mod 4.

technique: Reduce a size-n rectangle-parity condition to its largest divisor case by tiling every rectangle with congruent copies of the smaller rectangle.
how_used: Write n = 2^e·k with k odd; any a×b rectangle of area n dissects into k congruent rectangles each of shape 2^{ν2(a)}×2^{ν2(b)} of area 2^e. A coloring valid for 2^e makes each of the k pieces contain an odd count, and k (odd) odd numbers sum to an odd total, so validity for the power of 2 transfers to n. This reduces the whole problem to constructing colorings for n=2^k.

technique: Build a shape-selective coloring by marking one residue class per coordinate, so only rectangles of one aspect ratio catch the class an odd number of times.
how_used: For target shape 2^m×2^{k-m}, color (x,y) red iff x≡0 (mod 2^m) and y≡0 (mod 2^{k-m}). A 2^m×2^{k-m} rectangle hits each residue pair once, giving exactly one red cell (odd); for a mismatched 2^ℓ×2^{k-ℓ} rectangle the red count factors as (#x≡0 mod 2^m)·(#y≡0 mod 2^{k-m}), and when ℓ>m the x-factor is 2^{ℓ-m}, an even number, so the count is even.

technique: Superpose the single-shape basis colorings by XOR (summing mod 2) to satisfy all shapes simultaneously.
how_used: Every area-2^k rectangle is one of the k+1 shapes 2^m×2^{k-m}, m=0..k. Adding the k+1 shape-selective colorings mod 2 (a cell is red iff red in an odd number of them) yields a coloring where each shape gets its single odd contribution from its own basis coloring and even contributions from the others, so every area-2^k rectangle ends with an odd red count.

technique: Assign a local weight to each 2-edge path so that summing the weights over the three paths inside any triangle yields exactly the target linear combination of the triangle-type counts.
how_used: Charge each vee (two edges meeting at one vertex) +2 when its two edges share a color and -1 otherwise; then a monochromatic triangle sums to +6, a bichromatic triangle to 0, and a trichromatic (rainbow) triangle to -3, so the grand total over all vees equals exactly 6A - 3B, the coefficients matching the desired B <= 2A + n(n-1)/3.

technique: Recount the same weighted total of 2-edge paths by grouping them at their common apex vertex and expressing each apex's contribution through its color-degree distribution.
how_used: At a vertex with a red, b green, c blue incident edges the vees there contribute 2[C(a,2)+C(b,2)+C(c,2)] - (ab+ac+bc) = (a^2+b^2+c^2-ab-ac-bc) - (a+b+c), and since the vertex has degree n-1 the linear part is exactly -(n-1).

technique: Lower-bound a symmetric quadratic in nonnegative integer parameters by rewriting it as a sum of squares.
how_used: a^2+b^2+c^2-ab-ac-bc = (1/2)[(a-b)^2+(b-c)^2+(c-a)^2] >= 0, so each vertex contributes at least -(n-1), the total is at least -n(n-1), and 6A - 3B >= -n(n-1) rearranges to the claim.

technique: Force a minimum-two count on a cell that must return to its start side yet is provably touched at least once, by reading its required flip-count parity from the start-vs-target mismatch.
how_used: Because the flip walk takes unit steps its set of touched coins is a contiguous interval, and it must include both endpoints (leftmost and rightmost coins each need flipping), so every coin is flipped at least once. Each even-indexed coin starts and must end heads-up, so it needs an even number of flips; being also >=1 it is flipped >=2, giving the 2n+1 even-indexed coins at least 4n+2 flips.

technique: Exploit that each move lands on a cell of opposite position-parity from the previous, so the flip totals of the two parity classes differ by at most one, transferring a bound from the heavier class to the lighter one.
how_used: Successive flips are on adjacent coins, whose indices have opposite parity, so the sequence alternates between even- and odd-indexed coins; hence the odd-indexed total is at least (even-indexed total) - 1 >= 4n+1. Then, since there are an even number (2n+2) of odd-indexed coins each flipped an odd number of times, their total is even, rounding 4n+1 up to 4n+2, for the overall bound 8n+4.

technique: Tile the line with a fixed repeating block of moves that locally resolves a segment while ending adjacent to the next block, so blocks chain into one legal adjacency walk.
how_used: For k=0..n-1 flip the eight-move block (4k+1,4k+2,4k+3,4k+2,4k+3,4k+4,4k+3,4k+4) advancing four coins each time, then finish with (4n+1,4n+2,4n+3,4n+2); each block obeys the adjacency rule and the blocks concatenate into 8n+4 = 4044 flips reaching all heads.

technique: Assume nontermination forces a repeating state-cycle, then take the minimal-index object acted on within that cycle and show restoring it would require a forbidden smaller-index action.
how_used: Finite state space (≤ 2^2008 configurations) means a non-ending game repeats a state, giving a periodic cycle; let k be the smallest card number flipped during the period; flipping card k from black back to white requires selecting some card with number < k, contradicting minimality, so the game must end.

technique: Build a witness set as an arithmetic progression whose common difference equals the move's block length, so each move's window of consecutive positions contains exactly one witness and thus toggles exactly one.
how_used: Take the cards at positions 41k for 1≤k≤48 (i.e. 41,82,…,1968); since every legal move flips 41 consecutive cards k,…,k+40, that window contains exactly one multiple of 41, so each move flips precisely one card of this 48-card set (and 1968 is the highest selectable card).

technique: When each move flips exactly one element of a fixed set that starts uniform, use the resulting parity of same-colored elements as a turn invariant to guarantee the second player always has a legal move.
how_used: All 48 witness cards start white; each move flips exactly one, so after every A+B double-move the number of white witnesses is again even, meaning B always confronts an odd (hence positive) count of white witness cards and can always move, so B is guaranteed to make the last move and win.

technique: Checkerboard-color the board and use that a Hamiltonian-type path alternates colors, so a fixed color-imbalance between endpoints forces the color of the single omitted cell.
how_used: Color (i,j) black if i+j even, white if odd. On the 2m x 2n board there are equally many black and white cells, and both corners (1,1) and (2m,2n) are black. The snail visits every cell but the pawn's exactly once, alternating colors at each step; a path starting and ending black visits one more black than white. With one cell omitted, the counts can balance only if the omitted (pawn) cell is white, i.e. i+j odd. This is the necessary condition on the pawn's placement.

technique: To build a Hamiltonian path on a grid with one forbidden cell, decompose the board into full-width row-slabs plus the one slab containing the obstacle, serpentine each obstacle-free slab, and force the splice corners by the parity of the slab dimensions.
how_used: Say the pawn lies in the row-pair (2k-1,2k). Split into a lower slab (rows 1..2k-2), the two-row obstacle band (rows 2k-1,2k), and an upper slab (rows 2k+1..2m). Serpentine the lower solid rectangle from the snail's start (1,1): row1 L->R, up, row2 R->L, ...; since it has an even number of rows it ends at the far-left of its top row, and stepping up enters the band at its lower-left (2k-1,1). The band (built by the next crux) enters lower-left (2k-1,1) and exits top-right (2k,2n). Step up from (2k,2n) to (2k+1,2n), the far-right of the upper slab's bottom row, then serpentine the upper rectangle to terminate at (2m,2n)=the goal. Because each slab is a solid rectangle of even width 2n, its serpentine endpoint columns are forced by parity and match the left-entry / right-exit corners the band offers. Degenerate cases: k=1 the band starts directly at (1,1); k=m the band's top-right exit is the goal.

technique: To route a Hamiltonian path through the two-row band that contains the single forbidden cell, tile the band into 2x2 blocks swept with a fixed enter-corner/exit-corner handoff, and at the obstacle block replace the 4-cell tour by a 3-cell detour chosen to preserve the same exit corner so the sweep continues unbroken.
how_used: Partition the band (rows 2k-1,2k) into n consecutive 2x2 blocks, swept left-to-right. Corner names per block l: LL=(2k-1,2l-1), LB=(2k,2l-1), RB=(2k,2l), RL=(2k-1,2l). Before the pawn's block, traverse LL-LB-RB-RL, exiting lower-right and handing off to the next block's LL. The sweep reaches the pawn's block at its LL=(2k-1,2l-1) (an even cell, so the pawn cannot sit there); the pawn, being on an odd cell, is at LB or RL. Detour: if pawn=LB go LL-RL-RB; if pawn=RL go LL-LB-RB — either way exit at RB=(2k,2l) (top-right). After the pawn's block every block is traversed LB-LL-RL-RB, again exiting top-right, so the band enters at (2k-1,1) and exits at (2k,2n), matching the corners the slab construction requires.

technique: To force where a single removed cell of a Hamiltonian path with fixed endpoints must lie, 2-color the grid like a checkerboard and count: an alternating path with same-colored endpoints visits one more cell of the endpoint color, so the omitted cell must be the opposite color.
how_used: Color (i,j) black if i+j is even, white if odd. On the 2m x 2n board the two colors have equal counts (2mn each). The snail starts at (1,1) and ends at (2m,2n): both black. Its path alternates colors, so with both endpoints black it visits exactly one more black than white. It visits all 4mn-1 cells except the pawn's, i.e. 2mn black and 2mn-1 white, so every black cell is used and exactly one white cell is skipped. Hence the pawn must sit on a white cell (i+j odd). This is the necessity half of the answer; the construction crux supplies sufficiency.

technique: To force which single cell a color-alternating Hamiltonian path must omit, 2-color the grid like a checkerboard and count: an alternating path of known parity and fixed-color endpoints uses one color more than the other, pinning the omitted cell's color.
how_used: Checkerboard-color (i,j) black iff i+j even. The 2m x 2n board has equally many black and white cells, and the start (1,1) and end (2m,2n) are both black. A Hamiltonian path alternates black/white, so visiting all cells but the pawn's it hits one more black than white. Since it starts and ends black, the visited-black count exceeds visited-white by exactly one, which forces the single skipped cell (the pawn) to be white, i.e. i+j odd. This proves NECESSITY: only cells with i+j odd can work.

technique: To realize a Hamiltonian path avoiding one prescribed cell, tile the board into 2x2 blocks and route boustrophedon block-by-block, entering and leaving each block at a fixed corner; in the single block containing the removed cell, use the free 3-cell detour (an L-shaped traversal of the 2x2 minus one) to keep the same entry/exit corners.
how_used: Locate the pawn in rows 2k-1,2k and columns 2l-1,2l. Snake all full rows below row 2k-1 (odd rows left-to-right, even rows right-to-left), arriving at the far-left cell of row 2k-1. Traverse each 2x2 block of rows 2k-1,2k left-to-right in the order lower-left, upper-left, upper-right, lower-right, so each block is entered lower-left and exited into the next block's lower-left. On reaching the pawn's block, the snail stands at (2k-1,2l-1) (black, so pawn-free); the pawn is either upper-left or lower-right, and the L-detour (lower-left, lower-right, upper-right or lower-left, upper-left, upper-right) still exits upper-right. Continue the remaining blocks in that strip via upper-left, lower-left, lower-right, upper-right, always exiting upper-right, then step up to row 2k+1 and snake the remaining full rows to finish at (2m,2n). Every cell but the pawn's is hit exactly once.

technique: Strengthen the target into an induction that peels off one certified object at a time, leaving a smaller instance of the same shape for the hypothesis
how_used: Generalize the 100-gon claim to a 4n-gon whose two colors each appear at least (n-1) times, seeking (n-1) disjoint quads; induct on n by removing one valid quadrilateral Q_{n-1} so the remaining vertices form a convex 4(n-1)-gon to which the hypothesis applies (n=25 recovers the original, n=1 is vacuous).

technique: Slide a fixed-size window along a cyclic sequence and invoke a global count to force a window whose majority matches the dominant color
how_used: WLOG at least 2n of the 4n vertices are red. If the coloring is not alternating or 2-alternating there exist four consecutive vertices not split 2-2, hence four consecutive vertices with more red than blue (else red would be the minority). Take such a window with exactly three reds: those four span a valid quad Q_{n-1} (odd red count); removing this 3-red-1-blue block drops blue by only one, so both colors stay >= n-2 on the remaining 4(n-1)-gon and the IH applies. If all four are red, walk along the boundary to the first blue vertex (>= n-1 exist) and repeat.

technique: Handle the extremal periodic colorings that defeat the averaging step by hand with explicit spaced constructions
how_used: For the alternating and 2-alternating patterns (every 4-window is exactly 2-2 so no majority window exists), build the (n-1) quads directly: e.g. seed with P_2 P_3 P_4 P_{4n}, then advance one endpoint counterclockwise in steps of 3 and the other clockwise in steps of 1 so the quads stay pairwise disjoint and each picks up an odd red count under the periodic pattern.

technique: Use the parity of the cell-count on one side of a candidate fault line to upgrade 'at least one straddling tile' to 'at least two'.
how_used: The columns 1..k contain 4k cells (even); every domino lying entirely inside them covers 2 cells, so the horizontal dominoes straddling the seam between columns k and k+1 must be even in number. Since a fault-free tiling forces at least one straddler on each seam, there are at least two.

technique: Sum the forced minimum number of straddling tiles over every interior grid line and compare the total cells they cover against the board area for a contradiction.
how_used: Each of the 2009 vertical seams needs at least two horizontal dominoes and each of the 3 horizontal seams needs at least one vertical domino; these disjoint tiles cover (2*2009 + 3)*2 cells, which exceeds the 4*2010 cells of the board, contradicting the assumed fault-free tiling of the 4x2010 board.

technique: Build the extremal configuration inductively by splicing in a two-column block at a seam guaranteed to be crossed, re-routing the tiles that cross that seam into the new columns.
how_used: Starting from a fault-free 5x2n tiling (base case 5x6 given explicitly), choose a column carrying a vertical domino and insert two columns k1,k2 next to it; each horizontal domino spanning k,k+1 is split into one in columns k,k1 and one in columns k2,k+1, and the remaining exposed cells of k1,k2 (paired because column k had a vertical domino) are filled by horizontal dominoes, so every new seam is crossed and no fault line appears.

technique: Identify a modification whose net effect is 'wasted' because it shifts two competing aggregates by the same amount, so it cannot break their equality without a paired modification.
how_used: A changed cell that is the only changed cell in both its row and its column adds the same delta to that row's sum and that column's sum, so they stay equal ('insufficient cell'); since the final state needs all 4022 sums pairwise distinct, no cell may end up insufficient, forcing extra changes beyond one-per-line.

technique: Freeze the process at intermediate pauses and lower-bound total moves by charging a forced surplus quantity against the maximum number each later move can clear.
how_used: After changing one cell per column and n-1 rows, at least 2011-2n insufficient cells remain (2011 changed cells, one per column, spread over 2011-n occupied rows, so at least 2011-2n rows hold a unique changed cell); each change before the second pause clears at most one such cell, each after at most two, giving at least (2011-2n-(n-1))/2 extra changes and total 2011+(n-1)+that >= 3016 - n/2 >= 2681.

technique: Attain a distinctness target by adding to selected cells position-dependent increments that are strictly separated as a monotone function of the coordinates.
how_used: Abel raises 2681 chosen cells <m;n> each by 2(m+n)+1 (the cells <2;1> and, for l=1..670, <3l-1;3l-1>,<3l;3l-1>,<3l+1;3l>,<3l+1;3l+1>), the odd position-graded increments forcing all 4022 row and column sums to become pairwise distinct.

technique: Encode each element by the subset of players/sheets that 'expose' it, recasting a two-sided flip game as the question of whether some subset of the sheets fails to occur as any element's incidence set.
how_used: Give each of the k sheets a color; for each number 1..n form the set of colors of sheets that carry it on the front (its 'box'). Merlijn's move of turning a chosen set of sheets face-down corresponds exactly to picking a color-subset, and a number stays hidden iff its box equals that subset. So Merlijn wins iff he can name a color-subset that is not any number's box; since there are 2^k subsets but only n numbers, when 2^k > n one subset is unused (pigeonhole) and he wins, while when 2^k <= n Daniel makes the boxes surjective onto all subsets so every flip hides something.

technique: Build a blocking configuration for k+1 sheets by duplicating a k-sheet blocker onto a fresh disjoint block of elements and using the extra sheet to split the two copies, forcing whichever way it is turned into an already-blocked subproblem.
how_used: For the 2^k <= n direction: by induction, k sheets can block numbers 1..2^k. Copy the same front/back assignment shifted by 2^k so the sheets also block 2^k+1..2^{k+1}, and put every number > 2^{k+1} on all backs. Make sheet k+1 have 1..2^k on the front and 2^k+1..n on the back. Showing its front forces Merlijn to reveal 2^k+1..2^{k+1} on the first k sheets (impossible by IH); showing its back forces revealing 1..2^k (also impossible), so Daniel blocks whenever 2^k <= n.

technique: Process the objects one at a time with a greedy majority choice and track a count that at least halves at each step, giving geometric decay to below one.
how_used: For the winning direction via a constructive strategy: Merlijn decides each sheet in turn, always turning up the side that shows the most numbers not yet visible. If b_j is the number still hidden after sheet j, the first sheet shows at least half of 1..n so b_1 <= n/2, and each later sheet at least halves the remaining hidden set, b_j <= b_{j-1}/2. Hence b_k <= n/2^k < 1 when 2^k > n, and integrality forces b_k = 0, so all numbers are visible.

technique: Rule out a candidate line-count distribution by observing that a fully empty line, under an all-lines-even requirement, caps every crossing line two below its length.
how_used: Assuming all 18 lines even with total 10 forces the four rows (and the four columns) into (4,2,2,2) or (4,4,2,0). If some row were empty, each column could occupy only its other 3 cells, and even-parity rounds that down to at most 2, so all columns sum to at most 8 < 10; the (4,4,2,0) case is killed, leaving exactly one full row and one full column.

technique: Contradict achieving the perfect score by counting the lines already stuck at odd parity against the number of placements still available.
how_used: The forced full row plus full column consume 4+4-1 = 7 stones, leaving only 3. Casework on where they cross (corner / non-corner edge / interior) shows 5, 4, or the two length-2 NW-SE diagonals each already hold exactly one stone (odd); 3 remaining stones cannot make all those diagonals even, and in the interior case evening the two short diagonals turns an adjacent length-3 diagonal odd, so 18 points is unreachable and the maximum is 17.

technique: Certify a find-the-maximum value is attainable by exhibiting one explicit configuration realizing the claimed count.
how_used: Place the 10 stones on the 4x4 board in the displayed arrangement so that 17 of the 18 lines carry an even number of stones, proving 17 is achievable before the impossibility argument caps it there.

technique: Extend an n-sized extremal construction to n+1 by covering only the added border L-strip, using one new piece per orientation to preserve a balance constraint
how_used: To step from a valid k×k tiling to (k+1)×(k+1): embed the k×k solution in the lower-right, cover the whole left column with one width-1 height-(k+1) rectangle (type II) and the remaining top strip with one height-1 width-k rectangle (type I). This adds exactly one type-I and one type-II piece, keeping #type I = #type II, and grows N from 2k-1 to 2(k+1)-1. Base n=3: central 1×1 plus a pinwheel of four dominoes gives N=5.

technique: Lower-bound forced monominoes by counting the cells that lie in both a row and a column no long piece can occupy
how_used: With k = #(width-1, height>1) rectangles = #(height-1, width>1) rectangles (equal by the type balance) and l = #(1×1), so N=2k+l. Assuming k<n, the k tall pieces occupy at most k columns, leaving ≥ n-k columns with no tall piece, and symmetrically ≥ n-k rows with no wide piece. The (n-k)² cells in such a free row and free column can only be covered by 1×1 tiles, so l ≥ (n-k)², giving N ≥ 2k+(n-k)², minimized at k=n-1.

technique: Pin a boundary-crossing count's residue class row by row by inducting on the balance equation 'across-boundary items + within-row items = fixed width' with a vanishing edge condition.
how_used: Let b_i be the number of vertical dominoes straddling rows i and i+1, with b_0=b_m=0. In row i, the width splits as b_{i-1} + b_i + 2h_i = n (up-crossers + down-crossers + horizontal cells), and 2h_i is even, giving b_i = n - b_{i-1} (mod 2). Inducting from b_0=0 pins each b_i's parity: for n odd, b_i is odd for odd i and even for even i; for n even, b_i is even for all i (and its value mod 4 is what the coloring later reads). This is bookkeeping only — it does not yet build a coloring.

technique: To force a lower bound on a min-max quantity, hand the adversary one specific extremal configuration and read a parity obstruction straight off it.
how_used: The bound depends on n (columns). For n even, let Jetze tile every row entirely with horizontal dominoes: each row then contains n/2 dominoes, each monochrome, so a row's red-minus-blue cell count is 2*(#red dominoes - #blue dominoes), always even; when n/2 is odd (i.e. n=2 mod 4) this can never be 0, forcing V>=2, while n=0 mod 4 permits 0. Separately, for n odd the bound V>=1 needs no tiling at all: r+b=n is odd so |r-b| is odd in every row.

technique: Induct along a stack of rows on the count of shared (cross-boundary) objects, using that each in-row object covers an even number of the row's cells to pin the parity of that count row by row.
how_used: Number rows 1..m top-to-bottom; let b_i be the number of vertical dominoes with top cell in row i and bottom cell in row i+1, with b_0=b_m=0. In row i the n cells split as b_{i-1} cells (verticals entering from above), b_i cells (verticals leaving below), and an even number from horizontal dominoes (each covers 2 cells of the row). Hence b_{i-1}+b_i ≡ n (mod 2); inducting from b_0=0 forces: for n even every b_i is even; for n odd, b_i is odd exactly when i is odd. This forced parity is the ONLY structural fact about the tiling the coloring strategy needs. It is NOT pinned mod 4 (that depends on the free number of horizontals per row); the finer mod-4 balancing comes entirely from Merlijn's coloring freedom, not the tiling.

technique: For the matching lower bound, exhibit one explicit tiling that forces every row into an unavoidable parity mismatch, making the balance target unbeatable.
how_used: To show V cannot be smaller: (i) n odd — every row has an odd number n of cells, so red−blue is always odd, forcing |red−blue|≥1 for ANY tiling, hence V≥1. (ii) n≡2 mod4 — let Jetze lay every domino horizontally; each row then holds n/2 dominoes and n/2 is odd, so (#red−#blue) dominoes in a row is odd, whence red−blue cells (twice that) is ≥2 in absolute value, forcing V≥2. Combined with the constructions this pins V exactly: 0 (n≡0 mod4), 2 (n≡2 mod4), 1 (n odd).

technique: For a min-max (adversary chooses structure, you color) problem, get each lower bound on V by exhibiting ONE specific worst-case structure that forces an unavoidable parity/count obstruction in a single row.
how_used: The value V splits by n mod 4, and each branch's lower bound comes from a tailored Jetze tiling. For n odd: in any tiling the number of cells in a row covered by verticals plus (even) horizontals makes the red-minus-blue count in each row always odd, so |red-blue| >= 1 no matter how Merlijn colors, giving V >= 1. For n ≡ 2 mod 4: Jetze tiles every domino horizontally; then each row has n/2 dominoes, an ODD number, so red and blue domino counts differ by an odd number and each row's cell difference is >= 2, giving V >= 2. For n ≡ 0 mod 4 the target lower bound is 0 (nothing to force). This pins the answer V = 1 (n odd), 2 (n ≡ 2 mod 4), 0 (n ≡ 0 mod 4) as the quantity the construction must then match.

technique: To make a prefix/suffix cut of each row respect domino boundaries, first prove by induction on the row index that the count of dominoes crossing between consecutive rows has a forced parity, using that objects internal to a row contribute an even amount.
how_used: Let b_i be the number of vertical dominoes whose top cell is in row i (crossing into row i+1). Induct on i: a horizontal domino covers an even number of cells in any row, and the row has fixed width n, so the parity of b_i is forced by the parity of b_{i-1} and of n. This yields: b_i odd for odd i / even for even i when n is odd; b_i even for all i when n is even. This forced parity is exactly what guarantees Merlijn's red-prefix length (e.g. n_o cells for n odd, or 2n_o / 2n_0 cells for the even cases) lands on a domino boundary rather than splitting a vertical or horizontal, so the single per-row cut is legal.

technique: To color a shared boundary object consistently from BOTH sides using an independent local rule on each side, order the local list so shared objects sit at a fixed end, choosing the two orderings so each shared object lands at the SAME end in both lists it belongs to.
how_used: Merlijn colors each row by a single red-prefix / blue-suffix cut, applied independently per row; the danger is a vertical domino getting different colors from its two rows. Order each row's objects as three groups: verticals going DOWN (shared with the row below), horizontals (internal), verticals going UP (shared with the row above). For odd i use [down | horiz | up]; for even i use [up | horiz | down]. Then a vertical shared by odd row i and even row i+1 is a down-vertical of i and an up-vertical of i+1, and in both orderings it sits at the FRONT (red end) — so a red prefix in each row colors it red in both. Combined with the forced b_i parity making the prefix length (n_o, 2n_o, or 2n_0) land exactly at a group boundary, every shared vertical gets one color from both its rows with NO cross-row negotiation, and horizontals stay monochrome. This achieves |red - blue| = 1, 2, or 0 per row, matching the lower bound.

technique: Pair the cells of a region into dominoes and have the responding player always answer in the partner cell of whatever the mover just took
how_used: When at least one of m,n is even (say m even), tile every column into vertical dominoes (rows 1-2, 3-4, ...). Prik (the 2nd player, whose move must be side-adjacent to Stekel's last) maintains the invariant that after each of his moves every domino is empty or full. Whenever Stekel plays a cell, Prik plays its domino-partner: the partner is the same-column consecutive-row cell so it is side-adjacent (legal) and is empty by the invariant, restoring it. Prik thus never gets stuck and the board fills, so Prik wins.

technique: Settle a small base case that the general argument does not cover by an explicit forcing line
how_used: The 3x3 board (m=n=3) is not covered by the n>=5 wall/odd-parity argument (no full separating column with a nonempty column on each side to exploit). Stekel wins directly: play the center cell first; Prik must reply on an edge-midpoint (a neighbor of center), WLOG the top of the center column; Stekel completes the center column by playing its bottom cell; now the two flanking columns are empty and Prik's forced reply must enter a flanking column; Stekel then plays into the OTHER flanking column (the center column being full keeps Prik confined), and by keeping the tempo Stekel takes the last cell of that column, leaving Prik unable to move while empties remain. Verified exhaustively: center-first is a winning first move against all four of Prik's replies, and indeed every first move is winning on 3x3.

technique: Saturate a full separating line of cells so the board disconnects, after which the opponent's forced-adjacency reply can never cross from one side to the other
how_used: For the hard direction (m,n both odd so mn odd, with n>=5 giving a genuine middle column that has a full column of cells on each side), Stekel keeps placing his own pions in the central column until it is completely occupied. Adjacency between the left region and the right region can only pass through the central column, so once it is full no empty left-region cell is side-adjacent to any empty right-region cell. Load-bearing asymmetry to make explicit: Stekel himself has NO adjacency restriction (he may occupy any empty cell), so he can always keep filling the column; only Prik's reply must be side-adjacent to Stekel's last move. Prik's forced replies during the fill land in the column (helping fill it) or in a side region (harmless). This crux ONLY disconnects the board; who wins is the next crux. Do not over-claim 'two subgames handled one at a time' -- Stekel will only ever need one of the two regions.

technique: Strand the constrained opponent in an odd-sized walled-off region: the unconstrained player fills it freely so the odd cell-count forces the opponent to be the one left with no legal move
how_used: After the central column is full (previous crux), it is Stekel's turn and the number of pions on the board is automatically even (play strictly alternates, so every Stekel turn begins with an even count) -- this is NOT a tempo Stekel must engineer, it is free. Total cells mn is odd, so empties = odd - even = ODD, split between the two walled-off side regions; hence at least one region R has an odd number of empty cells. Stekel now plays only in R. Because Stekel has no adjacency constraint he can always place on any empty cell of R and NEVER gets stuck; each Stekel move forces Prik to reply on a cell side-adjacent to it, and since the wall (full central column) blocks all cross-region adjacency, Prik's reply stays inside R (or Prik cannot reply, in which case Stekel already wins because the other region still has empties). Each Stekel+Prik round fills 2 cells of R; R having an ODD number of empties means the final empty cell of R is filled on a Stekel move, after which Prik is to move but every empty cell left (in the other region) is non-adjacent to Stekel's last move by the wall -- so Prik cannot move while empties remain, and Stekel wins. This is NOT circular: it never asks 'who wins subgame R'; it is a direct fill-and-strand driven by Stekel's freedom plus the odd count.

technique: Assign the played values as a two-sided geometric (dyadic) sequence so that the single largest value strictly exceeds the sum of all the others.
how_used: Jesse writes only powers of two: he starts with 2^0 and each turn plays the next unused power either just smaller (2^{-(i+1)}) or just larger (2^{j+1}), so at any time the values form 2^{-i},...,2^j. Because 2^j > 2^{j-1}+...+2^{-i}, whichever box holds the current largest power outweighs the entire other box regardless of the split of all smaller stones.

technique: Defer committing the extreme value until the opponent's move vacates its target cell, playing a non-committal value elsewhere otherwise, to hold an invariant.
how_used: Jesse maintains the invariant 'the current largest power of two sits in the black box.' He waits to see Tjeerd's response: if Tjeerd moved that largest power out of black (freeing a black slot), Jesse plays the next-larger power into that freed black slot; if Tjeerd did anything else, the largest power is still in black, so Jesse instead plays the next-smaller power anywhere. Induction keeps the max in black through the final stone.

technique: Build the tightness example from many equal items so pigeonhole forces one part to hold more items than the target allows
how_used: Give one student 1001 cards each equal to 1000/1001 (total exactly 1000); over 100 boxes pigeonhole forces a box with at least 11 cards, whose sum is 11*(1000/1001) = 11 - 1/91, proving c cannot be smaller than 11 - 1/91.

technique: Pick the configuration minimizing the maximum part load, tie-broken by fewest parts attaining that maximum, so that any single-item transfer from the heaviest to the lightest part is non-improving
how_used: Order box sums d_1 <= ... <= d_100; by minimality, moving a positive card from box d_100 to box d_1 cannot lower the max or reduce the count of maximal boxes, which forces d_1 + (moved card value) >= d_100.

technique: Average an overloaded part with unit-capped items to guarantee an item at most load/count, then combine that transfer inequality with the global total bound
how_used: If d_100 > 10 then (cards <= 1) the heaviest box has >= 11 cards, so some card is <= d_100/11; the non-improving swap gives d_1 + d_100/11 >= d_100, i.e. 11 d_1 >= 10 d_100, and combining with 99 d_1 + d_100 <= 1000 yields 91 d_100 <= 1000, so d_100 <= 11 - 1/91.

technique: Track the running maximum as a monovariant and bound the answer by its total required rise: show every non-terminal position admits a move increasing the max, so the move-count is at most (target max) minus (current max).
how_used: The terminal state (all 3n stones in one box) has max = 3n. From any non-terminal position, pick a box achieving the max and pour any other nonempty box so at least one stone lands in it, raising the max by >=1. Hence f <= 3n - max(a_1,...,a_n). In particular max >= 5 already gives f <= 3n-5, and the extremal candidates must have small max.

technique: For a step-count lower bound on a token-shuffling process, partition the move sequence at the first and last 'big' (max-jumping) step and charge three disjoint costs on the three intervals -- a delayed onset before the first big step, one refill per box emptied between them, and a re-emptying cost afterward -- then sum to contradict the assumed bound.
how_used: From the uniform start (every box = 3), the max must climb from 3 to 3n, a rise of 3n-3; since each step raises the max by at most 2 (crux 0), fewer than 3n-4 steps would force at least two 'big' (+2) steps. A big step needs a source of >= n+1 but every box starts at 3, so the first big step is at turn i >= (n+1)-3, i.e. i >= n-1. Let j be the last big step and m the number of empty boxes at the start of turn j; since every box holds >=1 after turn i, emptying those m boxes costs >= m steps, so (j-1)-i >= m. After turn j no big steps remain, so re-emptying the n-1 remaining boxes (at most m holding a single stone) costs >= m + 2(n-1-m) = 2(n-1)-m. The three intervals are disjoint, so total >= (n-1) + (m+1) + (2(n-1)-m) = 3n-2, contradicting <= 3n-5. Hence f >= 3n-4, matched by the (3,...,3) construction, giving M_n = 3n-4 with equality only at the uniform config.

technique: To cap how much a single distribute-evenly move can boost the running maximum, note the recipient's post-move total is bounded by (global total minus source), so a source large enough to donate a big increment must itself be so large that it already dominates the max — forcing the per-move gain to a small constant.
how_used: A near-even pour of a source of size s adds at most ceil(s/n) to any one box, so a recipient gains +3 only from a source with s >= 2n+1. But that source held >= 2n+1 before the move, while the +3 recipient's new total is at most (3n - s) + 3 = 3n - (2n+1) + 3 = n+2 < 2n+1 <= s for n >= 3; equivalently two boxes each holding >= 2n+1 is impossible since 2(2n+1) > 3n. So the untouched source still exceeds the recipient and the max does not rise by 3. A +4 gain needs s >= 3n+1 > 3n, impossible. Hence every move raises max by at most 2 (Claim 3), and a '+2' move ('big move') requires a source of >= n+1 stones.

technique: To lower-bound a process's move count past an assumed budget, split the moves into two disjoint charges: bound how many moves must PRECEDE the first high-yield move by a threshold on the resource it consumes, and separately charge an unavoidable per-object cost across the objects still deficient after the last high-yield move, then add the two disjoint charges.
how_used: For all-3s start, assume all 3n stones reach one box in <= 3n-5 moves for contradiction. Claim 3 caps the max's rise at <= 2 per move and total rise is 3n-3, so >= 2 'big' moves (max +2) are needed. A big move needs a source box of >= n+1 stones; boxes start at 3, so the FIRST big move at turn i satisfies i-1 >= (n+1)-3, i.e. i >= n-1 (the threshold-before charge). With m boxes empty at the last big move (turn j), since every box holds >= 1 after turn i, emptying those m costs >= 1 move each so j >= i+m+1; after turn j at most m boxes hold exactly 1 and the other n-1-m hold >= 2, and with no big moves left, clearing the n-1 nonwinner boxes costs >= m + 2(n-1-m) = 2(n-1)-m (the per-deficient-object charge). Summing the disjoint charges: total >= j + 2(n-1) - m >= (n+m) + 2(n-1) - m = 3n-2 > 3n-5, contradiction, so f(3,...,3) >= 3n-4 (Claim 4). Combined with the upper bounds (max=3 gives <= 3n-4; max >= 4 gives <= 3n-5) this pins M_n = 3n-4, attained uniquely at (3,...,3).

technique: Turn a steady-state 'each site always holds exactly one token' condition into a conservation equation summing each neighbor's contribution rate.
how_used: Since the game never ends, every person holds exactly one balloon every round, so the rate at which a fixed person p receives balloons equals 1. Each friend q throws to p once every d(q) rounds (q cycles through its friend-list with period d(q)), contributing rate 1/d(q), giving the balance equation Σ_{q∈F(p)} 1/d(q) = 1.

technique: Apply the reciprocal-sum equation at a maximum-degree vertex so a per-term lower bound forces every term to equality, pinning all neighbors to the same extreme value.
how_used: Choose p with the most friends. The equation Σ_{q∈F(p)} 1/d(q) = 1 has d(p) terms, each 1/d(q) ≥ 1/d(p) since d(q) ≤ d(p); the total then is ≥ d(p)·(1/d(p)) = 1, forcing equality, hence d(q) = d(p) for every friend q of p — every neighbor of a max-degree person is also max-degree.

technique: Spread a vertex property that is closed under adjacency to the whole graph by walking along a connecting path.
how_used: Since 'has maximum degree' is closed under taking friends, and the friendship graph is connected, walk any path p=p_0,p_1,...,p_n=q from a max-degree p to an arbitrary person q to conclude d(p)=d(p_0)=...=d(p_n)=d(q), so everyone has the maximum (hence equal) number of friends.

technique: Sum a per-element integer quantity globally to express it as (count)×(a fixed modulus)×(a small parameter), then use the per-element range to bound that parameter to a short interval.
how_used: Each of the 2025 jump lengths is in {2,3,5}, and their total equals 2025·ℓ where ℓ is the combined number of laps. Since the average jump length lies in [2,5], ℓ∈{2,3,4,5}, cutting the problem to four cases. Combined with the given fact that π has exactly two cycles (one per frog): ℓ=2 forces every jump =2, so π(i)=i+2, a single 2025-cycle (gcd(2,2025)=1) — contradiction; ℓ=5 forces π(i)=i+5, giving gcd(5,2025)=5 cycles — contradiction. This leaves ℓ∈{3,4}.

technique: When a residual step-set (each step minus the global mean) has a UNIQUE most-negative value, force every cycle's net displacement to zero: a net-negative cycle would have to take that lone negative value at every one of its pads, but the only such all-negative map spans all pads and has nonzero average, contradicting the zero-mean normalization.
how_used: The two frogs' paths are exactly the cycles of the jump-permutation π on Z/2025 (each pad is the destination of exactly one jump, so following jumps from any start returns only after one full pass over that frog's pads = one cycle). Averaging the jump lengths (each in {2,3,5}) over 2025 pads gives total laps ℓ = mean ∈ {2,3,4,5}; ℓ=2 forces π(i)=i+2 (one cycle) and ℓ=5 forces π(i)=i+5 (five cycles), both excluded, leaving ℓ=3 and ℓ=4. For ℓ=4 set π''(i)=π(i)-4 so the residual step π''(i)-i ∈ {-2,-1,+1} with global average 0. Each cycle's net displacement is a multiple of 2025 lying in [-2c, +c] for a length-c cycle, and a negative multiple of 2025 with c ≤ 2025 must equal exactly -2025, forcing c = 2025 and every step = the most-negative value: the whole map π''(i)=i-2, whose average is -2 ≠ 0 — impossible. Hence every cycle nets 0, and with steps in {-2,-1,+1} the only net-0 cycles are the bicycle i→i+1→i and the tricycle i→i+1→i+2→i. (ℓ=3 is analogous with π'(i)=π(i)-3, steps {-1,0,+2}, unique negative -1, forcing cycles i→i and i→i+2→i+1→i.)

technique: For a permutation whose steps are bounded, subtract the average step from every image to form an auxiliary permutation with zero average net displacement; then observe that on a cyclic group the signed displacements around any single cycle sum to a multiple of the modulus, so 'zero total net displacement with individually small steps' forces every cycle to have net displacement exactly zero, collapsing the possible cycle shapes to a tiny explicit menu of short local cycles.
how_used: First an averaging count fixes the total winding: the sum of all jump lengths is 2025·ℓ where ℓ is the number of laps, and since every jump is 2, 3, or 5 the average jump ℓ lies in {2,3,4,5}; ℓ=2 and ℓ=5 are dispatched directly (all jumps equal, giving π(i)=i+2 with one cycle or π(i)=i+5 with five cycles). For ℓ=4, form π''(i)=π(i)−4, so each step π''(i)−i ∈ {−2,−1,+1}. The clockwise displacements around any cycle of π'' sum to a multiple of 2025, and the global average displacement is 0; a cycle with net negative winding would need all steps −1 or −2, forcing (since the only way to avoid net-negative across ALL cycles while averaging 0) every cycle to have net winding exactly 0. Checking which zero-net cycles are buildable from steps in {−2,−1,+1} yields exactly two shapes: the 'bicycle' i→i+1→i and the 'tricycle' i→i+1→i+2→i. This is the structural reduction that turns the raw {2,3,5}-jump permutation into the bicycle/tricycle skeleton whose starts tile Z/2025 by gaps 2 (after a bicycle) or 3 (after a tricycle). The identical maneuver with π'(i)=π(i)−3 handles ℓ=3 (steps {−1,0,+2}, cycles i→i and i→i+2→i+1→i).

technique: To count the cycles of a permutation from a known local cycle-menu, seed distinct tokens on a block of consecutive positions and push them through the permutation; each local cycle acts on the token block as a fixed even permutation, so the net token word after all cycles are exhausted lies in a short menu, and which word appears determines the number of underlying cycles.
how_used: With the ℓ=4 bicycle/tricycle skeleton fixed (starts tile Z/2025 by gaps 2 or 3), place tokens C,D,E,F on four consecutive pads i,i+1,i+2,i+3 at a cycle start and move them by π. Each cycle keeps the four tokens on four consecutive pads at the next cycle start and applies a fixed even permutation: a bicycle sends CDEF→EFDC, a tricycle sends CDEF→FECD. After all cycles are exhausted the tokens return to i..i+3 as one of CDEF, EFDC, DCFE, or FECD (the group these two even moves generate). Since the two frogs are exactly the cycles of π, the word reads off the cycle count: CDEF ⇒ four π-cycles, EFDC/FECD ⇒ one π-cycle, DCFE ⇒ two π-cycles. Having exactly two frogs forces the return word DCFE, so π's two cycles are the merged paths of {C,D} and of {E,F}, each traversing two laps (4050 positions). (For ℓ=3 the analogous three-token test returns only CDE/DEC/ECD, giving three or one cycle but never two, killing ℓ=3.)

technique: In a game/process forbidding cycles, bound the moves in a chosen vertex window against its size: when the edges placed inside a window are fewer than (its vertex count minus 1) the induced subgraph is disconnected, so the mover can add an edge joining two components — steer that forced-available edge to a component split that guarantees the extreme endpoints you want.
how_used: Alice's lower-bound strategy. For move i she looks at the window S_i = {1..i} ∪ {n-i+1..n} (2i vertices); any edge with one endpoint ≤ i and one ≥ n-i+1 has weight ≥ n-i and lives inside S_i. Before her i-th move only 2i-2 edges total have been placed, so the induced subgraph on S_i (2i vertices, ≤ 2i-2 edges) is disconnected; taking a vertex j in a different component from vertex 1 (she opened with (1,n)), she legally adds (j,n) or (1,j), an edge of weight ≥ n-i. So her i-th edge has weight ≥ n-i, giving her total ≥ (n-k)+…+(n-1) with k = ⌈(n-1)/2⌉.

technique: Prove the minimizer can always play a minimum-cost legal edge by a counting contradiction: if every cheap edge in a chosen window were illegal (cycle-forming), the window would have to be internally connected, forcing more edges than the number of moves played so far.
how_used: Bob's weight-1 strategy and its guaranteed contribution. Before Bob's (i-1)-st move consider S_i = {1..i} ∪ {n-i+1..n}. If no weight-1 (consecutive) edge inside S_i were legal, then (1,2),...,(i-1,i) blocked would force {1..i} connected and {n-i+1..n} connected, i.e. ≥ 2(i-1) edges; but only 2i-3 moves have been played, a contradiction. So a weight-1 edge is always available and Bob plays it; over his n-k-1 moves this contributes exactly n-k-1 to W, the additive '+(n-k-1)' term in the value.

technique: Cap how many heavy edges the maximizer can own by confining every heavy edge to a small vertex window and bounding the window's total edges by acyclicity (vertex count − 1), then subtracting the edges the minimizer has already forced there.
how_used: Bob's upper bound. Any edge of weight ≥ n-i needs both endpoints in S_i (2i vertices). Under Bob's weight-1 strategy he has placed ≥ i-1 edges inside S_i; since the forest on S_i holds ≤ 2i-1 edges, Alice holds ≤ (2i-1)-(i-1) = i edges inside S_i. Hence a_i := (# Alice edges of weight ≥ n-i) ≤ i, and also a_i ≤ k since Alice makes only k moves; together a_i ≤ min(i,k).

technique: Rewrite a weighted total as a sum over weight thresholds of tail-counts (number of items of weight ≥ the threshold), so a per-threshold cap can be applied termwise.
how_used: Alice's total edge weight = Σ_{i=1}^{n-1} a_i where a_i = # Alice edges of weight ≥ i. Applying the cap a_i ≤ min(k, n-i) from the window/acyclicity bound, the sum splits at the crossover i = n-k into a flat-cap head Σ_{i<n-k} a_i ≤ k(n-k-1) and a triangular-cap tail Σ_{i=n-k}^{n-1} a_i ≤ k+(k-1)+...+1; these add to exactly (n-1)+(n-2)+...+(n-k), Alice's k heaviest possible weights (verified for n=4..9). Adding Bob's guaranteed n-k-1 gives W = (n-k-1)+(n-k)+...+(n-1) = ½(k+1)(2n-k-2); sanity n=6,k=3 gives 12+2 = 14.

technique: For a 'find all values' partition problem, guess the extremal value by dissecting the region along every grid line in a single direction.
how_used: Cutting the sieve A along all n-1 horizontal grid lines decomposes each row at its single hole: the two rows whose hole sits in column 1 or column n split into one segment, the other n-2 rows into two, giving 2(n-2)+2 = 2n-2 sticks. This is a legal partition, so m(A) <= 2n-2 for every sieve A (and suggests 2n-2 as the common value, to be confirmed by the matching lower bound).

technique: Lower-bound the number of pieces in any partition by exhibiting a fooling set of cells, no two of which can lie in a single piece.
how_used: To prove m(A) >= 2n-2, reduce to finding 2n-2 cells of A such that no single stick (1xk or kx1) can contain two of them; each stick then covers at most one marked cell, so any dissection needs at least 2n-2 sticks. The separation criterion: two marked cells in one row (or column) must have a hole strictly between them. The actual construction of the 2n-2 cells is a separate move (see the Hall-matching crux).

technique: Produce the required system of distinct cells by verifying Hall's marriage condition on the bipartite graph of the two axis-aligned maximal-piece families.
how_used: Vertices are the 2n-2 horizontal maximal sticks G_h and 2n-2 vertical maximal sticks G_v from the full grid-line dissection, joined when they share a cell; a perfect matching selects 2n-2 cells, one per horizontal and one per vertical maximal stick, so no partition-stick (which lies inside a maximal stick) covers two — exactly the fooling set. Hall's condition on S subset G_h is checked by splitting S into the sticks meeting the leftmost vs rightmost column, with longest lengths l, r (distinct sizes per side since each column has one hole, so l >= |L|, r >= |R|, l+r >= |S|); if l+r <= n the vertical sticks along the two longest already give |N(S)| >= |S|, and if l+r > n the sticks span all columns so |N(S)| >= n, finished by a transposition/counting argument.

technique: Trap a pairwise sum strictly between two consecutive powers of two to force it to equal the unique power of two in that gap.
how_used: For a lower-half x (1<=x<=2^n) and upper-half y (2^n<y<=2^{n+1}) the sum satisfies 2^n < x+y < 2^{n+2}, so the funny-condition's required power-of-two sum can only be 2^{n+1}; this makes each upper-half y pair with exactly one lower-half partner x = 2^{n+1}-y.

technique: Recover the full object from its restriction to a self-similar sub-instance by reading the rest off as the forced complement, turning the count into a recurrence.
how_used: Restricting a funny M in B_{n+1} to B_n yields a funny A in B_n; then each upper-half element y=2^{n+1}-x lies in M iff x is NOT in A (since x+y=2^{n+1}), so A determines every element of B_{n+1} except 2^{n+1}, mapping funny subsets of B_n to those of B_{n+1}.

technique: Isolate the element that belongs to no constrained pair and treat its membership as an independent binary choice that doubles the count.
how_used: 2^{n+1} has no distinct partner whose sum is a power of two, so it is unconstrained; each funny A in B_n therefore extends to exactly two funny subsets of B_{n+1} (with or without 2^{n+1}), giving a_{n+1}=2 a_n and the answer 2^{n+1}.

technique: Take a maximal disjoint family of the objects that carry a color-boundary, so that maximality forces the leftover to contain no such object.
how_used: Call an (n+1)-set 'useful' if its n-subsets meet both classes. Take a maximal collection of p pairwise-disjoint useful sets; the remainder T (|T|=n^2+n-1-p(n+1)) can contain no useful (n+1)-set, so every (n+1)-subset of T has all its n-subsets one color.

technique: Convert a packing count plus a floor-of-division on the leftover into the target count by having each packed object donate one same-color piece.
how_used: T is monochromatic (say red); it yields floor(|T|/n) disjoint red n-sets, and each of the p useful sets (having both colors) donates one further red n-subset disjoint from these. Total p + floor(|T|/n) = p + floor(n+1-p-(1+p)/n) >= p+(n-p) = n disjoint same-color n-sets.

technique: Replace the fixed cardinality by a free parameter and induct, so the complement of an induction-sized subset is squeezed down to one block whose subsets are all forced into a single class.
how_used: Strengthen the target to: any set of size k(n+1)-1 contains k pairwise-disjoint same-class n-sets (the problem is k=n, since n^2+n-1=n(n+1)-1). Inductive step, by contradiction: assume size k(n+1)-1 has no k disjoint same-class n-sets. For ANY subset T with |T|=(k-1)(n+1)-1, the induction hypothesis gives k-1 pairwise-disjoint same-class n-sets inside T. The complement S\T then has size exactly n+1, and every n-subset of S\T must lie in the OTHER class (else adjoin it to the k-1 sets, which are disjoint from S\T, to reach k). So the whole (n+1)-block S\T is monochromatic in one class.

technique: Force a leftover block to be monochromatic by a completion-contradiction: if any of its members had the other class, it would complete the target configuration already assembled elsewhere.
how_used: Prove the stronger statement by induction on k: any |S| = k(n+1)-1 set has k pairwise-disjoint same-class n-subsets; the actual problem is k = n, |S| = n^2+n-1. Inductive step, by contradiction assume it fails. Pick ANY T of size (k-1)(n+1)-1; the induction hypothesis gives k-1 pairwise-disjoint n-subsets inside T all of one class c_T. The complement S\T has exactly n+1 elements, and every n-subset of it is disjoint from those k-1 sets. So if even one n-subset of S\T had class c_T, it would complete k pairwise-disjoint sets of class c_T -- contradiction. Hence ALL n+1 of the n-subsets of the (n+1)-block S\T are the OTHER class, i.e. S\T is monochromatic. This derives (not merely asserts) the block-monochromaticity the induction rests on.

technique: Upgrade a 'every block is constant' property to a single global constant by chaining blocks that pairwise overlap enough to share a common sub-object, so their constants agree along the chain.
how_used: From the previous crux, every (n+1)-subset of S is monochromatic (as T ranges over all size-((k-1)(n+1)-1) subsets, S\T ranges over ALL (n+1)-subsets of S). To conclude all n-subsets share one class, do NOT claim two arbitrary n-subsets sit in a common (n+1)-superset (FALSE for disjoint ones: two disjoint n-subsets need 2n > n+1 elements). Instead chain: two (n+1)-blocks overlapping in n elements share a common n-subset, so their single classes coincide; the overlap-in-n (Johnson) graph on (n+1)-subsets is connected since |S| = k(n+1)-1 >= n+2, forcing one global class for all n-subsets of S. That single global class trivially yields k pairwise-disjoint same-class sets, the contradiction closing the induction.

technique: Replace a bounded-degree connected figure by a spanning tree so that deleting one vertex splits it into at most (max-degree) connected pieces
how_used: Take the cell-adjacency graph of the polyomino (vertices = cells, edges = orthogonal adjacency) and pass to a spanning tree T. A grid cell has at most 4 orthogonal neighbors, so T has maximum degree <=4; deleting any vertex v breaks T into at most 4 subtrees, each a connected subpolyomino. This turns the whole primitivity question into a statement about one deletion in a max-degree-4 tree.

technique: Match the extremal bound with a symmetric cut-vertex construction where every piece avoiding the center is too small to be extremal
how_used: Build a plus/cross: one center cell with four straight arms of 2006 cells each, total 1 + 4*2006 = 8025. Any connected subpiece not containing the center lies inside a single arm, so has <=2006 cells and is not a dinosaur; hence every dinosaur subpiece must contain the center. Two disjoint pieces cannot both contain the center, so the cross cannot split into two dinosaurs and is primitive, attaining 8025.

technique: To force the existence of a cut vertex whose removal leaves only small components, run a descent that repeatedly steps the candidate vertex into the current heavy component, using the extremal hypothesis to cap the complement so the heaviest piece strictly shrinks each step.
how_used: Take a spanning tree T of the primitive dinosaur's adjacency graph; each cell has at most 4 orthogonal neighbors so T has maximum degree <=4. Claim: there is a vertex v* whose deletion leaves no component of size >=2007; then T-v* has at most 4 components each of size <=2006, so N <= 4*2006 + 1 = 8025. Descent to the claim: pick any v. If deleting v leaves a heavy component C (|C| >= 2007), its complement R (the side containing v, size N-|C|) cannot also be >=2007, since {C,R} would then split the animal into two dinosaurs, contradicting primitivity; so |R| <= 2006. Step v -> w = the neighbor of v inside C. Deleting w, the v-side piece is R plus v (bounded again by re-applying the primitivity cap, since its complement stays heavy), while every other new component is a proper subtree of C hanging beyond w, hence strictly smaller than |C|. So the size of the maximum heavy component strictly decreases at each step; a strictly decreasing sequence of positive integers terminates, yielding v* with all components <=2006. The matching construction is the cross: one center cell with four straight arms of 2006 cells (total 1+4*2006=8025), which is a dinosaur and primitive because any split must cut the center, leaving four arms of exactly 2006 < 2007, none a dinosaur.

technique: Split on whether a counting map between two equal-size sets is a bijection: if it is, the map itself is the desired object; if not, pigeonhole hands you an element in the codomain that is never hit.
how_used: The favorite-assignment sends n girls to n boys. If every boy is favorited exactly once it is a bijection, so matching each girl to her favorite already gives a valid perfect matching with every girl on her favorite. Otherwise some boy X is nobody's favorite.

technique: To shrink for the induction step, delete an element that lies OUTSIDE the protected set together with its partner in the given structure, so both the guaranteed property and the protected-set property survive on the smaller instance.
how_used: Remove the unfavorited boy X and his partner girl Y from the given valid matching. The rest is still a valid matching on k girls/boys, and since no remaining girl favorited X, every remaining girl's favorite is still among the k boys, so the induction hypothesis yields a favorite-edge; re-adding X-Y completes it.

technique: To force a line that meets exactly one marked piece, exploit that a set of distinct powers of two has its largest element strictly greater than the sum of all the smaller ones.
how_used: Assuming a distinct-dimensions covering has a width-1 rectangle, color every cell under a width-1 rectangle blue; the blue total M is a sum of distinct powers of two (the heights). With 2^k the largest such height, the other blue cells number < 2^k = height of that tallest strip, so some row of that strip's column carries a blue cell of it and no other blue cell.

technique: Get a contradiction on a single row by parity: after one unit-width piece takes one cell, the leftover cells are odd in number, yet every other piece meeting that line has even width.
how_used: In the isolated row, the single blue cell of the height-2^k strip is removed, leaving an odd number of cells; those must be covered by rectangles of width a power of two >1, hence all even width, which cannot sum to an odd count. This rules out width-1 rectangles (and symmetrically height-1), so every rectangle has even width and even height.

technique: When every tile of a covering has all-even side lengths, halve every dimension to reduce to the identical problem on a half-size board, and invoke a minimal counterexample to reach a contradiction.
how_used: Take the smallest n admitting a distinct-dimensions covering; since all rectangles and the 2^n x 2^n board have even sides (and integer power-of-two-area rectangles are exactly those with both sides powers of two), divide all dimensions by 2 to get a valid distinct-dimensions covering of a 2^{n-1} x 2^{n-1} square, contradicting minimality of n.

technique: For an edge count one above a triangular number, build the extremal graph as a clique with a single pendant vertex, so almost every edge inherits the clique's min-degree.
how_used: Model the problem as maximizing S(G)=sum over edges vw of min(deg v, deg w) over graphs with 2017 edges (vertices=entrees, edges=mathematicians, university pays the smaller endpoint degree). Since 2017 = C(64,2)+1, take L_64: a clique K_64 plus one extra vertex joined to a single clique vertex. The C(64,2)=2016 clique edges each contribute 63 and the lone pendant edge contributes min(64,1)=1, giving S=63*C(64,2)+1=127009. This is the lower bound / claimed answer; the matching upper bound is separate.

technique: Charge each edge's min-degree label to its smaller-degree endpoint in a fixed degree ordering, so the functional becomes a weighted sum of the sorted degrees with the weight on rank i capped by i-1.
how_used: Sort degrees d_1>=...>=d_n. For each edge min(deg u,deg v) is the degree of its lower-ranked (larger-index) endpoint; charging each edge there gives S(G)=sum a_i d_i, where a_i counts edges having vertex i as min-endpoint. The partner endpoint has degree >= d_i hence a strictly smaller index, and these partners are distinct, so a_i <= i-1. This cap plus monotone d_i is the input the algebraic-smoothing crux consumes; the smoothing of the a_i against the sorted d_i then yields the weighted bound d_2+2d_3+...+63 d_64+d_65.

technique: Maximize a fixed weighted sum of a sorted nonnegative integer sequence under a sum constraint by exchange-smoothing weight toward the higher-coefficient positions until the free coordinates equalize and the tail drains, then enumerate the few surviving profiles.
how_used: Bound A = x_2+2x_3+...+63 x_64+x_65 over integers x_1>=...>=x_65>=0 with sum <= 4034 (=2*2017). Exchange: if x_i>x_{i+1} and x_{j-1}>x_j for i<j<=64, move one unit x_i->x_j (larger coefficient) to strictly raise A, forcing x_1..x_64 within 1 of each other; and moving 4 units from x_65 into x_1..x_4 strictly raises A, forcing x_65<=3. With sum=4034 only four profiles survive; evaluating them gives A<=127010, with equality uniquely at x_1=...=x_64=63, x_65=2.

technique: To replace an extremal graph by one carrying a universal vertex without lowering a degree-weighted edge functional, delete a globally minimum-degree vertex and redirect each of its edges onto a currently non-adjacent pair, then repair any multi-edge by trading one duplicate for a missing edge; iterate until a universal vertex appears.
how_used: For S(G)=sum over edges of min(deg endpoints) with m=C(64,2)+1 edges, this is the inductive reduction on vertex count. Pick w of minimum degree d<k-1 (it exists because the average degree 2m/n<k-1, so no vertex is universal). For each neighbor w_i choose v_i with v_i w_i not an edge, delete w-w_i and add v_i-w_i, then delete w; a double edge appears only when v_i=w_j, which is fixed by removing one copy and inserting any absent edge (available since n-1>=k+1). This preserves m, lowers n by one, and by the monotonicity crux does not decrease S. NOTE: this move only manufactures the universal vertex; the actual upper bound is finished by a SEPARATE peel-off induction on that universal vertex (its own crux).

technique: To certify that a graph-surgery step cannot decrease a functional summing per-edge minima of endpoint degrees, verify two facts: no surviving vertex's degree drops, and each removed edge is matched by a new edge whose min-endpoint-degree is at least as large.
how_used: For the reroute (delete min-degree w of degree d, redirect its d edges to non-adjacent pairs, repair double edges), show S(G'')>=S(G) as follows. Every surviving vertex keeps degree at least its old value: the only edges removed are w's and one duplicate, and each removal is compensated by an added edge at the same or another vertex, so no degree strictly falls. Hence every retained edge's min-label is non-decreasing. Separately, the d edges at w each carried label exactly d (d is the global minimum, so every neighbor has degree >=d), and their d replacements have both endpoints of degree >=d, so each new label is >=d. The repair swap is absorbed by the same global 'no degree drops' fact. Together these give S(G'')>=S(G).

technique: Turn a per-edge min-of-endpoint-degrees functional into a weighted sum of the sorted degree sequence by charging each edge to its lower-degree endpoint, giving each vertex a charge count capped by its rank; then smooth the fixed total charge toward the high-degree end.
how_used: Entry point of the algebraic (Lin) solution. Order degrees d_1 >= ... >= d_n and charge each edge to its lower-degree (higher-index) endpoint, so S(G) = sum_i a_i d_i where a_i = #edges charged to vertex i. The other endpoint of such an edge is one of the i-1 higher-degree vertices with at most one edge each, giving the cap a_i <= i-1. The charges satisfy sum a_i = 2017 (fixed), not a_i = i-1 for all i; smoothing this fixed total mass toward the large-d_i (small-index) end subject to the caps yields S(G) <= d_2 + 2 d_3 + ... + 63 d_64 + d_65. This linearizes the graph functional into a pure inequality on the degree sequence, feeding the algebraic smoothing bound.

technique: Bound a weighted sum of a monotone bounded integer sequence by exchange smoothing: repeatedly move a unit toward the heaviest-weight entries whenever it strictly raises the objective, until only a few extremal profiles remain to check by hand.
how_used: Second hard move of the Lin solution: bound A(x) = x_2 + 2x_3 + ... + 63 x_64 + x_65 over integers x_1 >= ... >= x_65 >= 0 with sum <= 4034 (=2m). Unit-exchange smoothing forces the top 64 entries within 1 of each other and forces x_65 <= 3, leaving exactly four sequences: (63^63,62,3)->126948, (63^64,2)->127010, (64,63^63,1)->127009, (64,64,63^62,0)->127009. Direct evaluation gives A <= 127010, attained UNIQUELY at (63^64, 2). This yields S(G) <= 127010 and the unique equality profile d_1=...=d_64=63, d_65=2 that the subsequent equality audit attacks.

technique: When a relaxed optimum exceeds the target by a fixed gap and is attained only at one profile, close the gap by re-imposing on that exact profile a structural constraint the relaxation discarded, showing the true objective there falls strictly below the relaxed value.
how_used: The smoothing bound gives S(G) <= 127010 with equality forcing d_1=...=d_64=63, d_65=2 (delete isolated vertices, n=65), while L_64 attains only 127009 — so 127010 must be ruled out. Re-impose the charging structure the relaxation ignored: at this profile the last vertex actually collects BOTH its own edges, so a_65 = 2 exactly (not the relaxed tail weight 1), while a_i <= i-1 and sum a_i = 2017. Then S(G) = 63(a_1+...+a_64) + a_65 = 63(2017 - a_65) + a_65 <= 63*2015 + 2 = 126947 < 127010. This 126947 bounds ONLY the (63^64,2) profile — it does not touch L_64, whose degree sequence is genuinely different (L_64 has a degree-1 vertex and a degree-64 vertex, not sixty-four 63's), so L_64's 127009 survives. Hence no graph reaches 127010 and the maximum is 127009.

technique: To bound an edge-min-degree functional over a graph that has a universal vertex, delete the universal vertex and split the functional into its incident-edge contribution plus the residual-graph functional, using that deleting a universal vertex lowers every other degree by exactly one.
how_used: The upper-bound finish of the combinatorial (Evan Chen) solution once the maximizer is known to carry a universal vertex v. Write S(G)=sum over edges of min(deg u, deg w). Let H=G-v, let p=deg_G(v) be the number of edges at v, and m=e(H) the residual edge count. Because v is adjacent to all others, each edge (v,w_i) has min = deg_G(w_i)=deg_H(w_i)+1, so the incident edges sum to sum_i(deg_H(w_i)+1)=2m+p. Deleting v drops every other degree by exactly 1, so each edge inside H had its min-label raised by exactly 1 in G, contributing S(H)+m. Hence S(G)=(2m+p)+(S(H)+m). Key eps-handling: for a graph with C(k,2)+eps edges (eps in {0,1}), the universal vertex has p>=k-1+eps, forcing m<=C(k-1,2), so H falls in the PURE triangular-number case and the inductive hypothesis gives S(H)<=C(k-1,2)(k-2) with no eps carried into H. Plugging in collapses to S(G)<=C(k,2)(k-1)+eps. Base cases: clique K_k (eps=0) attains C(k,2)(k-1); L_k = clique plus one pendant edge (eps=1) attains +1. For k=64, eps=1: 63*C(64,2)+1=127009.

technique: To show a graph functional monotone under a local edge-rerouting move, verify the move never decreases any vertex's degree; since an edge-min-degree functional is monotone in degrees, no vertex dropping degree already forces the whole functional to weakly rise, so only the rerouted edges themselves need a direct label check.
how_used: The reduction that justifies the universal-vertex assumption crux 0 needs, in the combinatorial solution. Take a maximizer G with C(k,2)+eps edges and no universal vertex; pick a minimum-degree vertex w of degree d<k-1 (its neighbors w_1..w_d). By minimality every w_i has a nonneighbor v_i. Delete each edge w w_i and add v_i w_i, then delete w. THE INVARIANT: every surviving vertex's degree is at least what it was in G (each w_i keeps its degree via the swap; each v_i gains one; nobody loses), and because S is a sum of min(deg,deg) labels that is monotone nondecreasing in every degree, this ALONE guarantees no untouched edge's label drops -- there is no collateral loss to track. The only edges needing a direct check are the d newly added ones, whose labels are >= d (they replace edges that had label <= d at w). So S does not decrease. Multi-edges (when v_i=w_j) are repaired by deleting one copy and adding any missing edge, legal since the vertex count still exceeds k (or k+1 when eps=1); this again only raises degrees. Iterating drives to the near-clique carrying a universal vertex.

technique: Induct on the ambient dimension rather than the parameter, by pushing the whole configuration through a coordinate-forgetting quotient so the closure hypothesis transfers to the smaller-dimensional image where the full inductive claim already holds
how_used: Induct on n (string length). Assuming S has P_ell but not P_k, pick x_1..x_{2k+1} with majority y not in S. To force each single-bit neighbor y_i of y into S, apply the map s -> s-hat that forgets the i-th coordinate, sending S to T in {0,1}^{n-1}. T still satisfies P_ell (majority commutes with dropping a coordinate), so the induction hypothesis at dimension n-1 (the FULL equivalence P_ell => P_k for length n-1 strings) gives that T has P_k; hence y-hat = M(x_1-hat,...,x_{2k+1}-hat) is in T, so some s in S has s-hat = y-hat, i.e. s = y or s = y_i. Since y not in S, y_i is in S.

technique: Simulate a low-arity majority operation by feeding a high-arity majority repeated copies of its intended inputs, collapsing the redundant coordinates
how_used: Deduce P_1 from P_k directly: for any strings a,b,c, M(a,...,a (k times), b,...,b (k times), c) = M(a,b,c) since the k copies of a and k copies of b plus c is a valid 2k+1 majority, so P_k forces the 3-majority M(a,b,c) into S. This makes P_1 available for the upward step even though S was only assumed to have P_k.

technique: Realize a bitwise AND of two strings as a 3-input majority of those two strings with a chosen majority of the remaining inputs, exploiting a normalization that makes the third argument the low value
how_used: Work in solution 2 after WLOG M(x_1,...,x_{2k+3}) = 0...0. For any pair, M(x_1, x_2, M(x_3,...,x_{2k+3})) = x_1 AND x_2: coordinatewise, since the global majority is 0 there are at most k+1 ones among all 2k+3 strings, so among x_3..x_{2k+3} the inner (2k+1)-majority is 0 unless x_1,x_2 are both 1 at that bit, so the outer 3-majority reduces to x_1 AND x_2. By P_k the inner majority is in S and by P_1 the outer 3-majority is in S, hence x_1 AND x_2 in S (and by symmetry every x_i AND x_j).

technique: Assemble a higher-arity majority as the majority of the consecutive-neighbor ANDs, bounding via the global majority how many adjacent pairs can both be one
how_used: To prove P_{k+1} give M of any 2k+3 strings, WLOG their global majority is 0...0; show 0...0 is in S. Form the 2k+1 consecutive pairwise ANDs x_1 AND x_2, x_2 AND x_3, ..., x_{2k+1} AND x_{2k+2} (each in S by the AND-gate crux) and take their (2k+1)-majority via P_k. At any coordinate at most k+1 of the x_i are 1, so at most k of the 2k+1 consecutive ANDs are 1; the (2k+1)-majority is therefore 0 at every coordinate, i.e. equals 0...0. Thus 0...0 = M(consecutive ANDs) is in S, and 0...0 is the global majority M(x_1,...,x_{2k+3}) by the WLOG, giving P_{k+1}.

technique: To force a would-be-excluded point's single-coordinate neighbors into the set, identify (collapse) that one coordinate to project onto the lower-dimensional cube and apply the theorem's induction hypothesis in the smaller dimension.
how_used: Induct on the ambient dimension n (base case n=2 by hand; the step cannot reach n=2 from n=1, so verify n=2 directly). For the inductive step assume S satisfies P_ell but not P_k, so some x_1..x_{2k+1} in S have majority y = M(x_1,...,x_{2k+1}) not in S. Fix a coordinate i and let y_i be y with bit i flipped. Collapse coordinate i: map each string s to its image \hat{s} in {0,1}^{n-1} by deleting coordinate i, and set T = {\hat{s} : s in S}. Deletion commutes coordinatewise with the majority function, so T inherits P_ell; by the induction hypothesis on dimension n-1, T satisfies P_k, hence \hat{y} = M(\hat{x}_1,...,\hat{x}_{2k+1}) is in T. Some s in S has \hat{s} = \hat{y}, meaning s equals y or y_i; since y is not in S, we get y_i in S. This holds for every i, so all n single-bit neighbors of y lie in S.

technique: Recover a point as the coordinatewise majority of its single-bit neighbors by taking an odd multiset of those neighbors with multiplicities as equal as possible, so at each coordinate the lone dissenting neighbor is a strict minority.
how_used: Given that all n single-bit neighbors y_1,...,y_n of y lie in S, form a multiset of 2*ell+1 strings drawn from y_1,...,y_n with multiplicities differing by at most 1. At any coordinate j, the only strings that disagree with y's j-th bit are the copies of y_j; balancing keeps that count (at most ceil((2ell+1)/n)) a strict minority of 2*ell+1 whenever n>=3, so the coordinatewise majority is exactly y. Since S satisfies P_ell, this majority lies in S, i.e. y in S -- contradicting y not in S and completing the inductive step. (The n=2 case, where ceil((2ell+1)/2)=ell+1 is not a minority, is exactly why n=2 is the separate base case.)

technique: Characterize the unknown configuration as the unique N-point set maximizing a sum of per-point weights, choosing the weight to be a downward parabola in the defining invariant so that its top-N superlevel set is exactly the target region.
how_used: Bob first extracts N=|S| from the data. The claim is that among all N-point sets T, S={m<=x^2+y^2<=n} uniquely maximizes F(T)=sum over (x,y) in T of (x^2+y^2)(m+n-(x^2+y^2)).
