The weight w(r)=r(m+n-r) is a concave parabola in r=x^2+y^2 peaking between m and n with w(m)=w(n)=mn, so every point of the annulus has weight >=mn and every point outside has weight <mn; hence the N lattice points with largest weight are exactly those with m<=r<=n, making S the unique maximizer.

technique: Recover a forbidden cross-moment from only the marginal distributions of a variable set and their sums/differences by polarization: expand the fourth powers of the sum and difference to isolate the mixed term.
how_used: F(S)/N = (m+n)E[X^2+Y^2] - E[X^4] - E[Y^4] - 2E[X^2Y^2]. Bob knows the full marginal distributions of X, Y, X+Y, X-Y (the line counts for the four slopes), so he can compute any single-variable power moment, but not the cross term E[X^2Y^2] directly. Using E[X^2Y^2] = (E[(X+Y)^4] + E[(X-Y)^4] - 2E[X^4] - 2E[Y^4])/12, F(S) becomes a linear combination of known marginal moments, so any T sharing S's four marginals has F(T)=F(S).

technique: Recast a constrained one-out/one-in selection of directed edges as a perfect matching by splitting each vertex into an out-copy and an in-copy of an auxiliary bipartite graph.
how_used: Build bipartite Gamma with left vertices V_out and right vertices V_in, one copy of each city on each side; put edge v_out~w_in exactly when the directed road v->w exists in G. A perfect matching of Gamma covers each v_out once (picks one out-road of v) and each w_in once (picks one in-road of w), so matchings correspond bijectively to valid closings. Because G is 2-out/2-in regular, deg(v_out)=deg(w_in)=2, so Gamma is 2-regular bipartite.

technique: Count perfect matchings of a 2-regular bipartite graph by decomposing into even cycles, each contributing an independent factor of two.
how_used: A 2-regular graph is a disjoint union of cycles; Gamma being bipartite forces every cycle to have even length. Each even cycle has exactly two perfect matchings (the two alternating edge classes), and the choices across the n disjoint cycles are independent, so the total number of perfect matchings — hence of valid closings — is 2^n. Gamma is nonempty (cities have roads), so n>=1 and the count is a power of 2 greater than 1.

technique: Show an F_2 linear system's solution count is a positive power of two by pairing solutions under the fixed-point-free involution x -> x+1 and proving consistency by ruling out a 0=1 linear dependency among the equations.
how_used: The fresh solver reproduced the entire F_2 linear-algebra path (solution 2): x_e model, 2N two-variable equations, x -> x+1 fixed-point-free involution giving coset size 2^k with k>=1, and consistency via no 0=1 dependency, with each variable-in-S appearing exactly twice, the S-equations forming even (bipartite) cycles, and |S| even. Match is exact.

technique: Encode a parity-weighted count under a modular sum-constraint as a signed generating function run through the roots-of-unity filter, turning the even-minus-odd difference into one sum over the modulus's roots of unity.
how_used: With R(x)=sum over red x^s and B(x)=sum over blue x^s, weight each coordinate by +1 for blue and -1 for red so its generating function is B(x)-R(x); the roots-of-unity filter on the mod-100 sum condition then gives X-Y = (1/100) sum over 100th roots of unity omega of (B(omega)-R(omega))^n, collapsing both the mod-100 selection and the even/odd red split into a single closed sum.

technique: Use a global vanishing identity of the indicator polynomials at every nontrivial root of unity to rewrite each root term as a single manifestly nonnegative count.
how_used: Since B(omega)+R(omega)=0 for every 100th root omega != 1 (the full sum x+...+x^100 vanishes there), each nontrivial term (B(omega)-R(omega))^n becomes (2B(omega))^n; separating the omega=1 term gives X-Y = (1/100)[(-50)^n - 50^n] + 2^n Z where Z = (1/100) sum B(omega)^n counts all-blue tuples in T_n and is nonnegative, and for even n the bracket vanishes leaving X-Y = 2^n Z >= 0 for every coloring.

technique: To realize the failing case, engineer a residue-class coloring that forces the nonnegative slack term to be exactly zero, so the sign of the remaining constant term decides the inequality.
how_used: For odd n the bracket equals -(2/100)*50^n < 0, so a counterexample needs Z=0; color s red iff s not congruent to 2 mod 4 (blue = the 25 values congruent to 2 mod 4), whence any all-blue sum is 2n mod 4, which cannot be 0 mod 100 (0 mod 4) for odd n, giving Z=0 and X-Y = -(2/100)*50^n < 0, so odd n fail.

technique: To decouple a global modular sum-constraint, partition the constrained tuple set into classes by a finer tuple of block-sums, so that within each class the independent per-block choices restore a factored parity generating function.
how_used: Group the n coordinates into n/2 consecutive pairs and partition T_n by the (n/2)-tuple of pair-sums; fixing all pair-sums encodes the mod-100 condition (sum of pair-sums = 0) with no residual coupling, so each pair's monochrome-vs-nonmonochrome status is a free independent choice within its class. For a fixed pair-sum there are at least as many monochrome pairs as nonmonochrome ones (every nonmonochrome pair spends one of the 25 non-red elements), so the nonmonochrome probability p_i <= 1/2; since red-parity equals nonmonochrome-pair parity, the even-parity fraction is (f(1)+f(-1))/2 = (1 + prod(1-2p_i))/2 >= 1/2 for even n.

technique: Bound the count of moves that preserve a modular invariant by treating them as edges of a self-avoiding walk on that invariant class (at most |class|-1 of them)
how_used: Hops of size a multiple of 2^m keep the frog's position fixed modulo 2^m, so within each of the 2^m residue classes (each holding 2^{n-m} of the 2^n points) the large hops form a self-avoiding walk with at most 2^{n-m}-1 hops; summing over classes gives a_{n-1}+...+a_{n-m} <= 2^n - 2^m for every k=n-m

technique: Rewrite a weighted sum of counts as a sum of cumulative tail partial sums (Abel summation) so that available prefix/suffix-sum bounds can be plugged in term by term
how_used: S = a_0 + 2a_1 + ... + 2^{n-1}a_{n-1} is re-expanded into stacked rows of suffix sums (a_{n-1}+...+a_{n-k}), then each suffix is replaced by its bound 2^n - 2^{n-k}, and the resulting geometric total sums to (4^n-1)/3

technique: Achieve an extremal configuration by splitting the ground set into two sublattices each isomorphic to the smaller instance, solving each recursively, and linking them with a single connecting move
how_used: Split {0,...,2^{n+1}-1} into evens and odds, each a scaled copy of the size-2^n frog problem; recursively build Gray-code-style paths on each (giving 2^k hops of size 2^k) with controlled free endpoints, then join with one unit hop 2->1, yielding a full tour attaining S=(4^n-1)/3

technique: Average an incidence count over all nontrivial rotations of one point set against another and take the above-average rotation.
how_used: Over the 431 non-identity rotations of the 108 red points, each red point lands on a green point with 'probability' 108/431, so the mean number of red-green coincidences is (108/431)*108 > 27; hence some single rotation produces at least 28 coincidences, giving a red 28-gon that is a rotation of a green 28-gon.

technique: Iterate the rotational-averaging alignment on the surviving common subset, choosing the shrinking size schedule so each successive mean incidence stays above the next integer target.
how_used: Take the aligned 28-gon and average its 430 rotations against blue ((108/430)*28 > 7 gives a common 8-gon of red/green/blue), then average that 8-gon's 429 rotations against yellow ((108/429)*8 > 2 gives a common 3-gon); the schedule 108->28->8->3 is forced so each mean (27.06, 7.03, 2.01) clears the next integer. The four resulting monochromatic triangles are rotations of one another and hence congruent.

technique: Use a bounded per-step increment to show one side of a forbidden band is forward-invariant: once a term lands strictly below the band, the increment is too small to clear the band, so it stays below forever.
how_used: Assuming no index satisfies |a_i-i|<d, pick N>10^100 past all exceptions so for i>=N each term has a_i<=i-d or a_i>=i+d. If a_i<=i-d then |a_{i+1}-a_i|<=2d gives a_{i+1}<=a_i+2d<=(i+1)+(d-1), below the upper band, forcing a_{i+1}<=(i+1)-d. Induction yields the dichotomy: (A) a_i>=i+d for all i>=N, or (B) some M with a_i<=i-d for all i>=M.

technique: Contradict a claimed bijection of the positive integers by a cardinality mismatch: confining a cofinite set of indices to one side of the diagonal leaves too few index-slots for the values (or too few values for the terms).
how_used: Case (A): for i>=N, a_i>=i+d>N, so the N values 1..N can only be realized by the finitely many terms a_1..a_{N-1} — too few, contradicting surjectivity. Case (B): with k=max{M,a_1,...,a_M}, all k terms a_1..a_k lie in {1,...,k-1}, so pigeonhole forces a_i=a_j for some i<j, contradicting injectivity.

technique: To get the parity of a count invariant under a symmetry group, group the objects into orbits and keep only orbits whose size is odd, reading orbit size as a multinomial coefficient whose 2-adic valuation you test.
how_used: Each admissible ordered quintuple lies in the S_5-orbit of its underlying multiset, of size 5!/(t_1!...t_k!) with sum t_i=5. This multinomial is odd exactly when v_2 of the denominator equals v_2(5!)=3; with v_2(t!)=0,1,1,3,3 for t=1..5, the only multiplicity partitions hitting sum 3 are (5) and (4,1) — i.e. at least four of the five entries equal. So N mod 2 equals the number of unordered solutions of shape (a,a,a,a,b).

technique: Clear denominators of the small unit-fraction equation and complete the product into (linear)(linear)=constant (Simon's factoring), then enumerate the finitely many positive divisor pairs.
how_used: The surviving case 4/a + 1/b = 1 becomes 4b + a = ab, rewritten as (a-4)(b-1)=4; since b>=1 forces b-1 a nonnegative divisor of 4 (1,2,4), giving exactly (a,b) = (8,2),(6,3),(5,5) — three unordered solutions, so N is odd.

technique: Peel off a self-contained top block by reflecting a contiguous interval of indices through one fixed square, then recurse on the remaining prefix
how_used: For n=l+1, pick the square m^2 and index p with (l+1)+p=m^2, then set a_i = m^2 - i for all p<=i<=l+1; this reversal sends the block {p,...,l+1} onto itself with every i+a_i=m^2 a square, leaving {0,...,p-1} to be filled by the induction hypothesis (valid since p-1<=l)

technique: Verify a reflection/pivot point lands in range by bounding the smallest square above the target below twice the target
how_used: With m^2 the least square >= l+1, use l >= (m-1)^2 to get 2(l+1) >= m^2+(m-2)^2 >= m^2, guaranteeing p = m^2-(l+1) satisfies 0 <= p <= l+1 so the reflected block and the recursive prefix both make sense

technique: Sum a full symmetric cycle of pairwise lower bounds and halve to bound the total.
how_used: From N_x+N_y >= n, N_y+N_z >= n, N_z+N_x >= n, add to get 2(N_x+N_y+N_z) >= 3n, hence total >= 3n/2 = 3030.

technique: Reduce a global minimum-count bound to per-direction subtotals by proving a pairwise lower bound between each two transverse families, then sum the symmetric inequalities.
how_used: Let N_x,N_y,N_z count beams by direction (min>0 case). Establish the three symmetric inequalities N_x+N_y>=n, N_y+N_z>=n, N_z+N_x>=n; adding them gives 2(N_x+N_y+N_z)>=3n, i.e. N=N_x+N_y+N_z>=3n/2=3030, matching the construction. This move only sets up the reduction: the hard content is proving one such pairwise inequality (separate crux) and the degenerate min=0 case (separate crux).

technique: Build the extremal packing from three congruent axis-families of parallel unit prisms shifted by one cell along the main diagonal, so each family's long faces sit flush in the one-cell gaps the other two families leave.
how_used: For the n x n x n cube (n=2020) place n/2 beams in each axis direction, 3n/2 = 3030 total. Reconstruct the explicit corner-pairs from the n=6 picture: z-beams (0,0,0)->(1,1,n),(2,2,0)->(3,3,n),...; y-beams (1,0,0)->(2,n,1),(3,0,2)->(4,n,3),...; x-beams (0,1,1)->(n,2,2),(0,3,3)->(n,4,4),.... Each family staircases along the main diagonal in steps of 2 and is offset by one unit so its beams occupy the 1-wide channels flanking the transverse families. Verify the touching condition cell-by-cell: every 1xn long face of a beam abuts, over its whole length, either the cube wall or the interior face of a transverse beam of another family; the one-unit interlock is exactly what makes each long face flush end to end. Since 3n/2 equals the lower bound, this construction is optimal.

technique: Eliminate the degenerate case where one family is empty by slicing along the missing direction into independent unit slabs, each an isolated lower-dimensional touching problem whose per-slab cost multiplies to dominate the target bound.
how_used: Handle min(N_x,N_y,N_z)=0 separately, say N_z=0. Slice into the n horizontal unit slabs z in [k,k+1]. Every x-beam and y-beam lies entirely inside exactly one slab (its 1x1 cross-section pins its z-range to a single unit), so the slabs share no beams and are independent. Within one slab the beams form a 2D configuration of 1xn segments in an n x n grid whose long faces must all be touched, forcing on the order of n segments per nonempty slab; with n independent slabs this forces on the order of n^2 beams total (official bound n^2), far above 3n/2. Hence an empty family never competes with the min>0 optimum and is discarded. The slab-independence reduction is the load-bearing move; the per-slab 2D lower bound is the routine remaining work.

technique: Classify the placed objects by their axis-orientation into a few counts, prove one asymmetric inequality relating those counts under a nonemptiness hypothesis, then invoke the problem's rotational symmetry to get all cyclic copies and add them.
how_used: Split the beams into x-beams, y-beams, z-beams by which coordinate axis their long edge is parallel to, with counts N_x, N_y, N_z. First dispatch the degenerate case min(N_x,N_y,N_z)=0 (a whole axis-family absent forces at least n^2 beams, far above the target). In the main case all three counts are positive. The single hard inequality to establish is the asymmetric lemma: if N_z>0 then N_x+N_y >= n. Because the cube and the touching conditions are invariant under the cyclic rotation of the three axes, the SAME lemma gives N_y+N_z >= n and N_z+N_x >= n. Adding the three inequalities: 2(N_x+N_y+N_z) >= 3n, so N_x+N_y+N_z >= 3n/2 = 3030 for n=2020. This matches the construction (n/2 beams in each of the three directions), so 3030 is the answer. The reusable move here is ONLY the setup: partition-by-axis + prove-one + symmetrize-and-sum; the proof of the lemma itself is a separate step.

technique: To force a minimum number of transverse objects, do NOT trace a single monotone corridor (a corridor of same-orientation objects can legally reach a wall); instead count interfaces globally by projecting the whole configuration onto the plane perpendicular to the target axis and bounding a connectivity/interface quantity across all n layers at once.
how_used: Goal: prove N_z>0 implies N_x+N_y >= n. Fix a z-beam B. The tempting-but-FALSE argument is: in each of the n horizontal unit layers, walk in -y from B's unit-square cross-section and claim you must hit an x- or y-beam. This fails because a wall of mutually-flush z-beam cross-sections can satisfy the 2D touching condition among themselves and reach the cube wall, charging no transverse beam. So a per-layer monotone corridor walk does NOT work. The correct mechanism is a global interface/projection count: project all beams onto the xy-plane (z-beams become unit squares, x-/y-beams become full 1-wide strips) and, tracking heights, count that the x- and y-beams must supply at least n distinct backing interfaces over the whole n-tall stack, not one per layer independently. The transverse-beam lower bound comes from a global count of these interfaces, using that z-beams alone cannot self-back the required vertical/horizontal touching across all layers simultaneously.

technique: Read a 2x2 unimodular determinant condition on integer pairs as a lattice-triangle area, turning the algebraic constraint into a geometric counting problem about triangles of fixed minimal area through the origin
how_used: |a_i b_j - a_j b_i| = 1 is recognized as twice the area of triangle OP_iP_j (O the origin, P_k=(a_k,b_k)) equalling 1/2; N becomes the number of such 'good' area-1/2 triangles, so the whole problem is recast as maximizing good triangles among 100 lattice points

technique: Bound the incidences of the extremal element (the point farthest from the origin) by locating its partners on the two lattice lines parallel to it at unit determinant distance and using the coprimality of its coordinates to limit lattice points inside its bounding circle
how_used: Take P=(a,b) farthest from O; any Q with |det(P,Q)|=1 lies on one of two lines parallel to OP, and since gcd(a,b)=1 the lattice points along such a line are spaced by vector (a,b), so only two of them fall within the quarter-circle of radius OP, giving P at most 2 good triangles; deleting P then completes the induction n -> n-1

technique: Achieve the extremal count with a near-collinear lattice construction: place most points on a single line at consecutive lattice spacing plus one off-line anchor, so adjacent pairs and anchor pairs all give the minimal-area triangles
how_used: Use points (1,0) and (k,1) for k=1,...,99: the 98 adjacent pairs (k,1),(k+1,1) with O and the 99 pairs (1,0),(k,1) with O all have area 1/2, yielding 98+99=197=2n-3 good triangles

technique: Build the extremal configuration by stacking many points on the graph of a single low-degree polynomial so that every subset of them shares one witness polynomial.
how_used: Take A={(1,a),(2,b),(3,b),...,(n,b)} with a≠b nonzero: the last n-1 points all lie on the constant curve y=b (degree 0), so any subset of them of size ≥2 is overdetermined by P(t)=b (degree 0 ≤ |S|-2), while the full set with the outlier (1,a) is not overdetermined. This yields exactly 2^{n-1}-n overdetermined subsets, giving the matching lower bound.

technique: Cap how many size-(m-1) subsets of a set can carry a property by noting two such would each force a low-degree interpolant, and a nonzero difference of degree below the size of their overlap cannot have that many roots — so the interpolants coincide and extend to the whole set.
how_used: For a non-overdetermined ('flooded') m-set S (m≥3), if two (m-1)-subsets S-{p_i} and S-{p_j} were both overdetermined, their witness polynomials f,g each have degree ≤ m-3 and agree on the shared (m-2)-point set S-{p_i,p_j}; since m-3 < m-2, f-g (degree ≤ m-3 with m-2 roots) is zero, so the common polynomial witnesses that S itself is overdetermined — contradiction. Hence at most one (m-1)-subset of a flooded set is non-flooded.

technique: Turn a per-parent local bound (each good m-set has almost all children good) into a layer-by-layer binomial count by double-counting parent–child incidences up the subset lattice.
how_used: Since each flooded m-set has at most one non-flooded (m-1)-subset it has ≥ m-1 flooded (m-1)-subsets, and each (m-1)-set sits in n-(m-1) m-sets; the incidence count with the identity (m-1)/(n-(m-1))·C(n-1,m-1)=C(n-1,m-2) gives inductively ≥ C(n-1,m-1) flooded m-sets for each m, so overdetermined sets number ≤ Σ_{m=2}^n (C(n,m)-C(n-1,m-1)) = 2^{n-1}-n.

technique: Track the clockwise cyclic orientation of each unordered triple of points as a Z/2 invariant that flips with every swap of two of its members.
how_used: For any three tokens i<j<k the clockwise cyclic order is one of two states and flips exactly when two of the three are interchanged; since each of the three pairs is swapped exactly once, the triple undergoes 3 flips and ends reversed, forcing i+1 to be the counter-clockwise neighbor of i throughout, so the final arrangement is a mirror reflection of the initial one across some line l.

technique: Lower-bound the number of moves a moving object needs to touch two prescribed boundary crossings and compare it against its fixed move budget to rule out double crossing.
how_used: Each token makes exactly 2n-1 switches (odd, so its vertex changes parity, pinning l through the midpoints of opposite edges a and b); a token crossing l at BOTH a and b would have to travel from x to a, then a to b, then b to 2n+1-x, costing at least x+n+(n-x)=2n moves > 2n-1, so every token crosses l at exactly one of a or b.

technique: Take the first occurrence of each of two competing events and derive a contradiction by showing one participant gets permanently confined to an arc the other must later cross.
how_used: Assuming both edges a and b are used, take the first switch at a (moving x clockwise) and first at b (moving y clockwise); x,y start on opposite sides of l, and after x traces a it lies on the clockwise arc from y to b with no way to leave, yet y must still trace b afterward, which is impossible, so only one of a,b is ever chosen.

technique: Prove a process terminates by exhibiting an integer-valued quantity that strictly increases with every allowed move, choosing strictly increasing positional weights so that pushing a larger entry rightward raises the total.
how_used: Track S = a_1 + 2a_2 + ... + n a_n. Replacing (a_i, a_{i+1}) with (c, a_i) where a_i > a_{i+1} and c = a_{i+1}+1 or c = a_i-1 changes S by d = (a_i - a_{i+1}) + i(c - a_{i+1}); since a_i - a_{i+1} >= 1 and c - a_{i+1} >= 0, d is a positive integer, so S rises by at least 1 each step.

technique: Cap the strictly-increasing monovariant by identifying a quantity the operation leaves invariant, turning 'increases forever' into a contradiction with a fixed upper bound.
how_used: The operation never changes the maximum M of the sequence (each new entry lies between the two old ones), so every term stays <= M and S <= (1+2+...+n)M is constant. A quantity that gains >=1 per step but never exceeds this fixed bound forces finitely many steps.

technique: Sandwich a target count by bounding the same aggregate (the sum of the involved elements) below by its forced minimum and above by its forced maximum, then solve the resulting inequality for the count
how_used: Let x be the number of disjoint pairs. The total S of the 2x distinct involved elements is at least 1+2+...+2x = x(2x+1). Since the x pair-sums are distinct integers each at most n, S = sum of pair-sums <= n+(n-1)+...+(n-x+1) = nx - x(x-1)/2. Chaining the two bounds on the same S gives x(2x+1) <= nx - x(x-1)/2, which reduces to 5x <= 2n-1, so x <= floor((2n-1)/5).

technique: Match a construction to an extremal bound by splitting on the residue of n modulo the denominator, giving one explicit pattern for the tight residues and paring it down (drop a column, shift a row) for the others
how_used: Write n = 5k+r. For r in {3,4,5} (i.e. n = 5k+3,5k+4,5k+5) build a table pairing all of 1..4k+2 into 2k+1 disjoint pairs whose sums run consecutively from 3k+3 to 5k+3, all <= n. For r=2 (n=5k+2) delete the last column, removing the pair with sum 5k+3, to get 2k pairs. For r=1 (n=5k+1) delete the last column and subtract 1 from each first-row entry, giving 2k pairs with distinct sums <= 5k+1.

technique: Index each configuration by its middle/pivot element and count how many completions each choice admits, turning the count into a sum over that element
how_used: Each admissible triple (C1,C2,C3) has C2 a red cell (i,j); with a_i whites in its row and b_j whites in its column there are exactly a_i·b_j triples through it, giving T = Σ_{(i,j)∈R} a_i·b_j summed over red cells

technique: Bound a coupled product by the half-sum of squares (2ab≤a²+b²) so the double sum decouples, then regroup each square by the line it sits on
how_used: a_i·b_j ≤ (a_i²+b_j²)/2, and since row i has n−a_i red cells and column j has n−b_j red cells, Σ_{red}(a_i²+b_j²)/2 regroups to ½Σ_i(n−a_i)a_i² + ½Σ_j(n−b_j)b_j², separating into independent per-row and per-column sums

technique: Maximize a cubic like (n−x)x² by splitting its linear factor into equal weighted copies so three-term AM-GM applies with a balanced equality case
how_used: Write (n−x)x² = ½(2n−2x)·x·x and apply AM-GM to the three factors (2n−2x),x,x, giving ≤ ½(2n/3)³ = 4n³/27 with equality at x = 2n/3 = 666, which caps each line's contribution and yields T ≤ 4n⁴/27; matching construction: every line 666 white/333 red

technique: For the achievability half, pick a self-reproducing target configuration and show one player can restore it after any adversary move.
how_used: A maintains a 'regular' distribution (n-2 red boxes with 2 coins, 2 white boxes with 1 coin, total 2n-2); the claim is that after any B-move she can respond to a regular distribution again, so she survives indefinitely by induction.

technique: Pair the two units in each 2-coin box and send them opposite directions across B's forced move so every red box deposits exactly one coin into each neighbor.
how_used: Exactly one coin of a red box's pair was moved by B; A moves the other the opposite way, so the combined B+A pass drops one coin into the left neighbor and one into the right neighbor of every red box, guaranteeing each box with a red neighbor is non-empty and holds 1-2 coins.

technique: For the lower-bound half, define a size-weighted sub-interval as a potential and show the adversary can always strictly lower it after any response.
how_used: B works with an 'arc': a block of consecutive boxes of length l<=n-2 with N(alpha)<=2l-3 coins; B pushes coins outward at the arc ends so A can add back at most one coin to each extreme, forcing a new arc alpha' with strictly smaller coin count N(alpha')<N(alpha), and the integer potential cannot descend forever.

technique: Block the opponent's single repair coin by parking a coin at the interval's boundary that was just used by the adversary and is therefore frozen for that turn.
how_used: B arranges box l to hold exactly the one coin c received from box l-1 (possible because 3<=l<=n-2 and B pushes box l-1's coin clockwise into l); since c was in B's move A may not move it, so if A adds a coin to box l the extreme has 2 coins and dropping it yields a shorter arc with strictly fewer coins, otherwise the count already dropped. Only boxes 1 and l can receive A's coins (at most one each, k<=2 total), so a single end argument suffices.

technique: Split each doubled cell's two units and send them to opposite neighbors, one countering the adversary's forced move and one your free move, so together they deposit exactly one unit into every neighbor.
how_used: A starts from a 'regular' distribution: n-2 red boxes with 2 coins and 2 white boxes with 1 coin (total 2n-2). On B's move M exactly one of the two coins in each red box X is passed (say c1, to one side); A responds by passing the other coin c2 to the OTHER side. Combined, M and A's move M' push the two coins of every red box in opposite directions, so each neighbor of a red box gets exactly 1 coin that started in X. Where every box has a red neighbor, every box ends non-empty; and since each box receives at most 1 from a red neighbor and at most 1 from a white neighbor (white coins are frozen, being unused by A), every box holds 1 or 2 coins, N=2n-2 forces a regular distribution again, so the invariant is self-reproducing. The lone exceptional box lacking a red neighbor is handled separately.

technique: When one uniform response leaves a single exceptional configuration uncovered, detect that case reactively and give it a tailored do-nothing response, leaving the offending element untouched so it survives on its own residue.
how_used: The pairing move (send the two coins of each red box to opposite neighbors) fails only in situation S: a red box R with two WHITE neighbors that receives no coin from them on B's move M, so R would be fed by neither the pairing nor a neighbor. If S occurs, A leaves R untouched: R keeps exactly its 1 leftover coin and stays non-empty, while every other box still has a red neighbor DIFFERENT from R, so the pairing argument on the rest keeps all of them at 1-2 coins and non-empty. If S does not occur, R receives a coin from a white neighbor on M (that coin is frozen for A's move) so R stays non-empty. Because the response is chosen reactively after seeing M, A need not pre-commit where the two white boxes sit, and each move independently re-establishes a regular distribution.

technique: Run an integer monovariant equal to a deficient window's coin total: on your move drain the window's total by a fixed amount while the opponent's reply can push back strictly less, and reuse the window's own low-total slack to re-declare it as a valid (possibly shortened) deficient window each round, so a nonnegative integer keeps strictly dropping and cannot fall forever.
how_used: For N <= 2n-3 (n>=7), B wins. Call a block of 2<=L<=n-2 consecutive boxes an 'arc' if its total N(a) <= 2L-3; the inequality forces L>=2, and if both extremes are nonempty then N(a)>=2 forces L>=3, and any extreme holding >1 coin can be discarded to give a shorter arc, so every arc contains one whose two extreme boxes hold exactly 1 coin. Take an arc occupying boxes 1..L with ends 1 and L each holding exactly 1 coin. B moves so the arc loses coins: pass 1 coin counterclockwise out of box 1 and box n, clockwise out of every other box; this leaves N(a)-2 coins inside 1..L, and (using 3<=L<=n-2) leaves box L holding exactly the single coin c it received from box L-1. A can return coins to the arc only through its two ends (boxes 1 and L), at most 1 each, so A returns k<=2. If k<2: boxes 1..L now hold < N(a) coins, so the SAME block of length L is again an arc a' with N(a')<N(a) (the bound 2L-3 still holds since the total only dropped). If k=2: A adds a coin to box L, but A cannot move the frozen coin c (it was used in B's previous move), so box L now holds 2 coins while boxes 1..L again total N(a); discard the 2-coin extreme L to obtain a shorter arc a' of length L-1 with N(a')<=N(a)-2<=2(L-1)-3, so N(a')<N(a). Either branch produces a strictly smaller nonnegative arc total, which cannot decrease forever, so eventually the move that would drop it is blocked only by an empty box appearing after A's move.

technique: When a resource is only slightly below the uniform average, measure the deficit from that average as an additive potential; a global deficit of at least d, spread over a bounded cyclic/linear domain, forces some contiguous window whose local deficit is also at least d.
how_used: B wins when N<=2n-3. Define the deficit of a box as 2 minus its coin count; total deficit Sigma(2-c_i)=2n-N>=3. Call a block alpha of ell<=n-2 consecutive boxes an 'arc' when N(alpha)<=2ell-3, i.e. its local deficit is >=3. The seed step is: from a global deficit >=3 on the circle of n>=7 boxes, produce ONE arc. Every box has c_i>=1 so the deficit per box is at most 1; a deficit of >=3 means at least 3 singleton boxes carry it. The averaging/pigeonhole content is that these >=3 units of deficit cannot all sit in a single length-(n-1)-or-more sweep without some window of length <=n-2 accumulating deficit >=3: pick the shortest contiguous block that already contains 3 singletons (its two singleton extremes plus one interior singleton give deficit exactly 3 at the ends and >=3 total, N(alpha)<=2ell-3). Trim any extreme with >1 coin to keep singleton extremes. This is why the count '>=3 singletons' plus n>=7 yields an actual arc; the two singleton ENDS alone give only 2ell-2, so the third (interior) singleton is exactly what pushes the window's total to the strict threshold 2ell-3.

technique: To run a strict monovariant descent in an adversarial game, hand the opponent a designated forced move that both drains the potential and pins one boundary cell via a can't-be-touched token, so the responder cannot restore the potential no matter how they answer.
how_used: Given an arc alpha = boxes 1..ell (extremes singletons, ell in [3,n-2], N(alpha)<=2ell-3, all boxes nonempty), B forces N(alpha') < N(alpha) after ANY A-response, driving the arc-total monovariant down until a box empties. B's designated move: pass 1 coin counterclockwise from box 1 and from box n, and clockwise from every other box. Effect: the arc keeps only N(alpha)-2 coins (boxes 1 and ell each ship their single coin outward and box 2..ell-1 flow keeps interior inside), and box ell ends with exactly one coin c, the one just received from ell-1 - and c is 'involved in B's move' so A is FORBIDDEN to move it. A's reply can push at most 2 coins into the arc, only into boxes 1 and ell (<=1 each). If fewer than 2 enter, N(alpha')<N(alpha) directly. If exactly 2 enter, box ell now holds 2 coins but c is pinned, so N(alpha) is restored yet box ell (an extreme) has 2 coins - trim it to get a shorter arc alpha' with N(alpha')<N(alpha). Either way the monovariant strictly drops; it cannot drop forever, so eventually a box in the arc hits 0 after an A-move. The pinned token c (untouchable because it moved on B's turn) is the crux that defeats A's attempt to refill the boundary.

technique: Reduce a global rearrangement constraint to finding a single bounded-distance perfect matching between one target class and its same-type objects
how_used: Instead of building the whole color-correct permutation at once, observe it suffices to match the 3n^2 A-squares to the 3n^2 A-tokens within distance d+2 (the other colors follow by the cyclic A->B->C symmetry of the coloring and of pi), turning the problem into one bipartite matching existence question.

technique: Tile the board into blocks holding exactly one representative target cell, and edge each object to the representative of the block containing its own position and its images under the given near-map and that map's inverse
how_used: Split into 3x1 horizontal triminoes, each holding exactly one A-square; using the distance-d permutation pi (A->B->C->A), connect A-token T to the A-square of the trimino containing T, pi(T), or pi^{-1}(T). Block diameter 2 plus pi's reach d bounds every edge by d+2, and each A-token and each A-square lands with degree exactly 3.

technique: Certify Hall's condition on a k-regular bipartite graph by double-counting edges out of any vertex subset
how_used: Because both sides are 3-regular, any set S of A-squares emits 3|S| edges which must land on at least |S| A-tokens (each absorbing at most 3), so Hall's marriage condition holds and the desired perfect matching exists.

technique: Encode a candidate by binary-digit queries so that, whatever the yes/no answers come back, all of them are simultaneously inconsistent with exactly one common number.
how_used: In part a), to eliminate some y != x from a set T of size >2^k, Ben relabels T so it starts {0,...,2^k,...,m-1} and asks, for each i=1,...,k, whether the i-th binary digit of x is 0. Regardless of Amy's k answers, they are all inconsistent with a single number y in {0,...,2^k-1} (its digits are pinned by whatever was said). He first forces one extra inconsistent answer by repeatedly asking 'is x=2^k?' until a 'yes' (which is inconsistent with every y != 2^k); that gives a block of k+1 consecutive answers all inconsistent with y, so y=x would be k+1 lies in a row -- impossible -- proving y != x and letting Ben drop it, shrinking T down to size 2^k <= n. (Fallback: if Amy says 'no' k+1 times to 'is x=2^k?', one is truthful so x != 2^k and 2^k itself is dropped.)

technique: Track, for every candidate, the current run-length of answers inconsistent with it, and sum a geometric weight lambda^(run) over all candidates into a single potential the adversary greedily minimizes.
how_used: In part b), Amy sets N=n+1 and defines phi = sum over i=1..n+1 of lambda^{m_i}, where m_i counts her current streak of consecutive answers inconsistent with candidate i and 1<lambda<2. Keeping phi < lambda^{k+1} at all times forces every m_i <= k, so no candidate -- in particular the true x -- ever receives k+1 consecutive inconsistent (i.e. lying) answers, making her answers legal; and since phi and her choices never reference x, Ben learns nothing about x, so with n+1 candidates fully consistent at least one lies outside any n-element set Ben names.

technique: Bound a greedy minimizer's outcome by the average of its two available options, min(A,B) <= (A+B)/2, to get a clean recursive bound on the potential.
how_used: In part b), for a query set S the two possible new potentials phi_1 (answer yes) and phi_2 (answer no) satisfy each candidate contributing 1 to one and lambda^{m_i+1} to the other, so phi_1+phi_2 = lambda*phi + (n+1). Since Amy picks the minimizing answer, the new phi <= (1/2)(lambda*phi + n+1); plugging phi < lambda^{k+1}, lambda<2, and n = floor((2-lambda)lambda^{k+1}) - 1 yields new phi < (1/2)(lambda^{k+2} + (2-lambda)lambda^{k+1}) = lambda^{k+1}, preserving the invariant.

technique: Recast a 'pick many pairwise-compatible objects sharing one label' goal as a large independent set in the per-label conflict graph
how_used: Color each chord by the sum of its two endpoint labels (colors 3..4n-1 for labels 1..2n); observe two same-color chords cannot share an endpoint (a shared endpoint forces the other two labels equal), so 'disjoint' equals 'non-crossing'. For each color c build G_c on the color-c chords with edges between crossing chords; a set of pairwise disjoint equal-sum chords is exactly an independent set in one G_c, so it suffices to find a color whose graph has independence number >= 100

technique: Lower-bound the independence number of a graph by the sum over vertices of 1/(degree+1) (Caro-Wei), proved by repeatedly extracting a minimum-degree vertex and deleting its closed neighborhood
how_used: Prove and apply |independent set| >= f(G) := sum_v 1/(d_v+1): pick the min-degree vertex v0 of degree d, delete it and its d neighbors (all of degree >= d), so the removed terms sum to <= (d+1)/(d+1) = 1, giving f(G') >= f(G)-1; induction yields an independent set of size >= f(G_c) in each color graph

technique: Bound a chord's crossing-degree by the number of points on its shorter arc, since each such point anchors at most one same-color chord
how_used: For a chord l let m(l) <= n-1 be the points on its smaller arc; any same-color chord crossing l separates l's endpoints so has an endpoint among those m(l) points, and a point together with color c determines its partner label uniquely, so each point anchors at most one color-c chord; hence deg_{G_c}(l) <= m(l). With exactly 2n chords for each arc-count i=0..n-2, summing 1/(deg+1) >= 1/(m+1) over all chords gives sum_c f(G_c) >= sum_{i=0}^{n-2} 2n/(i+1) = 2n*H_{n-1}

technique: Prove a sum of reciprocals 1/i grows past a target constant by grouping its terms into consecutive dyadic blocks, each block contributing more than 1/2
how_used: There are 4n-3 colors, so averaging sum_c f(G_c) >= 2n*H_{n-1} over the colors yields a color with f(G_c) >= (2n/(4n-3))H_{n-1} > (1/2)H_{n-1}; to show this exceeds 100 for n=2^499, group the terms of H_{n-1} = sum_{i=1}^{n-1} 1/i into dyadic blocks [2^{k-1}+1, 2^k], each summing to > 1/2, giving H_{n-1} > 1 + 400*(1/2) = 201 > 200, hence (1/2)H_{n-1} > 100 and Caro-Wei yields >= 100 pairwise disjoint equal-sum chords

technique: Instead of directly building k objects of a target type, fix one blind tiling of the whole board and pigeonhole its two-class labeling to force at least half into one class
how_used: Tile the n×n board with floor(n^2/2) dominoes ignoring colors (all n^2/2 for even n; drop one cell and use (n^2-1)/2 for odd n, still an even count since 8|n^2-1); each tile is intrinsically colorful or plain, so one class holds >= floor(n^2/2)/2 = floor(n^2/4) tiles, and these lie in a single tiling so are non-overlapping and one type, giving k >= floor(n^2/4).

technique: For the matching extremal construction, make the color that caps both types an independent set carved out of a single checkerboard parity class, so it is pairwise non-adjacent and hits the target size
how_used: Checkerboard-color the board and let the MINORITY parity have floor(n^2/2) cells (for odd n put bottom-left white so black is minority); color exactly half of that parity class red (floor(n^2/4) reds), everything else blue. Reds are pairwise non-adjacent, so every colorful domino covers one red (<= floor(n^2/4) colorful) and every plain domino must be blue-blue containing a minority-parity cell (<= #minority-blue = floor(n^2/2) - floor(n^2/4) = floor(n^2/4) plain); pinning the minority parity is what makes both caps equal floor(n^2/4) (using the majority parity would give floor(n^2/4)+1 plain).

technique: Recast an 'exists a region avoiding the boundary' claim as its contrapositive, then use the boundary-covering hypothesis to force each region to own exactly one connected boundary arc, giving a bijection between regions and arcs.
how_used: Assume every rectangle meets the square's boundary; the line condition upgrades this to each rectangle having a full side on the boundary. A rectangle owning two disjoint boundary arcs would need them on opposite sides, but then a line along its other two sides would cross the square's interior without ever lying inside any rectangle — forbidden. Hence the perimeter splits into exactly n arcs, one per rectangle.

technique: Cap the number of interior vertices by subtracting the vertices forced onto the boundary from the fixed global vertex total.
how_used: The n rectangles have 4n corners total. At each of the n arc-endpoints two rectangles meet, contributing 2 corners each endpoint (2n), plus 4 corners coinciding with the square's own corners: 2n+4 corners lie on the boundary. So at most 4n-(2n+4)=2n-4 corners can lie in the interior.

technique: Assign to each boundary junction a distinct interior vertex where the perpendicular line, forced by the covering hypothesis to eventually enter a region's interior, first crosses a parallel region-side, then compare this count to the interior-vertex cap.
how_used: At each of the n boundary points P where two rectangles abut, the line perpendicular to that side initially runs along a side of both rectangles; to satisfy the hypothesis it must cross a rectangle side parallel to the original square side, at a branch point Q that is a corner of two rectangles. Distinct P give distinct interior Q, forcing at least 2n interior corners — contradicting the bound 2n-4.

technique: Recast a geometric legality condition as a monotone operation on an abstract multiset invariant of the position
how_used: Encode a position by the multiset {a,b,c} of the three arc-lengths between counters (a+b+c=n), and translate 'the triangle's area strictly increases' into 'replace two of the arcs by two numbers of the same sum that strictly increase the minimum of that pair', turning the geometry game into pure arithmetic on arc-lengths. Uses area = (R^2/2)(sin A+sin B+sin C) and sin A+sin B = 2 sin((A+B)/2)cos((A-B)/2) with A+B fixed under a slide.

technique: Prove a whole class of positions are N-positions by a strategy-stealing symmetry: reach a symmetric position, and argue any winning reply from it could have been played directly from the original
how_used: Show every non-isosceles configuration is a Win: slide one counter to form an isosceles triangle with apex Y; if that is a Loss we are done, otherwise the winning continuation cannot move the apex counter Y, so by the triangle's reflective symmetry it moves the other free counter to some Z'' that the original counter could have reached in one move directly, making the original a Win.

technique: Determine the game value by recursing on the 2-adic valuation of a difference that exactly halves at each relevant step, so the P/N status flips with each halving and depends only on the valuation's parity
how_used: From isosceles arcs (a,a,b) the only other reachable isosceles state has arcs (a, a±|a-b|/2, a±|a-b|/2), possible iff |a-b| is even; so (a,a,b) is a Win iff that halved-difference state is a Loss, giving an induction on v_2(a-b) and yielding: the start (1,1,n-2) is a Win iff v_2(n-3) is odd.

technique: Reduce an adversarial initial configuration to its worst case by enlarging it to a maximal symmetric shape you can analyze cleanly
how_used: Since flooding is monotone (a superset initial flood stays a superset at every later turn) and Hephaestus must enclose ALL flooded cells, adding flooded cells never helps him; so assume the flood starts as the full diamond |x|+|y|<=d containing Poseidon's finite set. Poseidon's spread grows it to |x|+|y|<=d+k-1 by Hephaestus's kth turn, a predictable symmetric linearly-expanding L1 front to fence in with a rectangle.

technique: Exploit a cumulative per-turn budget by banking slack in cheap early turns to afford a large bulk placement later
how_used: The wall-length cap is cumulative (length <= alpha*n after turn n), so early turns bank slack. Build the enclosing rectangle in phases: bulk-place a north cap in one turn, spend N1 turns extending the two vertical arms one unit each per turn to keep pace with the diamond, then once alpha*N1 > 2N1+(2d+3) bulk-place the east/west arms, spend N2 more unit-extension turns, and once alpha*(N1+N2) > 2N2+(6N1+8d+4) bulk-close the south. Both inequalities are simultaneously satisfiable for large N1,N2 exactly when alpha>2, since the budget grows like alpha*n while the geometric requirement grows like 2n, leaving linear headroom that dominates the O(d) overhead.

technique: Charge each boundary edge of a region to a distinct wall by shooting a ray from the source cell through that edge and proving no wall is hit twice
how_used: The flooded cells form a path c_0..c_n whose polyomino boundary has exactly 2n+4 exposed (green) edges. From each c_i's center shine a laser through each of its green edges; each laser crosses the enclosing loop. No wall is hit by two lasers: if the wall lies between two cells, the connecting segment would cross the loop once with both endpoints interior (contradicting Jordan-curve parity); if it lies above two cells c_i,c_j, they must form a straight column and their vertical lasers cannot coincide. So the loop has at least 2n+4 distinct walls, forcing alpha >= (2n+4)/(n+1) > 2.

technique: Count triangles as a monovariant under a neighbor-derived graph operation, choosing it so the count strictly rises exactly on the local configuration you want to forbid
how_used: The operation G to G' (u~v iff they share a common neighbor in G) never decreases the number of triangles (every triangle of G survives in G' since each pair shares the third vertex), and strictly increases it whenever G has a 'fatal' vertex (degree >=3 with two non-adjacent neighbors a,b; a third neighbor c makes a,b,c a new triangle in G'). Since G is isomorphic to G'' the triangle counts are equal, forcing G (and G') to have no fatal vertex.

technique: Characterize the graphs in which no vertex has degree at least 3 with two non-adjacent neighbors as disjoint unions of cliques, cycles, and paths
how_used: Having killed all fatal vertices, any vertex of degree >=3 has a clique neighborhood; a degree->=3 vertex v forces its component to be exactly the clique {v}∪N(v) (any outside neighbor of a clique member would make that member fatal), and all other components have max degree <=2, i.e. paths or cycles. So every component of G and G' is a clique (incl. single vertex), a cycle, or a path.

technique: Count connected components as a monovariant under the graph operation to eliminate the components that split
how_used: On a union of cliques/cycles/paths the operation acts componentwise (no cross-component edges in G'), so component count is non-decreasing. Isolated vertices, odd cycles, and cliques K_n (n>=3) are fixed; even cycles and paths of nonzero length break into strictly more pieces. Since G isomorphic to G'' equalizes component counts, no split can occur, so G consists only of the fixed types and hence G'=G, giving G isomorphic to G'.

technique: Encode a token-sliding process as a functional digraph where each mobile piece points to its forced target, so one slide reverses one edge and the reachable states biject with the vertices reachable from the hole in that graph.
how_used: Restrict to 'special' squares (those sharing both-coordinate parity with the empty cell); the hole stays on this class since every slide moves it by 2. Each special square except the hole is the near-square of exactly one domino: orient an edge from it to the special square that domino points at, giving a functional graph with the hole as unique sink. A legal slide reverses the single edge pointing at the hole, walking the hole one step along it. So reachable configurations correspond exactly to vertices of the connected component T containing the hole, and k(C) = |T|.

technique: To forbid a cycle in a lattice-embedded graph unless it encloses a distinguished point, apply Pick's theorem to the polygon the cycle bounds and force its interior lattice-point count to a fixed parity.
how_used: A cycle in the special-square graph is bounded by its dominoes, which enclose a polyomino of 2x2 blocks, so its area is a multiple of 4. In Pick's area = B/2 + I - 1, B is twice the number of dominoes on the cycle, and a parity argument on special squares makes that number even, so B is a multiple of 4. Then I must be odd. An odd count of interior special squares cannot be self-paired by dominoes unless one of them is the hole, so every cycle encloses the hole. Hence the hole's component T has no cycle avoiding the hole and is a tree.

technique: Encode a sliding/token-shuffling process as a directed functional graph — one out-edge per movable piece pointing to the cell it would vacate into — so that the reachable set becomes the connected component of the hole and each move is a single edge-reversal.
how_used: Restrict to 'special' squares: the hole plus all squares sharing both coordinate parities with it (sliding preserves this parity class). For each domino sitting on a special square s, draw a directed edge from s to the special square its far end points at. Every special square except the hole then has exactly one out-edge, so the graph is functional. The component T containing the hole has all its arrows oriented toward the hole; sliding a domino flips one arrow, and the reachable configurations correspond bijectively to the vertices of T, giving k(C) = |T|.

technique: To show every intermediate value of an extremal quantity is attained, exhibit an explicit maximizer (a spanning 'snake') and a local perturbation gadget that decrements the quantity by exactly one, then iterate the gadget across the board to sweep the whole range.
how_used: For the even-even case the cap is ((n-1)/2)^2; start from a snake configuration whose graph G is a spanning tree of the special squares (|T| at the maximum). A localized re-routing of a small block of dominoes detaches exactly one special square from the component T of the hole, lowering |T| by 1; sliding this perturbation along the board realizes every k in {1,...,((n-1)/2)^2}. The odd-odd top value ((n+1)/2)^2 is the isolated extra value achieved by the odd-odd snake spanning tree, so the achievable set is {1,...,((n-1)/2)^2} ∪ {((n+1)/2)^2}.

technique: Model a token-sliding puzzle's reachable states as a functional graph, so a single move reverses one edge along the path to the unique sink and the reachable positions are exactly one component.
how_used: Restrict to the 'special' squares (the empty cell plus all cells sharing its coordinate parity). Build a directed graph G on these squares: each domino sitting on a special square s draws an edge from s toward the special square it points at, so every special square except the empty one has out-degree exactly 1 and the empty cell is the unique sink. Sliding the domino adjacent to the empty square reverses that one arrow, walking the empty cell to an adjacent vertex, which becomes the new sink. Hence the set of reachable empty-cell positions is exactly the vertices of the component T containing the empty cell, and when T is a tree each reachable configuration is determined by which vertex is currently the sink, so k(C) = number of vertices of T. This reduces the problem to bounding and realizing |T|.

technique: To forbid a lattice cycle from bounding a region unless it encloses at least one lattice point, apply Pick's theorem to the polygon it bounds and pin the parity of the interior-point count from the area and boundary-point counts.
how_used: Call a square 'special' if it is the empty cell or shares the empty cell's parity in both coordinates. Put a vertex at each special square's center and, for each domino sitting on a special square, a directed edge from that square toward the special square the domino points at. A hypothetical undirected cycle in this graph bounds a lattice polygon. Show its area A is a multiple of 4 (the enclosed region decomposes into 2x2 blocks) and its boundary lattice-point count B is a multiple of 4 (B = 2 times the number of dominoes on the cycle, and a parity argument on special squares forces that domino count even). Pick's theorem A = I + B/2 - 1 then forces the interior count I odd, so I >= 1: any cycle strictly encloses at least one cell center, and the special-square parity structure makes the empty cell the only special square a cycle can enclose. Hence no cycle avoiding the empty cell exists.

technique: When slide/toggle moves on a rooted tree each just reverse one edge's orientation toward the root, count reachable states by identifying them bijectively with the choice of root vertex.
how_used: Once the component T containing the empty cell is shown acyclic (a tree), every domino's arrow points along T toward the empty cell, and one legal slide reverses exactly one arrow, moving the 'root' (empty cell) to an adjacent vertex. So each reachable configuration is determined by which vertex of T is currently the empty cell, giving a bijection between reachable configurations and vertices of T. Therefore k(C) equals the number of vertices of T, which is maximized (to ((n+1)/2)^2) when T is a spanning tree of the special-square graph.

technique: Reduce a two-player termination question to a single p-adic threshold: classify configurations by whether some token's p-adic valuation reaches the valuation of the fixed additive constant.
how_used: Set v = nu_2(a). The whole problem splits on the dichotomy 'every board number x has nu_2(x) < v' versus 'some x has nu_2(x) >= v'. The first case forces termination regardless of play; the second lets Alice play forever. Since the hypothesis is 'Bob can force termination', the second case is impossible (Alice would defeat every Bob strategy), so we are in the first case, and there termination is automatic for BOTH players -- which is exactly what must be shown.

technique: When adding a fixed constant whose valuation strictly exceeds each token's valuation, the addition preserves every valuation, so the total-valuation sum is a strict monovariant under the halving move.
how_used: In the regime nu_2(x) < v = nu_2(a) for all x: since nu_2(x) != nu_2(a), we get nu_2(x+a) = min(nu_2(x), v) = nu_2(x), so Alice's +a never changes any valuation and the invariant 'all nu_2 < v' persists. Take S = sum over tokens of nu_2(x), a nonnegative integer. Alice's move leaves S fixed; each Bob halving of an even token lowers that token's valuation by exactly 1, so S drops by exactly 1. Hence the game ends after at most S(initial) Bob moves, no matter how either player plays.

technique: To show a player can prolong a token-game forever, exploit that the prolonging player moves FIRST to carry a valuation witness one step ahead of the opponent: maintain a two-phase invariant (stronger bound before the opponent moves, weaker bound after) that is self-restoring because the first-mover always acts before the witness can be degraded.
how_used: Regime: some token has nu_2(x) >= v := nu_2(a). Boost fact: nu_2(y+a) > v exactly when nu_2(y) = v (equal leading 2-adic digits cancel). Alice moves first each round, so she maintains: (before Bob) some entry has nu_2 > v, (after Bob) some entry has nu_2 >= v. Given the after-Bob clause, if the witness sits at exactly v Alice adds a to it to push it above v; if it is already above v she adds a to a DIFFERENT entry, leaving the witness untouched -- either way before Bob some entry has nu_2 > v. Bob halving that witness drops it only to nu_2 >= v (restoring the after-Bob clause); Bob halving anything else leaves the witness above v. Since nu_2 > v >= 0 forces nu_2 >= 1, Bob always has an even token and never gets stuck, yet the invariant runs forever -- so whenever some token starts with nu_2 >= v, Alice survives forever.

technique: To show a token-game terminates under any play, find a regime preserved by both players' moves in which one player's move fixes every relevant valuation while the other's forced move strictly decreases a nonnegative-integer potential each round.
how_used: Let v = nu_2(a). Work in the regime where every board entry x has nu_2(x) < v. Key arithmetic fact: nu_2(n) < v implies nu_2(n+a) = nu_2(n), because n's lowest set bit sits strictly below a's lowest set bit and therefore survives the addition. Hence Alice's +a moves fix every entry's 2-adic valuation and keep the board inside the regime, while Bob is forced to halve some even entry (one with nu_2 >= 1), which drops that entry's nu_2 by exactly 1 and keeps it below v. So the potential Phi = sum_{x in S} nu_2(x) is a nonnegative integer that Alice cannot change and each Bob move strictly decreases; the game ends after exactly Phi Bob-moves. (This handles the case 'all tokens below v'.)

technique: To prove one player can force a token-game to run forever, have that player nurse a single chosen token so a driving valuation stays strictly above the opponent's reducing threshold, then close with a two-part induction showing the threshold holds both before AND after each opponent move so the opponent is never stuck yet never finishes.
how_used: Let v = nu_2(a) and suppose some board entry has nu_2 >= v; assume N >= 2. Alice fixes as her TARGET an entry that initially satisfies nu_2 >= v (such an entry exists by hypothesis -- it is NOT an arbitrary/first entry; an odd target makes the strategy fail, e.g. a=38, board=[3,40] with target=3). She plays to keep the target heavily even: if the target currently has nu_2 = v exactly, she adds a to it, producing nu_2(x+a) > v (equal lowest bits cancel and carry); otherwise she adds a to some OTHER entry (this branch needs N >= 2), leaving the target untouched with nu_2 > v. A double induction then maintains: just before each Bob turn nu_2(target) > v, and just after each Bob turn nu_2(target) >= v (if Bob halves the target its nu_2 drops from >v to >=v; if he touches another entry the target stays >v). In particular the target is always even on Bob's turn, so Bob always has a legal halving move and can never end the game -- play is infinite. Contrapositive of the given ('Bob can force the game to end') therefore forces every entry below v, which is exactly the always-terminating regime of crux 0.

technique: Count how many multiples of a chosen prime divide into one length-ℓ arithmetic progression to force a per-row dichotomy
how_used: For prime n=p, among 1..p^2 there are exactly p multiples of p, and a length-p AP with common difference d contains p multiples if p|d and exactly 1 otherwise. Since the p multiples split across p rows, either all p land in one row (that row is a p|d AP, forced by size to difference exactly p, i.e. the residue class {p,2p,...,p^2}) or they land one-per-row (every row is a complete residue system mod p). In both cases assigning column k the numbers ≡ k (mod p) makes each column the AP k,k+p,k+2p,... , so the finish after the dichotomy is immediate.

technique: Build a row-valid table that traps a chosen pair of values in one row by tiling a block of rows with fixed-common-difference arithmetic progressions
how_used: For composite n with prime divisor p, construct a row-valid table forcing n+2 and 2n+2 into the SAME row: row 1 is 1..n; rows 2..p+1 hold the block p+1..np+n split into common-difference-p APs of length n (each row a residue class mod p); the remaining rows hold the leftover numbers in reading order. Every row is a genuine AP so the table is row-valid, but n+2 and 2n+2 (differing by n) both land in one of the difference-p rows. Since row-permutations never move an entry across rows, this trapped pair survives any row-permutation. Concrete p=2,n=10: row 2 is 11,13,...,29 and row 3 is 12,14,...,30, with 12 and 22 sharing row 3.

technique: Pin an arithmetic progression's common difference by forcing its endpoints congruent modulo (length minus one) within a narrow window for the extremal endpoint
how_used: Assume the constructed composite-n table can be row-permuted to be column-valid; each column is a length-n AP, so min m and max M satisfy M = m + (n-1)d, hence m congruent to M mod (n-1). Column-minima lie in [1,n] and maxima in [n^2-n+1, n^2]. Track the entry 2 (a column minimum): its column's max must be congruent to 2 mod (n-1) inside the width-(n-1) window [n^2-n+1,n^2], which pins max = n^2-n+2 uniquely, forcing d = (n^2-n)/(n-1) = n. That column then contains 2, n+2, 2n+2, ..., putting n+2 and 2n+2 in different rows -- but the construction trapped them in the same row, and row-permutations preserve rows. Contradiction, so composite n fails.

technique: For a covering-with-forbidden-points lower bound, replace each forbidden point by a tiny cluster of new points around it and bound how many cluster-points a single admissible region can hold.
how_used: Points placed on the diagonal (s_i,s_i); each is blown up into a 4-point cross S' = S + {(±e,0),(0,±e)}, giving 4n perturbed points that all lie off the diagonal and so must be covered. Because any rectangle whose interior avoids the diagonal that catches two cross-points from different crosses i<j would have to contain some s_l (i<l<=j), a single admissible rectangle can cover at most 2 of the 4n points, and only from two adjacent crosses. The 4 extreme perturbed points at the two diagonal ends ((s_1-e,s_1),(s_1,s_1-e),(s_n+e,s_n),(s_n,s_n+e)) cannot be paired with any other point, so each needs its own rectangle, forcing k >= 4 + (4n-4)/2 = 2n+2.

technique: Cover the plane minus a finite point set by vertical slabs spanning each column to its neighbors, each slab punctured by removing the finitely many forbidden ordinates occurring in that column.
how_used: For each distinct x-coordinate x_i use |Y_i|+1 rectangles (x_{i-1},x_{i+1}) x ((0,1)\Y_i) where Y_i is the set of y-coords at x_i, plus two boundary slabs (0,x_1)x(0,1) and (x_m,1)x(0,1); this covers everything except points sharing a y-coordinate with horizontally adjacent columns, using m+n+2 rectangles.

technique: Orient the construction along the axis with fewer distinct coordinates so the residual leftover gaps are bounded by (points minus lines) along that axis.
how_used: Assume WLOG #distinct y-coords >= #distinct x-coords; the only uncovered points lie between same-y horizontally adjacent pairs, and there are at most n-m of them (sum over heights of r_y-1 = n - #distinct-y <= n-m), so n-m thin rectangles (x_i,x_{i+1})x(y-e,y+e) finish, totalling (m+n+2)+(n-m)=2n+2.

technique: Count the number of distinguishable outcomes and force at least one query bit per doubling of that count as an information-theoretic lower bound
how_used: The colorings of the 2022 vertices realizable by a halfplane cut number 2022*2021+2 > 2^21, so fewer than 22 truthful yes/no color queries can only separate 2^21 cases, forcing an error; gives the bound Q >= 22.

technique: Exploit convexity of each color class: any monochromatic set has monochromatic convex hull, so a color boundary between two known-different points on an arc is a single threshold locatable by binary search
how_used: Red and blue regions are each convex (halfplanes), so along equally spaced arc points B_0..B_{k+1} with B_0, B_{k+1} of known opposite colors there is exactly one switch; binary search finds all intermediate colors in ceil(log2 k) queries.

technique: Use a probed midpoint of a same-colored triple to certify one contiguous half is entirely that color, halving the uncertainty interval in one query
how_used: With B_0, B_{ceil(k/2)}, B_{k+1} all red on an arc, convexity forces at least one of the two halves fully red; a single extra query identifies which, cutting the unknown block of <=2^k-1 red-surrounded points to <=2^(k-1)-1.

technique: To pack quadratically many mutually distinguishable short windows into a bounded alphabet, concatenate blocks each of which is a full arithmetic progression over Z/n, letting the blocks' common differences run through a geometric sequence of ratios so that each block carries a distinct multiplicative slope-tag.
how_used: Block C_l lists (i-1)g^l mod n for i=1..n (an AP of slope g^l), with l running 0..a-1 for a fixed unit g; the a blocks each have length ~n giving total length a(n+2)+2, quadratic in n. Because the slopes g^0,...,g^{a-1} are distinct, a window's recovered AP common difference (a power of g) names which block produced it; the window's mean then names the offset inside that block.

technique: Recover the common difference of an arithmetic progression from only the unordered multiset of its residues by equating the multiset's power sums to their closed forms in (mean, difference), solving the second power sum for d^2, and taking a square root that is unique up to sign in an odd prime-power modulus.
how_used: For a window of length i<=k inside a block, the mean u = S1/i is recoverable (n=p^m coprime to i since p>k+1), and the sum of squares gives d^2 = 3(S2 - i u^2) * (fixed cubic-in-i factorial factor)^{-1} mod n; since n=p^m with p odd and gcd(d,n)=1, d is determined up to sign, so the block-slope g^l and hence the window's block are forced.

technique: Turn block boundaries into readable positional anchors by planting deliberately repeated adjacent symbols there, and choose the scale parameters so that within any short window the ONLY possible coincidence of two values is one of the planted repeats — a small-coefficient coprimality bound forbidding accidental collisions.
how_used: Each C_l duplicates its endpoints (g^l,g^l and (n-1)g^l,(n-1)g^l). For a window straddling C_{l-1},C_l an accidental repeat would need (n-u)g^{l-1} = v g^l, i.e. u+gv=0 mod n with 0<u,v<k; but g<n/k-1 gives 0<u+gv<k+kg<n, impossible. Hence any in-window repeat is a planted anchor whose value reveals l; dividing the window by g^{l-1} normalizes it and the split index is read off from where residues cross the n/2 threshold.

technique: To prove a short arithmetic progression with unit common difference is recoverable from just its multiset of residues mod p^m, use low-order power sums: the first power sum pins the center and the second power sum pins the squared common difference, hence the difference up to sign.
how_used: For a length-i AP (i<=k) of residues mod n=p^m with difference d coprime to n, the average u of the residues (i invertible since p>k+1) gives the center, and the sum of squares X satisfies X ≡ i u^2 + d^2 * (an explicit integer with denominator invertible mod n), so d^2 is determined, hence d up to sign. Recovering d from d^2 up to only two roots needs n=p^m with p odd and gcd(d,n)=1 (so squares have exactly two square roots). This identifies each AP-block window from its multiset up to reflection, which suffices because reflection fixes a block and the sign ambiguity is killed across blocks by the block-count choice (crux 0).

technique: To show a window straddling two adjacent blocks has no hidden repeated value in non-consecutive positions, turn a would-be collision into a small linear congruence in the scaling ratio and bound both sides strictly below the modulus so only the zero solution survives.
how_used: A window crossing from C_{l-1} into C_l repeats a residue in non-consecutive spots only if (n-u)g^{l-1} ≡ v g^l (mod n) for indices 0<u,v inside the window, i.e. u + g v ≡ 0 (mod n). Since the two pieces have combined length < k, u and v are < k, and g < n/k - 1 gives 0 < u + g v < k + kg < n, so the congruence is impossible. Together with p>k+1 (which forbids in-block accidental repeats away from the doubled markers), this proves the lemma: in any window of length <=k, equal residues occur only in consecutive positions. That lemma then feeds the routine global casework (0-marker, single-repeat, double-repeat cases) that pins each window's location.

technique: To find a primitive root below a small bound modulo p^2, lift each mod-p primitive root and count: expanding the (p-1)-th power shows at most one lift of each fails, and an inverse-pairing argument forbids all small-order units from clustering in the initial interval.
how_used: The construction needs a unit g with 0

technique: To extend a short-window uniqueness property to a very long low-alphabet string, concatenate scaled copies of the same recoverable block using successive powers of one scalar as the per-block parameter, and bound the number of blocks by that scalar's multiplicative order so distinct blocks stay distinguishable to the block-recovery lemma.
how_used: Work mod n=p^m, p>k+1. Pick a unit g with 0<g<n/k-1. Block C_l is the AP with common difference g^l (0,g^l,...,(n-1)g^l), with the first and last nonzero terms doubled as markers, and S_n=0,C_0,...,C_{a-1},0. Since a window inside C_l recovers its difference only up to sign (the recovery lemma), two windows from different blocks C_l,C_{l'} collide only if g^l ≡ ±g^{l'}; taking a = smallest positive integer with g^a ≡ ±1 caps l<a so g^{l-l'} ≢ ±1 for l≠l', killing all cross-block collisions. Within-block and boundary-straddling windows are located via the doubled-endpoint markers and delimiter 0's: a window's multiset reveals whether it touches a block boundary (repeated marker residue) pinning its block and offset, and the g<n/k-1 bound keeps boundary APs from wrapping so i_1,i_2 split unambiguously. Length is a(n+2)+2.

technique: To make a short arithmetic progression recoverable from its unordered multiset of residues mod n, compute a symmetric power-sum (the sum of squares) of the residues, reducing to a closed form linear in the squared common difference and thus pinning that difference up to sign.
how_used: For a length-i AP with residues {u-jd,...,u+jd} mod n=p^m (p odd, gcd(d,n)=1), the mean u is recovered as the average of the residues (i invertible since p>k+1>=i), and the sum of squares X satisfies X = i*u^2 + d^2*(sum of squared offsets) mod n; solving gives d^2 = 3(X - i u^2)*(offset-sum)^{-1}, and since n=p^m with p odd and gcd(d,n)=1, a square root recovers d up to sign. This is the recovery lemma the construction leans on: a single AP-window determines its common difference only up to +/-, and the identity is a congruence in Z/nZ independent of ordering or wraparound. Even/odd length are handled by the same power-sum with the appropriate offset multiset.

technique: To force a scalar parameter below a required threshold while keeping its multiplicative order maximal, lift a primitive root mod p to mod p^2, use that at most one lift per residue class fails to stay primitive, then rule out the failing residues occupying the target range via an inverse-pairing/size argument.
how_used: Need g with 0 1 pushes the length past 0.499 n^2 for large n.

technique: To build a long string over an n-letter alphabet with all short-window multisets distinct, concatenate scaled arithmetic-progression blocks whose common differences are successive powers of a fixed generator, so that any window either lies in one block (an AP recovered by the recovery lemma) or straddles a block seam where a size bound on residues separates the two sides.
how_used: For 0<=l<a define block C_l as the residues 0, g^l, g^l, 2g^l, ..., (n-1)g^l mod n (the AP with common difference g^l, with the endpoint terms doubled), and form S_n by concatenating C_0,...,C_{a-1} with a 0 prepended and appended, giving length a(n+2)+2. A window of length <=k either sits inside one C_l (an AP with difference g^l coprime to n, uniquely located by the recovery lemma) or straddles a seam between C_{l-1} (tail -u g^{l-1}) and C_l (head v g^l); a non-consecutive residue repeat would need u+gv = 0 mod n, but 0<u+gv<k+kg<n, impossible. Dividing a straddling window by g^{l-1} normalizes it to negative small residues (near n) on one side and small multiples of g (<n-k) on the other, so the seam position, and hence the window, is uniquely identified. This is precisely where the constraint g<n/k-1 is spent.

technique: Turn a forced zero in a derived difference-sequence into a forced repeat in the base sequence, then add that duplicate to the count of mandatory distinct values to get a length lower bound
how_used: Since edge value 0 must appear and k_i=|e_{i+1}-e_i|, some adjacent pair e_i=e_{i+1} coincide; the vertices must still realize all m+1 values 0..m, so beyond those m+1 distinct values one extra (the duplicate) is needed, giving n >= m+2

technique: Interleave a rising and a falling run into a single zigzag sequence so that consecutive absolute differences descend through every target value exactly once
how_used: Take (e_1,...,e_n)=(0,m,1,m-1,2,m-2,...) alternating low/high toward the middle; the successive |differences| are m,m-1,...,1 each once, the terminal equal pair e_{n-1}=e_n yields a 0 edge, and the wrap difference |e_n-0| duplicates a value <m, matching the doubled vertex value — realizing n=m+2

technique: Encode a configuration as an integer in positional notation whose highest place sits at the position a legal move is forced to alter, so every move strictly decreases the integer.
how_used: Read the 2009 cards left-to-right as a 2009-digit binary number (gold=1, black=0). Any move flips a block whose leftmost card is gold, turning the most-significant altered digit from 1 to 0 while only lower places change, so the number strictly decreases; nonnegative integers are well-ordered, so the game must terminate.

technique: Pick a subset of positions with period equal to the block length so that every legal move meets the subset in exactly one element, making the count of marked members flip parity on each move.
how_used: Label cards 1..2009 from the right and take S = {50i : i=1..40} (every 50th card). Each 50-card block contains exactly one multiple of 50, so g_n (golds in S) changes by exactly 1 per move; starting from g_0=40, after any odd number of moves g_n is odd hence positive, so the nonstarting player always finds a gold card in S to move on and thus wins — no winning strategy for the starter.

technique: Lower-bound a sum over a set of pairwise-distinct nonnegative integers by the triangular number 0+1+...+(N-1), then aggregate that bound across all coordinates against the fixed coordinate-sum invariant.
how_used: Since the a_i are distinct their sum is at least 0+1+...+(N-1)=N(N-1)/2, and likewise for b_i and c_i; summing the three bounds and using a_i+b_i+c_i=n gives 3N(N-1)/2 <= nN, hence N <= floor(2n/3)+1.

technique: Match an extremal counting bound with an explicit construction built from two interleaved blocks of consecutive first-coordinate values, casing on the residue class of the parameter.
how_used: For each residue n=3k-1, 3k, 3k+1, tabulate floor(2n/3)+1 triples as two consecutive runs of a_i (0..k-1 then k..2k-1, etc.) with b_i and c_i stepping through arithmetic progressions so all three columns are permutations of distinct values summing to n, attaining the bound.

technique: Encode a family of coefficient-driven recurrences as a single functional indexed by the driving binary word, so that a mirror-image construction becomes the same functional evaluated on the reversed word.
how_used: Define recursively a two-parameter word functional $(u,v)^w$ matching the branching rule ($\varepsilon=0$ vs $\varepsilon=1$), so that with word $w=\varepsilon_1\ldots\varepsilon_{n-1}$ one gets $a_n=(1,7)^w$ and, because $b$ runs the same rules in reversed index order, $b_n=(1,7)^{\bar w}$. This turns the goal $a_n=b_n$ into the reversal-invariance statement $(1,7)^w=(1,7)^{\bar w}$ for every binary word.

technique: Transfer a recurrence step from the tail of a word to the head of its reverse by re-encoding the step's coefficients as a modified seed of the word functional (using seed-multilinearity and the fact that the seed evaluated on any single letter reproduces the base value).
how_used: In the induction on $w\sigma\varepsilon$: apply the back-recurrence, e.g. for $\varepsilon=0$, $(1,7)^{w\sigma 0}=2(1,7)^w+3(1,7)^{w\sigma}$, then use the induction hypothesis to reverse to $2(1,7)^{\bar w}+3(1,7)^{\sigma\bar w}$. Since $(2,1)^\sigma=7=(1,7)^\emptyset$ for either letter $\sigma$, the front-peel relation $(u,v)^{\varepsilon w}=(v,(u,v)^{\varepsilon})^w$ gives $(1,7)^{\bar w}=(2,1)^{\sigma\bar w}$; multilinearity in the seed then merges $2(2,1)^{\sigma\bar w}+3(1,7)^{\sigma\bar w}=(7,23)^{\sigma\bar w}=(1,7)^{0\sigma\bar w}$, so appending $0$ at the tail of $w$ equals prepending $0$ at the head of $\bar w$ (and analogously for $\varepsilon=1$, giving $(7,10)$).

technique: Recount the total boundary length of a rectangle partition by summing, over each grid line, the number of pieces that meet that line.
how_used: Total perimeter is written p = 2(Σ r_i + Σ c_i), where r_i is the number of rectangles covering some cell of row i and c_i the number covering some cell of column i; summing r_i over rows recovers the total of all rectangle heights and summing c_i the total of all widths, so this line-incidence count reproduces Σ 2(height+width).

technique: To bound a sum of exponential weights 2^{-x_i}, attach to each index a family of subsets of a fixed universe whose cardinality realizes that weight, then prove the families for distinct indices are disjoint so their total cannot exceed the universe's size.
how_used: For diagonal index i, a subset S of the partition's rectangles is 'type i' if it contains all r_i rectangles meeting row i but none of the c_i meeting column i, giving 2^{n-r_i-c_i} such subsets; the rectangle covering cell C_{ij} (i<j) must lie in S by type-i yet lie outside S by type-j, so no S is two types at once; disjointness plus a universe of 2^n subsets forces Σ 2^{-(r_i+c_i)} ≤ 1.

technique: In a perimeter-minimizing partition, apply a merge-or-shift local exchange to the piece covering the extreme corner to force its opposite corner onto the symmetry line, producing a self-similar split for induction.
how_used: For the staircase board B_k, the rectangle R covering corner cell C_{1k} has upper-left corner (i,j); if i<j one either merges R with the neighboring rectangle sharing its full top side (Case 1) or slides the whole row of lower sides up by one (Case 2), each strictly decreasing total perimeter and contradicting minimality; hence the corner is (i,i), cutting B_k into congruent copies of B_i and B_{k-i} for the induction bound D_k = 2k log_2 k.

technique: For an adversarial capacity game, hand the defender a self-reproducing invariant family of configurations and show each legal move can restore it, so the bound holds forever by induction
