how_used: Cinderella maintains the invariant that two adjacent buckets are empty, the two flanking buckets have combined content at most 1, and the last bucket at most 1; after the Stepmother pours, choosing the right adjacent pair to empty re-establishes all three conditions, capping every bucket at 1 < 2 forever

technique: Bound a bounded total by splitting the covered quantities into two (or more) disjoint complementary sub-collections so at least one sub-collection lies below the average threshold, pinning which choice to make
how_used: From y0+y1+y2+y3 <= 2, the two disjoint diagonal pairs y0+y2 and y1+y3 sum to <= 2, so one of them is <= 1, telling Cinderella which adjacent pair to empty; the alternate solution sums all five overlapping diagonal pairs to 2*(total) <= 5 to force a non-critical pair

technique: Choose a cell-coloring on which the constrained move type forces the sequence of visited colors to be periodic, so a closed route uses each color equally and is capped by the rarest color's supply.
how_used: Color each cell by (i,j) mod 2 into four classes A,B,C,D. Because every limp-rook move must turn, moves strictly alternate horizontal/vertical, so from an A-cell the color sequence is forced into the fixed 4-cycle A,B,D,C,... (or A,C,D,B,...); a cyclic route therefore hits all four colors equally, and since there are only 499^2 A-cells the route has at most 4*499^2 cells.

technique: Checkerboard-two-color a sublattice and exploit its odd cardinality so that the route cannot perfectly alternate the two classes, forcing two consecutive route-cells of the same class.
how_used: Assuming the route visits all A-cells, color the A-cells (a diagonal sublattice) black/white so distance-2 A-cells differ; their count 499^2 is odd, so somewhere two same-colored A-cells (four rook-steps apart, at (a,b) and (a+2,b+2)) are visited consecutively, which up to reflection pins a unique local staircase path between them. (This forces the local configuration only; the actual contradiction is deferred to the Jordan-curve crux.)

technique: Close one required path into a loop with a straight chord and show the loop separates the two endpoints of another required path (one inside, one outside), so by the Jordan-curve property that second path must cross the first.
how_used: With the forced staircase between (a,b) and (a+2,b+2), and the forced passage through A-cell (a,b+2) via (a-1,b+2)->(a,b+2)->(a,b+3) (each A-cell is followed by a B-cell), the closing paths must join (a,b+3) to (a,b) and (a+2,b+2) to (a-1,b+2); these four cells are opposite vertices of a convex quadrilateral, so closing (a,b)-(a,b+3) with the chord yields a loop with one of (a-1,b+2),(a+2,b+2) inside and the other outside, forcing the second path to cross it — a revisited cell contradicting non-intersection.

technique: To make one large object outweigh several duplicated smaller copies inside an exponential potential, pick the exponential base b so that a guaranteed +1 in an exponent (b^{a+1}=b*b^a) beats the fixed number of copies (here b> number of copies).
how_used: At the split digit r, before the step the block R=zr contributes one term 4^{f_r(zr)} = 4^{f_r(z)+4^{f_{r+1}(z)}} to the level-(r-1) sum; the extra +4^{f_{r+1}(z)}>=1 in the exponent (r is the final digit, so it acts as a level-(r-1) separator picking up the trailing +) makes this >= 4*4^{f_r(z)}. After the step z(r-1)z(r-1) contributes at most three terms 4^{f_r(z)} at that level, totaling 3*4^{f_r(z)}. Since base 4 > 3, 4*4^{f_r(z)} > 3*4^{f_r(z)}, so the changed block's rank strictly drops.

technique: To prove a string-rewriting/branching process terminates, assign each string an ordinal-valued rank via a tower of exponentials nested by a monotone parameter, one exponential level per value of that parameter, and reduce termination to showing the rank strictly drops.
how_used: Index levels by the digit threshold k=9..0. Define f_k on strings whose digits are all >=k by splitting at each occurrence of the separator digit k into blocks x_s of digits >=k+1 and summing 4^{f_{k+1}(x_s)}, with f_9 counting nines. The point that makes this tractable: h only rewrites the maximal right part R=zr (r the last digit, z digits >=r) into z(r-1)z(r-1) with NO borrow, since r>=1 decrements cleanly and z is untouched; the left part L is copied verbatim. So f_0(n) is a positive integer and the whole problem reduces to Fact 3: f_0(h(n)) < f_0(n).

technique: To lift a strict rank-drop that occurs only in one inner block up to a drop of the global rank, use the recursion's collapse identity (levels below the minimal digit of the untouched prefix reduce the whole rank to a pure exponential of the inner rank) and induct downward on that minimal digit.
how_used: The change sits inside the right block; the prefix L=yk is copied verbatim. Fact 1 says a string with no digit below level i has f_i = 4^{f_{i+1}}, so at every threshold level below the minimal digit d(y) the total rank is a fixed monotone (base-4 exponential) function of the inner-level rank. Thus f_0(n)-f_0(h(n))>0 follows from the inner drop by monotonicity of x->4^x, handled by induction on d(y)=k,k-1,...,0: writing y=utv with t=d(y), f_t(n)-f_t(h(n)) = 4^{f_{t+1}(vkzr)} - 4^{f_{t+1}(vkz(r-1)z(r-1))} > 0 using the level-(t+1) drop.

technique: To make a duplication-type rewrite strictly decrease a potential, rank strings by a tower of exponentials with a base chosen larger than the number of copies the rewrite spawns, so one forced increment of an exponent outweighs the added copies.
how_used: This is the base inequality Case 1 (d(y)>=k) reduces to: show f_{r-1}(zr) > f_{r-1}(z(r-1)z(r-1)) at the level where r is the separator. By Fact 1, f_{r-1}(zr)=4^{f_r(zr)} with f_r(zr)=f_r(z)+4^{f_{r+1}(z)}, while the RHS splits at the two (r-1) separators into blocks z,z,eps giving 4^{f_r(z)}+4^{f_r(z)}+4^{f_r(eps)} < 3*4^{f_r(z)}. Fact 2 forces f_{r+1}(z)>=1, so the extra exponential factor 4^{f_{r+1}(z)}>=4, whence 4^{f_r(z)+4^{f_{r+1}(z)}} >= 4*4^{f_r(z)} > 3*4^{f_r(z)}. Base 4 (not 2) is exactly what beats the factor 3 = two duplicated copies plus one leftover block; this is why the ranking uses 4^{...} and why the strict drop survives the duplication.

technique: When a rewrite acts strictly inside one fixed positional block of a positionally-additive potential while everything outside that block is copied unchanged, lift the inner strict decrease to the top by inducting outward on the nesting level, using that the level-to-level aggregator is strictly increasing so a strict drop in one summand forces a strict drop in the whole level.
how_used: This is the Case 2 step (d(y) < k) that the base inequality alone does not settle. The rewrite h changes a fixed positional sub-block; the left part L and every separator of index below the acting level are copied verbatim, so at each level exactly one position-summand changes. Induct on t = d(y) = k, k-1, ..., 0: at level t write y = u t v with v free of digits <= t, so f_t(n) - f_t(h(n)) = 4^{f_{t+1}(v k z r)} - 4^{f_{t+1}(v k z (r-1) z (r-1))}; the induction hypothesis gives the inner argument strictly decreasing, and because x |-> 4^x is strictly increasing while every other summand at level t is identical (block at a fixed position, neighbors copied), the drop propagates. Descending to t=0 gives f_0(n) > f_0(h(n)) every step, and f_0 lands in a well-ordered set so the process terminates. Requires the potential to be predefined as the recursive positional aggregate f_k(x) = sum over blocks x_s (cut by the separators = k) of 4^{f_{k+1}(x_s)}, f_9(all-nines-of-length m) = m+1; the base case t=k is exactly Crux 2.
technique_tags: monotone lifting of an inner decrease

technique: To show a rewrite that lengthens a string still strictly lowers a base-b positional potential, pick the base b large enough that b times the surviving weight strictly exceeds the total weight of the copies-plus-separators the rewrite creates, so the exponential jump from one nested digit beats the linear blow-up in count.
how_used: This is Case 1 (d(y) >= k), the base of the whole argument and the only place a genuine inequality (not mere bookkeeping) is proved. Here h sends R = z r to two copies of R-1, i.e. z r -> z(r-1) z(r-1), so the block gets longer and gains a separator. Reduce by Fact 1 to level r-1 and compute f_{r-1}(zr) = 4^{f_r(zr)} = 4^{f_r(z) + 4^{f_{r+1}(z)}} >= 4^{f_r(z)} . 4^{4^{f_{r+1}(z)}} >= 4 . 4^{f_r(z)} (since the inner exponent 4^{f_{r+1}(z)} >= 1) which strictly exceeds 3 . 4^{f_r(z)} = 4^{f_r(z)} + 4^{f_r(z)} + 4^{f_r(z)} = f_{r-1}(z(r-1) z(r-1)). The number 3 counts the two copies of z plus the separator (r-1); base 4 is chosen precisely because 4 > 3, so the factor-of-4 gain from removing the digit r beats the factor-3 cost of duplicating. With f_10(eps)=0 the r=9 corner is covered. This strict drop initializes the outward induction of Crux 1.
technique_tags: tune the base so exponential gain beats linear count blow-up
reduce a potential inequality to its innermost level

technique: Assign position-dependent weights to the cells and choose them so every allowed move leaves the weighted total unchanged modulo n, forcing the move's net weight-change to vanish.
how_used: Label vertices 0..4 and weight vertex i by i, making S = N1+2N2+3N3+4N4 (mod 5) invariant: a move puts -m on two neighbors and +2m on the opposite vertex, and the weight combination is chosen so this net change is 0 mod 5. Distinct winning configurations (2011 on one vertex, 0 elsewhere) give distinct residues of S, so at most one vertex can win.

technique: Replace an unordered sequence of reversible moves by one net-amount variable per move-type, so reachability becomes existence of a solution to a linear balance system (order and sign of moves irrelevant since the step parameter ranges over all integers).
how_used: Let x_i be the total m summed over all moves in which vertex i receives +2m; since m can be any integer, the final value at each vertex is a_i + 2x_i - x_{i-2} - x_{i+2}. Winning at vertex 0 reduces to integer-solving the five balance equations (one redundant), which after substitution collapses to a two-variable linear system in x_2, x_3.

technique: Confirm the reduced linear system has an integer (not merely rational) solution by exhibiting a key combination whose divisibility is guaranteed precisely by the invariant's congruence condition.
how_used: The solution needs x_2 - x_3 = (a_1 - 3a_2 + 3a_3 - a_4)/5 to be an integer; that numerator is congruent to a_1+2a_2+3a_3+4a_4 which is 0 (mod 5) exactly when vertex 0 is the invariant-selected winner, so the same mod-5 condition that forces uniqueness also certifies integral solvability, proving the game is winnable at that vertex.

technique: Count pairwise set-intersections by summing a binomial-of-multiplicity over ground elements
how_used: Assign each element a multiplicity x_i = number of the 11 sets containing it; then Σ|A_i∩A_j| = Σ_element C(x_i,2), which with the given |A_i∩A_j|=9 yields Σx_i²=1485, while summing |A_i| gives Σx_i=495.

technique: Lower-bound the number of support terms via Cauchy-Schwarz on their first and second moments, n ≥ (Σx)²/Σx²
how_used: With Σx_i=495 and Σx_i²=1485 known, n·Σx_i² ≥ (Σx_i)² gives n ≥ 495²/1485 = 165, the desired bound on |A_1∪...∪A_11|.

technique: Realize the equality case as the uniform incidence design of all fixed-size subsets of an index set
how_used: Take the ground set to be all 165 three-element subsets of {1,...,11}, and let A_i be those 3-subsets containing i; then |A_i|=C(10,2)=45 and |A_i∩A_j|=C(9,1)=9, giving equality (every x_i=3, the Cauchy-Schwarz equality condition).

technique: Strengthen the induction by conjecturing the exact multiset of the whole initial segment rather than the asked-for property, then carry that multiset forward step by step
how_used: Instead of directly chasing 'all N occur', posit that a_0,...,a_k is always exactly the two consecutive-integer staircases {0,1,...,ell-1} and {0,1,...,k-ell} for some ell with 2ell<=k+1; proving this stronger form makes the k->k+1 step tractable and immediately yields that every N shows up by index 2N

technique: Fold a lower-tail binomial partial sum with C(n,i)=C(n,n-i) so two lower tails together become the full row minus a single middle term, then subtract against the row-sum 2^n
how_used: The hypothesis makes the given sum equal (C(m+1,0)+...+C(m+1,ell-1)) + (C(m+1,0)+...+C(m+1,m-ell)) + C(m+1,a_{m+1}); reflecting the second tail into C(m+1,m+1)+...+C(m+1,ell+1) covers every index of row m+1 except ell, so subtracting from 2^{m+1}=sum of the whole row isolates C(m+1,a_{m+1})=C(m+1,ell)

technique: From an equality of two binomial coefficients in the same row, use strict unimodality of that row to pin the index to one of exactly two reflected values
how_used: C(m+1,a_{m+1})=C(m+1,ell) with the row increasing up to (m+1)/2 and decreasing after forces a_{m+1}=ell or a_{m+1}=m+1-ell, precisely the two ways to extend the staircase structure and keep the inductive form

technique: Strengthen the claim before inducting: replace the rigid boundary value with an inequality and widen the free parameter's range so the induction hypothesis actually applies to the smaller instance
how_used: Instead of proving the result only for total weight exactly s=2n and 0<=r<=2n-2, prove the more general 'n blocks each >=1 with total s<=2n, and every -2<=r<=s is achievable within a window of 2'. The looser 's<=2n' is what lets the residual set (after deleting a block) satisfy s-x<=2(n-1), and extending r down to -2 is what makes the two covered sub-intervals meet

technique: Split the achievable subset-sum range into the sums that exclude a chosen element and those same sums shifted up by that element's weight, so covering a whole interval reduces to the two shifted copies overlapping
how_used: Deleting the largest block x, the inductive hypothesis covers r in [-2, s-x]; adding x back to each of those subsets covers r in [x-2, s]. The union is all of [-2,s] provided x-2 <= s-x, which holds because the remaining n-1 blocks each weigh >=1 (so x <= s-(n-1)). Sol 2 uses the same move as S_k = S_{k-1} u (x_k + S_{k-1}), reducing 'mesh <=2' to the single gap condition x_k <= (sum of smaller blocks) + 2

technique: Prove a per-element gap bound by contradiction: order the quantities and assume the bound fails at one index, forcing every later (larger) quantity to also violate it, then contradict a global total via a counting bound
how_used: With weights sorted increasingly, if x_k > sum_{j<k} x_j + 2 >= k+1 then every x_l (l>=k) exceeds k+1, so 2n = sum x_j > (n+1-k)(k+1) + (k-1); this rearranges to n > k(n+1-k), false for 1<=k<=n, contradicting the total weight 2n

technique: Reduce a deterministic bit-string process to its smaller instance by exhibiting a complement-and-reverse symmetry that conjugates the dynamics on a chosen subset of states onto the dynamics on the shorter strings.
how_used: The n-string state graph G_n is built from two copies of G_{n-1}: appending T leaves the flip-rule unchanged, while the map s_1...s_{n-1} -> \bar s_{n-1}...\bar s_1 H (flip every coin, reverse, append H) sends a config with k heads to one with n-k heads and mirrors each step, so that half runs as a copy of G_{n-1} that reaches HH...H then takes n extra steps. This yields E(n)=E(n-1)+n/2 with E(0)=0.

technique: Posit a closed-form nonnegative-integer potential equal to the total number of times each element is acted on, then verify it decreases by exactly one at every operation so the process length is its total value.
how_used: Set t(i)=I_i + 2(min{i,H_n} - H_i), where I_i marks coin i heads, H_i counts heads in positions 1..i, H_n total heads. A four-way case check (i<k, i>k, i=k head, i=k tail with k=H_n) shows exactly t(k) drops by 1 each flip. Then averaging sum t(i) by linearity — with the min-term evaluated via binomial identities — gives n(n+1)/4.

technique: Recast the process as a back-and-forth pointer walk and biject configurations with strictly increasing sequences of maximal same-direction run lengths, so each possible run length contributes to the count in exactly half the cases.
how_used: A Turing head starts at the k-th coin (k heads), stepping left on H (flip) and right on T (flip); a maximal run of a moves forces the next opposite run to have length >= a+1, so run lengths a_1<...<a_t <= n strictly increase (proving termination). Reversing the moves from all-tails shows each ascending sequence comes from a unique configuration, matching 2^n to 2^n; each i in 1..n appears in half the sequences contributing i, giving E(n)=(1/2)(1+...+n)=n(n+1)/4.

technique: Bound the number of connected components below by (vertices) minus (edges), using that each edge merges at most two components.
how_used: Regions of the line arrangement are the vertices of a reachability graph and doors are its edges. Count vertices by induction (each new wall crosses the n-1 others once, splitting n regions, giving C(n+1,2)+1 regions) and count edges as exactly one door per intersection = C(n,2), independent of the painting. Adding edges one at a time drops the component count by at most 1 each, so components >= C(n+1,2)+1 - C(n,2) = n+1; Morgana seats one knight per component.

technique: Bound the number of connected components of a planar-region adjacency graph from below by (number of regions) minus (number of adjacency edges), using that each edge merges at most two components.
how_used: The regions cut by n generic lines are the vertices of the door-graph G; by induction the k-th line meets the previous k-1 lines and splits k regions, so there are C(n+1,2)+1 regions = |V|. Each of the C(n,2) intersection points contributes exactly one door (the unique diagonal pair of differ-colour corners), so |E| = C(n,2) no matter how Merlin paints. Since adding edges one at a time drops the component count by at most 1, #components >= |V| - |E| = (C(n+1,2)+1) - C(n,2) = n+1. Morgana puts one knight per component, forcing k >= n+1 for every painting (the lower-bound direction).

technique: Attach to each region an integer read off from a canonical orientation of the walls, and check it is invariant across every door, so it partitions the regions into color-independent classes.
how_used: For the upper-bound construction, choose axes so no wall is N-S or E-W and have Merlin paint every wall red on its west face, blue on its east face. Label each region by the number of walls it lies strictly east of, an integer in 0..n. A door sits at an intersection of two walls a,b at the diagonal pair where colours differ; crossing it flips the region's side with respect to exactly a and b, and the fixed west-red/east-blue orientation makes one east-count go up and the other down, so the label is unchanged. Hence label is constant on each component, so there are at least n+1 classes; this is the invariant half of showing the count is exactly n+1.

technique: To show every element of a labeled class lies in one component, from any element walk monotonically along one fixed direction until it reaches the class's unique unbounded representative.
how_used: Having shown the east-count label is a door-invariant, prove each label class i is a single component. From any label-i region, walk due north: each region is convex, so if it is bounded to the north it has a single northernmost vertex, and the door at that vertex leads north into another region, which still has label i (the invariant). The north-coordinate strictly increases, so the walk never repeats and never sticks; it terminates at the unique label-i region unbounded to the north. So every label-i region reaches that canonical representative, class i is connected, and there are exactly n+1 components under this painting, giving k <= n+1.

technique: Lower-bound the number of connected components of a graph by (#vertices) minus (#edges), using that each edge drops the component count by at most one.
how_used: Delivers the lower bound k >= n+1, holding for EVERY Merlin painting. Model the labyrinth as a graph G whose vertices are the plane regions cut by the n lines and whose edges are the doors. Two paint-independent counts feed the inequality: (i) the n lines in general position create binom(n+1,2)+1 regions (separate induction: the k-th line meets the k-1 earlier lines and splits exactly k regions); (ii) there are exactly binom(n,2) doors, one per intersection point, regardless of colouring, since each crossing has a unique diagonal pair of different-colour corners. Then components >= V - E = binom(n+1,2)+1 - binom(n,2) = n+1. Placing one knight per component gives n+1 knights who can never meet. The reusable move is only the components >= V - E bound; the two counts are its inputs.

technique: To show a hard-to-analyze combinatorial count matches a target value, hand-design a special base configuration where the count is transparent and prove the target value there by induction on building the configuration one element at a time.
how_used: Supplies the base case for Merlin's sharp upper-bound painting (Solution 2/4). Merlin ignores the target labyrinth and builds his OWN: n walls added in turn with increasing positive gradients, each placed so far to the right that all previous intersection points lie to its left, painted blue-on-left/red-on-right. Call a region 'on the right' if its x-coordinate is unbounded above. Induct on the number of walls with the invariant: after placing m walls there are m+1 connected components, each containing exactly one 'on the right' region. Base m=0 is one region. The (m+1)-th wall, being right of all prior crossings, cuts exactly the m 'on the right' regions; it leaves each old component with still one right-region and creates one brand-new single-region component that is also on the right. Hence m+1 -> m+2 components, giving exactly n+1 for the designed labyrinth. The reusable move is: don't attack the general count directly — construct an easy base where an inductive build makes the exact count provable.

technique: Prove a discrete quantity is constant across all configurations of a continuous family by moving between them so that the only combinatorial event encountered is one generic local move, then verifying that single move preserves the quantity.
how_used: Transports the count from Merlin's designed base labyrinth to the target labyrinth for the upper bound k <= n+1. Continuously translate and rotate the walls (each carrying its own paint) from the base positions into the target positions, never letting two walls become parallel. Between events the arrangement's combinatorial type is fixed, so the door-graph's isomorphism type and component count are locally constant; the ONLY combinatorial event is one wall sweeping through the intersection of two others (a triple-line crossing). The required local check: in this move a small triangular region flips, but the incoming colouring — inherited from the base, where no crossing triangle has all three inner edges the same colour — is preserved by the rotation rule, and one verifies by direct inspection of the local door reconnection that the number of components is unchanged. So the target inherits the base's n+1 components. The reusable move is the deformation-invariance principle: reduce 'the count for an arbitrary configuration' to 'the count survives the one generic local transition,' anchored by an easy base.

technique: To manufacture a vertex with two non-adjacent neighbours in a connected non-complete graph, take a maximal clique K and use a vertex outside K adjacent to K: by maximality it misses some vertex of K.
how_used: In a >=3-vertex component that is not complete, pick a maximal complete subgraph K. Connectivity gives a vertex D outside K adjacent to some A in K. By maximality of K, D is non-adjacent to at least one other vertex B of K (else K + D would be a larger clique). Then A is adjacent to both D and B while D,B are non-adjacent, so A is the vertex with two non-adjacent neighbours needed to perform a refriending.

technique: When an operation preserves acyclicity, argue a forest on which no operation is possible must have max degree <=1, because in a forest any two neighbours of a vertex are automatically non-adjacent and hence give a legal operation.
how_used: Refriending preserves being a forest: deleting AB, AC and adding BC creates a cycle only if B,C had another connecting path, but that path plus A would already be a cycle in the forest. So once the graph is a forest, keep refriending until stuck; a stuck forest has no vertex with two neighbours (two neighbours of a vertex in a forest are non-adjacent, so would allow a move), i.e. max degree <=1 — the target. This is Step 2 of the tree route, and terminates because the edge count strictly decreases.

technique: When a process has a strictly monotone integer quantity, drop the goal 'reach a terminal configuration' and prove instead 'a legal move exists whenever the target does not yet hold' — the monovariant makes termination free, so the process must halt at the target.
how_used: Each refriending deletes edges AB, AC and adds BC, a net loss of one edge, so the edge count strictly decreases and the process must terminate. It therefore suffices to prove that whenever the graph is NOT yet a disjoint union of edges and isolated vertices (i.e. some component still has max degree >=2 AND is not stuck), a legal refriending is available. Caution: 'max degree >=2' alone does NOT guarantee a move — a clique K_{>=3} has every degree >=2 yet is stuck (every pair of a vertex's neighbours is adjacent). So the real content the later cruxes must supply is showing the process can never get trapped in a clique or clique-union; this crux only provides the monovariant/termination half of the reduction and the fact that the halting state, once move-existence is secured, has max degree <=1.

technique: To break every cycle while keeping a graph connected, locate a cycle together with an off-cycle vertex adjacent to one endpoint of a cycle-edge but not the other, and redirect that pendant edge onto the cycle-edge's far endpoint; find such a configuration by splitting on whether the graph has a triangle (use a maximal clique) or is triangle-free (use a shortest cycle).
how_used: It suffices, while a cycle exists, to have a connectivity-preserving refriending: find a cycle Z, an edge AB of Z, and a vertex C outside Z with C~A and C not~B, then delete AB, AC and add BC — Z keeps A,B connected via its other arc and C is reattached through BC, so the component stays connected while an edge is destroyed and a cycle is killed. Triangle case: take a largest clique K (>=3 vertices); non-completeness gives C outside K adjacent to some A in K, maximality gives B in K with C not~B, and Z runs through edge AB inside K. Triangle-free case: take a shortest cycle Z, choose an off-cycle C adjacent to a vertex A of Z; triangle-freeness makes C non-adjacent to A's cycle-neighbour B. Combined with the edge-count monovariant, iterating leaves a forest.

technique: Rule out the extremal sub-object that would leave no 'outside' vertex to act on, by showing that object forces a global structure contradicting a preserved parity feature of the graph.
how_used: In the triangle-free branch of the shortest-cycle reduction, the minimal cycle Z might a priori span every vertex, leaving no off-cycle vertex C to redirect an edge. Rule this out: if Z is Hamiltonian, minimality forbids any chord (a chord would split Z into a strictly shorter cycle), so G would be exactly the cycle Z, giving every vertex degree 2 — all even. But a refriending preserves the presence of a vertex of odd degree, and initially G has odd-degree vertices (1010 vertices of degree 1009). Contradiction. Hence Z is non-Hamiltonian, so a vertex C off Z adjacent to some A in Z exists; triangle-freeness makes C non-adjacent to A's cycle-neighbour B, giving the cycle-breaking move.

technique: To show a legal move never runs out under an edge-decreasing process, carry a component-level structural invariant strong enough to both force a move to exist and survive any move, and prove survival by casework on how deleting the moved vertex splits its component.
how_used: Invariant (1): every connected component with >=3 vertices is non-complete AND has a vertex of odd degree. It holds initially: any two vertices have degree sum >=1009+1009=2018>2017=n-2, so they are adjacent or share a neighbour, making G connected; and G is non-complete (max degree 1010<2018), and odd degrees are present. Non-completeness gives a vertex A whose neighbours are not all mutually adjacent (take a maximal clique K; a vertex A of K has a neighbour outside K not adjacent to all of K), so a legal refriending exists whenever some vertex has degree >=2. KEY PARITY FACT (used to survive the move): a refriending on A,B,C removes AB,AC and adds BC, so B and C keep their degrees (each -1 to A, +1 between them) and only deg(A) drops by 2 - hence pointwise parity is PRESERVED and an odd-degree witness is never destroyed. Survival casework: delete A, splitting its component G' into G_1..G_k. Case k>=2 with two edges to some G_i: pick B in G_i, C in another G_j (non-adjacent); move keeps G' connected, parity unchanged. Case k>=2 single edge each: A has degree 1 into each G_i, so by 'even number of odd-degree vertices' each G_i already contains an odd-degree vertex; any resulting big component keeps a witness and stays non-complete. Case k=1, >=3 edges: A has non-adjacent neighbours B,C, move keeps connectivity, finish as first case. Case k=1, exactly 2 edges: B,C the two neighbours; move leaves an isolated vertex plus a component with an odd-degree vertex - done unless that component is complete on >=3 vertices, i.e. G_1=K_m minus edge BC with m>=4; then a SECOND refriending at B (remove BA,BD, add AD for a third vertex D) keeps G' connected and escapes. Edges strictly drop each move, so the process ends at maximal degree <=1.

technique: To drop one edge of a graph while keeping it connected, find a cycle and an edge AB on it together with a vertex C off the cycle adjacent to A but not B, then replace edges AB, AC by the single edge BC.
how_used: This is the connectivity-preserving move that powers the 'reduce every cycle away' step: since each refriending removes one edge (deletes AB, AC, adds BC = net -1), it suffices to show that as long as the graph has a cycle, SOME refriending leaves it connected. The move above does exactly that: after deleting AB, B still reaches A around the rest of the cycle Z, and C stays attached via the new edge BC, so connectivity survives while the edge count drops. Exhibiting such (Z, A, B, C) whenever a cycle exists is the content of the two branches (clique branch / shortest-cycle branch) and the odd-degree exclusion in the other cruxes. Once no cycle remains the graph is a forest, and a forest on which no refriending is possible has max degree <= 1: a vertex of degree >= 2 in a forest has two neighbours that are non-adjacent (an edge between them would close a cycle), so a refriending would still be available.

technique: Establish that the whole graph is connected up front by a Dirac-type degree-sum bound: if any two vertices have degree-sum at least (n-1), they are adjacent or share a neighbour, so the graph is connected.
how_used: The initial graph has 2019 vertices of degree 1009 or 1010, so any two vertices have degree-sum at least 1009+1009 = 2018 = n-1; hence they are adjacent or have a common neighbour, and the graph is connected. Connectivity is the load-bearing fact that lets the later per-component / per-cycle arguments be run globally: because there is exactly ONE component, ruling out a Hamiltonian shortest cycle (via the parity crux) truly forces a vertex OFF the cycle adjacent to it — there is no separate component where the odd-degree vertex could hide, and no cycle-only component can arise. Every later 'a vertex outside Z adjacent to Z exists' step depends on this single-component setup.

technique: To forbid a Hamiltonian shortest cycle in a triangle-free graph, use a parity invariant: refriending changes only deg(A) by -2, so 'some vertex has odd degree' is preserved, while a graph equal to a single cycle is 2-regular (all even), a contradiction.
how_used: In the triangle-free branch, one needs a vertex C off the shortest cycle Z adjacent to Z; combined with connectivity (separate crux), this reduces to showing Z is not Hamiltonian. If Z (a shortest cycle) spanned all vertices, any additional edge would be a chord creating a strictly shorter cycle, contradicting minimality, so the graph would BE the cycle Z: 2-regular, every degree even. But refriending removes AB, AC and adds BC, changing only deg(A) by -2 and leaving every other vertex's parity fixed, so 'the graph has a vertex of odd degree' is an invariant; the initial graph has odd-degree vertices (the 1009 users of degree 1009... and the degree-1010 vertices are even, but the degree-1009 vertices are odd). A 2-regular graph has no odd-degree vertex, contradicting the preserved invariant. Hence Z is non-Hamiltonian, and by connectivity a vertex C off Z adjacent to Z exists, so triangle-freeness gives C not adjacent to A's cycle-neighbour B and the redirect move is formed.

technique: Recast a 'split a multiset into two equal-sum groups' target as a +/-1 signing of the terms summing to zero.
how_used: The two required angle-groups are encoded by walking the cyclic path A_1...A_{2n} and signing each of the 2n angles +1 at a left turn and -1 at a right turn; the two groups are then complementary with equal sums exactly when this signed angle sum vanishes, so the combinatorial demand becomes the single scalar condition (signed sum) = 0.

technique: Force a target value of an integer-quantized quantity by a discrete intermediate-value argument: exhibit an operation that negates it and a move that changes it by at most one quantum, then walk between the two matched endpoints.
how_used: The signed angle sum S is always a multiple of 360 degrees. Reversing the whole ordering (A_k -> A_{2n+1-k}) traverses the same closed path backwards, exchanging all left/right turns, so S(reverse) = -S. Transposing two consecutive path points reverses one central segment and reshapes its two neighbouring triangles; using anticlockwise directed angles mod 360, each of the two affected triangles shifts the directed-angle total by +/-180 degrees, so the net change to S is +/-180 +/- 180 = one quantum (+/-360) or 0 -- never a jump of 720. Along a chain of such transpositions from an ordering to its reverse, S goes from S_0 to -S_0 changing by at most one 360-quantum per step, so it must hit 0.

technique: Force a directed angular total that is a priori a multiple of a half-turn down to exactly zero by keeping the rotating direction permanently inside one open half-turn sector, so it can never wind past the forbidden boundary orientation.
how_used: Pick a line ell splitting the 2n points n/n and label so consecutive path vertices alternate sides (L={A_1,A_3,...}, R={A_2,A_4,...}); then every path edge A_iA_{i+1} crosses ell, so no edge direction equals the direction of ell. Introduce a moving line s starting as A_{2n}A_1, and pivot it about A_1 to lie along A_1A_2, then about A_2 to A_2A_3, etc., for 2n pivots, after which s returns to its starting line. At vertex A_i the pivot turns s from the direction of edge A_{i-1}A_i to that of edge A_iA_{i+1}, so its signed amount is exactly the interior angle angle A_{i-1}A_iA_{i+1} (sign = clockwise vs anticlockwise); the total directed turn Theta is the signed sum of the 2n interior angles, and since s ends on its starting line Theta is a priori a multiple of 180 degrees. Choosing each pivot's direction so s is never parallel to ell keeps s's orientation strictly inside the single open arc of R/180 obtained by deleting the ell-direction point; a direction confined to an open half-turn sector cannot accumulate a nonzero multiple of 180, forcing Theta=0. Then Theta=0 says the anticlockwise interior angles and the clockwise interior angles have equal sums -- the required two-group partition.

technique: To locate a vertex with no known outgoing edge, run a king-of-the-hill sweep: hold one current candidate, query it against each not-yet-tested vertex, and pass the candidacy to the other vertex whenever the queried edge leaves the current candidate.
how_used: Start from the first answer A->B and set candidate T=B; repeat n-2 more times, each time querying T against a fresh untested town X and promoting X to be the new T when the road runs T->X (the old T now has a known outgoing road). After n-1 total queries the surviving T has no known outgoing road, every other town has exactly one known outgoing road, and the known-direction edges form a spanning tree (in-arborescence toward T).

technique: Engineer an invariant in which every surviving candidate already carries exactly one known outgoing edge, so that a single query between two candidates is guaranteed to disqualify one of them by revealing its second outgoing edge (amortized one-query elimination).
how_used: Track S = towns not yet known to have more than one outgoing road; after the sweep (and after resolving T) every town in S has exactly one known outgoing road. Then querying any unresolved pair inside S makes the tail town's second outgoing road known, deleting it from S, so each single query shrinks S rather than costing two queries per town — this is what keeps the total linear toward the 4n bound. A genuinely good town (out-degree <=1) can never acquire a second outgoing edge, so it can never be deleted from S.

technique: Maintain that the known-edge subgraph on the candidate set stays a forest, guaranteeing there is always an untested pair whose resolution shrinks the set, so the elimination can be run down to a constant number of survivors before individual checking.
how_used: Whenever Alice queries a pair inside S the loser immediately leaves S, so no new known edge is ever added between two vertices that both remain in S; hence the known edges within S stay acyclic (a subgraph of the original tree). A forest on m>=3 vertices has fewer than C(m,2) edges, so while |S|>=3 an untested S-pair always exists and can be queried, deleting one more non-good town, down to at most 2 survivors; then finish by asking each survivor's remaining incident edges (saving a query because its tree outgoing edge is already known), giving the 4n-7 total.

technique: To bound the size of a set under a per-element cap on the number of distinct 'types' each element sees, assign each element the weight 2^{-(its type count)} and control the sum of these weights instead of the size directly.
how_used: Here each x in F sees at most k distinct scales r_F(x)<=k. Setting w(S)=sum_x 2^{-r_S(x)} and proving w(S)<=1 for all finite real sets forces |F|*2^{-k} <= sum 2^{-r_F(x)} <= 1, hence |F|<=2^k, matching the construction {0,1,...,2^k-1}.

technique: Exploit that two gaps each at least the minimal scale sum to at least the next scale up, to show only consecutive elements in sorted order can realize the minimal scale.
how_used: With d the minimal scale in S and x_1<...<x_n sorted, any i,j with j-i>1 give |x_i-x_j| >= 2^d+2^d = 2^{d+1}, so D(x_i,x_j)>d. Thus all scale-d pairs are adjacent neighbours, letting one isolate a maximal run x_i,...,x_j whose consecutive gaps all have scale d.

technique: Bound a fractional weight by splitting the configuration into two overlapping sub-configurations that share a common part and each retain only one parity class of a chosen chain, then show the weight is at most the average of the two.
how_used: Split the minimal-scale run by index parity into E (even) and O (odd), with R the rest; form S_O=R∪O and S_E=R∪E. Each x in O loses its only scale-d partners (all in E), so r_{S_O}(x)<=r_S(x)-1, giving 2^{-r_S(x)} <= (1/2)2^{-r_{S_O}(x)} (likewise for E), while R elements only drop, yielding w(S) <= (1/2)(w(S_O)+w(S_E)) <= 1 by induction.

technique: Recover an unknown string one coordinate at a time by counting, within the given set of words, how many members agree versus disagree at that position and reading off the strict majority.
how_used: For each position i, among the C(n,k) board words at Hamming distance k from u, exactly C(n-1,k) match u at position i and C(n-1,k-1) differ; when n != 2k these two binomials are unequal, so the majority value at position i equals u's i-th bit, reconstructing all of u in one guess.

technique: Exhibit a second preimage producing the identical neighbor-set by taking the bitwise complement, using that Hamming distance to the complement equals n minus the distance to the original.
how_used: When n=2k, the all-positions-flipped word u-bar has d(w,u-bar)=n-d(w,u), so a word sits at distance k=n/2 from u iff at distance k from u-bar; u and u-bar write the exact same board, so Bernhard cannot tell them apart and needs at least 2 guesses.

technique: Eliminate every remaining candidate by constructing a word inside that candidate's k-neighborhood but at distance greater than k from the true word, using the spare positions where they already agree.
how_used: For any w != u, u-bar differing from u in a positions with 0<a<=k=n/2, flip k of the n-a>=k positions where w agrees with u to build w' at distance k from w but distance a+k>k from u; w' is not on the board, so w's board differs from u's, proving only u and u-bar collide and 2 guesses always suffice.

technique: Read a mod-2 invariant off the generating operation: since a point reflection sends x to 2y-x, each coordinate is unchanged modulo 2, so the coordinatewise parity triple is preserved by every allowed move.
how_used: Reflecting one point in another gives S_y(x)=2y-x; each of the three coordinates of the image has the same parity as x regardless of the mirror point y. This colors all lattice points with 2^3=8 parity-classes that are invariant under the move, so reflections of a set never produce a point in a new parity-class.

technique: Show the target objects already exhaust every invariant class exactly once, so any one of them is unreachable from the rest under an operation that cannot change class.
how_used: The eight cube corners (0/1 in each coordinate) realize all eight parity-combinations, one per class; hence the missing eighth corner sits in a parity-class none of the other seven occupies, and since reflection preserves class it can never be produced.

technique: Neutralize an over-covered category-combination by matching each such item with a complementary single-category item, so every resulting block covers all categories an equal number of times.
how_used: Classify students by the language-subset they speak (DFS, FS, SD, DF, D-only, F-only, S-only) and count them on a Venn diagram (a FS, b SD, c DF, d DFS, with 50-t+a D-only, 50-t+b F-only, 50-t+c S-only where t=a+b+c+d). WLOG a<=b<=c, then build blocks each speaking every language equally: a triples of FS+SD+DF (each covering all three twice); then absorb the excess double-language speakers by pairing each of the leftover b-a SD-speakers with one F-only and each of the leftover c-a DF-speakers with one S-only (each pair covers all three once); the d DFS students each stand alone (each covers all three once); and the remaining single-language speakers, which after the pairings are equal in number (all = 50-d-b-c), split into D+F+S triples (each covers all three once). The complementary counts of single-language speakers exactly absorb the excess double-language speakers, so every block covers the three languages equally (all twice, or all once).

technique: Once every unit is identical across all coordinates, assemble them into equal-size targets by greedy largest-first packing, collapsing the multi-coordinate balancing to a single count.
how_used: After crux 0, each block speaks all three languages either twice (the a double-blocks) or once (the 50-2a single-blocks, an even number), and each language is spoken 50 times total. Fill groups to a per-language count of 10 by first merging the twice-blocks until near 10 and then topping up with once-blocks; since every block contributes equally to all three languages, reaching 10 in one language reaches 10 in all, and size-1 (once) blocks let each bin hit the target exactly, yielding exactly 5 groups of (10,10,10).

technique: Encode each non-tree edge of a spanning forest by its unique fundamental cycle and record which tree edges that cycle uses
how_used: A spanning forest F (union of spanning trees of components) has |A| <= v-1 edges, leaving |B| >= (1+eps)v-(v-1) = eps*v+1 extra edges; adjoining each b in B to F closes one simple cycle C_b, and S_b is the set of tree edges of F lying on C_b, turning the extra edges into cycles whose tree-edge supports can be counted.

technique: When a family of quantities is forced to take distinct values, lower-bound their sum by the smallest possible distinct integers (a triangular number), then average over the ground set to find a heavily-covered element
how_used: Since all cycles have distinct lengths the sizes |S_b| are distinct, so sum over b in B of |S_b| >= 2+3+...+(|B|+1) > |B|^2/2 > eps^2 v^2/2; dividing this among the <= v tree edges of A forces some single tree edge a to lie in more than eps^2 v/2 of the fundamental cycles, giving a set B' of that many extra edges whose cycles all pass through a.

technique: From two distinct cycles sharing a common path build a theta-graph and extract a third cycle through both private edges, giving an injective map from unordered pairs to new cycles
how_used: For b1,b2 in B', the cycles C_b1 and C_b2 share exactly the tree path through a, so their union is a theta-graph containing a third simple cycle through both b1 and b2; since that third cycle meets B' only in {b1,b2}, the map {b1,b2} -> C_{b1,b2} is injective, producing at least C(|B'|,2) > C(eps^2 v/2, 2) distinct cycles, which exceeds the upper bound of v cycles (one per length class) once v is large, giving the contradiction.

technique: To realize a product of two linear-extension counts, take the disjoint union of the two posets and add to every element of one the constraint that it come after every element of the other, so each good order splits uniquely into (whole first block)(whole second block) and the counts multiply.
how_used: Realizability is shown multiplicative: n1 by k1 singers and n2 by k2 singers give n1*n2 by k1+k2 singers (each B-singer must perform later than all A-singers). This reduces '2010 by 20 singers' to factoring 2010=6*5*67 and realizing the factors with 3+4+13=20 singers separately.

technique: Engineer a prescribed count of linear extensions by fixing a rigid backbone chain (a total order forced by wishes) so the only freedom is where a few 'free' elements slot into the chain's gaps; count these placements as an independent product, then correct the gaps where two free elements can co-occupy (giving 2 orders instead of 1).
how_used: For 67 with 13 singers: chain a1..a11 is forced; x may precede any of a1..a9 (9 slots), y may follow any of a5..a11 (7 slots) giving 9*7=63; but when x and y land between the same pair (a_i,a_{i+1}) for i=5..8, their mutual order doubles that case, adding 4, for 63+4=67. Similarly 30 is hit via 5*6 sequential insertions of x,y into a fixed a1..a4 chain.

technique: Fix a few coordinates across an entire product family to forbid every target configuration, sizing the family by the free-coordinate count
how_used: For the lower bound M>2^{N-2}: take all 2^{N-2} flags with 1st square yellow and 2nd square blue. Any N of them placed on the diagonal put some flag in row 1 (diagonal entry yellow) and some in row 2 (diagonal entry blue), so no diagonal is monochrome; this family of size 2^{N-2} has no diverse subset, forcing M>=2^{N-2}+1.

technique: Recast a 'pick one object per slot, all of one color' feasibility task as a saturating matching in a bipartite graph and read the obstruction off Hall's condition
how_used: Upper bound via matchings: with columns V and flags V', put edge (c,f) in G_y iff column c of flag f is yellow, in G_b otherwise. A monochrome-yellow (resp blue) diagonal is a V-saturating matching in G_y (resp G_b). Assuming no diverse set means neither saturates V, so Hall gives deficient column-sets S_y, S_b with |E_y(S_y)|<=|S_y|-1 and |E_b(S_b)|<=|S_b|-1.

technique: Bound the objects avoiding both deficient sets by their free-coordinate count and clash it against the population size
how_used: Disjoint case S_y ∩ S_b = ∅: flags in V'\(E_y(S_y)∪E_b(S_b)) are blue on all of S_y and yellow on all of S_b, fixing y+b coordinates (disjoint, so no clash), so their count is <=2^{N-y-b}. But that count is >=|V'|-|E_y(S_y)|-|E_b(S_b)|>=2^{N-2}+1-(y-1)-(b-1). With c=y+b this gives 2^{N-c}+c>2^{N-2}+2, impossible for N>=c>=2.

technique: When a coordinate lies in both deficient sets, use that every object is one-or-other color there to force the two neighborhoods to cover the whole population
how_used: Overlapping case S_y ∩ S_b ≠ ∅: pick a shared column c; every flag is yellow or blue at c, so it lies in E_y(S_y) or E_b(S_b), giving E_y(S_y) ∪ E_b(S_b)=V'. Then 2^{N-2}+1=|V'|<=|E_y(S_y)|+|E_b(S_b)|<=|S_y|+|S_b|-2<=2N-4 (using S_y,S_b != V, so each has size <=N-1, valid since N<=2^{N-2}+1), impossible for N>=4.

technique: Peel a chosen non-constant coordinate, pigeonhole its majority color to keep enough sub-objects for the induction hypothesis, then re-insert one element whose peeled coordinate matches the sub-object's realized diagonal color
how_used: Inductive step (N>4) of M_N<=2^{N-2}+1. Given 2^{N-2}+1 distinct flags: some column is non-monochrome (else all flags identical); relabel it column 1, so both colors occur there. Pigeonhole gives a majority color, say blue, with >=ceil((2^{N-2}+1)/2)=2^{N-3}+1>=M_{N-1} 'good' (blue-in-col-1) flags. Strip column 1 (good flags stay distinct on cols 2..N since they agreed in col 1), apply IH to get a monochrome-diagonal (N-1)-square Q on cols 2..N using N-1 good flags. Top Q with a row-1 flag matching Q's diagonal color: if Q blue-diagonal, use one of the >=2^{N-3}+1-(N-1)>0 leftover good flags (this surplus is positive only for N>4, which is why the base case is handled separately); if Q yellow-diagonal, use a yellow-in-col-1 flag, which exists because col 1 was chosen non-monochrome and is unused in Q.

technique: Establish the induction's base case by splitting each object over a small alphabet and settling it with a counting bound plus manual pairing facts about the pieces
how_used: Base case N=4 of M_N<=2^{N-2}+1: among any 5 distinct length-4 flags, find a diverse 4-set. Write each flag as LR with L,R in S={BB,BY,YB,YY}. Manual facts: (i) each A in S has exactly one C in S that cannot pair with it into a monochrome-diagonal 2x2; (ii) any three distinct elements of S contain a pair forming a yellow-diagonal 2x2 and a pair forming a blue-diagonal 2x2. From 5<=(#distinct L)(#distinct R) one factor is >=3, say r>=3, and two flags share a right part R1 (L1R1,L2R1). Using (i) one of (L',L1),(L',L2) forms a monochrome 2x2 (say blue), giving the top-left block; using (ii) two of three flags with distinct right parts form a blue-diagonal 2x2, giving the bottom-right block. Stack the two blue 2x2 squares on the diagonal of a 4x4 square to get four diverse flags. This distinct argument replaces the peel/pigeonhole induction because its surplus count vanishes at N=4.

technique: Prove a threshold's lower bound by exhibiting an explicit family with two coordinates fixed to opposite values so the target monochrome configuration is structurally impossible
how_used: Lower bound M_N>2^{N-2}: take all 2^{N-2} flags whose first square is yellow and second square is blue. In any N x N square arranged from these flags, some diagonal cell lies in column 1 (value yellow) and some in column 2 (value blue), so the diagonal is never monochrome; hence no diverse N-set exists among these 2^{N-2} flags. Combined with the upper bound M_N<=2^{N-2}+1 this pins the answer M=2^{N-2}+1.

technique: Tile the board into equal blocks whose count matches the object total, so a local exclusion caps each block at one and the global count forces exactly one per block.
how_used: Partition the 100x100 board into 2500 disjoint 2x2 blocks; non-attacking forces at most one king per block, and there are exactly 2500 kings, so pigeonhole makes every block hold exactly one king, reducing the problem to a 50x50 grid of blocks.

technique: Label each cell by the position of its object within its block, then use the adjacency-exclusion to force that binary label to propagate in a fixed direction, so it is constant along each whole line.
how_used: Tag each block T/B by whether its king is in the top/bottom half and L/R for left/right. Non-attack forces: a B-block at (i,j) makes (i+1,j) a B-block (and analogues), so a single B-block in the first row makes its whole column a B-column; counting (25 per row/column) then yields exactly 25 T-columns, 25 B-columns, 25 L-rows, 25 R-rows.

technique: At the interface of two oppositely-oriented regions, use the diagonal-neighbor exclusion to force the transverse label to be monotone across the whole strip, pinning the configuration.
how_used: Between an adjacent T-column j and B-column j+1, a BL-block at (i,j+1) forbids (i+1,j) from being a TR-block, forcing it TL, so the L-rows propagate downward; with exactly 25 L-rows this fixes rows 1-25 as R and 26-50 as L, and the same argument on columns then leaves only two total arrangements.

technique: Build a reusable growth gadget by alternating a coin-multiplying move with a position-resetting move so a linear count becomes exponential inside a fixed window of stacks.
how_used: Lemma 1: to realize (a,0,0)->(0,2^a,0), the atomic gadget is (x,m,0)->(x-1,2m,0): empty the middle stack via Move 1 (each coin becomes two in the next stack) giving (x,0,2m), then Move 2 on the first stack swaps the empty middle with the doubled pile back into position, giving (x-1,2m,0). Chaining the gadget inducts (a,0,0)->(a-k,2^k,0) up to k=a.

technique: Escalate an exponential-growth gadget to an iterated-exponential (tower) by recursively feeding its output back as the input of the same gadget one stack over.
how_used: Lemma 2: define the power tower P_n and prove (a,0,0,0)->(0,P_a,0,0) by inducting (a,0,0,0)->(a-k,P_k,0,0), where each step applies Lemma 1 to the sub-block (S2,S3,S4) to turn P_k into 2^{P_k}=P_{k+1}, then a Move-1 shift on the first stack. Applying it twice from (0,3,0,0,0,0) reaches P_{16} coins, vastly exceeding A=2010^{2010^{2010}}.

technique: Hit an exact large target reachable only by monotone growth: overshoot it enormously, then use an available decrementing move to walk the count back down to the precise required value.
how_used: After reaching (0,0,0,P_16,0,0) with P_16 >> A, apply Move 2 to stack S_4 repeatedly (each removes one coin while harmlessly swapping the empty S_5,S_6) until S_4 holds exactly A/4, then double twice via Move 1 into (0,0,0,0,0,A).

technique: Count an induced subconfiguration by summing over each vertex the number of subsets in which that vertex plays a fixed distinguished role, giving a binomial-coefficient sum.
how_used: A player i is the unique local champion of a k-company iff the other k-1 members are drawn from the w_i players he beat, so he heads C(w_i,k-1) of them; total local champions over all k-companies is Sum_i C(w_i,k-1), and symmetrically total local losers is Sum_i C(l_i,k-1).

technique: Turn the forbidden induced pattern into a per-subset inequality between two double-counts, then sum over all subsets to get a global inequality.
how_used: 'No bad 4-company' means any 4-company having a local loser must also have a local champion, so within each 4-company (#local losers) <= (#local champions); summing over all 4-companies gives Sum_i C(w_i,3) >= Sum_i C(l_i,3).

technique: Express the target power as an integer linear combination of lower binomial-coefficient differences plus a linear term, exploiting a fixed sum of the two variables to absorb the degree.
how_used: Using w_i+l_i=n-1, write (x-y)^3 = 24(C(x,3)-C(y,3)) + 24(C(x,2)-C(y,2)) - (3(n-1)^2-4)(x-y); summing, the C(.,3) term is >=0 (from the 4-company bound), the C(.,2) term is 0 (3-companies balance), and the linear term is 0 (total wins = total losses).

technique: Replace a single fragile survival inequality by a DISJUNCTIVE invariant whose second clause carries a reserve buffer, chosen so the exact transition where the plain inequality fails is caught by the other clause.
how_used: Invariant maintained at every stage: there exist a u-b-string and v-w-string with either (i) u>v>=1, OR (ii) 2<=u<=v<2u together with k-1 further strings all longer than v/2. Both clauses force u>1, so a (>=2)-black string survives to the terminal stage, which is the claim. Base case: b>w gives clause (i). Clause (ii)'s k-1 reserve is exactly the buffer that survives a halving step where the longest black and white lengths cross; a single-clause invariant breaks precisely there.

technique: In the phase where every string is cut each step, track both color classes as balanced binary halvings and propagate an initial strict length gap through matched ceiling/floor halving of the extremes.
how_used: This is the key lemma of the ALTERNATE (powers-of-two) solution, independent of the disjunctive-invariant solution. For i<=min(s,t) every (>1)-string is cut, so A_i has exactly 2^i black and 2^i white strings. Longest evolves by ceiling: B_i=ceil(B_{i-1}/2); shortest by floor: b_i=floor(b_{i-1}/2). Monotonicity of ceil and floor and B_0=b>w=W_0 give B_i>=W_i and b_i>=w_i for all i in range, so black dominates white at both extremes throughout the saturated phase. Used in Case 1 (s<=t): if s=f the chain 2=B>=W>=b>=w>1 collapses to all-2s giving b=2^s=w, contradicting b!=w; hence s<f, so the s-th step cuts every string and a 1-b-string forces a simultaneous 1-w-string.

technique: In a length-ordered greedy process, split the inductive step on whether the SHORTER paired string is cut, using the order rule that any string at least as long as a cut string is also cut.
how_used: The cut rule takes the k longest strings, so if a string of length L is cut, every (>=L)-string is cut. In clause (ii) we have u<=v (black shorter than the paired white). Three subcases: (2c) if a u-b-string is cut then all (>=u)-strings are cut, so the v-w-string is cut too and both halve to ceil(u/2),floor(v/2); (2b) if no v-w-string is cut then (since u<=v) no u-b-string is cut either and every cut string exceeds v, refreshing the (>v/2) reserve; (2a) the mixed case where the white is cut but the black is not gives floor(v/2)<u restoring clause (i). The reserve set S of k-1 strings is transported by keeping, for each s in S, its larger half (if cut) or s itself (if not), all staying >v/2>=v'. The u'=1 collapse is excluded because it would force cutting a u-b, a v-w, and all k-1 of S simultaneously, i.e. k+1 strings, exceeding the k-cut budget.

technique: Track paired extremal quantities of two symmetric sub-populations under a length-halving process and prove by induction that an initial strict dominance between them is preserved by the monotone ceil/floor split map.

When a per-step cut budget of k caps how many strings can shrink, lower-bound the surviving count of one class, pigeonhole an unshrunk member, and force it to a terminal value via the process's ordering rule.
Encode a modular structure as a grid by writing each residue's mixed-radix / base-p digit expansion as coordinates, so a divisibility-defined family becomes an axis-aligned coordinate slice.
how_used: Via CRT each m in {0,...,n-1} is split into residues mod p_i^{alpha_i}, then each residue is written in base p_i; the digit tuple r(m) places m in a p_1^{alpha_1}...p_k^{alpha_k} grid (alpha_i axes of size p_i for prime p_i). r is a bijection {0,...,n-1} -> N. A progression P_j with step d_j = prod p_i^{gamma_i} becomes exactly the subgrid fixing the low gamma_i base-p_i digits of each block i, turning membership 'q'-q divisible by p_i^{gamma_i}' into equality of those fixed coordinates. Condition (i) becomes 'subgrids cover N', condition (ii) becomes 'each subgrid has a private point', and for each axis some subgrid fixes it (since p_i^{alpha_i} | d_{j(i)}); the target 1+sum alpha_i(p_i-1) = 1+sum(size-1 over axes).

technique: To force an uncovered point when a product grid is covered by axis-fixing subgrids, run a maximum-deficiency (defect Hall) argument: peel off the largest subgrid-set whose neighborhood is deficient, apply Hall to the remainder to match each surviving subgrid injectively to a distinct axis it fixes, then build the miss coordinate-by-coordinate.
how_used: Solution 1's Lemma. Grid N = prod_i [0,n_i-1]; a subgrid L fixes a nonempty index set I of axes ("orthogonal to axis i" iff i in I). Assume for contradiction s <= sum_i(n_i-1). Bipartite graph: left = the s subgrids, right = slots v_{ij}, n_i-1 per axis i; edge (L,v_{ij}) iff L fixes axis i. Take W = a maximum-size subgrid-set with |W|>|f(W)| (empty if none); by (iii) f(V)=V', and |V'|>=|V| forces W a proper subset. On U=V\W, U'=V'\f(W), maximality of W gives Hall's condition |f(X) cap U'|>=|X| for all X in U, so each L in U is matched to a distinct axis g(L) it fixes; since only n_i-1 slots exist per axis, at most n_i-1 U-subgrids fix each axis i (for i in the U'-axes), leaving a free value a_i on each. Pick b not covered by any W-subgrid (W proper); then (a_1,...,a_ell,b_{ell+1},...,b_k) misses every U-subgrid (wrong fixed coordinate) and every W-subgrid (else, differing from b only in the first ell coords, it would fix a first-ell axis, contradicting f(W)'s axes). Contradiction gives s >= 1 + sum(n_i-1).

technique: Prove a covering-count lower bound by minimal-counterexample descent that divides one prime out of a composite step, splitting the covering into two sub-coverings of strictly smaller period whose separate bounds are then recombined by the identity x = (x-y)_+ + min(x,y).
how_used: Solution 2. Prove the strengthened Claim: for I subset [k] and beta_i<=alpha_i, |T| >= 1 + sum_{i in I} beta_i(p_i-1) where T = {j : p_i^{alpha_i-beta_i+1} | d_j for some i in I}. Base case (all d_j prime) via CRT: if <p_i APs of step p_i for every i, an uncovered residue exists. For the descent, take a counterexample minimizing n then sum of steps; some d_1 is composite, p_1|d_1, d_1'=d_1/p_1>1, enlarge P_1 to P_1' of step d_1'. Two derived coverings: (P') a minimal subcovering of {P_1',P_2,...} with period n' = n/(prime powers removed), exponents sigma_i; (Q) the traces R_i = P_i cap P_1' rescaled by 1/d_1', period n''<n. Minimality applies the Claim to each: from P' with I'={i: beta_i>sigma_i}, exponents beta_i-sigma_i, get |T cap [s']| >= 1 + sum (beta_i-sigma_i)_+(p_i-1); from Q with I''={i: sigma_i>0}, exponents min(beta_i,sigma_i), get G indices in T cap {s'+1,...,s}. Private numbers h_j survive the split (if P_j dropped from P', then h_j in P_1', forcing Q_j into Q), so the two counts live on disjoint index ranges. Recombine with (beta_i-sigma_i)_+ + min(beta_i,sigma_i) = beta_i to get |T| >= 1 + sum beta_i(p_i-1), contradiction.

technique: To count arithmetic progressions in a covering of Z whose steps have lcm n, encode residues mod n as points of a product grid via CRT plus base-p digit expansion, turning each progression into an axis-fixing subgrid so the AP problem becomes a grid-covering problem.
how_used: Solution 1's reduction to the Lemma. With n = prod p_i^{alpha_i}, encode 0<=m<n by its CRT residues m_i mod p_i^{alpha_i}, then by the base-p_i digits of each m_i, giving r(m) in the grid N with alpha_i axes of side p_i per prime i (total size n); r is a bijection Z/n -> N. A progression P_j of step d_j = prod p_i^{gamma_i} is the coset of residues congruent to a fixed value mod d_j, which is exactly fixing the low-order digits t<=gamma_i of each prime-block to specific values while high digits range freely; hence r(P_j)=L_j is a subgrid (product of pinned singletons on the fixed low axes with the full range on free axes). Covering (i) => union L_j = N; private element (ii) => (ii') each L_j has a private point; and since n=lcm of steps, for each prime i some j(i) has p_i^{alpha_i} | d_{j(i)}, so L_{j(i)} fixes ALL alpha_i axes of prime i, giving hypothesis (iii) that every axis is fixed by some subgrid. The reduction converts the target s >= 1 + sum alpha_i(p_i-1) into the same bound for the grid Lemma. The one nontrivial insight: an AP is a coset, and coset-membership mod p_i^{gamma_i} coincides exactly with agreement on the low-order base-p_i digits, so residue structure maps onto grid structure under the bijection r.

technique: To turn a covering of the integers by arithmetic progressions whose steps divide n into a covering of a finite product grid by coordinate-fixing subgrids, encode each residue mod n by its CRT components and then the base-p digits of each prime-power component, one grid axis per digit.
how_used: The reduction that converts the AP problem into the grid Lemma. Write n = prod p_i^{alpha_i}. Map m in {0,...,n-1} to r(m) = (r_{11},...,r_{1 alpha_1}, r_{21},...,r_{k alpha_k}), where m_i = m mod p_i^{alpha_i} and r_{i1},...,r_{i alpha_i} are its base-p_i digits; this lands in the grid N = prod_i (p_i x ... x p_i, alpha_i times), and r is a bijection {0,...,n-1} -> N because r(m)=r(m') forces p_i^{alpha_i} | m-m' for all i, hence n | m-m'. An AP P_j with step d_j = prod p_i^{gamma_i} becomes the subgrid L_j fixing exactly the first gamma_i digit-coordinates on each block i (q' in P_j iff p_i^{gamma_i} | q-q' iff r_{i,t}=r'_{i,t} for all t<=gamma_i), so L_j is orthogonal to those digit-axes. Since n = lcm of the steps, for each i some d_{j(i)} is divisible by p_i^{alpha_i}, so L_{j(i)} fixes all alpha_i digit-axes of block i — giving Lemma condition (iii) that every axis has an orthogonal subgrid. Condition (ii) (each AP has a private integer) transfers to (ii') (each subgrid has a private point), and the target 1 + sum alpha_i(p_i-1) is exactly 1 + sum_axes (n_axis - 1) with n_axis = p_i. The nonobvious part is choosing base-p DIGITS as separate axes (not the residues themselves), which is what makes each factor p_i^{alpha_i} contribute alpha_i axes each of size p_i.

technique: When a covering lower bound needs each object assigned to a distinct slot but the full assignment graph may violate Hall's condition, take a maximal deficient vertex set, delete it with its neighborhood, and apply Hall's theorem to the induced subgraph on the complement, where maximality restores the marriage condition.
how_used: The core of the grid Lemma: covering N by subgrids L_1,...,L_s with (ii') private points and (iii) every axis fixed by some subgrid forces s >= 1 + sum_i (n_i - 1). Suppose not: s <= sum_i (n_i-1). Build bipartite G with left V = {L_1,...,L_s} and right V' = {v_{ij}: 1<=j<=n_i-1} (n_i-1 slots per axis i), edge (L_m, v_{ij}) iff L_m is orthogonal to (fixes) axis i. Condition (iii) gives f(V)=V'. Let W be the LARGEST set with |W|>|f(W)| (empty if none); since |V'|=|f(V)|>=|V|, W != V, so U=V\W is nonempty. Set U'=V'\f(W). Maximality of W is exactly what makes the induced graph on U u U' satisfy Hall: if some X<=U had |f(X) cap U'|<|X| then W u X would be a larger deficient set. Hall then injectively assigns each L in U a distinct slot v_{ij}; since axis i has only n_i-1 slots, at most n_i-1 subgrids of U fix axis i. The single load-bearing move is applying Hall not to the whole graph but to the deficiency-complement subgraph, using the maximal-defect set to guarantee the marriage condition there.

technique: Given a partial injective assignment of covers to axis-slots, construct an uncovered point by picking, on each assigned axis, a coordinate value avoided by the few covers routed to it, and inheriting the remaining coordinates from a point already free of the deleted deficient block.
how_used: The finish of the grid Lemma, consuming the Hall assignment g from the companion crux. After deleting the maximal deficient set W (with f(W)=W'), permute axes so U' = {v_{ij}: i<=ell} and W' = {v_{ij}: i>ell}. Because W != V, pick a base point b=(b_1,...,b_k) in N not covered by any subgrid in W. For each axis i<=ell, the at most n_i-1 subgrids L in U with g(L)=i each fix that axis to some value c_L; since only n_i-1 values are used out of n_i, choose a_i in [0,n_i-1] with a_i != c_L for all such L. Set a=(a_1,...,a_ell, b_{ell+1},...,b_k). Then a escapes every L in U: a's g(L)-th coordinate a_{g(L)} differs from c_L. And a escapes every L in W: a and b differ only in the first ell coordinates, so if a were in L then L would fix one of the first ell axes, putting an edge from L in W into U' -- contradicting that W's neighborhood is W' (disjoint from U'). So a is uncovered, contradicting the covering. The delicate point: b need only dodge the W-subgrids (from W != V), and the a/b split works precisely because W's edges avoid the first ell axes.

technique: Bound a swap process by counting a configuration-specific set of tuples that each move destroys at a color-dependent rate, then divide the initial count by the smallest per-move drop.
how_used: Define a 'feisty triplet': an unordered rock-paper-scissors triple with the paper duck sitting between the rock and scissors on the arc and facing the rock. A paper-rock swap kills c triplets (one per scissors), a rock-scissors swap kills b, a scissors-paper swap kills a, and no move increases the count; so every move removes at least min(a,b,c). Since the count starts at most abc and stays nonnegative, the number of moves is at most abc/min(a,b,c) = max(ab,bc,ca).

technique: Attain the extremal bound by grouping each type into one contiguous block and letting an entire block filter through an adjacent block.
how_used: Assuming WLOG a = min(a,b,c) (only cyclic, not full, symmetry is allowed, so max(ab,bc,ca)=bc), place the a rocks, b papers, c scissors as three contiguous arcs in clockwise order; hold the rocks fixed and let each of the c scissors ducks filter through all b paper ducks, producing bc = max(ab,bc,ca) swaps, after which no move remains.

technique: Find an element to induct on by locating a maximal boundary object whose associated count has the required parity
how_used: Locate a pivotal point p in the stable set S that is MAXIMAL in S (no larger point of S, i.e. p+(1,0), p+(0,1), p+(1,1) all not in S) AND has the capped rectangle R(p)={q<=p} of EVEN size. Existence is forced by inspecting the top row (max y): if it has length >=2 one of its two rightmost points works (their R-sizes are consecutive multiples of the row's height, so one is even); if length 1, the top point or the one directly below it works (R-sizes differ by 1, so one is even). Maximality comes automatically from choosing the top-row-rightmost / topmost point.

technique: Split the structure at the chosen pivot so that objects using it decompose as an independent product of two sub-structures
how_used: For stable subsets that CONTAIN p, use the partition S = R(p) ⊔ S1 ⊔ S2, where S1 = points of S strictly above p in its column-region and S2 = points of S strictly to the right. Because p+(1,1) is not in S, no point of S2 sits above row of p and no point of S1 sits right of p's column, so once R(p) is forced in (stability), membership in the S1-region and the S2-region are independent stable-subset choices. Hence the count of such subsets factors as (stable subsets of S1) × (stable subsets of S2).

technique: Prove a parity-count inequality by factoring the even-minus-odd difference into a product of the two sub-part differences
how_used: With |R(p)| even, subsets containing p are even in E1E2+O1O2 ways and odd in E1O2+E2O1 ways (Ei,Oi = even/odd stable-subset counts of Si); the difference telescopes to (E1-O1)(E2-O2), which is >=0 since each sub-region satisfies Ei>=Oi by the inductive hypothesis. This gives even>=odd among subsets containing p; the complementary subsets NOT containing p are exactly the stable subsets of the smaller stable set S\{p} (p maximal), handled by the same inductive hypothesis, completing f(S)>=0.

technique: Bound the vertices adjacent to a fixed clique by pinning each such vertex to finitely many rigid geometric loci, then intersect those loci against the mobility constraint of the clique's own vertices
how_used: A firefly e friending three of the K4 {a,b,c,d}, say a,b,c, must sit at one of the two apexes E1,E2 of a fixed-shape tetrahedron over triangle ABC (intersection of three spheres = two points). Requiring each of a,b,c,d to itself be able to move forces (via the coplanarity lemma) E1,E2 onto specific loci: E1 on line CD, E2 in plane ABD (E1 = line CD meeting the reflection of plane ABD in plane ABC; E2 symmetric). This uniquely fixes {E1,E2} per WLOG choice, capping the count of such e at 12, which yields the '2n+O(1)' edge bound when the clique is removed.

technique: Set up an extremal-count recurrence by peeling a fixed-size substructure and iterate it to a closed-form bound compared against the conjectured optimum
how_used: Let g(n) be the max friendships. If the extremal graph contains a K4, peel {a,b,c,d}: the previous crux caps its incident edges at 2n+10, giving g(n) <= max{f(n), (2n+10)+g(n-4)} with f(n)=floor(n^2/3). Iterating in steps of 4 down to a base ~24 sums the arithmetic series to (n/4-5)(n+37)+C(24,2), which is < f(n) for n>=70, forcing g(n)=floor(n^2/3); at n=10^7 this is floor(10^14/3).

technique: Realize an extremal graph geometrically by placing vertices on parallel lines and using reflection through the plane of the other lines as the allowed distance-preserving motion
how_used: Distribute n fireflies as evenly as possible among three pairwise-parallel lines forming an equilateral triangular prism; friends iff on different lines (complete tripartite, floor(n^2/3) edges). Every friendship of a line-L firefly goes to the other two lines, whose plane the reflection through it fixes pointwise, so all friend distances are preserved; reflecting each line in turn carries every firefly arbitrarily far, witnessing the construction attains floor(n^2/3).

technique: When a point must keep fixed distances to a fixed set of anchor points, its only distinct alternative position is the mirror image across the affine hull of those anchors; so it can move at all iff the anchors span a proper flat, and every move is a reflection fixing that flat.
how_used: A firefly's admissible new positions are the common intersection of spheres centered at its friends. In R^3, once a firefly has friends that affinely span R^3, that intersection is a single point (itself) and it is frozen; a genuinely distinct second position exists iff all of its friends are coplanar, and the move is exactly the reflection of the firefly across that plane. This converts the hypothesis 'this firefly moves' into the static fact 'at that instant all of its friends are coplanar', and makes every displacement a plane-fixing reflection — the premise the downstream plane-membership arguments consume.

technique: To build the extremal graph under a rigid-motion mobility constraint, place vertices on a few parallel affine flats and join two iff they lie on different flats, so an entire flat can be displaced at once by reflecting it in the flat spanned by the others (which fixes every one of its neighbors).
how_used: Do NOT default to the tempting two-parallel-planes guess (friends iff on different planes) — it gives only ~n^2/4 and is a known trap, not optimal in R^3. Use THREE pairwise-parallel lines l_A,l_B,l_C forming an infinite triangular prism (mutual spacing > 1, so no three points coplanar). Split the n fireflies as evenly as possible among the three lines and declare two friends iff they lie on different lines, giving floor(n^2/3) friendships (balanced split maximizes n1*n2+n1*n3+n2*n3). Mobility: every firefly on l_A has all its friends on l_B U l_C, which span the plane P_BC; reflecting l_A across P_BC is a rigid motion fixing all those friends, so the whole line moves at once (realized as single-firefly hops). Reflect each of the three lines in the plane of the other two to translate the prism arbitrarily far, so all fireflies escape. This is the tight lower bound the counting argument must match.

technique: To upper-bound edges under a rigid geometric constraint, fix a densest forbidden core, bound how many outside vertices can attach to enough of it to be pinned, delete the core, and recurse into a self-improving inequality whose iterate falls below the construction's value.
how_used: Let g(n) be the max friendships given four pairwise friends a,b,c,d exist; if none exist you are in the no-K4 regime already bounded by f(n)=floor(n^2/3). Note a firefly can move only if all its friends are coplanar at that instant. First prove no four pairwise friends are coplanar (a coplanar K4 freezes its own vertices). Then the key pinning claim: at most 12 fireflies e are friends with >=3 of a,b,c,d — such an e sits at one of two reflection-image points E1,E2 of the tetrahedron across a face, and requiring each of a,b,c,d to still have coplanar friends at its own move instant forces E1,E2 onto specific lines/planes of ABCD, and only one of each pair may be occupied. So edges meeting {a,b,c,d} number at most 6 internal + (2n+4) external, giving g(n) <= 6+(2n+4)+max{f(n-4),g(n-4)} = max{f(n),(2n+10)+g(n-4)}. Iterating the second branch down to a base case below 24 yields (r+1)(2n-4r+10)+g(n-4r-4) <= (n/4-5)(n+37)+C(24,2), which is < f(n) for n>=70; hence g(n)<=f(n) and floor(n^2/3) is optimal. For n=10^7 the answer is (10^14 - 1)/3 = floor(10^14/3).

technique: Recast an object carrying a distinctness constraint on labeled pairs as a maximal matching in a labeled complete graph, after using a self-inverse symmetry to restrict to the involution case.
how_used: Permutations with distinct ratios x_k/k: sigma -> sigma^{-1} is an involution on the valid set (the ratio multiset inverts, distinctness preserved), so a_n mod 2 equals the count of valid involutions, i.e. permutations with all cycles of length <=2. Such an involution is a matching on {1..n}; a fixed point gives ratio 1 so at most one is allowed, forcing the matching to be maximal (perfect if n even, one unmatched vertex if n odd). An edge {i,j} with i<j gives ratios i/j and j/i, so all ratios distinct reduces exactly to: the labels i/j on the edges of K_n (edge {i,j}, i<j, labeled i/j) are pairwise distinct. Call such a maximal matching 'fantastic'; then a_n mod 2 = number of fantastic maximal matchings.

technique: Deduce the parity of a count of degree-0 (special) vertices from the handshake lemma, using that the total vertex count has known parity and all non-special vertices have odd degree.
how_used: In the graph Gamma on all maximal matchings (adjacency = neighbor relation, self-loops excluded), fantastic matchings are exactly the isolated vertices (neighbor count 1, degree 0) and every other vertex has odd degree (neighbor count odd minus itself). The handshake lemma gives an even number of odd-degree vertices, so the number of non-fantastic matchings is even. The total number of maximal matchings is (2*ceil(n/2)-1)!!, a product of odd numbers hence odd. Therefore #fantastic = total - #non-fantastic = odd - even = odd, so a_n is odd.

technique: To count a set modulo 2, pair each element with an order-2 involution that preserves the property being counted; the count reduces mod 2 to the number of fixed points of the involution.
