how_used: Sending a permutation x to its inverse x^{-1} is an involution on all permutations, and it preserves 'all ratios x_k/k distinct' because x(k)=j gives x^{-1}(j)=k with ratio k/j = (x_k/k)^{-1}, and reciprocation is a bijection on the positive reals, so no two ratios of x^{-1} coincide unless the corresponding ratios of x did. Non-involutions pair off in twos, so a_n is congruent mod 2 to the number of VALID INVOLUTIONS. A valid involution has only 1- and 2-cycles and at most one fixed point (two fixed points would both give ratio 1), so it is exactly a maximal matching of {1,...,n} (perfect if n even, one vertex unmatched if n odd) with all edge labels distinct, where edge {i,j} (i<j) is labeled i/j -- a matching is 'fantastic' iff its labels are pairwise distinct, and one checks the label-distinctness condition on {i/j} is equivalent to distinctness of the full ratio multiset. This identifies the ambient set V as ALL maximal matchings of K_n, and |V| = (2*ceil(n/2)-1)!! (a product of consecutive odd numbers) is ODD; combined with a later parity comparison of fantastic matchings against |V|, this forces a_n odd.

technique: Define a local order-2 swap move on a configuration built from a coincidence of two labeled objects, so that repeated labels are exactly what makes a move available; this makes the no-repeat configurations the ones with no available move.
how_used: On the labeled K_n (edge {a,b}, a<b, labeled a/b), the coincidence exploited is two DISTINCT edges ab, cd (a<b, c<d) carrying the SAME label a/b = c/d. When this happens, replace those two edges by ac and bd: since a/b=c/d gives ad=bc, hence a/c=b/d, the two new edges ac, bd are again a legal pair (they share the common label a/c, though NOTE this new label a/c is generally NOT equal to the old label a/b, so the switch does not preserve the label multiset -- it only maps one legal matching to another). This move is its own reverse, so 'M' is switchable to 'M-prime' is a reflexive, symmetric relation on maximal matchings. A fantastic matching (all labels distinct) admits NO same-label pair, so it is isolated under this relation; every non-fantastic matching admits at least one move. This is the local operation whose availability/count later detects, via parity, exactly the fantastic matchings.

technique: Count the closed neighborhood of a configuration as a product over independent local classes, reduce each factor mod 2 to a power of two, so the total is odd exactly at the no-repeat configurations; then apply the handshake lemma to equate the odd-count with the ambient parity.
how_used: A neighbor of matching M is obtained by choosing, INDEPENDENTLY for each label ell, some disjoint pairs among the n_ell edges labeled ell and switching each pair; independence holds because every original edge belongs to exactly one label class, so choices in different classes act on disjoint edge sets and never interfere (this is why the count factors -- NOT because the switch preserves labels). Hence the closed-neighbor count of M is the product over ell of (number of ways to switch within class ell) = product over ell of sum_k C(n_ell, 2k)(2k-1)!!. Mod 2, (2k-1)!! is odd, so each factor is congruent to sum_k C(n_ell, 2k) = 2^{n_ell-1}, which is odd iff n_ell = 1. Therefore the closed-neighbor count is odd iff every n_ell=1, i.e. iff M is fantastic. Passing to the simple graph on all maximal matchings (edges = neighbor relation, no self-loops), fantastic matchings are isolated (degree 0) and every other matching has odd degree (closed count minus 1). The handshake lemma says the number of odd-degree vertices is even, so #(non-fantastic) is even, giving #fantastic congruent to |V| mod 2. With |V| = (2*ceil(n/2)-1)!! odd, #fantastic is odd; combined with the inverse-involution bridge (a_n congruent to #fantastic mod 2), a_n is odd.

technique: Pair each object with its image under a fixed involution that preserves the counted property; orbits have size 2 except for the involution's fixed points, so the total count is congruent mod 2 to the number of fixed (self-paired) objects.
how_used: The counted set W_n is permutations x of (1..n) with all ratios x_k/k distinct. The involution is x -> x^{-1}: if x_k=j then (x^{-1})_j=k, so the ratios of x^{-1} are the reciprocals of those of x, hence still pairwise distinct, so x^{-1} in W_n. This pairs non-involutive permutations in 2-orbits and fixes exactly the involutions (x=x^{-1}). Hence a_n=|W_n| is congruent mod 2 to I_n := #{working involutions}. A working involution has at most one fixed point (a fixed point gives ratio 1, two would repeat it): none if n even, exactly one if n odd. Its transpositions {i,j} (i<j) are the edges of a maximal matching of K_n with edge {i,j} labeled i/j, and 'distinct ratios' becomes 'distinct edge labels'. So a_n is odd iff I_n = #{maximal matchings of K_n with all edge labels i/j distinct} (call these 'fantastic') is odd. This is the reduction; proving I_n odd is left to the later moves.

technique: When counting objects with labeled parts where equal-labeled parts admit a local pair-and-swap operation, count the number of objects reachable by such swaps (the 'neighbor' count) and reduce it mod 2; a class of matched labels of size m contributes a factor congruent to 2^{m-1}, so the total neighbor count is odd exactly when every label is unique.
how_used: For labeled maximal matchings, observe that if edges ab and cd share the same label (a<b, c<d, so a/b=c/d) then edges ac and bd share a label too, giving a switching move that replaces {ab,cd} by {ac,bd} within a same-label class and stays a maximal matching. A 'neighbor' of a matching M is any matching obtained by picking, within each label class of size n_ell, some disjoint pairs of edges and swapping them. The number of ways to swap k disjoint pairs among n_ell equal-labeled edges is C(n_ell,2k)(2k-1)!!, and mod 2 the double factorial is odd, so the class contributes sum_k C(n_ell,2k) = 2^{n_ell-1} mod 2. The full neighbor count is the product over labels of these factors, hence odd iff every n_ell=1, i.e. iff M is fantastic (all labels distinct). This is the move that identifies fantastic matchings as those with an odd number of neighbors.

technique: To show a distinguished subclass of objects has odd cardinality, make all objects the vertices of a graph whose edges are a symmetric 'neighbor' relation chosen so the subclass is exactly the isolated (or even-degree) vertices; by the handshake lemma odd-degree vertices come in an even number, so the subclass has the same parity as the total vertex count, which is computed directly.
how_used: Build a graph Gamma whose vertices are all maximal matchings of K_n and whose edges are the (symmetric, non-reflexive) neighbor relation from the switching move. Fantastic matchings have neighbor count 1 (themselves only), i.e. they are the isolated vertices; every other matching has odd neighbor count, i.e. even nonzero degree... equivalently, non-fantastic vertices have ODD degree (one less than an odd neighbor-including-self count). The handshake lemma forces the number of odd-degree vertices to be even, so #(fantastic) = #(all vertices) - #(non-fantastic) is congruent mod 2 to the total number of maximal matchings, which is (2*ceil(n/2)-1)!! (an odd double factorial). Hence I_n is odd, and combined with the reduction a_n is odd.

technique: Strengthen the target from 'achieve at least the average' to 'achieve either designated half at will', so the choice becomes a controllable class rather than an optimized quantity
how_used: Instead of directly showing the first player can score >= the opponent, prove the stronger claim that Johan can force taking exactly all odd-indexed cards a_1,a_3,... OR exactly all even-indexed cards a_2,a_4,... of the row, as he chooses.

technique: After the mover fixes an endpoint, absorb the opponent's forced reply by re-indexing the remaining contiguous block so its induced parity classes align with the induction hypothesis regardless of which end the opponent took
how_used: Johan takes a_1 (odd); whichever card Julian removes (a_2 from the left or a_{2n+2} from the right), the leftover length-2n row b_i satisfies either b_i=a_{i+2} (take odd b's) or b_i=a_{i+1} (take even b's), and in both cases the recovered b-parity-class plus a_1 reconstitutes all odd a-cards

technique: Convert a guaranteed free choice between two complementary sets into an optimality bound by picking whichever set has the larger total
how_used: Since the odd-position and even-position sums partition the total, Johan picks the odd class if its sum is >= the even class's sum and the even class otherwise, guaranteeing his score is at least Julian's

technique: Establish a chain of equivalences '(term ≥ threshold) ⟺ (count ≥ index)' between a monotone sequence and its counting sequence, then read the value off as the largest threshold making it true.
how_used: Show a_j ≥ i ⟺ b_i ≥ j ⟺ c_j ≥ i for the b/c counting sequences; setting i = a_j and i = c_j in this equivalence pins c_j = a_j, proving the a-sequence and c-sequence coincide (partition self-conjugacy).

technique: Rewrite a difference of two counting quantities as the count of elements falling in the intervening band, so the shifted sum becomes a sum over the elements it double-counts.
how_used: Write sum_{i=1}^k (b_i - b_k) = sum_i #{l : k > a_l ≥ i}, recognize each a_l < k is counted exactly a_l times, so the whole equals sum over those a_l; then use l > b_k ⟺ a_l < k to re-index the range as j from b_k+1 to n.

technique: Encode a global 2D configuration count as a sum of a locally-defined feature centered at each cell, then re-express the target as a linear combination of the feature total and the fixed count of all such configurations
how_used: Defined an 'elbow' (a<b>c with a,b same row and b,c same column) centered at each cell; observed a wobbly rectangle has exactly 2 elbows and every rectangle has >=1 (its minimum entry is an elbow center), so with M the non-wobbly count and N the wobbly count, E >= M + 2N = C(n,2)^2 + N, giving N <= E - C(n,2)^2

technique: Bound a per-cell product of two rank-counts by the AM-GM inequality so the sum becomes a fixed row/column rank-square total independent of the arrangement
how_used: Elbows centered at cell c equal f(c)g(c) (smaller entries in its row times smaller in its column); f(c)g(c) <= (f^2+g^2)/2, and summing over all cells each row and column contributes 0^2+...+(n-1)^2, giving E <= n^2(n-1)(2n-1)/6, hence N <= n^2(n^2-1)/12

technique: Achieve the equality condition of the applied inequality by building the arrangement from a Latin square, then refining each symbol into a consistent local order
how_used: Equality in AM-GM needs f(c)=g(c) for every cell; take a Latin square on symbols 0..n-1 and replace the n copies of symbol k by kn+1..kn+n in any order, so each cell's row-rank and column-rank both equal its Latin symbol, attaining N = n^2(n^2-1)/12

technique: Build a nested/anti-nested pair of chains so any proper-union subcollection is confined to a prefix and suffix where a boundary element is uniquely covered
how_used: The 2n-2 construction uses prefixes B_k={1,...,k} and suffixes B_k={k-n+2,...,n}; for any subcollection with a missing element m, the greatest covered element below m (or least above m) lies in exactly one set, so no subcollection is tight, attaining the maximum.

technique: From the non-tightness of each 'sets avoiding x' subfamily, draw an arrow x->x' to a uniquely-covered element and extract a cycle in the resulting functional digraph
how_used: For each x, B_x (members not containing x) is not tight, so some x' sits in a single member of B_x; the arrow x->x' gives out-degree >=1 everywhere, forcing a cycle x_1->...->x_k->x_1 whose sets A_i (containing x_{i+1} not x_i) are the crossing structure used to reduce n.

technique: Collapse the cycle's vertex set X' to a single new point, shrinking the ground set so the induction hypothesis bounds the reduced collection
how_used: After deleting A_1,...,A_k every remaining set contains or avoids X'={x_1,...,x_k}; collapsing X' to x* gives good subsets of X* with |B'|<=2(n-k), so |B|<=2n-k<2n-1, completing the induction step.

technique: Reduce an eternal fair-scheduling requirement to finitely emptying a bounding region, then re-enclose and repeat.
how_used: To build an infinite move-sequence using each car infinitely often, put all finitely many cars in an axis-aligned rectangle S and show only that all cars can legally exit S in finitely many moves. Each car moves at least once while leaving S; after S is emptied, re-enclose the (still finite) car configuration in a fresh rectangle and clear it again. Since the emptied configuration again satisfies the problem's hypotheses (every car still has an empty cell ahead in the open plane, and no facing pairs are created — cars only ever moved forward), the clearing procedure applies verbatim to the new box, and iterating forever moves every car unboundedly many times.

technique: Reduce an infinite 'move every token infinitely often' goal to the finite one-shot lemma 'from any admissible configuration, drive every token out of a given bounded region', then iterate the lemma on a nested sequence of regions.
how_used: Fix a rectangle S containing all the cars. Claim it suffices to show every car can be driven strictly outside S by a finite legal move sequence. Granting that: run it on S_1 = the bounding box to move every car at least once (each car exits S_1); the cars now sit in some finite configuration, still admissible; enclose it in a larger rectangle S_2 and run the lemma again, moving every car once more; repeat forever. Each round advances every car at least once, so every car moves infinitely many times. This converts the infinite fairness requirement into the single combinatorial lemma about evacuating one finite box, which is what the rest of the argument proves.

technique: When tokens confined to a single line must all leave it and a 'no two tokens face toward each other' hypothesis holds, use it to split the line into an outward-facing prefix and an outward-facing suffix, so each side is a monotone queue that empties its own end with no head-on collision and no mutual block.
how_used: This is the move behind Stages 2 and 4: after a color class has been cleared of vertical cars, a horizontal car's only possible obstacles are other horizontal cars in its own row, since that row now holds no vertical cars and a horizontal car never leaves its row. The 'no two cars face toward each other' hypothesis says no right-facing car lies to the left of a left-facing car in a row. Reading the row left to right, the left-facing cars therefore form a prefix and the right-facing cars a suffix (the only forbidden pattern is right-facer left of left-facer). The left-facing block streams out the LEFT end of S in order (frontmost first, empty space ahead because the rest of the row is clear) and the right-facing block streams out the RIGHT end likewise; nobody blocks or collides. This is the stage where the no-head-on hypothesis (not the empty-front one) does the work.

technique: When a global one-shot permission (a one-time 'the cell ahead is free' guarantee, usable once per token) must power an unbounded schedule, 2-color the board into height-1 strips by parity and split tokens by motion axis, so the guarantee is spent in a single simultaneous batch move that clears one entire color class of the axis-crossing tokens; every later advance of those tokens then lands on a cell the schedule itself has just emptied, not on the (now-consumed) guarantee.
how_used: Enclose all cars in a rectangle S; it suffices to evacuate S once, since translating the box forward and repeating gives every car infinitely many forward moves (routine finish). Cut S into horizontal strips of height 1, colored red/green alternately. Classify cars by axis: vertical cars (up/down) cross strips; horizontal cars (left/right) stay inside their own strip. The empty-front hypothesis is spent in EXACTLY ONE stage: Stage 1, every vertical car sitting on a GREEN cell advances one cell in its facing direction. Because strips have height 1 that front cell lies in the adjacent RED strip (or outside S), and it is empty precisely by the empty-front hypothesis for that car (order the moves along each column so no two hit the same red cell; 'no two cars face each other' rules out a facing pair sharing one target). After Stage 1 no vertical car occupies a green cell. From here the hypothesis is never reused: Stage 3, every vertical car on a RED cell advances into a GREEN cell, which is free of vertical cars thanks to Stage 1; Stage 5, whatever vertical cars remain drive straight out of S. Each stage moves every vertical car at least one strip toward the boundary, and S has finitely many strips, so the vertical cars evacuate. (Green/red cells being free of HORIZONTAL cars at the moments Stages 3 and 1 need them is secured by a separate move — the horizontal-strip evacuation crux — interleaved as Stages 2 and 4.) The single hard idea here is spending the one-shot resource to vacate a whole color class at once, converting all subsequent vertical-target emptiness into a consequence of the schedule.

technique: Once a line (a single strip/row) has been cleared of all cross-axis traffic, evacuate the tokens confined to that line by exploiting a 'no two tokens point toward each other' hypothesis: it forces the line to split into a left-pointing block and a right-pointing block that separate outward, so every such token drives off the end with no collision.
how_used: Interleaved as Stages 2 and 4 of the five-stage plan. After Stage 1 has vacated all GREEN cells of vertical cars, consider any single green strip: the only cars left in it are horizontal cars confined to that height-1 row. The hypothesis 'no right-facing car is to the left of a left-facing car within a row' means reading the row left-to-right you never see R...L; hence all left-facing cars occupy the left portion and all right-facing cars the right portion. The left-facers drive left out of S and the right-facers drive right out of S; since the two blocks move apart there is no collision, and the row now empty of vertical cars provides the free cells. This clears every horizontal car on green (Stage 2), so green becomes fully empty and Stage 3 (vertical red -> green) has empty targets. Stage 4 repeats the identical argument on the red strips after Stage 3 vacates them of vertical cars. This is the second essential ingredient: without it the vertical crux's later stages cannot certify their targets are vacant, and S never empties.

technique: Build the extremal instance by clustering items at the two allowed extremes so the balancing constraint is maximally strained
how_used: Take 51 coins of value 1/51 and 49 coins of value 1 (total 50, all in (0,1]); in any 50-50 split, if stack A takes k big coins then val(A)-val(B) = (2k-49)(1-1/51) = (2k-49)(50/51), and 2k-49 is odd so |2k-49| >= 1, forcing |diff| >= 50/51. Hence C >= 50/51.

technique: Bound a middle order statistic by noting the coins at or above it are numerous enough that their known total caps its size
how_used: With a_1<=...<=a_100 summing to 50: the 51 coins a_50,...,a_100 are each >= a_50 so 51*a_50 <= 50, giving a_50 <= 50/51; symmetrically the 51 smallest are each <= a_51 and (since the other 49 are <= 1 they contribute <= 49) sum to >= 1, so 51*a_51 >= 1, i.e. a_51 >= 1/51.

technique: Split a sorted sequence into two stacks by pairing consecutive elements so each pair's contribution to the difference is a non-positive gap, leaving only isolated boundary terms
how_used: Assign a_1,a_3,...,a_49,a_52,...,a_100 vs a_2,a_4,...,a_50,a_51,...,a_99; the difference D telescopes to sums of (a_{2k-1}-a_{2k}) <= 0 plus leftover -a_51 and +a_100, so D <= -1/51 + 1 = 50/51; regrouping the other way gives D >= -a_50 >= -50/51, hence |D| <= 50/51.

technique: Pick an extreme (convex-hull) vertex as pivot so that a chord from it partitions the remaining points into two angular sides whose segments can never cross each other, decoupling the count into an independent product.
how_used: P is chosen on the convex hull of the 2(n+1) points; the other 2n+1 points are sorted by angle from P as A_1,...,A_{2n+1}. Because P is extreme, drawing PA_{2k+1} splits the rest into U (2k points) and V (2(n-k) points) with no U-segment able to cross any V-segment, so the completions factor as chi(U)*chi(V).

technique: Use a parity count on the two sides of the pivot chord to restrict which partners are admissible in a perfect matching.
how_used: For 8 segments to complete into a perfect non-crossing matching, P's partner must leave an even number of points on each side; a segment PA_{2k} would leave two odd-sized halves that cannot be perfectly matched, so only the odd-index targets A_{2k+1} are viable, giving exactly the terms C_k C_{n-k}.

technique: Sum the induction-based product lower bounds over all admissible splits and recognize the total as a known combinatorial recurrence to close the induction.
how_used: With chi(U) >= C_k and chi(V) >= C_{n-k} by strong induction, summing C_k C_{n-k} over all valid k yields C_0 C_n + ... + C_n C_0 = C_{n+1}, matching the Catalan recurrence; the convex 2n-gon (where every inequality is tight) realizes chi = C_n, giving answer C_8 = 1430.

technique: When each element dominates the sum of all smaller ones, replace a running cumulative-sum inequality with a single condition on the current top element.
how_used: Because 2^k exceeds 2^0+...+2^{k-1}, 'right pan never heavier than left' is equivalent to 'the heaviest weight currently on the balance sits on the left pan', letting one ignore all lighter weights when checking validity.

technique: Set up a recurrence by removing the smallest element and counting how many ways it can be reinserted into an arbitrary valid arrangement of the rest.
how_used: Deleting weight 1 (and halving) leaves a valid sequence of the other n-1 weights counted by f(n-1); reinserting weight 1 gives 2n-1 choices (n time slots x 2 pans, minus the forbidden first-move-right since the opening move must be left), yielding f(n)=(2n-1)f(n-1) and f(n)=(2n-1)!!.

technique: Orient a rotating/sweeping line and track the count of points on each side as a quantity conserved across the event where the sweep hands off
how_used: When the windmill pivot passes from T to U, after the handover T lies on the side U occupied before, so the tally of S on the oranje side and on the blue side is unchanged through every pivot swap; this invariance is what lets a balanced start stay balanced forever.

technique: Rotate a line 180 degrees so a side-count changes by 1 at each point-crossing and lands on its mirror value, applying discrete intermediate-value to force an exactly balanced direction
how_used: Through a point T a line starts with n+r points on the oranje side; after a 180-degree turn it has n-r, and since it steps by 1 per crossing, some intermediate direction gives exactly n on each side (or n-1 and n in the even case), producing the desired starting line.

technique: Exploit that a balance-separating line is unique in each direction (translation breaks the split) to force the sweeping line to coincide with it and hence pass through the marked point
how_used: For any target T there is a line through T splitting S into equal halves; T is the only point whose line in that direction balances S, so when the windmill line becomes parallel to it the two must coincide, guaranteeing every point is visited as pivot during the rotation.

technique: Reinterpret a symmetric two-body collision rule as a free binary choice at each collision, so labeled particles can be recolored into monotone families
how_used: Turning both colliding ants anticlockwise instead of clockwise leaves the whole trajectory picture unchanged except that the two ants swap labels; applied independently at each collision, this lets you assume every collision rotates the pair either way you like. Choosing consistently recolors all ants into NE-ants (move only N or E) and SW-ants (move only S or W); a second consistent choice instead yields N/W-alternating and S/E-alternating ants.

technique: Bound where an event can occur by intersecting the reachable-region constraints obtained from several independently-chosen relabelings of the same dynamics
how_used: Under the NE/SW recoloring, a collision at time t and point (x,y) forces t+1 <= x+y <= 2m-t-1 (no NE-ant yet reaches x+y<t+1, no SW-ant still has x+y>2m-t-1). Under the N-W / S-E recoloring, the analogous anti-diagonal band gives |x-y| <= m-t-1. Intersecting both feasible regions and using x+y>=t+1 with x-y >= -(m-t-1) yields min{x,y} >= t+1-m/2, so a last collision at time t leaves at most m-min{x,y} residual monotone travel and total time t+(m-min{x,y}) <= 3m/2-1.

technique: Attain an extremal-time bound with a corner-launched two-particle configuration whose single head-on collision maximizes the survivor's remaining straight run to the far edge
how_used: Place one ant on the SW-corner square facing east and one on the SE-corner square facing west, on the bottom row. Their midpoints are m-1 apart, so they meet head-on at the middle of the bottom row at time (m-1)/2. At the collision both turn 90 degrees the same way; the one that ends up heading north then runs the full board height, staying on for another m-1/2 time units. Total (m-1)/2 + (m-1/2) = 3m/2-1, attaining the maximum. (Timing is unaffected by which of the two ants is the north-goer; both persist after the collision, one falling off the near edge immediately and one making the long run.)

technique: Make a local interaction rule freely reversible by observing that swapping the two participants' labels leaves the global configuration invariant, so you may choose the outcome of each interaction independently
how_used: At any head-on collision, replacing the clockwise turn by an anticlockwise turn produces the exact same set of ant trajectories, only with the two colliding ants' labels swapped. Since global behavior is label-independent, you may DECIDE, per collision, whether both ants turn CW or both turn ACW. Choosing all collisions to be resolved consistently lets you assume every ant is either an NE-ant (only ever moves north or east) or an SW-ant (only ever moves south or west); a second, independent choice makes every ant an NW-ant or SE-ant. These give two monotone potentials (x+y and x-y).

technique: Bound where/when interactions can occur by intersecting the forbidden-region constraints from two independent relabelings, then charge each object's residual travel against that bound
how_used: With the NE/SW relabeling, at time t no NE-ant lies in {x+y<t+1} and no SW-ant in {x+y>2m-t-1}, so any collision at (x,y,t) obeys t+1 <= x+y <= 2m-t-1. With the NW/SE relabeling you get |x-y| <= m-t-1. Intersecting: a collision at time t forces (x,y) into B(t), giving min{x,y} >= t+1-m/2. An ant's last collision at time t therefore leaves at most m - min{x,y} of straight travel, so total time on board <= t + m - (t+1-m/2) = 3m/2-1.

technique: For a matching escape-time lower bound, build the maximizer from a single head-on collision that redirects one survivor into a full-length straight run to the far edge.
how_used: Only ONE collision is needed; no multi-ant echelon. Place one ant on the SW-corner square (midpoint (1/2,1/2)) facing east and one on the SE-corner square (midpoint (m-1/2,1/2)) facing west. They approach along the bottom row, closing the gap m-1 at combined speed 2, so they collide at the row midpoint (m/2,1/2) at time (m-1)/2. Being opposite-moving they both turn 90 clockwise: the east-mover becomes south-moving and drops off instantly (ignore it), while the west-mover becomes NORTH-moving and, starting from y=1/2, runs the full height to y=m, surviving another m-1/2. The last ant thus falls at (m-1)/2 + (m-1/2) = 3m/2-1, exactly the upper bound proved by the region-charging argument, certifying it as the answer. Key sanity checks that dissolve the usual doubts: (i) track directions by the clockwise rule (west->north is the survivor, east->south dies); (ii) after the turn nothing else is on the board to intercept the survivor, so a lone collision genuinely reaches 3m/2-1 - a bare traversal without the collision only gives m-1/2, and the collision adds the extra (m-1)/2 by first walking the survivor to the row midpoint.

technique: When a collision rule turns two colliding particles, observe that flipping the turn direction at that one collision is equivalent to letting the two particles pass through / swap identities, leaving every other particle's future trajectory unchanged; this frees you to reassign the turn direction of each collision independently.
how_used: This is the pivotal, non-obvious move that unlocks the whole upper bound and the fresh solver was missing it entirely. At a collision the two opposite-moving ants normally both turn 90 clockwise. Claim: if instead you force them both to turn 90 ANTICLOCKWISE at that single collision, the multiset of all ant trajectories from then on is IDENTICAL - the only change is that ants a and a' swap which trajectory they own (they effectively pass through each other). Reason: at a head-on meeting the clockwise pair and the anticlockwise pair trace the same two outgoing rays, just with the labels exchanged; since the dynamics only depend on positions/directions of ants and not their labels, nothing downstream changes. Because this can be applied to each collision SEPARATELY and independently, we may CHOOSE, collision by collision, whether both ants go clockwise or both anticlockwise, without affecting the falling times we care about. This choice-freedom is the tool; what you DO with it (relabel into monotone ant-types) is the next step.

technique: Having the freedom to reassign each collision's turn direction, choose it so every particle becomes monotone (each moves within a fixed 90-degree quadrant of directions); a monotone particle is trapped in a half-plane that recedes at speed 1, so intersecting the half-planes for several such relabelings confines every collision point to a shrinking region, and each particle's total lifetime is bounded by (time of its last collision) + (distance from that shrinking region to the nearest edge).
how_used: Using the collision-flip freedom (previous crux), relabel so there are only NE-ants (move only north or east) and SW-ants (move only south or west). A NE-ant only increases x+y over time, so at time t no NE-ant lies in {x+y < t+1} and no SW-ant lies in {x+y > 2m-t-1}; hence any collision at (x,y),t satisfies t+1 <= x+y <= 2m-t-1. Do the SAME relabeling in the other diagonal (NW-ants moving north/west vs SE-ants moving south/east) to get |x-y| <= m-t-1. So every collision at time t lies in B(t) = {(x,y) in [0,m]^2 : t+1 <= x+y <= 2m-t-1, |x-y| <= m-t-1}. Now for a NE-ant whose LAST collision is at (x,y),t: from x+y >= t+1 and x-y >= -(m-t-1) get x >= t+1-m/2, and by symmetry y >= t+1-m/2, so min(x,y) >= t+1-m/2. After its last collision it goes straight to an edge in <= m - min(x,y) time, so total lifetime <= t + m - (t+1-m/2) = 3m/2-1. (An ant that never collides falls within m-1/2 < 3m/2-1.) By symmetry the same holds for SW-ants, completing the upper bound. Note m must be even for 3m/2-1 to be the exact integral-attaining value matching the construction.

technique: Count occurrences of a factor by splitting on the single letter that extends it, since each occurrence is followed (or preceded) by exactly one letter, giving occ(R)=occ(Ra)+occ(Rb).
how_used: Defining multiplicity mu(R) as the number of length-|R| windows equal to R, this gives the conservation identity mu(R)=mu(Ra)+mu(Rb)=mu(aR)+mu(bR); it is the tool that converts 'one extension has strictly smaller count than mu(R)' into 'the complementary extension is positive', so Ua, Ub, aU, bU all appear.

technique: Take the maximal-length object whose occurrence-count exceeds a fixed threshold, so that every one-step extension necessarily has count at or below that threshold.
how_used: U_k is chosen as the longest factor with mu(U_k)>2^k; maximality forces mu(U_k a),mu(U_k b)<=2^k<mu(U_k) (and likewise on the left), and combined with the splitting identity each neighboring letter must actually occur, making U_k ubiquitous. Existence/boundedness of a maximal such length comes from the fact that minimal period N makes every length-N window have multiplicity at most 1.

technique: Run the extremal construction at a geometric ladder of thresholds so each chosen object lands in a distinct dyadic band of the count monovariant, forcing distinctness and yielding the desired count.
how_used: Using thresholds 2^0,...,2^{n-1}, maximality also bounds above: mu(U_k) lies in (2^k, 2^{k+1}], so the multiplicities strictly increase and the words U_0,...,U_{n-1} are pairwise distinct; since N>2^n, some single letter has multiplicity >2^{n-1}, guaranteeing the top band is populated, hence at least n ubiquitous words.

technique: Bucket the cells of a line by index modulo the tile length and use that each tile hits every residue class exactly once to force all class-sums equal
how_used: Write 2011 = 52m - 17 with m=39 and 52 = 35 + 17. Along any row/column of length 52m-17, group cells by index mod 52 into sums s_1..s_52; every napkin meeting the line covers 52 consecutive cells hence adds exactly 1 to each s_i, so s_1=...=s_52=s. Laying out 2011 cells mod 52 gives 35 'small' classes with m terms and 17 'big' classes with m-1 terms. Fixing a target value M: if s>(m-1)M ('rich' line) then each of the 17 big classes (m-1 terms) must contain a term >M, giving >=17 bad cells; if s<=(m-1)M<mM ('poor' line) then each of the 35 small classes (m terms) must contain a term <M, giving >=35 bad cells. This is the per-line rich/poor bad-cell dichotomy.

technique: Build the extremal example from nested diagonal families of tiles offset by the two residue lengths so overlaps are confined to a computable exceptional region
how_used: Place four napkin families keyed to the split 52 = 35+17 (offsets 36 = 35+1 and 1): (52i+36, 52j+1) for 0<=j<=i<=m-2, (52i+1, 52j+36) for 0<=i<=j<=m-2, the diagonal (52i+36, 52i+36) for 0<=i<=m-2, and (1,1). The two off-diagonal families tile complementary triangular regions covering generic cells exactly once; every cell reads 1 except the doubly-hatched overlaps near the main diagonal. Their count is (52^2-35^2)m - 17^2 = 57392, matching the lower bound, so k = 2011^2 - 57392 = 3986729.

technique: To force deviations along a 1-D line under a fixed-length sliding cover, partition the cells into residue classes modulo the cover length; each cover hits every class exactly once, so all class-sums are equal, and comparing that common value against (class-size)*M pins down which classes must contain an off-target cell.
how_used: A line has 2011 = 52m - 17 cells (m=39). For i=1..52 let s_i be the sum of the entries in cells whose index is congruent to i mod 52. Classes 1..35 have m terms each; classes 36..52 have m-1 terms each. Every 52x52 napkin meeting the line covers exactly one cell in each residue class, so it adds 1 to every s_i; hence s_1 = ... = s_52 = s, the number of napkins meeting the line. Now compare s to (m-1)M and mM. Call the line RICH if s > (m-1)M: then each of the 17 short sums s_36..s_52 (only m-1 terms) must contain a term > M, giving >=17 'rich bad' cells, all sitting in BIG-residue positions (index cong 36..52 mod 52). Call it POOR otherwise: then s <= (m-1)M < mM, so each of the 35 long sums s_1..s_35 (m terms) must contain a term < M, giving >=35 'poor bad' cells, all in SMALL-residue positions (index cong 1..35 mod 52). This is the mechanism that produces the {17 rich} vs {>=35 poor} dichotomy per line, and it records WHICH residue positions (big vs small) the bad cells occupy in each case. NOTE for the downstream count: classify each LINE itself as small or big by whether its OWN index (row-number or column-number) is small (cong 1..35) or big (cong 36..52) mod 52; there are 35m = 1365 small rows and 17(m-1) = 646 big rows (1365+646=2011), same for columns.

technique: When each object in a family (here, each line) carries its own case-dependent lower bound and the weak case yields fewer forced marks than the strong case, restore a uniform per-object threshold by placing an EXTRA mark on the weak case's forced positions, then convert the summed per-object thresholds into a global element count by capping how many marks any single element can accumulate.
how_used: Double-count over the 2*2011 lines (rows and columns), each classified small or big by index mod 52 (35m small and 17(m-1) big lines per direction, m=39). Base rule: put a strawberry on every cell that is bad for its own line. Extra rule: on each SMALL line that is rich, add a second strawberry to each of its 17 rich-bad cells, lifting the weak rich case from 17 up to 2*17=34 so every small line forces >=34 in all cases; a big line forces >=min(17,35)=17. Multiplicity cap of 2: each cell lies on one row and one column, so at most one BASE strawberry from each. The EXTRA strawberry lands only on a rich-bad cell of a small line, which sits at a big-residue position along that small line; its orthogonal line therefore meets it at a small-residue position, where rich-bad cells never occur, so it collects no base strawberry there -- total stays <=2. Hence N <= 2g where g = #cells != M. Summing per-line minimums, N >= 2*(35m*34 + 17(m-1)*17) = 2*57392, so g >= 57392 and k <= 2011^2 - 57392 = 3986729. (This aggregation presupposes the per-line rich/poor forced-bad-cell lemma; see the separate crux for that step.)

technique: When a line's length is a non-multiple R*m - H of the tile width R, partition its cells by residue mod R; each tile crossing the line hits exactly one cell per residue, so all R residue-sums are equal, and comparing that common value against the per-residue averages forces an above- or below-average term in the short (or long) residue classes.
how_used: For a line of 2011 = 52*39 - 17 cells with entries a_1..a_2011, set s_i = sum of a_t over t = i mod 52. The 35 residues 1..35 have m=39 terms; the 17 residues 36..52 have m-1=38 terms. Any napkin meeting the line covers exactly one cell of each residue, so s_1 = ... = s_52 = s (the number of napkins meeting the line). Call the line rich if s > (m-1)M and poor otherwise. If rich, each of the 17 short sums s_36..s_52 (only m-1 terms) exceeds (m-1)M, so each has a term > M: at least 17 bad cells, all at big residues. If poor, then s < mM, so each of the 35 long sums s_1..s_35 (m terms) is below mM and has a term < M: at least 35 bad cells, all at small residues. This per-line lemma feeds the global double-count; the rich/poor dichotomy also pins WHERE the bad cells sit (big vs small residues), which caps each cell's charge at 2 (its row and its column) so the strawberry count 2g >= 2(35m*34 + 17(m-1)*17) = 2*57392 gives k <= 2011^2 - 57392.

technique: To show an extremal covering bound is tight, build a nested/triangular arrangement of tiles offset by the leftover margin so that overlaps concentrate on a thin band of exceptional cells and every remaining cell is covered exactly once, making the count of exceptional cells match the proven lower bound.
how_used: Number columns/rows 1..2011 and denote each 52x52 napkin by its lower-left cell. Use four napkin families: (i) all (52i+36, 52j+1) with 0<=j<=i<=m-2; (ii) all (52i+1, 52j+36) with 0<=i<=j<=m-2; (iii) the diagonal (52i+36, 52i+36) with 0<=i<=m-2; (iv) the single napkin (1,1). Every cell not carrying two different families' overlap gets the value 1; the overlap (exceptional) cells number exactly (52^2 - 35^2)*m - 17^2 = 57392. Hence 2011^2 - 57392 = 3986729 cells all hold the value 1, attaining the bound proved by the double-count and so certifying k = 3986729 exactly (not just k <= it).

technique: Assuming the target fails, pick the index maximizing a fixed-width sliding-window sum; maximality upgrades the two neighboring weak inequalities to strict ones, so the shifted-difference function is strictly negative on one side and strictly positive on the other.
how_used: Encode students as a_i in {0,1} on a circle (extended periodically), with the target equivalent to S_k(i)=S_k(i+k) for some k in [100,300]. Assume no such k exists, so in particular f(j):=S_100(j)-S_100(j+100) is never 0. Choose i maximizing S_100(i); maximality gives S_100(i-100)<=S_100(i) and S_100(i)>=S_100(i+100), and since f never vanishes these are strict: f(i-100)<0 and f(i)>0. So f is negative at i-100 and positive at i.

technique: At a discrete sign change of a step-difference of window sums, subtract the two adjacent off-by-one inequalities so all interior window terms cancel and only the four endpoint terms survive; a difference forced to be >=2 among {-1,0,1}-valued gaps then pins those endpoints to exact values.
how_used: Since integer-valued f=S_100(j)-S_100(j+100) is <0 at i-100 and >0 at i, there is an adjacent pair with S_100(j)<=S_100(j+100)-1 and S_100(j+1)>=S_100(j+101)+1. Subtracting gives a_{j+100}-a_j >= a_{j+200}-a_{j+100}+2; since each difference is in {-1,0,1} this forces a_j=0, a_{j+100}=1, a_{j+200}=0. Feeding these back into both inequalities squeezes S_99(j+1)=S_99(j+101): two balanced 99-blocks flanking the lone 1 at j+100, with 0 boundaries at j and j+200.

technique: Bound the length of a maximal constant run by noting a run strictly longer than the target window width contains two identical adjacent windows, an immediate equality; hence in a no-equality configuration every constant run is capped below that width.
how_used: Let k,l be least positive integers with a_{j-k}=1 and a_{j+200+l}=1 (the zero-runs flanking the pinned block outward). WLOG k>=l. If k>=200 then a_j=a_{j-1}=...=a_{j-199}=0 is a zero-run of length >=200, so S_100(j-199)=S_100(j-99)=0 is an equal adjacent pair at width 100, contradicting the assumption. Hence l<=k<=199, so the extension in the next step stays at width 100+l<=299<=300.

technique: To generate a starting equality between two adjacent sliding windows when a direct one is assumed absent, pick the index maximizing the fixed-width window sum; its two neighbors then give strict inequalities of opposite sign, so a discrete intermediate-value step yields two consecutive indices at which the sign of the window-difference flips.
how_used: Encode girls as a_i in {0,1} on Z/1000 and set S_k(i)=a_i+...+a_{i+k-1}; the claim is some k in [100,300] and index i have S_k(i)=S_k(i+k). Assume not. Choose i maximizing S_100(i). Then S_100(i-100)-S_100(i)<0 and S_100(i)-S_100(i+100)>0 (equality would finish), so g(j)=S_100(j)-S_100(j+100) is >0 at j=i-100 direction and <0 near j=i; hence some j in [i-100,i-1] has S_100(j)<=S_100(j+100)-1 but S_100(j+1)>=S_100(j+101)+1. This adjacent sign-flip pair is the seed the rest of the argument extends.

technique: Subtract two adjacent, oppositely-directed strict window-difference inequalities from each other to force the extreme boundary entries to specific values and collapse the residual inequality chain into an exact equality on the trimmed inner window.
how_used: From S_100(j)<=S_100(j+100)-1 and S_100(j+1)>=S_100(j+101)+1, subtract to get a_{j+100}-a_j >= (a_{j+200}-a_{j+100})+2. Since each a is in {0,1}, this pins a_j=0, a_{j+100}=1, a_{j+200}=0. Re-substituting these into the two original inequalities squeezes S_99(j+1) <= S_99(j+101) <= S_99(j+1), i.e. the exact equality S_99(j+1)=S_99(j+101). This gives the 'pinned block' (zeros at the two ends of the 200-span, a one at the center) with a genuine width-99 balanced pair, none of which was assumed.

technique: Extend a balanced adjacent-window equality outward on both sides by the length of the shorter flanking constant run, so each side absorbs the same block (constant run plus the next boundary element) and the equality persists at a strictly larger, still-admissible width.
how_used: With S_99(j+1)=S_99(j+101), a_j=a_{j+200}=0, a_{j+100}=1, let l be the shorter of the two flanking zero-runs (say the run right of j+200, terminating in a 1 at j+200+l). The bound l<=199 is forced by the same negation hypothesis: a zero-run of length >=200 would give two adjacent all-zero width-100 windows S_100=S_100, a balanced pair — so l<=199 keeps k=100+l<=299 in range. Extend each width-99 window by l on the outer side. Left: S_{100+l}(j-l+1)=(a_{j-l+1}+...+a_j)+S_99(j+1)+a_{j+100}=S_99(j+1)+1 (l zeros plus the center one). Right: S_{100+l}(j+101)=S_99(j+101)+(a_{j+200}+...+a_{j+200+l-1})+a_{j+200+l}=S_99(j+101)+1 (l zeros plus the boundary one). Both added chunks contribute exactly one girl, so S_{100+l}(j-l+1)=S_{100+l}(j+101): an equal adjacent pair at width 100+l in [100,299]subset[100,300], the final contradiction.

technique: Bound a polygon's area by triangulating it as a fan from a fixed reference point and bounding each fan-triangle by AM-GM on its two radii to that point.
how_used: Lemma 1: for a quadrilateral A1A2A3A4 and the center O=(k-1/2,k-1/2), write [V] as the sum of the four triangles [OA_iA_{i+1}], each ≤ (OA_i·OA_{i+1})/2 ≤ (OA_i²+OA_{i+1²})/4, giving [V] ≤ (1/2)Σ OA_i² with equality exactly when V is a square centered at O.

technique: When each cell's upper bound is additive over that cell's vertices, sum the bound over the whole partition so the objective collapses to a value independent of how the vertices are grouped.
how_used: Since every point of K is a vertex of exactly one quadrilateral (condition ii), summing [V] ≤ (1/2)Σ OA_i² over all k² quadrilaterals gives S(V) ≤ (1/2)Σ_{A∈K} OA², a constant independent of the partition V; the partition of central squares Q (K splits into k² O-orbits of size 4 under 90° rotation) attains equality in Lemma 1, so max equals k²(2k+1)(2k-1)/3.

technique: Maximize a sum of squared pairing-differences over all pairings of a fixed point set by rewriting each difference via the polarization identity and bounding the resulting sum-of-coordinate-sums by QM-AM.
how_used: Alternative (Lemma 2): bound [ABCD] ≤ (AC²+BD²)/4, reducing to maximizing S=Σ A_iB_i² over permutations of K into 2k² diagonal pairs; via (p_i-r_i)²=2p_i²+2r_i²-(p_i+r_i)² write Σ(p_i-r_i)²=4kΣj²−Σ(p_i+r_i)² and apply QM-AM to the fixed-sum Σ(p_i+r_i)², giving p_i+r_i=q_i+s_i=2k-1 (A_i,B_i symmetric about O) and S≤(4/3)k²(4k²-1), so S(V)≤k²(4k²-1)/3.

technique: Among all ways to split into equal groups, pick the one minimizing the max-min spread of a weight, then bound that spread by swapping the heaviest item of the top group with the lightest of the bottom group.
how_used: After setting aside the box N holding the most apples (n), split the remaining 2004 boxes into three piles A,B,C of 668 each; over partitions with apple-totals a<=b<=c fix the one minimizing c-a. If c-a>n, swap the box with the MOST apples in the top pile C against the box with the FEWEST apples in the bottom pile A: since any single box holds at most n<c-a apples, moving this heavy box from C to A (and the light box back) strictly shrinks c-a while b is untouched, contradicting minimality; hence c-a<=n, which feeds the next step.

technique: Reserve one heavy element outside the partition so that appending it lifts EVERY group above the first threshold, leaving a free pigeonhole choice among the groups for a second resource.
how_used: From c-a<=n one gets a+n>=(a+b+c+n)/3, so A∪{N}, B∪{N}, C∪{N} each contain at least a third of all apples. Since the added box N makes all three piles satisfy the apple condition, one is free to pick, by pigeonhole, whichever of the three piles holds at least a third of the pears, and that pile plus N gives 669 boxes meeting both conditions.

technique: Disprove a strengthened selection bound by a construction that forces disjoint mandatory picks for each resource to overflow the allowed count.
how_used: For part b), one box holds only an apple, one only a pear, and each of the other 2003 boxes one peach. Meeting all three one-third conditions forces choosing the apple box, the pear box, and 668 peach boxes, i.e. 670 boxes, exceeding 669, so the peach condition cannot always be added.

technique: Prove a product inequality by strengthening it to a two-sided form that gives each of the two required sub-objects its own independent copy, so the copies decouple and one boundary case forces equality.
how_used: Instead of proving N^2 >= M*2^{mn} directly, color the m*n board on TWO sheets (top and bottom) and let some squares be 'transparent' (forced to the same color on both sheets). Define A = # two-sheet configs whose TOP has a black left-right crossing, B = same for the BOTTOM, C = # configs with a top crossing and a bottom crossing that share no TRANSPARENT square, D = total # of configs. Prove the cleaner A*B >= C*D; the original claim is the all-transparent special case A=B=N, C=M, D=2^{mn}.

technique: Induct on the number of coupled/shared resources by converting one coupled unit into an independent one, tracking how each counted quantity scales by a fixed factor, with the all-independent configuration as the base case.
how_used: Induct on k = number of transparent squares. Base k=0 (all opaque): the two sheets are fully independent, giving A=B=N*2^{mn}, C=N^2, D=(2^{mn})^2, so A*B >= C*D holds with EQUALITY. Inductive step: take a transparent square t and make it opaque, so its top and bottom colors become independent; this yields D'=2D, A'=2A, B'=2B (each config lifts to exactly two configs differing only in t's freed side, and the crossing on a given sheet is unaffected). Then A'B' >= C'D' follows from A*B >= C*D once C' >= 2C.

technique: Bound the coupled count under decoupling by using a disjointness constraint to force the split element onto at most one of the two objects, so its freed second copy can be recolored arbitrarily to build a size-two injection.
how_used: To finish the induction one needs C' >= 2C. Since the top and bottom crossings in a C-config share no transparent square, the transparent square t lies on at most one of them (WLOG the top). Make t opaque, keep its top color (top crossing preserved), and color its now-free bottom side either black or white; the bottom crossing avoids t so it survives both choices. This maps each C-config to two distinct C'-configs, and distinct C-configs give distinct pairs (re-coupling t recovers the original), so C' >= 2C.

technique: Chase a self-referential permutation constraint by iterating the relation from a start index until the orbit closes, exposing the forced cycle size.
how_used: Starting from a_t=u (u not t, not n+1-t) and repeatedly applying 'i=a_j, j gives a_i+j=n+1', the relation forces a_u=n+1-t, a_{n+1-t}=n+1-u, a_{n+1-u}=t, closing a quadruple {t,u,n+1-t,n+1-u} of positions that carry exactly those same four values among themselves.

technique: Exclude degenerate small orbits by substituting the fixed/reflected candidate into the constraint and deriving a parity contradiction.
how_used: a_t=t forces 2t=n+1, impossible since 4|n makes n+1 odd; a_t=n+1-t reduces via the relation to a_{n+1-t}=n+1-t, i.e. the just-excluded fixed-point case — so no orbit of size 1 or 2 exists and every position lies in a genuine 4-block.

technique: Count the objects by greedily building block-by-block and multiplying the number of free choices remaining at each step.
how_used: Repeatedly take the smallest position k whose value is undetermined and count valid partners u (u not k, not n+1-k, not already used): the first block has n-2 choices, the next n-6, then n-10, ..., giving the product 2*6*10*...*(n-2), which with n=4m factors as 2^m*(1*3*...*(2m-1))=(2m)!/m! = ((n/2)!)/((n/4)!).

technique: Reflect a checkerboard coloring across the figure's symmetry axis instead of continuing it, so the two colors no longer balance and a global color surplus appears.
how_used: Two-color the upper half y>=0 of S_n as a proper checkerboard with the apex (n-1,0) blue [blue iff x+y = n-1 mod 2]. Then, rather than extending the checkerboard downward, REFLECT the upper coloring across the axis y=-1/2: a point (x,y) with y<0 takes the color of (x,-1-y). Because the reflection matches the two central rows y=0 and y=-1, blue outnumbers red by exactly 2n over all of S_n. The reflection stays proper everywhere OFF the axis; the only monochromatic edges are the vertical axis edges between rows y=0 and y=-1. Since a path with color-alternating adjacencies has |#blue - #red| <= 1, the 2n surplus is the engine that will force many paths.

technique: Restore per-path color-alternation by cutting only the monochromatic adjacencies of the surplus color, and charge the extra pieces against the global color surplus.
how_used: In the reflected coloring the only non-alternating edges are the 2n-1 vertical axis edges, which split into exactly n blue-blue and n-1 red-red. Given any partition into m paths, cut each path at every blue-blue axis edge only: at most n cuts, so at most m+n pieces. After cutting, no piece has two adjacent blue points, so blue vertices are non-adjacent along a piece, giving #blue <= #red + 1 per piece. (Red-red axis edges need NO cut: extra reds never violate blue <= red + 1 — this one-sidedness is why the constant is n.) Summing over p <= m+n pieces gives surplus = 2n = #blue - #red <= p <= m+n, hence m >= n.

technique: To induct on a lattice region, peel off a boundary layer chosen so that the complement is congruent to the same region one size smaller, reducing the count bound to forcing a single object to occupy exactly that layer.
how_used: For the diamond S_n = {(x,y) in Z^2 : |x| + |y+1/2| < n} (2n^2 points, symmetric about y=-1/2), take the right-hand boundary layer S = {(x,y) in S_n : x + |y+1/2| >= n-2}: a single connected staircase from the top point (0,n-1) down through (n-1,0),(n-1,-1) to the bottom point (0,-n), and S is Hamiltonian-traversable top-to-bottom. Its complement S_n \ S is congruent (a translation) to S_{n-1}. So once one shows a minimal partition contains a path P whose vertex set is exactly S, deleting P leaves a partition of S_{n-1}, which by the inductive hypothesis needs >= n-1 paths, giving >= n for S_n. The whole problem reduces to forcing one path to equal the layer S.

technique: Set up an induction on the size parameter by peeling off one canonical outer layer whose removal leaves a scaled-down copy of the same region, so a lower bound on the number of parts reduces to the same bound one size smaller.
how_used: Reformulate first: a partition of S_n into k paths is a degree-<=2 acyclic unit-edge graph with #paths = |S_n| - #edges, so a minimal partition maximizes edges. To lower-bound the path count by n, induct on n (base n=1 trivial). Choose the outer layer to be the L-shaped/boundary staircase S = {(x,y): x + |y+1/2| >= n-2}, running from the top point (0,n-1) down the right side through a=(n-1,0), b=(n-1,-1), to the bottom point (0,-n). The point of picking THIS S is that S_n minus S is exactly a translated/shrunk copy of S_{n-1}. So if one can show some minimal partition contains S as a single path P=S, deleting P leaves S_{n-1}, which by induction needs >= n-1 paths, giving S_n >= n paths. The whole difficulty is thus offloaded to producing a minimal partition in which P=S actually occurs.

technique: To guarantee a minimal/extremal configuration contains a desired canonical sub-structure, among all optimal configurations select one maximizing a secondary alignment statistic, then show any local deviation from the target admits an edge-count-preserving delete-one/add-one exchange that strictly increases the statistic, contradicting maximality.
how_used: We need a minimal partition of S_n in which the path P through a=(n-1,0) equals the staircase S. Among all minimal (edge-maximal) partitions, pick one maximizing N = number of vertices of S in the component of P containing a. Claim P=S. Minimality first forces edge a-b (b=(n-1,-1)): else a,b are both path-ends and adding a-b would merge two paths, lowering the count. Walk along P from a away from b; each way P can fail to hug S is a stall killed by a single delete-edge/add-edge swap that keeps #edges (hence optimality) but raises N: (i) P steps to v not in S -> with w the prior point and x the S-neighbor of w, delete vw and add wx; (ii) P dead-ends at an interior S-point v not the top (0,n-1) -> with w the next S-point, delete an edge touching w and add vw. Each swap preserves degrees (<=2) and acyclicity because the deleted edge frees exactly the degree the new edge consumes, and it strictly increases N, contradicting maximality. So P follows S up to (0,n-1) and, symmetrically, down to (0,-n), i.e. P=S.

technique: Enumerate the finitely many triangles that can rest on a fixed boundary edge by imposing the equal-length (isosceles) constraint on that edge
how_used: Chords of a regular n-gon have length determined by arc-span; a boundary edge A1A2 has span 1, and a triangle A1A2Ak has arc-spans (1, k-2, n-k+1). Isosceles means two spans are equal: span 1 = k-2 gives the small ear at A3, span 1 = n-k+1 gives the small ear at An, and k-2 = n-k+1 gives 2k = n+3, solvable only when n is odd (the big triangle at apex A_{(n+3)/2}). So each boundary edge admits exactly two legal triangles when n is even, three when n is odd.

technique: To constrain how a fixed object can be built, take a forced boundary edge and enumerate every admissible piece that can rest on it, reading off the possibilities from the equality condition (here, arc-length equalities) the admissibility demands.
how_used: Inscribe the vertices A_1..A_n on a circle and measure every chord by the number of arcs it subtends, so two chords are equal iff they subtend equal arcs and a polygon triangle is isosceles iff two of its three arc-lengths coincide. A short side A_kA_{k+1} (arc 1) with apex A_j has legs of arc |j-k| and |j-k-1|. Leg=base forces A_j adjacent, giving the two small 'ear' triangles A_{k-1}A_kA_{k+1} and A_kA_{k+1}A_{k+2}; leg=leg forces A_j on the base's perpendicular bisector, which for n even hits no further vertex but for n odd hits the single 'big' apex A_{k+(n+1)/2} whose two legs each subtend arc (n-1)/2. Menu: n even -> {two ears}; n odd -> {two ears, one big triangle}. Both descents run on this enumeration.

technique: When every forced boundary edge admits only a fixed local piece, delete all those pieces at once; the leftover boundary is a scaled copy of the same object, reducing the instance to a smaller one.
how_used: For even n>4, crux 0 leaves only ears on every short side, so each short side lies in an ear cutting off one endpoint vertex. An ear on A_kA_{k+1} simultaneously uses the neighbor short side, so the ears pair adjacent sides and must cut off alternate vertices; deleting all ears leaves the arc-2 chords A_1A_3, A_3A_5, ... which are all equal and bound a regular n/2-gon whose interior must again be isosceles-triangulated. Hence n works iff n/2 works; iterating strips all factors of 2, with base n=4 (two right-isosceles triangles) seeding the powers of 2. The alternation of the cut vertices is the execution detail: no two ears can claim the same short side, forcing a perfect alternating cover.

technique: Classify which triangles containing a forced boundary edge satisfy the shape constraint, by writing every triangle as its triple of boundary-arc lengths and testing the constraint on that triple, so each such edge gets a finite explicit menu of admissible triangles.
how_used: Every short side A_kA_{k+1} of the regular n-gon must lie in some triangle of the triangulation. Label a chord by its arc length (1..n-1); the chord length is a function of the arc, symmetric under arc j <-> arc n-j, so two chords are equal iff their arcs are equal or sum to n. A triangle on the short side has arcs (1,b,c) with b+c=n-1, and is isosceles iff two of its three chords are equal. Testing each equality: (i) the two arc-1... no; b=c gives b=c=(n-1)/2, possible only when n is odd (the 'big' triangle); (ii) arc 1 = arc b via 1+b=n forces b=n-1,c=0, impossible; (iii) an 'ear' where one of b,c equals 1, i.e. arcs (1,1,n-2). So the admissible menu on a short side is exactly {two ears} when n is even, and {two ears, one big triangle A_{(n+3)/2}A_1A_2 with both legs of arc (n-1)/2} when n is odd. This finite menu is the foundation both the even reduction and the odd forcing run on.

technique: When a forced boundary edge's isosceles menu contains only the two 'ear' triangles, each ear removes one vertex and fuses its two incident edges into a single next-scale edge; iterate to reduce the instance to the same problem on the alternate-vertex sub-polygon.
how_used: Inscribe the regular n-gon in a circle; a triangle on vertices spanning arcs (x,y,z) with x+y+z=n is isosceles iff two spans are equal. A short side has span 1, so edge A_kA_{k+1}'s third vertex at span-distance d gives spans (1,d,n-1-d), isosceles only for d=1, d=n-2 (the two ears A_kA_{k+1}A_{k+2}, A_{k-1}A_kA_{k+1}) or d=(n-1)/2 (a big triangle). For n EVEN, (n-1)/2 is non-integral so the big triangle is impossible: every short side's only options are the two ears. Cutting an ear deletes a vertex and merges two arc-1 sides into one arc-2 chord, so short sides get consumed two at a time and the surviving arc-2 chords form a regular n/2-gon that must itself be isosceles-triangulated (arc-2 chords are the unit edges at the next scale). Hence for even n>4, n works iff n/2 works; with n=4 working this gives all powers of 2 and reduces the even case to the odd case, contributing the factor 2^a in n=2^a(2^b+1).

technique: When a symmetric region's forced edges can only be paired off two at a time but their count is odd, a parity mismatch forces at least one edge into the single non-pairing piece; locate that piece and exploit its mirror symmetry to cut the region into two congruent sub-regions.
how_used: For n ODD, (n-1)/2 is an integer, so besides the two ears each short side A_kA_{k+1} also admits the big triangle T=A_kA_{k+1}A_m with m=k+(n+1)/2 and two equal legs of span (n-1)/2. Ears consume short sides two at a time (as in the even case), but n is odd so the n short sides cannot all be paired off by ears: at least one short side must lie in a big triangle T. T is symmetric across the perpendicular bisector of its base A_kA_{k+1}, and its two equal legs are chords that split the n-gon into two congruent 'fans', each bounded by one long leg (span (n-1)/2) and (n-1)/2 consecutive short sides. This is the entry move for the odd case: parity produces exactly the central big triangle whose symmetry halves the polygon, setting up a recursion on each identical half.

technique: After a symmetric split creates two congruent sub-regions each bounded by one long chord plus a run of unit edges, recurse the same triangulation argument on a half, treating the long chord as the base of its own forced central piece, to reduce the run-length to a smaller instance.
how_used: Each fan from the odd-case split has (n-1)/2 short sides sitting on a long base of span (n-1)/2. Running the same analysis inside a fan: the short sides again get paired off two at a time by ears, and by the same parity/symmetry argument the fan's forced structure reduces just as the whole polygon did, so triangulability of the fan drives (n-1)/2 down through repeated halving. Iterating the reduction forces n-1 to be a power of 2, i.e. n=2^b+1 for the odd factor. Composed with the even reduction's factor 2^a, the full classification is n=2^a(2^b+1) (a,b nonnegative, not both zero).

technique: Encode a per-vertex parity constraint as a single linear system over F_2 using the adjacency matrix as the operator
how_used: A 2-coloring is a vector v in F_2^n; "each mathematician sees an even number of friends in their own room" becomes A v = d, where A is the graph's adjacency matrix over F_2 with its diagonal reset to deg(v) mod 2 and d is that same diagonal. The solution set is then an affine coset of ker A, so its size is 0 or 2^(dim ker A) — a power of two — reducing the whole problem to showing the system is consistent.

technique: Over F_2, evaluate the quadratic form x^T A x for symmetric A so off-diagonal symmetric pairs cancel and only the diagonal survives
how_used: To prove A v = d is consistent, show d lies in the column space, i.e. d is orthogonal to every left-null covector ξ (ξ^T A = 0). The key identity: for symmetric A over F_2, ξ^T A ξ equals the diagonal dotted with ξ (the symmetric off-diagonal terms a_ij + a_ji cancel mod 2), and here the diagonal IS d, so ξ^T d = ξ^T A ξ = (ξ^T A) ξ = 0. Hence d has no obstruction and a valid coloring exists.

technique: Create a double threat where the opponent's single allowed response cannot block both winning lines simultaneously (a fork)
how_used: After x is fully surrounded and B is forced to remove x, A plays the two marked green cells, opening two distinct completions to 5-in-a-line through the region; whichever counter B removes next, the other red completion still yields 5 consecutive counters on A's following move, forcing the win.

technique: Plant a standing one-move threat whose only legal parry is a repair, so the opponent's turns are consumed repairing while your surplus placement enriches elsewhere
how_used: A places a counter-pair two cells apart on one line so the two inner empty cells x and y are each one placement short of completing the target run; to avoid an immediate loss B must spend his single removal each turn deleting whichever of x,y A just refilled. Because A's move places TWO counters, she uses one to repair the threatened cell and the other to add a counter adjacent to x, so B stays pinned to the x/y threat and can never touch the growing neighborhood. A keeps enriching around x until x is completely surrounded by counters.

technique: Close a forced position by making a single move that creates two independent one-move winning completions, so the opponent's one removal per turn cannot block both
how_used: After x has been surrounded and B is forced to remove x itself, A plays her two counters in the two marked green cells so that TWO distinct single-cell completions of a 5-run become simultaneously live. B can delete at most one per turn, so whichever of the two red completions he removes, the other still lets A finish the 5-in-a-line on her next move. This double threat converts the enriched neighborhood of x into the k=5 win.

technique: Bound the number of allowed moves by case-splitting a single move on its position within a run and reading off the fixed signed change it makes to the monovariant
how_used: Track the divider count D. Removing a TST (or, identically, an STS) sits inside one zigzag; case-split on where: at a zigzag endpoint the move deletes one divider and merges two zigzags (D decreases by 1); strictly interior the move creates one divider and splits the zigzag (D increases by 1). So every move changes D by exactly +/-1. Since the game must reach D=0 (empty necklace) in 2n moves and can lower D by at most 1 per move, a Tasty-first win forces the starting D0 <= 2n. This gives the NECESSITY half of the symmetric criterion, and it uses no color information, so it applies verbatim to a Stacy-first start.

technique: When two population counts are equal, invoke the forced balance between the two types to guarantee each player always has a legal move, patching the all-even degenerate case with a length threshold that must be hit on average
how_used: For sufficiency (D0 <= 2n, no length-1 zigzag => winnable): because #S = #T, the number of odd-length zigzags (length >=3) with T-endpoints equals the number with S-endpoints. So if any odd zigzag exists, both a TST endpoint move (for Tasty) and an STS endpoint move (for Stacy) are simultaneously available; if all zigzags are even, some has length >=4 (average length is 6n/D >= 3), and Tasty removing TST from its T-end yields an odd, S-ended zigzag that hands Stacy her move. Endpoint moves lower D by 1 and never create a singleton (zigzags merge, not split), so both players can drive D to 0 and win. Since move-availability is argued symmetrically in S and T, the identical alternation works with Stacy first — completing the criterion's sufficiency for both start orders.

technique: Re-encode a two-colored cyclic word by placing a marker on every same-color adjacent pair, so the state is described by the color-blind marker count rather than by which color sits where
how_used: Draw a divider between any two adjacent beads of the SAME color. The dividers cut the necklace into maximal alternating 'zigzag' runs, each with two endpoints. The 'no three consecutive same color' hypothesis becomes exactly 'no zigzag of length 1' (a singleton run would force its two neighbors, both of the opposite color to it, to match each other across it only if... precisely: a length-1 zigzag means a bead flanked by dividers on both sides, i.e. its two neighbors share its... ) — operationally: singleton run <=> three same-color beads in a row is forbidden. The divider count D equals the number of same-color adjacent pairs, and is DEFINED without reference to which color is which. So D, and any statement phrased purely in D, is automatically invariant under the color-swap involution S<->T. Because the number of S and T beads are equal, #SS = #TT, so the same-color adjacency structure is genuinely symmetric under the swap. This color-blind coordinate is what makes a Tasty-first and a Stacy-first game comparable at all; it does NOT by itself prove anything about winnability.

technique: Show a natural integer statistic of the state is a monovariant under every legal move, then use its monotone/bounded behavior to pin down exactly which starting states can reach the terminal state
how_used: Track D = number of dividers (same-color adjacent pairs), equivalently the number of maximal alternating zigzags; the no-triple hypothesis says exactly that no zigzag has length 1. Check by casework where the removed triple sits inside a zigzag: a move at a zigzag ENDPOINT merges two neighboring zigzags and gives dD = -1, while a move from the INTERIOR splits a zigzag and gives dD = +1, so every move changes D by exactly +1 or -1. The whole game consumes all 6n beads in exactly 2n moves and ends at the empty necklace with D = 0, so the 2n unit steps sum to -D_initial, forcing #(+1 moves) = (2n - D_initial)/2 >= 0, i.e. D_initial <= 2n. This is the necessity half, and since D counts same-color pairs irrespective of which color, the bound D <= 2n is stated in a color-blind coordinate and holds identically for Tasty-first and Stacy-first games. (This direction does not use the no-triple hypothesis.)

technique: Prove sufficiency of a bound by exhibiting, at every non-terminal position, a legal move for each player that decreases the monovariant without violating the state constraint, via a parity/counting argument on the run structure
how_used: Assuming D <= 2n and no length-1 zigzag, show both players can always take an endpoint (merge, dD = -1) move, which never creates a singleton zigzag (a merge joins two runs of length >=1 into one of length >=3), so D descends to 0 where the necklace is a single alternating cycle TSTS... and removal completes trivially. The counting engine: since #S = #T, an even zigzag carries equal S and T while an odd (>=3) zigzag has one surplus of its endpoint color, so #(odd zigzags with T endpoints) = #(odd zigzags with S endpoints). If at least one of each exists, Tasty removes TST from the T end of one and Stacy removes STS from the S end of another. Otherwise all zigzags are even, so a length-4 zigzag exists (average length 6n/D >= 3); Tasty removes TST from its T end, the merged zigzag becomes odd with S endpoints, and Stacy can now move. Either way both players get an endpoint move each turn, sustaining the descent. Carried out in the D/zigzag language, this applies identically to a Stacy-first game.

technique: Build the set from a linear recurrence where each element is the sum of two earlier ones, so swapping an element for its two predecessors keeps a subset's sum fixed while raising its cardinality by one.
how_used: Elements are chosen so s_{2i+1}=s_{2i}+s_{2i-1} (concretely the pairs 1*3^k, 2*3^k with 2*3^k + 1*3^k = 3^{k+1}=1*3^{k+1}); replacing one term by its two smaller summands grows an m-subset to an (m+1)-subset with the same total 3^n, generating all required A_m for m=2,...,n from a single seed subset A_2={3^{n-1},2*3^{n-1}}. Explicitly A_m={2*3^k: k=n-m+1..n-1} union {3^{n-m+1}} sums to 3^n.

technique: Set the total to a clean target by adding two glue elements (a small one and a large complementary one) so the whole set sums to exactly twice the half-target you need to hit.
how_used: Adjoin 1 and (3^n+9)/2 - 1 to the geometric pairs so that the total telescopes to Sigma = 2*3^n (since the pairs sum to (3^{n+1}-9)/2), making the needed subset sum exactly 3^n; the two extra elements are picked non-divisible by 3 to guarantee all 2n integers are distinct from the 3-divisible geometric terms.

technique: Restrict a placement game to a large independent set of the conflict graph so alternation alone guarantees a player at least half of it
how_used: Horst places knights only on the 200 same-color squares; since a knight always jumps to the opposite color these form an independent set (same-color knights never attack), so no move is ever blocked by an attack, only by occupancy. As the players alternate, each round removes at most 2 of the 200 pool squares, so Horst still finds an empty same-color square on each of his first 100 moves, forcing at least 100 knights

technique: Cap each cycle of a conflict-cycle partition at one piece by responding on the antipodal vertex, whose occupancy plus the placed piece's two neighbor-attacks seal the cycle
how_used: With the 400 cells partitioned into 100 knight 4-cycles A-B-C-D-A, whenever Horst places a knight on a cycle vertex, Queenie places her queen on the antipodal vertex of that same cycle. The antipode is empty (the cycle was untouched before Horst's move), so the response is legal. Afterwards the two occupied vertices are opposite, and the other two are the knight's cycle-neighbors hence attacked by it, so no further knight can enter the cycle. At most one knight per cycle gives at most 100 knights, the matching upper bound.

technique: Partition every cell into vertex-disjoint short conflict-cycles by tiling with a small block and repeating one fixed choice of covering cycles per block
how_used: Tile the 20x20 board with 25 disjoint 4x4 blocks. Inside one 4x4 block, hand-pick four vertex-disjoint knight 4-cycles that together cover all 16 cells using only knight moves internal to the block (one valid choice: {(0,0),(1,2),(3,3),(2,1)}, {(0,1),(1,3),(3,2),(2,0)}, {(0,2),(1,0),(3,1),(2,3)}, {(0,3),(1,1),(3,0),(2,2)}). Because every chosen cycle stays inside its block, repeating the same choice in all 25 blocks partitions the 400 cells into 100 disjoint knight 4-cycles A-B-C-D-A. The block's induced knight graph is NOT 2-regular, so this is a chosen sub-collection of 4-cycles, not the whole induced subgraph. This partition is the scaffold on which Queenie's pairing response (a separate move) runs.

technique: Secure a guaranteed placement count by restricting the mover to a large monochromatic conflict-free class and counting alternating turns against its size
how_used: Color the board in the usual chessboard pattern; a knight move always changes color, so two knights on same-color cells never attack each other, and all 200 black cells form a conflict-free class where any placement is legal. Horst always plays an empty black cell. Before his k-th move (k<=100) at most 2k-2<=198 cells are occupied, so fewer than 200 black cells are taken and an empty black cell always remains; hence Horst places at least 100 knights regardless of Queenie. This is the achievability half matching the 100 upper bound.

technique: Cap each disjoint conflict-cycle at one placement by having the responder immediately occupy the mover's cyclic-opposite vertex in that cycle
how_used: On the partition of the 400 squares into 100 knight 4-cycles A-B-C-D-A (consecutive vertices attacking: A~B, B~C, C~D, D~A; opposite vertices non-attacking: A,C and B,D), the ONLY way Horst gets two knights into one cycle is by taking a non-attacking opposite pair. Queenie's response rule: whenever Horst plays a square A in cycle A-B-C-D-A, she immediately plays the opposite square C of that same cycle (empty because Horst's move was the cycle's first touch). Afterward Horst cannot use A or C (occupied) nor B or D (both attacked by the knight on A, since A~B and A~D), so each cycle ever holds at most one Horst knight, giving at most 100 knights total. This is the response that turns the partition scaffold into the upper bound K<=100.

technique: For a lower bound in a placement game with a mutual-conflict constraint, have the mover confine all placements to an independent set of the conflict graph so no placement can ever be blocked by an earlier one of his own
how_used: Horst's guaranteed-100 half: checkerboard-colour the 20x20 board. A knight always moves to the opposite colour, so two knights on same-colour squares never attack: the 200 black squares form an independent set in the knight-attack graph. Horst plays only on empty black squares, so his non-attacking rule is automatically satisfied no matter where his previous knights sit. The only way he can be stopped is running out of empty black squares. Before his k-th move, k-1 knights and k-1 queens have been placed, so at most 2(k-1) black squares are gone; for k<=100, 2(k-1)<=198<200, so an empty black square always remains. Hence Horst can make 100 moves, giving K>=100.

technique: For an upper bound in a placement game, partition the conflict graph into small identical components each of which can hold at most one non-conflicting piece, and have the blocker respond inside the same component the mover just used to exhaust it
how_used: Queenie's cap-at-100 half: view squares as vertices with an edge between any two squares a knight-move apart. On a 4x4 board these attack-edges organize the 16 squares into 4 disjoint 4-cycles A-B-C-D-A; tiling the 20x20 board with twenty-five 4x4 blocks partitions all 400 squares into 100 such 4-cycles. When Horst plays a square A in a cycle A-B-C-D-A, Queenie plays the opposite vertex C (equivalently, reflect A through the centre of its 4x4 block). Now A and C are occupied and B, D are both attacked by the knight on A, so no further knight can go in that cycle. Every Horst move thus permanently uses up one whole cycle, so he places at most one knight per cycle, i.e. at most 100 knights: K<=100. Combined with K>=100 gives K=100.

technique: Impose a labeling/tie-breaking rule on interchangeable objects so a per-object invariant becomes provable, exploiting that the choice of which object to move is free.
how_used: Since the n stones are indistinguishable, number them 1..n and always move the highest-numbered stone available in the chosen square. Because the labels present in any square are distinct positive integers, their count is at most their maximum; so when stone k (the current max) is moved, its square holds at most k stones, hence stone k advances by at most k squares per move.

technique: Turn a fixed total displacement plus a per-step size cap into a per-object move-count lower bound via a ceiling, then sum the independent bounds over all objects.
