(Boundary care: because the children sit on a CIRCLE, the naive weight i^2 need not increase at the sink-adjacent cell n-1, since one of its coins crosses into the excluded sink; a fresh solver must either restrict to a linearized potential or invoke the abelian/finiteness of chip-firing to close halting there.)

technique: Establish a long-range transport primitive that moves surplus across an intervening run of unit cells in one net move -- prove it by induction on the run length, using the base operation to bump-and-relay the surplus one cell outward per inductive step.
how_used: This is the load-bearing lemma the M-reduction treats as a black box, and it must be PROVEN, not assumed. Claim: from a block a, 1^k, b, 1^k, c with b>=2 (b coins flanked by two equal runs of k ones, then endpoints a,c), a legal sequence of single fires reaches a+1, 1^k, b-2, 1^k, c+1 -- i.e. the pile b ships one coin out each side across the k ones to the endpoints. Induct on k. k=0 is the raw operation. k>=1: fire the b-child, then fire both freshly-created neighbors, producing ...,2,0,b,0,2,... then discharge every interior 2 outward until none remain, which shrinks both runs to 1^{k-2} and re-centers to the SAME pattern a+1,0,1^{k-2},b,1^{k-2},0,c+1 with gap k-2; the induction hypothesis then delivers the coins to the two zeros. This proves the primitive is always executable (no cell gets stuck below 2 before the coin arrives), which is precisely the feasibility the solver could not verify.

technique: Drive an integer defect monovariant strictly down by repeatedly invoking the transport primitive to bleed a single surplus toward its two nearest deficits, with casework on the two flanking gap lengths and an inner monovariant (a strictly shortening block) guaranteeing each round terminates.
how_used: From a semi-uniform state of irregularity M, reduce M. If M>3 then (only n coins) at least two children are empty, so the pile sits in an arc 0,1^a,M,1^b,0. If a=b, long-pass (transport primitive) the pile out both sides into the two zeros, dropping M. If a!=b (WLOG a>b) long-pass symmetrically only to distance b, filling the near zeros but leaving a stray 2 at distance one further out: 0,1^alpha,2,1^beta,M-2,... Then repeatedly long-pass that stray 2 toward its nearest 0 plus one other cell; the inner monovariant is the length of the block between the two relevant zeros, which strictly shrinks each pass (so the inner loop cannot run forever), and an alpha=beta alignment lets a final long-pass reach irregularity M-1. Each outer round strictly lowers M, an integer bounded below, so the process halts at a semi-uniform state with M<=2 -- the input the endgame invariant argument consumes. Rely on the separately-proven transport primitive for every long-pass; the ONLY new content here is the M-monovariant plus the inner shrinking-block monovariant.

technique: Close the endgame by evaluating the preserved linear-weight invariant on the single non-uniform terminal state and reading off a divisibility contradiction that rules that state out.
how_used: After reduction the only non-trivial terminal case is irregularity M=2: one child with 0, one with 2, rest 1. Place the M-child at index n; let the empty child be index k (1<=k<=n-1). The invariant sum_{i=1}^n i c_i = n(n+1)/2 (mod n) is preserved from the start, and here equals (sum_i c_i) - k = n(n+1)/2 - k (mod n), forcing k = 0 (mod n) -- impossible since 1<=k<=n-1. Hence M=2 is unreachable, so reduction must stop at M=1 = all-ones. This is the step that converts the (necessary) invariant into a SUFFICIENCY-completing contradiction; it is the reason the invariant is not just necessary but exactly characterizes reachability.

technique: To count objects with a hard-to-verify property, build an injection from a full easily-counted domain by perturbing each element into one that provably has the property.
how_used: Inject all n^n functions f: X->{1,...,n} into the set of nice functions X->{1,...,n+1}: given f, pick a set X_l maximizing f(X_l) and define f^+ = f+1 on X_l, f^+ = f elsewhere; this lands in the nice-function count, giving the >= n^n bound.

technique: Turn a non-tie among aggregate sums into a strict inequality by comparing whole-set weight against overlap weight of the added increment.
how_used: After bumping f by +1 on X_l, f^+(X_i)=f(X_i)+|X_i cap X_l|. Since X_l maximizes f, X_l is not a subset of any X_j, so |X_l|>|X_j cap X_l|; then f^+(X_l)=f(X_l)+|X_l| >= f(X_j)+|X_l| > f(X_j)+|X_j cap X_l|=f^+(X_j), making X_l the unique maximizer.

technique: Guarantee injectivity of a perturbation map by making the perturbation reversible: read off from the image the unique locus that was modified, then undo the modification.
how_used: Reconstruct f from f^+: the unique maximizer X_l of f^+ is forced, so decrease f^+ by 1 on X_l to recover f, proving distinct f give distinct nice f^+.

technique: Find an odd modulus whose divisibility of every pile is forced to persist backward through the move, so a target divisible by it is unreachable from an indivisible start
how_used: The move replaces piles of sizes a,b (and an empty pile) by a-c, b-c, 2c. If an odd m divides all three resulting sizes, then m|2c with m odd gives m|c, hence m|(a-c)+c=a and m|(b-c)+c=b: divisibility by any fixed odd m>1 is preserved backward along every move. A single final pile of n is divisible by an odd m>1 whenever n is not a power of two, so it would force the all-ones start to be divisible by m, which is false. This gives the lower bound of at least 2 piles for non-powers-of-two.

technique: To hit an arbitrary target pile size, over-build one pile past the target, then shrink it one unit at a time by repeatedly applying the operation between it and a small shuttling auxiliary pile.
how_used: For n not a power of two, pick N with 2^N<n<2^{N+1} and set m=n-2^N, so 0<m<2^N. First assemble a pile of size 2^N (the routine power-of-two doubling), leaving m single-pebble piles untouched. Now shrink this large pile from 2^N down to exactly m: take one pebble from the large pile plus one single-pebble pile to form a 2-pile; thereafter each step takes one pebble from the large pile and one from the current 2-pile, forming a fresh 2-pile (the old 2-pile becomes a single pebble). Each application lowers the large pile by 1 and conserves the total at n. Stop when the large pile equals m. The endpoint is one m-pile, one 2-pile, and 2^N-2 single pebbles. The solver still must reassemble those 2^N-2 singletons plus the 2-pile into one pile: pair the singletons into 2-piles giving 2^{N-1} piles of size 2, then double up to a single pile of 2^N, leaving exactly the two piles {m, 2^N}. Key discipline: the move never transfers pebbles between two existing piles; it deletes c from each of two piles and creates a new pile of 2c, so every intermediate configuration has total exactly n.

technique: Prove an operation cannot reach a target state by exhibiting a divisibility property that the move preserves under time-reversal: if every pile after a move shares an odd common factor, so did every pile before it.
how_used: This is the lower-bound / impossibility half: show that when n is not a power of two, you can never reduce to a single pile. Write a move as: from piles of sizes a and b remove c from each and create a pile of size 2c (view the created pile as starting from a phantom 0-pile). Suppose an odd integer d>1 divides every pile AFTER the move; then d|2c, d|a-c, d|b-c, and since d is odd d|c, hence d|a and d|b — so d divided every pile BEFORE the move too. Thus the odd-common-divisor property propagates backwards along any sequence of moves. A single final pile of n pebbles is divisible by every odd divisor of n; since n not a power of two has some odd d>1 dividing it, reaching that single pile would force d to divide every pile in the starting all-ones configuration — impossible, since single-pebble piles are only divisible by d=1. Hence at least two piles must remain, giving the bound 2 (matched by the construction).

technique: Encode a per-coordinate indicator by evaluating a downward quadratic in the coordinate index that peaks at a chosen target index, then take the coordinatewise max over all targets to assemble the all-ones and standard-basis tuples
how_used: With seeds a_i=-i^2 and b_i=i and constant c=(-1,...,-1), the additive combination d(j)=2a+4j*b+(2j^2-1)c has d(j)_i = 1-2(i-j)^2, equal to 1 at i=j and <=-1 elsewhere; d(1) v ... v d(n) is the all-ones tuple 1, then 0 = 1+c and e(j) = d(j) v 0 isolates each standard basis tuple

technique: Reduce generating an arbitrary target to producing a fixed generating set by writing the target as a nonnegative combination of the basis indicators plus a uniform negative-constant shift
how_used: Given e(1),...,e(n) and c=(-1,...,-1), any tuple v equals k*c + sum_i (k+v_i)*e(i) for k large enough that k+v_i>0, so v is reachable using only additions of nonnegative integer multiples of the generating tuples

technique: Exhibit a homogeneous two-coordinate linear inequality x_j >= a*x_k (a>=0) that is closed under both operations, so any property shared by all seeds is shared by every generated tuple
how_used: For a>=0, if v_j>=a*v_k and w_j>=a*w_k then (v+w)_j >= a*(v+w)_k, and for m=v v w one has m_j >= a*v_k and m_j >= a*w_k while m_k is v_k or w_k, so m_j>=a*m_k; hence a common such inequality on the two seeds is inherited by everything they generate, blocking tuples that violate it

technique: Find a monoid invariant that survives a max/join operation by using a homogeneous two-coordinate inequality x_j >= a x_k: it is preserved under coordinatewise sum trivially and under coordinatewise max because the max's k-coordinate equals one operand's, which already dominates a times the corresponding j-side.
how_used: Observation for the s>=3 lower bound: if seeds v,w both satisfy v_j>=a*v_k and w_j>=a*w_k (a>=0), then v+w satisfies it by adding the inequalities, and m=v v w satisfies it because m_j>=v_j>=a*v_k and m_j>=w_j>=a*w_k while m_k equals v_k or w_k, so m_j>=a*m_k. By induction every generated tuple obeys the inequality; but all integer tuples include ones violating any nontrivial such inequality (e.g. large x_k, x_j=0), so two seeds sharing one homogeneous inequality can never generate everything — this is the contradiction the pigeonhole/ratio cruxes feed into, forcing s>=3.

technique: Under a sign-based obstruction on two vectors, split each coordinate by whether the two vectors weakly agree in sign there (zero-inclusive >=) versus strictly disagree, so the strictly-disagreeing coordinates realize only a bounded number of sign patterns and pigeonhole forces two coordinates into the same pattern.
how_used: To show s=2 fails, suppose only seeds v,w. Case A: some coordinate i has v_i,w_i >= 0 (or both <= 0) — the weak, zero-inclusive inequality makes any coordinate where either seed is 0 fall here; then sign of coordinate i is preserved by + and by max, so no tuple with the opposite strict sign in coordinate i is reachable, contradiction. Case B (complement): every coordinate has v_i,w_i strictly opposite signs (v_i>0>w_i or v_i<0<w_i), so each coordinate is strictly nonzero and its (sign v_i, sign w_i) is one of only TWO patterns (+,-) or (-,+). With n>=3 coordinates, pigeonhole gives j!=k in the same pattern, so v_j,v_k share a strict sign and w_j,w_k share a strict sign; WLOG v_j,v_k>0 and w_j,w_k<0. The zero-inclusive split makes the surviving coordinates strictly signed so the ratio a=v_j/v_k in the next crux is well-defined and positive.

technique: Given two coordinates where each of two vectors is single-signed, take one vector's coordinate ratio as the slope and compare the other vector's ratio against it to select which of the two directions of a homogeneous two-coordinate inequality is satisfied by BOTH vectors at once.
how_used: With v_j,v_k>0 and w_j,w_k<0 (from the pigeonhole crux), set a=v_j/v_k>0, so v satisfies x_j>=a*x_k with equality. Compare w_j/w_k to a: if w_j/w_k<=a then clearing the negative denominator w_k gives w_j>=a*w_k, so BOTH seeds satisfy x_j>=a*x_k; otherwise w_j/w_k>a gives w_k>=(1/a)*w_j and also v_k>=(1/a)*v_j, so both seeds satisfy x_k>=(1/a)*x_j. Either branch yields one nontrivial homogeneous inequality x_p>=a'*x_q (a'>0) satisfied by both seeds, which the invariant crux then propagates to every generated tuple, forcing the contradiction.

technique: To prove a closure process (generated from seeds by given operations) cannot reach every element, find a homogeneous pairwise inequality of the form (one coordinate) >= a*(another coordinate), a>=0, that every operation preserves, so if all seeds satisfy it then every generated tuple does.
how_used: The two operations are coordinatewise sum and coordinatewise max. If v_j >= a*v_k and w_j >= a*w_k (a>=0), then for v+w add the inequalities: (v+w)_j = v_j+w_j >= a*v_k+a*w_k = a*(v+w)_k; and for m = v v w, m_j >= v_j >= a*v_k and m_j >= w_j >= a*w_k while m_k equals v_k or w_k, so m_j >= a*m_k. Hence any such inequality holding on all starting tuples is inherited by everything generated. Since a huge/tiny integer tuple violates any fixed such inequality, if the seeds all satisfy one, not every tuple is reachable. This is the invariant the lower bound rests on.

technique: To build a coordinatewise indicator (peak at a chosen index, low elsewhere) from a few fixed integer seeds, take an integer combination of the seeds whose i-th coordinate is a negated perfect square in (i - target) so it peaks at the target and drops off, then clamp and combine targets with coordinatewise max.
how_used: Three seeds suffice: a_i=-i^2, b_i=i, c_i=-1. For each target j form d(j)=2a+4j*b+(2j^2-1)*c (all coefficients nonnegative, so reachable by repeated addition), whose i-th coordinate is -2i^2+4ij-(2j^2-1)=1-2(i-j)^2: equal to 1 at i=j and <=-1 otherwise. Then 1=(1,...,1)=d(1) v ... v d(n); 0=1+c; and the indicator e(j)=d(j) v 0 (off-target coords clamp up to 0). Having all e(j) and c, any integer tuple v is reachable as k*c + sum_i (k+v_i)*e(i) with k large enough that k+v_i>0, since the i-th coordinate is -k+(k+v_i)=v_i. This proves s<=3.

technique: To prove a target state is unreachable under a set of closed operations, find a homogeneous linear inequality between two coordinates that every operation preserves, then show the seeds satisfy it but the target does not.
how_used: The invariant is a pairwise inequality x_j >= a*x_k for a fixed real a >= 0 and fixed coordinates j,k. Check closure under both allowed operations: under coordinatewise addition, x_j+y_j >= a*x_k + a*y_k = a*(x+y)_k; under coordinatewise max m = x V y, m_j >= x_j >= a*x_k and m_j >= y_j >= a*y_k, and since m_k equals x_k or y_k, m_j >= a*m_k. Hence if BOTH seeds satisfy x_j >= a*x_k, so does every reachable tuple. But the all-integer-tuple target contains tuples violating any such inequality (e.g. one with j-th coordinate one unit below a times the k-th), so if the two seeds can be forced into one such inequality, not everything is reachable. (Also the degenerate single-coordinate inequality x_i >= 0, i.e. a=0 with k=i, or x_i <= 0, is preserved the same way.)

technique: To force any two given seeds into a common preserved pairwise inequality, first sign-split the coordinates: a shared same-sign coordinate gives a one-coordinate obstruction outright; otherwise pigeonhole two coordinates with matching sign-patterns and pick the ratio direction both seeds obey.
how_used: With only two seeds v,w: Case 1, if some coordinate i has v_i,w_i both >= 0 (or both <= 0), the preserved inequality x_i >= 0 (resp. x_i <= 0) already blocks reaching any tuple with negative (resp. positive) i-th coordinate. Case 2, otherwise every coordinate i is strictly sign-split (v_i>0>w_i or v_i<0<w_i), giving each coordinate one of only TWO sign-pattern labels; with n >= 3 coordinates, pigeonhole yields j != k with v_j,v_k the same sign and w_j,w_k the same sign. WLOG v_j,v_k>0 and w_j,w_k<0. Set a = v_j/v_k > 0. If w_j/w_k <= a then (note w_k<0, so this rearranges with a sign-flip to) w_j >= a*w_k and also v_j >= a*v_k, so both seeds obey x_j >= a*x_k; otherwise both obey x_k >= (1/a)*x_j. Either way both seeds satisfy one preserved inequality — this is exactly where n >= 3 is used.

technique: To build a coordinate-selector or indicator tuple, engineer an affine-in-index quadratic whose discriminant makes it a downward parabola in (index - target), peaking at a single index, then take a coordinatewise max over targets to extract a constant/indicator tuple.
how_used: Show 3 seeds suffice by producing e(1),...,e(n) and c=(-1,...,-1), from which any tuple v is reachable as k*c + sum_i (k+v_i)*e(i) for k large enough that k+v_i>0. Take seeds a with a_i = -i^2, b with b_i = i, and c with c_i = -1. For each target j form d(j) = 2a + 4j*b + (2j^2-1)*c by repeated addition; its i-th coordinate is -2i^2 + 4ij - (2j^2-1) = 1 - 2(i-j)^2, which equals 1 exactly when i=j and is <= -1 otherwise. Then d(1) V ... V d(n) = the all-ones tuple 1; add c to get 0; and e(j) = d(j) V 0 (picking out the single coordinate where d(j) is 1). This yields all e(j), completing the construction.

technique: Recast a global count as a per-endpoint tally satisfying a local recurrence, then sum that auxiliary array.
how_used: Instead of counting good paths directly, put in each cell B the number of good paths ending there; a well (local minimum) gets 1, every other cell gets the sum of its smaller-valued neighbors' B-values, and the answer is the sum of all B-entries.

technique: Charge each summand of a neighbor-sum quantity down to the adjacent edge it came from, turning the total into an edge count bounded below by the minimum per-edge weight.
how_used: Each non-well B-value is a sum over smaller neighbors; ascribe to every adjacent pair the lower of its two B-values, so the non-well total equals a sum over the 2n(n-1) grid edges, each term at least 1, plus at least one well, giving 2n(n-1)+1 = 2n^2-2n+1.

technique: Count objects by a per-vertex tally obeying a sum-over-smaller-neighbors recurrence, then lower-bound the total by charging each non-base unit to the incident edge whose lower endpoint carries it.
how_used: Let B(v) = number of good paths ending at field v. A well (a field all of whose neighbors are larger) has B=1 (the length-1 path); every other field has B(v) = sum of B over adjacent fields of smaller value, since a good path enters v only from a lower neighbor. The answer is sum_v B(v). Split this sum: the base contribution equals the number of wells, which is >= 1 (the field labeled 1 is always a well). The rest is sum over each adjacent pair of B(lower endpoint); since B >= 1 everywhere, each of the 2n(n-1) grid edges contributes >= 1. Hence total >= 2n(n-1) + 1 = 2n^2 - 2n + 1. Equality forces exactly one well and B(lower endpoint) = 1 on every edge.

technique: Translate the equality case of a per-edge bound into a structural constraint on which vertices carry the base value, reducing the extremal problem to constructing a marked set with prescribed domination/independence/acyclicity.
how_used: Equality needs exactly one well and every edge's lower endpoint to have B=1. Call B=1 fields 'marked'. No edge may have its lower endpoint unmarked, so unmarked (B>1) fields form an independent set and marked fields form a dominating set. A non-well marked field must have exactly one smaller neighbor and it must be marked, so ordered by value the marked fields form a rooted tree (each attaches to one earlier marked field), i.e. the marked set induces a connected acyclic subgraph rooted at the single well. Conversely any marked set M that is dominating, has independent complement, and induces a tree realizes equality: number M first in a tree order from the root (each marked cell then has one smaller marked neighbor, B=1), then number all unmarked cells afterward (their neighbors are all smaller and marked, so every incident edge charges 1 and they are never wells). Reduction: build M dominating, independent complement, tree-inducing.

technique: On a grid, realize a required dominating spanning tree with independent complement as a comb: a connected acyclic backbone along one edge plus periodically spaced teeth, offsetting the period per residue class so the leftover complement cells stay pairwise non-adjacent up to the boundary.
how_used: The remaining task is to exhibit, for every n, a marked set M that is dominating, has independent complement, and induces a tree. Use a comb: a connected backbone of marked cells running down the first two columns (a path, not a solid 2xn block, so it stays acyclic and connected) plus teeth attached periodically and reaching across each row so every unmarked cell is adjacent to a marked one (domination). Space the teeth on row-period 6 with an offset s depending on n mod 3 (s=2 for n=0,2 mod 3; s=1 for n=1 mod 3) so the unmarked cells never touch, placing successive teeth on columns of opposite parity so consecutive unmarked cells sit in non-adjacent columns. Verify per residue class that domination, independence of the complement, and acyclicity hold including at the ragged bottom/right boundary. Handle n=1 (single cell) and n=2 (L-tromino) explicitly. This attains total 2n^2-2n+1 for all n.

technique: Count the extremal objects by their terminal element, giving each cell a count equal to the sum over its already-processed smaller neighbors, so a global total becomes a quantity read off the adjacency structure.
how_used: Build an auxiliary board B whose entry at a cell is the number of good increasing paths that END there. A 'well' (a cell all of whose neighbors carry larger numbers) has exactly one path ending in it (itself); any other cell's entry equals the sum of the entries of its smaller-valued neighbors, since a good path can only enter it from a lower neighbor. Filling B in increasing order of the values in A makes this a well-founded fill: a cell with no already-filled neighbor is exactly a well and gets 1, every other cell gets the sum of its filled neighbors. Because every good path has a unique terminal cell, the total number of good paths equals the sum of all entries of B, converting the objective into 'minimize sum(B)'.

technique: To lower-bound a sum of per-cell contributions where each contribution is a sum over smaller neighbors, recharge each summand to the incident edge (assign it to the edge's lower endpoint), so the total becomes a sum over edges of a per-edge quantity that is at least 1, and read the equality conditions off directly.
how_used: Each non-well entry of B is a sum over its smaller neighbors, so ascribe to each adjacent pair the entry written on its lower-valued endpoint; summing over all adjacent pairs recovers exactly the sum of non-well entries. Each ascribed value is at least 1, so the non-well sum is at least the number of edges of the n x n grid, which is 2n(n-1); adding the forced 1 from the global-minimum well gives total >= 2n(n-1)+1 = 2n^2-2n+1. Equality forces exactly one well and forces every edge to have a lower endpoint with entry 1, i.e. no two entries exceeding 1 are adjacent.

technique: To realize an extremal bound, translate the equality conditions into a marking problem and exhibit an explicit periodic construction: mark a connected spanning set whose unmarked complement is an independent set, then order the values so the marked cells receive the small counts.
how_used: Equality requires the entry-1 cells (the marked set) to form a connected tree spanning the board while the entry->1 cells (unmarked) form an independent set with no two adjacent. Concretely one marks a snake of cells running through the first two columns as a connected backbone, then attaches marked 'combs' on a period-6 schedule (offset s = 2 for n ≡ 0,2 mod 3 and s = 1 for n ≡ 1 mod 3), arranged so the leftover unmarked cells sit in columns of opposite parity and are therefore pairwise non-adjacent, and no cycle is created. Base cases n=1 (single cell) and n=2 (L-tromino) are handled directly. Assigning values so that A increases outward from the single well along this marked tree makes every marked cell get B=1, attaining 2n^2-2n+1.

technique: Attain an extremal parity/rank count by tuning the ordering slope just below or above an integer so the rank formula collapses on the boundary rows, then propagate parities across the grid through the local square identity.
how_used: Pick alpha ~= 199.999 (just under 200): then f(n,0)=#{(x,y): x+199y<n}=n gives the bottom row parity alternating, and f(0,k)=200A-k gives f(0,k)=k mod 2 for the left column. Feeding these two boundary sequences into f(x,y)+f(x+1,y+1)=f(x+1,y)+f(x,y+1)+1 propagates parities so that even-index rows alternate (50 odds each) and odd-index rows are all odd (100 odds each), giving N=50*50+50*100=7500. Taking alpha ~= 200.001 swaps the pattern and yields N=2500. With the [2500,7500] bound this shows both extremes are attained.

technique: When an order-preserving shift hypothesis forces every translate to compare consistently, define a real threshold as the infimum of the direction-ratios whose translation stays orientation-consistent, and bridge back to the map by a sign-casework lemma: split on the signs of the two coordinate differences and route each case to the correct side of the threshold.
how_used: Call (k,l) a 'needle' if f(x+k,y)>f(x,y+l) for all (x,y); the strengthened equivalence form of the hypothesis makes needles and non-needles each closed under addition (hence integer scaling/division), so a needle depends only on its ratio k/l, which is upward-closed. Grades exist and small ratios are non-grades, so alpha := inf(grades) is real. The load-bearing move (the Key Property) is the sign-casework: if x1+y1*alpha > x2+y2*alpha, case on the signs of x1-x2 and y1-y2 — when the two differences have opposite signs, the ratio (x1-x2)/(y2-y1) lands strictly above alpha (a grade, so a needle) or strictly below (a non-needle), each forcing f(x1,y1)>f(x2,y2); the same-sign case is immediate. This makes f order (x,y) by the linear functional x+y*alpha; perturbing alpha to a nearby irrational leaves f unchanged on the 100x100 window and kills ties, giving the rank formula f(a,b)=#{(x,y): x+y*alpha < a+b*alpha}.

technique: Prove a fixed local additive identity on every unit cell by double-counting the lattice points a rank/count formula assigns to two adjacent half-open strips, matching them via a boundary-row bijection that accounts for the +1.
how_used: Using f(a,b)=#{(x,y): x+y*alpha<a+b*alpha}, compute f(x+1,y+1)-f(x,y+1) as the count of points in the strip x+(y+1)alpha <= a+b*alpha < (x+1)+(y+1)alpha; peel off the b=0 boundary row and shift it (drop one alpha-layer) to align with the strip for f(x+1,y)-f(x,y), the shifted row contributing exactly one extra point, giving the exact identity f(x,y)+f(x+1,y+1)=f(x+1,y)+f(x,y+1)+1. Mod 2 the four corners of any unit square sum to 1, so each unit square has an odd count (1 or 3) of odd values; tiling the 100x100 grid into 2500 disjoint 2x2 blocks gives N between 2500*1 and 2500*3, i.e. 2500 <= N <= 7500.

technique: Double-count one local feature of all cells against the global vertex population by weighting each vertex by how many cells meet there.
how_used: Classify every corner-vertex of the axis-parallel dissection by cell-multiplicity: the 4 corners of R lie in 1 cell each, T-junctions in exactly 2, crossings in exactly 4 (these are the only possibilities). Counting the 4k cell-corners two ways gives 4k = 4 + 2b + 4c with b = #T-junctions, c = #crossings; dropping the c-term yields b <= 2k - 2.

technique: Lower-bound a structural population by injecting each marked object into it, using a genericity hypothesis to make the assigned targets distinct.
how_used: Each given point p_i lies strictly inside some cut (an interior border between sub-rectangles, not on R's boundary, since no rectangle contains p_i in its interior). Extend that cut straight through p_i maximally along the border network to a segment S_i; its two endpoints are T-junctions of the dissection (points where exactly TWO sub-rectangles meet at a common corner while S_i passes straight through as the crossbar). Because p_i is interior to S_i, S_i passes straight through each endpoint, so each endpoint is such a two-rectangle corner (B-junction). Injectivity is what the hypothesis buys: a B-junction lies on a unique straight crossbar line, and no two given points lie on a common line parallel to a side, so the S_i lie on distinct lines and no B-junction is the crossbar-endpoint of two different p_i. Hence the 2n endpoints are 2n distinct B-junctions: b >= 2n.

technique: Bound the number of interior meeting-points of a cell complex by double-counting cell corners: each cell contributes a fixed number of corners, each meeting-point absorbs a fixed multiplicity depending on its type.
how_used: Partition all corner-points of the dissection by how many sub-rectangles have that point as one of their four corners: A = the four corners of R (each a corner of exactly 1 sub-rectangle), B = T-junctions where exactly 2 sub-rectangles share a corner (b of them; at a T-junction the far-side rectangle has the point on its edge-interior, not at a corner, so the multiplicity is 2, not 3), C = crossings where exactly 4 share a corner (c of them). Every sub-rectangle has exactly 4 corners, so summing corner-incidences: 4k = 4*1 + 2*b + 4*c. Dropping the nonnegative 4c term gives 4k >= 4 + 2b, i.e. b <= 2k - 2. Combined with the injection bound b >= 2n this forces 2k - 2 >= 2n, hence k >= n+1.

technique: Track the product of all quantities as a monovariant, bounding its per-step multiplicative growth by an AM-GM inequality on the two locally-changed factors
how_used: Let P be the product over all 2^m sheets; replacing a,b by a+b on both sheets swaps factor ab for (a+b)^2, and (a+b)^2 >= 4ab forces P_{k+1} >= 4 P_k, so from P_0=1 the product after m2^{m-1} steps is at least 4^{m2^{m-1}} = (2^m)^{2^m}

technique: Convert a proven lower bound on a product into a lower bound on the sum via AM-GM on the fixed number of terms
how_used: With P_{m2^{m-1}} >= (2^m)^{2^m} over the 2^m sheets, AM-GM gives sum >= 2^m * P^{1/2^m} >= 2^m * 2^m = 4^m

technique: Anchor a strip at an extremal row so a subsequent deletion removes a guaranteed occupant, leaving a deficit below the count needed to fill every cell of a partition
how_used: To show n>ℓ² forces an empty ℓ×ℓ square: pick the row whose rook sits in the leftmost column, take ℓ consecutive rows around it (exactly ℓ rooks), then delete the n-ℓ²≥1 leftmost columns — this deletion is guaranteed to remove that anchored rook, leaving an ℓ²×ℓ rectangle with ≤ℓ-1 rooks partitioned into ℓ squares, so one is empty by pigeonhole

technique: Index rows and columns by mixed-radix digit pairs and place a marked point at each digit-swap coordinate so every window of consecutive rows spreads its occupants evenly across all column blocks
how_used: For the n=ℓ² lower-bound construction: write each index uniquely as iℓ+j (0≤i,j≤ℓ-1) and place a rook at (iℓ+j, jℓ+i). Any ℓ consecutive rows then have their rooks in columns forming an ordered list running from ≤ℓ-1 up to ≥(ℓ-1)ℓ with consecutive gaps ≤ℓ, guaranteeing every ℓ-column window (hence every ℓ×ℓ square) contains one

technique: Adapt an extremal construction to smaller size by deleting rows and columns, then repair the resulting empty lines by bijecting empty rows to empty columns and seating one point at each pairing
how_used: To extend the n=ℓ² construction to n<ℓ²: delete the ℓ²-n bottom rows and ℓ²-n rightmost columns (no ℓ×ℓ square becomes empty), then since equally many rows and columns are left empty, match them bijectively and place a rook at each crossing to restore the happy (one-per-row/column) property

technique: Design a periodic two-coloring of the board so that one chiral tile family always covers an even count of marked cells while its mirror family always covers an odd count, turning tile-type parity into a fixed cell-count parity invariant
how_used: One picks a specific non-checkerboard periodic black/white pattern (the checkerboard fails, since it makes both chiralities cover 2 black + 2 white) under which every S-tetromino, in all rotations and translations, covers an EVEN number of black cells while every Z-tetromino covers an ODD number. Then B = (number of black cells of P) satisfies B ≡ #Z (mod 2) in any S/Z tiling. B depends only on P; since P has an all-S tiling, B ≡ 0 (mod 2), forcing #Z even. (A working pattern is obtained as the mod-2 sum of two simpler stripe colorings.)

technique: Weight each cell by a signed geometric monomial base^i·(-base)^j so that translating any fixed tile shape merely multiplies its cell-weight sum by a monomial, collapsing every placement of a shape to one signed constant times a unit
how_used: Write 3^i·(-3)^j in cell (i,j). Every S-tetromino sums to -32·3^i·(-3)^j or to 0 — always divisible by 32. Every Z-tetromino sums to 0 (first type) or to 16·3^i·(-3)^j, i.e. 16 times an odd number (second type). Because P is S-tileable, the fixed total board sum is ≡ 0 (mod 32); so in ANY tiling the Z-contribution must also be ≡ 0 (mod 32), and since each Z of the second type contributes 16·(odd), an EVEN number of them is forced. Rotating 90° handles the first Z-type. (Note the roles: it is the Z shape, not S, that carries the nonzero 16·odd residue.)

technique: Take a maximal (inclusion-maximal) valid substructure so every element outside it is certified to violate the property, turning the existence target into a lower bound on the maximal set's size
how_used: Pick a maximal blue subset B (|B|=k) whose lines make no finite region all-blue; then adding any red line would create an all-blue region, and the goal reduces to proving k >= ceil(sqrt(n/2))

technique: Extract a witness object from each element's maximality-violation and injectively associate it to that element to seed a counting inequality
how_used: For each red line l, maximality of B guarantees a finite region A whose only red side lies on l; since A has >=3 sides it has a blue vertex, and one such blue vertex is associated to l

technique: Bound the number of associated elements by a fixed local incidence count at each target point, then compare against the total to get a quadratic-in-k inequality
how_used: Each blue point (intersection of two blue lines) lies in exactly four regions, so at most four red lines associate to it; with C(k,2) blue points, n-k <= 4*C(k,2)=2k(k-1), giving n <= 2k^2 and k >= ceil(sqrt(n/2))

technique: To upgrade a rule's verdict from a few calibrated configurations to all pairs, interpolate the arbitrary pair through auxiliary sets whose internal order-type is isomorphic to the calibrated configurations, chaining coordinatewise-domination comparisons with the calibrated verdicts by transitivity.
how_used: Given the pivot k and arbitrary increasing X,Y with x_k<y_k, choose reals building U,V,W (size n) with u's mostly below both sets, v's mostly above, and the middle block x_k<v_1<...<v_k<w_1<...<w_n<u_k<...<u_n<y_k. Then u_i<y_i and x_i<v_i give U≺Y and X≺V by condition 2; U∪W is order-isomorphic to A_{k-1}∪B_{k-1} so U≻W, and V∪W to A_k∪B_k so V≺W (the two calibration verdicts). Transitivity (condition 3) closes X≺V≺W≺U≺Y, so X≺Y, matching 'compare k-th elements' on every pair.

technique: To show a rank-only, monotone, transitive order ignores its extreme coordinate (enabling a descent to smaller size), assume that coordinate flips a verdict, then shift the two witnessing configurations by an order-preserving epsilon in opposite directions to manufacture a cyclic triple that transitivity forbids.
how_used: Alternative (induction on n) route. To prove a_1,b_1 irrelevant: fix the order of all elements except b_1; if b_1=x makes B win and b_1=y makes A win, set B_x={x,b_2,...}, B_y={y,b_2,...} and pick epsilon below half the min gap. Then A≺B_x-ε and A≻B_y+ε (order-types preserved by condition 1), while B_x-ε≺B_y+ε (by condition 2 if y>x, else by the calibrated relation of size n on the shifted pair). This yields A≺B_x-ε≺B_y+ε≺A, contradicting condition 3; hence the rule factors through the top n-1 coordinates, and induction pins it to comparing one index.

technique: To locate the single coordinate on which a rank-only, domination-monotone, transitive order keys, sweep a one-parameter family of paired configurations whose two extreme members have opposite verdicts forced by the domination axiom, and take the minimal index where the verdict flips as the candidate pivot.
how_used: For sets of size n with ranks among 2n cards, define A_k={1,...,k, n+k+1,...,2n} and B_k={k+1,...,n+k}. At k=n the pair degenerates to A_n={1,...,n} ≺ B_n={n+1,...,2n}, whose verdict is forced by condition 2 (coordinatewise domination). Let k be MINIMAL with A_k ≺ B_k; it exists since it holds at k=n. The only facts extracted are the two adjacent calibration verdicts A_k ≺ B_k (definition of k) and A_{k-1} ≻ B_{k-1} (minimality), and k is the conjectured compared index. No monotonicity of the sweep is needed — only these two boundary verdicts.

technique: To pin down which coordinate an order-only, domination-respecting, transitive comparison rule secretly reads, run the rule along an explicit one-parameter staircase family of set-pairs interpolating between a forced-win and a forced-loss, and take the index where the verdict first reverses as the definition of that coordinate.
how_used: Define the family A_j = {1,...,j, n+j+1,...,2n} and B_j = {j+1,...,n+j} for j=0,...,n. At j=0, A_0={n+1,...,2n} dominates B_0={1,...,n} coordinatewise so A_0 succ B_0 by condition 2; at j=n, A_n={1,...,n} is dominated by B_n={n+1,...,2n} so A_n prec B_n. Let k be minimal with A_k prec B_k; then A_{k-1} succ B_{k-1}. This k is the candidate coordinate: the claim to be proved next is that X prec Y iff x_k < y_k. The staircase is engineered so that consecutive pairs A_{k-1}/B_{k-1} and A_k/B_k are exactly the two 'calibrated' order-types the later sandwich reuses; without first defining this family and extracting k, there is no index to compare against.

technique: To upgrade a comparison verdict known only on special 'calibrated' configurations into a verdict on an arbitrary pair, sandwich the arbitrary pair between auxiliary sets placed so that each consecutive link is settled either by the coordinatewise-domination axiom or by copying one of the calibrated order-types, then close by transitivity.
how_used: Given disjoint increasing X,Y with x_k < y_k, choose reals forming U,V,W with u_1<...<u_{k-1}<min(x_1,y_1), max(x_n,y_n)<v_{k+1}<...<v_n, and x_k<v_1<...<v_k<w_1<...<w_n<u_k<...<u_n<y_k. Then: u_i<y_i and x_i<v_i for all i give U prec Y and X prec V by condition 2; U cup W has the same order-type as A_{k-1} cup B_{k-1}, so from A_{k-1} succ B_{k-1} we get U succ W; V cup W copies A_k cup B_k, so from A_k prec B_k we get V prec W. Chaining X prec V prec W prec U prec Y through condition 3 forces X prec Y. The placement (V just above x_k, W in the middle, U just below y_k, with the outer u's low and outer v's high) is exactly what makes the domination inequalities and the two order-type copies hold simultaneously, using the slack x_k<y_k. Symmetry gives the converse, so the rule is exactly 'compare coordinate k'.

technique: Replace a real-valued termination potential with an integer count of how many fixed objects a configuration element crosses, so 'the process ends' upgrades to an explicit polynomial step bound
how_used: Instead of total Euclidean segment length (which only forces finiteness via the triangle inequality but yields no polynomial step count), define value(seg) = number of 'red lines' (lines through two points of M) crossing the segment's open interior, and let the potential be the sum of these values over the n current segments; this is a nonnegative integer, so any per-step decrease by a fixed integer bounds the number of steps.

technique: Bound a summed monovariant at the start by multiplying a per-term ceiling by the number of terms
how_used: There are C(n,2) < n^2/2 red lines total, so each of the n initial segments has value < n^2/2; hence the initial total value < n * n^2/2 = n^3/2, and with a drop of >=2 per move the move count is < n^3/4.

technique: To show a local replacement cannot increase a crossing-count, route any line meeting a new segment through the triangle it forms with the crossing point, forcing a second boundary crossing on a sub-edge of an old segment
how_used: For the swap AB,CD (meeting at interior S) -> AC,BD, consider triangle ACS: side AS lies on segment AB and side CS lies on segment CD. A red line crossing the interior of AC enters triangle ACS through AC, so (being a full line and, by no-three-collinear, missing the vertices) it must exit through AS, CS, or S -- i.e. it crosses AB or CD. Hence X_AC subset X_AB union X_CD, and via triangle BDS symmetrically X_BD subset X_AB union X_CD. This yields ONLY the union-side containment |X_AC union X_BD| <= |X_AB union X_CD|; it does NOT by itself give the intersection inequality.

technique: Prove the companion intersection inequality for a swap by a case split on whether the crossing line passes through the shared crossing point
how_used: To get |X_AC intersect X_BD| <= |X_AB intersect X_CD|: a red line h in X_AC intersect X_BD crosses both new segments AC and BD. Split on S: if S in h, then h through S already forces h to cross both old segments AB and CD near S; if S not in h, the two triangle-routing exits (crossing AC forces an exit on AS or CS, crossing BD forces an exit on BS or DS) can be matched so h lands in both X_AB and X_CD. Either way h is in X_AB intersect X_CD. This is the 'similar but easier' half the solution needs, distinct from the union containment.

technique: Turn a pair of set-containments (union side and intersection side) into a strict decrease of a sum of set-sizes by expanding each side via inclusion-exclusion into its union and intersection terms and bounding the two terms separately
how_used: Since value(s)=|X_s|, inclusion-exclusion gives value(AB)+value(CD) = |X_AB union X_CD| + |X_AB intersect X_CD| and likewise value(AC)+value(BD) = |X_AC union X_BD| + |X_AC intersect X_BD|. The intersection crux gives |X_AC intersect X_BD| <= |X_AB intersect X_CD|. For the union term, the containment gives <=, and strictness comes from two specific members of X_AB union X_CD absent from X_AC and X_BD: the red lines through A,B and through C,D. Line AB crosses segment CD at S (so it is in X_AB union X_CD) yet passes through A and B, endpoints of AC and BD, so by no-three-collinear it crosses the interior of neither new segment; symmetrically for line CD. That gives |X_AC union X_BD| + 2 <= |X_AB union X_CD|. Adding the two term inequalities: value(AC)+value(BD)+2 <= value(AB)+value(CD).

technique: Recast a parity win-condition as one global XOR-sum invariant that both players are forced to share
how_used: Cards are the subsets of {0,...,9}, i.e. vectors in F_2^10 under symmetric difference. 'Can discard one card leaving every digit-count even' means the XOR-sum of your hand equals one of your own cards. Because each digit lies on exactly 512 of the 1024 cards, ALL cards XOR to the empty set, so F's hand-XOR must equal S's hand-XOR; call this common value C. Exactly one player physically holds card C, and that player (and only that player) can discard it, so the holder of C wins and no draw is possible.

technique: Pair the ground set by a fixed nonzero translation and show any transversal's XOR lands in the two-element coset {0, B}
how_used: Fix a nonempty card B and pair every card X with X△B (a fixed-point-free involution, 512 pairs). Picking one card per pair gives a transversal. Take the 512 representatives that avoid a chosen digit b of B: these are exactly all cards not containing b, so every other digit appears on 256 (even) of them and they XOR to ∅. Any other transversal differs by flipping some pairs, each flip adding B, so its XOR is ∅ or B. Thus every full transversal sums to ∅ or B.

technique: In a pairing/misère take-turns game, have the responder answer each opponent pick with its fixed involution-partner, and seed the responder with one full pair up front so that whatever coset value the final invariant lands on is a card the responder is guaranteed to already hold.
how_used: Identify cards with F_2^10 under symmetric-difference XOR. Total XOR is ∅ (each digit on 512 cards), so both hands have the same sum C, and the player holding card C wins (throw it out). Case F opens ∅: S takes an arbitrary A; when F takes B, S takes A△B, so the first two pairs are {∅,B} (F) and {A,A△B} (S) under the involution X↦X△B. Thereafter S always takes the partner of F's pick, so S ends with exactly one card per pair EXCEPT he holds the full pair {A,A△B}. Temporarily swap A→∅: now S holds one card from every pair, so by the pinning lemma his sum is ∅ or B; swapping A back, S's real sum C is A or A△B — and S owns BOTH of those. Hence S holds C and wins. The reusable move is the mirror-by-partner response plus the deliberately-taken opening full pair that pre-owns both possible coset outcomes.

technique: To run a partner-mirroring strategy when exactly one involution-pair is broken, keep a single unpaired 'floating' card and hand it off (take a fresh card whenever the opponent grabs the floater, promoting the new card's partner to floater) so the opponent is forced to take the floater on the final move.
how_used: Case F opens A≠∅: S takes some B≠∅, F replies A△B. Under the pairing X↦X△B the untaken cards are complete pairs plus ONE extra element (∅ is untaken but its partner B was taken by S). F mirrors: if S takes from a complete pair, F takes its partner; if S takes the current extra element, F takes an arbitrary Y and Y's partner becomes the new extra element. This invariant (always exactly one floating card) forces S to take the extra element on his LAST move. The end state is F holding the full pair {A,A△B} plus one card per other pair, S holding {∅,B} plus the complementary transversal — i.e. Case 1 with roles reversed, so F wins. (If S opens ∅, F first names any untaken card B and takes A△B to reach this setup.)

technique: To pin the XOR of a system of representatives (one element per pair of an involution X↦X△B) to a 2-element coset, choose the canonical representatives that all avoid a fixed element b∈B: those are exactly the sets missing b, whose XOR is ∅ by a counting/parity symmetry, and any other transversal differs from it by adding B some number of times.
how_used: For nonempty B, split the 1024 cards into 512 pairs (X, X△B). Fix b∈B. In each pair one card contains b and one doesn't; the b-free representatives are precisely all sets not containing b. Every other digit a≠b appears on exactly 256 of those sets, so their total XOR is ∅. Replacing any representative by its partner adds B to the running sum, so any transversal's XOR is ∅ or B. This is the keystone that makes the mirroring strategies work: it forces the responder's swapped hand-sum into {∅,B}, hence (after undoing the swap of the seeded card A) into {A, A△B}.

technique: Resolve each transversal crossing into a non-crossing pair of arcs so a dynamical traversal becomes a static family of disjoint simple closed curves
how_used: At each of the double intersections, the two circles are locally rewired into two small arcs encoding which circle the snail leaves on; this converts the snail's direction-dependent path into 'snail orbits' that are simple closed curves with no mutual or self intersections, reducing 'one path covers all circles' to 'the number of orbits equals 1', and letting the target parity claim be proven for the orbit count instead of the trajectory.

technique: Track a count's parity under a local surgery that changes it by exactly +/-1, then apply the surgery an even number of times to restore parity
how_used: Define 'flipping a cross' (swap which arcs are joined at an intersection); casework on how the four arcs a,b,c,d are externally connected shows one case is impossible and the other two either merge two orbits into one or split one into two, so each flip changes the orbit count by exactly +/-1 (flips its parity). Since every intersecting circle pair contributes exactly 2 crosses, the total number of crosses is even, so flipping all crosses restores the original orbit-count parity, reducing the claim to the fully-flipped configuration.

technique: Double-count total turning (curvature) of a closed-curve family two ways to extract a signed orbit count
how_used: Orient the flipped orbits so the snail always turns anticlockwise on arcs; each orbit contributes +/-2*pi total curvature, giving total (P-N)*2*pi. Counting the same total curvature circle-by-circle gives 2*pi per circle with the paired turnings at each cross cancelling, so total is n*2*pi. Equating yields P-N=n, and since the orbit count P+N has the same parity as P-N, the orbit count matches n mod 2.

technique: Combine two opposing constraints by taking a signed linear combination that cancels the shared middle terms and pairs the survivors positionally.
how_used: Subtract twice the k-subset bound (N/2 >= a_{k+1}+...+a_{2k}) from the full-sum bound (N+1 <= a_0+...+a_{2k}); the top-k terms cancel against their doubles, leaving a_0 >= 1 + sum_{i=1..k}(a_{k+i} - a_i), pairing each large element with an element k positions below it.

technique: Bound each positional gap in an increasing integer sequence below by its index gap.
how_used: For distinct increasing positive integers, a_{k+i} - a_i >= k for each i, so the paired-difference sum >= k*k, forcing a_0 >= k^2+1; equality holds exactly for a consecutive-integer run (difference 1), matching the optimal set {k^2+1,...,k^2+2k+1}.

technique: Convert a bound on the smallest element into a bound on a sum of larger elements by writing each as the smallest plus its distinctness offset.
how_used: Lower-bound the top-k sum a_{k+1}+...+a_{2k} >= sum (a_0 + (k+i)) = k*a_0 + ((k+1)+...+2k); substituting a_0 >= k^2+1 gives N/2 >= k(k^2+1) + k(3k+1)/2, hence N >= k(2k^2+3k+3), attained by the consecutive set as construction.

technique: Show a deletion of elements from a process preserves a legality constraint by proving the deleted elements only shift later states by multiples of a modulus that the surviving legality checks are insensitive to
how_used: Fix an exponent e and delete every later jump whose length is divisible by 2^e. Each surviving position is then shifted by a sum of deleted lengths, i.e. a multiple of 2^e. A surviving big jump taken from x has length 2^{nu2(x)+1} < 2^e, so nu2(x) < e; hence nu2(x) is determined by x mod 2^e and is unchanged by shifting x by a multiple of 2^e. Therefore the required jump length 2^{nu2(x)+1} is unchanged and the surviving jump stays legal (unit jumps are always legal).

technique: To turn a valid path to a target into a strictly shorter valid path, delete steps from the tail largest-first by length, so that every step still present is legal after its start point is shifted down by a multiple of the deleted lengths
how_used: A frog step from n has length 1 or the big jump 2^{v2(n)+1}. Given a valid path to 2^i k (k>=2), sweep an exponent e from large down to 0; at threshold e, delete every step of length exactly 2^e whose endpoint exceeds the target 2^i. Deleting a length-2^e step shifts the whole subsequent tail down by 2^e. The order (largest-first) is what makes this legal: when a length-2^e step's start is shifted down by earlier-deleted multiples of >=2^e, and every remaining big jump has length 2^{m'+1} <= 2^e, subtracting a multiple of 2^e from that jump's start preserves v2(start)=m' (since the change is >= its own length), so the jump stays exactly the big jump legal at its new start. Since k>=2 at least one big jump ends past 2^i and is deleted, giving a strictly shorter valid path. This crux supplies only the legality of the pruning engine; where the pruned path ENDS is a separate move.

technique: To show a process that removes selected steps of a path leaves it legal, delete only steps whose length is divisible by a fixed power of the modulus, so every later position shifts by a multiple of that power and its residue-dependent legality is unchanged.
how_used: Legality of a jump from n depends only on v_2(n) (a legal long jump has length 2^{v_2(n)+1}). Delete, after some index, all jumps whose length is divisible by 2^e. Then each later position x is shifted to x' = x - (sum of deleted lengths), and that sum is a multiple of 2^e. For any surviving long jump its length 2^{v_2(x)+1} is not divisible by 2^e, so v_2(x)+1 < e, i.e. v_2(x) < e; since x and x' differ by a multiple of 2^e and v_2(x) < e, the valuation is determined by the residue mod 2^e and so v_2(x') = v_2(x). Hence the surviving jump's required length 2^{v_2+1} is unchanged and it remains legal (a +1 jump is always legal). This is the legality-preservation lemma the deletion-sweep crux presupposes.

technique: Pin the endpoint of a top-down deletion sweep to a single target value by carrying a two-sided invariant down the sweep: a fixed floor it never drops below, plus a divisibility that grows as the deletion threshold falls, trapping it between the floor and the target.
how_used: Sweep e from large down to 0; at stage e delete every surviving jump of length 2^e whose endpoint exceeds the target 2^i. Each such batch is deletable (legality preserved) by the valuation-preservation lemma. Downward-induction claim: after all jumps of length > 2^e are gone, the endpoint E satisfies E >= 2^i and 2^{min(i,e)} | E. Floor: a jump is deleted only when its endpoint exceeds 2^i, and the divisibility invariant fed back (E divisible by 2^{min(i,e)} and > 2^i forces E >= 2^i + 2^{min(i,e)}) keeps E from dropping below 2^i after removal. Divisibility: between thresholds E changes only by multiples of 2^e (surviving length-2^e jumps), preserving its residue and lifting divisibility to 2^{min(i,e)}; the smallest multiple of 2^{min(i,e)} exceeding x is 2^i. At e=0 the floor gives E >= 2^i and the construction (unit jumps past 2^i also deleted) gives E <= 2^i, forcing E = 2^i. Since k >= 2 forced at least one overshooting deletion, the pruned legal path to 2^i uses strictly fewer jumps than the original to 2^i k.

technique: Reach the target structure by repeatedly deleting any element made redundant by the others, then argue the terminal irreducible state already IS that structure
how_used: Start with S = all teams. Repeatedly delete any team all of whose signature colors are also signature colors of some OTHER team still in S. When no such team remains, every surviving team has a signature color that no other survivor carries, so assigning each survivor that private color makes S color-identifiable — exactly the object sought.

technique: Bound the terminal set's size by a quantity the deletion step provably preserves, then divide that conserved total by the per-element capacity
how_used: Each deletion removes only a team all of whose colors are still carried by others, so the set of distinct colors present is unchanged — all n colors survive to the terminal state. Since each surviving team carries at most t colors and the survivors must together cover all n present colors, k survivors give kt >= n, so k >= ceil(n/t).

technique: Greedy on the least-used resource, deleting simultaneously the picked resource's owners AND the chosen owner's resources; the two deletions certify mutual non-conflict while the resource pool shrinks by a bounded amount per round
how_used:
Lower bound g(n,t) >= ceil(n/t). Model: colors vs teams, each team a palette of <= t colors, n colors present. Each round: among CURRENTLY-PRESENT colors pick C with the FEWEST teams using it, and one team T with C in its palette; add the pair (T,C) to the selected set. Then perform BOTH deletions: (i) delete every team that uses C, and (ii) delete from the present-color pool all (<= t) colors of T. Repeat until no colors remain.

The selected pairs {(T_i,C_i)} are mutually non-conflicting (color-identifiable), and the two deletions handle the two directions SEPARATELY:
  - Direction j>i (C_i not in a LATER team's palette): deletion (i) at round i removes all teams using C_i, so any T_j selected later does not use C_i.
  - Direction j<i (C_i not in an EARLIER team's palette): deletion (ii) at round j removed ALL of T_j's colors from the pool; C_i is chosen at round i>j from surviving pool colors, hence C_i is not in T_j's palette. (Team-persistence in the selected set and color-pool-survival are different things: T_j persists as a chosen team even though its colors left the pool at round j.)

Color-loss per round is at most T's <= t colors, giving >= ceil(n/t) rounds. Correctness of the bound needs the minimality lemma: any color C' that SURVIVES (is not one of T's colors) still has a user after deletion (i). Proof: if C' lost all users, then users(C') is contained in users(C); minimality of C gives |users(C)| <= |users(C')|, so users(C')=users(C); but T is in users(C)=users(C'), so T uses C', meaning C' WAS one of T's colors and was deleted by (ii) -- contradiction. So deletion (i) removes no surviving color's last user, and the pool drops by at most the <= t colors of T each round. This is the 'adding colors' greedy of the official solution (sol 2 / USAMO 2015 P3).

technique: In a finite-target-over-unbounded-time game, discard every round that can only help you and freeze your own score, so the game collapses to a fixed local move on the other players' scores alone.
how_used: Rescale weights to +1/-1/0 (no effect on who leads), WLOG all opponents start at 0, and discard rounds where all answers agree AND rounds where you answer correctly (those never shrink any lead). Since you always copy an existing answer-group, your own score is treated as fixed; what remains is a game where each round you pick an equal-answer group to lose 1 point while some disjoint group (the correct-answer class) gains 1 point. The whole problem becomes how much an opponent group can net-gain, not about your play.

technique: To shrink the label space of a counting bound over set-partitions, always record the MINORITY side by first consuming a majority block, forcing every recorded set below half-size.
how_used: This is the else-branch of the same one-guess-per-round strategy (the if-branch is crux 1's cancellation, so the two copy-choices never conflict — exactly one fires per round). When recording a new set, first copy a group T with |T| >= n/2 (a largest answer-class always exists at that size when there are >=2 classes). The correct-answer set S you then record is disjoint from T, so |S| <= n/2. Hence every set placed in L has size <= n/2, so a fixed contestant c lies in at most half of the 2^{n-1} subsets that could contain it, i.e. 2^{n-2}. With crux 1's ledger bound, c's total gain is at most 2^{n-2}, so a lead of 2^{n-2}+1 (already stronger than the required 2^{n-1}) can never be caught.

technique: Reframe a comparative-scoring game by an affine reweighting of the payoffs that zeroes out the protagonist's own contribution, then discard the rounds the protagonist controls, leaving a normal form in which only relative gaps move.
how_used: Replace payoffs (0,-2,-1) for (correct, wrong-other, wrong-you) by (+1,-1,0); an affine shift preserves every score DIFFERENCE and makes your own answer contribute 0. WLOG all other contestants start at 0 and your lead exceeds the target. Discard rounds where everyone answers alike (nothing moves) and rounds where you answer correctly (you only gain relative ground, so dropping them can only hurt you). What remains, tracked via gaps d_c = your score minus c's score (you win iff every d_c stays positive forever): your score is effectively frozen, and each round you copy some wrong same-answer group T, whereupon the correct set S (disjoint from T) each closes 1 point on you while the copied group T loses 1 point to you and everyone else is unchanged. So the round's only net effect is: correct set S banks +1 on you, copied group T loses 1 to you.

technique: Reverse a banked gain by spending a later round to copy exactly the set that gained, docking it back the point — exploiting that closures are non-monotone because copying a group is a real move that penalizes it.
how_used: KEY OBSERVATION. In the reduced game a set S banks +1 on you in round R1 when S was the correct group while you copied a different wrong group. If in a LATER round R2 that same set S is again a single answer-group, copy S: either S is correct (you tie, harmless) or S is wrong, in which case S's members get -2 and you get -1, so each member of S loses exactly 1 to you, cancelling the +1 from R1. The +1 and the forced -1 cancel, so R1 and R2 together contribute nothing net to any contestant's gain over you and both can be ignored forever. The realization is that a banked gain is a debt you can retire by copying the same set later, so an unbounded horizon is survivable.

technique: To cap a total accumulated over unbounded time, greedily maintain a DUPLICATE-FREE ledger of the configurations that banked a gain — reverse-and-remove when the current configuration is already listed, otherwise record it — so each net gain charges one distinct listed configuration and the horizon collapses to a finite subset count.
how_used: Keep a list L of subsets, initially empty. Each round: if some same-answer group equals a set S already in L, copy S (forcing S to lose the banked point — the cancellation) and delete S, adding nothing. Otherwise copy any group T, taking |T| >= n/2 WHEN POSSIBLE; let S be the correct set. INVARIANT: L never holds duplicates, since a set is added only when no equal copy is present, so each listed set stands for exactly one still-un-reversed +1. Hence contestant c's net gain over you is at most the number of currently-listed sets containing c, i.e. the number of DISTINCT subsets that can ever be listed and contain c — a finite count over infinite time. The naive ledger over all nonempty proper subsets gives a bound near 2^n; charging per-contestant-c already halves it.

technique: Sharpen a subset-counting bound by choosing the copied object as large as possible, so the adversarially-revealed complement you must record is forced into the small half — halving the subset population that can ever be charged.
how_used: The listed set S is the correct set, which is disjoint from the copied group T. By copying T with |T| >= n/2 (when possible), the recorded correct set S has |S| <= n/2. So each contestant c is charged only by DISTINCT subsets of size <= n/2 containing it, of which there are at most sum_{k<=n/2} C(n-1,k-1) <= 2^{n-2}. Combined with the per-contestant charging (crux 2), a lead of 2^{n-2}+1 (hence 2^{n-1}) over each of the n contestants is never erased. Note the official solution states the |T| >= n/2 selection with an 'if possible' caveat and gets exactly this bound; the halving is the second of the two independent optimizations (per-contestant charging being the first) that jointly push 2^n down to 2^{n-2}+1.

technique: From a minimal-length nonnegative-sum certificate at one index, deduce every index it spans is also certified, so a left-to-right greedy sweep tiles the certified set into disjoint consecutive blocks of nonnegative sum
how_used: Call k good with minimal length L=L(k)<=m if a_k+...+a_{k+L-1}>=0 and no shorter window works. Minimality forces every proper prefix a_k+...+a_{k+j-1}<0 (1<=j<=L-1), so the complementary suffix a_{k+j}+...+a_{k+L-1}>0 has length L-j<=m; hence each interior index k+j is itself good. Thus the whole run [k,k+L-1] is good with nonnegative sum. Greedily grab the first uncovered good index, seize its minimal block, jump past it, repeat: the blocks are disjoint, every good index lands in some block (a good index in a gap would have been grabbed first), the blocks cover exactly T, and each has sum>=0, so sum_{k in T} a_k >= 0 in the non-cyclic (no wraparound) version.

technique: Reduce a cyclic (mod-n) statement to its already-proved linear version by periodizing: concatenate N copies of the sequence, run the linear result, and let N grow so the fixed boundary defect washes out under division by N
how_used: Lay N copies of a_1,...,a_n end to end and apply the linear blocking result to this length-Nn word. Because every certifying window has length <=m<n it spans at most two adjacent copies, so away from the two ends each copy reproduces the cyclic good set T faithfully; only an O(1) band of terms near each concatenation end fails to tile into a clean copy of T. The total contribution of good indices is therefore N*(sum_{k in T} a_k) plus a leftover c_N supported on that fixed-size boundary band, whence |c_N| is bounded by sum|a_i|, a constant not depending on N. The linear result gives N*(sum_{k in T} a_k)+c_N>=0; divide by N and send N->infinity to get sum_{k in T} a_k>=0.

technique: Prove the whole-line (non-wrapping) version by greedily tiling the flagged indices into consecutive blocks: repeatedly take the leftmost still-ungrouped flagged index, attach exactly the shortest nonnegative-sum window it starts, and note minimality forces its interior indices to also be flagged so no block ever swallows an unflagged index
how_used: For the LINEAR version, call k l-good if l≤m is the SMALLEST length with a_k+···+a_{k+l-1}≥0. Minimality makes every proper prefix a_k+···+a_{k+j-1}<0 for j<l, so each interior tail a_{k+j}+···+a_{k+l-1} = (whole)−(prefix) > 0, a length-(l−j) nonnegative window at k+j, so k+1,…,k+l-1 are all good. Greedy sweep: take the leftmost ungrouped good index (l-good for some l≤m), swallow it with the next l−1 indices as one block of sum≥0; those l−1 are themselves good by inheritance, so blocks tile ALL good indices disjointly. Summing the nonnegative block sums gives ∑ over linear-good indices ≥ 0.

technique: Recover a cyclic (mod-n) averaged inequality from its already-proved linear (non-wrapping) version by applying the linear version to N concatenated periods, absorbing the linear-vs-cyclic mismatch into a boundary defect bounded independently of N, then dividing by N and sending N to infinity.
how_used: The linear lemma only certifies windows that do not wrap past the end of the finite sequence. To recover the true cyclic claim ∑_{k∈T} a_k ≥ 0 (windows taken mod n), concatenate N copies of a_1,…,a_n into a length-Nn sequence and apply the linear lemma to it. An index k in an interior copy is linearly good in the concatenation iff it is cyclically good in the original, because copies to its right supply the wrap-around continuation of any cyclic good window of length ≤ m; only indices within the last m-1 positions (the right boundary) can be certified cyclically but fail linearly. Hence the linear-lemma inequality reads (N − O(1))·∑_{k∈T} a_k + c_N ≥ 0 with the boundary error |c_N| ≤ ∑|a_i| independent of N. Divide by N and let N→∞: c_N/N→0 forces ∑_{k∈T} a_k ≥ 0.

technique: To prove a sum over a hard-to-describe 'good' index set is nonnegative, certify each good index by a minimal witnessing window and greedily tile the good indices into consecutive blocks, each carrying a nonnegative window-sum.
how_used: Work first with the sequence on the line (indices NOT reduced mod n). Call index k ℓ-good when ℓ is the least length in [1,m] with a_k+…+a_{k+ℓ-1} ≥ 0. Key sub-fact: if k is ℓ-good then every interior index k+j (1 ≤ j < ℓ) is good, because by minimality the prefix a_k+…+a_{k+j-1} < 0, so the complementary suffix a_{k+j}+…+a_{k+ℓ-1} = window − prefix > window ≥ 0 and has length ℓ−j ≤ m. Then sweep left to right: at the leftmost good index not yet covered, which is ℓ-good, emit the block [k, k+ℓ−1] (all members good by the sub-fact) with its nonnegative window-sum, and jump to k+ℓ. Every good index either starts a block or lies inside one (gaps between blocks contain only non-good indices, since the sweep would otherwise have started a block there), so the good set is exactly partitioned into these blocks and Σ_{good} a_k = Σ (block sums) ≥ 0. This proves the claim for the linear (non-cyclic) sequence.

technique: To transfer a bound proven for a linear sequence to its cyclic version, apply the linear result to N concatenated copies and let N→∞ so the fixed O(1) boundary discrepancy is dominated by the N-fold main term.
how_used: The good-index set and the target sum are cyclic (windows may wrap past index n), but the greedy-tiling result only holds on the line. Form the sequence of N concatenated copies of a_1,…,a_n and apply the linear result to it. In the interior of this length-Nn sequence each period reproduces the cyclic good set T, so the linear sum is N·Σ_{k∈T} a_k plus an error term c_N coming only from the two ends (indices whose good-status differs from the cyclic one because their forward windows run off the concatenation). This end error is bounded independently of N by |c_N| ≤ Σ|a_i|. Hence N·Σ_{k∈T} a_k + c_N ≥ 0 for all N; dividing by N and letting N→∞ forces Σ_{k∈T} a_k ≥ 0.

technique: Encode a computation into a token-game move-set by making each coordinate a program variable and each element of the move set a labeled instruction whose negative entries act as legality guards active only in the intended state
how_used: The k-tuple coordinates are split into a data register X (later Y) holding n plus a bank of one-hot 'state' flags and turn counters A,B; each element of S is a named move (Init, Kill, Sleep, Begin, ClaimX, Win, etc.) that flips the current state flag to the next and edits X/Y, with negative entries making it illegal (losing) except in the intended state, so the abstract Nim-style game simulates a small machine operating on n

technique: Force a player off any off-protocol move by giving the opponent a punishing move that repeatedly drains a guard counter to a negative value, so deviating is a forced loss
how_used: Playing Init a second time (or moving when A=B=0) lets the opponent answer with Kill/PunA/PunB repeatedly, decrementing X until it goes negative; this makes the 'death part' a guaranteed loss for the deviator and pins both players onto the intended main-part protocol

technique: Simulate halving of a counter as a guarded phase that can only complete without going negative when the counter is even, chaining phases so survival is possible exactly when repeated division by two reaches 1
how_used: Each X-phase / Y-phase converts (x,0) with x>1 to (0,x/2), completable without loss iff x is even (odd x forces WrongX and a loss); iterating these phases from n survives down to (1,0)/(0,1) enabling ClaimX/Win exactly when n=2^k, else a mid-chain odd value forces the loss on the intended player

technique: Recast the existence claim as a strict count inequality: bound the number of 'bad' objects and show it stays below the total number of objects, so a good one must exist.
how_used: To show some 1x3/3x1 triple has all-distinct colours, count the 2n(n-2) total triples and prove that the triples that are 'bad' (bear a repeated colour) number strictly fewer, forcing a good triple to exist. Concretely #bad <= sum_C 3(p_C-1) = 3(n^2-N) < 2n(n-2) since N = [(n+2)^2/3] > (n^2+4n)/3.

technique: Bound the count of qualifying objects by an incidence double-count: sum the cell-in-triple incidence two ways, using a floor on incidences per object and a ceiling on incidences per point, with a stronger cap at boundary points.
how_used: For a colour C appearing q times in one row, count pairs <cell, monochromatic 3-cell window>: each bad window contains >=2 such cells and each cell lies in <=3 windows (<=2 if leftmost/rightmost), giving 2r <= 2 + 3(q-2) + 2 = 3q-2, so r <= 3q/2 - 1 per row.

technique: Aggregate per-line bounds into a per-object bound using the geometric spread across rows and columns as a subtracted slack term.
how_used: Summing the per-row bound 3p/2 - k and per-column bound 3p/2 - l over the k rows and l columns holding a colour used p times, and using k + l >= 3 whenever p > 1, gives total bad triples for that colour <= 3p - (k+l) <= 3(p-1).

technique: Design a cell coloring so that the two piece types you must distinguish cover opposite parities of the marked cells
how_used: Color the unit squares of the grid so that every S-tetromino covers an even number of black squares while every Z-tetromino covers an odd number; this makes the two orientations distinguishable purely by a mod-2 black-square count.

technique: Pin a tiling invariant's value from a known reference tiling, then read it off any other tiling to constrain that tiling's piece counts
how_used: Because P admits an all-S tiling, its total black-square count is even (sum of even contributions); any mixed S/Z tiling must reproduce this same even total, so the number of odd-contributing Z-tetrominoes is forced to be even.

technique: To force a chosen local-extremum object to be 'nice for two sides' at once, minimize the extremal quantity over triangles constrained to bridge a partition, so both cross-part sides inherit the extremal property simultaneously
how_used: Over all triangles with at least one vertex in A and one in B, pick one of minimal area; for each of its two sides joining A to B, any competitor PRX with P in A and R in B also straddles, hence has area at least the minimum, so the triangle is nice for both cross-part sides and thus beautiful. This 'straddling-minimal triangle is beautiful' observation is the engine of the whole proof.

technique: Model the extremal objects as hyperedges and argue the hypergraph is connected, then invoke that a connected 3-uniform (or k-uniform) hypergraph on n vertices has at least (n-1)/(k-1) edges
how_used: Beautiful triangles are hyperedges on the n points; since every bipartition yields a beautiful triangle bridging it, the hypergraph is connected, so a connected 3-uniform hypergraph on n vertices has at least (n-1)/2 hyperedges, giving at least (n-1)/2 beautiful triangles.

technique: Grow one part of a partition by repeatedly absorbing the vertices of the current cross-part extremal object, counting a new distinct extremal object each step until the other part is exhausted
how_used: Start with A a single point; take an (A,B)-minimal (hence beautiful) triangle, move its B-vertices into A, repeat. Each step gives a new beautiful triangle (it uses a vertex still in B, absorbed thereafter, so it differs from all earlier ones) and B loses at most two points, so the process runs at least (n-1)/2 steps, producing at least (n-1)/2 distinct beautiful triangles.

technique: Reframe an edge-labeling/assignment target as an edge clique cover, letting each shared label be one clique
how_used: Building the friendship graph (vertices = orphans, edges = friendships), the requirement that each parent be shared by exactly a set of mutual friends becomes: cover the edges by cliques, one parent per maximal clique, so friends in a common clique share that parent and enemies (non-adjacent) never do.

technique: Translate a forbidden local induced configuration into 'each neighborhood is a disjoint union of cliques' and bound the number of pieces
how_used: The hypothesis that any three of an orphan's friends contain an even number of enemy pairs forbids the exactly-one-enemy-pair triple (an induced P3) inside a neighborhood; this forces each vertex's friend-set to split into cliques, and forbidding a 3-enemy-pair triple (one friend from each of three cliques) pins it to at most two cliques, so every vertex lies in at most two maximal cliques.

technique: Prove a per-vertex bound on how many maximal cliques can contain a single vertex by turning a local even-parity hypothesis on triples into a coboundary condition that splits the vertex's neighborhood into at most two classes.
how_used: Decompose the friendship graph into maximal cliques (peel off maximal cliques until no edges remain; every edge lies in one). Establish the claim that every vertex lies in at most two maximal cliques. Fix an orphan v; the hypothesis says among v's friends N(v) every triple has an even number (0 or 2) of enemy pairs. Even parity on every triple is exactly the cocycle condition e(x,y)+e(y,z)+e(z,x)=0 mod 2, so the enemy relation on N(v) is e(x,y)=g(x)+g(y) mod 2 for a 2-coloring g: enemies form a complete bipartite graph between the two color classes and friends are 'same color'. Hence N(v) is a union of at most two mutual-friend cliques, and since v is friends with all of N(v), every maximal clique through v corresponds to one of these at most two classes. So v lies in at most two maximal cliques. This bound is the whole engine; the construction downstream is bookkeeping.

technique: Read the required construction directly off the clique decomposition — one label per maximal clique, shared by all its members — so the pairwise conditions become automatic and the forbidden triple is discharged by a per-vertex clique-count bound rather than global reasoning about overlapping cliques.
how_used: Give each maximal clique its own parent, assigned to every child in it, padding any child short of two with fresh distinct private parents. Two children are friends iff their edge lies in a common maximal clique iff they share exactly one parent (uniqueness: if both lay in two cliques C1,C2 then C1 union C2 would be a clique, contradicting maximality); enemies lie in no common clique and padding parents are private, so enemies share no parent. No love triangle: three parents pairwise sharing a child are all clique-parents (padding is private), giving a in P cap Q, b in Q cap R, c in P cap R; at vertex a, N(a) splits into two friend-parts, P and Q land in distinct parts, so c (in P) and b (in Q) fall in opposite parts and are enemies — yet both lie in clique R, hence friends, contradiction. The already-proven bound (a lies in at most two maximal cliques) is exactly what forbids the third clique through a, killing the love triangle by pinning the forbidden configuration onto one vertex's clique-membership count.

technique: Model finite sets as vectors over F_2 so that symmetric difference becomes addition in a field of characteristic 2
how_used: The 2^n+1 sets are viewed as binary indicator strings of length ell (the number of distinct objects), i.e. elements of the field F = F_{2^ell}; symmetric difference of a red and blue set is exactly their sum in F, turning the count of distinct symmetric differences into |B+R| for the subsets B,R of F, and reducing the problem to: for nonempty B,R with |B|+|R| = 2^n+1, show |B+R| >= 2^n.

technique: To lower-bound a sumset, assume it fits inside a small target set and build the product polynomial vanishing on the grid, then invoke the Combinatorial Nullstellensatz on its top monomial
how_used: Assuming |B+R| <= 2^n - 1, choose X containing B+R with |X| = 2^n - 1 and set P(b,r) = prod_{x in X}(b+r-x); this degree-(2^n-1) polynomial vanishes on all of B x R because b+r lies in X. Since (|B|-1)+(|R|-1) = 2^n-1 = deg P, the monomial b^{|B|-1} r^{|R|-1} is an admissible top term with exponents |B|-1<|B|, |R|-1<|R|, so a nonzero coefficient forces some (b,r) with P(b,r) != 0, contradicting the vanishing.

technique: Certify a binomial coefficient is nonzero in characteristic 2 by reading it off the leading form of the product polynomial and applying Lucas' theorem
how_used: The degree-(2^n-1) part of P = prod_{x in X}(b+r-x) is (b+r)^{2^n-1} (the -x terms only lower degree), so the coefficient of b^{|B|-1} r^{|R|-1} is C(2^n-1, |B|-1).
