Since 2^n-1 is all ones in binary, Lucas' theorem makes every such binomial coefficient odd, hence 1 (nonzero) in F of characteristic 2, giving the nonzero leading coefficient the Nullstellensatz needs to close the contradiction.

technique: Match a global count to a target total to force an exact one-per-line incidence
how_used: The number of red cells equals 1+2+...+n, exactly the combined area of tiles 1x1,...,1xn, so tiles occupy only red cells with no waste. Because the horizontal cover contains the n-tile, every column meets a red cell, so the vertical cover puts at least one tile in each column; with exactly n tiles this forces exactly one vertical tile per column (and symmetrically exactly one horizontal tile per row). Hence each row/column carries exactly one tile and the tile lengths per row (and per column) are a permutation of 1..n.

technique: Use a single-piece contiguity requirement to force the position/label sequence to be monotone-up-then-down
how_used: Read off the sequence of tile-number labels along the rows top-to-bottom (equivalently the row block-lengths). For two vertically adjacent rows with labels a>b, column n-b is red in row a but not in row b, so a red cell on the far side of row b would split column n-b into two pieces that the single (n-b)-tile cannot cover; hence once labels drop they cannot rise again. Since row n (the longest) has strictly smaller labels on both sides, the labels must increase up to n then decrease: the sequence is unimodal. The same argument gives unimodal column labels.

technique: Count unimodal (up-then-down) orderings of a set by encoding them as subsets, one per side of the peak
how_used: An up-then-down arrangement of 1..n with peak n is determined by choosing which of the remaining n-1 values go on the ascending side (uniquely sorted increasing before n); the rest are forced descending after n. That gives 2^{n-1} valid row-label orderings and independently 2^{n-1} column-label orderings, and each (row-ordering, column-ordering) pair yields exactly one valid coloring, so the total is 2^{n-1} * 2^{n-1} = 2^{2n-2}.

technique: Relabel each line by the object it carries so the constraint collapses to a single canonical incidence pattern
how_used: Rename rows and columns by tile number: 'row i' is the row whose horizontal tile has length i, 'column j' the column whose vertical tile has length j (first argue every row/column holds exactly one tile). In THESE relabeled coordinates a short induction on i shows cell (i,j) is red iff i+j >= n+1 (the staircase): row 1 has its single red cell forced into column n, and knowing column j's red count in rows 1..k forces its remaining n-k reds into rows k+1..n. This does not fix the physical board; it says every valid coloring becomes the SAME staircase once rows/columns are reindexed by tile number, so a coloring is determined by how those labels map back to physical positions. It deliberately does NOT tell you which label-maps are physically legal — that is a separate move.

technique: Count up-then-down (unimodal) orderings of 1..n by the subset that precedes the maximum
how_used: An ordering of 1..n that first increases then decreases is determined by choosing which of {1,...,n-1} lie before the maximum n: that subset must be arranged in increasing order before n and its complement in decreasing order after n, so orderings correspond bijectively to subsets of an (n-1)-element set, giving 2^{n-1}. Applied independently to the physical row-labels and column-labels, and using that each (unimodal, unimodal) pair yields exactly one legal coloring, the total is 2^{n-1} * 2^{n-1} = 2^{2n-2} (check: n=1 gives 1, n=2 gives 4).

technique: After indexing each row/column by the unique object it is forced to hold, induct on the index to prove the marked region has an exact threshold (staircase) shape
how_used: Because red cells equal the total tile area, the horizontal covering forces exactly one tile per row and the vertical covering exactly one per column, so label row i by the tile of length i in it and label columns analogously. With this labeling prove by induction on i that cell (i,j) is red iff i+j>=n+1. Base: row 1 has a single red cell, forced into the column holding the n-tile (column n). Step: assuming the pattern for rows<=k, column j (which must hold exactly j red cells) already has j+k-n of them in rows 1..k, so it still needs n-k more, filling every remaining row including k+1; hence row k+1 is red exactly for j>=n-k, i.e. (k+1)+j>=n+1. This pins the coloring to a fixed staircase read through the label permutation, which the later counting relies on.

technique: Compare two physically adjacent parallel lines to convert each perpendicular line's single-contiguous-run requirement into a no-valley (unimodal) constraint on the sequence of line labels
how_used: Given the staircase (cell (i,j) red iff i+j>=n+1 in tile-label coordinates), take two vertically adjacent physical rows with labels a>b. In column n-b, row a is red (a+(n-b)>n) but row b is not; for column n-b's red cells to be contiguous (so the (n-b)-tile can lie there), the row on the far side of b must also be non-red there, forcing its label below b. Hence row-labels cannot decrease then increase: top to bottom they rise to the all-red row (label n) then fall — unimodal — and identically for column-labels. Conversely any unimodal row ordering and any unimodal column ordering makes every row's red run {j: j>=n+1-i} contiguous, giving a valid coloring, exactly one per label pair; so colorings = (unimodal row orderings) x (unimodal column orderings), the two axes independent.

technique: In an adversarial game, bound the requester by having the adversary commit every requested item to one orientation, then count the disjoint lines each such item must occupy.
how_used: Julian labels all m tiles horizontal; since n<=2k-1 a length-n row cannot hold two disjoint horizontal k-tiles, so the m tiles occupy m distinct rows among only n, forcing m<=n.

technique: Bound the count of one type by choosing an adversary mix that saturates a guaranteed-overlap strip, then count the residual capacity left there for the other type.
how_used: Every vertical k-tile must cover a cell in each of the 2k-n central rows; with n-k+1 verticals each central row loses n-k+1 cells leaving k-1<k, so no horizontal fits in those rows, confining the 2n-2k+1 horizontals to 2n-2k rows -- contradiction, giving m<=3(n-k)+1.

technique: Prove achievability of the bound by exhibiting a few extreme packings, then cover the whole feasible parameter region by casework that discards surplus items from whichever extreme dominates.
how_used: A pinwheel packs 2(n-k) horizontal + 2(n-k) vertical; a second config packs n vertical + (n-k) horizontal. WLOG A<=B; split on A<=n-k (use second config) vs A>=n-k+1 (then A,B<=2(n-k), use pinwheel), dropping tiles as needed, so every demand with A+B<=min(n,3(n-k)+1) is met.

technique: To bound the count of extremal objects, take the globally largest element in the interval spanned by two candidates; it wins every one-on-one confrontation, so it forces one of the candidates to lose its extremal status.
how_used: For the uniqueness half (at most one un-sweepable town): suppose towns A (left) and B (right) are both un-sweepable. Among all bulldozers strictly between them, including A's right bulldozer and B's left bulldozer, take the largest, b. WLOG b is a left bulldozer, sitting in some town T to the right of A. Since b is the largest in the whole region, it exceeds every opposing (right) bulldozer between T and A, so nothing stops it: T sweeps A away, contradicting A un-sweepable. (Symmetrically if b is a right bulldozer.) Hence at most one un-sweepable town.

technique: To force existence of an object with a closure property, assume none exists, follow the assumed escape route to build an infinite chain, and exhibit a positional coordinate that strictly moves one way each step so the chain cannot fit on the finite ground set.
how_used: Existence half (at least one un-sweepable town). Assume every town can be swept away. Let t_1 = leftmost town; for each k pick t_{k+1} = a town that sweeps t_k away. Show t_{k+1} lies strictly to the right of t_k (the strict-advance step, isolated as its own crux). A strictly rightward chain among finitely many towns is impossible, so the assumption fails and some town is un-sweepable.

technique: Use a directional blocking lemma: if X's advancing agent passes over Y, then Y is blocked by X and can never pass X, so Y cannot reach anything on X's far side.
how_used: Closes the strict-advance step of the existence chain. If t_{k+1} lay left of t_k, then since prior links satisfy t_j < t_{j+1}, t_{k+1} lies between some t_j and t_{j+1}. Then t_{j+1} swept t_{k+1} away, so t_{k+1} cannot sweep t_{j+1} away, hence cannot reach t_k which is at or beyond t_{j+1} — contradicting that t_{k+1} sweeps t_k. So t_{k+1} is strictly right of t_k.

technique: To prove at most one object has the closure property, suppose two candidates exist, take the extremal (largest) obstacle strictly between them, and show its owner can act on one candidate because nothing between them outranks it.
how_used: Uniqueness half (at most one un-sweepable town). Suppose towns A (left) and B (right) can both not be swept away. Among all bulldozers strictly between them — including A's right bulldozer and B's left bulldozer — take the largest, b. WLOG b is a left bulldozer, sitting in a town to the right of A. Since b outranks every bulldozer between it and A, nothing stops that town from sweeping A away (larger right-facing bulldozers do not exist between them, and rear-approaches are automatic wins), contradicting A's un-sweepability. Hence at most one un-sweepable town.

technique: Realize an equidistant-witness requirement on a regular polygon by taking the witness vertex to be the index-midpoint of the two given vertices modulo n.
how_used: For an odd regular n-gon A_1..A_n, given A_i,A_j choose k with 2k ≡ i+j (mod n); n odd makes 2 invertible so k exists uniquely, and k-i ≡ j-k (mod n) makes the two arcs A_kA_i and A_kA_j equal, hence chords A_iA_k = A_jA_k, so A_k witnesses the pair. This gives a balanced n-point set for every odd n.

technique: Build a balanced witness structure from equilateral triangles that all share one apex, so the shared apex balances every rim pair and each triangle's third vertex balances the apex-with-rim pair.
how_used: Place O plus rim points on a circle centered at O, arranged so OA_iB_i is equilateral for each pair: O is equidistant from all rim points (balances any rim pair), and for the pair (O,A_i) the third triangle vertex B_i has B_iO = B_iA_i so it witnesses that pair. Choosing the number of triangles (and a small extra CDE cluster) realizes any even cardinality, completing the even-n case of part (a).

technique: When a heavily-loaded witness cannot lie in any pair it witnesses, count endpoint slots: too many witnessed pairs on too few remaining points cannot be pairwise disjoint, so two of them must share an endpoint.
how_used: In a balanced center-free set of even size n, average the ~n(n-1)/2 associated (pair,witness) incidences over n points to get a point P associated with >= n/2 pairs. None of these pairs contains P, so they live on the other n-1 points; n/2 vertex-disjoint pairs would need n distinct points, but only n-1 are available, so two witnessed pairs {A,B},{A,C} share A. Then PA=PB and PA=PC give PA=PB=PC, contradicting center-free -- so n cannot be even.

technique: Use the sandwich inequality forced by the defining equation to prove the split must be an initial segment in sorted order
how_used: Since lcm(A1)=d=gcd(A2), every a_i in A1 satisfies a_i <= d and every a_j in A2 satisfies d <= a_j; after sorting a_1<...<a_n this forces A1={a_1,...,a_k}, A2={a_{k+1},...,a_n}, so each good partition corresponds to exactly one 'partitioning' index k where l_k=lcm(a_1..a_k)=gcd(a_{k+1}..a_n)=g_k.

technique: From two adjacent objects both satisfying the defining relation, deduce a rigid equality that forbids a third adjacent object of the same type
how_used: If a_{k-1} and a_k are both partitioning, l_{k-1}=g_{k-1} divides a_k gives g_k=l_k=lcm(l_{k-1},a_k)=a_k and g_{k-1}=gcd(a_k,g_k)=a_k; hence three consecutive partitioning elements would force a_{k+1}=g_k=a_k, contradicting strict increase, so no 3 consecutive partitioning indices exist.

technique: Cap the count of a marked type via a no-three-consecutive density argument to turn the target count into a lower bound on n
how_used: No three consecutive partitioning indices plus endpoint exclusions (a_1,a_2 not both; a_{n-2},a_{n-1} not both) yields at most ceil(2(n-2)/3) partitioning elements; setting ceil(2(n-2)/3) >= 2015 gives n >= 3024.

technique: Build a periodic multiplicative tower on primes 2,3 whose consecutive lcm/gcd chains realize the extremal 2-in-3 pattern
how_used: The set {2*6^i, 3*6^i, 6^{i+1} : 0<=i<=1007} of size 3024 makes each element of form 3*6^i or 6^i (except 6^1008) partitioning, giving exactly 2015 good partitions and matching the lower bound.

technique: To show a player who moves second never gets stuck, cut the ground set by the opponent's committed picks into contiguous components and pigeonhole your fewer occupied elements against the component count, so some component is entirely yours-to-play
how_used: B first picks n. When A has made k>=2 picks (pairwise non-consecutive by rule (ii)), A's picks split [n]\A into k contiguous components (if 1 in A) or k+1 (else), so the component count is >= k. B has made only k-1 picks, so by pigeonhole at least one component contains no B-number. Any number x in that B-free component is legal for B: it is unchosen (rule (i)), and it is at distance >=2 from every B-number, since B-numbers lie in other components separated from x by an interposed A-element and none lie in x's own component, so rule (ii) is not violated. Hence B always has a legal move and can never be the stuck player.

technique: To rule out the opponent's draw outcome, characterize a draw as a forced partition of the board into complementary independent sets, note the board (a path) admits only the parity 2-coloring, then make a first move that lands you in the class the opponent would need to own entirely.
how_used: A draw means all of [n] is chosen and neither player ever picked two consecutive integers, so A's set and B's set are complementary independent sets of the path P_n. The connected path has a unique proper 2-coloring up to swap, {odds} and {evens}, so any draw forces one player to own all odds and the other all evens. B picks n on move 1 (A's opening normalized to <=(n+1)/2 by the reflect-through-center symmetry, justified separately). For odd n>=3: n is odd, so B owns an odd, hence A cannot own all odds — no draw. For even n>=8: n even means a surviving draw needs A to own all odds of [n-1]; on move 2 B grabs an odd from {1,3,...,n-3} (which has (n-2)/2>=3 elements, more than A's 2 picks), an odd A can never complete — no draw. (n=4,6 are genuine draws outside the B-win range.)

technique: To prove a player never gets stuck (liveness), count the contiguous components the opponent's chosen positions cut the board into and show that count exceeds the number of positions the replier has used, so some component holds a free legal reply by pigeonhole.
how_used: B opens with n. Claim: whenever A has just made its k-th move (k>=2), B can make a k-th move. Let S be A's first k picks; S is independent, so [n]\S splits into k contiguous components if 1 in S and k+1 components otherwise. B has chosen only k-1 numbers so far, so by pigeonhole some component C of [n]\S contains none of B's picks. B plays any number of C: it is unchosen, non-adjacent to A's picks (it lies strictly inside a gap between them), and non-consecutive to B's own picks (C contains none, and any B pick sits in a different component). So the reply is legal. Iterating, B never gets stuck; with the no-draw guarantee, A is the one who eventually cannot move.

technique: To reuse a winning strategy known only for one specific opponent-opening on a different opening, run a shadow game coupled to the real one by a position map, and verify a ONE-directional legality implication per player (in the direction each player needs), not a full automorphism.
how_used: B knows a winning strategy S when A opens 1. For a real opening a>1, B couples a shadow (imaginary) game to reality by the flip of the segment [1,a]: x maps to a+1-x if x<=a, and to x if x>a; this sends real opening a to imaginary opening 1, so S is available. B reads A's real move m, plays phi(m) for A in the shadow game, lets S answer with r, and plays phi(r)=phi^{-1}(r) in reality (phi is an involution). The ONLY thing to check is the legality transfer, and crucially it is one-directional and OPPOSITE for the two players: (A) every A-move legal in REALITY maps to an A-move legal in the SHADOW (so B can always feed A's move to S); (B) every B-reply legal in the SHADOW maps to a B-reply legal in REALITY (so B's S-reply is always playable). Both hold. Note phi is NOT a graph automorphism: it breaks the consecutiveness of the seam pair {a,a+1} (a maps to 1, a+1 stays fixed, and 1,a+1 are not adjacent). But the breakage is harmless because it only ever makes a cell that is BLOCKED in reality LOOK free in the shadow (or vice versa), i.e. it costs a player options in exactly the direction that does NOT hurt B's coupling. So one must state the correspondence as 'shadow-blocked implies real-blocked for A, and real-blocked implies shadow-blocked for B' (the exact single directions above), never as a two-way adjacency equivalence. This legitimizes reducing every opening to opening 1 (and the WLOG a<=(n+1)/2 by the same flip about the center).

technique: In a take-turns 'no-consecutive among your own picks' game, show the second player can always reply by a component-counting/pigeonhole invariant: the unpicked region splits into more gaps than the responder has used, so a fresh gap always remains.
how_used: This is the actual engine of B's win (the crux the solver noted was missing). B's very first pick is n. Lemma: after A has made the k-th move (k>=2), B can also make a k-th move. Proof: let S be A's first k picks. Since A's picks contain no two consecutive numbers, [n]\S breaks into k contiguous components if 1 is in S, else k+1 components. B has so far made only k-1 picks, so at least one of these >=k components contains no number B has picked; B chooses any number from that untouched component (it is unpicked and, lying in its own component, is not adjacent to any earlier B-pick). Hence B never gets stuck before A, so B does not lose. This move is what guarantees B can always respond; it must be established BEFORE the draw-avoidance upgrade and before the opening-1 strategy transfer are meaningful.

technique: To upgrade 'the responder never loses' to 'the responder wins' in a draw-possible pairing game, characterize the unique drawing end-configuration (an explicit parity/structure pattern) and have the responder permanently occupy one cell of that pattern so a draw becomes impossible.
how_used: The Lemma gives B a non-losing strategy, but a full board is a draw; B must also kill the draw. Observation: the board fills completely (a draw) only if the two players' picks partition [n], and analyzing the no-consecutive rule shows the only way this happens is A ending up with all the odd numbers. B pre-empts this by owning an odd cell A would need. Odd n>=3: B's first pick n (which is odd) is one of those odds, so A can never collect all odds; draw impossible. Even n>=8: n is even, so B additionally spends its second move on some odd number in {1,3,...,n-3} not yet taken by A (this set has (n-2)/2>=3 elements while A has picked only 2, so one is free); now A cannot obtain every odd of [n-1], killing the draw. Combined with the Lemma, A eventually cannot move, so A loses; this covers all n except the small exceptions n=1,2,4,6 handled by direct check.

technique: Reindex an injectivity-of-shifts condition as a directed graph where n points to n+a_n, so each target receives at most one arrow and the integers decompose into disjoint monotone paths.
how_used: From i+a_i != j+a_j, draw an arrow n -> n+a_n of length a_n (<=2015); each integer receives at most one arrow, so following arrows from the arrow-free 'starting points' gives disjoint strictly-increasing rays covering all of Z_{>0}.

technique: Bound the number of covering paths by forcing them all to hit one fixed short interval and invoking that they occupy distinct points there.
how_used: Each ray meets every window [n,n+2014] at least once (arrow length <=2015); if there were >=2016 starting points, a window past all of them would need 2016 distinct meeting points in 2015 slots, so the number b of rays satisfies 1<=b<=2015.

technique: Rewrite a block sum as a telescoping difference of the first ray-positions past each endpoint, converting the sum into positions-within-a-length-2015-window.
how_used: Sum_{i=m+1}^n a_i = sum_j (y_j - x_j) where x_j,y_j are the first ray points exceeding m,n; hence sum(a_i - b) = sum_j(y_j-n) - sum_j(x_j-m), turning the target into differences of window-offsets.

technique: Bound the spread between two same-size subsets of {1,...,K} by placing one at the bottom and the other at the top, then close with AM-GM on the two complementary factors.
how_used: The offsets x_j-m (and y_j-n) are b distinct elements of {1,...,2015} including 1, so their sums differ by at most (b-1)(2015-b), which by AM-GM is <= ((b-1+2015-b)/2)^2 = 1007^2.

technique: Adjoin a fresh element larger than everything involved to inject a representation of one parity into the regime where representations are guaranteed unique, so assumed non-uniqueness contradicts the guaranteed uniqueness.
how_used: Under the contradiction hypothesis every n>N has a unique odd representation. To bound even reps of any n: pick x in S with x>max(n,N); x cannot appear in an even rep of n, so adjoining x turns each even rep of n into an odd rep of the clean number n+x, injectively, forcing at most one even rep. For odd reps of a small n, adjoin two fresh y,z. Same move gives Property 4: for N<s<t, adding s to the even rep of t and adding t to the even rep of s are two odd reps of the large clean number s+t, so uniqueness forces the even rep of t to contain s.

technique: Cover the positive integers by the residue progressions of a fixed modulus and show each progression contains only finitely many exceptional elements, so the exception set is globally finite.
how_used: Fix s in S. Property 2 shows that n+2as gains an even representation for a>=1, so within each progression Z_r={r+2as : a>=0} (r in {1,...,2s}) the property of having an even rep propagates upward and at most one element exceeding N lacks one. Since Z_{>0} is the union of these 2s progressions, only finitely many integers lack an even representation, hence every large n has exactly one even rep.

technique: Pick the index minimizing a bounded leftover term so the growth relation forces a multiplicative doubling gap, producing an empty interval containing no set element between a value and its double.
how_used: Property 4 gives s_i = sigma_{i-1} - sigma_{k-1} + R_i with 0 <= R_i <= sigma_{k-1}. Choose p>j_0 minimizing R_p over the finite range; then s_{p+1} = (s_p - R_p) + s_p + R_{p+1} >= 2 s_p, so no element of S lies in (s_p, 2 s_p). The guaranteed even rep of 2 s_p then cannot use any element above s_p, so it must contain s_p itself; removing s_p yields a second odd rep of s_p, contradicting Property 1.

technique: Prove a lower bound on a family of substructures by producing one distinct instance per subset of a ground set, indexing them so that a distinct subset gives a provably distinct substructure.
how_used: After reformulating (contrapositive: a non-11-colorable enemy graph has chromatic number k>=12), the solution proves G has at least 2^{k-1}-k odd cycles by producing, for every odd-size subset C of the k color classes with |C|>1, an odd cycle visiting EXACTLY the classes in C. A cycle's set of visited classes recovers C, so different C give different cycles; the number of odd-size subsets with |C|>1 is 2^{k-1}-k, and 2^{11}-12=2036>2015 closes the problem. Crux 0 supplies only this packaging/counting; the per-C cycle construction is cruxes 1-2.

technique: Take the extremal coloring under a lexicographic tie-break on the class-size vector, so any recoloring that shrinks an earlier class is forbidden and yields a local structural constraint.
how_used: A proper k-coloring V_1 ⊔ ... ⊔ V_k is chosen leximinimal in (|V_1|,...,|V_k|). For a chosen v in V_1, if v had no neighbor in the (post-process) class W_2 then moving v there would give a lexicographically smaller proper coloring, contradiction. So v has a neighbor w in W_2 — the seed constraint that starts the colorful odd cycle. (Sol 2 variant: fix V_1={v} in a critical graph and instead minimize the neighbor-count vector (n(V_2),...,n(V_k)).)

technique: In a leximinimal (lexicographically-smallest class-size) proper coloring with classes in a fixed cyclic order, run a directed reachability process that from each already-reached vertex marks its unmarked neighbors in the NEXT class, then shift every marked vertex one class forward; leximinimality of the shifted coloring forces a returning edge from the seed to a marked vertex sitting in the LAST class.
how_used: Pick v in the class chosen first by leximinimality (V_1), arrange the remaining classes V_2,...,V_k cyclically (V_{k+1}=V_2). Mark v's neighbors in V_2, and repeatedly mark unmarked next-class neighbors of marked vertices. After marking, no marked vertex in V_i has an unmarked neighbor in V_{i+1}, so shifting each marked vertex one class forward keeps the coloring proper. If v had no neighbor in the new class W_2, moving v there would give a lexicographically smaller coloring - contradiction; so v has a neighbor w in W_2. w cannot be an unmarked V_2 vertex (those all got marked and shifted out), so w is a marked vertex that shifted into W_2 from V_k. The directed root-path v->...->w steps through the classes in cyclic order, so its edge-count is a multiple of (k-1); when k is odd this length is even, and the closing edge w->v yields an odd cycle visiting every class. This is Lemma 1: a leximinimal coloring with ODD number of classes contains a colorful odd cycle.

technique: To count many odd cycles at once, index them by odd-size subsets of the color classes: restrict the leximinimal coloring to the induced subgraph on a chosen subset of classes, observe the restriction is itself leximinimal (a lex-smaller restricted coloring would splice back to a lex-smaller global one), apply the single-odd-cycle lemma to each subgraph, and read distinctness off the color-set.
how_used: For every C subset of {1,...,k} with |C| odd and >1, let G_C be the induced subgraph on the union of classes indexed by C. The global coloring restricts to a proper |C|-coloring of G_C; it is leximinimal on G_C because any lexicographically smaller coloring of G_C, recombined with the untouched classes V_i (i not in C), would beat the global leximinimal coloring - contradiction. Since |C| is odd, Lemma 1 applied to G_C yields an odd cycle visiting EXACTLY the classes in C. Because each cycle's color-set equals its own C, distinct C give distinct cycles. The number of odd subsets of size >1 of a k-set is 2^{k-1}-k, so a k-chromatic graph has at least 2^{k-1}-k unsociable groups; with k>=12 this exceeds 2015 (2^{11}-12>2015), forcing an 11-coloring in the contrapositive.

technique: Encode a constrained assignment count as a filtered coefficient sum of a product of linear forms, one factor per structural object
how_used: Give worker k the variable x_k; give each brigade spanning workers i..j the linear form f_ij = x_i + ... + x_j, and form f = prod over all brigades (single-worker brigades included) of f_ij. The coefficient of x_1^{a_1}...x_17^{a_17} in f counts the leader-assignments giving worker k exactly a_k leaderships, so the augmented count N equals Sigma(f), the SUM of coefficients over exactly those monomials whose every exponent is congruent to 1 mod 4. N is thus a partial (filtered) coefficient sum of f, not the total.

technique: Show a product of linear forms vanishes at every point of F_p by exhibiting, for each input, one factor forced to be a zero contiguous block-sum via a pigeonhole on prefix sums
how_used: Over F_17, for any (a_1,...,a_17) the 18 prefix sums s_0=0, s_1,...,s_17 lie in F_17, so two coincide, giving indices i<=j with a_i+...+a_j = 0 in F_17; the corresponding factor f_ij (present as a real factor because single-index blocks i=j are included) evaluates to 0, so f(a_1,...,a_17)=0 for every point of F_17^17.

technique: Reduce each variable below degree p via x^p = x, then use that a polynomial with per-variable degree < p vanishing on all of F_p^n is the formal zero polynomial, forcing every coefficient (and any partial coefficient sum) to vanish
how_used: Replace each x_i^17 by x_i (Fermat), which preserves both the vanish-everywhere property on F_17^17 and every coefficient sum; the result g has degree <= 16 in each variable and still vanishes on all of F_17^17, so by induction on variables g is the zero polynomial. Hence ALL coefficients of g are 0 in F_17, so in particular the filtered coefficient sum Sigma(g) = Sigma(f) = N vanishes — no roots-of-unity filter needed, since g being formally zero kills every coefficient sum at once. Thus 17 | N.

technique: Absorb an awkward divisibility constraint by adjoining phantom copies of a structural object that each contribute a fixed forced increment, shifting every target residue by a controlled amount
how_used: Adjoin a single-worker 'brigade' for each of the 17 workers (each with its unique forced leader). Each phantom brigade adds exactly 1 to its worker's assignment count, so the original constraint 'each count divisible by 4' becomes 'each count congruent to 1 mod 4' in the augmented setting, and the augmented valid-count equals the original N. This also promotes the row of length-≥2 brigades into the clean uniform product over ALL intervals ∏_{1≤i≤j≤17} f_ij with f_ij = x_i+...+x_j, which is what the vanishing argument later needs.

technique: Turn 'vanishes at every point of F_p^n' into 'is the zero polynomial' by collapsing each exponent below p via x^p→x (which preserves both evaluations by Fermat and the coefficient functional), then invoking uniqueness of low-per-variable-degree polynomials.
how_used: Σ(f) is invariant under replacing any x_i^17 by x_i: this drops an exponent by 16≡0 mod 4, so it preserves the '≡1 mod 4' membership of every α_i, and by Fermat's Little Theorem it preserves all F_17-evaluations. Iterate to reduce f to g with each variable of degree ≤16<17. Since g still vanishes on all of F_17^17 and has per-variable degree <17, an induction on the number of variables shows g≡0 identically, so Σ(g)=0; as Σ is preserved, Σ(f)=0, i.e. N≡0 mod 17.

technique: Enlarge the counted family by adjoining forced/degenerate members so the count acquires a clean algebraic index set, absorbing the added members by shifting the per-object divisibility target by their fixed contribution.
how_used: Instead of counting leader-assignments to genuine brigades (blocks [i,j] of length >=2) with each worker's assignment count ==0 mod 4, adjoin a single-worker 'brigade' [i,i] for every i, each of which has a UNIQUE forced leader (worker i itself). Adjoining these is a bijection on assignments (nothing to choose for singletons) so it preserves the count, but forces every worker to gain exactly one extra assignment; hence the target 'each worker's count ==0 mod 4' becomes 'each worker's count ==1 mod 4' in the enlarged setting. Now the family of blocks runs over ALL i<=j (length >=1), which is exactly the index set needed so that a length-1 consecutive block can later appear as a genuine factor; with the original i<j (length >=2) family the later vanishing argument fails.

technique: Encode a residue-constrained count as the coefficient-sum of a product of linear forms, one form per structural sub-object, so a monomial's exponent vector records how many sub-objects selected each element.
how_used: Enlarge the count by declaring each single worker [k,k] a brigade with its unique leader k, so every worker gains a fixed +1 and the target congruence becomes 'each worker's leadership total ≡ 1 mod 4'; call this enlarged count N. For each block [i,j] (now 1≤i≤j≤17) set f_ij = x_i+...+x_j and f = prod_{i≤j} f_ij. Expanding, each factor f_ij contributes exactly one variable x_k with i≤k≤j = the chosen leader of that block, so the coefficient of x_1^{a_1}...x_17^{a_17} in f counts leader-assignments giving worker k exactly a_k leaderships. Hence N = Σ(f), the sum of coefficients over all exponent vectors with every a_k ≡ 1 mod 4, and the goal reduces to Σ(f) ≡ 0 mod 17.

technique: Show a product of linear forms vanishes at every point of F_p^n by pigeonholing the n+1 prefix sums of the coordinates: two coincide, forcing a contiguous block-sum to zero, and that block's factor is a genuine factor of the product.
how_used: Work over F_17. For any point a=(a_1,...,a_17) in F_17^17, the 18 prefix sums s_0=0, s_t=a_1+...+a_t all lie in F_17, so by pigeonhole s_{i-1}=s_j for some i≤j, giving a_i+...+a_j = 0, i.e. f_ij(a)=0. Because f = prod over ALL blocks 1≤i≤j≤17 includes this f_ij as a genuine factor (adjacent-prefix collisions give a length-1 block [k,k], which is why the enlargement to length-≥1 blocks is essential), f(a)=0. Hence f vanishes at every point of F_17^17 — the input needed for the coefficient argument.

technique: To convert 'polynomial vanishes everywhere on F_p^n' into a statement about its coefficients, first collapse each variable's degree below p using x^p = x, then use that a polynomial of per-variable degree < p vanishing on all of F_p^n is identically zero.
how_used: f vanishes on all of F_17^17 and we want Σ(f)=0, the coefficient-sum over monomials with every exponent ≡ 1 mod 4. Repeatedly replacing x_i^17 by x_i (Fermat: x^17=x on F_17) leaves the value at every point of F_17^17 unchanged and yields g of per-variable degree ≤ 16. This preserves Σ: the reduction sends an exponent e≥1 to its representative ≡ e mod 16, and since 4|16 the exponent's mod-4 class is unchanged, so the target class (all exponents ≡ 1 mod 4) is preserved and merged coefficients sum — hence Σ(g)=Σ(f). A polynomial with each variable-degree < 17 vanishing at every point of F_17^17 is identically zero (induction on the number of variables: fixing all but one gives a univariate polynomial of degree <17 with 17 roots, so all coefficients vanish; peel off variables). Thus g≡0, Σ(g)=0, so Σ(f)=0, i.e. N≡0 mod 17, and 17 divides the original count.

technique: Fill cells in increasing-label order and stop at the least label where a whole orientation of lines first becomes saturated
how_used: Color cells black one by one following labels 1,2,..., stopping at the least label k such that after coloring it, every line of one orientation (all rows, or all columns) contains at least two black cells; minimality forces that just before k at least one row and one column had at most one black cell, and it also forces at most one line of the saturated orientation to be entirely black. This pins the exact first moment the filled region is spread across every line.

technique: At the stopping moment, give each line its own boundary quota to lower-bound the filled cells adjacent to an unfilled cell
how_used: Call a black cell red if it is torus-adjacent to a white cell. Each non-all-black row has >=2 black and >=1 white, so on its length-N cycle it crosses the black/white boundary >=2 times, contributing >=2 red cells; the single possible all-black row still contributes >=1 red cell via a white vertical neighbor in an adjacent row, totaling >=2(N-1)+1=2N-1 red cells. The least red label is <= k+1-(2N-1); its eventual white neighbor gets label >= k+1, forcing a neighbor difference >= 2N-1. The per-line ownership of >=2 boundary cells is what yields 2N-1 rather than the planar N.

technique: In a monotone incremental filling of a grid in label order, halt at the first moment a global coverage threshold is met and read off the count of filled/unfilled adjacent pairs forced at that stopping moment.
how_used: Lower bound M >= 2N-1 on the N x N torus (N=2011, answer 4021). Color cells black in label order 1,2,3,..., stopping at the least label k after which every line of one orientation (WLOG every row) first contains >= 2 black cells; by minimality just before k some row AND some column still had <= 1 black cell, forcing at most one row to be all-black. Recolor RED each black cell adjacent to a white cell: every non-all-black row keeps a white cell so contributes >= 2 red cells, and the possible all-black row contributes >= 1 red via a white cell in a neighboring row, giving >= 2(N-1)+1 = 2N-1 red cells. These occupy distinct labels <= k, so the smallest red label s <= k+1-(2N-1); its white neighbor is filled only at some label >= k+1, so that adjacent pair differs by >= (k+1)-s >= 2N-1. This is the load-bearing half.

technique: To force a global extremal quantity with no obvious extremal configuration, run a monotone filling/coloring process in label order and freeze it at the FIRST label that crosses a structural threshold, then extract the count/inequality from the objects present at exactly that frozen instant.
how_used: This is the LOWER bound M >= 2N-1 (the genuinely hard half; N=2011 so 2N-1=4021, which decides the problem). Color all cells white, then walk labels 1,2,3,... coloring each cell black, and STOP at the least label k whose coloring first makes every line of one orientation contain >= 2 black cells (so just before k, at least one row AND at least one column still had <= 1 black cell). WLOG this is rows. Structural fact read off AT the stop: at most one row is entirely black (two all-black rows would have already forced every column to >= 2 black, triggering the stop earlier). Now color RED every black cell adjacent to a white cell; each of the N-1 non-all-black rows is a cyclic sequence with >= 2 black and >= 1 white so contributes >= 2 red cells (2(N-1) total), and the lone possible all-black row contributes >= 1 more via a white cell in a neighboring row, giving >= 2N-1 red cells all with labels <= k. Hence the smallest red label is <= k+1-(2N-1); its white neighbor is eventually labeled >= k+1, so that adjacent pair differs by >= 2N-1. The torus (cyclic rows/columns, Z_N x Z_N) is what makes '2 per line' the threshold and supplies the '+1', beating the planar bound N.

technique: To meet an adjacency bound on a torus, lay the consecutive labels along a single center-out traversal by nested square shells (boustrophedon within each shell), symmetric about the center, so that the two ENDS of each shell are the cells brought together by the seam identifications and per-shell label spread — not radius — controls every gap.
how_used: This is the UPPER bound / explicit construction M <= 2N-1 (N=2011, 2N-1=4021), which together with the lower bound pins M = 2N-1. It is the Table V spiral (verified on N=3,5,7 in Tables I, III, IV). WARNING, the naive 'concentric rings => same-ring cells get near-equal labels' idea is FALSE: an outer ring holds ~4N cells spanning a label range ~4N, so same-ring / around-ring neighbors can differ by ~4N (a plain Chebyshev-ring labeling gives max gap ~16 for N=5, not 9). The actual construction places 1 at the center and threads consecutive integers OUTWARD shell by shell in a boustrophedon (snake) order chosen so that (i) planar around-shell and inward/outward neighbors differ by <= 2N-1, and (ii) the two seam identifications (top<->bottom, left<->right) each glue the two ENDS of a shell, which by the symmetric-about-center layout carry labels within 2N-1 of each other. The real work a solver must still do: pin the exact shell traversal / closed form from Table V (odd N=2n+1; e.g. read off the entries n(2n-1)+1, 2n^2, 2n(n+1), (2n+1)^2-k), then check EVERY adjacency class -- planar neighbors, the top/bottom seam, the left/right seam -- attains max difference exactly 2N-1. The reusable pointer is 'route consecutive labels along a center-out shell traversal so seam-glued cells are shell-ENDS, not same-radius cells'; the executable content is the explicit snake ordering and the two seam checks.

technique: Propagate a consistent orientation of covering dominoes along a monochromatic diagonal by induction, using the no-2x2 condition to rule out an orientation flip between consecutive diagonal cells
how_used: 2-color so (0,0) is white; the ith white diagonal is {(2i+k,k)}. Claim: if the K lowest cells of a white diagonal are all covered, every covering domino faces right or up (its black cell is right or above its white cell); mirror for black diagonals (face left or up). Induct on k up the diagonal: base k=0 from the fully-covered bottom row (condition iv); step — if (2i+k,k) faces up/right but (2i+k+1,k+1) faces down/left, the two dominoes form a 2x2 square, contradiction. This orientation rigidity is the engine of the alternative proof; the subsequent tally of forced-empty white cells (via an L/R split counting distinguished dominoes) is a separate downstream step.

technique: Reduce an extremal bound to a fixed target configuration by a count-non-decreasing local repair applied to the lowest deviating cell, using the number of deviations as a monovariant with a well-founded (bottom-up) order that prevents already-fixed deviations from re-breaking
how_used: Fix a target 'staircase' of fictitious horizontal dominoes: with rows labeled 0..m-1 upward, row i carries a vertically-centered block of n-i fictitious dominoes (omitting i cells on each side). A fictitious domino is bad if not fully covered by a real domino. The bottom row is fully covered by condition (iv), so it has no bad ones; take the LOWEST bad fictitious domino D. Because the repair (separate crux) only touches D's row and the cell above, choosing the lowest bad one guarantees repairing D cannot re-break any lower already-good fictitious domino, so bad-count strictly decreases while the real-domino count does not; finitely many repairs reach a normal form with all fictitious dominoes good, and its count bounds the original.

technique: Repair an uncovered target cell without losing count by casework on the covering status of its cells, using a forbidden-2x2 hypothesis to force any conflicting cover to be perpendicular so it can be re-laid onto the target (or a fresh piece inserted)
how_used: At the lowest bad fictitious horizontal domino D with left cell ℓ and right cell r: the cells directly below ℓ and r are the right cell of one horizontal domino D_1 and the left cell of a DIFFERENT horizontal domino D_2 in the good row below. Case (a) ℓ covered by real D_ℓ: since D is bad, D_ℓ is not the horizontal ℓ-r; and D_ℓ cannot be horizontal at all without forming a 2x2 with the horizontal below, so D_ℓ is VERTICAL (covers ℓ and the cell above ℓ). If r were also covered, that cover would be vertical too and form a 2x2 with D_ℓ — contradiction; so r is free, and D_ℓ is re-laid as the horizontal ℓ-r. This creates no new 2x2 with the row below because the two cells under ℓ,r belong to distinct dominoes D_1≠D_2, not a single horizontal domino. Case (b) r covered: mirror. Case (c) neither covered: add a fresh horizontal on D and, if that makes a 2x2 with the domino directly above D, delete exactly that one domino (net count ≥ 0). Each case yields a valid arrangement with count non-decreasing and one fewer bad fictitious domino.

technique: Set up a per-region monovariant that strictly decreases under a local re-packing move, so an arbitrary configuration can be pushed to a canonical 'all-good' normal form without losing count.
how_used: Overlay a fixed template of 'fictitious' horizontal dominoes: in row i (rows numbered 0..m-1 upward) place a vertically-symmetric block of n-i fictitious horizontal dominoes, leaving i cells bare on each side. Call a fictitious domino GOOD if the real arrangement fully covers its two cells, BAD otherwise; the monovariant is the number of bad fictitious dominoes. To decrease it, take a bad fictitious domino D of minimal row rank (never the bottom row, which is fully covered). Because the cells directly below D's two cells are inner cells of real dominoes and no two real dominoes form a 2x2 square, a short case analysis on whether D's left/right cell is already covered shows one can always re-pack locally: slide the vertical real domino covering one endpoint of D to instead cover D, or (if both endpoints of D are free) add a domino on D and delete the domino directly above it to avoid a new square. Each move keeps the arrangement valid, does not decrease the domino count, and strictly lowers the count of bad fictitious dominoes; iterate to reach an all-good configuration.

technique: In a normal form where a fixed skeleton is fully covered, confine the remaining free cells to a boundary region and lower-bound its uncovered cells by its chessboard color imbalance (each domino covers one cell of each color).
how_used: In the all-good configuration every fictitious domino is covered, so the only real dominoes not pinned to the fictitious skeleton lie in the two triangular corner regions of side-length m-1 at the upper-left and upper-right (the cells the shrinking blocks leave bare, i cells per side in row i). Because the skeleton is fully covered, no room remains for a domino to poke out of a triangle, so each triangle behaves as a self-contained region. Chess-color the board; in each side-(m-1) triangle the counts of black and white cells differ by exactly floor(m/2). Since any domino covers one black and one white cell, at least floor(m/2) cells of the majority color stay uncovered in each triangle, giving 2*floor(m/2) uncovered cells overall. With 2mn cells total, the number of dominoes is at most (2mn - 2*floor(m/2))/2 = mn - floor(m/2), matching the brick-like construction.

technique: Compute an average degree in a graph as (total edge-endpoint count)/(vertex count) by counting ordered edges directly instead of per-vertex
how_used: Average coziness = E/V where V = number of distributions of n+1 stones into n boxes = C(2n,n+1) (stars and bars) and E = number of ordered neighbor pairs (a,b); dividing gives (n^2-1)/2 without needing the per-vertex degree distribution.

technique: Encode each ordered edge of a move-graph by the intermediate object obtained by removing the moved element plus the ordered (source,target) label
how_used: An ordered neighbor pair (a,b) is bijected with a distribution c of n stones into n boxes (remove the moved stone) together with an ordered pair (i,j), i!=j, of source/target boxes; hence E = C(2n-1,n)*n(n-1).

technique: Compute the expected count of a sum of indicators by linearity, reducing to one symmetric event's probability
how_used: Coziness = (n-1)*(number of non-empty boxes) since each of the f(a) non-empty boxes yields n-1 neighbors; writing f(a)=sum f_i(a) and using symmetry, mean f = n*P(box i non-empty) = n*(1 - C(2n-1,n+1)/C(2n,n+1)) = n*(n+1)/(2n), giving average (n-1)(n+1)/2.

technique: Bound the number of rounds below by counting how many distinct across-round membership patterns the process can assign to objects and forcing that count to reach the number of objects
how_used: Each switch is described by whether it sits in start vs. flipped state over the r rounds, giving at most 2^r distinct patterns; with 15 switches, r=3 yields only 2^3=8 patterns, so two switches must share a pattern and stay indistinguishable, forcing r>=4.

technique: Recover a hidden edge-subset of a cycle from its vertex-parity boundary by propagating the forced local parity constraint around the cycle, then break the resulting complement ambiguity with a globally known parity
how_used: A lit lamp is an odd-degree vertex of the flipped-switch edge set; fixing membership of one edge forces every subsequent edge around the 15-cycle by the parity constraint at each vertex, pinning the set to exactly two complements (sizes summing to 15, hence opposite parity), and Raymond's known count of flipped switches selects the right one, revealing that round's toggled lamp-pairs.

technique: Identify each object by a per-round membership pattern using a binary-digit labeling, so ceil(log2 N) rounds separate all objects
how_used: Label the 15 switches with distinct 4-bit codes; resetting all switches before each round, in round j flip exactly those whose j-th bit is 1, use the recovery step to learn which lamp-pairs were active that round, and read each lamp-pair's unique 4-bit across-round membership to match it to its switch.

technique: Reindex nested set-intersection conditions by typing each element by the exact family it belongs to, so each intersection becomes a superset-sum of the type-count function
how_used: Type each integer by the binary string v in F_2^100 recording which of S_1..S_100 contain it, and let f(v) count elements of type v; then for nonempty T with indicator u, |cap_{i in T} S_i| = sum_{v superset u} f(v). Each condition '|T| divides the intersection size' becomes P(u): |u| divides sum_{v superset u} f(v) for every nonempty u, the nonempty-intersection hypothesis becomes f(1..1) >= 1, and the objective 'in at least 50 sets' becomes A = sum_{|v| >= 50} f(v). Any nonnegative f realizes as an actual set system, so the problem becomes minimizing A over nonnegative f meeting all P(u).

technique: For the achievability bound, guess a closed-form assignment linear in the coordinate weight and verify the divisibility constraints by collapsing a weighted binomial sum
how_used: Take f_0(v) = 2|v| - 100 (nonnegative on the relevant levels |v| >= 50, which is all that matters since it suffices to assign f on |v| >= 50). For |u| = 100 - k the constraint sum is sum_{j=0}^k C(k,j)(100 - 2j) = (100 - k)*2^k = |u|*2^k, a multiple of |u|, so every P(u) holds; and A = sum_{i=50}^{100} C(100,i)(2i-100) = 50*C(100,50), the claimed optimum.

technique: Prove the matching lower bound by a mass-conserving redistribution move that pushes count from a set to its immediate subsets, applied top-down to reduce every level (including the top) to the minimal representative of its forced residue class
how_used: Define push-down on v with |v| >= 50 and f(v) >= |v|: subtract |v| from f(v) and add 1 to each w subset v of size |v|-1. This preserves every congruence P(u) (for u subset v the superset-sum drops by exactly |u|, so |u| | sum is untouched; for others unchanged) and never increases A (A is unchanged for |v| > 50, drops by 50 for |v| = 50). Apply it FIRST at the full set 1..1 repeatedly until f(1..1) equals exactly 100 (the smallest positive multiple of 100), THEN sweep levels |v| = 99, 98, ..., 50 pushing each down until f(v) < |v|. Bringing the TOP down to 100 (not leaving it at an arbitrary multiple) is what fixes the residue tower: with f(1..1)=100 and 0 <= f(v) < |v| below, the mod-|v| congruence forces f(v) = f_0(v) at every level, so A >= A(f_0) = 50*C(100,50).

technique: Encode a polygon area as the imaginary part of a shoelace determinant, then row-reduce so the area becomes an element of the cyclotomic ring generated by the vertices' roots of unity.
how_used: Place the regular n-gon at vertices omega^k (omega = e^{2 pi i/n}). Writing the signed area of triangle (omega^k, omega^{k+a}, omega^{k+b}) as (1/2i)det of the 3x3 shoelace matrix and subtracting the first row from the others factors it into T(a,b) = (omega^a-1)(omega^b-1)(omega^{-a}-omega^{-b})/(2i); rotation-invariance (|omega^k|=1) removes the base index k, so every triangle's area is (1/2i) times an algebraic integer in Z[omega]. This sets up any color-class area sum as (1/2i)(element of Z[omega]).

technique: Show a residue-class subsum over roots of unity is independent of the residue by isolating the residue-dependent part and killing it as a complete geometric series whenever the step properly divides the order.
how_used: For the construction when m | n, triangulate the regular n-gon by the fan from vertex 1 (all diagonals from omega^0) and color triangle (omega^j, omega^0, omega^{j+1}) by j mod m, admitting the degenerate zero-area triangles at j in {-1,0} so the index j runs over a FULL residue system of n/m terms per color (this fixes the n vs n-2 count without changing any area). Color-r area = sum_{j = r mod m} T(-j,1) = ((omega-1)/2i)[ (n/m)(1+omega^{-1}) + sum_{j = r mod m}(omega^{-j}-omega^j) ]. The residue-dependent inner sum is the only r-dependent piece; both sum_{j=r mod m} omega^j = omega^r(1+omega^m+...+omega^{n-m}) and its conjugate are complete geometric progressions equal to 0 when m | n (m<n), so the inner sum vanishes and every color gets n/m * (omega-1)(omega^{-1}+1)/(2i), independent of r. NOTE: the triangles are NOT rotations of a single base triangle; equal-area comes purely from the residue-dependent part vanishing.

technique: Rule out a target value by an algebraic-integrality test: any attainable value is a finite sum of algebraic integers, so if the forced target is not an algebraic integer it is unattainable.
how_used: Necessity direction. Repeating the shoelace with no divisibility assumption, any valid m-coloring of any triangulation forces each color's area to equal S = (n/m)(omega-1)(omega^{-1}+1)/(2i) (each color = A/m, A the polygon area). Each triangle contributes T(a,b) = (1/2i)(algebraic integer), since omega is an algebraic integer and the shoelace numerator is a Z-combination of powers of omega; a color's area is a finite sum of these, so 2i*S is a finite sum of algebraic integers, hence an algebraic integer. Then 2i*S = (n/m)(omega-1)(omega^{-1}+1) must be an algebraic integer. Concluding m | n from this requires reducing to 'n/m is an algebraic integer' -- that reduction is the separate divisibility move (see next crux); with it, a rational algebraic integer is an ordinary integer, forcing m | n, so m does not divide n is impossible.

technique: Justify dividing every ring element in a sum by a common factor by proving that factor divides each summand over the algebraic integers, via a parity/residue casework on the summand's own factors.
how_used: Each triangle area T(a,b) = (omega^a-1)(omega^b-1)(omega^{-a}-omega^{-b})/(2i) is divisible by (omega-1)(omega^{-1}+1) over the algebraic integers: (omega-1) always divides omega^a-1 and omega^b-1 (via omega^a-1 = (omega-1)(1+...+omega^{a-1})), and casework on a,b mod 2 shows at least one of {omega^a-1, omega^b-1, omega^{-a}-omega^{-b}} is a multiple of omega+1 (~ omega^{-1}+1 up to a unit) -- e.g. a even gives (omega+1)|(omega^a-1); a,b both odd gives (omega+1)|(omega^{-a}-omega^{-b}). Crucially, (omega-1) and (omega+1) are drawn from DISTINCT factors so their product divides N(a,b) in every parity case (no double-counting). Hence rescaling by 2i/((omega-1)(omega^{-1}+1)) instead of 2i keeps every triangle's contribution an algebraic integer, so their sum is, and the forced color area rescales to exactly n/m, which must therefore be an algebraic integer. This makes the integrality obstruction valid without invoking O_K = Z[omega].

technique: Bound the number of distinct objects by the size of the finite value-set their invariant lives in
how_used: Fix any one of the n cuts; it splits the mn beads into m disjoint blocks of n consecutive beads, and each block's red-count is an integer in {0,1,...,n}, a set of only n+1 values. The condition forces these m counts pairwise distinct, so m distinct integers must fit in an (n+1)-element set, giving m <= n+1 (the necessity direction).

technique: Lay the objects into a 2D array read row-by-row around the cycle, so a one-bead cyclic shift of the cut acts as a synchronized one-step shift of every row-window at once
how_used: For the extremal case m=n+1, place the mn beads as an (n+1) x n staircase array where row k has its first k beads red and the rest blue (row k has k reds), and read the array row-by-row around the circle. Because each block has length exactly n = one row and the m blocks sit exactly one row apart, the n cuts T_0,...,T_{n-1} are the cyclic shifts of the cut window by 0,1,...,n-1 positions, and each block of T_i is a length-n window that takes the last n-i beads of some row k and the first i beads of row k+1 (indices mod n+1). Its red-count is max(0,k-i)+min(i,k+1), which for each fixed i is exactly the map giving counts (i,0,1,...,k-1,k+1,...,n) from bottom to top -- a permutation of {0,1,...,n}. So within every shift the n+1 block-counts are distinct, and m=n+1 is achievable.

technique: To force a windowed statistic to hit all extremal values, lay the object as a staircase/triangular array whose k-th row carries exactly k of the marked element, placed so a one-step slide of every window changes each row's count by a controlled unit.
how_used: Build the tight m=n+1 case as an (n+1)-by-n array read in reading order, where row k from the bottom is a staircase holding exactly k reds, giving the n+1 distinct counts 0,1,...,n at offset 0. Orientation matters and must be pinned: put the k reds in the LAST k columns of row k (right-justified staircase); the left-justified version fails distinctness from offset 1. With the right-justified staircase the n cyclic one-bead shifts T_1,...,T_{n-1} obey the closed form: #reds in row k of T_i equals k if k>i, k-1 if i>=k>0, and i if k=0. For each fixed i these n+1 values read bottom to top are (i,0,1,...,k-1,k+1,...,n) -- a permutation of 0..n -- hence all distinct. Verifying this explicit formula (rather than any recursion) settles the extremal m=n+1 necklace; every larger construction bottoms out here.

technique: Reduce a small-parameter instance to an already-built larger-parameter extremal object by prepending equal inert (monochromatic) padding to each block, sized so the padding is silently absorbed by the first few window-shifts and later shifts replay the base object's cuts.
how_used: For m < n+1 (so m <= n), take the ALREADY-CONSTRUCTED extremal (m, m-1) staircase necklace -- note m = (m-1)+1 is exactly the tight case at n'=m-1, so it is the base built by the staircase crux, NOT a fresh recursion -- and prepend pad = n+1-m beads of a single color (treated as blue) to the front of each of the m rows, extending each block from length m-1 to n and giving mn beads. Blocks are spaced exactly n apart, so a global one-bead cut-shift moves every block-window by the same amount within its own row. For the first pad shifts the window only drops a leading pad bead and picks up a padding bead of the next row, leaving every red count unchanged, so offsets 0..pad reproduce the base necklace's offset-0 distinct profile; once the shift exceeds pad, each further shift replays the (m,m-1) necklace's genuine cuts, which are distinct by that base construction. Hence all n cuts of the padded necklace have distinct block counts, giving every m <= n; with the m=n+1 crux this settles all m <= n+1.

technique: Represent each quadratic-form term as a Euclidean inner product of vectors, so the whole double sum collapses to the squared norm of one summed vector.
how_used: Assign to subset A_i the vector v_i indexed by ordered pairs (p,q) with entry 1/|A_i| when both p,q in A_i and 0 otherwise; then |A_i∩A_j|^2/(|A_i||A_j|) = <v_i,v_j>, making the target double sum equal to ||sum_i x_i v_i||^2 = ||v||^2.

technique: Lower-bound a vector's norm by testing Cauchy-Schwarz against a well-chosen probe vector, then optimize the probe's free parameters to make the resulting bound sharp.
how_used: Test v against w = α·e + β·1 (e = diagonal indicator, 1 = all-ones over pairs); Cauchy-Schwarz gives ||v||·||w|| >= <w,v> = α·sum x_i + β·sum x_i|A_i| >= (α+ℓβ)sum x_i, then choosing α=n-ℓ, β=ℓ-1 yields the sharp c=(n+ℓ^2-2ℓ)/(n(n-1)).

technique: Certify a Cauchy-Schwarz bound is tight by exhibiting an extremal configuration whose summed vector is a scalar multiple of the probe vector.
how_used: Take all C(n,ℓ) subsets of size exactly ℓ with x_i=1; compute v's diagonal entry C(n-1,ℓ-1)/ℓ and off-diagonal entry C(n-2,ℓ-2)/ℓ and check these are proportional to w's entries (n-1 on diagonal, ℓ-1 off), so equality holds and c cannot be larger.

technique: Prove sufficiency by tiling the board into copies of a small block on which the allowed moves flip every cell exactly once
how_used: Assuming WLOG 3|m, cover the grid with 3-row-by-2-column blocks; in each block apply an A-move on the top 2x2 (flipping (1,1),(1,2),(2,2)) and a B-move on the bottom 2x2 (flipping (2,1),(3,1),(3,2)), so their two L-trominoes cover all six cells of the block once; stacking the bands flips every coin exactly once and yields all heads

technique: Assign cell weights from an abelian group so that either choice-variant of a single move changes the weighted head-count by the same fixed amount, making that count an invariant
how_used: Weight cell (i,j) by (i+j) mod 3; then the two optional off-diagonal cells (TR and BL of a 2x2) have equal weight, and the three flipped cells always occupy all three residue classes once each, so every move flips the parity of each class-count simultaneously; from all-tails the class-count parities stay equal, and reaching all-heads needs the three residue-class sizes equal in parity, which on an m x n board holds iff 3|mn

technique: Build the extremal sequence by indexing each term through the 2-adic valuation of its position, so every window has a unique maximal-valuation position
how_used: Set a_i = 2^{k - v_2(i)} for i = 1..2^{k+1}-1; in any window i..j exactly one index x attains the maximal v_2, so a_x is the unique term of minimal 2-adic valuation and every other term is divisible by 2^{k-v+1}, forcing any signed sum to be a nonzero odd multiple of 2^{k-v} (values stay in 1..2^k).

technique: Greedily choose each sign to pull the running partial sum back toward zero, then induct to confine every prefix sum to a fixed bounded window
how_used: Set s_i = +1 when the current partial sum b_{i-1} <= 0 and s_i = -1 when b_{i-1} >= 1; induction confines every b_i to [-n+1, n] (n = 2^k), a window of exactly 2n integers.

technique: Force two equal prefix sums by pigeonholing more prefix values than the bounded range allows, then subtract to realize the forbidden zero-sum window
how_used: With L >= 2n there are >= 2n+1 prefix sums b_0..b_L but only 2n possible values in [-n+1,n], so two are equal and their difference gives a consecutive signed subsequence summing to 0, proving L <= 2n-1 = 2^{k+1}-1.

technique: Force a logarithmic bound on the worst-case count by placing the marks on a doubling schedule so any monotone path meets at most one mark inside each geometrically-growing block of rows.
how_used: For row i = 2^a + b (0<=a<=N=floor(log2 n), 0<=b<2^a) colour the (2b+1)-th circle. As a ninja-path descends its column index rises by at most 1 per row, while within one block (rows 2^a..2^{a+1}-1) the coloured columns 2b+1 are spaced 2 apart across only 2^a rows, so a path can catch at most one red per block; over the N+1 blocks that is at most N+1 = 1+floor(log2 n) reds.

technique: Turn a longest-monotone-path count into a per-vertex potential by labelling each vertex with the maximum number of marked vertices on a monotone path ending there.
how_used: Assign to each circle C the maximum number of red circles on a top-to-C ninja-path. A red circle with label m witnesses a ninja-path through m reds, so proving k>=N+1 reduces to forcing some red label to exceed N; and equal-label reds are automatically pairwise unreachable from one another (a red reached from another same-or-lower red would get a strictly larger label).

technique: Close a per-level count into a geometric bound by an induction where each level is bounded by one more than the running total of all lower levels, then sum against the global total to force a level beyond the range.
how_used: Combine e_i<=l with row-minimality: if l is the lowest row carrying a label-i red, every red above row l has label <i, so l-1 <= e_1+...+e_{i-1}. Induction then gives e_i <= 1+(e_1+...+e_{i-1}) <= 2^{i-1}. Summing, e_1+...+e_N <= 2^N-1 < n (since 2^N<=n), so not all n reds fit in labels 1..N; some red has label >=N+1, yielding a ninja-path with >=1+floor(log2 n) reds.

technique: To bound the size of one antichain in a geometric poset, cover the whole ground set by pieces each of which is a 'downward cone' or a single line, so that each piece can contain at most one antichain element.
how_used: Reds are assigned number = max reds on a downward ninja-path ending at them; two reds with the same number i are pairwise unreachable, so number-i reds form an antichain. Take the lowest number-i red, in row l. Cover the triangle by the sub-triangle hanging below that red (a cone: any two reds in it would be comparable, so it holds at most one number-i red) together with l-1 lines covering rows 1..l-1 (each meets the antichain at most once). Hence e_i <= l.

technique: Turn a per-class size bound of the form (class size <= its lowest occupied row) into a geometric bound by induction: the rows strictly above that lowest row are exactly filled by the earlier classes, so the lowest row is at most one plus the running total of previous class sizes.
how_used: With e_i <= l where l is the lowest row holding a number-i red, note every red in rows 1..l-1 has number < i, so l-1 <= e_1+...+e_{i-1}. Inductively assuming e_j <= 2^{j-1} gives l-1 <= 2^{i-1}-1, so l <= 2^{i-1} and e_i <= 2^{i-1}. Summing e_1+...+e_N <= 2^N-1 < n forces some red with number >= N+1, i.e. a ninja-path through >= N+1 reds.

technique: For a tight upper-bound construction on a layered/triangular structure, place the marked cells by a dyadic (binary-block) rule that partitions the rows into blocks of sizes 1,2,4,... so that any monotone path meets each block at most once.
how_used: In row i = 2^a + b (0 <= a <= N, 0 <= b < 2^a) color the (2b+1)th circle. The rows split into blocks {2^a, ..., 2^{a+1}-1} of size 2^a; the offsets 2b+1 are spaced so any ninja-path passes through at most one red in each block, giving at most N+1 reds per path and matching the lower bound.

technique: Encode each maximal run of consecutive values as an edge whose endpoints are its first value and one-past-its-last value, turning a tiling-by-runs into a multigraph on the residue set
how_used: Labels are read mod n. A cut piece a, a+1, ..., b-1 becomes an edge a->b on vertices 1..n, so #pieces = #edges of the multigraph Gamma; the k-th reversed strip k, k+1, ..., k+n-1 traces a closed cycle gamma_k through vertex k, so Gamma's edges partition into the n edge-disjoint cycles gamma_1,...,gamma_n.

technique: Read a global end-to-end traversal that uses every piece exactly once as an Eulerian trail of the encoding multigraph to force connectivity
how_used: Because the pieces reassemble into one contiguous 1xn^2 strip (consecutive labels have consecutive residues), reading that strip left-to-right traverses every edge of Gamma once, an Eulerian cycle; a graph with a trail through all edges is connected, so Gamma is connected. This connectivity is what the edge-count bound consumes.

technique: Lower-bound edge count by deleting one edge from each of several edge-disjoint spanning cycles: since each cycle alone spans all vertices, connectivity survives and a spanning tree's worth of edges must remain
how_used: The n cycles gamma_1,...,gamma_n are pairwise edge-disjoint and each visits all n vertices; delete one edge from each, giving Gamma'. Deleting one edge from a spanning cycle cannot disconnect it, and the cycles are edge-disjoint, so Gamma' stays connected, hence has >= n-1 edges. Adding back the n deleted edges gives |E(Gamma)| >= (n-1)+n = 2n-1, i.e. at least 2n-1 pieces.

technique: To realize a claimed extremal value, exhibit one explicit instance whose piece-count equals the bound and verify it produces the required arrangement.
how_used: Give a construction with exactly 2n-1 pieces. E.g. cut the 1xn^2 strip into sizes n,1,n,1,...,n,1,1 -- that is (n-1) pieces of length n plus n pieces of length 1 (sum (n-1)n + n = n^2, count (n-1)+n = 2n-1) -- placing each length-n piece as one of the first n-1 rows under pure translation and gluing the length-1 pieces to form the last row, so that a_ij = i+j-1 (mod n) throughout. (An equivalent construction cuts into n,1,n-1,2,n-2,...,n-1,1 and swaps each consecutive pair summing to n.)

technique: Reverse the process to its target pieces, then encode each maximal run of consecutive labels as an edge of a multigraph on the residue classes, so a piece a,a+1,...,b-1 becomes an edge from a to b.
how_used: Run the assembly backwards: the goal state is the n rows, the k-th being labels k,k+1,...,k+n-1 (mod n). Any cut piece is a block a,a+1,...,b-1, which becomes an edge a->b on the vertex set Z/nZ = {1,...,n}. The n original rows become n closed walks (cycles) gamma_1,...,gamma_n, gamma_k passing through vertex k; the number of edges of the resulting multigraph Gamma equals the total number of pieces. Reassembling all pieces into the single 1xn^2 strip means Gamma admits an Eulerian circuit, hence Gamma is connected. This encoding is what converts 'count the minimum pieces' into 'lower-bound the edges of a connected multigraph.'

technique: To beat the trivial connectivity bound on a multigraph's edge count, delete one edge from each of a family of edge-disjoint cycles; connectivity survives every such deletion, so the survivor still needs a spanning-tree's worth of edges on top of the deleted ones.
how_used: In the multigraph Gamma (connected, n vertices) the n row-cycles gamma_1,...,gamma_n are pairwise edge-disjoint. Pick and delete one edge from each gamma_k: removing a single edge of a cycle never disconnects a graph, and disjointness lets all n deletions happen simultaneously, so the remaining graph Gamma' is still connected on all n vertices and thus has at least n-1 edges. Adding back the n deleted edges gives at least (n-1) + n = 2n-1 edges, i.e. at least 2n-1 pieces -- matching the construction, so the minimum is exactly 2n-1.

technique: Bound the max-minus-min spread of a growing multiset by finding a reference multiset with the same total that majorises it for all time, since majorisation forces the top and bottom coordinates to be sandwiched by the reference's
how_used: To show sorted gem counts a_1<=...<=a_n (sum = t, growing without bound) satisfy a_n^t - a_1^t <= n-1, one seeks a sequence (b_i^t) with the same sum t that majorises (a_i^t) for every t. Majorisation gives a_n^t <= b_n^t and a_1^t >= b_1^t (the k=1 prefix and suffix dominations), so a_n^t - a_1^t <= b_n^t - b_1^t; if b has fixed spread, the dynamic process is bounded by that constant. This reduces the whole problem to constructing such a b and proving the majorisation is preserved each step.

technique: Build the majorising reference as a fixed arithmetic-progression template that absorbs the same total per-step growth via a round-robin increment (each index gets exactly one increment per full cycle) so its sum tracks the real process while its sorted spread stays constant
how_used: Set b_k^0 = k-(n+1)/2 (an AP of common difference 1, sum 0, spread n-1); define b_i^t = b_i^0 + floor((t-i)/n) + 1, i.e. index i receives +1 exactly when t ≡ i (mod n). Then sum_i b_i^t = t (one +1 per day) and b_i^t <= b_{i+1}^t with strict inequality unless t ≡ i (mod n), so the sorted spread stays exactly b_n^t - b_1^t = n-1 forever. This gives the reference with same total and constant narrow spread. (Sol 2's variant d_i^0 = 3n(i-(n+1)/2), d_i^t = d_i^0 + t uses a wider fixed AP gap 3n, giving a looser constant but an easier majorisation proof.)

technique: To bound a greedy actor against an adversary that can block at most r objects, pigeonhole on the r+1 smallest objects: at least one of the smallest r+1 is unblocked, so the greedily-chosen minimum is dominated by every object ranked above r
how_used: Elisa always adds a gem to a smallest-count UNLOCKED chest (call its value a_{m(t)}^t). At end of day t exactly r = (t mod n) chests are locked. Sort counts a_1^t <= ... <= a_n^t. For any sorted rank j > r: the j smallest chests (ranks 1..j, all value <= a_j^t) number more than r, so since only r chests are locked at least one of them is unlocked and available; Elisa's greedy pick took a minimum over unlocked chests, hence a_{m(t)}^t <= (that available chest) <= a_j^t. This is a pigeonhole on the bottom-j sorted chests, NOT a claim that the locked chests occupy the bottom ranks (the fairy may lock a large chest). It yields the domination fact the majorisation induction needs: (t mod n) <= k-1 forces a_k^t >= a_{m(t)}^t. A trivial companion fact (a_j^t > a_{m(t)}^t for every sorted rank j above m(t)'s rank, since a_{m(t)}^{t+1} <= a_j^{t+1} = a_j^t) is used to locate where the increment lands.

technique: To show a fixed comparison sequence keeps majorising an evolving one, take the least prefix index where majorisation would first break; the resulting tightness of the shorter prefix plus a strict gap at the next term contradicts the hypothesis at index k+1
how_used: Prove by induction that a hand-built sequence (b_i^t), strictly increasing at t=0 with b_n^0 - b_1^0 = n-1 and b's round-robin increment b_i^{t+1}=b_i^t+[t+1==i mod n], majorises the sorted counts (a_i^t). Suppose k is the least prefix where sum_{i<=k} b <= sum_{i<=k} a FAILS at t+1. Each prefix rises by <=1, so failure forces: the t-prefix was tight (equality at k), b incremented inside the prefix (t+1==j mod n, j<=k, so (t mod n) <= k-1), and a did NOT (m(t) > k). Tightness + minimality give b_k^t >= a_k^t. Now plug in the greedy-domination crux: (t mod n) <= k-1 gives a_k^t >= a_{m(t)}^t, and m(t) > k with monotonicity collapses a_k^t = a_{k+1}^t = a_{m(t)}^t; combined with the STRICT reference gap b_k^t < b_{k+1}^t (strict because t is NOT == k mod n, so b's construction left b_k < b_{k+1} at that step) this gives sum_{i<=k+1} b^t > sum_{i<=k+1} a^t, contradicting the induction hypothesis at k+1. Hence no first-failure index; majorisation persists and a_n^t - a_1^t <= b_n^t - b_1^t = n-1 = C.

technique: Encode a partition-into-monotone-objects as a tiling of a region, so 'minimum number of objects' becomes 'minimum leftover area of the tiling'
how_used: Each step of a right-down/right-up path (a move between two adjacent cells) is drawn as a 'good parallelogram' (two glued isosceles right triangles straddling the shared edge). A partition of the N x N grid into k paths uses N^2 - k steps, so it packs N^2 - k good parallelograms and leaves exactly k units of triangular area uncovered; the map is a bijection (the packing recovers the partition uniquely). Proving 'at least N paths' is thus reduced to 'any packing of good parallelograms in the N x N grid leaves at least area N empty'.

technique: Extend a corner object into a full boundary-to-boundary monotone cut, so that deleting it and re-gluing yields a smaller instance of the same problem for induction
how_used: Induct on N. Take the path P through the top-left cell; if right-up it lives in the top row/left column and the induction hypothesis on the lower-right (N-1)x(N-1) subgrid finishes. If right-down, greedily grow P into a right-down staircase Q from the top-left to the bottom-right corner, maintaining the invariant (*) that the cells below and to the right of Q's current endpoint lie in OTHER paths. At each step, depending on which path the below/right neighbor belongs to (right-down tail, right-up column/row segment, or a two-cell bridge when both neighbors share one right-up path), splice in cells so (*) is preserved. Deleting Q's cells and gluing the two remaining regions gives an (N-1)x(N-1) grid; each cut path stays a valid right-down or right-up path, so induction gives >=N-1 paths there, plus P gives >=N.

technique: Reduce a minimize-count-of-objects problem to a minimize-empty-area problem by encoding each object as a fixed-shape tile so that a k-object cover corresponds bijectively to a tile packing leaving exactly k units of area empty.
how_used: Encode each right-down or right-up path by a chain of 'good parallelograms' (each a unit square split by a diagonal into two isosceles right triangles), laid along consecutive cells of the path. A partition into k paths corresponds bijectively to a packing of good parallelograms into the NxN grid leaving total empty area exactly k, and the packing uniquely recovers the paths. Thus 'the grid needs >= N paths' becomes 'any good-parallelogram packing leaves empty area >= N'. This is the conceptual bridge that turns a path-counting problem into a geometric area-deficit problem.

technique: To lower-bound the number of defect regions in a tiling, overlay a mirror pattern that makes a traced ray direction-neutral through every tile, so any net change in the ray's direction certifies it crossed at least one defect.
how_used: After the reduction to a good-parallelogram packing, in each unit cell draw the diagonal that does NOT cut any good parallelogram, and treat these diagonals as 45-degree mirrors. Shoot a laser perpendicularly inward from each of the 4N boundary edges, reflecting off the mirrors until it exits. Passing through one good parallelogram is two reflections that restore the incoming direction (direction-neutral). Hence a laser can only change direction by crossing an EMPTY triangle: a laser exiting perpendicular to its entry crossed >= 1 empty triangle, one exiting reversed crossed >= 2. This converts 'count empty triangular area' into 'classify each boundary laser by its entry-vs-exit direction change'.

technique: Turn a non-crossing constraint into a compensating count: use planarity to forbid a 'cheap' pairing type from occurring on two transversal families at once, forcing the saved cost to reappear as an 'expensive' pairing type on the other family.
how_used: Pair each laser's entry edge with its exit edge, splitting the 4N boundary edges into 2N pairs of three types: (1) one vertical + one horizontal edge (crosses >= 1 empty triangle), (2) two edges on the same side (>= 2 empty triangles), (3) two edges on opposite sides (0 needed). Because beams do not cross, type-(3) pairs cannot occur on the vertical sides AND the horizontal sides simultaneously; say all t of them are vertical. That leaves 2N horizontal edges and 2N-2t vertical edges, forcing at least t type-(2) pairs on the horizontal side. Summing per-type lower bounds gives >= (2N-2t) + 2t = 2N empty triangles, i.e. empty area >= N.

technique: To force every Hamiltonian path to hit a target color, build a vertex-partition into nested size-classes and color each edge by its endpoint in the smaller class, sizing the top class above half the vertices and each lower class one more than everything strictly beneath it.
how_used: Take k=floor(log2 n). Label nodes 1..n, give node i color min(floor(log2 i)+1,k), so class j (for j<k) has exactly 2^(j-1) nodes and the top class k has n-2^(k-1)+1 > n/2 nodes; color edge ij (i<j) by node i's color. Top class: >n/2 same-color nodes force two of them adjacent on any Ham path, and that edge is color k.
