Non-top class i<k: if a Ham path avoided color i, every color-i node could only be adjacent to color-(<i) nodes, forcing the alternating shape (i)-(<i)-(i)-...-(i); but that already uses every color-i node (2^(i-1) of them) and every color-(<i) node (2^(i-1)-1 of them) with no slot for any node of color >i (which exist since i<k), a contradiction. Hence no color can be deleted, so this coloring is good and uses k colors.

technique: To show a single monochromatic edge is freely recolorable in an extremal-avoidance coloring, assume recoloring creates an avoiding path through it, then at each split reroute by swapping which endpoint leads; each reroute that must fail pins one incident edge of the deleted color, and double-counting those forced incidences lower-bounds the two endpoints' color-degrees.
how_used: Lemma 1: for a color-i edge AB with d_i(A)+d_i(B) <= n-1, recoloring AB stays good. If not, some Ham path A_s..A_0=A, B_0=B..B_t has AB as its only color-i edge. Reversing the A-arm and re-attaching forces edge B_0 A_s to be color i; symmetrically A_0 B_t is color i; and for each split index p, at least one of B_0 A_p / A_0 A_{p+1} (resp. A_0 B_q / B_0 B_{q+1}) is color i, else you'd exhibit a color-i-avoiding Ham path. Each edge A_0 X and each edge B_0 X is charged exactly once (A_0 B_0 and B_0 A_0 counted separately), so d_i(A)+d_i(B) >= (s+1)+(t+1) = n, contradicting <= n-1. Iterating this single recolorability fact drives every edge onto its lower-indexed endpoint's color.

technique: In a coloring where each edge takes its lower-indexed endpoint's color, build a color-avoiding Hamiltonian path by interleaving each target-color vertex with a distinct earlier off-color vertex, which is possible exactly when no prefix of the ordering holds a strict majority of the target color.
how_used: Claim 2: after canonicalization (edge A_u A_v, u<v, has color c_u), suppose color i has NO prefix A_1..A_p with more than p/2 nodes of color i. List color-i nodes A_{x_1}<...<A_{x_t} and off-color A_{y_1}<...<A_{y_s}; the no-majority hypothesis gives t<=s and y_j<x_j for every j (else the prefix up to x_j would have a color-i majority). Then the path A_{x_1}-A_{y_1}-A_{x_2}-A_{y_2}-...-A_{x_t}-A_{y_t}-A_{y_{t+1}}-...-A_{y_s} uses no color-i edge, because each edge joins some A_x to a LOWER-indexed A_y (off-color) or two off-color nodes, so its color is the lower off-color endpoint's. This avoiding path contradicts goodness, so goodness forces some prefix with a strict color-i majority.

technique: Turn per-object local-majority thresholds into a global exponential lower bound by ordering the minimal thresholds and summing rounded-up half-contributions, so each threshold dominates a doubling of the previous ones.
how_used: Each color i has a smallest prefix length p_i with a strict color-i majority among A_1..A_{p_i}; order p_1<p_2<...<p_k (strict by minimality). Within A_1..A_{p_i} there are at least ceil((p_j+1)/2) nodes of color j for every j<=i, and distinct colors occupy disjoint nodes, so p_i >= sum_{j<=i} ceil((p_j+1)/2); this recursion forces p_i >= 2^i - 1, hence n >= p_k >= 2^k - 1. To exclude n=2^k-1: equality forces every p_i=2^i-1 with color-i nodes exactly A_{2^{i-1}}..A_{2^i-1}, and then the explicit interleaved path A_{2^{k-1}}-A_1-A_{2^{k-1}+1}-A_2-... avoids color k, contradicting goodness. So n >= 2^k.

technique: Recolor the passable cells by which side of an obstacle they abut, so each obstacle-crossing becomes one of a few typed symbolic events on a finite local alphabet.
how_used: Relabel each white square red/blue/green according to whether its adjacent black square lies horizontally, vertically, or there is none (well-defined because black squares are isolated with upper-right corner at (even,even), so each white cell touches at most one black cell). Then every lattice-line crossing of the laser is exactly one of four typed events: a horizontal event that is either a red<->green color swap or a wall-rebound flipping the x-velocity (staying in blue), or a vertical event that is either a blue<->green color swap or a wall-rebound flipping the y-velocity (staying in red). This recodes the continuous reflecting trajectory as a discrete stream of typed events.

technique: Reduce a coordinate at integer times to a single scalar whose one-step map is either identity or the reflection x->1-x, then use that a half-period reversal composed with itself closes the orbit.
how_used: Let x_t be the fractional part of the x-coordinate at integer seconds (y is 0 at these moments by the time-zero convention). Then x_{t+1}=x_t if the number of vertical wall-collisions that second is even and x_{t+1}=1-x_t if odd; these are involutions. From the odd count of vertical collisions over 3 seconds, x_3=1-x_0, a mirror-symmetric position, and the velocity is reversed. Because 1-x is an involution and the velocity reversed, running another identical 3-second window sends x_6=1-(1-x_0)=x_0 with velocity un-reversed, so position and velocity coincide with the start at t=6 and the path is a closed loop of period 6.

technique: Over a window whose event-count in each orientation is odd, use that the two-state color toggles must fire an even number of times to return to the start, so the complementary velocity-flipping events number odd — reversing that velocity component.
how_used: Because the per-second event sequence repeats (the coloring has period 2 and the free direction is fixed within a second), over a 3-second window the laser meets 3r horizontal and 3s vertical events, both odd since r,s are odd. The only color changes are the toggles red<->green (horizontal) and blue<->green (vertical); for the color to be periodic every 3 seconds each orientation's toggles must total even. Subtracting these even toggle-counts from the odd totals 3r, 3s leaves an ODD number of wall rebounds in each orientation. Odd-many horizontal rebounds flip the y-velocity and odd-many vertical rebounds flip the x-velocity, so after 3 seconds the velocity is exactly reversed.

technique: Recolor the passable cells by which side their blocking obstacle sits, so that each obstacle-line crossing becomes one of a small fixed set of colored event-types and the reflecting dynamics turns into a symbolic stream of letters.
how_used: Recolor each white square as red, blue, or green according to whether it has a black square directly to its left/right, directly above/below, or neither (well-defined because no two black squares are adjacent, so a white cell abuts a black cell on at most one axis). Then every lattice-line crossing is exactly one of four colored event-types: a horizontal event that switches red<->green, a horizontal wall-rebound that stays blue and flips the x-velocity, a vertical event that switches blue<->green, and a vertical wall-rebound that stays red and flips the y-velocity. This recoloring makes 'wall collision' vs 'harmless pass' readable off the local color and converts the whole reflecting trajectory into a discrete stream of h/v letters. Fix time zero to be just before the laser crosses a horizontal lattice line so the y-coordinate's fractional part is pinned at these sample times. (rx - sy irrational rules out ever exactly hitting a lattice corner, so the four cases are exhaustive.)

technique: Recolor the passable region by which side each cell's obstacle sits on, giving each lattice-crossing a fixed two-outcome menu per orientation (a color-toggle or a perpendicular wall-rebound) with no inert pass-through.
how_used: Black squares are the cells whose upper-right corner is (2a,2b); they are pairwise non-adjacent, so a white cell can touch black across a vertical edge OR a horizontal edge but never both. Color white cells: red = black square directly left/right, blue = black square directly above/below, green = neither. Fix t=0 just before the beam passes a HORIZONTAL lattice line. Track every lattice line the beam meets (wall or not). KEY PAIRING the solver must nail down: a horizontal crossing (crossing a y=integer edge) is either (a) a rebound off a horizontal black wall, which occurs precisely when a black square is directly above/below, i.e. the cell is BLUE, and the beam stays blue while v_x flips; or (b) a non-wall pass-through, which necessarily changes whether a black square lies left/right of the beam's cell, i.e. toggles RED<->GREEN. Symmetrically a vertical crossing either rebounds inside RED (v_y flips) or toggles BLUE<->GREEN. The reason horizontal crossings govern the red/green (left-right) bit and NOT the blue bit: the only way a horizontal step lands you in a blue cell is by hitting its wall (rebound), so among non-wall horizontal crossings the above/below status can only be 'no black above/below' on both sides, leaving the left/right status (red vs green) as the only thing that can change. This makes the menu exhaustive: exactly two event-types per orientation, one color-toggle and one perpendicular rebound.

technique: Over a window on which a bounded two-valued state returns to itself, the number of toggling events is even; subtracting that even count from a known-odd raw total leaves an odd number of the other event-type.
how_used: GIVEN (established separately, treat as input): the per-second keyword is fixed, so each second has exactly r horizontal and s vertical crossings (r,s odd), and the induced color pattern is periodic with period 3 seconds. Take that periodicity as the hypothesis; do NOT re-derive it here. Over one 3-second period there are 3r horizontal crossings and 3s vertical crossings, both ODD. Because the state has period 3, the red/green bit and the blue/green bit each return to their starting value across the period. By the setup crux the ONLY color-changing events are horizontal red<->green toggles and vertical blue<->green toggles, so a net return forces an EVEN number of toggles of each orientation. Each orientation's raw crossings split into toggles + perpendicular rebounds, so ODD raw minus EVEN toggles = ODD rebounds of each orientation. Odd horizontal rebounds flip v_x an odd number of times and odd vertical rebounds flip v_y an odd number of times, so after 3 seconds the beam points in exactly the reversed direction. This odd-rebound-per-orientation fact feeds the closure crux.

technique: Reduce the live positional state to a single fractional coordinate whose only nontrivial action is reflection across the cell center on each perpendicular rebound, so an odd rebound-count over a window sends it to its mirror and two such windows return it to start.
how_used: Sample x_t = frac(x-coordinate) at the instants just before each horizontal crossing; at these instants the y-fractional phase is pinned to 0 by the t=0 setup, so x_t is the only free positional coordinate. Between samples, ordinary advance moves x by whole units (vanishing mod 1), and each vertical wall-rebound reflects x across the cell center, x -> 1 - x. Hence over one 3-second period the map is x -> x for an even vertical-rebound count and x -> 1 - x for an odd one. Feeding in the parity crux's ODD vertical-rebound count per period: x_3 = 1 - x_0. CLOSURE (do NOT invoke any reflection symmetry of the lattice): the keyword is identical every second, so the SECOND 3-second period again has an odd vertical-rebound count, so the SAME map x -> 1 - x applies again, giving x_6 = 1 - x_3 = 1 - (1 - x_0) = x_0. Velocity is reversed after 3 seconds and reversed again after 6, hence restored; the y-phase is pinned to 0 throughout. So the full state repeats at t = 6 and the path is a closed loop.

technique: For each independent binary choice, form a two-element residue set of the two achievable values, so the reachable totals become a sumset of these sets (and handle the degenerate equal-values case as an immediate win).
how_used: Each of the p-1 disjoint triangles, once known to have nonzero sum mod p, gives a choice between routing u_i->v_i through x_i (weight u_i x_i + x_i v_i) or taking edge u_i v_i directly; set A_i = {u_i x_i + x_i v_i, u_i v_i}. If the two values coincide mod p their difference is the triangle's own 3-cycle sum ~= 0 mod p, done immediately; otherwise A_i is a genuine 2-element subset of Z_p, reducing 'route each triangle' to 'pick a_i in A_i'.

technique: Bound the size of an iterated sumset of small sets in Z_p by inducting with Cauchy-Davenport so the sum eventually covers the whole group.
how_used: Applying Cauchy-Davenport inductively over the p-1 two-element sets gives |A_1+...+A_t| >= min{p, t+1}; at t = p-1 the sumset A_1+...+A_{p-1} equals all of Z_p, so 0 is representable as a_1+...+a_{p-1} with a_i in A_i, i.e. some combined choice of triangle routings yields total 0 mod p.

technique: Chain independent sub-structures end-to-end into a single cycle so each local binary choice is realized simultaneously within one global object.
how_used: Join the p-1 triangles into one cycle by identifying consecutive endpoints (v_i = u_{i+1}) and closing v_{p-1} to u_1 (uses ~2(p-1) << 1000p vertices); in each triangle delete either the pair u_i x_i, x_i v_i or the single edge u_i v_i, independently realizing the chosen element a_i of A_i, so the cycle's total label sum equals sum_i a_i, chosen (via crux 1) to be 0 mod p.

technique: Make a cyclic group act on the counted objects by rotating their circular labeling, so the count becomes a sum of orbit sizes each dividing the group order.
how_used: Place labels 1..n on a circle; the forbidden edges (labels differing by 1, plus {1,n}) are exactly the n arcs of C_n, so admissible spanning trees are the spanning trees of the complement of C_n. Rotation i -> i+1 (mod n) preserves the forbidden edge set, hence permutes admissible trees, giving a Z/nZ action on the set of size T_n; by orbit-stabilizer T_n is a sum of divisors of n, reducing the divisibility claim to controlling orbit/stabilizer sizes.

technique: To bound the stabilizer of a tree under a group of automorphisms, invoke that any automorphism group of a finite tree fixes a vertex or an edge (the tree-center/fixed-point theorem).
how_used: The forbidden edges {i,i+1} and {1,n} are exactly the edges of the cycle C_n on the natural cyclic order, so the admissible-edge set is invariant under the rotation sigma: i -> i+1 mod n; hence Z/n acts on the set of admissible spanning trees. To stabilize a tree T, sigma^k (0<k<n) acts as an automorphism of the finite tree T. Since k != 0 fixes no label, it fixes no vertex, so by the tree-center theorem it fixes a central edge {u,v} and must swap u<->v; then sigma^{2k} fixes u, forcing n | 2k, so k = n/2 (only when n is even). Thus for odd n stabilizers are trivial (free action, all orbits size n => n | T_n), and for even n stabilizers have order 1 or 2 (orbits size n or n/2 => (n/2) | T_n).

technique: Partition the objects by a size class and bound each class's contribution to the chain using the adjacency restriction it forces on neighbors
how_used: On S={1,...,7}, a set of size >=4 forces both neighbors to have size <=2 (a neighbor is disjoint and its union with the large set must not be all of S, so it is a proper subset of the size-<=3 complement); there are only C(7,1)+C(7,2)=28 such small sets, so each interior large set consumes two small-neighbor slots and the chain has at most 29 large sets, plus at most 28 small sets and C(7,3)=35 size-3 sets, totaling <=92<100, so |S|=7 is impossible and |S|>=8.

technique: Build a chain on the larger ground set by doubling a valid chain, gluing the two copies through the empty set, and inserting the new element into alternating positions
how_used: From a valid chain on {1,...,n} of length 2^{n-1}+1, delete one set to get even length, concatenate two copies with the empty set between them, and insert n+1 into every other set starting from the first; this preserves consecutive-disjointness and union-not-full, yielding a length-(2^n+1) chain on {1,...,n+1}. Starting from the explicit length-9 chain on {1,2,3,4}, iterating reaches length 129 for n=8, exceeding 100.

technique: Prove a position unwinnable by an adversary that keeps a hidden set information-free and, on any mixed query, answers with the complement so revealed cards stay all-distinct
how_used: For k=n: after the first move (if not already won) there is a set S of n cards, one of each label, whose internal order the player has zero information about. A query inside S alone or inside its complement S-bar alone shows n distinct labels, no match. For a query mixing S and S-bar, since the player knows nothing about S's order the wizard is free to arrange S's chosen cards to be exactly the labels complementary to the chosen S-bar cards, keeping all n revealed labels distinct; so no query ever forces a match and no finite m guarantees a win.

technique: To prove a game with a re-randomizing adversary is unwinnable, maintain an adversary invariant of total ignorance and answer every move by choosing a hidden configuration that avoids a win while staying consistent with all prior answers.
how_used: For k=n, after the first move the adversary keeps a set S of n cards holding each value exactly once, about whose internal order the player has zero information, plus the complementary set Sbar. Any n-query lying wholly in S or wholly in Sbar has all distinct values (no match). A mixed query taking A from S and B from Sbar is answered by choosing S's still-free order so the values shown on A are exactly the complement of the values shown on B, making all n revealed cards distinct; the player cannot rule this out because it has no information on S's order. After each reveal the adversary re-randomizes S, restoring total ignorance and preserving the invariant, so no finite strategy can force a match when k=n.

technique: To show a game with a hidden-permutation adversary is unwinnable, maintain a symmetry invariant under which the adversary retains full freedom over an unrevealed ordering, so that any single move the player makes can be dodged into an all-distinct reveal.
how_used: For k=n prove NOT winnable. Invariant after the first move (if the player has not already won, the first move revealed n distinct values): the row splits into a set S of n cards carrying each value 1..n exactly once and its complement S-bar likewise, and the player has no information about the internal order of S. A move picking only within S (or only within S-bar) can never match, since each value occurs once there. A move mixing a cards of S and n-a of S-bar: because the player has no information on S's arrangement, the wizard may have arranged S so the a chosen S-cards are exactly the value-complement of the n-a chosen S-bar cards -- then all n picked values are distinct, no match. Since every possible move is dodgeable, no finite-m strategy is guaranteed to win, giving the k=n side of the answer (winnable iff k<n).

technique: When each query returns only the value-set of a fixed-width window that slides one position at a time, recover a genuine card value by set-differencing the value-sets of two consecutive overlapping windows.
how_used: For 2<=k<n, query positions {1..k},{2..k+1},...,{2n-k+1..2n}; each query returns the value-set S_i of that window (and if any window shows a repeat you have already won). Compare S_i to S_{i+1}: position i is in W_i but not W_{i+1}, so S_i\S_{i+1} is the value that sat at position i. The mandatory reshuffle only permutes values AMONG the k currently-queried positions, so it never changes WHICH set of values occupies a window; the set-difference is therefore a genuine value. The degenerate case S_i=S_{i+1} (window value-set unchanged) is resolved by the face-up detail: the k cards are turned face up BEFORE the reshuffle, so you directly read which value is about to leave at position i. This gives a genuine (value, position i) read for each i=1..2n-k.

technique: When a sliding-window scan's forced perturbation touches only positions currently inside the window, note that a position permanently exits after its last window, freezing its value, so all per-window deductions are simultaneously valid at the end of the scan.
how_used: Position j appears only in windows whose start s satisfies s<=j<=s+k-1, i.e. s in [j-k+1, j]; the LAST window containing position j is W_j (start s=j). Once W_j has been queried and reshuffled, position j is never queried again, so the wizard can never move its card again -- position j's value is frozen for the remainder of the scan. Hence the value deduced for position i via the consecutive-window set-difference stays put; after the full pass of queries you simultaneously KNOW the current true value at each of the 2n-k frozen positions 1..2n-k. Since 2n-k>n and every one of the n labels appears exactly twice, two of these known positions hold the same value; point at any k cards including both of them to win. This is the step that turns per-window value-recovery into a single guaranteed matching move.

technique: Turn a multiplicative constraint on set values into closure of the nonzero-value locus under the meet and join operations
how_used: From f(T1)f(T2)=f(T1∪T2)f(T1∩T2), a nonzero product on the left forces both factors on the right nonzero, so supp(C)={T:f(T)≠0} is closed under union and intersection; combined with being upward-closed this pins the support to an interval [X,S]={T:X⊆T⊆S}.

technique: Pin down a lattice function by prescribing it on singletons and reconstructing the rest inductively by size
how_used: For a full-support coloring the blue singletons B determine f({b}) for each b, then f(T) is forced inductively on |T|, giving the unique formula f(T)=2^{|T∩B|} (verified via inclusion–exclusion); this shows each B⊆{1..n} yields exactly one full-support coloring, so 2^n of them.

technique: Sum a count over an anchoring subset by weighting each anchor size with a binomial coefficient and collapsing via the binomial theorem
how_used: A general nontrivial coloring with support [X,S] is a full-support coloring on the (n-|X|) elements above X; summing 2^{n-k} full-support colorings over the C(n,k) choices of X with |X|=k (i.e. Σ C(n,k)2^k) and adding the all-red coloring gives 1+3^n.

technique: Identify a coordinate-wise conserved quantity that the move leaves fixed, and count its attainable values to bound the classes from above
how_used: The ordered column-count vector (c_1,...,c_n) and row-count vector (r_1,...,r_n) are each unchanged by any stone move (a rectangle swap adds and removes one stone in the same two rows and same two columns, so per-row and per-column totals are preserved), so the 'signature' (c;r) is invariant; stars-and-bars gives C(m+n-1,n-1) choices for each vector (compositions of m into n nonnegative parts), so there are at most C(m+n-1,n-1)^2 non-equivalent pilings. This is only the upper bound.

technique: Re-encode the configuration as a multiset of coordinate pairs so the move becomes a transposition of one coordinate between two elements
how_used: Replace the grid by the multiset of m stones as (x,y) pairs; a stone move is exactly swapping the y-coordinates of two pairs while fixing their x-coordinates, and the invariant becomes the multisets X (of x's) and Y (of y's). Since such transpositions generate all reassignments of the y-multiset onto the fixed x-slots, any two pilings with the same (X,Y) are equivalent, so the signature is a COMPLETE invariant; and every (X,Y) with |X|=|Y|=m is trivially realized by some placement, so all C(m+n-1,n-1)^2 signatures occur, matching the upper bound.

technique: Introduce a nonnegative slack variable measuring the gap to the constraint bound, then Abel-sum the weighted count to convert the target inequality into a recurrence in the slacks.
how_used: Set x_n = nλ - #A_n ≥ 0 and expand Σ_{a∈A_n} a = n#A_n - (#A_1+...+#A_{n-1}) by parts; substituting the x_n makes the λ-terms cancel exactly, turning the assumed failure (n+1)nλ/2 < Σ a into the clean recurrence x_n < (x_1+...+x_{n-1})/n for all large n, i.e. each slack is strictly below the average of its predecessors.

technique: Extract a fixed positive lower bound on consecutive differences from an integrality/quantization constraint that the main inequality has not yet used.
how_used: Since #{n∈A} is an integer and x_{n+1}-x_n = λ - #{n∈A}, and λ∈(0,1) is non-integer, x never lands on an integer: |x_{n+1}-x_n| ≥ ε with ε = min{λ, 1-λ} > 0. This rules out the slacks clustering together and supplies the rigidity that the averaging bound alone (which permits bounded non-convergent sequences) cannot.

technique: Recast a claimed inequality on a weighted partial sum by Abel summation into a claim about how each term of an auxiliary slack sequence compares to the running average of its predecessors.
how_used: Set x_n = nλ - #A_n ≥ 0 (the constraint #A_n ≤ nλ gives nonnegativity). Write the target sum via Abel summation: Σ_{a∈A_n} a = n·#A_n - (#A_1+···+#A_{n-1}). Substituting #A_k = kλ - x_k collapses this to Σ_{a∈A_n} a = n(n+1)/2·λ - n·x_n + (x_1+···+x_{n-1}). So the target 'Σ_{a∈A_n} a ≤ n(n+1)/2·λ' is EXACTLY 'x_n ≥ (x_1+···+x_{n-1})/n', i.e. x_n meets the average of its predecessors. Negating the conclusion (fails for all large n) becomes: x_n < (x_1+···+x_{n-1})/n for all n ≥ N_0 — each slack strictly below the running average of all preceding slacks.

technique: To rule out a nonnegative integer-derived sequence sitting forever below the running average of its predecessors, use a fixed lower bound on consecutive gaps to iterate a single 'adjacent pair can't both hug the ceiling' estimate that lowers a uniform upper ceiling by a fixed amount each stage until it drops below zero.
how_used: After reducing (via Abel summation on the elementwise sum) the failing conclusion to x_n < (x_1+···+x_{n-1})/n for all n ≥ N_0, where x_n = nλ − #A_n ≥ 0, first get boundedness for free: being below the running average forces that average to be non-increasing past N_0, so x_n < M := avg(x_1,…,x_{N_0}) is a uniform ceiling. The gap floor comes from INTEGRALITY: x_{n+1}−x_n = λ − #{n+1 ∈ A} is λ minus a nonnegative integer, so |x_{n+1}−x_n| ≥ ε := min{λ, 1−λ} > 0 (uses 0<λ<1). The single estimate: for n > N_0, x_n and x_{n+1} both lie below M yet differ by ≥ ε, so x_n + x_{n+1} < 2M − ε; a long tail block therefore averages < M − ε/2, and since each x_n is below the average of its predecessors this becomes a new ceiling x_n < M − ε/3 past some N_1. Iterating the SAME estimate drops the ceiling by ~ε/3 per stage, so after finitely many stages it crosses below 0, contradicting x_n ≥ 0.

technique: Encode a joint parity condition on a rectangle's four side-distances as the shared checkerboard color of the unit squares sitting in its four corners
how_used: Checkerboard-2-color the a*b unit squares by (i+j) mod 2. Because a and b are BOTH odd, all four corner unit squares of R share one color (call it green). For a small tile with side-distances (x,y,u,v) = (left i0, right a-i1, bottom j0, top b-j1), the corner unit square touching R's top-left corner is green iff x and u have the SAME parity, and similarly each of the other three green corner-squares of a tile forces one more equal-parity pair among {x,u},{x,v},{y,u}. All four corner squares green therefore forces x,y,u,v to be all-even or all-odd — exactly the target tile. KEY, and where a naive reading fails: this is NOT the claim 'all four corner unit squares are the same color as each other' (a yellow tile also has monochromatic corners); it is 'all four are R's corner color', and the equivalence to same-parity distances is driven by comparing each tile-corner square against R's corner square. The single (i+j)-checkerboard DOES suffice precisely because a,b odd make R's corners monochromatic; verify on a small a=5,b=3 grid that green-corner tiles are exactly the same-parity-distance tiles (they are, with zero exceptions), and note right-distance is a-i1 using the FULL width, not i1.

technique: Force a special tile to exist by summing a per-tile signed count that is additive over the partition and equals a nonzero value for the whole region
how_used: Give each rectangle (R or a tile) the weight (number of green unit squares it contains) minus (number of yellow unit squares). This count is trivially additive over any partition into sub-rectangles, since each unit square lies in exactly one tile — no telescoping or signed corner machinery is needed; it is a plain census of the interior unit squares. A rectangle with all-green corner squares contains exactly one more green square than yellow (weight +1); all-yellow corners give -1; mixed corners give 0. R is green so its weight is +1; the tile weights sum to +1, so at least one tile has weight +1, i.e. is a green-corner tile — which by the encoding crux is a target tile with all-even or all-odd distances.

technique: Lower-bound a minimum-swap distance by a counting quantity that changes by exactly 1 per adjacent transposition
how_used: Define f(X) = f_ab + f_ac + f_bc, where f_uv(X) counts ordered position-pairs with the left one holding u and the right one holding v (fixed orientation per letter-pair). An adjacent swap of two distinct letters u,v flips exactly the relative order of that one pair, so exactly one f_uv changes by 1 and the others are untouched; equal-letter swaps change nothing. Hence |f(X)-f(X')|=1 per swap and d(X,Y) >= |f(X)-f(Y)|. For P = a^n b^n c^n, all pairs are in-order so f(P)=3n^2; for Q = c^n b^n a^n all are reversed so f(Q)=0, giving d(P,Q) >= 3n^2.

technique: Force a far target from an arbitrary start by placing it at least half the diameter away via the triangle inequality
how_used: The swap-distance d is a metric (symmetric, triangle inequality). For arbitrary chameleon X, d(X,P)+d(X,Q) >= d(P,Q) >= 3n^2, so max{d(X,P),d(X,Q)} >= 3n^2/2 (the larger of two numbers is at least their average). Take Y to be whichever of P, Q realizes the max, giving d(X,Y) >= 3n^2/2 as required (radius >= diameter/2).

technique: Split a merge process into independent sub-processes by backward-coloring: color the tokens feeding the final merge, then propagate each color backward so every token inherits one color and no move but the last mixes colors
how_used: The last move merges two 2^{n-1} tokens; paint them blue and red and trace all moves backward, painting the two parents of each reversed merge with their child's color. Every token gets one color and, except the last move, no move touches both colors, so blue moves alone build one 2^{n-1} and red moves alone build the other. Because the FIRST inserted number is WLOG blue, some cell holds a blue token throughout, so the red sub-process runs on only k-1 cells while blue uses all k, giving m(n,k) <= m(n-1,k)+m(n-1,k-1)+1 (equality by running the two blocks in sequence). Routine induction on the recurrence yields 2*sum_{j=0}^{k-1} C(n,j) - 1.

technique: Bound the number of occupied cells below by the base-2 popcount of their total, via the lemma that a fixed sum of powers of two needs at least as many terms as its binary weight and equals the binary form only when all terms are distinct
how_used: Let S be the sum of all cell entries (unchanged by merges, increased by inserts). Lemma: any way to write an integer A as a sum of powers of 2 uses at least popcount(A) terms, and a minimal (popcount-many) representation must be A's distinct binary digits (merge two equal summands to shrink any non-distinct one). Apply with A=S over the occupied cells: if S ever had k nonzero binary digits, the k cells could only realize S in exactly one way (the k distinct binary powers), so all k cells are full with distinct values -- no insert (no empty cell) and no merge (all distinct) is possible, yet the game is not finished: contradiction. Hence after every move S has at most k-1 nonzero binary digits.

technique: Show a strictly-increasing potential attains its reachable-value cap by proving consecutive reachable values differ by a single legal step, so every value is hit
how_used: The insert count is capped by |A(n,k-1)| = sum_{j=0}^{k-1} C(n,j), the number of integers <= 2^n with at most k-1 nonzero binary digits, since each insert strictly raises S and popcount(S) <= k-1 always. To attain it, order A(n,k-1) as a_1<...<a_m and show from any state with S=a_j one legal insert (after clearing merges to distinct powers) reaches a_{j+1}: if a_j has < k-1 ones then a_{j+1}=a_j+1; else a_j = 2^{b_1}+...+2^{b_{k-1}} and adding 2^{b_1} is the smallest increase keeping popcount <= k-1 (any smaller addition overflows the bit count, and a_j+2^{b_1} collapses to fewer distinct powers by the minimality lemma), so a_{j+1}-a_j = 2^{b_1} is an insertable power. Thus all |A(n,k-1)| inserts are realized; with #merges = #inserts - 1 (token conservation), total moves = 2*sum_{j=0}^{k-1} C(n,j) - 1.

technique: Recast a two-constraint selection as 'keep only same-part pairs' by partitioning the ground set along one of the two dual attributes, so that any pair kept inside one part is automatically un-separable in that attribute once the rest of the part is deleted
how_used: Each of the N(N+1) players carries two coordinates: spatial position and height rank; the coach's condition forbids a survivor from separating a designated pair in EITHER coordinate. Partition by ONE attribute: e.g. split by height into N groups G_1..G_N of N+1 consecutive height-ranks (G_1 = tallest N+1, etc.). If from each group you keep exactly 2 players and delete the other N-1, then (a) the two survivors of G_i are height-adjacent among survivors, since every player of intermediate height lay in G_i and is gone, and (b) because the groups are height-separated, the 2N survivors sorted by height fall exactly into the N designated pairs {survivors of G_1},...,{survivors of G_N}. So the whole problem collapses to: choose 2 players per group that end up SPATIALLY consecutive among survivors. (The dual choice — partition by position into N blocks of N+1 consecutive players and control heights instead — gives the other solution; either works, pick one.) This crux only sets up the target; a separate move must actually exhibit the 2-per-group spatially-consecutive selection.

technique: Scan a sequence until the FIRST pair sharing a class (pigeonhole forces this by the (#classes+1)-th item); stopping at the first collision guarantees no OTHER class repeats in the scanned prefix, which is exactly what makes a per-class deletion charge close.
how_used: Group the N(N+1) players into N height-classes, each a contiguous interval of N+1 consecutive heights (G_1 = the N+1 tallest, ..., G_N = the N+1 shortest); this grouping is what makes any within-group survivor-pair automatically a valid consecutive-rank final pair. Scan the row left-to-right and stop at the first person completing a same-group pair; with N groups this happens by the (N+1)-th scanned person (pigeonhole). Take that colliding pair (a,b) in some G: they are spatially un-separable (everyone strictly between them was already scanned, hence deleted) and height-un-separable (the rest of G will be deleted). Commit (a,b), delete the rest of G AND everyone scanned so far, recurse on players to the right of b. The accounting turns on WHY each surviving group loses at most one person to the deleted prefix: because we stopped at the FIRST collision, the scanned prefix contains no repeated group except G, so every other group had at most one member in the prefix. Thus after k rounds the N-k remaining groups each still have >= (N+1)-k people (>0 for k<=N), so the scan keeps finding a fresh collision for N rounds, yielding 2 per group = 2N players.

technique: Under a noisy/approximate observation, hide a binary decision inside the sensor's tolerance so both choices produce an identical observation stream, keeping the adversary unable to distinguish them.
how_used: The rabbit picks one of two symmetric targets Y1, Y2 each 1 unit off the reveal line r and hops 200 rounds toward it; since every hop stays within radar tolerance (R_nR'_n <= 1), all pings can lie exactly on r, so the hunter cannot tell whether the rabbit chose Y1 or Y2.

technique: Bound the pursuer's best guaranteed outcome from below by exploiting the mirror symmetry of the two hidden targets: any response is at least as far from one target as the symmetric on-axis response is from both.
how_used: For any hunter path over the 200 rounds, moving above r increases distance to Y2 and below r increases distance to Y1, so the straight-ahead endpoint H' (distance y = H'Y1 = H'Y2 to the symmetric pair) is the best case; hence the hunter's guaranteed distance is at least y.

technique: Quantify a per-phase gain via the sagitta N - sqrt(N^2 - 1) of a chord and show a bounded positive increment per phase, so the invariant crosses a fixed threshold within the allotted number of phases.
how_used: With Z the midpoint of Y1Y2 and offset eps = 200 - sqrt(200^2 - 1) > 1/400, expanding y^2 = 1 + (d_n - eps)^2 = d_n^2 + eps(400 - 2 d_n) gives d^2 increase > 1/2 per 200 rounds while d_n < 100, reaching 10^4 in < 4*10^6 < 10^9 rounds.

technique: Stratify the objects by the multiplicity with which each shared attribute occurs, weight each stratum by the reciprocal of its minimum multiplicity, and split the resulting weighted total into a uniform part plus a residual that a local bound can control.
how_used: Colors are split into C_1, C_2, C_3 (appearing exactly once, exactly twice, at least thrice); with M_i the cubes of those colors and n_i=|M_i|, the count satisfies C <= n_1 + n_2/2 + n_3/3 since n_i >= i|C_i|. Rewriting as (n_1+n_2+n_3)/3 + (4n_1+n_2)/6 = n^3/3 + (4n_1+n_2)/6 isolates the residual 4n_1+n_2, which the per-line bound then feeds in.

technique: Bound one line/box's contribution by charging each of its rare-multiplicity elements to the forced position of that element's color-partner, defining an injection into an off-line intersection of the two matched partner boxes.
how_used: For an x-box X and color-matched y-box Y, z-box Z: a once-colored cube must lie in X∩Y∩Z (so |X∩M_1|<=1); of the twice-colored cubes in X, those not in X∩Y or X∩Z have their unique twin a' forced into (Y∩Z)\X, an injection into a set of size n-1, giving |X∩M_2| <= 2(n-1)+(n-1)=3(n-1) and 4|X∩M_1|+|X∩M_2|<=3n+1; summing over n x-boxes yields 4n_1+n_2 <= n(3n+1).

technique: Relax the problem so its defining property is closed under deletion, then peel one matched layer of the shared structure across all orientations to expose a smaller instance and induct.
how_used: Introduce 'invisible' cubes so the relaxed ('strange') property survives deletion; pick any nonempty matched triple X,Y,Z, blank out all cubes of that color set, and discard those three slabs to get an (n-1)^3 strange cube whose remaining matched sets are exactly preserved. At most n^2 colors are lost per peel, giving D(n) <= D(n-1) + n^2, which telescopes to n(n+1)(2n+1)/6.

technique: Build the extremal object from the orbits of a cyclic coordinate-permutation, assigning one color class per orbit so that slices indexed identically across the permuted directions carry the same class set.
how_used: Color classes are orbits of the cyclic shift (a,b,c)->(b,c,a): n singletons {(i,i,i)}, 3C(n,2) doubletons like {(i,j,j),(j,i,i)}, and 2C(n,3) triples {(i,j,k),(j,k,i),(k,i,j)}, totaling n+3C(n,2)+2C(n,3)=n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 colors; since the shift rotates the axes, the i-th x-slice, y-slice, and z-slice share the same color set, satisfying the matching requirement.

technique: Encode a set operation as a function on the integers by representing each set through its complement-enumerator (the map sending k to the kth positive integer absent from the set), then identify the operation with composition of those enumerators.
how_used: Define f_X(k) = kth positive integer not in X; since range(f_X)=Z_{>0}\X, show f_{X*Y}=f_X∘f_Y by checking both are increasing with equal range. This turns * into composition, giving associativity and translating A*B=B*A into g∘h=h∘g with g=f_A, h=f_B, and A^{*b}=B^{*a} into g^b=h^a.

technique: Reduce a targeted equality of two composite objects to a cancellation law: prove that among objects of equal size, commuting under the operation forces equality, then apply it to the two composites which have equal size and commute.
how_used: Note |A^{*b}|=ab=|B^{*a}| and, from A*B=B*A plus associativity, that A^{*b} and B^{*a} commute. Prove Lemma 2 (equal-size commuting sets are equal) and apply it to X=A^{*b}, Y=B^{*a} to conclude A^{*b}=B^{*a}.

technique: To prove two commuting equal-size sets coincide, take the largest element lying in exactly one of them and show the two enumerators must agree at that index, producing an element that is in one commuted product but not the other.
how_used: Let s be the largest number in exactly one of X,Y, say s∈X\Y. Using |X|=|Y| and agreement of X,Y above f_X(s), deduce |X∩[1,f_X(s)]|=|Y∩[1,f_X(s)]|, hence f_X(s)=f_Y(s). Then f_X(s)∉X*Y (since s∉Y) but f_Y(s)∈Y*X (since s∈X), contradicting X*Y=Y*X.

technique: Recast a monotone erosion process by its limit: the final set is the unique inclusion-maximal subset closed under the survival rule, so characterize that maximal stable set directly instead of tracking the removals.
how_used: The occupied sets form a nested decreasing chain from Q; since Q is up-right closed and the rule preserves that, any stable (no-lonely-point) subset of Q survives forever and lies in every stage, while the terminal set F is itself stable. Hence F is the largest stable up-right-closed subset of Q, and the problem becomes 'describe that maximal stable set and count its comfortable points,' bypassing the minute-by-minute dynamics.

technique: Build the extremal boundary as a broken line whose edge vectors are the primitive rays through a chosen finite lattice region, ordered by slope, with edge length equal to the region's multiplicity along each ray.
how_used: Take K_n = {(i,j): 1≤i≤n, -n≤j≤-1}; the rays from O through K_n, ordered by slope, give edge vectors v_i to the farthest K_n-point on ray r_i with k_i = |r_i ∩ K_n| lattice points. Concatenating the v_i in slope order yields the V-curve, whose up-right shadow D is the target final set. Each segment contributes k_i lattice points besides its start, so the curve carries 1 + Σk_i = 1 + |K_n| = n²+1 lattice points.

technique: Certify a point's survival status by covering the occupied half of its neighborhood with two shifts of the region along consecutive slope-ordered edge vectors, using that each edge vector is long enough that the window meets only its adjacent segments.
how_used: For a curve point p on segment d_i d_{i+1}, exactly half of N(p)∩l lies in D; the covering shows the rest of N(p) above l is filled, so p is comfortable. For an interior p, shift D_L by d_i→p and D_R by d_{i+1}→p (consecutive in slope) to cover all of N(p) above l plus the extra neighbors d_i, d_{i+1}, tipping p to crowded. The covering works because each v_i has a coordinate > n/2, so within the (2n+1)-window N(p) meets at most two segments on each side and the shifted 'gap' angles between consecutive rays hold no lattice points. Comfortable points are exactly the V-curve, count n²+1.

technique: To force a long collinear run inside a stable/no-lonely set, take the supporting line parallel to a chosen direction, then apply the local survival threshold to a point on it using the reflection symmetry of the neighborhood across that line.
how_used: For a target direction v_i, take the supporting line l of the stable set S parallel to v_i and a point b of S on l. l splits N(b)\l into two congruent halves related by reflection across l, and one half lies entirely in the empty side (outside S). So to keep b from being lonely, at least half of the 2k_i lattice points of l ∩ N(b) must survive, giving S a boundary segment of ≥ k_i+1 collinear points codirected with v_i (length ≥ |v_i|). This is only the per-direction local bound.

technique: To turn a family of per-direction length bounds into a single coordinatewise dominance, exploit that a slope-ordered monotone boundary curve has ONE pivot vertex splitting any direction-family into a left block and a right block, and read off the dominance at that pivot.
how_used: A boundary vertex p' of S's V*-curve splits it into a down-right arc X and up-left arc Y; correspondingly the target directions V split into V_X (whose matched segments lie in X) and V_Y. Because the V-curve is slope-ordered, its V_X-segments all precede its V_Y-segments, so a SINGLE V-curve vertex p separates them. Claim 1 gives, for each direction in V_X, a codirected S-segment of length >= that of the V-curve on p's down-right side, and symmetrically for V_Y on the up-left side; these place p' up-right of the pivot, i.e. p' >= p, so p' in D. Over all vertices this gives S subset of D, hence F subset of D.

technique: To pin down the terminal state of a monotone shrinking process, recognize it as the largest-by-inclusion stable set, then guess that extremal set explicitly and verify by two-sided containment instead of tracking the dynamics.
how_used: The final butterfly set F is stable and contains every stable subset of Q, so F is the largest up-right-closed stable set. One guesses it explicitly as D: from the ray-set K_n = {(i,j): 1<=i<=n, -n<=j<=-1}, take for each ray through O the primitive vector v_i to the farthest K_n point on that ray, order the v_i by slope into a V-curve d_0...d_m, and let D be all lattice points weakly up-right of that curve. The entire solution is then organized as proving F = D (every stable set lies in D; D is itself stable). Choosing this exact ray-geometry curve is the move that makes the terminal set concrete and countable.

technique: To force a lower bound on a boundary edge of a stable region in a prescribed direction, take the supporting line in that direction and use that it cuts the local neighborhood into two congruent halves with one half empty, so non-deficiency of a boundary point forces enough occupied points on the line itself.
how_used: For target vector v_i, let l be the supporting line of the stable hull S parallel to v_i and pick a butterfly b on l. Line l splits N(b)\l into two congruent halves, and one half lies entirely outside S since l supports S. For b to be non-lonely, at least half of N(b) must be occupied; all occupied points lie in the interior half plus l, so at least half of the 2k_i points of l∩N(b) must be in S. This gives a collinear boundary segment of >= k_i+1 points through b, i.e. a codirected hull edge v_i* with |v_i*| >= |v_i| (Claim 1).

technique: To verify a guessed extremal boundary is stable, show each boundary lattice point is exactly balanced by writing its neighborhood's occupied side as translated copies of the set that stay inside, using that the boundary's slopes turn slowly enough that any one neighborhood meets only a few boundary segments.
how_used: To close F = D one must show D is stable (the reverse of the containment half). Because each v_i has a coordinate > n/2, N(p) of radius n meets at most two V-curve segments on each side of p's own segment d_i d_{i+1}. For p on the curve (Claim 3): line l through d_i d_{i+1} meets D in exactly k_i+1 lattice points, so exactly half of N(p)∩l lies in D; and every point of N(p) above l lies in D, because the only candidates lying outside D sit in the shifted angular sectors between consecutive rays r_j,r_{j+1} (or r_j',r_{j-1}'), and N(O) — hence each shifted copy — contains no lattice points in those empty sectors. So p is comfortable. This identifies the V-curve lattice points as exactly the comfortable ones; counting them gives 1 + sum_i k_i = 1 + |K_n| = n^2 + 1.

technique: To show a guessed extremal region is over-occupied at every interior point, cover its neighborhood above the local support line by translating the left and right parts of a boundary point's neighborhood by two boundary vectors whose slopes keep the shifts inside the region.
how_used: For interior p of D (Claim 4): if p is up-right of a curve point p', the shift of N(p')∩D by p'p stays in D and N(p) has an extra point, done. Otherwise p sits in the right triangle on hypotenuse d_i d_{i+1}, with d_i,d_{i+1} in N(p). Split D by the vertical line h through d_i into D_L,D_R. Since the slopes of d_i p, d_{i+1}d_{i+2}, d_i d_{i+1}, d_{i-1}d_i, p d_{i+1} are non-increasing, shifting D_L by d_i p and D_R by d_{i+1}p both land in D, and together they cover all of N(p) above l plus the on-l points left of p; adding d_i,d_{i+1} makes strictly more than half of N(p) occupied, so p is crowded. With Claim 3 this proves D is stable, hence F = D.

technique: Bound a stable/extremal up-right-closed configuration by comparing it, direction by direction, to a candidate boundary: for each candidate boundary vector take the supporting line of the configuration parallel to it and use a balance/non-lonely condition to force a boundary segment at least as long in that direction.
how_used: This is the containment half F ⊆ D (Claims 1-2), which the stability cruxes presuppose. For a stable up-right-closed S with convex hull having boundary V*-curve: for each v_i in V, take the supporting line l of S parallel to v_i, pick b in l∩S. Line l splits N(b) into two congruent halves, one disjoint from S, so for b not to be lonely at least half of l∩N(b) (which has 2k_i points) must lie in S — forcing a boundary segment of l∩S with ≥ k_i+1 lattice points, i.e. a co-directed v_i* in V* with |v_i*| ≥ |v_i| (Claim 1). Summing these across directions and matching vertices (Claim 2) shows every vertex of the V*-curve lies up-right of a V-curve vertex, so S ⊆ D. Applied to S = F gives F ⊆ D.

technique: When a strictly increasing chain of integers is confined to a range with exactly as many slots as chain entries, force it to be the full enumeration of that range in order
how_used: The window sums S(vn,(v+1)n] satisfy 0 <= S(0,n] < S(n,2n] < ... < S(n^2,n^2+n] <= n, which is n+1 strictly increasing integers inside [0,n] (n+1 values); this pins S(vn,(v+1)n]=v for every v, and later inside a shifted chain of length n-v+1 in [v,n] pins each subsequent block sum to its index t

technique: Recover individual terms from overlapping fixed-length window sums by differencing two windows shifted by one index
how_used: Since a_{u+tn}-a_{u+(t-1)n} = S(u+(t-1)n,u+tn] - S((u-1)+(t-1)n,(u-1)+tn], subtracting the two known block-sum values gives 0/1 telescoping increments, and summing from a_u=0 up the column reconstructs a_{u+vn}=[u+v>=n+1]

technique: In a minimal counterexample, merge two pieces that share a full common edge into their union, checking the merge destroys neither forbidden feature so it contradicts minimality.
how_used: Among dissections with no splitting line and no interior rectangle, take one with fewest rectangles (necessarily >2, else the single interior edge is a splitting line). If two rectangles share a full common side, replace them by their union: still no interior rectangle and no splitting line, but fewer pieces, contradicting minimality. Hence no two rectangles share a full common side, a normalization used by all later steps.

technique: Locate a rectangle blocked from three of the square's four sides by its neighbors; being forced to touch the remaining side, one of its edges runs uninterrupted across the square and is a splitting line.
how_used: Label ABCD (A,B lower-left/right). Corner pieces a at A, b at B with height(a) <= height(b); c is the neighbor at a's lower-right corner (height(c) != height(a) by the no-shared-edge normalization). The piece d adjacent to both a and c cannot touch AB, AD (blocked by a) nor BC (since a is no taller than b), so d touches CD; whichever of the two height cases holds, d's free vertical side runs from CD across the square, a splitting line — contradiction.

technique: To force two oppositely-attached families to touch, route a polygonal cut hugging one family's boundary from one side to the opposite side; its two endpoints lie in the two remaining opposite families, so along the cut those two families must meet.
how_used: Each rectangle is attached to exactly one side (attachment to two opposite sides would give a splitting line). Let L be the union of left-attached rectangles. If L met no right-attached rectangle, a polygonal line skirting L's right boundary from top to bottom would pass only through top- and bottom-attached pieces, yet its upper endpoint is in a top piece and lower endpoint in a bottom piece; so a top and a bottom rectangle meet on it. Either way, some opposite-attached pair is adjacent.

technique: To force two regions attached to opposite boundary sides to touch, run a polygonal curve hugging the outer boundary of one region's union from top edge to bottom edge; its endpoints lie in different opposite-side regions, so somewhere along it those two opposite regions meet.
how_used: Assume no interior rectangle and no splitting line, so every rectangle is attached to some side and none to two opposite sides. Let L be the union of all left-attached rectangles. If L never touched a right-attached rectangle, draw a polygonal line p from the top side to the bottom side of the square running just to the right of L's boundary; every point of p lies in a top- or bottom-attached rectangle, but its upper end is in a top-attached one and its lower end in a bottom-attached one, so along p a top-attached and a bottom-attached rectangle must meet. Either way a pair of opposite-attached rectangles shares a point, giving the neighboring opposite pair a and b (a left, b right) meeting at X that the rest of the argument needs.

technique: From a point on a non-splitting line, march along the line to the nearest rectangle whose interior it crosses; the entry point is a shared corner of two rectangles boxed on their inner sides, so their forced boundary attachments make their aligned outer edges a splitting line.
how_used: Take the opposite neighboring pair a (left), b (right) meeting at X. If X lies on their horizontal sides, those collinear sides already give a horizontal splitting line. Otherwise X lies on a common vertical line l. Since l is not splitting, it crosses some rectangle's interior; let c be the nearest such rectangle above X, and Y = l meets c's bottom edge. Y is the upper-right corner of a rectangle a' and upper-left corner of b' lying directly below c (possibly a'=a, b'=b). Because a' sits above a, below c, and left of b', it can only be attached to the left; symmetrically b' only to the right. Neither is attached to the top, so their top edges both run along the horizontal through Y uninterrupted; those two aligned top edges form a horizontal splitting line, the contradiction.

technique: Count a structured configuration by assigning each unwanted (bichromatic) instance to a bounded fiber and dividing by the constant fiber multiplicity, then subtract from the known total.
how_used: Each pair (x,y) determines a unique z making x+y+z divisible by n, so there are n^2 divisible triples. Each bichromatic divisible triple contains exactly one ordered pair in R×B among its three cyclic pairs, and each R×B pair is assigned to exactly 3 distinct triples; so bichromatic count = 3rb and monochromatic = n^2 - 3rb = r^2 - rb + b^2.

technique: Bound a quadratic form's variable by completing to a sum of squares to trap one variable in a short integer range, then finish by testing each candidate.
how_used: After reducing r^2-rb+b^2=2007 via 9| gives r=3s, b=3c and s^2-sc+c^2=223, writing 892=(2c-s)^2+3s^2 forces 223≤s^2≤297, so 15≤s≤17; testing s=15,16,17 leaves c(17-c)=66 with c=6,11, giving n=69,84.

technique: Track a sum-of-squares potential under the ±1 update and reduce its increment to a signed partition gap
how_used: Define S_k = sum of x_i^2 over A_k; the +1 on I / -1 on J update gives S_{k+1}-S_k = n + 2(sum_I x_i - sum_J x_j) = n + 2G, so S strictly increases exactly when the signed gap G of the chosen partition exceeds -n/2.

technique: Prove a balanced-partition bound by induction, placing the new element on the currently smaller side
how_used: By induction on n: if all |x_i| < a there is a partition with |sum_I - sum_J| < a. Split x_1..x_{n-1} with gap in [0,a), then append x_n to the smaller side so the new signed gap lies in (-a,a). Applied with a = n/2, this forces the algorithm's minimal |G| < n/2, hence G > -n/2, making crux 0's increment n+2G > 0.

technique: Bound the reachable state space to force a repeated configuration contradicting a strict monovariant
how_used: Each b_i - a_i is an integer and under the contradiction hypothesis every term stays in (-n/2, n/2), giving at most n values per coordinate, so at most n^n sequences. Among A_1..A_{n^n+1} two coincide (A_p = A_q, p<q), so S_p = S_q, contradicting the strictly increasing S from cruxes 0 and 1.

technique: Assume the negation of the trivial monochromatic configuration to force a rigid functional constraint on the coloring that later constructions exploit.
how_used: If any two strips at horizontal distance a share a color, an axis-aligned a-by-b rectangle with left side in S_n and right side in S_{n+a} is monochromatic; so assume S_n and S_{n+a} are always opposite-colored, and likewise for b, turning color into a sign function with color(n+a)=-color(n), color(n+b)=-color(n) for all n.

technique: Extract a parity constraint by choosing an integer combination of the two step lengths that vanishes and demanding the induced sign rule be self-consistent at the identity shift.
how_used: With color(n+pa+qb)=(-1)^{p+q}color(n), pick p=b_1, q=-a_1 (a_1=a/d, b_1=b/d) so b_1 a - a_1 b = 0 is a null shift, forcing (-1)^{b_1-a_1}=1, i.e. a_1+b_1 even; coprimality of a_1,b_1 then forces both odd, whence (via Bezout k a_1 - l b_1 = 1 with k+l odd) color flips every d and the coloring is periodic with period 2d.

technique: Tilt the target rectangle so one side projects onto the periodic axis to exactly one full period, making that side's two endpoints automatically monochromatic and collapsing the four-vertex condition to a single pair.
how_used: Order a>b so a_1>b_1>=1 with both odd gives a_1>=3, hence a>2d; place ABCD (AB=a, AD=b) with AB projecting to length exactly 2d on the x-axis (real y-projection d*sqrt(a_1^2-4) since a>2d). By period-2d periodicity A,B share a color and C,D share a color, so only the color of the pair A,D — offset along x by (bd/a)*sqrt(a_1^2-4), which is irrational since a_1^2-4 is a non-square integer for a_1>=3 — remains to be matched.

technique: To land a point at a fixed irrational offset from a chosen anchor onto a prescribed color, anchor inside a maximal monochromatic run (fixing the anchor's color for free) and slide it so the offset image traverses an open window of length equal to the maximal run whose irrational endpoints force it to meet one more strip than any run can fill.
how_used: Let w be the largest number of consecutive same-colored (say red) strips S_{n_0},...,S_{n_0+w-1} (w<=d). Taking t in (n_0,n_0+w) makes A=(t,0) automatically red. As t ranges over this run, u=t+(bd/a)*phi ranges over I=(n_0+(bd/a)phi, n_0+(bd/a)phi+w), an interval of length w with irrational endpoints, so I meets w+1 consecutive strips; by maximality of w they cannot all be blue, so I contains a red point u. Setting t=u-(bd/a)phi keeps t in (n_0,n_0+w), making A=(t,0) red and D=(u,y_3) red; since A,B and C,D are already color-linked, all four vertices are red, contradicting the negation.

technique: Under the assumption that a monochromatic configuration is forbidden, turn each 'two positions must differ in color' constraint into generators of a lattice and induct on word length so the color becomes the parity of the lattice word, then evaluate the parity function on a relation that returns to the same object to force a parity/coprimality constraint on the reduced generators.
how_used: Assuming no monochromatic a-by-b axis-aligned rectangle, S_n and S_{n+a} must be opposite colors (else (n,0),(n,b),(n+a,0),(n+a,b) are monochromatic), and likewise S_n vs S_{n+b}. Inducting on |p|+|q|, S_n and S_{n+pa+qb} agree iff p+q is even. With d=gcd(a,b), a1=a/d, b1=b/d, the word p=b1,q=-a1 gives S_0 = S_{0+b1 a - a1 b} (the same strip), so same color forces b1 - a1, i.e. a1+b1, even; since a1,b1 are coprime both must be odd. Choosing k,l with k a1 - l b1 = 1 gives ka-lb=d with k+l odd, so S_n and S_{n+d} are opposite, hence the coloring is periodic with period 2d.

technique: To make a tilted figure's vertices depend on as few free parameters as possible, orient it so that one side's projection onto the coloring axis equals an exact period of the coloring, collapsing that side's two endpoints to one color and leaving a single displacement between the two still-independent vertices.
how_used: Place rectangle ABCD with AB=a, AD=b, right angle at A, vertex A=(t,0) on the x-axis, and the x-projection of side AB equal to 2d (possible since a=a1 d >= 3d as a1>=3 odd). Then A=(t,0), B=(t+2d,y1), C=(u+2d,y2), D=(u,y3). Because the coloring has period 2d and depends only on the x-strip, A,B share a color and C,D share a color automatically; only A vs D remain. Pythagoras gives y1=sqrt(a^2-4d^2)=d*phi with phi=sqrt(a1^2-4), and similar triangles ADD_0 ~ BAB_0 give the single constraint u - t = (bd/a)*phi. Since a1-1 < phi < a1 with phi^2 an integer, phi is irrational, so u-t is an irrational displacement.

technique: To force two points separated by a fixed irrational horizontal offset into the same color class of a coloring with bounded monochromatic runs, slide one endpoint across a maximal monochromatic run so its image interval has that run's length but irrational endpoints, hence meets one more cell than any run can be monochromatic and must contain a matching-color point.
how_used: Let w be the length of a longest monochromatic run S_{n0},...,S_{n0+w-1}, say red (w ≤ d since S_{n0+d} is blue). Take t in (n0, n0+w). The image interval I = (n0 + (bd/a)φ, n0 + (bd/a)φ + w) has length w with IRRATIONAL endpoints, so it intersects w+1 consecutive strips; since at most w consecutive strips are monochromatic, I contains a red point. Pick u ∈ I with x=u red and set t = u - (bd/a)φ; then t ∈ (n0,n0+w) so A=(t,0) is red, and D=(u,y_3) is red. Combined with A,B same-color and C,D same-color (from the periodic construction), all four vertices are red, contradicting the assumption of no monochromatic rectangle.

technique: When a strip/lattice coloring has no monochromatic configuration of two prescribed step lengths, force each single step to FLIP the color, then propagate the flip along all integer combinations of the two steps by induction on the combination's total weight, so the color at an index depends only on the parity of the combination.
how_used: same

technique: To turn an integer side of a rectangle into an IRRATIONAL horizontal shift between colored classes, tilt the rectangle so one side projects onto the axis with a chosen integer length; the perpendicular leg then has an irrational length (square root of an integer that is not a perfect square), and by similar triangles the other side inherits a proportional irrational horizontal offset.
how_used: same

technique: To force two color classes to agree under a fixed irrational horizontal offset when the coloring has a bounded monochromatic run of length w, slide an axis interval of length w whose endpoints are irrational: it meets w+1 consecutive strips, so it cannot be monochromatic and must contain a point of the target color, which fixes the free translation parameter.
how_used: new

technique: Since each unit move changes a monitored integer quantity by at most one, invoke discrete intermediate-value to force two competing quantities to land within one of each other.
how_used: Fix a maximum clique M with |M|=2m; put all of M in Room A and everyone else in Room B, so c(A)=|M| >= c(B). Then repeatedly send one person A->B while c(A)>c(B): each such move drops c(A) by exactly one and raises c(B) by at most one. Room A strictly shrinks so the loop halts, and since the two quantities can differ by at most one per step, at halt c(A) <= c(B) <= c(A)+1 -- either the desired equality, or a gap of exactly one to be resolved.

technique: Show every vertex on the target side is adjacent to all of a common witness set, so any clique there merges with that witness set into one big clique whose size the global maximum caps.
how_used: With the witness set W = B cap M and (from the dichotomy) every (k+1)-clique in B containing W: repeatedly drain a member of C\M from a (k+1)-clique C in B into A (nonempty since |C|=k+1 > m >= |B cap M|), until c(B) drops to k. Now every competitor in A is friends with all of W -- M-members trivially (M is a clique), and each drained competitor because it shared a clique C that contained W. Hence for any clique Q in A, Q union W is a clique, so |M| >= |Q| + |W| = |Q| + |M| - |A cap M|, giving |Q| <= |A cap M| = k. Thus c(A) = k = c(B), completing the equalization.

technique: Turn a global extremal object into a self-correcting arrangement by relocating its members one at a time and halting the instant a monovariant crosses, so a single-element move bounds the overshoot to at most one.
how_used: Let M be a max clique, |M|=2m; send all of M to room A and everyone else to B, so c(A)=|M|>=c(B). While c(A)>c(B), move one competitor A->B; each step drops c(A) by exactly 1 and raises c(B) by at most 1. Halt at the first moment c(A)<=c(B); because only one person moved last, the overshoot is bounded: c(A)<=c(B)<=c(A)+1 (one-sided gap). Reading M's split into the rooms then forces the size floor: c(A)=|A cap M|=k>=m and |B cap M|<=m, since m+1 members of M in B against m-1 in A would give c(B)-c(A)>=2. This is exactly the setup that makes the residual gap at most 1 and guarantees the extra clique in B (when c(B)=k+1) must reach outside B cap M.

technique: In the residual gap-1 case, split on whether a distinguished extremal vertex can be avoided by some optimal object: if some optimal object dodges it, relocate that vertex for an immediate equalization; otherwise conclude every optimal object contains the whole distinguished set.
how_used: At halt with c(A)=k>=m and c(B)=k+1 and |B cap M|<=m: ask whether some x in B cap M lies outside some (k+1)-clique C of B. If yes, move x back to A: then |A cap M|=k+1 so c(A)=k+1, while C avoided x so c(B) stays k+1, giving c(A)=c(B)=k+1 and STOP. If no such x exists, then every (k+1)-clique of B contains B cap M as a subset -- the universal-containment premise handed to the finishing move.

technique: Drain an over-large extremal object down to the target size by repeatedly extracting a member forced to lie outside a distinguished core, then cap the receiving side using that every extracted vertex, and the core, are jointly adjacent to the distinguished set.
how_used: Hard branch: every (k+1)-clique of B contains B cap M, and |C|=k+1>m>=|B cap M| forces C\M nonempty. While c(B)=k+1, pick a (k+1)-clique C and move one vertex of C\M from B to A; each move drops c(B) by at most 1, so the loop ends at c(B)=k. Now cap c(A)=k: take any clique Q in A. Every vertex of Q is either a member of M (friends with all of B cap M since M is a clique) or was moved in this loop from a (k+1)-clique containing B cap M (hence friends with all of B cap M). So Q and B cap M are jointly adjacent, making Q union (B cap M) a clique; maximality of M gives |M|>=|Q|+|B cap M|=|Q|+|M|-|A cap M|, i.e. |Q|<=|A cap M|=k. Thus c(A)=c(B)=k and STOP.

technique: Force cross-intersection between two set families by a containment-vs-hitting relation on a shared block partition
how_used: Partition {1,...,n=km} into k disjoint blocks A_1,...,A_k of size m. Let S = subsets meeting every block, and T = subsets that contain some full block A_i (minus S, to keep the families disjoint). Any S in S meets that A_i, and A_i sits inside T, so S cap T contains S cap A_i which is nonempty; every S-set thus intersects every T-set with no pairwise checking. Take p = min(|S|,|T|); disjointness of S and T makes all 2p sets distinct.

technique: Count a family defined by independent per-block membership constraints as a product over blocks
how_used: Each of the k blocks contributes an independent choice for the set's intersection with that block, so cardinalities are k-fold products: |S| = (2^m-1)^k (nonempty per block); complement of T_1 = (2^m-1)^k (avoid the full block per block); S minus T_1 = (2^m-2)^k (nonempty and proper per block). Routine inclusion-exclusion then assembles |T| = 2^{km} - 2(2^m-1)^k + (2^m-2)^k, with densities |S|/2^n = (1-2^{-m})^k and |T|/2^n = 1 - 2(1-2^{-m})^k + (1-2^{1-m})^k.

technique: Tune an integer growth parameter to a target density by matching an exponential limit and a fixed-point identity
how_used: The positive root delta = (3-sqrt5)/2 of x = (1-x)^2 is the target density. Set k = floor(2^m log(1/delta)) so k/2^m -> log(1/delta); then (1-2^{-m})^k -> exp(-log(1/delta)) = delta, giving |S|/2^n -> delta, and (1-2^{1-m})^k -> delta^2, giving |T|/2^n -> 1 - 2delta + delta^2 = (1-delta)^2 = delta by the fixed point. Both densities converge to delta, so for large m each exceeds any alpha < delta, forcing p > alpha*2^n.

technique: Charge each object to a bounded set of its constituents by selecting only the extremal constituent(s), capping the total count of (object, constituent) incidences
how_used: Each good triangle is charged to a vertex A only through an EXTREMAL unit-direction at A: among all unit-neighbors of A (which by convexity span an arc < 180 deg on the unit circle omega_A centered at A), only the two boundary directions AL_A (CCW-extreme) and AR_A (CW-extreme) qualify. Each of AL_A, AR_A lies in a unique good triangle (the 60-deg-inward partner is forced by the ordering of neighbors along the arc), so A receives at most 2 charges. Summing over all n vertices caps total charges at 2n; combined with >=3 charges per good triangle this gives t <= (2/3)n.

technique: Force a would-be extreme point into the interior of the convex hull of other named points by summing directed angles around it to a full turn, contradicting that all points are polygon vertices
how_used: Proving every good triangle ABC (vertices clockwise) receives at least three assignments. By the cyclic symmetry of A,B,C it suffices to prove ABC is assigned counterclockwise to C OR clockwise to B (the other two of the three needed assignments follow by rotating roles A->B->C->A). Suppose both fail: L_C != A and R_B != A. Let A',B',C' be the second intersection points of the unit circles omega_A, omega_B, omega_C (besides A,B,C). Since arc L_C A subtends less than 120 degrees, one of L_C and its partner L_C' (the good triangle C L_C L_C') lands as a point X on arc B'A of omega_C, past A; symmetrically the good triangle B R_B' R_B drops a point Y (!= A) onto arc A C' of omega_B. Then AX and AY sit on OPPOSITE flanks of angle BAC, so the four clockwise-oriented angles XAY, YAB, BAC, CAX are each at most 180 degrees and sum to a full turn around A. Hence A lies in the interior of quadrilateral XYBC (or on segment XY) — impossible, since A,X,Y,B,C are all vertices of the convex polygon P.

technique: Charge each element to the two EXTREME neighbors it forces on a shared cyclic structure, so extreme-endpoint uniqueness caps its out-charges at two.
how_used: Cap half of the double count K on assignments of good (unit-equilateral) triangles. Fix a vertex A. Every vertex at unit distance from A lies on the unit circle omega_A centered at A; by convexity of P they all lie on an open arc of less than 180 degrees. Let L_A R_A be the SHORTEST such arc, oriented clockwise, so L_A is the counterclockwise-extreme unit-neighbor and R_A the clockwise-extreme one. Segment A-L_A lies in a unique good triangle (assign it 'counterclockwise to A'); segment A-R_A lies in a unique good triangle (assign it 'clockwise to A'); if A is in only one good triangle it gets assigned twice. Since L_A and R_A are the two UNIQUE extreme endpoints of the arc, A emits at most two assignments. Summing over the n vertices gives the cap K <= 2n. Combined with the separately established floor 3t <= K (each good triangle collects at least 3 assignments), this yields t <= 2n/3.

technique: To lower-bound how many times an object is charged in a double count, argue by contradiction from convex position: assume it is NOT charged at a chosen site, use the objects that failure produces to force one polygon vertex into the convex hull of the others.
how_used: The solve double-counts assignments: give each good triangle >=3 charges and each polygon vertex <=2 charges (its two extremal arc-endpoints), so 3t <= K <= 2n and t <= (2/3)n. This crux supplies the hard half, 3t <= K. For a good triangle ABC (clockwise), by cyclic symmetry it suffices to show it is assigned counterclockwise to C (L_C = A) or clockwise to B (R_B = A); the other two of the three charges follow by rotating roles. Suppose not: L_C != A and R_B != A. Let A',B',C' be the second intersection points of the unit circles omega_A, omega_B, omega_C (besides A,B,C). From the good triangle C L_C L_C' the arc L_C A on omega_C subtends < 120 degrees, so one of L_C, L_C' lies on arc B'A; call it X (if L_C=B', L_C'=A take X=B'). Symmetrically from B R_B' R_B, one of R_B, R_B' lies on arc A C' of omega_B; call it Y != A. Then clockwise angles XAY, YAB, BAC, CAX are each <= 180 degrees and sum to 360, so A lies in quadrilateral XYBC (interior or on segment XY). But X,Y,B,C,A are all vertices of convex P, so none can lie in the hull of the others - contradiction. Hence >= 3 charges per triangle, i.e. 3t <= K.

technique: Forbid a homogeneous linear relation on a symmetric set by choosing all elements of one fixed parity, so every constrained sum lands in a residue class the target avoids.
how_used: To avoid a+b+c=0 with a,b,c in {-n,...,n} (repeats allowed), take all odd integers {±1,±3,...}: three odds sum to an odd number, never 0. Count gives n elements when n is even (largest odd is n-1) and n+1 when n is odd (largest odd is n), matching the claimed optimum, so this is the lower-bound construction.

technique: Reduce a symmetric-interval extremal bound by an induction that strips only the outermost symmetric shell, so the residual is the same problem on a step-smaller symmetric interval and the hypothesis applies verbatim.
how_used: For even n, induct by removing the four extreme values {-n,-n+1,n-1,n}. In the branch where at most 2 of these lie in A, the remaining A∩{-(n-2),...,n-2} still avoids a+b+c=0, so the induction hypothesis bounds it by n-2, giving |A| <= (n-2)+2 = n. The other extreme-heavy branches are separate critical steps (a different move closes them).

technique: Reduce to even parameter and induct by stripping the two outermost symmetric shells; when few enough shell-elements survive, the remainder lands inside the smaller instance and the hypothesis closes it.
how_used: It suffices to prove |A|<=n for n even (odd n reduces to the next lower even case, and the all-odds construction gives n or n+1). Induct on even n>=2, base n=2 trivial. Look at the four outermost values {-n,-n+1,n-1,n}. If |A intersect {-n,-n+1,n-1,n}| <= 2, then A\{these four} is a sum-free-of-zero subset of {-(n-2),...,n-2}, so by the induction hypothesis it has <= n-2 elements, and adding back the <=2 shell elements gives |A| <= n. This reduction is what makes the remaining casework finite: only configurations with 3 or 4 of the four outermost values present survive to be handled by the pairing move.

technique: With a fixed element forced into the set, split the remaining values into complementary pairs each of which together with the fixed element sums to the forbidden value, so at most one member of each pair may be kept; the pair count bounds the survivors.
how_used: In the surviving heavy-extreme configurations, use a present extreme element as the fixed third summand. If n and -n are both in A, then for each k the triple k+(n-k)+(-n)=0 forbids keeping both k and n-k; the pairs (1,n-1),(2,n-2),... on the positives and their negations admit at most one member each, capping |A\{±n}| at n-2 so |A|<=n. If instead n,n-1,-n+1 in A with -n absent, the same move with these fixed elements forms pairs (1,n-2),(2,n-3),... and (-2,-n+2),(-3,-n+3),... (forcing -1 absent), adding at most n-3 more, again |A|<=n. Each branch is one application of this single pairing move with a different fixed element supplied by the induction reduction.

technique: Induct by peeling the domino on an extremal corner cell, casing on whether that cell is coverable in the exceptional orientation in some tiling versus forced into the other orientation in every tiling
how_used: WLOG the lower-left cell s of the polygon. If some tiling covers s by a vertical domino, delete it and induct on the rest; because s is an extremal corner (its down and left neighbors lie outside the polygon) the restored vertical domino cannot complete either forbidden 2x2 pattern, so tastefulness is preserved automatically. Otherwise s is horizontal in every tiling (this case genuinely occurs), which is handled separately.

technique: Rule out the forbidden 2x2 next to a just-restored domino by observing that such a block admits a flip whose existence contradicts the case hypothesis
how_used: In the forced-horizontal case, delete the horizontal domino h on s, tastefully tile the rest by induction, and restore h. A forbidden pattern with h would require a second horizontal domino directly above h (below is outside the polygon). But two stacked horizontals fill a 2x2 that could be re-tiled by two verticals, covering s vertically — contradicting that s is horizontal in every tiling. Hence no such neighbor exists and h stays tasteful.

technique: Propagate the tasteful constraint deterministically along a diagonal staircase of cells, forcing consecutive domino orientations to alternate
how_used: Comparing two distinct tastefulk tilings, their symmetric difference is a union of alternating cycles; on the region Q bounded by such a cycle, fixing the corner p0=(0,0) vertical forces p1=(1,0) horizontal, p2=(1,1) vertical, p3=(2,1) horizontal, and so on up the staircase, each next orientation forced to avoid a distasteful 2x2 with the previous domino, pinning the tiling uniquely as far as the staircase stays inside Q.

technique: Terminate the argument by tracking where the forced-alternation path re-crosses a fixed diagonal and showing the color-side of the forced domino there contradicts the cycle's orientation-induced sense.
how_used: Draw the diagonal ell: y = x - 1; gamma crosses it at b=(1,0) where the staircase departs. Let a be the first staircase point after p1 at which gamma re-crosses ell. By the V/H alternation (crux 1), the domino at a is vertical, and its black point lies to the RIGHT of ell. But ell splits Q into two parts and, because gamma is oriented CCW, gamma's path enters at a from the right of ell as well; the global white->black invariant (crux 0) then forces the black point to the opposite side. These two determinations of which side a's black point sits on clash: contradiction. Hence no nontrivial symmetric-difference cycle exists, so the two tilings coincide and the tasteful tiling is unique. (Existence that gamma re-crosses ell: the staircase advances monotonically NE inside the bounded region Q while gamma is a closed cycle, so the path started at b must return across ell.)

technique: To compare two tilings, pass to their symmetric-difference alternating cycles and re-embed the cells as a 2-colored point lattice so each domino becomes an oriented edge whose direction is fixed by one corner choice plus a global cycle orientation.
