how_used: For uniqueness (b): given two distinct tasteful tilings, their symmetric difference is a nonempty union of alternating cycles (each edge of a cycle is a domino belonging alternately to the two tilings). Re-embed: treat the unit SQUARES as points of Z^2, colored black/white by parity, so a domino is exactly an edge joining a white point to an adjacent black point. Pick one cycle gamma, orient it counterclockwise, and let Q be the enclosed lattice polygon (gamma included). At the lower-left point s of Q (WLOG black), one of the two tilings covers s horizontally and the other vertically; keep the VERTICAL-at-s tiling. The claimed global invariant: along gamma, every domino points from its white point to its black point (i.e. traversing gamma CCW, within each crossed domino you go white->black). PREREQUISITE the solver was missing: the tasteful condition forbids exactly two adjacent-domino color patterns, namely two parallel dominoes side-by-side whose two touching cells have the SAME color arrangement that creates the bad 2x2 color-domino pattern shown; state these two forbidden patterns explicitly, because both this invariant and the later staircase forcing are read off them. The corner choice (vertical at s) fixes the sense of the domino at s, and the forbidden patterns are what let that sense be read consistently as the white->black rule around all of gamma.

technique: Probe the enclosed region with a monotone right-up staircase of cells and use the forbidden adjacent-domino patterns to force domino orientations to strictly alternate cell-by-cell along it.
how_used: With s=(0,0) covered by a vertical domino in the kept tiling, walk the staircase p0=(0,0), p1=(1,0), p2=(1,1), p3=(2,1), ... (alternately step right, then up). Consecutive staircase cells are edge-adjacent, so the dominoes covering p_i and p_{i+1} sit in a shared 2x2 window governed by the tasteful rule (all within the SAME kept tiling). The forbidden patterns force: vertical at p0 => horizontal at p1 (a vertical domino at p1 would complete a forbidden 2x2 color-domino pattern), => vertical at p2, => horizontal at p3, and so on, alternating V,H,V,H,... as long as p_i lies in Q. To apply the forcing at each step the solver must plug in the two explicit forbidden patterns from crux 0: at a rightward step a vertical p_i forbids a vertical p_{i+1}, and at an upward step a horizontal p_i forbids a horizontal p_{i+1}. This gives a rigid comb of alternating dominoes emanating from the corner, the local structure that will collide with the global white->black invariant.

technique: Characterize which outputs a sequential insertion/typing process can produce by a forbidden-pattern (pattern-avoidance) condition on the induced permutation
how_used: Model reachability as a permutation sigma sending position i of A to position sigma(i) in B, and prove B is reachable from A iff sigma is 213-avoiding (no i<j<k with sigma(j)<sigma(i)<sigma(k)), converting the dynamic left-arrow typing process into a static combinatorial condition on sigma.

technique: Reduce a symmetric relation to a class of permutations being closed under inversion
how_used: Show the reachability-witnessing class (213-avoiding permutations) is closed under taking inverses; since reversing the roles of A and B corresponds to replacing sigma by sigma^{-1}, closure under inversion makes reachability symmetric.

technique: Rule out a small forbidden clique by showing every 2-coloring of its complete edge set is forced to contain one of the forbidden monochromatic subgraphs, then feed the clique-free conclusion into Turan's theorem
how_used: Show the underlying uncolored graph has no K5: on any 5 mutually adjacent vertices the 10 red/blue edges cannot avoid a monochromatic C3 or C5 (if both color classes are triangle-free on 5 vertices they must be complementary self-complementary C5's, forcing a monochromatic C5). Both are forbidden, so no K5; Turan for K5-free on 60 vertices gives E <= binom(4,2)*15^2 = 1350.

technique: Achieve the extremal count by making each color class bipartite so it carries no odd cycle at all
how_used: Construction: a red K_{30,30} between two sides A,B of size 30, plus on each side a blue K_{15,15} (split A and B each into 15+15). Every color class is bipartite hence has no odd monochromatic cycle (no C3 or C5), giving 30^2 + 2*15^2 = 1350 edges, matching the upper bound.

technique: Classify each cell by its intersection pattern with the closed path and total over all cells to get one equation.
how_used: Each of the mn unit squares meets the non-self-crossing path P in exactly one of five ways (since m,n>=4 rules out a fully-enclosed square): opposite pair (B), no side (C), one side (D), adjacent pair (E), three sides (F). Summing gives mn = B+C+D+E+F.

technique: Double-count incident (cell, used-boundary-edge) pairs, once by summing per-cell contributions and once by summing per-edge contributions.
how_used: Counting pairs (Q,S) of a square Q and one of its sides S lying on P: per-cell counts give 2B+0C+1D+2E+3F; per-edge, each of the (m-1)(n-1) unit segments of P borders exactly two squares, giving 2(m-1)(n-1). Hence 2(m-1)(n-1)=2B+D+2E+3F.

technique: Count interior vertices by a straight-through vs turn dichotomy and charge each turn to the cell tucked into its corner.
how_used: At each of the (m-1)(n-1) interior vertices P either goes straight (A of them) or turns; every turn encloses a square of type E or F, with each E-square getting one turn and each F-square two, giving (m-1)(n-1)=A+E+2F.

technique: Apply the operation twice in a row to its own outputs to turn {a,b} into {2a,2b}, giving a reusable primitive that scales a chosen pair up by 2 while leaving all other numbers untouched.
how_used: From a>b, move 1 gives {a+b,a-b}; move 2 on those gives (a+b)+(a-b)=2a and (a+b)-(a-b)=2b. So any two board numbers can be simultaneously doubled. This never shrinks the count (its outputs are generically new), so it is only the rescaling tool feeding the halving/descent argument.

technique: To shrink a full initial block by a controlled amount, pair up the elements so that for each pair BOTH the sum and the absolute difference are values already on the board, so the move erases two elements and writes nothing.
how_used: On {1,...,n}, take n=4k or 4k-1 and pair the odds as (1,4k-1),(3,4k-3),...,(2k-1,2k+1). Each pair (2i-1, 4k-2i+1) has sum 4k and difference 4k-4i+2, both even numbers in [2,4k] already present (for n=4k-1 the top value 4k is absent, so it is written once on the very first pairing and present thereafter). Deleting all k odd pairs leaves exactly the evens {2,4,...,4k}=2*{1,...,2k}, an isomorphic rescaled copy of the game on {1,...,2k}={1,...,ceil(n/2)}, giving the induction step to a smaller board. The families n=4k+1,4k+2 first play one collision-free opening move on (4,2k+1) (sum 2k+5<=n already present) to reach the same even-string outcome; n=2,5,6 are the explicit induction base cases. Answer: it is possible for EVERY n>=2 (no obstruction).

technique: Prove a size-reduction step by contradiction on a minimal-sum counterexample: assume an irreducible configuration exists, pick one of minimum sum, then reach a strictly-smaller-sum configuration of the SAME size to contradict minimality.
how_used: To show any board of size k>=3 can be reduced in count, suppose not and pick an irreducible size-k set S of minimal sum sigma; every set reachable from S has sum >= sigma. If two entries are even, halve them (via the pair-doubling gadget applied to the others plus clearing a common factor), giving a same-size set of smaller sum — contradiction. Otherwise pick two odds a1<a2; one move sends them to the evens a1+a2 and a2-a1, then halve those to (a1+a2)/2 and (a2-a1)/2, again a smaller sum — contradiction. So no irreducible size-k set exists; repeat to descend k->k-1->...->2, proving reaching exactly two is possible for every starting configuration (hence every n>=2).

technique: To show a size-reducing move always exists on any board with at least three entries, argue by contradiction on a minimal-sum extremal object: among all boards that can NEVER be shrunk by any move-sequence, take one of least sum, and manufacture from it another never-shrinkable board of strictly smaller sum.
how_used: A move erases a,b and writes each of {a+b,|a-b|} only if not already present, so the count drops exactly when a written value collides with an existing one. 'Reducible to two' follows once we prove: any board of k>=3 distinct positive integers admits some move-sequence that lowers the count. Suppose not; pick an irreducible set S={a_1,...,a_k}, k>=3, of MINIMAL sum sigma. Key consequence of irreducibility, and the fact that closes the solver's collision worry: since NO sequence of moves on S ever lowers the count, every move actually performed on S or any board reachable from it is automatically collision-free (writes exactly two new values), keeps k entries, and yields sum >= sigma. So any construction built purely from legal moves on S can be run without ever accidentally reducing the count -- a collision would itself be the win we sought. The contradiction: exhibit, via such moves, a k-element board of sum < sigma, impossible by minimality. Dividing the whole board by a common factor is itself a LEGAL move here (the process runs identically on the divided board), so once the construction has forced every entry to share a factor g, clearing g yields a genuine k-element board of smaller sum -- not a mere bookkeeping rescale. The engine that legitimately creates such a common factor (and thus the smaller-sum board) is the separate crux.

technique: Build a 'double any two entries in place' primitive from two consecutive moves, then use it to engineer a global common factor on all-but-two chosen even entries so that dividing it out halves exactly those two.
how_used: Doubling primitive: for a>b, one move sends {a,b} to {a+b,a-b}; a second move on those two sends them to {(a+b)+(a-b),(a+b)-(a-b)}={2a,2b}. So any two board entries can be doubled while the rest stay put. To halve two even entries a,b with everything else fixed: if k is even, pair up the OTHER k-2 entries and double each pair, so every entry except a,b now carries a factor 2 while a,b do not; the board equals 2 times {a/2, b/2, rest}, so dividing out the common factor 2 leaves a,b halved and the rest restored. If k is odd, double all entries except a (in pairs), then double all entries except b, so a and b each end multiplied by 2 while every other entry is multiplied by 4; since a,b were chosen EVEN, 2a and 2b are divisible by 4, so the whole board shares the factor 4 and clearing it nets a,b halved with the rest restored. Either way the sum strictly drops (a,b replaced by a/2,b/2, rest unchanged), the contradiction the descent needs. Since we work inside the minimal irreducible board, every doubling move is collision-free by hypothesis, so no double accidentally lands on an existing value. When no two entries are even, two are odd, say a_1<a_2; one move replaces them by the evens a_1+a_2 and a_2-a_1, and applying the halving above gives (a_1+a_2)/2,(a_2-a_1)/2, again strictly lowering the sum.

technique: Force a contradiction from a simple (non-self-intersecting) planar curve by exhibiting two of its sub-arcs whose endpoints interleave along a line, so the arcs are compelled to cross.
how_used: Assume both sides of every wall are hit. Take the leftmost vertical trajectory segment Q_iP_{i+1} and the rightmost vertical segment Q_jP_{j+1}. The bulldozer's broken line then supplies an arc from P_{i+1} to Q_j and an arc from P_{j+1} to Q_i; because the leftmost-segment and rightmost-segment endpoints interleave, these two arcs must intersect, contradicting that the single trajectory is a simple curve (and that the disjoint walls cannot be crossed).

technique: When a comparison is defined only on pairs whose projections overlap, upgrade it to yield an extreme element by proving the relation has no directed cycle (its transitive closure is a strict partial order), so a minimal element exists.
how_used: Call wall v 'above' wall w if some point of v is directly above a point of w (same x, larger y). Non-crossing of the disjoint segments makes this antisymmetric on each overlapping pair. But antisymmetry alone does NOT give a lowest wall, since the relation is partial (non-overlapping walls are incomparable). The real work is showing there is no cycle v_1 above v_2 above ... above v_1: a cycle in 'above' would force the walls to enclose a region and hence some pair to cross, contradicting disjointness. With no cycles the relation extends to a strict partial order, so a wall that is above no other (a 'lowest wall') exists; symmetrically a highest wall exists. This lowest wall is the anchor for the main argument. (This sub-claim is Iran TST 2010.)

technique: To contradict 'every object is used on both sides', anchor at the extreme element and route the trajectory into two arcs whose four endpoints interleave along the boundary of the unbounded region, forcing the two arcs of a single non-self-crossing path to cross.
how_used: Assume the bulldozer hits both sides of the lowest wall L (and every wall). Look at the leftmost vertical trajectory segment Q_iP_{i+1} and the rightmost vertical segment Q_jP_{j+1}. Because both sides of walls get hit, the trajectory contains one broken-line arc from P_{i+1} to Q_j and another from P_{j+1} to Q_i. Since L is lowest and these are the extreme (leftmost/rightmost) vertical segments, the four endpoints P_{i+1},Q_i,P_{j+1},Q_j sit on the boundary of the unbounded outer region in interleaved cyclic order; two arcs joining interleaved endpoint pairs must intersect. But the whole trajectory is one non-self-intersecting broken line, so it cannot cross itself — contradiction. (If instead the bulldozer eventually moves up forever it never hits the underside of L, and if down forever it never hits the top of the highest wall, again contradicting both-sides.)

technique: Identify a forbidden pattern that each constraint object rules out, then count distinct forbidden patterns as a lower bound on unreachable outcomes
how_used: Since every customer must buy one fish from stall i, their origin in that coordinate is forced away from the stall's complement, so the complement vector c_i of stall i's origin-vector a_i can never be a customer profile; when the 10 vectors c_i are distinct this forces at least 10 unreachable profiles out of 2^10.

technique: When two constraint objects coincide, substitute the neighboring 'one-coordinate-off' patterns as the forbidden set to keep the lower bound intact
how_used: If stalls i and j share the same origin-vector (a_i=a_j), the single complement c_i only gives one exception, so instead take the 10 vectors d_k obtained by flipping one species of c_i (the profiles agreeing with a_i in exactly one coordinate); such a profile can share at most one fish with stalls i and j, contradicting that the customer buys from both, so all 10 d_k are unreachable.

technique: Realize a target labeling via a cyclic-shift assignment on the mismatched index set so each element gets served by a neighbor rather than itself
how_used: With the market where stall i is all-N except species i is M, to achieve any target profile b that does not have exactly one N: buy each M-species i from stall i, and for the set B of N-species (size >=2) buy species i_k from stall i_{k+1} indexed cyclically mod n, so i_{k+1}!=i_k guarantees an N-origin fish; this realizes all 2^10-10 targets.

technique: Bound a per-vertex quantity by routing it through the vertex's extremal (highest-degree) neighbor used as a shared hub
how_used: Each vertex v lies in at least m(v)-1 amicable pairs: let u be a neighbor of v of maximum degree m(v); u is a common neighbor witnessing amicability of v with each of u's other m(v)-1 neighbors, giving m(v)-1 distinct amicable pairs through v. Summing over v and halving (each pair counted at both endpoints) yields #amicable >= (1/2) sum_v (m(v)-1) = (1/2)(sum_v m(v) - n).

technique: Symmetrize a vertex-indexed neighbor-sum into per-edge terms of the form t+1/t so a single AM-GM bounds it
how_used: To get sum_v m(v) >= 2#E, first prove the friendship-paradox bound for average neighbor degree a(v)=(1/deg v) sum_{w~v} deg w. Rewriting sum_v a(v) as a sum over ordered adjacent pairs and grouping each edge's two orientations gives sum_{edges vw} (deg w/deg v + deg v/deg w); AM-GM (t+1/t>=2) makes each edge contribute >=2, so sum_v a(v) >= 2#E = sum_v deg v. Then m(v)>=a(v) upgrades to sum_v m(v) >= 2#E, and #E=n^2/4, #V=n turn Crux 0's reduction into #amicable >= n^2/4 - n/2 = 2*C(n/2,2).

technique: Pair the moves into fixed two-element cells so the second player can always complete the cell the opponent touched
how_used: A midline is fixed as a discard bin; all left segments are partitioned into disjoint LL-corners and all right segments into disjoint UR-corners (two segments sharing a joint). Whenever Bob orients one segment of a corner, Ann orients its partner; middle segments are answered by another middle segment. Ann's first move spends a middle segment to keep parity, so she is always the responder.

technique: Orient each paired unit so its shared joint is forced to be a common source or a common sink, making it un-traversable by any directed cycle
how_used: For each corner, Ann orients the partner t so the joint is either the source of both arrows or the target of both. A directed cycle passing through a vertex must enter along one edge and leave along another, but a common-source or common-sink joint has both incident corner-edges pointing the same way, so no cycle can route through such a joint via those two edges.

technique: Locate a contradiction by taking an extremal vertex of the offending cycle under a lexicographic order
how_used: Given a putative oriented cycle C, take X = lowest of the leftmost points of C and Y = topmost of the rightmost points. X (if left of midline) is the joint of a fully oriented LL-corner, or Y (if right) of a UR-corner; by Ann's orientation rule that joint is a common source/sink, so C cannot pass through it, contradicting X or Y being on C.

technique: Introduce a symmetric auxiliary count over ordered pairs of the two sides, then double-count it against each side separately to force a parity match
how_used: Count pairs (X,Y) of a boy-set X and girl-set Y that are 'separated' (no edge between them); mutual acquaintance makes 'separated' symmetric in the two sides, so the same total n can be evaluated once as a sum over boy-sets and once as a sum over girl-sets, tying the two covering-set counts to a common n

technique: Collapse the count of objects extending a base object by 2^(free-choices), so mod 2 only the base objects with zero free choices survive
how_used: For a fixed boy-set X, the girl-sets separated from X are exactly the subsets of the maximal separated set Y_X, giving 2^{|Y_X|} choices; so n = sum_X 2^{|Y_X|} is congruent to (number of X with Y_X empty) = number of covering boy-sets mod 2, since 2^{|Y_X|} is even unless Y_X is empty

technique: Encode a boolean covering/hitting predicate as a polynomial product of indicator factors, then reduce mod 2 by swapping the sign in each factor so the product expands into a symmetric sum
how_used: With f(b,g)=1 iff b,g don't know each other, X covers iff prod_g (1 - prod_{b in X} f)=1; summing over X and replacing 1-t by 1+t mod 2 turns the count into sum_{X,Y} prod_{b in X, g in Y} f(b,g), a form symmetric between boys and girls

technique: Reduce a linear-growth bound to a uniform bound on consecutive differences
how_used: Instead of directly bounding f(x) <= ax, reduce to proving f(z+1)-f(z) <= D for all z above some z0; the uniform gap bound telescopes to f(x) <= f(z0) + D(x-z0) <= a x, and the finitely many small x are absorbed by monotonicity, giving the required linear bound.

technique: Expand one target value two ways along two coprime step-lengths and equate to force a contradiction from a same-color assumption
how_used: Take two reds x,y with f(x)/x != f(y)/y (the degenerate case where every same-color pair shares a common ratio is settled directly at the outset). Set m=xy and assume a whole segment [k,k+m] is monochromatic red. Then f(k+xy) is split additively in steps of x (each addend x and each endpoint red, giving f(k)+y f(x)) and in steps of y (giving f(k)+x f(y)); equality forces y f(x)=x f(y), i.e. f(x)/x=f(y)/y, contradicting the choice, so every length-m segment contains a blue number.

technique: When no monochromatic window exists, manufacture a same-color additive triple by shifting the anchor by a fixed constant offset and case-splitting on the color of the shifted point
how_used: Case 2: every length-m window contains both colors, so consecutive same-color numbers are within 2m and color changes infinitely often; fix a red R>=2m with R+1 blue, set D=max{f(R),f(R+1)}. To bound f(z+1)-f(z) for z>2m: let r=largest red <= z, b=largest blue < r; then 0<z-b<=2m and b+1,...,r are all red (maximality of b), so b+1 is red. Let t=b+R+1>z. Split on the color of t: if t is blue, then (b, R+1, t) is an all-blue additive triple (b+(R+1)=t) so f(t)=f(b)+f(R+1)<=f(b)+D and monotonicity b<=z<z+1<=t gives f(z+1)-f(z)<=f(t)-f(b)<=D; if t is red, then (b+1, R, t) is all-red so f(t)=f(b+1)+f(R)<=f(b+1)+D and b+1<=z<z+1<=t gives f(z+1)-f(z)<=f(t)-f(b+1)<=D. Either way the jump is <=D.

technique: Force a fixed color into every window of a chosen length by expanding one additive quantity two different ways and equating
how_used: Enabling density lemma. Since not all same-color pairs share the ratio f/x, pick two red numbers x,y with f(x)/x != f(y)/y and set m=xy. Claim: every segment [k,k+m] of length m contains a blue number. Suppose [k,k+m] is entirely red; then f(k+xy) is expanded two ways using property (b) with all intermediate endpoints red: stepping by x (x red) gives f(k+xy)=f(k)+y*f(x), and stepping by y (y red) gives f(k+xy)=f(k)+x*f(y). Equating yields y*f(x)=x*f(y), i.e. f(x)/x=f(y)/y, contradicting the choice. Hence every length-m window contains a blue number. (Note: this gives 'blue in every window' only; it does NOT by itself force an all-blue window to exist — that dichotomy is handled downstream.)

technique: Bound a local jump by straddling the target with a same-color pair whose difference lands inside a known monochromatic window, then apply additivity plus monotonicity
how_used: Case 1: assume some length-m window [k,k+m] is entirely blue; set D=max{f(k),...,f(k+m)}. For z>k, let b1 be the largest blue <= z, so z-b1<=m by the density lemma. The translated window [b1+k, b1+k+m] contains a blue b2 (density lemma), and b2>z since the window's top exceeds z. The addend b2-b1 lies in the all-blue window [k,k+m], hence is blue with f(b2-b1)<=D, and b1 is blue, so property (b) gives f(b2)=f(b1)+f(b2-b1)<=f(b1)+D. Monotonicity b1<=z<z+1<=b2 then gives f(z+1)-f(z)<=f(b2)-f(b1)<=D. Summing the uniform bound D over consecutive z yields f(x)<=a*x.

technique: When no window is monochromatic, transport across a fixed same-color anchor pair and case-split on the color of the translate so one of two additive splittings always applies
how_used: Case 2 (the complementary hard case): every length-m window contains both colors, so no all-blue window exists and Case 1 does not apply. Fix a red number R>=2m with R+1 blue (such an R exists because colors alternate densely). Set D=max{f(R),f(R+1)}. Claim f(z+1)-f(z)<=D for z>2m. Take r=largest red <=z and b=largest blue <r; then 0<z-b=(z-r)+(r-b)<=2m, and b+1 is red (b is the top blue below r). Let t=b+R+1>z. Case-split on t's color: if t is blue, then b blue and R+1 blue give f(t)=f(b)+f(R+1)<=f(b)+D, so f(z+1)-f(z)<=f(t)-f(b)<=D; if t is red, then b+1 red and R red give f(t)=f(b+1)+f(R)<=f(b+1)+D, so f(z+1)-f(z)<=f(t)-f(b+1)<=D. Either way the jump is capped by D, and summing gives f(x)<=a*x.

technique: When each vertex of an edge-colored graph sees only finitely many colors, pigeonhole the incident colors to extract an infinite monochromatic star at one vertex
how_used: Model S as a complete graph with edge {x,y} colored gcd(x,y). Some vertex alpha has >=2 colors among its incident edges (else every gcd would collapse to one global value, contradicting the hypothesis). Since gcd(alpha,beta) always divides alpha and alpha has finitely many divisors, the infinitely many edges at alpha use finitely many colors; pigeonhole gives a divisor d of alpha with B = {beta in S : gcd(alpha,beta)=d} infinite.

technique: Pigeonhole a fixed outside vertex's edge-colors into an infinite monochromatic class to pull out two class-members joined to it by the same color
how_used: Choose gamma with gcd(alpha,gamma)=e != d (exists because alpha shows >=2 colors). gamma has finitely many divisors and B is infinite, so gcd(gamma,beta) over beta in B takes finitely many values; pigeonhole yields two distinct beta1,beta2 in B with gcd(gamma,beta1)=gcd(gamma,beta2)=d'. Now gcd(alpha,beta_i)=d, gcd(gamma,beta_i)=d', gcd(alpha,gamma)=e!=d.

technique: Case-split on whether two candidate colors coincide, using that a single edge-color cannot equal two distinct values to force a bichromatic triangle
how_used: If d=d': triangle alpha,gamma,beta1 has gcd(alpha,beta1)=gcd(gamma,beta1)=d != gcd(alpha,gamma)=e. If d!=d': f=gcd(beta1,beta2) cannot equal both d and d', so if f!=d then alpha,beta1,beta2 is bichromatic (two edges d, third f) and if f!=d' then gamma,beta1,beta2 is bichromatic (two edges d', third f). Either way the required x,y,z with two equal gcds at y and the third differing appears.

technique: Pick the sparsest class, use its few occurrences as separators, and pigeonhole on the gap they leave to force one gap longer than the window.
how_used: At m=n(n-1)-1, some colour (blue) appears at most n-2 times (its count is below the average m/n < n-1); these <= n-2 blue marbles cut the remaining >= (n-1)^2 non-blue marbles into at most n-2 arcs, and since (n-1)^2 > n(n-2) one arc has >= n+1 marbles, giving n+1 consecutive marbles with no blue and violating the window.

technique: For a circular window constraint, tile the circle by concatenating fixed-length blocks that each already satisfy the window, padding count via a modular decomposition of the total to absorb the remainder.
how_used: Writing m = nk + j with k >= n-1, 0 <= j <= n-1, place k-j copies of the full-rainbow block [1,2,...,n] and j copies of the padded block [1,1,2,...,n]; lengths sum to m and every n+1 consecutive marbles then span all n colours, realizing all m >= n(n-1).

technique: Negate the existence target to turn it into a uniform local constraint holding at every step, collapsing each step into a same-side dichotomy.
how_used: Assume no move k swaps thimbles a<k<b. Then at move k the two neighbors of thimble k that get swapped are either both numbered below k ('low move') or both above k ('high move'), a clean per-move binary classification (with the forced extremes: move 2021 is low, move 1 is high).

technique: When a local operation always acts on two elements lying on the same side of the acting element by a total order, use that same-sideness to attach a well-defined signed orientation (a clockwise/counterclockwise arrow) to the site of the operation.
how_used: Assume for contradiction no move k swaps a<k<b. Then at move k the two neighbors of thimble k (the central thimble) are BOTH smaller than k ('small' move) or BOTH larger ('large' move), never straddling. This same-side dichotomy is what makes 'the direction of the swap' well-defined: the two swapped values u,v satisfy u != v and both lie strictly on one side of k, so 'the larger swapped value' is unambiguous and exactly one of the two central slots receives it after the swap. Define the arrow at move k to point from the central position toward the slot ending up with the larger swapped thimble for a small move, with the opposite convention for a large move (convention tuned so the arrow's meaning is uniform across move-types). This produces 2021 well-defined local CW/CCW labels, one per central position. The one hard content here is ONLY well-definedness at each site; it does NOT yet claim the arrows agree with each other.

technique: Break the symmetry of a locally-symmetric configuration by using a global forbidden-pattern hypothesis to pick a comparison BETWEEN the two swapped elements (not a comparison of each against the pivot), turning each swap into a definitely-oriented edge.
how_used: Assume for contradiction no move straddles, so in move k the two neighbors of central thimble k are either both smaller than k ('small move') or both larger ('large move'). The hard move is to make each move carry a DEFINITE arrow on the circle. The naive attempt fails exactly as the fresh solver found: 'which side the smaller-than-k neighbor sits on' is not well-defined, because in a small move BOTH neighbors are smaller than k, so comparing each neighbor to k breaks nothing. The correct use of the hypothesis is to compare the two neighbors TO EACH OTHER and let the move's type choose the direction of that comparison: at move k orient the arrow at the central position toward the LARGER of the two swapped neighbors on a small move and toward the SMALLER on a large move (a fixed convention; the point is it is single-valued and forced by the small/large label, not chosen). This crux only establishes that the no-straddle hypothesis supplies a well-defined per-move orientation via a neighbor-vs-neighbor comparison; it does NOT yet claim these orientations cohere around the circle (that is the next crux).

technique: Derive a contradiction from an odd-length cycle by showing each of the n sites carries a sign that flips exactly once when passed to the next site, so the product around the loop is (-1)^n = -1 yet must be +1 on return to the start.
how_used: Take the per-move oriented arrows from the previous crux and lay them out over the 2021 positions arranged on the circle. The real content is a local consistency computation, done on a FIXED reference configuration (resolving the solver's value-vs-position worry: fix the circle of positions and read off, for each position, the arrow of the move whose central thimble ends up governing that site, so the transport is around the frozen 2021-position circle, not a moving picture). Show that moving the reference from one position to the geometrically adjacent one multiplies the accumulated orientation sign by exactly -1 every time: the swap at each move relocates precisely the one neighbor that serves as the reference for the adjacent site, and the small/large convention forces that hand-off to reverse orientation exactly once (never zero, never twice) — this is the single lemma the solver must prove. Because the walk closes on itself after 2021 steps, the total product must be +1; but 2021 unit flips give (-1)^2021 = -1. The impossibility +1 = -1 refutes the no-straddle assumption, so some move k swaps a and b with a < k < b. This crux fixes only the SHAPE: an odd cycle obstructs closing a sign that flips once per step.

technique: Reinterpret the maximum number of edge-disjoint directed paths between two vertices as the minimum directed edge-cut between them (Menger's theorem), replacing a path count by a cut count.
how_used: A diverse collection of paths from A to B is exactly a set of edge-disjoint A->B paths, so N_AB is the max number of edge-disjoint A->B paths, which by Menger equals the minimum size of an (A,B)-cut (edges directed from S to T over partitions with A in S, B in T); likewise N_BA is the min (B,A)-cut. The equality N_AB=N_BA thus becomes a comparison of minimum cut sizes in the tournament.

technique: Convert an optimal cut for one source-sink pair into a candidate cut for the reversed pair by moving only the two distinguished vertices to the opposite sides of the partition, leaving every other vertex fixed.
how_used: From an (A,B)-cut (S_A,T_A) build the (B,A)-cut S_B = S_A\{A}∪{B}, T_B = T_A\{B}∪{A}. This is a valid (B,A)-cut, and applied to the OPTIMAL cut in each direction it yields both N_BA <= N_AB+(b-a) and N_AB <= N_BA+(a-b), whose combination forces N_BA-N_AB = b-a (the routine finish once the size change is computed in the next step).

technique: To compare the max edge-disjoint path counts from A-to-B versus B-to-A, build a size-preserving-up-to-a-constant bijection between (A,B)-cuts and (B,A)-cuts by swapping only the two terminals across the partition, then read the min-cut via Menger.
how_used: Model N_AB, N_BA as min-cut sizes (Menger / max-flow min-cut). Given an (A,B)-cut (S_A,T_A), define S_B = S_A\{A}∪{B}, T_B = T_A\{B}∪{A} — only A and B move sides, everything else fixed. Every arc incident to neither A nor B crosses (S_A,T_A) iff it crosses (S_B,T_B), so those cancel (common count c). The surviving cut-arcs are exactly the out-arcs of whichever terminal sits on the S-side: |cut_A| = c + a_t + (|S_B|-b_s-1) and |cut_B| = c + b_t + (|S_A|-a_s-1), where a_s,a_t (resp. b_s,b_t) split a=out-deg(A) (resp. b=out-deg(B)) by destination side. Since the swap keeps |S_A|=|S_B|, subtracting gives |cut_B|-|cut_A| = (b_s+b_t)-(a_s+a_t) = b-a on EVERY cut. Minimizing both sides yields N_BA = N_AB + (b-a), so N_AB=N_BA iff a=b.

technique: Normalize a maximum edge-disjoint path family toward a prescribed set of short target paths by a local exchange: for each missing target path, either delete the at-most-one existing path blocking one of its arcs and insert the target, or splice the two paths that separately use its two arcs, discarding the resulting cycle — each move preserves edge-disjointness and never lowers the count.
how_used: In the path-side (non-Menger) proof, WLOG arc A→B exists. Classify each city C≠A,B by its two arcs to A,B: I={A→C,B→C}, O={C→A,C→B}, 𝒜={A→C,C→B}, 𝒵={C→A,B→C}. The short A→B paths are A→B itself and A→C→B for C∈𝒜, i.e. |𝒜|+1 of them (|𝒜| is the CLASS size, not out-degree). Take a maximum diverse collection of N_AB paths A→B; process each short path once: if A→C→B is absent and at most one existing path uses arc A→C or C→B, delete that path and insert A→C→B; otherwise two distinct paths carry A→C and C→B respectively, so recombine them into A→C→B plus a leftover A-⋯-B walk (drop the cycle). Each operation is independent and non-decreasing, giving P' with |P'|≥N_AB that contains all |𝒜|+1 short A→B paths.

technique: Once a path family is normalized to contain every prescribed short path, pin the two interior endpoints of each remaining long path into fixed vertex-classes by observing edge-disjointness forbids it from reusing the arcs the short paths already occupy.
how_used: With P' containing every short A->B path (previous crux), take any non-short path A->C->...->D->B in P'. Its first arc A->C needs A->C so C is in I or A_cls; but if C in A_cls the short path A->C->B is in P' and already uses A->C, so diversity forces C in I. Symmetrically the last arc D->B needs D->B so D in A_cls or O; if D in A_cls the short path A->D->B claims D->B, so D in O. Hence every residual path is A->C->...->D->B with first interior C in I and last interior D in O. This structural pinning is exactly what makes the terminal-arc swap of the next crux legal (C in I supplies B->C, D in O supplies D->A).

technique: To force a maximum edge-disjoint path family to physically contain a prescribed short path on its own arcs, delete or locally recombine only the family paths that use either arc of the short path, keeping the count and disjointness.
how_used: Normalization Lemma. Classify each city C (other than A,B) by the orientation of its arcs to A and B: I = {A->C and C->B}, O = {C->A and B->C}, and the classes A_cls = {A->C and C->A... i.e. A<-C->B: C->A? } — concretely A_cls is the set of C with the length-two path A->C->B available and B_cls the set with B->C->A available. The 'short' A->B paths are the direct arc A->B (if oriented that way) and A->C->B for every C in A_cls, so there are |A_cls|+1 of them. Take a maximum diverse A->B family P (|P|=N_AB) and install each missing short path: first add the direct arc A->B if present (it is a single arc, at most one P-path uses it — delete that path, insert the arc). For each C in A_cls with A->C->B absent: if at most one P-path uses arc A->C or arc C->B, delete it and insert A->C->B; else exactly two P-paths use these arcs, one of form A~>C->B and one of form A->C~>B, and you recombine their edges into A->C->B plus the leftover walk A~>...~>B (delete any cycle to make it a genuine path). Each step preserves the count and diversity and only touches arcs A->C, C->B, so previously installed short paths (using different arcs) are untouched. Result P' of size >= N_AB contains all short A->B paths and none of its arcs is an arc of a short B->A path.

technique: Turn a maximum edge-disjoint s->t path family into a t->s family by keeping every path's interior segment intact and only re-attaching its two endpoints, using that the pinned first/last interior vertices lie in classes where the two needed new terminal arcs exist.
how_used: Terminal-arc swap. After the Normalization Lemma, split P' into its |A_cls|+1 short A->B paths plus the remaining 'long' paths, each of the form A->C->...->D->B. The first interior vertex C satisfies A->C but is not in A_cls (else the length-two short path already used arc A->C), forcing C in I, where B->C exists; symmetrically the last interior vertex D lies in O, where D->A exists. Build Q: for each long path replace its endpoints, keeping the interior C->...->D verbatim, to get B->C->...->D->A; also throw in all |B_cls| short B->A paths B->C->A. Q is diverse: the interior segments were pairwise arc-disjoint and unchanged; the new head arcs B->C use distinct C (two long paths sharing head C would have shared arc A->C in P'); the new tail arcs D->A are distinct likewise; and none collides with the short-B->A-path arcs since I, O, B_cls are disjoint classes. So |Q| = (number of long paths) + |B_cls| = |P'| - (|A_cls|+1) + |B_cls|.

technique: In a tournament, read off each terminal vertex's out-degree by partitioning the other vertices according to their arc orientations toward the two terminals, so the out-degree difference becomes a difference of class sizes; combine the two mirror inequalities to force equality.
how_used: Out-degree counting close. With classes I = {A->C, C->B}, O = {C->A, B->C}, A_cls = {A->C, B->C}... more precisely: every out-neighbor of A is a city C with A->C, which lands in I (A->C, C->B), in A_cls (the length-two-path class, A->C), or is B itself (assuming WLOG A->B). Every out-neighbor of B is a city with B->C, landing in I (B->C) or B_cls (B->C, C->A). This gives a = |I| + |A_cls| + 1 and b = |I| + |B_cls|, hence a - b = |A_cls| - |B_cls| + 1. Substitute into the previous crux's |Q| = |P'| - (|A_cls|+1) + |B_cls| = |P'| - (a - b) = |P'| + (b - a) >= N_AB + (b - a), so N_BA >= N_AB + (b-a). The mirror construction (B->A family into A->B family) gives N_AB >= N_BA + (a-b). Adding the two inequalities forces N_BA - N_AB = b - a exactly, so N_AB = N_BA iff a = b, the desired equivalence.

technique: Rephrase a paired-window count as a shifted-difference indicator whose values lie in {-1,0,1} and sum to a fixed constant over one period
how_used: Encode girls as 1 and boys as 0 to get the periodic sequence a_i (period 2n+1, sum n+1), then define b_i = a_i + a_{i-k-1} - 1 in {-1,0,1}. Over any full window of 2n+1 consecutive indices the b_i sum to (n+1)+(n+1)-(2n+1)=1, forcing a marked index b_{i0}=1. The key identity b_{i+1}+...+b_{i+k} = (girl-neighbours of i) - k reduces the target 'a girl with >=k girl-neighbours' to finding a marked index (b_i=1) whose forward k-window b_{i+1}+...+b_{i+k} is nonnegative.

technique: To refute 'no index has a nonnegative forward window', greedily chain marked indices by a gap>k successor rule so each block sums nonpositively, then use pigeonhole mod the period to close a cycle and contradict the positive period-sum
how_used: Assume every marked index i (b_i=1) has forward window b_{i+1}+...+b_{i+k}<0. Build i_0<i_1<... with i_j the least marked index >i_{j-1}+k; each half-open block [i_j,i_{j+1}) sums to S_j = b_{i_j}+...+b_{i_{j+1}-1} <= b_{i_j}+...+b_{i_j+k} <= 0 (trailing b's are non-marked hence <=0). Among i_0,...,i_{2n+1} two agree mod (2n+1); take i_0,i_T with i_T-i_0=m(2n+1). Then sum_{i=i_0}^{i_T-1} b_i = S_0+...+S_{T-1} <= 0, but by the period-sum it equals m*1=m>0, a contradiction.

technique: Combine several independent finite colourings into one product colouring whose colour is the tuple of the component colours, so a single legal colouring reports every component's label at once
how_used: The hunter merges C1..C5 into one colouring whose colour on a cell is the 5-tuple of its C1..C5 colours; since each Ci uses finitely many colours the product is still a finite legal colouring, and every reported tuple simultaneously delivers x mod 3, y mod 3, and the three sparse-line readouts, so all five tracking schemes run off one colour stream.

technique: Colour by a coordinate's residue mod 3 so consecutive reports reveal each unit step's direction (increment, decrement, or a move along the other axis)
how_used: C1 = x mod 3, C2 = y mod 3. A rabbit step changes exactly one coordinate by +/-1; using modulus 3 > 2 makes +1 and -1 distinguishable as residue changes, and no change means the step was along the other axis. So each minute the hunter reads the exact signed step vector and accumulates the rabbit's position relative to its unknown start.

technique: Since three linear functionals of position are pairwise linearly dependent, argue that an unbounded walk keeps at least two of them unbounded, guaranteeing enough absolute readouts fire
how_used: If the rabbit never gets stuck its self-avoiding path is infinite, so it leaves every bounded region. Among x, y, and x+y, any one is an integer combination of the other two (x=(x+y)-y, etc.), so if two were bounded the third and hence the whole trajectory would be bounded, a contradiction. Thus at least two of x, y, x+y are unbounded, so at least two of the distinct-gap readouts C3/C4/C5 eventually fire; two of {x,y,x+y} determine the third and thus the current cell, which the mod-3 displacement tracking then back-solves to the start.

technique: Colour a family of parallel lines so the gaps between consecutive marked lines are pairwise distinct, turning the coordinate of a line into something a passer-by can read off from the two marks bracketing it
how_used: In C3 blacken columns (constant-x lines) so consecutive black-column gaps are all different; do the same for rows (C4) and for anti-diagonals x+y=const (C5). Once a coordinate is unbounded the walk eventually lands on two black cells in distinct black lines of that family. Because every neighbouring-gap is distinct, the separation between those two black lines names a unique consecutive pair, hence the exact line, hence the absolute value of that coordinate. This crux only supplies the readout of the ABSOLUTE value GIVEN that the separation between the two black hits is known; making that separation observable from the colour stream is a separate move (the mod-3 tracking crux).

technique: Colour cells by a coordinate's residue mod 3 so that each reported colour-change reveals the sign of the step in that coordinate, making the walk's signed displacement recoverable from the colour stream alone
how_used: The hunter sees only colours, never moves, so before he can use any absolute-value readout he must recover relative displacement. C1 colours each cell by x mod 3; since x changes by 0 or +/-1 per minute, consecutive reported residues distinguish +1 (residue advances 0->1->2->0), -1 (residue retreats), and a vertical move (residue unchanged), telling the hunter whether each step was left, right, or vertical. C2 does the same with y mod 3 for up/down/horizontal. Merged, C1 and C2 let the hunter reconstruct the full signed x- and y-displacement between any two minutes. This is what supplies (a) the separation between the two black-column hits needed by the distinct-gap crux, and (b) the back-solve from a later located cell to the starting cell.

technique: Run several independent colourings simultaneously by taking their product colouring: colour each cell with the tuple of its colours under the separate schemes, so every piece of information decodable from any one scheme is decodable at once
how_used: The hunter needs mod-3 movement tracking (C1,C2) AND three distinct-gap self-locating patterns (C3,C4,C5) all active on the same board with finitely many colours. He gives each cell the 5-tuple of its colours under C1..C5; the total palette is the finite product of the individual palettes. Then a single colour report simultaneously yields the x mod 3 residue, the y mod 3 residue, and whether the cell is black in each of the column/row/diagonal patterns, so all trackers read the same colour stream in parallel while keeping the colour count finite as required.

technique: Merge the values that are mutually indistinguishable under the separation tolerance into one symbol, and count the resulting patterns as the upper bound
how_used: Since property (ii) is violated exactly when two rows agree within tolerance 1 in every column, replace both 2k-1 and 2k by a single symbol x_k for k=1..50; each row becomes an arrangement of 50 symbols each used twice. Two rows with the same symbol-pattern differ by at most 1 in every column (same pair per column), violating (ii), so distinct rows have distinct patterns, and the number of patterns 100!/2^50 is an upper bound on N.

technique: Build a canonical section of the quotient map by an inductive local-placement rule that fixes, for each new pair of values, its order relative to one already-placed anchor
how_used: To realize every symbol-pattern as an actual permutation, process k=1..50: place 2k-1,2k into x_k's two known columns so that the triple 2k-2,2k-1,2k reads (left-to-right) in one of exactly three chosen orders relative to the already-placed 2k-2, namely 2k-2,2k-1,2k or 2k,2k-2,2k-1 or 2k-1,2k,2k-2. This picks exactly one permutation per pattern, so the family has exactly 100!/2^50 rows. (This crux only builds the family and matches the count; that the family satisfies (ii) is a separate move.)

technique: Characterize the maps lying within a per-coordinate tolerance of a given map by inducting from the extreme value downward, peeling off at each step either a fixed value or a forced adjacent swap
how_used: The Lemma: for two permutations of 1..n with |pi1(i)-pi2(i)|<=1 in every coordinate, normalize pi1 to the identity and induct on n from the largest value. At value n: either pi2(n)=n (n is fixed; delete it and recurse on 1..n-1), or pi2(n)=n-1, in which case the tolerance forces pi2(n-1)=n, i.e. n-1 and n are swapped as an adjacent pair; delete both and recurse. This peels the permutation into a set S of DISJOINT adjacent transpositions (j,j+1), elements of S pairwise >=2 apart, with pi2 obtained from pi1 by applying exactly those swaps. This is the structural lemma controlling what 'close' rows can look like; note swapping an adjacent value-pair keeps the tolerance yet genuinely changes the row, so closeness does not collapse to identical merged patterns and a finer invariant (next crux) is needed.

technique: Prove a constructed family is an antichain under near-equality by exhibiting a block-suborder parity invariant that every admissible swap-set is forced to break
how_used: The constructed family is the permutations whose induced subpermutation on each overlapping window {1,2},{2,3,4},{4,5,6},...,{98,99,100} is even. To verify property (ii): suppose two family rows are close; by the Lemma their difference is a set S of disjoint adjacent transpositions (elements pairwise >=2 apart). Let r=min(S). If r=2k-1 is odd, the swap (r,r+1) sits inside window {2k-2,2k-1,2k} (or {1,2}) and flips that window's suborder parity, so pi1,pi2 induce opposite parities there, contradicting the shared even parity. Hence r=2k is even; but then keeping window {2k,2k+1,2k+2} at equal parity forces 2k+2 in S, and iterating forces 2k+4,...,98 in S, so window {98,99,100} ends with opposite parities — contradiction. The solver supplies the min-extraction and the forced-chain up the windows; the reusable move is choosing the block invariant that no allowed swap-set can respect.

technique: For an antichain-counting upper bound, merge indistinguishable-under-the-relation values into a coarser symbol pattern so that same-pattern objects are forced too close, then pigeonhole rows into patterns
how_used: This is the upper bound N<=100!/2^50, which neither prior crux delivers and where the fresh solver stalled. In each row replace both of {2k-1,2k} by a single symbol x_k for k=1..50, producing a pattern: an arrangement of 50 symbols each used twice. There are 100!/2^50 distinct patterns. If two rows share a pattern, then in every column their entries lie in the same pair {2k-1,2k}, so |T(r,c)-T(s,c)|<=1 for all c, violating property (ii). Hence distinct rows must have distinct patterns, capping N at the number of patterns, 100!/2^50. The reusable move is the value-merging quotient that makes 'no two rows too close' equivalent to 'no two rows share a pattern', turning the extremal bound into counting merged patterns.

technique: On a longest shortest path, bound how many path vertices a single off-path vertex can neighbor: too many, and splicing through it shortcuts the path, contradicting minimality.
how_used: Each interior path vertex A_i has a third neighbor B_i off the path. If some off-path B_i were adjacent to four path vertices A_i,A_m,A_n,A_p (i<m<n<p), rerouting A_i->B_i->A_p replaces >=3 path edges by 2, strictly shortening the shortest path. Hence each off-path vertex is adjacent to at most 3 of the A_j (indices within a window of span <=2). So the third-neighbors of the interior indices 3<=i<=k-3 comprise at least (k-5)/3 distinct off-path vertices.

technique: Attain an extremal shortest-path length by chaining identical constant-size gadget blocks along a single spine, so a source-to-sink path must cross every block and each block forces a fixed number of interior detour vertices.
how_used: Split the 2018 cities into 504 diamond groups (two groups of five, the rest of four). Within group i wire A_i-B_i, A_i-C_i, B_i-D_i, C_i-D_i, and connect groups only by the single spine edge D_i-A_{i+1}. Since A_i and D_i are non-adjacent, crossing a diamond costs a detour through B_i or C_i, so >=3 of the 4-5 vertices per group lie on the A_0-to-D_503 route: 3*504=1512 vertices, 1511 edges. To make EVERY vertex degree exactly 3 (the min-degree-3 hypothesis): for interior groups 1<=i<=502 add the edge B_i-C_i (this is what raises B_i,C_i from degree 2 to 3); the two endpoint groups of five use E_0 joined to A_0,B_0,C_0 and E_503 joined to B_503,C_503,D_503 to fix the degrees at the open ends. Count: 502*4 + 2*5 = 2018.

technique: Bound the extremal length by forcing enough distinct off-path vertices (via the minimum-degree condition) and packing all path plus off-path vertices into the fixed vertex budget.
how_used: The k+1 path vertices A_0..A_k, the >=(k-5)/3 distinct interior third-neighbors B_i (3<=i<=k-3, from the splice lemma), and the endpoint extras must all fit in 2018. Distinctness is secured by the index-window restriction, which is the point of the 3<=i<=k-3 range: it carves out the endpoint region so the interior B_i cannot collide with the endpoint neighbors. Concretely A_0,A_k each have only one path-neighbor so need two off-path neighbors: B_0,C_0 and B_k,C_k. Because B_0,C_0 adjacent to A_0 cannot equal any B_i with i>=3 (else splice to shorten), and B_k,C_k cannot equal any B_i with i<=k-3, these four are distinct from the counted interior set. Also every B_i,C_i differs from all A_j (a coincidence would be a path chord). So (k-5)/3 + (k+1) + 4 <= 2018, giving 4k <= 6044, k <= 1511.

technique: To prove a local swap process terminates, weight each edge by a combinatorial multiplicity (a subtree count computed from the tree the edge sits in) and sum weighted lengths into a monovariant.
how_used: Each edge e is weighted by p_T(e), the number of A-vertices in the component of T-e holding e's A-endpoint; f(T)=sum over edges of p_T(e)*|e|. Since only finitely many trees exist, a strictly decreasing f forbids repetition and forces termination.

technique: Show the swap changes the potential by isolating exactly which edge-weights change and reindexing them so the difference collapses to the given strict inequality times a positive multiplicity.
how_used: Under T'=T-A1B1+A1B2, only the weights on A1B1->A1B2, A2B1, A2B2 change; substituting p_{T'}(A2B1)=p_T(A2B1)+p_T(A1B1) and p_{T'}(A2B2)=p_T(A2B2)-p_T(A1B1) makes f(T')-f(T)=p_T(A1B1)*(A1B2+A2B1-A2B2-A1B1), negative by the transformation hypothesis A1B1+A2B2>A1B2+A2B1.

technique: Encode each object by a coarse statistic and prove that statistic ranges bijectively over all its possible values
how_used: Map each good configuration C to its source set O(C) (the n points from which arrows emerge); claim every n-subset of the 2n cyclically-labeled points equals O(C) for exactly one good C, so the count is the number of n-subsets = C(2n,n). This is the framing move; the bijection itself is proved by the boundary-forcing induction (separate crux).

technique: At an index where a chosen membership property flips between two cyclically adjacent elements, use the forbidden-pattern rule to force a direct link between them
how_used: Pick k with a_k a source but a_{k+1} not. If a_k pointed to a farther a_l (k+1<l), non-crossing forces the arrow into a_{k+1} to emerge from some a_m with k+2<=m<=l-1; then a_k->a_l and a_m->a_{k+1} form a prohibited quadrangle. Hence a_k->a_{k+1}. This adjacent arrow can be stripped (it never crosses or joins a prohibited quadrangle), reducing to 2n-2 points for the routine induction that finishes both existence and uniqueness.

technique: Count decorations of a fixed skeleton by splitting on one distinguished feature's state, where one state reduces to the sub-skeleton (induction) and the reversed state admits exactly one completion
how_used: Fix a Catalan chord-diagram (C_n of them). Choose the chord ab of MINIMAL length; its endpoints are cyclically adjacent, so relabel {a,b}={1,2}. Good orientations split into: (i) those with arrow 1->2 (this arrow can never join a prohibited quadrangle, so deleting chord 1-2 gives a Catalan (n-1)-config, contributing exactly n by induction), and (ii) those with 2->1, of which there is EXACTLY ONE valid orientation (every other chord forced to emerge from its smaller endpoint). Hence n+1 good orientations per skeleton, independent of the skeleton, giving (n+1)C_n = C(2n,n).

technique: Recognize a forced strictly-increasing chain of subsets (one element added per step across the full ground set) as an arbitrary ordering of the ground set, and factor out its relabeling as a symmetric-group factor.
how_used: The boundary path S_{00}⊊S_{01}⊊...⊊S_{0n}⊊S_{1n}⊊...⊊S_{nn} runs through all sizes 0,1,...,2n adding exactly one element per inclusion, so it is a maximal chain in the subset lattice of {1,...,2n}, i.e. an ordering of the 2n elements; there are (2n)! such orderings, so fix the canonical one S_{0i}={1,...,i}, S_{in}={1,...,n+i} and multiply the interior count by (2n)!.

technique: To count the completions of one unknown set wedged between a fixed smaller set and a fixed set two sizes larger (both inclusions forced), enumerate which of the two available extra elements it contains.
how_used: In the 2-by-2 corner with fixed A (size k), its two one-step supersets on the two sides, and the size-(k+2) opposite cell C fixed, the unknown cell S is the fourth cell of the 2-by-2, of size k+1, forced to satisfy A subseteq S subseteq C. Writing C=A cup {x,y} (two elements x,y not in A), S must be A plus exactly one of x,y, so S is either A cup {x} or A cup {y}: exactly 2 valid choices. This is the constant factor 2 the induction multiplies over each interior cell. Note S is the cell diagonally opposite the size-(k+2) cell, at the same size level as the two intermediate cells, so both extra elements x,y are genuinely free.

technique: When a distinguished part of the configuration is forced to be a maximal chain of nested sets (each step adds one element to a ground set), factor the count as (size of ground set)! times the count with that chain pinned to a canonical labeling, since relabeling the ground set acts freely and transitively on the possible chains.
how_used: The sizes |S_{ij}|=i+j together with monotonicity force the border read as top row then down the right column, i.e. empty=S_{00} subsetneq S_{01} subsetneq ... subsetneq S_{0n} subsetneq S_{1n} subsetneq ... subsetneq S_{nn}={1,...,2n}, to be a maximal chain with consecutive sizes 0,1,2,...,2n. Such a chain is exactly a total ordering of {1,...,2n}, so there are (2n)! of them, and the symmetric group on {1,...,2n} relabels one into any other. Hence the total equals (2n)! times the number of configurations with this chain fixed to the canonical S_{0j}={1,...,j} (top row) and S_{in}={1,...,n+i} (right column). The n-by-n block of remaining cells (i>=1, j<=n-1) is what is then counted.

technique: To count monotone set-fillings of a grid, induct on Young tableaux: add cells one at a time so the growing region stays a Young tableau, and for the just-added corner cell read its number of legal values off the two already-fixed cells that pin it from below and above in size — the count is the size gap between the smaller neighbor it must contain and the larger cell it must sit inside.
how_used: Orient the grid so |S_{ij}| = i+j increases both UP and to the RIGHT (empty set at one corner, the full 2n-set at the opposite corner). After factoring out the (2n)! ways to build the boundary chain, prove by induction on a Young tableau T of cells-to-fill that there are exactly 2^{|T|} fillings. When you enlarge T by one corner cell S, the tableau condition guarantees that both S's smaller-side neighbor A (with |A|=|S|-1, so A must be contained in S) and S's larger-side neighbor C (with |C|=|S|+1, so S must be contained in C) are ALREADY filled. Write C = A cup {x,y} with x,y not in A; since A subseteq S subseteq C and |S|=|A|+1, S is A plus exactly one of x,y — exactly 2 choices, and both automatically respect the remaining diagonal neighbor. Hence each added cell contributes a clean factor 2, independent of prior fills, giving 2^{n^2} interior fillings and total (2n)! 2^{n^2}. The factor 2 comes from a size-|S|-1 neighbor and a size-|S|+1 neighbor sandwiching S; it is NOT the standard orientation where the two adjacent fixed neighbors are both size |S|-1 (which would force S uniquely) — the larger cell C of size |S|+1 is a genuine fixed constraint here precisely because the induction is on Young tableaux, not a fixed row-major sweep.

technique: Count how many entries are forced to exceed a threshold and compare against how many admissible values remain above that threshold, deriving a contradiction when the forced count overshoots the supply.
how_used: Let a_k=n (or more generally a_t=k with the prefix already fixed to {1,...,k-1}). The monotone chain i*a_i >= k*a_k = kn forces every entry in the block of slots from k up to the top to exceed k. That block has one more slot than there are integers in {1,...,n} exceeding k, so by counting the placement is impossible unless the block has length <=2, pinning a_n=n (or the short block a_k=t) as the only surviving option.

technique: When a chain of inequalities is squeezed between equal endpoints, force every link to equality, then multiply the individual slot-value equalities into one product identity and contradict it by pairing factors whose products each strictly exceed the common value.
how_used: Inside a saturated block with k*a_k = ... = t*a_t = kt whose values are exactly {k,...,t}, take the product of the interior equalities: (kt)^{t-k-1} = prod (k+i)a_{k+i}. Since the a's are the values {k+1,...,t-1}, pair each slot (k+i) with value (t-i); then (k+i)(t-i) = kt + i(t-k-i) > kt for every interior i, so the product strictly exceeds (kt)^{t-k-1}, contradicting equality. Hence no interior indices exist: the block has length <=2, giving a_k=k or the adjacent swap a_k=k+1, a_{k+1}=k.

technique: Turn a local two-option structural lemma into a linear recurrence by peeling the top element(s) in each option, then identify the recurrence as Fibonacci via a domino/unit-square tiling bijection.
how_used: The lemma gives two disjoint exhaustive branches at the top: a_n=n (delete one slot, leaving a valid permutation of 1..n-1, the freed top link automatic) or (a_{n-1},a_n)=(n,n-1) (delete two slots, leaving a valid permutation of 1..n-2, the two top links automatic). So P_n = P_{n-1} + P_{n-2} with P_1=1, P_2=2, giving P_n = F_{n+1}; equivalently each valid permutation is a set of disjoint adjacent swaps on {1,...,n}, bijecting to 1xn tilings by dominoes (swaps) and unit squares (fixed points).

technique: Convert a monochromatic run into a skew object by walking to the nearest opposite-colored vertex and taking its immediate predecessors, yielding a consecutive-vertex object
how_used: The block from crux 1 has >= 3 white. If it is 3 white / 1 black it is already a skew quad. If it is 4 white (all white), scan forward from the block to the first black vertex V_j (exists because V_{4k+1} is black by crux 1's relabeling); then V_{j-3}, V_{j-2}, V_{j-1} are white and V_j is black, giving FOUR CONSECUTIVE vertices with a 3-white/1-black split. Any 4 vertices of a convex polygon are in convex position, so they form a convex skew quadrilateral.

technique: Replace a fixed numeric target with a color-symmetric parametrized family, then induct by removing one object that drains the abundant side hard and the scarce side barely, so the per-color floor survives the step
how_used: Prove P(k): any (4k+1)-gon 2-colored with each color used >= k contains k pairwise-disjoint skew-colored quadrilaterals (3 of one color, 1 of the other). The 100-gon (41 black, 59 white) follows by deleting 3 arbitrary vertices to reach 97 = 4*24+1 with both colors still >= 24, then P(24). Disjoint means only vertex-disjoint, and any 4 vertices of a convex polygon are automatically in convex position, so a skew quad is just any 3-of-one-color-plus-1-of-other set. In the step, WLOG white is the majority (w >= 2k+1, b in [k,2k]); extract any skew quad using 3 white and 1 black. Removing it leaves 4(k-1)+1 vertices with b-1 >= k-1 black and w-3 >= 2k-2 >= k-1 white, so P(k-1) applies. Load-bearing: the quad drains the abundant color by 3 and the scarce color by only 1, so the scarce floor b >= k is preserved as k drops by 1. Color-symmetry of P(k) lets the WLOG be re-taken each step, so the extracted quad's type flips (3-black-1-white) once black becomes majority, which is why the total count is achievable even though 24 all-3W1B quads would demand 72 > 59 white.

technique: Encode each relation's reachability as one coordinate of a product invariant, and choose the two encodings to be independent so no element pair shares both coordinates.
how_used: Company A links only (i,i+1) with n not dividing i, making A-linked pairs share ceil(i/n) (the block index); company B links only (i,i+n), making B-linked pairs share i mod n (the residue). Block-index and residue are independent coordinates on the n^2 checkpoints, so no pair is linked by both, giving the k=n^2-n construction that shows k<=n^2-n fails.

technique: Label each element by the pair of maximal chains (one per relation) it lies in, then pigeonhole on the product of the two chain-counts.
how_used: Each checkpoint lies in a unique maximal A-chain and unique maximal B-chain (elements of one chain are mutually reachable, hence linked); with n-1 A-chains and n-1 B-chains there are (n-1)^2 chain-pairs, and since n^2 > (n-1)^2 at k=n^2-n+1, two distinct checkpoints share both a chain, hence are linked by both companies.

technique: Count the maximal chains of a relation by counting the elements that are not the image of any relation-step (the chain-heads), using distinctness of the step targets.
how_used: All k finishing points of A-cars are distinct, so exactly n^2-k=n-1 checkpoints are never a finishing point; each such checkpoint heads exactly one A-chain (each checkpoint starts at most one car since starts are distinct, so the step-graph is a union of simple paths), giving n-1 A-chains and symmetrically n-1 B-chains, feeding the (n-1)^2 pigeonhole count.

technique: Model a lower bound on set size as a graph where each required difference contributes one edge, then bound the vertex count by the forest inequality (a forest with E edges has at least E+1 vertices).
how_used: Vertices are the elements of S; for each 1<=k<=d=ceil(n/2) pick one pair with difference F_{2k-1} as an edge (odd-index Fibonaccis, with F_1=F_2 covering the value 1). Once these d edges are shown acyclic, the forest inequality forces |S| >= d+1 = ceil(n/2)+1.

technique: Prove an edge set on the integer line is acyclic by showing the longest edge length strictly exceeds the sum of all admissible shorter edge lengths, so the triangle-inequality path around any cycle cannot reach across the longest edge.
how_used: In any cycle the longest edge has length F_{2m+1}; the remaining edges have distinct lengths in {F_1,F_3,...,F_{2m-1}}, and the telescoping identity F_1+F_3+...+F_{2m-1}=F_{2m}<F_{2m+1} makes the path sum too short to span the longest edge's endpoints, a contradiction.

technique: Attain the extremal bound with an explicit anchored construction where each target value is realized as a difference from a common base point or from an adjacent chosen element.
how_used: Take S={F_0,F_2,F_4,...,F_{2d}}; then F_{2k}-F_0=F_{2k} and F_{2k}-F_{2k-2}=F_{2k-1} (Fibonacci recurrence) realize every F_1,...,F_{2d} as a difference, using exactly d+1 elements to match the lower bound.

technique: Bound one indexed extremal quantity below by another using that the underlying counting function is monotone nondecreasing along the same index
how_used: Writing n_a = p*m_a and R(n_a)=a*m_a, the fact that R (red count) is nondecreasing gives, whenever m_a<m_b, that b*m_b = R(n_b) >= R(n_a) = a*m_a, i.e. m_b >= (a/b) m_a; applying it to the blue count B (color swap) gives the parallel m_b >= ((p-a)/(p-b)) m_a. The same reduction fixes n_a as the value with r=a/p (forcing p|n_a) and reads off the a priori cap m_a <= N/p < (p^2-1)/4.

technique: Pivot on the extremal (largest) value in an index-block, then apply the available amplifying inequality once against the top index so the top index collapses the denominator and the block's size forces the pivot past its a priori cap
how_used: Setup (standard, assume for contradiction): for each a in {1,...,p-1} pick n_a with r(n_a)=a/p; then p|n_a, write n_a=p*m_a, and R(n_a)=a*m_a. The a priori CAP comes straight from N=(p^3-p)/4 - 1: every m_a <= N/p < (p^2-1)/4, STRICTLY. The 'Claim' gives, whenever m_a<m_b: (red count) m_b >= (a/b) m_a and (swap colors) m_b >= ((p-a)/(p-b)) m_a. THE MOVE: let q=(p-1)/2, WLOG m_1<m_{p-1}. In the main case all of m_1,...,m_q are below m_{p-1}. Let m_a be the MAXIMUM VALUE among m_1,...,m_q. Two independent facts, not one chained inequality: (i) as a VALUE, the max of q distinct positive integers is >= q, so m_a >= q; (ii) its INDEX a lies in {1,...,q}, so a <= q hence p-a >= p-q. Now apply the second (blue) Claim inequality EXACTLY ONCE with b=p-1: the top index makes the denominator p-b = p-(p-1) = 1 collapse, giving m_{p-1} >= (p-a) m_a >= (p-q)*q = ((p+1)/2)((p-1)/2) = (p^2-1)/4, contradicting the cap m_{p-1} < (p^2-1)/4. This is a SINGLE Claim application, not a telescope: the top index kills the denominator and the max-of-block pivot supplies the size >= q. (The remaining case, some m_k>m_{p-1} with k minimal, runs the same one-shot amplification off m_{p-1} and the max of m_1..m_{k-1}, using both Claim inequalities once each with the same telescope-free structure.)

technique: Pair up elements into complementary pairs of constant sum so any equal-count split of the pairs automatically balances the total.
how_used: Pair coins {k, 4n+1-k} for k=1..2n; each pair sums to 4n+1, so distributing the 2n pairs n-to-a-side makes the two weight totals equal automatically, reducing the task to splitting the pairs with two coins of each color per side.

technique: Encode a two-side partition with per-type balance constraints as a 2-edge-coloring of a multigraph whose edges join the two 'types' of each element.
how_used: Build a 4-regular multigraph on n color-vertices, one edge per complementary pair (joining the colors of its two coins). A valid partition = coloring edges red/blue so every vertex has red-degree = blue-degree = 2, i.e. equal red and blue degree at each color.

technique: Take an Euler circuit of an even-degree graph and alternate two colors along it to split each vertex's degree evenly between the colors.
how_used: Every component has all even degrees, so it has an Euler circuit of even length (= twice its vertex count); traverse it coloring edges alternately red/blue, so each degree-4 vertex is passed twice getting 2 red and 2 blue edges, yielding the desired coin partition.

technique: Compose two cross-domination maps into a self-map so its image factors through the smaller side and caps its own size.
how_used: The saddle property of each pair supplies rho_1: R2->R1 and rho_2: R1->R2 (and column analogues sigma_1,sigma_2) with a(rho_1(r2),c)>=a(r2,c) etc. Setting rho=rho_1 o rho_2 : R1->R1 forces |rho(R1)| <= |rho_1(R2)| <= |R2|, so the self-map on R1 can never occupy more than |R2| rows.

technique: Chain the row-domination and column-domination inequalities of the composed maps into a single interleaved comparison a(rho(r),c) >= a(r,sigma(c)).
how_used: Threading a(rho_1(rho_2(r_1)),c_1) >= a(rho_2(r_1),c_1) >= a(rho_2(r_1),sigma_2(c_1)) >= a(r_1,sigma_2(c_1)) >= a(r_1,sigma_1(sigma_2(c_1))) yields a(rho(r_1),c_1) >= a(r_1,sigma(c_1)) for all r_1,c_1, coupling the row self-map rho to the column self-map sigma.

technique: Stabilize a descending chain of images of a self-map on a finite set, then take the power that restricts to the identity on the stable core.
how_used: R^i=rho^i(R1) and C^i=sigma^i(C1) descend and stabilize at index n; rho^n restricted to R^n is a surjection of a finite set onto itself hence a bijection, so some power rho^{nk} is the identity on R^n (and sigma^{nk} on C^n). The periodicity converts the shift inequality into a(r_*,c)=a(rho^{nk}(r_1),c) >= a(r_1,sigma^{nk}(c))=a(r_1,c), certifying (R^n,C^n) as a saddle subpair with |R^n| <= |R2|.

technique: Force the pursuing player's moves to keep all board quantities inside a restricted algebraic set, so the terminal position is structurally constrained
how_used: A always pairs two equal nonzero numbers; induction shows every number stays a power of 2 or 0, so when A can no longer pair, the nonzero entries are distinct powers of 2 and the largest exceeds the sum of the rest, forcing termination with the board still a set of powers of two

technique: Assign each board entry a conserved 'weight' (count of original units it descends from) and bound the entry count below via subadditivity of a digit-sum on those weights
how_used: Each number's 'range' = number of original 1's it came from; nonzero k has range k, zeros have power-of-2 range, so ranges are powers of 2 summing to n; since S_2(a+b) <= S_2(a)+S_2(b), n needs at least S_2(n) powers of two, forcing at least S_2(n) numbers on the board

technique: Define a potential as the count of a sign-labeling structure and preserve a chosen 2-adic residue of that count as a game invariant
how_used: B tracks N = number of sign collections with signed sum 0 (balanced), and keeps the situation 'good' meaning 2^{s+1} does not divide N; initial N = binom(n, n/2) has 2-adic valuation exactly S_2(n) by Legendre's formula

technique: Split the invariant's count over the two possible responses as N = N_+ + N_-, so an odd-valuation total forces at least one branch to inherit that valuation
how_used: When A erases x_p, x_q, balanced collections split by whether their signs on the two entries agree (N_+, choosing x_p+x_q) or differ (N_-, choosing |x_p-x_q|); since 2^{s+1} does not divide N=N_++N_-, it fails to divide one summand, so B can pick the move keeping the situation good; at termination a dominating number gives N=0 and all-zeros gives N=2^k, forcing k <= s

technique: Recast a binary-string local constraint as a sum-free condition on the index set of one letter
how_used: Read the positions of T as an increasing sequence a_1<a_2<...; property (b) (i,j both T forces i+j to be S) becomes exactly 'no a_i+a_j equals any a_k', i.e. the T-positions form a sum-free set, and (c) becomes a_k=2k-1 for infinitely many k

technique: Sandwich an extremal quantity between matching upper and lower bounds via the difference set of a prefix, forcing equality
how_used: For a k with a_k=2k-1, the prefix A_k={a_1,...,a_k} lies in [1,2k-1] with |A_k|=k; the positive-difference set D and A_k are disjoint (a difference equalling a member would give a sum in the set, violating sum-free) and both live in [1,2k-1], so 2k-1 = a_k >= (|A_k-A_k|-1)/2 + |A_k| >= (2|A_k|-2)/2 + |A_k| = 2k-1, making every inequality tight so |A_k-A_k|=2|A_k|-1

technique: Use the minimal-difference-set characterization: a set whose difference set has the smallest possible size is an arithmetic progression
how_used: Equality |A_k-A_k|=2|A_k|-1 (the minimum for a k-element set) forces A_k to be an arithmetic progression; matching a_1+(k-1)d=2k-1 for the infinitely many equality indices k pins d=2 and a_1=1, so a_n=2n-1 for all n (T exactly at odd positions)

technique: Encode which of a pairwise two-sided constraint is tight as a directed edge, turning a set of elements into a tournament whose orientation records local blocking
how_used: On the last row's n entries x_i=a_{i,n}, the triple (i,j,n) forces x_i-x_j-a_{i,j} in {0,1}; orient i->j when the lower bound is tight (a_{i,n}=a_{i,j}+a_{j,n}) and j->i when the upper bound is tight. The arrow points at the entry blocked from increasing, so a source is the unique entry that can be incremented by 1 and a sink the unique entry that can be decremented by 1 while preserving stability (earlier rows are frozen so their triples are unaffected).

technique: Rule out a directed 3-cycle in a constraint-tournament by summing the three tightness equations around the cycle into an off-by-integer contradiction
how_used: For entries x,y,z on the last row with frozen inter-values p=a_{i,j}, q=a_{j,k}, s=a_{i,k}, a cycle x->y->z->x gives x=y+p, y=q+z, x=s+z+1, forcing s=p+q-1, which contradicts stability's own lower bound a_{i,k}>=a_{i,j}+a_{j,k}; the reverse cycle forces s=p+q+2, contradicting the upper bound. No 3-cycle => the tournament is transitive => a total order with a unique source and unique sink.

technique: Induct on a global scalar total by stepping between adjacent instances through the extremal element of the acyclic orientation, incrementing the source to go up and decrementing the sink to go down
how_used: Induct on N=s_n (last-row sum), earlier rows fixed: base N=s_{n-1} is row n-1 copied with a trailing 0 (this is the minimal attainable sum since a_{i,n}>=a_{i-1,n}+a_{n-1,n}). Existence N->N+1: increment the unique source. Uniqueness at N>s_{n-1}: decrement the unique nonzero sink to reach N-1 and apply the hypothesis. The needed fact that the sink is nonzero for N>s_{n-1} is exactly the Lemma's clause 'a 0 entry is never a source except at N=s_{n-1}' transported to the sink via the total order.

technique: Find a small set of rewrite identities that are sound under EVERY operation in the allowed class, turning them into universally-valid reduction rules on the objects
how_used: For any simple (associative, x*y in {x,y}) operation, x=y gives x*x=x, and casework gives xyxzx=xyzx; both hold for every simple op, so they descend to the equivalence classes and act as the reduction engine.

technique: Normalize an object by first replacing it with a self-concatenated copy (s -> ss), which exposes redundancy the reduction rules can then delete
how_used: Since any full string s equals ss, applying the interior-deletion identity xyxzx=xyzx to ss squeezes it down to two consecutive full permutations of S; there are n! choices per block, giving the upper bound (n!)^2 on the number of classes.

technique: Realize the abstract structure by a concrete evaluation model (assign reals, take the max with a fixed left/right tiebreak) to separate non-equivalent inputs
how_used: Model x*y as the larger real with a side-choice on ties; to distinguish two double rainbows differing in the order of a pair a,b, make a,b the two largest values so all other letters are inert, reducing evaluation to the a,b subsequence, and separate the four patterns abab/abba/baab/baba by choosing the tiebreak side.

technique: Case-split on whether the vertex set admits a monochromatic edge cut
how_used: Partition the argument on whether V splits as A ⊔ B with every crossing edge the same color (say blue). If such a monochromatic cut exists, one branch handles it (the cut edge is forced into every spanning tree, enabling contraction); if no monochromatic cut exists, then the boundary of any vertex set carries at least two colors, which is precisely the hypothesis the color-matching exchange in the other branch needs.

technique: Swap an edge for a same-color partner along the fundamental cycle it creates, keeping all per-color counts fixed
how_used: In the monochromatic-blue-cut branch, fix a blue cut edge e. For any of the three given trees T not containing e, T+e has a unique cycle which must recross the cut at another edge e'; since the cut is all blue, e' is blue, so T-e'+e is a spanning tree with identical (red,green,blue) counts but now containing e. Doing this to T_r, T_g, T_b forces all three to contain e; contracting e (routine descent) drops b→b-1 and closes by induction on r+g+b.

technique: Split on whether some vertex cut is monochromatic; in the monochromatic-cut case, force one fixed cut-edge into every given object by a same-color cycle-exchange, then contract that edge to descend to a smaller instance and induct.
how_used: Induct on n = r+g+b (base n=1 trivial). Given the three spanning trees T_r, T_g, T_b (with r red, g green, b blue edges respectively), split on the existence of a vertex partition V = A ⊔ B all of whose crossing edges share one color, say blue. Connectivity gives a blue crossing edge e (this branch is only entered when such a cut exists, so a crossing edge is present; if the monochromatic color has count 0 the branch is vacuous). For each of the three trees T not already containing e, the cycle of T ∪ {e} crosses the cut A|B an even number ≥ 2 of times, so it contains a second crossing edge e', which is also blue; swap e' out for e, producing a tree with identical per-color counts that now contains e. After doing this to all three trees, contract e (identify its endpoints) to get Γ*; each tree loses exactly one blue edge, so Γ* satisfies the hypotheses with (r, g, b-1). By induction Γ* has a spanning tree with r red, g green, b-1 blue; restoring e gives the desired tree in Γ. This is the branch that makes the induction go and is absent from any purely extremal argument.
