technique: Among all count-fixed feasible selections (each color class individually acyclic), minimize the number of connected components of the union, then break any surviving cycle by a same-color boundary-edge exchange to contradict minimality.
how_used: Complementary branch: NO vertex partition has all crossing edges one color. Range over triples (R, G, B) of edge sets with |R|=r red, |G|=g green, |B|=b blue, each color class individually acyclic (one exists: take the correctly-colored edges of the three given trees); the union R ∪ G ∪ B need NOT be acyclic. Pick one minimizing the number k of components of the union. If k=1 the union is connected on n+1 vertices with r+g+b = n edges, hence a spanning tree with the exact counts — done. If k ≥ 2, count: a graph on n+1 vertices with k components and n edges has at least one component K carrying more edges than (its vertices − 1), so K contains a cycle C. Since each single color is acyclic, C carries ≥ 2 colors, say red and green. KEY PIGEONHOLE: the cut (V(K), rest) is non-monochromatic by hypothesis, so its crossing edges bear ≥ 2 of the three colors; since only ONE color (blue) is not on C, at most one crossing color can be blue, so at least one crossing edge is red or green — a color appearing on C. Take such an edge e, say red; delete a red edge e' of C from R and add e. Since e' lay on a cycle, deleting it keeps K connected; adding the boundary edge e merges K with another component, so k drops by 1 while counts and per-color acyclicity are preserved — contradicting minimality. Hence k=1.

technique: When a cut is monochromatic, force a common cut-edge into each given tree by cycle-exchange, then contract it to reduce the induction parameter by one and invoke the smaller instance.
how_used: This is the induction on n = r+g+b (base n=1 trivial), Case 1: there is a partition V = A ⊔ B all of whose crossing edges share one color, say blue. Pick a crossing blue edge e (exists since Γ is connected). Force e into each of T_r, T_g, T_b: if a tree T misses e, then T ∪ {e} has a unique cycle through e that must recross the cut on a second edge e', which is necessarily blue; swap T + e - e', a blue-for-blue exchange preserving all three color counts, so T now contains e. With e in all three trees, contract e (identify its endpoints) to get Γ* on n vertices; each tree loses exactly the blue edge e, so Γ* meets the hypotheses for (r, g, b-1). The induction hypothesis gives a spanning tree of Γ* with counts (r, g, b-1); un-contract e (adding back one blue edge) to obtain the desired spanning tree of Γ with counts (r, g, b). The single non-obvious move: recognizing a monochromatic cut lets you force one common cut-edge and contract it to drop b by one, reducing to a strictly smaller instance.

technique: When a color-swap exchange is blocked, minimize the number of connected components over all valid monochromatic acyclic edge-sets and use the extremal choice to force any remaining cycle to be breakable.
how_used: Case 2: no cut is monochromatic (every cut sees ≥2 colors). Consider all collections (R, G, B) where R, G, B are acyclic sets of exactly r red, g green, b blue edges respectively — at least one exists by hypothesis. Among all such collections pick one for which the graph on V with edge set R ∪ G ∪ B has the fewest components k. If k = 1 the total edge count is (r+g+b) = |V|-1 and the collection is exactly the desired spanning tree. If k ≥ 2, some component K contains a cycle C (else the graph would be a forest with more than |V|-1 edges, impossible); since R, G, B are each acyclic, C carries ≥2 colors, say red and green. Because the cut separating V(K) from the rest is NOT monochromatic, it has an edge of a color appearing on C, say a red edge e leaving K. Swap: let e' be a red edge of C and set R' = R \ {e'} ∪ {e}; then (R', G, B) is still valid (still r red, still acyclic since we removed a cycle edge and added an edge to a different component) and it has strictly fewer components — contradicting minimality. The one hard move: choosing the components-count as the monovariant to minimize, so that the non-monochromatic-cut hypothesis directly supplies a cycle-edge-colored bridge that merges two components.

technique: Bound a global count of local operations by charging each operation to the unordered pair of elements it involves and summing an independent per-pair cap.
how_used: Each permitted switch involves two students h_i, h_j; charge the switch to the pair {i,j}. Granting a per-pair cap of |j-i|-1, group pairs by gap g=j-i (there are n-g of gap g) and sum: sum over pairs of (|j-i|-1) = sum_{g}(n-g)(g-1) = C(n,3).

technique: Cap how often one local operation repeats by restricting to the minimal set of elements it touches and showing each repeat must be preceded by the same operation on a strictly smaller instance, giving an inductive descent.
how_used: For gap j-i>=2, restrict attention to only h_i, h_{i+1}, h_j. After h_j and h_i first switch, the relative order is forced to h_i -> h_j -> h_{i+1} (h_i, h_{i+1} can never swap, being adjacent-index). To switch {i,j} again, h_j must first pass back behind h_i, which within this trio requires an {i+1,j} switch (gap j-i-1) in between. Hence f(gap) <= 1 + f(gap-1), and induction gives f(gap) = gap-1.

technique: Recast a selection-with-adjacency objective as a graph where the count becomes edges incident to a chosen vertex set
how_used: Build a multigraph on vertices a_i = -b_i (one class per absolute value); the 68 ordered pairs become 68 edges (pairs (k,k) are self-loops), the erasing rule 'no two erased sum to zero' becomes 'pick at most one of {a_i,b_i} per class', and the 'no both (k,k) and (-k,-k)' hypothesis lets you place all self-loops on the a_i side (WLOG). The score = number of edges incident to the chosen vertices.

technique: Set a single random-choice probability so the two weakest coverage cases become equal, forcing every edge's coverage above the common value
how_used: Choose a_i with probability p and b_i with 1-p independently per class. Given all self-loops are on the a-side (from crux 0), the two weakest coverage probabilities are the a-self-loop (p) and the b_i b_j edge (1-p^2); setting p = 1-p^2 gives p = (sqrt5-1)/2, so every edge is covered with probability >= p and E[score] >= 68p ~ 42.02 > 42, hence some selection scores >= 43.

technique: Build the tight extremal instance by mixing one class's loops with a clique on the other class and optimizing the count over the split
how_used: Take n=8, five self-loops on each a_i and a full K_8 on the b_i (68 edges total, loops only on a-side). Selecting m of the a_i and 8-m of the b_i scores 5m + (C(8,2) - C(m,2)); maximizing over m gives 43 (at m=5,6), matching the lower bound so the answer is exactly 43.

technique: Read the whole evolution as a space-time matrix (rows = successive states) and prove a claim about a distinguished final row rather than tracking one step at a time
how_used: Stacked the states of the n=2^k lamp system into a 2^k x 2^k matrix A_k whose top row is [1,0,...,0]; the whole task reduces to showing the bottom row (state after 2^k-1 steps) is all 1s, since one more step then zeroes everything (a lamp equal to all its neighbours switches off).

technique: Prove non-termination by showing the state trajectory hits a reflection of an earlier state; left/right symmetry of the rule then makes the run periodic from that earlier state onward, and the target state lies outside the cycle
how_used: For n=2^k+1 the first 2^k rows are A_k with a trailing zero column; row 2^k is [0,...,0,1,1], which is the reverse of row 1 = [1,1,0,...,0]. Since the rule is left/right symmetric, evolving from a reversed state gives the mirror of the original evolution, so the trajectory from row 1 recurs periodically (n=5: period 6; n=9: period 14), and every state in the cycle is a mirror of a nonzero state, so the all-off state never appears.

technique: Prove a corner sub-block of a cellular-automaton space-time diagram is a scaled copy of the whole by supplying its missing outer-boundary neighbour from a reflection symmetry of the diagram, so the block obeys the identical local rule and the induction hypothesis transfers to it
how_used: Take n = 2^k and let A_k be the 2^k x 2^k 0/1 space-time matrix (row t = state after t steps, top row the initial [1,0,...,0]); the inductive claim is that the bottom row of A_k is all 1s. Split A_{k+1} into four 2^k x 2^k blocks [[A_k, O_k],[B_k, C_k]]. A light-cone bound (the last 1 in row m sits at column m+1) makes the top-right block O_k all zero, so by the hypothesis the bottom row of the top half is [1,...,1,0,...,0], and the next row (first row of the bottom half) is [0,...,0,1,1,0,...,0], symmetric about the FULL-width midpoint of A_{k+1}. Because the switching rule is left/right symmetric, every later row stays midpoint-symmetric, so B_k is the mirror image of C_k; hence the column just left of C_k equals C_k's own leftmost column. Viewing C_k in isolation, its leftmost cell's needed left neighbour is thus a self-copy, which is exactly the endpoint boundary condition of the isolated n=2^k automaton (endpoint cell depends only on itself and its one neighbour). Since C_k's top row is [1,0,...,0], C_k evolves identically to A_k, so C_k = A_k; the hypothesis then gives the bottom rows of C_k and its mirror B_k all 1s, so the bottom row of A_{k+1} is all 1s. This closes the induction, and one further step turns the all-1s row into all-0s, proving n=2^k is eventually all off (part a).

technique: Force a periodic (never-terminating) orbit by choosing the size one larger than a self-terminating one so a reflecting boundary bounces the first non-trivial state back, making the evolution enter a cycle that skips the all-zero state
how_used: For part (b), take n = 2^k + 1 (one wider than the eventually-off case). Run the width-(2^k) evolution A_k inside this width-(2^k+1) strip with an extra column of zeros on the right; after 2^k steps the row A_k would-be-all-1s instead lands as [0,...,0,1,1] because the extra boundary column changes the endpoint behaviour, and crucially this vector is the REVERSAL of the second row [1,1,0,...,0]. Since the entire rule (interior and both symmetric endpoint conditions) is invariant under left-right reflection of the strip, the orbit from a reflected state is the reflection of the orbit from the original state; so from this reversed state the future rows are mirror copies of the earlier rows, and after equally many steps the pattern [1,1,0,...,0] (the second row) reappears and the sequence of states cycles periodically. Because the second row is nonzero and the cycle only revisits already-seen nonzero rows, the all-zero state never occurs; running k over all integers gives infinitely many such n, proving part (b).

technique: Set up an induction on the number of boundary sides subtended by a dissecting chord, reducing a bound on the whole configuration to the same bound on the shorter arcs each chord cuts off
how_used: For a dissecting diagonal AB cutting off the shorter boundary arc L of n sides, prove the iso-odd triangles with all vertices on L number at most n/2 by induction on n; the base n=2 is immediate, and the step splits L at an apex into shorter arcs to which the hypothesis applies. Finally instantiate on the shorter arc cut by the longest dissecting diagonal to bound all triangles by 1003.

technique: Choose the extremal (longest) member of the counted family as the pivot of the induction step, so its maximality forbids any other member from straddling across it
how_used: In arc L take PQ, the longest diagonal that is an equal side of an iso-odd triangle PQS on L. Since every triangle inscribed in the sub-semicircular arc is obtuse/right, S is the summit and PQ the base; maximality of PQ means no other iso-odd triangle can have a side longer than PQ, so none can have vertices in both outer pieces L_AP and L_QB. Hence L splits into four pieces L_AP, L_PS, L_SQ, L_QB and every iso-odd triangle except PQS lies wholly in one piece.

technique: Recover the extra slack to pay for the pivot object from the strictness of the induction bound on pieces of odd size
how_used: The two central pieces L_PS and L_SQ each span an odd number of sides, so an integer count strictly below (odd)/2 is at most (odd-1)/2, losing a full 1/2 each versus the naive bound; the two half-units together pay for the extremal triangle PQS itself, so the four sub-arc bounds plus PQS still total at most n/2, closing the induction.

technique: Attain the even-count maximum with a closed zig-zag broken line skipping every other vertex, then complete the triangulation arbitrarily
how_used: From a chosen vertex of the 2006-gon draw the broken line joining every second vertex; because 2006 is even the line closes, cutting off 1003 ear-triangles each with two polygon sides (both odd), i.e. 1003 iso-odd triangles. Triangulating the remaining central region arbitrarily leaves these 1003 intact, showing the bound 1003 is attained.

technique: To bound a count on a nested region by induction, peel off the object built on the LONGEST relevant diagonal: extremality forces its triangle to have that diagonal as base (all other vertices give shorter sides), so no counted object can straddle the outer sub-regions it separates, and the sub-region bounds add with no double-count.
how_used: Alternative to the parity proof. Lemma: for a dissecting diagonal AB with shorter boundary arc L of n sides, the number of iso-odd triangles with all vertices on L is at most n/2 (induct on n; n=2 trivial). Since L spans at most half the 2006-gon, every triangle with vertices on L is obtuse or right, so its longest side is a well-defined base. Take the iso-odd triangle PQS whose base PQ is the LONGEST iso-odd diagonal on L; S is its summit, PS=SQ the equal odd legs, and A,P,S,Q,B lie in this order splitting L into L_AP, L_PS, L_SQ, L_QB. Because PQ is longest, no iso-odd triangle can have vertices on both L_AP and L_QB (its base would exceed PQ), so every other iso-odd triangle lies within a single piece. Summing the induction hypothesis over the four pieces bounds the iso-odd triangles other than PQS by n/2; the two legs' pieces L_PS, L_SQ have ODD side-count so their bounds are strict, and the two saved halves absorb PQS itself, giving n/2. Top level: apply the same to the longest dissecting diagonal XY (triangle XYZ acute/right, so no iso-odd triangle straddles), split the whole polygon by Z into three arcs each of at most half, apply the lemma to each, and (with strictness when XYZ is itself iso-odd) sum to 2006/2 = 1003.

technique: To attain an even-parity extremal count on a regular n-gon, draw a closed broken line joining every SECOND vertex: with n even it closes into an n/2-gon whose congruent step-2 chords are all odd diagonals, forcing a full family of the target triangles, then triangulate the interior arbitrarily.
how_used: Supplies the lower bound matching the 1003 upper bound. Pick a vertex of the regular 2006-gon and join every second vertex by a broken line; since 2006 is even the line closes after 1003 chords, forming an inscribed 1003-gon. Each chord skips exactly one 2006-gon vertex, cutting off an arc of 1 side (odd) on one side and 2005 sides (odd) on the other, so every chord is an odd diagonal; together with the single skipped side, each of the 1003 'ear' triangles is isosceles (two equal chord-sides) with two odd sides, i.e. iso-odd. That gives 1003 iso-odd triangles; complete the remaining interior 1003-gon into triangles arbitrarily. Since the upper bound is 1003, the maximum equals 1003.

technique: To bound counted structures by charging each to a private boundary unit, exploit that every rival structure occupies an EVEN number of units inside any ODD-sized region it meets: the parity mismatch leaves a residual unit charged to no rival, making the charge an automatic injection.
how_used: Call a dissection triangle iso-odd if it is isosceles with its two equal sides both odd (each subtending an arc of an odd number of 2006-gon sides). For iso-odd ABC with odd equal sides AB, BC, the (odd) block of 2006-gon sides under AB and the (odd) block under BC 'belong to' ABC. Claim: some side in each block belongs to no OTHER iso-odd triangle. Belonging is via the arc-under-an-odd-side, and the dissecting diagonals are NON-CROSSING, so the belonging-arcs of the triangles are laminar (properly nested, never straddling): hence any other iso-odd triangle DEF meeting this block does so only through one of ITS two odd sides, whose arc lies wholly inside the block, and since DEF is odd-isosceles its two odd sides contribute odd+odd = an EVEN number of the block's sides. (This is exactly the parity/strict-inequality gain that solution 1 makes rigorous by strong induction on block length: the two odd sub-arcs PS, SQ each force a STRICT inequality, whose spare 1/2 + 1/2 pays for the apex triangle.) So all other iso-odd triangles together claim an even number of the block's sides; the block is ODD, so one side is claimed by none. Reserve one such side per block. The map triangle -> {two reserved sides} is injective for free: a reserved side belongs to no other iso-odd triangle, so it can be reserved for at most one. Two reserved sides each among 2006 sides gives at most 1003 iso-odd triangles.

technique: Insert a factor that equals 1 to turn a fixed exponent sum into an expandable binomial power
how_used: Set y=1-x so x+y=1. Since no three points are collinear, a(P)+b(P)+c(P)=n for every convex polygon P, where c(P) counts points of S strictly inside P. Multiply each term x^{a(P)}y^{b(P)} by (x+y)^{c(P)}=1 and expand the binomial, so the sum becomes homogeneous of degree n and each interior point is independently tagged x or y.

technique: Interpret a coefficient of the expanded generating function as choosing an object plus a subset, then collapse it via a unique-decomposition bijection into choosing a plain subset
how_used: After expansion, the coefficient of x^r y^{n-r} counts pairs (convex polygon P, subset T of the points of S strictly inside P) with |V(P)|+|T|=r. Map (P,T) to U=V(P)∪T. No-three-collinear forces every point of an arbitrary U to be either a vertex of conv(U) or strictly interior (never on an edge), so each r-subset U of S splits uniquely as V(conv U) plus interior points; the map is a bijection, the coefficient is C(n,r), and the total is (x+y)^n=1.

technique: Apply the inductive hypothesis to the point set with a chosen subset deleted, then reconcile the difference in what an exponent counts before vs. after deletion
how_used: Induct on n=|S|. For a nonempty set X of convex-hull vertices, apply the hypothesis to the smaller set S\X: the sum over convex polygons P with vertices in S\X, weighted by y to the count of S\X-points outside P, equals 1. Every point of X is a hull vertex hence lies outside every such P, so the S\X-outside-count equals b(P)-|X| where b(P) is measured against the full S. Substituting back, the same sum weighted by the full b(P) equals y^{|X|}.

technique: Sieve a family by inclusion-exclusion over a set of markers so each member is counted with net multiplicity one and a distinguished member is isolated
how_used: A convex polygon P with vertices in S is excluded from the S\X-sum exactly when X meets the hull vertices missing from P; every polygon except the full hull C is caught by at least one nonempty X subset C. Form the alternating sum over k=|X|>=1 of (-1)^{k-1} times the S\X-sums (each equal to y^{|X|}): this gives sum_k (-1)^{k-1} C(m,k) y^k = 1-(1-y)^m = 1-x^m, counting every P!=C once. Adding the single hull term x^m for P=C completes the total to 1.

technique: Drive a reconfiguration proof by a monovariant that is squeezed between the current and target states, so each allowed move strictly increases it and the target caps it.
how_used: Define a(X) = number of A-strawberries and b(X) = number of B-plums in the top-left rectangle [OX]; the hypothesis gives a(X) <= b(X) everywhere. Show it suffices to find one switch producing A' with a(X) <= a'(X) <= b(X) for all X and strict increase in sum_X a(X); since all sums are bounded by sum_X b(X), iterating forces every a to reach b, i.e. A reaches B.

technique: Locate the move by taking the topmost row where the two configurations disagree, then descend to the first misplaced piece below it to fix the corners of the operating rectangle.
how_used: Take the uppermost row where plum P and strawberry S differ (P left of S); in P's column the strawberry sits below P, so region [BS] below [PS] holds a strawberry; let V be the uppermost such strawberry, W its intersection with S's column, U the intersection of P's row with V's column. The switch moves strawberries from S and V to U and W.

technique: Establish a strict slack margin over a whole rectangle by decomposing each prefix-count into a below-balance region, a perfectly-matched region, and a region containing only a target piece.
how_used: For X in [PR], split [OX] into: the part left of P's column (plums >= strawberries by hypothesis), the part above P/S's row (perfect A-B balance), and the remaining rectangle [PX] (holds plum P and no strawberry). This yields a(X) < b(X) strictly on all of [PR], guaranteeing the switch's +1 increment on [UR] subset [PR] keeps a' <= b.

technique: Model a schedule/pairing structure as translation by group elements over an abelian group so the closure condition becomes a group-law identity
how_used: Label the 2^t players by F_2^t vectors; round i pairs alpha with alpha+omega(i) where omega(i) is the binary expansion of i. Condition (ii) (A~B, C~D, A~C in round j implies B~D) reduces to the associative/commutative XOR identity beta+omega(j)=[alpha+omega(i)]+omega(j)=[alpha+omega(j)]+omega(i)=delta, making it automatic. For general n=2^t*s, take s disjoint copies so cross-block triples never all meet and (ii) is vacuous across blocks.

technique: When a local pairing propagates along paths, use the structural axiom to lift a single cross-edge into a full block-to-block matching, forcing two merging classes to be equinumerous
how_used: When A (in i-component Gamma) meets B (in i-component Delta) in round i+1, take any C in Gamma with a path A=X_1,...,X_m=C using rounds 1..i, where X_j meets X_{j+1} in round r<=i. Let Y_j be X_j's round-(i+1) partner. Apply (ii) with i:=r, j:=i+1 (edges X_j~X_{j+1} and Y_j~Y_{j+1} in round r, cross-edges X_j~Y_j, X_{j+1}~Y_{j+1} in round i+1) to get Y_j~Y_{j+1} in round r, so the Y-path stays in Delta; hence every C in Gamma meets a partner in Delta and vice versa, proving |Gamma|=|Delta|.

technique: Track a size invariant across a merge step to show it can only stay fixed or double, forcing it to be a power of two by induction
how_used: The (i+1)-component of A is Gamma union Delta with |Gamma|=|Delta|, and since two i-components are disjoint or coincide, |Gamma_{i+1}| equals |Gamma_i| or 2|Gamma_i|; starting from |Gamma_1|=2 this makes every |Gamma_i|=2^u.

technique: Convert a counting lower bound on distinct neighbors into a threshold on a power-of-two invariant to pin the divisibility level
how_used: Player A has k distinct opponents all lying in its final component Gamma_k of size 2^u, so 2^u >= k+1, forcing u >= t_k where 2^{t_k} is the least power of two at least k+1. Since every player meets k distinct opponents, every final component has size >=k+1 hence a power of two >=2^{t_k}, and the player set partitions into these components, so 2^{t_k} divides n.

technique: For a tiling necessity bound, restrict the tiling to the tiles meeting a chosen sub-region and count the two cell-types it covers, using that each tile pairs one of each type
how_used: Restricting a diamond tiling to the diamonds meeting a size-k subtriangle T' gives a figure with (k^2+k)/2 - h upward cells (h = holes) and at least (k^2-k)/2 downward cells; since each diamond covers one upward and one downward cell, (k^2+k)/2 - h >= (k^2-k)/2, yielding h <= k, so the hole condition is necessary

technique: Prove a closure property for extremal (equality) sets by combining the modularity identity size(A)+size(B)=size(A meet B)+size(A join B) with the constraint's inequalities on the meet and join
how_used: The 'full' triangles (size k containing exactly k spread-out holes) are closed under smallest-containing-triangle: for touching full triangles of sizes a,b with intersection size c and join size d, the identity a+b=c+d, the spread-out bounds x<=c (meet holes) and y<=d (join holes), and a+b<=x+y (the overlap is counted twice on the left) force x=c and y=d, so both meet and join are full

technique: In an inductive peeling argument, replace each removed boundary object by the just-outside cell of a maximal extremal region anchored at it, and use the closure lemma to show the swap preserves the global constraint
how_used: To peel the bottom row, replace bottom hole u by cell w: let Delta be u's associate (the maximal full triangle through u's top vertex with base on line ell), and w the upward cell just right of Delta sharing a vertex; w is not a hole (else Delta extends) and lies left of the next hole v; if some Gamma contained w but not u and were full, then Gamma+Delta would be full of H minus u yet strictly larger than Delta (contradicting maximality if above ell) or would contain u (contradicting spread-out if it reaches row B), so replacing u by w keeps holes spread out for the induction

technique: Encode a two-parallel-support-plane (antipodality) condition on a convex body via the Gauss map: send each boundary stratum to its outward-normal image on the sphere and reflect through the origin, so 'contained between parallel planes' becomes 'a normal image overlaps the antipodal reflection of another normal image'.
how_used: Each face F -> its outward-normal point S^+(F); each edge E -> the great-circle arc S^+(E) of outward normals of its support planes (joining the two adjacent face-normals, perpendicular to E); each vertex V -> the spherical polygon S^+(V) of outward normals of its support planes (bounded by the incident edge-arcs). Writing S^-(X) for the origin-reflection (inward normals): U in stratum X and V in stratum Y are antipodal iff S^-(X) meets S^+(Y). Hence a vertex pair is antipodal iff S^-(V_i) overlaps S^+(V_j) (Lemma 1), and an edge-midpoint pair is antipodal iff arc S^-(E_i) meets arc S^+(E_j) (Lemma 2). The three no-parallel hypotheses make these meetings transverse (arcs cross at isolated interior points, polygons overlap in open regions), so A and B are honest incidence counts.

technique: Superimpose a spherical cell-decomposition and its origin-reflected copy, tally the combined vertices/edges/faces of the overlay with each transverse crossing counted, and read the unknown incidence counts off a single Euler characteristic of the overlaid complex.
how_used: Draw all outward arcs S^+(E_i) together with all reflected arcs S^-(E_j). Knots = the 2ℓ face-image points (S^+ and S^- copies, distinct by the no-parallel-faces hypothesis) plus the 2B arc-crossings (each antipodal edge-midpoint pair gives two origin-symmetric crossings). Segments = the original 2m arcs, each of the 2B crossings splitting two arcs to add 4B, giving 2m+4B. The overlay's regions are exactly the overlaps of S^-(V_i) with S^+(V_j), which by convexity are contiguous, so their number is 2A (each antipodal vertex pair giving two symmetric overlaps). Euler V-E+F=2 reads (2ℓ+2B)-(2m+4B)+2A=2; with n-m+ℓ=2 for Γ this gives A-B=m-ℓ+1=n-1.

technique: Replace a body's antipodal-pair structure by the boundary combinatorics of its difference body K-K: points on the boundary correspond exactly to antipodal generating pairs, and stratify that boundary by the (feature-type of U, feature-type of V) of the unique generating pair.
how_used: Δ=Γ-Γ is convex, centrally symmetric, and W=U-V lies on ∂Δ iff U,V are antipodal (parallel support planes with opposite normals), with the representation W=U-V unique because the no-parallel hypotheses force the separating intersection (Γ-U)∩(Γ-V) to be the single point {0}. Classifying ∂Δ by the type-pair of the generating pair: (vertex,vertex) gives the vertices of Δ, numbering 2A; (edge,edge) with independent directions gives Minkowski-sum parallelogram 2-faces, numbering 2B; (face,vertex) gives translated/reflected congruent copies of each face, numbering 2ℓ; (face,edge) and (face,face) are excluded because they would require a parallel edge/face. Hence V(Δ)=2A and the 2-faces of Δ number F(Δ)=2B+2ℓ.

technique: Count a polytope's edges indirectly through the handshake/degree-sum identity: sum the side-counts over all its 2-faces (equal to twice the edge number) instead of enumerating 1-cells directly.
how_used: For Δ=Γ-Γ, the 2-faces are the 2B parallelograms (4 sides each) and the 2ℓ face-copies (each copy of F_i has d_i sides). Using the handshake identity on Γ, Σd_i=2m, the total side-sum over ∂Δ is 2B·4 + 2·(Σd_i) = 8B+4m, so E(Δ)=(8B+4m)/2=4B+2m. Feeding V(Δ)=2A, E(Δ)=4B+2m, F(Δ)=2B+2ℓ into Euler on Δ gives 2A-(4B+2m)+(2B+2ℓ)=2, i.e. A-B=m-ℓ+1, and Euler on Γ (n-m+ℓ=2) reduces this to A-B=n-1.

technique: Exploit a data-preserving involution on the hidden object that becomes a symmetry exactly at the critical parameter value, forcing indistinguishability
how_used: Complementing every bit of the leader's string X to X' maps each deputy string Y to its complement and sends the distance-k condition to distance n-k; when n=2k these coincide so X and X' produce the identical deputy set, making them indistinguishable and forcing at least 2 guesses (while for n!=2k the same map lets one WLOG assume k>=n/2).

technique: Recover a hidden coordinate by comparing how many revealed objects carry each value there, using that the two counts differ away from the symmetric parameter
how_used: Fixing coordinate i, among the C(n,k) deputy strings exactly C(n-1,k) agree with X at i and C(n-1,k-1) disagree; since n!=2k gives C(n-1,k)!=C(n-1,k-1), the value with the larger (publicly computable) count is X_i, and repeating over all i reconstructs X so one guess suffices.

technique: Double-count incidences of (structure, distinguished feature) two ways, once through the object's internal contribution and once through the feature's global multiplicity
how_used: Count pairs (isosceles triangle, side with differently-colored endpoints). Assuming no 3-colored triangle, every counted triangle is exactly 2-colored so contributes exactly 2 such sides, giving 2a_2 for the total; this side of the count is forced even.

technique: Count how many of the target structures a fixed pair of vertices lies in by placing the pair in each possible role, using a number-theoretic hypothesis to force those placements into distinct structures
how_used: Any two vertices A,B lie in exactly 3 isosceles triangles: two with AB as a leg, one with AB as base (n odd); gcd(n,3)=1 forbids an inscribed equilateral triangle so all three are distinct. Summed over bichromatic pairs this gives the count 3(bc+cd+db).

technique: Derive a contradiction by forcing the two evaluations of a double count to have opposite parities, using the hypothesis to fix the parity of one side
how_used: 2a_2 is even, while 3(bc+cd+db) is odd because b,c,d are each odd (odd number of vertices per color), so each product and their sum is odd. Even != odd contradicts a_3=0, so a rainbow isosceles triangle exists.

technique: Rule out perpendicular chords in an odd regular polygon by reflecting to force a nonexistent antipodal vertex
how_used: If diagonals AB and CD are perpendicular, let E be the vertex on the perpendicular bisector of AB and E' its antipode on the circumcircle; perpendicularity gives EC = E'D, so E' would have to be a polygon vertex. But an odd regular n-gon has no pair of antipodal vertices, a contradiction. Hence for odd n no two selected diagonals are perpendicular, so the 'or perpendicular' clause is void and selected diagonals must be pairwise non-crossing; a non-crossing family of a convex n-gon has at most n-3 diagonals (a triangulation), attained by a fan from one vertex, giving n-3.

technique: After a family is forced into a fixed small set of parallel classes, isolate the extremal (longest) member of each class to shave its endpoints, then bound the total by a per-vertex degree count
how_used: After the collapse, all selected diagonals lie in two perpendicular directions, so within each direction they are pairwise parallel (non-crossing) and each vertex carries at most one diagonal per direction, i.e. degree at most 2 in the selection graph. Take the LONGEST selected diagonal in one direction: no other selected diagonal can share either of its endpoints, because any parallel selected diagonal sharing an endpoint would be shorter and would have to cross a still-longer parallel selected diagonal (parallel chords sharing an endpoint are nested), forcing an illegal non-perpendicular crossing. Same for the longest in the other direction. This pins down 4 vertices of degree exactly 1. Each of the remaining n-4 vertices has degree at most 2, so the sum of degrees is at most 2(n-4)+4 = 2n-4, giving at most (2n-4)/2 = n-2 selected diagonals. The bound n-2 is attained: take all diagonals from a vertex A plus the diagonal joining the two neighbours of A's antipode (the only crossing pair being that diameter and that short diagonal, which are perpendicular).

technique: When a perpendicular crossing pair partitions the circumcircle into four arcs each smaller than a semicircle, classify every other admissible chord by which arc its endpoints occupy: a crossing pair whose four endpoints fall in a single such arc cannot subtend perpendicular angles, forcing each admissible chord to align with one of the two frame directions.
how_used: Even case, all-crossing subcase (every selected diagonal meets another). Fix a selected perpendicular crossing pair d1 perp d2 meeting at interior point P; because d1 perp d2, the four arcs A,B,C,D they cut satisfy arcA+arcC=180 and arcB+arcD=180 (intersecting-chords angle theorem: crossing angle = half the sum of the two vertical intercepted arcs), so EACH single arc is < 180 deg, i.e. lies strictly on one side of a diameter of Gamma. The move: take any selected crossing pair e1,e2 with neither parallel to d1 nor d2. The claim the solver must establish (the official solution states it flatly and this is the real work) is that all four endpoints of e1,e2 then lie in a single one of the four arcs; being confined to one arc of measure < 180 deg, e1,e2 subtend a crossing angle < 90 deg (their two vertical intercepted arcs are proper sub-arcs of that one arc, summing to < 180 deg), so e1,e2 are NOT perpendicular -- forbidden. Hence no selected crossing pair avoids both frame directions, so every selected diagonal runs parallel to d1 or to d2.

technique: Given a family split into two direction classes, note the longest member of each class has endpoints that cannot be reused (a second chord there crosses a longer parallel member at a forbidden angle), then bound the family size by a vertex-incidence double count charging at most two per ordinary vertex and one per protected extreme endpoint.
how_used: Even case, finishing the all-crossing subcase after crux 0 gives: every selected diagonal is parallel to one of the two perpendicular directions d1, d2. Take L1 = longest selected diagonal in direction 1. Its two endpoints carry no other selected diagonal: a second selected diagonal through an endpoint of L1 would be direction 2 (a parallel one would coincide), and it must cross a direction-1 diagonal strictly longer than / beyond L1 at that vertex at a non-right angle -- forbidden. Same for L2 = longest in direction 2. So these 4 endpoints are used by exactly these 2 diagonals; each of the other n-4 vertices lies on at most 2 selected diagonals (at most one per direction). Double count endpoint-incidences: 2*(#selected) <= 2*(n-4) + 1*4 = 2n-4, so #selected <= n-2. Combine with the lonely-diagonal branch of the induction (a selected diagonal crossing no other splits the n-gon into an m-gon lying on one side of a diameter, at most m-3 non-crossing diagonals, and an l-gon giving l-2 by induction, plus the diagonal itself: (m-3)+(l-2)+1 = n-2 since m+l=n+2). Even bound n-2, attained by all n-3 diagonals from a vertex A plus the chord joining the two neighbours of A's antipode A' (only crossing pair AA' perp d', both perpendicular, allowed).

technique: Track a complete-bipartite (biclique) substructure as the invariant a graph-rewriting process preserves, rather than tracking the whole graph.
how_used: Define two disjoint island sets A and B forming a 'network' (every island of A joined to every island of B) and carry this biclique through all years instead of the full adjacency; base case is any single edge A-B plus, from the connectivity hypothesis, a third island joined to A, giving a 3-vertex network. Preservation and growth of this object are handled by the later cruxes.

technique: When a symmetric 'toggle-if-adjacent-to-exactly-one' rewrite fires because an edge between two chosen vertices is removed, exploit that any third vertex already joined to one endpoint is forced joined to the other endpoint afterward (regardless of its prior adjacency to that other endpoint).
how_used: When network edge A-B closes (A in A, B in B), take any C in A-{A}: C is joined to B by the network property. If C was not joined to A, C is now adjacent to exactly one of {A,B}, so the rule adds C-A; if C was already joined to A, it stays. Either way C ends joined to both. Symmetrically for B-{B}. So {A,B} vs the rest re-forms a network on the same vertex set. KEY: pre-existing adjacency to the 'other' endpoint never blocks this - the vertex ends joined to both no matter what.

technique: Maintain a complete-bipartite structure between two named vertex sets as the induction invariant, and restore it after a single edge is lost by RE-SPLITTING the same vertex set into a new two-part partition rather than repairing the old one.
how_used: Call two disjoint island-sets A and B a 'network' if every island of A is joined to every island of B (complete bipartite across A,B; edges inside A or inside B are irrelevant). Seed it from one route A-B (put A in A, B in B) plus a third island C joined to A (forced by connectivity) placed in B. The network's only cross-edge type is A-B (A in A, B in B); it can only be destroyed when the specific route A-B is closed. When that happens, re-split the SAME set A cup B as A'={A,B}, B'=(A cup B) minus {A,B}. Check A' vs B' is again a network: take any C in A minus {A}; C was joined to B (network), and if C was not joined to A the toggle adds route C-A, so C is now joined to both A and B; symmetrically for islands of B minus {B}. So the toggle rule converts the lost edge into exactly the edges needed for the new bipartition. B' is nonempty since |A cup B|>=3.

technique: Grow the tracked structure by feeding a SELF-CHOSEN partition (structure-so-far vs everything outside) to a hypothesis that some cross-edge must eventually be cut, then use that cut's own toggle to promote the newly touched outside vertex into the structure.
how_used: While the network A cup B is not all n islands, apply the 'every partition eventually loses a cross route' hypothesis to the partition (A cup B) vs (outside islands). It forces some cross route to close: between a network island A and an outside island D; WLOG A in A. Because A vs B is a network, every island of B was joined to A, so closing route A-D adds, by the toggle, a route from D to every island of B that lacked one (those already joined to D stay joined). Hence D becomes joined to all of B, so putting D into A keeps A vs B a network while enlarging A cup B by one. |A cup B| strictly increases and is bounded by n, so eventually A cup B is all n islands.

technique: When a closing/toggling operation breaks an invariant across a bipartition, re-split around the endpoints of the just-closed edge and show the same toggle that broke it re-establishes completeness across the new split.
how_used: Call disjoint island-sets A, B a 'network' if every island of A is joined to every island of B. This complete-bipartite relation can be lost only when a closed route is a cross route A-B (A in A, B in B) - no other operation touches a cross pair. At that moment re-split: A'={A,B}, B'=(A cup B)-{A,B} (nonempty). For any C in A-{A}: the network already gave C-B, and the toggle rule (any island joined to exactly one of the two closed-edge endpoints gets a route to the other) means if C was not joined to A it becomes joined to A now; either way C ends joined to both A and B, i.e. to all of A'. Symmetrically for C in B-{B}. So A'|B' is a network on the SAME vertex set A cup B. The network relation is only about cross-side completeness (edges inside a side are irrelevant), so this is the load-bearing invariant: closing the cross route re-establishes a network rather than destroying it.

technique: To grow an invariant complete-bipartite core to the whole vertex set, invoke the eventual-cross-cut hypothesis on core-vs-outside, then read the per-vertex toggle to see the outside vertex become complete to one whole side, and absorb it.
how_used: Seed a network A|B from an edge A-B plus a third island C joined to A (the hypothesis forces such a C) placed in B, so 3<=|A cup B|<n. While |A cup B|<n, apply the hypothesis to the partition (A cup B) vs outside: some cross route eventually closes, say A-D with A in A, D outside. Crucially the toggle rule fires PER ISLAND, not just for the two endpoints: it toggles every island joined to exactly one of {A,D}. Every island B' in B was joined to A by the network; whichever ones were not joined to D now get a route to D. Hence after this single cut EVERY island of B is joined to D, so D is complete to B. Move D into A: the new A|B is a network with |A cup B| increased by one. Iterate until |A cup B|=n.

technique: To force some distinguished vertex to become universal, freeze two symmetric vertices as one side of a two-element split over all vertices; the eventual-cross-cut hypothesis must cut one of their edges, and by the symmetry of the two frozen vertices the other is left complete to everyone.
how_used: Once |A cup B|=n, cut a cross route A-B and apply crux 0: A'={A,B}, B'=all remaining islands form a network, so BOTH A and B are joined to every island of B'. The two frozen vertices A and B play symmetric roles as the side A'. The network breaks only when a cross route A'-B' closes; by the hypothesis (applied to A'|B') this must eventually happen, and it is a route from one of {A,B} to some C in B'. By the A<->B symmetry take WLOG the cut route to be A-C. Then B's routes are untouched: B is still joined to A and to every island of B', hence to all n-1 other islands, so B is universal. (Symmetrically, if the cut were B-C then A is universal.) Either way one of the two frozen vertices ends connected to all others.

technique: Extend a finite arrangement of crossing segments to full lines cutting a bounding circle, so each segment becomes a chord with two endpoints on the circle and the dynamics become static incidence data on the 2n boundary points.
how_used: Enclose all segments in a big disk D and extend each segment s_i to a line l_i meeting the boundary circle at two points A_i, B_i; the 2n boundary points are distinct and, since every two segments cross in the interior, every two chords cross inside D (so each chord has n-1 crossings and each arc between A_i and B_i holds n-1 of the other endpoints). A snail's start endpoint is a choice of one chord-end as origin, and the clap-time at which it reaches P = l_i ∩ l_j equals the number of other chords whose crossing with l_i lies between the origin and P. Two snails coincide at P iff these two crossing-counts are equal, converting the dynamic 'never meet' condition into equality/inequality of static crossing-counts.

technique: To compare crossing-counts on two arms meeting at a point, classify each third object by which arc its endpoint falls on: objects on the arc between the two arm-origins cross exactly one arm, all others cross both or neither.
how_used: For snails from A_i and A_j meeting at P = l_i ∩ l_j, arrival is simultaneous iff the crossing-counts on arms A_iP and A_jP are equal. A third chord l_k crosses exactly one of the two arms iff its boundary endpoint lies on the arc A_iA_j (else it crosses both or neither), so the SUM of the two arm-counts has the parity of the number of endpoints on arc A_iA_j. When A_i, A_j have opposite marks the arc holds an odd number of endpoints, making the sum odd so the counts cannot be equal (no meeting) — this closes part (a) since the odd-n orientation makes the two starting ends opposite-marked for every pair. When A_i, A_j share a mark (the even-n forced neighbours) the arc count is even and the equal-count / simultaneous-arrival case is realized, forcing the meeting for part (b).

technique: Extend crossing segments to full chords of an enclosing circle and alternately two-color the 2n boundary points around the circle, so a chord's two endpoint colors are read off the parity of how many other endpoints lie on the arc between them.
how_used: Put all n mutually-crossing segments inside a disk and extend each to a line cutting the circle at A_i, B_i. Because every pair of lines crosses inside the disk, exactly n-1 of the other endpoints lie on each arc from A_i to B_i. Mark the boundary points 'in'/'out' alternately around the circle; then A_i and B_i get OPPOSITE colors iff the number of points strictly between them (n-1) is odd, i.e. iff n is even, and the SAME color iff n is odd. This turns 'which endpoint each snail starts from' into a color, so a placement is a choice of one colored end per chord.

technique: To decide whether two moving points can meet at a crossing, compare the parity of how many transversals cut each of the two half-segments up to the crossing, classifying each transversal by whether its two boundary endpoints separate the two start endpoints on the boundary arc.
how_used: Two snails on l_i, l_j can collide at P = l_i ∩ l_j only if they arrive at the same clap, i.e. only if segments A_iP and A_jP carry the SAME number of other intersection points. Count those crossings by their line l_k: a line whose two boundary endpoints separate A_i from A_j (its endpoints lie on opposite arcs of the boundary determined by A_i, A_j) meets exactly ONE of A_iP, A_jP (odd, +1 to the parity of the sum); every other line meets both or neither (even). Hence parity(count on A_iP + count on A_jP) = parity(number of boundary endpoints on arc A_iA_j). If A_i, A_j lie an ODD arc apart, count_i and count_j have different parity, so they can never be equal — that pair never collides; if the arc is EVEN, equal counts are possible and (when both are 'in' starts) forced, so they collide at P. This is the local per-pair collision test used for both directions.

technique: Extend each object to a full line meeting a bounding circle, so a global structural count (each object crosses all others) fixes how many endpoints lie on each arc; then alternately 2-color the boundary endpoints to turn that count into a parity relation between an object's two endpoints.
how_used: Enclose all n segments in a disk and extend segment i to a line l_i meeting the circle at A_i, B_i, so the 2n endpoints sit on the circle. Because every two segments (hence lines) cross inside the disk, each of the other n-1 lines has exactly one endpoint on each open arc between A_i and B_i; so each arc A_iB_i contains exactly n-1 boundary points. Mark the 2n boundary points 'in'/'out' alternately around the circle. Since A_i and B_i are separated by n-1 points, for ODD n they get OPPOSITE colors (so 'start at the in-endpoint of l_i' is a well-defined choice for every line), while for EVEN n they get the SAME color (so two neighbouring boundary points must both be 'in'). This is the geometry-to-parity reduction that sets up the collision analysis; it does NOT by itself decide whether any given pair collides.

technique: To decide whether two tokens advancing step-by-step along two crossing tracks reach the crossing point at the same step, reduce 'same arrival step' to 'equal number of intervening crossings on each track', then recount that total by how many other tracks separate the two starting ends — a track with exactly one end strictly between the two starts contributes an odd amount, all others an even amount.
how_used: Extend the n segments to lines l_i cutting a bounding disk at endpoints A_i,B_i on the circle. A snail's position after t claps on l_i is its t-th intersection point counted from its start end, so two snails from A_i,A_j meet iff they meet at P=l_i∩l_j, i.e. iff (#crossings strictly between A_i and P) equals (#crossings strictly between A_j and P). Classify every other line l_k by its two circle-endpoints relative to the open arc between A_i and A_j: if exactly one endpoint of l_k lies on that arc, l_k separates the starts and crosses exactly one of the two segments A_iP, A_jP (contributes 1); otherwise it crosses both or neither (contributes 0 or 2). Hence the combined crossing count on A_iP and A_jP has the same parity as the number of endpoints strictly on the arc between A_i and A_j. If that arc-count is ODD the two side-counts have opposite... unequal parity so cannot be equal — the snails never meet. This is the meeting-obstruction engine used for both parts; combined with the odd-n construction it kills every pair (a), and combined with the even-n adjacency it is upgraded to a forced meeting (b).

technique: To choose a consistent start-end for every chord of a circle so that any two chosen starts have an odd number of other endpoints between them, 2-color the cyclic sequence of all endpoints alternately and take the 'in'-colored end of each chord — this works exactly when each chord spans an EVEN number of intervening endpoints, which makes its two ends receive opposite colors.
how_used: The 2n line-endpoints A_i,B_i sit in cyclic order on the disk boundary. Color them alternately 'in','out' around the circle. Any chord l_i has exactly n-1 endpoints strictly between A_i and B_i (every other line crosses it inside the disk). Two points with k endpoints strictly between them on an arc get opposite colors iff k is even. For n ODD, n-1 is even, so A_i and B_i always get opposite colors — Jeff can start each snail at the 'in'-colored end. Then for any pair, the arc between the two 'in' starts contains an odd number of endpoints (the two chosen ends are same-colored, forcing an odd count of points between them), so the separator-parity engine gives an odd combined count and the pair never meets. This is the constructive half of part (a): it produces the placement, which the obstruction crux then certifies.

technique: When a parity count only shows two quantities are congruent, force EXACT equality by choosing the configuration so the two endpoints are adjacent on the boundary (no separator between them): then every separator lies wholly on one side and contributes equally to both counts. Guarantee such an adjacent equal-colored pair exists by noting the required alternating coloring is impossible — each chord spans an ODD number of intervening points, so its ends must share a color, breaking perfect alternation.
how_used: For n EVEN, mark each endpoint 'in'/'out' by the direction each snail actually starts. A perfectly alternating in/out pattern around the 2n endpoints would give every chord's two ends OPPOSITE marks; but each chord l_i spans n-1 endpoints, and n-1 is ODD for even n, forcing A_i and B_i to share a mark under any alternating pattern — contradiction, so the marks cannot perfectly alternate and two neighbouring endpoints A_i,A_j must carry the same mark, which can be taken 'in' (both are start-ends). Since A_i,A_j are adjacent on the circle, NO other endpoint lies on the arc between them, so every other line has both ends on the same side and crosses both of A_iP,A_jP or neither — the crossing counts on A_iP and A_jP are not merely equal in parity but EXACTLY equal. Hence the snails from A_i and A_j arrive at P together and collide, proving (b) for every placement.

technique: Superimpose a perfect matching with its reflection across an axis so red (original) and blue (reflected) edges give every vertex degree 1 in each color, decomposing the union into alternating red/blue cycles whose per-cycle red<->blue swap produces another valid configuration
how_used: Given a valid partition P of the 2n x 2n board with fewer than 2n marks, build a graph on all cells: red-join the two cells of each domino of P; blue-join x,y iff their reflections across the main diagonal d are a red domino. Reflection of a domino is a domino, so both colors are perfect matchings (degree 1 each), and the union splits into cycles alternating red/blue. On any single cycle, deleting its red edges and inserting its blue edges rebuilds P into a different domino partition P' that differs only along that cycle.

technique: Bound the number of alternating cycles from below by counting how the reflection's fixed elements distribute (each fixed element pairs into a cycle of length >=4 with exactly one other fixed element), then pigeonhole the scarce resource onto a cycle carrying at most one unit to flip it
how_used: Each of the 2n cells on the main diagonal d is a fixed point of the reflection; its red and blue edges are mirror images so go to two different cells, forcing its cycle to have length >=4. A symmetric-path argument (walk from a diagonal cell to the next diagonal cell hit, then mirror the path) shows each such cycle contains exactly two diagonal cells, so the 2n diagonal cells lie in exactly n cycles. With k<2n marks spread over these n cycles, pigeonhole gives a cycle with at most one mark; its red<->blue swap yields a valid partition P' (a cycle with <=1 mark has no domino covering two marks, and dominoes off the cycle are unchanged) that is distinct from P, contradicting uniqueness and proving k>=2n.

technique: Force a tiling to be unique by placing obstructions so one corner cell has a single legal domino orientation, then let that forced orientation propagate cell-by-cell.
how_used: Mark the 2n cells (i,i) and (i,i+1) for i=1..n. The cell (1,1) cannot lie in a horizontal domino (it would cover the two marked cells (1,1),(1,2)), so its domino is vertical; this forces the domino at (2,2) vertical, and by induction every domino in the diagonal region is vertical. The 90-degree rotational symmetry of the whole configuration forces the analogous orientation in the other three regions cut out by the board's two diagonals, so a legal partition exists and is unique. This shows 2n marks suffice, i.e. k <= 2n.

technique: To show a marking is too small to force uniqueness, overlay the tiling with its reflection across a symmetry axis: red edges = the tiling's dominoes, blue edges = the reflected dominoes; the two perfect matchings decompose into alternating cycles, and swapping the red/blue edges on one cycle produces a distinct valid tiling.
how_used: Suppose k < 2n cells are marked and a valid partition P exists. On the cells as vertices, put a red edge for each domino of P and a blue edge joining cells whose reflections across the main diagonal d are red-joined. Every vertex has red-degree and blue-degree 1, so the graph splits into cycles with colours alternating. A domino never reflects to itself across d, so at each diagonal cell the two edges differ; hence every diagonal cell (i,i) sits on a cycle of length >= 4, and by the reflection symmetry each such cycle meets d in exactly two cells, so the 2n diagonal cells lie in n cycles. Since k < 2n, by pigeonhole some cycle contains at most one marked cell; recolour that cycle (replace its red dominoes by its blue dominoes). The result P' differs from P (cycle length >= 4) and still has no domino covering two marked cells, since any new domino lies on that cycle and the cycle holds <= 1 mark. Hence uniqueness fails, so k >= 2n.

technique: To prove a configuration is not forced, overlay it with its image under a symmetry of the domain to obtain a 2-regular bicolored graph, so the two configurations decompose into alternating cycles along which a local swap produces a second valid configuration.
how_used: Take any legal tiling P. Put a red edge on the two cells of each domino of P (a perfect matching). Reflect P's dominoes across the main diagonal d and put a blue edge on each reflected pair (also a perfect matching, since reflection is an involution on cells). Every cell has red-degree 1 and blue-degree 1, so red union blue is a disjoint union of cycles with colors alternating (length-2 cycles = dominoes fixed by the reflection). On any cycle of length >= 4, deleting its red dominoes and laying its blue dominoes gives another legal tiling P' differing from P only along that cycle. This converts 'P is unique' into 'no such swappable cycle can avoid the mark constraint.'

technique: To find a constraint-free swap when a scarce resource is spread over disjoint orbits, count the orbits and pigeonhole the resource against them: with fewer resource units than orbits' minimum requirement, some orbit is under-loaded and can be swapped freely.
how_used: The 2n diagonal cells are partitioned into exactly n alternating cycles, each of length >= 4. If a legal marking uses k < 2n cells, then since there are n cycles and 2n cells to distribute along them, by pigeonhole some cycle C_i carries at most one marked cell. Swapping red <-> blue on C_i yields a tiling P' that differs from P (|C_i| >= 4) and agrees with P off C_i; since C_i holds at most one mark, no domino of P' covers two marks, so P' is a second legal tiling, contradicting uniqueness. Hence k >= 2n.

technique: To realize a prescribed unique configuration, seed a forced choice at an extremal cell by having the marks kill one of its two options, then run the forced-choice induction inward and finish the remaining regions by the domain's symmetry.
how_used: Mark (i,i) and (i,i+1) for i=1..n. The two board diagonals split the 2n x 2n board into four triangular regions. In the top-left region the corner cell (1,1) cannot be covered by a horizontal domino, since that domino would cover (1,1) and (1,2), both marked; so (1,1) is covered vertically. Peeling off column 1 (or equivalently moving to the next diagonal cell), (2,2) is now the exposed corner of the remaining region and its horizontal option covers (2,2),(2,3), both marked, so it too is vertical; inductively every domino in the top-left region is vertical. Rotating the whole picture by 90/180/270 degrees carries the mark pattern to itself, so the bottom region is forced all-horizontal, the right region all-vertical, etc.; the four forced regions fit together into exactly one tiling. This exhibits 2n marks with a unique legal tiling, giving k <= 2n.

technique: When an alternating red/blue cycle is invariant under the reflection defining the blue matching, trace one red/blue arm from a fixed point of the reflection and use that the reverse-color arm is exactly its mirror image, forcing the cycle to return to the fixed-point set after one mirrored pair.
how_used: Each cell c on the diagonal d is fixed by the reflection, so its red partner and blue partner are mirror images of each other and hence distinct; thus c lies on a cycle of length >= 4. Walk the cycle c = c_0, c_1, ..., c_m taking m minimal with c_m on d (c_m != c). The construction (blue = reflection of red) makes the mirror image of this path also a path of the graph, and the two arms together close up into the whole cycle C(c). Hence each such cycle contains EXACTLY two cells of d, so the 2n diagonal cells lie on exactly n cycles, each of length >= 4.

technique: Double-count a chosen letter over a restricted family of lines by summing the incidence count two ways: once line-by-line, and once cell-by-cell with each cell weighted by how many family-lines pass through it.
how_used: Set n=3k, tile the table into k×k blocks of 3×3, mark each block-center as a 'vital' cell, and call any row/column/diagonal through a vital cell a 'vital line'. Count pairs N = #{(vital line, M-cell on it)}. Every vital line has length a multiple of 3, so it holds (length/3) copies of M; and cell-by-cell each entry lies on exactly 1 or 4 vital lines (the '4' cells being exactly the vital centers). This sets up the two totals to be equated by the later steps.

technique: Sum the equal-letter count over all diagonals of one direction using the triangular profile of how many marked cells each successive diagonal contains.
how_used: For vital diagonals in one direction, the number of vital centers per diagonal runs 1,2,…,k−1,k,k−1,…,2,1; each vital diagonal contributes one M per vital center it meets, so one diagonal direction yields 1+2+⋯+k+⋯+1 = k² copies of M, and the other diagonal direction gives k² likewise. Each vital row and each vital column (k of each, length 3k) holds k copies of M, contributing k² per family. Summing the four families gives N = 4k².

technique: Force a divisibility condition by equating the two double-count totals modulo the per-cell multiplicity, exploiting that every occurring multiplicity is congruent mod that modulus.
how_used: Each cell lies on 1 or 4 vital lines and 1≡4≡1 (mod 3), so the cell-side total N is ≡ (number of M-cells) = 3k² ≡ 0 (mod 3). Equating with the line-side N = 4k² gives 4k² ≡ 0 (mod 3), hence k² ≡ 0 (mod 3), so 3 | k and 9 | n.

technique: To show some diagonal/transversal of a grid meets a count quota, average the count over all transversals using that every cell lies in equally many, then invoke the extremal principle.
how_used: In the (a+b+1)x(a+b+1) grid every cell lies in the same number ((a+b)!) of the (a+b+1)! transversals (permutation diagonals), so the mean number of amber cells over all transversals equals (#amber)/(a+b+1) >= (a^2+ab-b)/(a+b+1) = (a-1)+1/(a+b+1) > a-1. Since amber-count is integer-valued, some transversal T_a attains at least a amber cells; symmetrically, from #bronze >= b^2+ab-a some transversal T_b attains at least b bronze cells (equivalently at most a+1 amber). This yields the two anchor transversals but does NOT yet give one transversal meeting both quotas.

technique: To interpolate between two transversals/permutation-diagonals of a grid, connect them by single moves each of which reassigns two rows' columns by swapping two chosen cells for the opposite corners of the rectangle they span (a single transposition of the underlying permutation).
how_used: T_a is turned into T_b by a sequence of moves, each move choosing two cells c=(r1,c1), c'=(r2,c2) of the current transversal and replacing them with the rectangle's other two corners (r1,c2),(r2,c1); this stays a transversal and equals composing with one transposition, and transpositions generate the symmetric group so a connecting path always exists. A single move replaces two cells by two others, so the amber count changes by AT MOST 2 per move (do NOT try to force a unit step; a change of 2 is fine and is what crux 2 exploits).

technique: When a step-bounded integer quantity starts at/above and ends at/below a TARGET INTERVAL whose width is at least the per-step bound, apply the discrete intermediate value theorem: the process cannot skip the interval, so some state lands inside it.
how_used: The goal is a transversal with amber-count in {a, a+1} (amber >= a gives a amber cells; amber <= a+1 means bronze >= b, and dropping one surplus cell yields exactly a amber and b bronze with no two sharing a row/column since a+b < a+b+1). Along the swap sequence from T_a to T_b, amber changes by at most 2 per move; T_a has amber >= a and T_b has amber <= a+1, so consider the first move after which amber <= a+1 -- the previous value was >= a+2, and a drop of at most 2 forces the new value to be >= a, hence in {a, a+1}. The interval {a, a+1} has width 2, matching the step bound 2, so it cannot be jumped over.

technique: Encode each element by which subset of the k functions is nonzero on it, cap the number of distinct nonzero patterns at 2^k-1, and pigeonhole two elements into the same pattern to force a monotonicity contradiction.
how_used: Choose the adversarial input x_n = -n (strictly decreasing) for n=1..N. Since each column sum x_n != 0, the support S(n)={i : f_i(n)!=0} is a nonempty subset of {1,...,k}, giving at most 2^k-1 patterns. If 2^k-1 <= N-1 (i.e. 2^k-1 < N), two indices n<n' share S(n)=S(n'); on every i in the common support both values are nonzero so the essentially-increasing condition forces f_i(n) <= f_i(n'), summing to x_n <= x_{n'}, i.e. -n <= -n', contradicting n<n'. Hence 2^k-1 >= N, giving k >= floor(log2 N)+1 = 11 for N=2022.

technique: To hit the extremal count of a construction, build it by a middle-pivot recursion: split the index block around one element handled alone by a fresh object, and hand each half-block to the previously-built objects, so the recurrence T(k)=2T(k-1)+1 forces the exact extremal size.
how_used: To realize N = 2^k - 1 rows with k essentially-increasing functions, order the rows 1..N and recurse: the newest function f_k is the one used to correct the top block, with a single 'leaf' row (index 2^k-1) it covers alone, while the two half-blocks of length 2^{k-1}-1 are each decomposed independently by the previous k-1 functions. This gives T(k)=2T(k-1)+1, T(1)=1, so T(k)=2^k-1, matching the pigeonhole threshold. The k=4 table exhibits the binary structure: rows 1,3,7,15 (= 2^i-1) are single-function leaf rows, and f_4 is active only on the top block rows 8..15. For N=2022 <= 2^11-1 this yields k<=11.

technique: For a lower bound on how many monotone summands a decomposition needs, tag each index with its support set (which summands are nonzero there), force a repeated support by pigeonhole on the nonempty subsets of the k-set, then derive a contradiction from the monotone constraint applied to the two indices sharing that support.
how_used: Test with the strictly decreasing input x_n = -n for n = 1..N. For each row n let S(n) = {i : f_i(n) != 0}, a nonempty subset of {1,...,k} (nonempty since the summands total x_n != 0). There are only 2^k - 1 nonempty subsets, so if 2^k - 1 < N pigeonhole gives two rows n < n' with S(n) = S(n'). Every function active on both is essentially increasing and nonzero at both, so f_i(n) <= f_i(n'); summing over the shared support gives x_n <= x_{n'}, i.e. -n <= -n', contradicting n < n'. Hence 2^k - 1 >= N, so k >= floor(log2 N)+1 = 11 for N = 2022.

technique: To force a monotone additive decomposition to hit arbitrary prescribed row-targets, reserve on each row one summand as a free corrector and freeze every other active summand to a fixed dominant value; set the corrector to target minus the frozen sum, so the dominant frozen values (not the bounded targets) dictate each summand's order along its support.
how_used: For N = 2^k - 1 give each row n a distinct nonempty support S(n) subset of {1,...,k}. On row n every active index except the largest gets a fixed 'backbone' value equal to an increasing power of a base B (B chosen after seeing the x_n, B > max|x_n|), and the largest active index i* = max S(n) is the corrector: f_{i*}(n) = x_n - (backbone sum on row n), so the row total is exactly x_n. Backbone functions take increasing B-powers hence are increasing; a corrector's values are dominated by -(the B-power it offsets), which beats all |x_n|, so the corrector inherits a monotone order across its support. In the k=4, B=10 table f_2 corrects rows 2,3 as -9,4; f_3 corrects rows 4-7 as -299,-195,-91,2; f_4 corrects rows 8-15 as -6994,...,-993,9 -- each increasing. Thus k functions suffice whenever N <= 2^k - 1, so k = 11 handles N = 2022.

technique: To lower-bound how many essentially-increasing summands a decomposition needs, test it against a strictly DECREASING target sequence and track, for each index, its nonempty support set (the rows where it is nonzero); a pigeonhole on the finitely many possible supports pairs two rows, and the essentially-increasing hypothesis on their common support contradicts the decreasing targets.
how_used: Suppose k functions f_1..f_k work for all N-tuples. Feed the adversarial strictly decreasing sequence x_n = -n for n=1..N. For each row n set S(n) = { i : f_i(n) != 0 }; since sum_i f_i(n) = -n != 0, each S(n) is a nonempty subset of {1,...,k}, of which there are 2^k - 1. If 2^k - 1 < N there are more rows than available supports, so by pigeonhole S(n) = S(n') for some n < n'. On that common support every f_i is nonzero at both n and n', so the essentially-increasing condition gives f_i(n) <= f_i(n') for each such i; summing over i in S(n) yields x_n <= x_{n'}. But x_n = -n > -n' = x_{n'}, contradiction. Hence 2^k - 1 >= N is forced, i.e. 2^k >= N+1, giving k >= floor(log2 N) + 1 = 11 for N = 2022.

technique: To realize the extremal case of a support-counting bound, index the objects by the distinct nonempty support patterns themselves and enforce the required monotonicity by scaling each coordinate with widely separated magnitudes (large powers of a common base), so that within any single coordinate the nonzero entries automatically appear in increasing order regardless of the target values.
how_used: Match the lower bound by constructing, for N = 2^k - 1, k essentially-increasing functions summing to ANY given x_1,...,x_N. Assign to each index n one of the 2^k - 1 distinct nonempty subsets S(n) of {1,...,k} as its support (so support determines n and vice versa), ordered so that supports refine down a recursive binary splitting. Build the entries as sums/differences of large powers of a base B: give each function f_i, on the indices where it is active, values dominated by a huge positive B-power term plus lower-order corrections, chosen so the algebraic sum across the support of index n equals x_n exactly, while the dominant B-power makes each individual f_i strictly increasing across the (ordered) indices in its own support -- so f_i is essentially increasing on {n : f_i(n) != 0}. For k=4, N=15 this is the explicit table (powers of 10 as B): e.g. f_1 active on odd-support indices with entries 3,10,100,1000,...; the highest function f_4 carries one giant negative correction -6994 etc. so each row sums to its x_n while every column, restricted to its nonzero cells, is monotone. Since B can be taken arbitrarily large, the dominant terms swamp the bounded corrections and monotonicity within each column always holds; this proves k = 2^k - 1 supports suffice, so k = floor(log2 N)+1 is achievable, pinning the answer to 11.

technique: Build the extremal starting configuration from many copies of the smallest closable gadget all sharing one common core, so each gadget closes independently and the shared core then cascades the closures together.
how_used: For even n, take a single edge ab and hang n/2-1 copies of C4 that all reuse ab as an edge (each copy adds 2 new vertices and 3 new edges); each C4 completes to a K4, then the two shared vertices a,b are joined to every other vertex, cascading to K_n; odd n adds one extra vertex joined to a,b. Edge count is exactly 1+3(n/2-1)=3n/2-2, matching the target.

technique: To lower-bound the initial size of a graph closure process, run a canonical greedy version of the operation (tracking a clique cover plus an edge-to-clique label map) until it gets stuck; then any graph that can reach the full object must have this canonical run terminate at the full object, giving a well-defined merge sequence to induct over.
how_used: Maintain a clique cover C (initially one K2 per edge) and a label map L: E->C. Each step picks a C4=abcd whose four edges do not all share one label, adds the two diagonals, completes the union V of the involved 2-4 cliques to a clique on V, and merges those cliques into a single clique K_V (relabeling their edges and the new edges to K_V). Stop when every C4 is single-labeled. If G was ever completable to K_n, this run must end with C={K_n}, providing the canonical target and merge sequence.

technique: Assign each clique of the cover a potential counting only ORIGINAL edges it carries, and prove a linear lower bound on this potential in terms of clique size by induction over the merges, charging the vertex overlap forced by the operation against the additive slack.
how_used: Define theta(K) = number of original edges of G labeled by clique K, so theta is exactly additive under merges. Prove theta(K) >= 3|K|/2 - 2 by induction: a C4-merge of m cliques (2<=m<=4) forces at least m of the four cycle-vertices a,b,c,d to be shared, so |K| <= (sum of sizes) - m; then theta(K) = sum theta(K_i) >= 3/2(sum sizes) - 2m >= 3/2(|K|+m) - 2m = 3|K|/2 - m/2 >= 3|K|/2 - 2 for m<=4 (equality at m=4). At termination C={K_n}, so #original edges = theta(K_n) >= 3n/2 - 2.

technique: Bound each nonlinear term below by the line tangent at the equality point, choosing the tangent so it also passes through the value at the boundary equality point, then verify the bound by factoring the difference.
how_used: Replaced 1/(b^3+4) by the linear underestimate 1/4 - b/12, the tangent at b=2 forced to also pass through (0,1/4); verified via 12-(3-b)(b^3+4)=b(b+1)(b-2)^2 >= 0, so the bound holds for all nonnegative b.

technique: Group a cyclic sum of products into a single product of two paired sums, then bound that product by AM-GM against the fixed total.
how_used: After the tangent bound the residual cross term is ab+bc+cd+da=(a+c)(b+d); since (a+c)+(b+d)=4, AM-GM gives (a+c)(b+d) <= ((4)/2)^2=4, pinning the whole expression at (a+b+c+d)/4 - (ab+bc+cd+da)/12 >= 1 - 1/3 = 2/3.

technique: Solve a two-term recurrence in closed form as a sum over index-subsets, encoding the recurrence's 'take or skip the last term' branching as a forbidden-adjacency (no two chosen indices consecutive) constraint on the subsets.
how_used: Prove by induction that $u_k=\sum a_{i_1}\cdots a_{i_t}$ over all $0<i_1<\dots<i_t<k$ with $i_{j+1}-i_j\geq 2$; the recurrence $u_{k+1}=u_k+a_k u_{k-1}$ splits the subsets of range $<k+1$ into those omitting $k$ (giving $u_k$) and those containing $k$ (giving $a_k\cdot u_{k-1}$, forcing $k-1$ excluded).

technique: Exhibit the reversal symmetry of the target quantity by reindexing the closed-form sum under $i\mapsto n-i$, showing the set of admissible index-tuples is invariant and the summand is unchanged.
how_used: Applying the closed form to $b_k=a_{n-k}$ gives $v_k$ as a sum over decreasing tuples $n>i_1>\dots>i_t>n-k$ with gaps $\geq 2$; at $k=n$ this reindexed sum is term-for-term identical to the sum for $u_n$, yielding $u_n=v_n$.

technique: Encode a scalar recurrence as a product of $2\times2$ transfer matrices chosen so that reversing the coefficient order corresponds to transposing the whole product, making a scalar entry manifestly reversal-invariant.
how_used: Write $\binom{u_{k+1}}{u_{k+1}-u_k}=A_k\binom{u_k}{u_k-u_{k-1}}$ with $A_k=\begin{psmallmatrix}1+a_k&-a_k\\a_k&-a_k\end{psmallmatrix}$, so $u_n=(1\;0)A_{n-1}\cdots A_1\binom{1}{0}$ while the $v$ side is the row-vector transpose $(1\;0)A_{n-1}\cdots A_1$ acting the same way; the $1\times1$ product equals its transpose, so $u_n=v_n$.

technique: Sort a finite family of quantities and dichotomize on consecutive ratios: either some adjacent pair is within the target factor (giving the near-equal ratio directly), or every consecutive ratio exceeds the threshold.
how_used: List all m=C(2000,2) pairwise distances as D_1<=...<=D_m. If some D_{i+1}/D_i < 1+10^{-5}, that adjacent pair already gives 0 <= D_{i+1}/D_i - 1 < 10^{-5}, so |ratio-1| < 10^{-5}; otherwise assume every consecutive ratio D_{i+1}/D_i >= 1+10^{-5}.

technique: Telescope the ratio of extremes as a product of consecutive ratios each bounded below, then blow the extreme up using the (1+1/n)^n >= 2 exponential lower bound.
how_used: Write D_m/D_1 = prod (D_{i+1}/D_i) >= (1+10^{-5})^{m-1}; with m-1 > 19*10^5 and (1+10^{-5})^{10^5} >= 2, get D_m = v-u >= 2^{19} > 2*10^5, so the diameter of the set exceeds 2*10^5 times the minimal gap (normalized D_1 = 1).

technique: Nest the smallest gap inside a much larger difference to a shared far endpoint, so two overlapping differences have ratio automatically within the tolerance.
how_used: With minimal gap y-x=1 and diameter forcing |x-z|>10^5 for some z in {u,v}, form (z-y)/(z-x) or (y-z)/(x-z): the two pairs share endpoint z, differ in the other coordinate (so a!=c or b!=d), and the ratio deviates from 1 by exactly 1/|x-z| < 10^{-5}.

technique: Amplify a lossy additive bound f(x) > x - c by feeding a power of the argument through the same bound and taking the n-th root, so the constant error becomes negligible as n grows
how_used: Having only f(x) > x-1 for x>1 (from f(x) >= f(floor x) >= floor x > x-1), apply the submultiplicative iterate f(x)^n >= f(x^n) > x^n - 1, giving f(x) >= (x^n - 1)^{1/n}; since (x^n-1)^{1/n} -> x from below, this upgrades to the sharp f(x) >= x for all x>1

technique: Convert a one-sided bound into equality by sandwiching against a known exact value at a large point, splitting that point additively and letting the superadditive inequality force each summand to be tight
how_used: From f(a)=a and submultiplicativity a^n = f(a)^n >= f(a^n) >= a^n one gets f(a^n)=a^n exactly; then for any x>1 pick n with a^n - x > 1 and use superadditivity a^n = f(a^n) >= f(x) + f(a^n - x) >= x + (a^n - x) = a^n, forcing f(x)=x

technique: Bound a sum of monotone terms by double-counting: pair each below-threshold index with the count of above-threshold indices whose value exceeds a shifted level, and bound that count using the nested-value constraint.
how_used: Given a_1 <= n (from the auxiliary bound), pick t with a_1 <= ... <= a_t <= n < a_{t+1} <= ... <= a_n. For each i let b_i = #{j in {t+1,...,n}: a_j >= n+i}; double-counting rewrites sum_{j>t}(a_j - n) = sum_i b_i. The key inequality is a_i + b_i <= n for i <= t: since a_{a_i} <= n+i-1 and a_i <= n, every j with a_j >= n+i has a_j > a_{a_i}, forcing j into {a_i+1,...,n}, so b_i <= n-a_i. Combined with b_i = 0 for i > t, summing a_i + b_i <= n over all i gives total <= n^2.

technique: Turn a sum bound into an area/disjointness count by reflecting a staircase region across the diagonal and translating it a fixed distance, then proving the original and reflected shapes never overlap inside a target square.
how_used: Shade the bottom a_i cells of column i (dark); reflect across x=y and shift n units left to shade the leftmost a_j cells of row j (light). Dark cells in the n x n square S at origin count sum min(a_i,n) and light cells count sum max(a_i-n,0), together sum a_i. No cell of S is both dark and light: for the top dark-and-light cell in column i, if a_i <= n it is (i,a_i), the (n+i)-th cell of row a_i, but only a_{a_i} < n+i cells are light there; if a_i >= n+1 it is (i,n), the (n+i)-th cell of row n with only a_n <= a_1+n light cells, forcing i <= a_1 hence a_i <= a_{a_1} <= n, a contradiction. Disjointness inside S gives sum a_i <= n^2.

technique: Bound each term of a monotone periodic sequence by taking a minimal-index counterexample and using a nested-value constraint plus periodicity to forbid a whole residue window, forcing the offending term to jump up by a full period.
