how_used: As an auxiliary bound (NOT the finisher): to prove a_i <= n+i-1 for all i, take the smallest i with a_i >= n+i; monotonicity a_n >= ... >= a_i >= n+i together with a_{a_i} <= n+i-1 and periodicity forbid a_i from being congruent to i, i+1, ..., n mod n, so a_i >= 2n+1; then a_1+n >= a_n >= a_i gives a_1 >= n+1, and minimality forces i=1, a contradiction. The ONLY consequence used downstream is the corollary a_1 <= n (equivalently a_{a_1} <= n), which the finishing argument needs; this lemma does not by itself give the sum bound.

technique: To bound a sum whose terms split at a threshold into 'small' and 'large' parts, count the large excess by level: for each level count how many terms exceed it, and pair that per-level count against a matching small term so the two cancel to a fixed constant.
how_used: This is the FINISHER; it takes a_1 <= n as input (supplied by the first-claim crux). If a_n <= n the bound is trivial; else pick t in [1,n-1] with a_1<=...<=a_t<=n<a_{t+1}<=...<=a_n. From a_1<=n and a_{a_1}<=n get a_1<=t, hence a_n<=n+t. For each i>=1 let b_i = #{ j in {t+1,...,n} : a_j >= n+i } (so b_1>=b_2>=...>=b_t>=b_{t+1}=0). Key per-level bound: a_i + b_i <= n for 1<=i<=t, because n+i-1 >= a_{a_i} with a_i<=n forces every j with a_j >= n+i to satisfy a_j > a_{a_i}, so j in {a_i+1,...,n}, giving b_i <= n - a_i. Then the large terms satisfy a_{t+1}+...+a_n <= n(n-t) + (b_1+...+b_t) (each large term = n + its excess, and summing excesses over levels equals sum of b_i); adding a_1+...+a_t and using a_i + b_i <= n yields a_1+...+a_n <= n(n-t) + nt = n^2.

technique: To prove a self-referential index bound of the form a_i <= n+i-1 for a periodically-extended sequence, take a minimal counterexample and use periodicity to convert the constraint on the composed index a_{a_i} into a modular exclusion on the value a_i: rule out an entire residue block mod n so the value is forced to jump into the next period, then collapse via minimality.
how_used: Establishes the first claim a_i <= n+i-1 (in particular a_1 <= n), which the finisher crux then builds on. Assume i is the smallest counterexample, so a_i >= n+i while a_{a_i} <= n+i-1. Since a_i <= a_{i+1} <= ... <= a_n are all >= n+i and a_{a_i} <= n+i-1, periodicity a_{n+k}=a_k forces that a_i cannot be congruent to i, i+1, ..., n mod n (each such residue r would give a_{a_i}=a_r >= a_i >= n+i, contradicting a_{a_i} <= n+i-1). Hence the residue lies in {1,...,i-1} and a_i >= 2n+1. Then a_1 + n >= a_n >= a_i >= 2n+1 gives a_1 >= n+1, so a_1 itself violates the bound; minimality forces i=1, but the i=1 case (a_1 >= n+1 with a_{a_1} <= n) is directly contradictory. This yields a_i <= n+i-1 for all i, in particular a_1 <= n.

technique: To turn a per-index constraint on a composed index into a global sum bound, split the indices at the threshold where the values cross n, then define a counting function on the over-threshold block measuring how many large values exceed each level, and prove a pointwise 'value plus count <= n' bound by reading the composed-index constraint as a range restriction on where those large values can land.
how_used: Supplies the missing finisher after the Lemma a_i <= n+i-1 (hence a_1 <= n) is known. If a_n <= n the sum is trivially <= n^2, so assume a threshold t with 1 <= t <= n-1 and a_1 <= ... <= a_t <= n < a_{t+1} <= ... <= a_n. Note a_1 <= t (since a_{a_1} <= n forces a_1 not to exceed the low block) and a_n <= n+t. For each i define b_i = #{ j in {t+1,...,n} : a_j >= n+i }, so b_1 >= b_2 >= ... >= b_t >= b_{t+1}=0. The one hard move: prove a_i + b_i <= n for 1 <= i <= t. Because a_{a_i} <= n+i-1 and a_i <= n, any j with a_j >= n+i satisfies a_j > a_{a_i}, so (by monotonicity and a_i <= n) that j must lie in {a_i+1,...,n}; hence b_i <= n - a_i. The routine finish then sums the high block a_{t+1}+...+a_n <= n(n-t) + (b_1+...+b_t) by double-counting the b_i, adds a_1+...+a_t, and uses a_i+b_i <= n to get a_1+...+a_n <= n(n-t)+nt = n^2.

technique: Compute one higher iterate of the unknown function two ways—peel the outermost application vs. apply the functional equation at a shifted argument—and equate to collapse the awkward triple composition into a clean shift-recurrence for that iterate.
how_used: From f^3(n)=f(n+1)+1 evaluate f^4(n)=f(f^3(n))=f(f(n+1)+1), and separately apply the FE at argument f(n+1) to get f^4(n+1)=f^3(f(n+1))=f(f(n+1)+1)+1; equating yields f^4(n+1)=f^4(n)+1, so by induction f^4(n)=n+c for a constant c=f^4(0), i.e. the fourth iterate is a pure translation.

technique: Once an iterate equals translation by a constant, apply the base function to that relation to show the function commutes with the constant-shift, hence permutes residue classes modulo that constant.
how_used: Apply f to f^4(n)=n+c: f(n+c)=f^5(n)=f^4(f(n))=f(n)+c, and likewise g(n+c)=g(n)+c for g=f+1. So m≡n (mod c) ⟺ f(m)≡f(n) (mod c) ⟺ g(m)≡g(n) (mod c); f and g each permute Z/cZ, and iterating, {f^k(n):n=0..c-1} and {g^k(n):n=0..c-1} are complete residue systems mod c for every k. This is the structural fact that makes the period-sum counting well-defined.

technique: Pin a translation constant by summing the per-step displacement over one full period two different ways—decomposing the same net shift into the composing steps of one map vs. another map that carries an extra fixed increment per step—and equating the two totals.
how_used: With δ(n)=f(n)-n=g(n)-n-1 and S=sum_{n=0}^{c-1} δ(n): since each of {f^k(n):n=0..c-1} is a complete residue system, the net shift of f^4 over a period, c^2=sum_{n=0}^{c-1}(f^4(n)-n), telescopes as four δ-layers = 4S; using g^2=n+c instead, c^2=sum(g^2(n)-n) telescopes as two g-layers where each g-step contributes δ+1, giving 2S+2c. Equate 4S=2S+2c with 4S=c^2 to get c^2=4c, so (c≠0) c=4.

technique: For a shrinking chain of iterate-ranges, use injectivity to make consecutive range-defect sets equinumerous, then bound one common size from above by classifying every out-of-range element by a forced preimage relation.
how_used: Let R_i=range(f^i), S_i=R_{i-1}\R_i; injectivity (forced because f(m)=f(n) makes f eventually periodic, contradicting that Z≥0\R_1 is finite via f^4(n)+1=f^4(n+1)) gives a bijection S_i→S_{i+1}, so all |S_i|=k. Classify each b in S_1∪S_2∪S_3: if b>0 and b-1=f(n) for some n>0 then f^3(n-1)=f(n)+1=b puts b∈R_3, contradiction; so the only survivors are b=0, b=f(0)+1 (the n=0 case), or b-1∈S_1. Hence 3k=|S_1∪S_2∪S_3|≤1+1+k, forcing k=1 and {a,f(a),f^2(a)}={0,a+1,f(0)+1}.

technique: Apply the base map to the whole functional equation to turn a fixed iterate into a unit-increment recurrence in n, which integrates to that iterate being a pure translation.
how_used: Apply f to (*) f^3(n)=f(n+1)+1: LHS becomes f^4(n)=f(f(n+1)+1), while writing (*) at n+1 gives f^3(n+1)=f(n+2)+1 and substituting n->f(n+1) in (*) gives f^4(n+1)=f(f(n+1)+1)+1. Comparing, f^4(n+1)=f^4(n)+1. A first-difference-equals-1 recurrence integrates to f^4(n)=n+c where c=f^4(0). Via g=f+1 one has g^2=f^4, and since g(n)>=1 one gets c=g^2(0)>=1. This translation fact is the structural input every later counting/residue argument presupposes (it also gives injectivity of f and g).

technique: Bootstrap a functional equation into a global affine identity h^N(n)=n+c by producing a one-step shift relation for a high iterate and inducting from a single base value.
how_used: Set g(n)=f(n)+1. Substituting f(n) for n in f(f(f(n)))=f(n+1)+1 gives f^4(n)=f(f(n)+1)+1=g^2(n). Applying f to the original relation and reusing that identity gives f^4(n)+1=f^4(n+1): a pure +1 shift as n increases by 1. With c:=f^4(0)=g^2(0), induction on n yields the global affine identity g^2(n)=f^4(n)=n+c for ALL n. This is the structural fact the rest of the solve rests on: it forces f (and g) injective (f(m)=f(n) gives m+c=f^4(m)=f^4(n)=n+c), and since g(n)>=1 gives c>=1. Without this step there is no constant c to pin.

technique: To pin the modulus/constant of a residue-preserving map, sum the per-point displacement delta(n)=h(n)-n over one full residue system and evaluate that total two ways using iterates of two different depths.
how_used: Take as given the affine identity f^4(n)=g^2(n)=n+c (g=f+1) and its consequence f(n+c)=f(n)+c, g(n+c)=g(n)+c, which make residues mod c preserved (m===n mod c iff f(m)===f(n) mod c) so delta(n)=f(n)-n is residue-determined and each layer {f^k(n):n<c} is a complete residue system. Let S=sum_{n=0}^{c-1} delta(n). Telescoping f^4(n)-n over one residue system four layers deep gives c^2=4S. Doing the same for g^2(n)-n two layers deep (g contributes delta+1 per step) gives c^2=2S+2c. Eliminating S: c^2=4S=2(c^2-2c), so c^2=4c, and c!=0 forces c=4. This fixes the modulus, reducing the problem to determining f on {0,1,2,3}.

technique: Compare the leading surviving coefficient of a polynomial shift-identity to constrain the degree
how_used: Write P of degree n; the two top powers cancel because the leading cubics agree, so the first surviving power x^{n+1} gives a_n(n-2m)(n-1)=0, forcing n=1 or n=2m and localizing all further work to the n=2m branch.

technique: Propagate roots of a shift-invariant relation by integer steps until each chain end is blocked by a root of a fixed factor
how_used: Plugging integer-shifted values into the equation shows: if s-1,s are roots of S and A(s)!=0 then s+1 is a root; symmetrically down through B. So a maximal consecutive run r-a,...,r+b of S-roots is forced to terminate with r-a a root of B and r+b a root of A, converting the chain into the constraint that a B-root and an A-root differ by the integer a+b.

technique: Rule out a shared root of two integer polynomials via the rational-root test, forcing one to be an integer shift of the other
how_used: r-a is a common root of B(x) and A(x+a+b), hence of their gcd in Z[x]; a proper gcd would give B a rational root, but B(±1)=m,m+2>0 forbids it, so B(x)=A(x+c) with c=a+b; expanding A(x+c)-B(x)=(3c-2m)x^2+c(3c-2m)x+c^2(c-m) forces 3c-2m=0 and c-m=0, giving m=0, a contradiction.

technique: Multiply a symmetric three-term relation by x and regroup into a first-order shift relation between two factors
how_used: Multiplying the identity by x and regrouping gives A(x)Q(x)=B(x)Q(x-1) with Q(x)=xP(x+1)-(x+1)P(x); reading roots with multiplicity yields the multiset identity {roots A} u R_Q = {roots B} u (R_Q+1), which organizes all roots into three integer chains each running from a root of B up to a root of A (so corresponding B- and A-roots differ by an integer).

technique: Count the real roots of a one-parameter cubic from the sign of its non-trivial local-extremum value
how_used: For A_a(x)=x^3+ax^2+1 the extrema are at x=0 (value 1>0) and x=-2a/3 (value 1+4a^3/27), positive for integer a>=-1 and negative for a<=-2, so A_a has three real roots iff a<=-2 and one iff a>=-1; since the chain (crux 4) forces A_m=B and A_{-m}=A to have equal real-root counts, this pins m=±1, and then the single real roots of x^3±x^2+1 lie in disjoint unit intervals so cannot differ by an integer.

technique: Subtract a scalar multiple of a known solution of a linear functional equation, chosen via an auxiliary polynomial, to plant a prescribed pair of adjacent roots in a new solution.
how_used: The FE (x^3-mx^2+1)P(x+1)+(x^3+mx^2+1)P(x-1)=2(x^3-mx+1)P(x) is LINEAR in P, and P(x)=x is a solution, so S(x)=P(x)-kx is again a solution for any constant k. Comparing x^{n+1} coefficients forces n=1 or n=2m, so a solution of degree >=2 has n=2m. Build the AUXILIARY polynomial Q(x)=xP(x+1)-(x+1)P(x): its x^{n+1} terms cancel, leaving degree n with leading coefficient (n-1)a_n (nonzero since n=2m>=2), so Q has a complex root r. At r, rP(r+1)=(r+1)P(r), so k:=P(r)/r=P(r+1)/(r+1) is well-defined (edge cases: r=0 take k=P(1); r=-1 take k=-P(-1)). Then S(x)=P(x)-kx has S(r)=S(r+1)=0, the adjacent-root seed the FE propagates into an integer-spaced chain of roots.

technique: At the two ends of a maximal integer-spaced chain of roots, read off that each endpoint is a root of a specific factor, then equate the two factors as a shifted polynomial identity and match coefficients to force a contradiction.
how_used: S(x) satisfies the FE with A(x)=x^3-mx^2+1, B(x)=x^3+mx^2+1. Evaluating the FE at x=s shows: if s-1,s are roots of S and s is not a root of A then s+1 is a root; if s,s+1 are roots and s not a root of B then s-1 is a root. So take the maximal chain r-a,...,r+b of roots of S (with r-a-1 and r+b+1 NOT roots). Maximality forces r-a to be a root of B and r+b to be a root of A, hence r-a is a root of both B(x) and A(x+a+b). Their integer-polynomial gcd C(x) can't be a proper divisor of B (that would give B a rational root, but by the rational-root theorem the only candidates are +-1, and B(1)=m+2 and B(-1)=m are both >0 because n=2m>0 forces m>0), so B(x)=A(x+c) with c=a+b>=1. Expanding A(x+c)-B(x)=(3c-2m)x^2+c(3c-2m)x+c^2(c-m)=0 forces 3c-2m=0 and c-m=0, giving m=0, contradicting m!=0. Hence deg P<=1 and P(x)=tx.

technique: Attach to each equivalence class its convex hull as an interval of consecutive integers, so that the classes covering the index set becomes intervals covering it
how_used: Under the contradiction hypothesis every ratio-value class S_lambda={k: a_k/k=lambda} has >=2 elements; replacing S_lambda by T_lambda={m_lambda,...,M_lambda} (min to max index) turns each into a run of >=2 consecutive integers, and since every index k lies in some S_lambda these T_lambda cover all of N, converting the problem into a covering-of-N-by-intervals statement

technique: Prune an interval cover to bounded overlap using the Helly-type fact that among three intervals sharing a point one lies in the union of the other two
how_used: Each integer lies in only finitely many T_lambda (finitely many possible left endpoints m_lambda below it), so wherever a point is covered >2 times, discard one T_lambda (contained in the union of two others) while keeping the cover; iterate to a subcollection {T_lambda : lambda in Lambda} still covering N but with every integer in at most two intervals, giving the factor-2 bound on the total telescoped increase

technique: Lower-bound each interval's telescoped increment by a harmonic block, so summing a bounded total increase over a cover of N yields the divergent harmonic series
how_used: On T_lambda the telescoped rise sums to a_{M_lambda}-a_{m_lambda}=(M_lambda-m_lambda)lambda; rewriting lambda=a_{m_lambda}/m_lambda>=a_1/m_lambda and using (M_lambda-m_lambda)>=(M_lambda-m_lambda+1)/2 gives 2*sum_{k in T_lambda}(a_{k+1}-a_k) >= a_1 * sum_{k in T_lambda} 1/k; since the increments telescope to at most 1 (a_k in (0,1) increasing) and overlap is <=2, the left side is <=4 while the right sums over a cover of N to a_1*sum 1/k, contradicting harmonic divergence

technique: Reindex a single covering orbit by position g(k)=f^k(start) to turn the relation into a symmetric identity in the index
how_used: With one half-infinite chain from c, g(k):=f^k(c) is a bijection Z>=0 -> N with f(g(k))=g(k+1). Writing m=g(a), n=g(b), the tower f^{f(n)}(m) applies f a total of f(n)=g(b+1) times to g(a), giving g(a+g(b+1)); symmetrically the other tower is g(b+g(a+1)). So Delta becomes delta(a,b)=g(g(b+1)+a)-g(g(a+1)+b); since g is a bijection, delta(a,b) != 0 for a != b reduces to g(b+1)+a != g(a+1)+b, i.e. injectivity of x -> g(x)-x, and boundedness becomes |delta(a,b)| <= N.

technique: Force a contradiction by making a bounded relation output a value pinned by an extremal (maximal-preimage) choice, then read off a fixed offset injectivity forbids repeating
how_used: Pick B with g(B)+N<=B (exists via the lemma that g(x)<=x-M for arbitrary M, so g(B)-B is arbitrarily negative). Let t be the largest index among preimages of the window [g(B)-N, g(B)+N]. The bound |delta(t-1, B-g(t))| = |g(B) - g(t-1+g(B+1-g(t)))| <= N puts the index t-1+g(B+1-g(t)) into that same preimage set, so maximality of t forces g(B+1-g(t))=1, hence B+1-g(t)=g^{-1}(1). Since g(t) is within N of g(B), this gives |(B-g(B)) + 1 - g^{-1}(1)| <= N for infinitely many B; but x -> g(x)-x is injective, so B-g(B) takes infinitely many distinct values, which cannot all lie in a fixed width-2N window. Contradiction.

technique: Model an iterated injective self-map by its functional (arrow) graph n -> f(n), so orbit shape replaces nested iterates
how_used: Under the bounded-Delta assumption f is injective: f(m)=f(n) makes both nested iterates in Delta(m,n) equal (same value iterated the same number of times), so Delta(m,n)=0, and the hypothesis forces m=n. With f injective, every vertex of the graph n -> f(n) has out-degree 1 and in-degree at most 1, so G is a disjoint union of chains (two-sided infinite, half-infinite) and cycles; the nested iterate f^{f(n)}(m) becomes 'walk f(n) steps forward from m along its chain', reducing Delta to a comparison of forward-walk endpoints.

technique: Cap the number of orbits by feeding one representative per orbit into the bounded quantity so their distinct outputs must fit a fixed-width window
how_used: Pick one representative m_i per chain. For a common large B apply the bound to the pair (m_i, f^{B-f(m_i)}(1)): the second nested iterate collapses to f^B(1) (i-independent), so |Delta(m_i, f^{B-f(m_i)}(1))| <= N becomes |f^{f(x_i)}(m_i) - f^B(1)| <= N with x_i = f^{B-f(m_i)}(1). Every representative's iterate value lies in the width-2N window [f^B(1)-N, f^B(1)+N]. Because the m_i lie in different chains and forward-walks preserve chains (injectivity), those values are pairwise distinct integers; at most 2N+1 fit the window, capping the number of chains at 2N+1.

technique: Upgrade a finite-orbit bound to a single cofinite orbit by counting how many index-window outputs each length-(B-A) window can miss
how_used: With finitely many chains, n -> f^{f(c)}(n) has cofinite image, hitting all integers >= M. For B>A>=M, whenever f^{f(c)}(n) in [A,B] the bound puts f^{f(n)}(c) in [A-N,B+N], and distinct n give distinct outputs (graph structure), so >= B-A+1 'good' values fill [A-N,B+N], leaving <= 2N 'bad' values; letting B grow, only <= 2N bad values exceed A-N in total. Hence all but finitely many integers lie on one half-infinite chain from a start c, so every integer is f^k(c) (k>=0). Setting g(k):=f^k(c) gives a bijection Z>=0 -> N, and Delta reformulates as delta(a,b)=g(g(b+1)+a)-g(g(a+1)+b); Delta!=0 on distinct arguments becomes g(a+1)-a != g(b+1)-b, i.e. g(x)-x is injective.

technique: Force the displacement of a diagonal-anchored bijection to be unbounded below via a prefix-image counting argument against surjectivity.
how_used: For the bijection g: Z>=0 -> N with displacement d(x)=g(x)-x injective, prove the Lemma: for every M there is x with g(x) <= x - M (g dips arbitrarily far below the diagonal). Suppose d(x) >= -M for all x. Since g is onto the positive integers, the values {1,...,V} have V distinct preimages, and d(x) >= -M forces the preimage of value v to be <= v+M, crowding all V preimages into the indices {0,...,V+M-1}; the V displacements are distinct and confined, so surjectivity onto an initial segment cannot be sustained past a bounded point. Hence d is unbounded below, giving infinitely many B with g(B)+N <= B (and independently g(B) > N) -- the raw material B-g(B) -> +infinity for the terminal contradiction.

technique: Pin an iterate to a boundary/extreme value by choosing the maximal preimage inside a bounded output window, so the bound cannot push it out except by hitting the extreme value.
how_used: Given B with g(B)+N <= B and g(B) > N (from the Lemma), set t = max of the preimages g^{-1}(g(B)-N), ..., g^{-1}(g(B)+N). The transferred bound |delta(t-1, B-g(t))| = |g(B) - g(t-1+g(B+1-g(t)))| <= N forces t-1+g(B+1-g(t)) back into that same window of preimages; by maximality of t this can only hold if g(B+1-g(t))=1, i.e. B+1-g(t)=g^{-1}(1). Since |g(t)-g(B)| <= N, this yields |(B-g(B))+1-g^{-1}(1)| <= N. Because B-g(B) takes infinitely many distinct values (Lemma) and g(x)-x is injective, infinitely many distinct integers are trapped in a fixed width-2N window -- impossible, the contradiction that finishes the proof.

technique: To rule out a periodic component of an injective map's functional graph under a boundedness constraint, use that the deep iterate over a finite cycle is confined to a bounded set, so the boundedness constraint traps its paired term in a bounded set across infinitely many inputs, then pigeonhole that paired term against the injectivity of a single fixed iterate.
how_used: Assume for contradiction |Delta(m,n)| <= N for all m,n and let G be the arrow graph (edges n->f(n)); injectivity of f makes G a disjoint union of chains and cycles. To kill a length-L cycle C, pick m on C. For every n, the on-cycle term f^{f(n)}(m) equals f^{(f(n) mod L)}(m) and so lies in the finite set C, i.e. it is bounded by max(C) independent of n. Then from |Delta(m,n)| = |f^{f(n)}(m) - f^{f(m)}(n)| <= N, the partner term f^{f(m)}(n) lies in [1, max(C)+N] for EVERY n in N. But f(m) is a fixed exponent, so n |-> f^{f(m)}(n) is a single fixed iterate of f, hence injective; an injective map cannot send the infinitely many inputs n into the finite set [1, max(C)+N]. Pigeonhole gives n1 != n2 with f^{f(m)}(n1) = f^{f(m)}(n2), contradicting injectivity. So G has no cycles. NOTE: the contradiction is with INJECTIVITY of the fixed iterate (driven by the |Delta|<=N boundedness hypothesis), NOT with the 'Delta != 0 on distinct arguments' hypothesis; do not try to manufacture distinct a,b with Delta(a,b)=0 -- equal nonzero Delta values are allowed and confinement never forces a numeric zero. The lever is boundedness + fixed-iterate injectivity, not position-matching among cycle points.

technique: To bound the number of connected components (chains) of an injective map's graph under the same boundedness constraint, plug one component representative per component into the bounded difference against a common reference point routed through a fixed target, so each component contributes a distinct value into a fixed-width window, and count.
how_used: After cycles are eliminated, G is a disjoint union of chains and we want to show there are at most 2N+1 of them. Fix the reference value 1 and a large exponent B. For a representative m_i of the i-th chain, evaluate Delta(m_i, f^{B - f(m_i)}(1)): one branch becomes f^{f(x)}(m_i) with x = f^{B-f(m_i)}(1) chosen so the OTHER branch is exactly f^B(1), a single value independent of i. So |Delta| <= N forces f^{...}(m_i), a point ON the i-th chain, to lie within N of the fixed number f^B(1). Because the m_i sit in DIFFERENT chains, these chain-points are all distinct integers, yet they are all crammed into the length-2N window [f^B(1)-N, f^B(1)+N]; distinctness plus the window width caps the number of chains at 2N+1. The move is: force one distinct representative per component into a common bounded window and count the window's capacity.

technique: After collapsing an injective graph to a single half-infinite chain, transport the whole problem onto the chain's index coordinate via the bijection sending index k to the k-th iterate of the chain root, turning the functional equation into a scalar identity in the reindexing function and reading the non-vanishing hypothesis as injectivity of that function minus the identity.
how_used: Once G is shown to be exactly one half-infinite chain with root c, every natural number is uniquely f^k(c) for k>=0, so g(k):=f^k(c) is a bijection Z_{>=0} -> N. Rewrite Delta in these coordinates: with m=f^a(c), n=f^b(c), one gets delta(a,b):=Delta(f^a(c),f^b(c)) = g(g(b+1)+a) - g(g(a+1)+b). The hypotheses become |delta(a,b)| <= N for all a,b and delta(a,b)!=0 for a!=b; the latter unpacks to g(a+1)-a != g(b+1)-b for a!=b, i.e. the map x |-> g(x)-x is INJECTIVE for x>=1. This scalar reformulation (bounded delta plus injectivity of g(x)-x) is the object the endgame descent runs on. The move is the coordinate change to the chain index plus reading off the g(x)-x injectivity invariant; it does NOT yet derive a contradiction.

technique: To finish a bounded scalar functional equation on a bijection whose displacement is injective, first show the displacement must drop arbitrarily far below the identity, then run a maximality/extremal-index argument that pins a preimage exactly, forcing infinitely many displacement values into a fixed window and contradicting the displacement's injectivity.
how_used: Working with g and delta(a,b)=g(g(b+1)+a)-g(g(a+1)+b), bounded by N, and g(x)-x injective. Lemma: for every M there is x with g(x) <= x - M (the displacement g(x)-x is unbounded below); otherwise g(x)-x bounded below plus injectivity would let g not be surjective, contradicting g being a bijection. Pick B with g(B)+N <= B and g(B)>N (infinitely many, by the Lemma). Let t = max over j in [-N,N] of g^{-1}(g(B)+j), the largest preimage of the 2N+1 values near g(B). Compute delta(t-1, B-g(t)) = g(B) - g(t-1+g(B+1-g(t))), which is <= N in absolute value, so t-1+g(B+1-g(t)) is itself a preimage of some value in [g(B)-N, g(B)+N]; by maximality of t this forces g(B+1-g(t))=1, i.e. B+1-g(t)=g^{-1}(1). Since |g(t)-g(B)|<=N, this yields |(B-g(B)) + 1 - g^{-1}(1)| <= N. Holding for infinitely many B, and hence (by injectivity of g(x)-x) infinitely many distinct values of B-g(B), all trapped in a fixed 2N-wide window -- contradiction. The move is the extremal-preimage pin that converts the bound into a fixed-window trap on the injective displacement.

technique: Sum over all indices a term-wise nonnegative product formed from the extreme values, turning a min/max constraint into one global inequality
how_used: Since a=min and b=max, each factor (r_i-a)>=0 and (b-r_i)>=0, so sum over all i of (r_i-a)(b-r_i) >= 0; this single global inequality carries all 2019 terms at once.

technique: Expand the product sum and substitute the given power-sum values to collapse it to a linear relation in the target quantity
how_used: Expanding gives sum(-r_i^2 + (a+b)r_i - ab) = -(sum r_i^2) + (a+b)(sum r_i) - 2019 ab; plugging in sum r_i=0 and sum r_i^2=1 yields -1 - 2019 ab >= 0, i.e. ab <= -1/2019.

technique: Reduce to the minimal instance by passing to just enough roots to make the hypothesis bite on maximal-degree divisors
how_used: The divisibility hypothesis applies to any degree-(k+1) factor; assuming for contradiction all roots real/distinct, pick any k+1 of the roots and work with that sub-product, so WLOG n=k+1. Then the divisors of interest are exactly the n polynomials P_i=P/(x+r_i), each of degree n-1=k.

technique: Pigeonhole on the position of a forced vanishing coefficient across many sibling factors
how_used: Each P_i=P/(x+r_i) has nonzero leading and constant coefficient (P(0)!=0, r_i!=0), so its forced zero coefficient sits in one of only n-2 interior positions; with n siblings and n-2 slots, two siblings P_a,P_b have their zero coefficient at the SAME interior position x^t.

technique: Factor two siblings through a common core and equate a matched coefficient at two distinct linear factors to kill two consecutive core coefficients
how_used: With Q=P/((x+r_a)(x+r_b)) so P_a=(x+r_b)Q, P_b=(x+r_a)Q, the x^t coefficient of (x+r)Q is b_{t-1}+r*b_t; setting it to 0 for the two distinct nonzero r_a,r_b forces b_t=b_{t-1}=0, i.e. Q has two consecutive zero coefficients.

technique: Turn two consecutive zero coefficients into a forced double root under repeated differentiation, contradicting Rolle-preserved distinctness of an all-real-rooted polynomial
how_used: Consecutive zeros b_{t-1}=b_t=0 of Q mean its (t-1)-th derivative has both constant and linear term zero, a double root at 0; but if all roots of Q were real and distinct, Rolle forces every derivative to keep all its roots real and (by degree count) distinct, so no derivative can have a double root -- contradiction, so P has a nonreal root.

technique: Rewrite each summand as a square over a chosen denominator so the Cauchy-Schwarz (Titu) bound produces the target squared-sum in the numerator
how_used: Write the LHS term (k+1)/k^3 = (1/k^2)^2 / (1/(k(k+1))); Titu then gives sum >= (sum 1/k^2)^2 / (sum 1/(k(k+1))), whose numerator is exactly the (sum 1/k^2)^2 that appears on the RHS

technique: Engineer the Titu denominator to be a partial-fraction quantity that telescopes, then bound its telescoped closed form to match the target coefficient
how_used: The chosen denominators 1/(k(k+1)) = 1/k - 1/(k+1) telescope to 1/m - 1/(n+1) < 1/m; dividing (sum 1/k^2)^2 by a quantity strictly less than 1/m yields >= m*(sum 1/k^2)^2, the target

technique: Show the unknowns are roots of a polynomial with real coefficients, then invoke the reality dichotomy: a real-coefficient polynomial's non-real roots come in conjugate pairs, so it has a real root or a conjugate pair — each of which contradicts a forbidden property of the unknowns
how_used: Once the elementary symmetric functions e1=a+b+c and e2=ab+bc+ca (with abc=1) are certified real, a,b,c are the roots of x^3-e1 x^2+e2 x-1 (real coefficients): the guaranteed real root makes some a,b,c real (banned). In the sibling case where e1,e2 are conjugates, the conjugate-reversed cubic x^3-e2bar x^2+e1bar x-1 has roots 1/abar,1/bbar,1/cbar and coincides with the original, so the multiset {a,b,c} is invariant under inversion x->1/x, forcing one root of modulus 1 (also banned). Either way the assumed reality is impossible.

technique: Pair an asymmetric quantity with its reverse-orientation twin and use their sum and product as the coefficients of a quadratic, converting reality of the target into one polynomial identity among the elementary symmetric functions
how_used: Introduce the reversed twin q'=b/a+c/b+a/c. Then q+q'=f-3 and qq'=p^3-(3p+6)f+9 where f=e1 e2 and p=e1+e2 (all verified). So q,q' are the roots of t^2-(f-3)t+(p^3-(3p+6)f+9); substituting t=q and regrouping by f gives (3p+q+6)f=p^3+q^2+3q+9. With p,q real and f non-real (certified by the real-coefficient-cubic dichotomy applied to whether f=e1e2 real), the real multiplier must vanish: 3p+q+6=0 and p^3+q^2+3q+9=0, whence (p+3)^3=0 and (p,q)=(-3,3).

technique: Re-express asymmetric ratio data by introducing new variables whose cyclic ratios are the original unknowns, turning ratio sums into symmetric-function fractions of the new variables
how_used: Set x,y,z (up to scale) so that a=y/x, b=z/y, c=x/z (consistent since abc=1). Then p becomes the sum of all six ratios = (x+y+z)(xy+yz+zx)/xyz - 3, and q=a/b+b/c+c/a becomes (x^3+y^3+z^3)/xyz. This ratio substitution is what exposes the symmetric structure that the next move collapses; without it the given p,q look irreducibly asymmetric.

technique: Form a rational combination of the two given real quantities engineered so all cross-terms cancel into a single perfect symmetric block, whose reality is then read off directly
how_used: After the ratio substitution, p+3=(x+y+z)(xy+yz+zx)/xyz and q-3=(x+y+z)(x^2+y^2+z^2-xy-yz-zx)/xyz. The combination 3(p+3)+(q-3) makes the second factor become x^2+y^2+z^2+2(xy+yz+zx)=(x+y+z)^2, collapsing everything to (x+y+z)^3/xyz. Scaling x,y,z so x+y+z is real (nonzero case; the x+y+z=0 case directly gives p=-3,q=3), xyz becomes real, and since p+3 is real this forces xy+yz+zx real — certifying that x,y,z satisfy a real-coefficient cubic, whose real-root dichotomy the hypotheses then bar.

technique: Reinterpret a weighted-average functional inequality as a supporting-line (supergradient) bound: rewrite so the secant slope of the outer interval becomes the slope of a line touching the graph at an interior anchor point.
how_used: The given inequality f(y) - [((z-y)/(z-x))f(x)+((y-x)/(z-x))f(z)] <= f((x+z)/2) - (f(x)+f(z))/2 is rearranged. Writing L(t) for the chord over [x,z] (affine, slope s=(f(z)-f(x))/(z-x)), the RHS is f(mid)-L(mid) with mid=(x+z)/2, and the LHS is f(y)-L(y); so f(y)-L(y) <= f(mid)-L(mid), i.e. f(t) <= f(mid)+s*(t-mid) for all t in (x,z). Thus the secant slope s is a supergradient of f at the midpoint (x+z)/2 on (x,z), for every x<z.

technique: Derive concavity by evaluating a supporting-line bound at the two endpoints of a convex combination, so the linear terms cancel.
how_used: Using the supergradient a=s at an interior point y, f(x) <= f(y)+a(x-y) and f(z) <= f(y)+a(z-y). Taking the convex combination with weights (z-y)/(z-x) and (y-x)/(z-x), the coefficient of a is (z-y)(x-y)/(z-x)+(y-x)(z-y)/(z-x)=0, so ((z-y)/(z-x))f(x)+((y-x)/(z-x))f(z) <= f(y): exactly the concavity (Jensen) inequality. Concave f on R is automatically continuous.

technique: Force a one-sided nonnegative quantity to zero by adding two shifted copies of the hypothesis into a contraction of the same quantity at a larger scale, then iterate the scale down.
how_used: Let g(t) = [f(y)-f(y-t)]/t - [f(y+t)-f(y)]/t, the left-minus-right slope gap at y (>=0 by concavity, itself from the tangent-line/supergradient reading of the hypothesis). Apply the problem inequality to two width-4eps triples with evaluation point y but offset window midpoint: (i) (y-3eps, y, y+eps) gives f(y) <= f(y-eps) + [f(y+eps)-f(y-3eps)]/4; (ii) (y-eps, y, y+3eps) gives f(y) <= f(y+eps) - [f(y+3eps)-f(y-eps)]/4. Adding and rewriting via g(eps)*eps = 2f(y)-f(y-eps)-f(y+eps) and g(3eps)*3eps = 2f(y)-f(y-3eps)-f(y+3eps) yields exactly 5/4*eps*g(eps) <= 3/4*eps*g(3eps), i.e. g(eps) <= (3/5) g(3eps). Iterate with eps = 3^{-n} eps0: g(3^{-n} eps0) <= (3/5)^n g(eps0) -> 0, giving differentiability.

technique: Rewrite a 'derivative-at-midpoint equals secant slope' relation as a two-variable functional identity, then differentiate it into Jensen's equation for the derivative.
how_used: With differentiability established, the midpoint m=(x+z)/2 is an interior maximizer of the differentiable gap gap(y)=f(y)-secant*(y-x)-f(x); the first-order condition gap'(m)=0 forces f'(m) = (f(z)-f(x))/(z-x) for every window. Put x=X-Y, z=X+Y (midpoint X) to convert this into the pure identity f(X+Y)-f(X-Y)=2 f'(X) Y for all X,Y. Differentiate in Y: f'(X+Y)+f'(X-Y)=2 f'(X), Jensen's equation for f'. f' is continuous (from f'(X)=f(X+1)-f(X-1) at Y=1, f continuous as concave), so Jensen forces f' affine, hence f(y)=a y^2+b y+c; concavity gives a<=0.

technique: Choose the substitution that makes the inner argument of a nested composition cancel, collapsing the composed term into a bare function value
how_used: Setting y=-2x makes 2x+y=0, killing the (2x+y)g(y) term and turning g(f(x+y)) into g(f(-x))=f(x); this identity g(f(-x))=f(x) lets every later occurrence of the composition g(f(...)) be replaced by a plain f-value, dissolving the outer g

technique: Set one variable to zero in a two-variable relation to express one unknown function explicitly in terms of the other, then back-substitute to reduce to a single unknown
how_used: With x=0 the reduced relation gives f(-y)=f(0)+y g(y), so f is determined by g; substituting this f back into the relation (5) eliminates f entirely and leaves a functional equation purely in g

technique: Swap the two variables in a symmetric-looking two-variable identity and equate the two forms to extract a proportionality constraint forcing linearity
how_used: In (7) (x+y)h(x+y)=(2x+y)h(y)+x h(x) for h=g-g(0), swapping x and y and equating gives x h(y)=y h(x), so h(x)/x is constant, forcing h(x)=cx and hence g(x)=cx+b

technique: After deriving the parametric form of the functions, feed it into a leftover constraint and compare coefficients to solve for the parameters
how_used: Plugging g(x)=cx+b, f(x)=a-bx+cx^2 into g(f(-x))=f(x) yields a polynomial identity whose coefficient comparison gives c^2=c, bc=-b, ac+b=a, splitting into c=0 (trivial (0,0)) and c=1 (giving g=x, f=x^2+a)

technique: Encode coupled quadratic recurrences as power sums of the roots of a fixed polynomial by choosing coefficients so the squaring-minus-cross-terms folds into the doubling of exponents.
how_used: Let r,s,t be roots of p(lambda)=lambda^3 - a_1 lambda^2 + b_1 lambda - 1, so by Vieta a_1=r+s+t, b_1=1/r+1/s+1/t (since rst=1 makes 1/r=st etc.). Then a_n = r^{2^{n-1}}+s^{2^{n-1}}+t^{2^{n-1}} and b_n is the same in the reciprocals; the map a_{n+1}=a_n^2-2b_n becomes exactly (sum of squares) = square of sum minus twice sum of pairwise products, doubling every exponent.

technique: Detect a dominant root of magnitude exceeding a threshold by evaluating the polynomial at that threshold and reading off a sign change.
how_used: Because p(1)=b_1-a_1<0 (given a_1>b_1), the cubic p has a real root greater than 1; take r to be the largest such root, giving a root of magnitude >1 whose 2^{n-1}-th power dominates the power sum a_n.

technique: Establish eventual monotonicity of a power sum by isolating the term of largest magnitude and controlling the rest as a vanishing-relative remainder.
how_used: With m=max(|r|,|s|,|t|)>1 and k the multiplicity of that magnitude, a_n ~ k m^{2^{n-1}} when s,t are real; when s,t are non-real conjugates of magnitude 1/sqrt(r)<1 their contribution is bounded so r^{2^{n-1}}-2 < a_n < r^{2^{n-1}}+2. Since n>=2 makes the exponent 2^{n-1} even, even a negative dominant root contributes +m^{2^{n-1}}>0, and the double-exponentially growing dominant term forces a_k < a_{k+1} for large k.

technique: Iterate a two-term averaging recurrence n steps to expand a value as a binomial-weighted average over a diagonal of arguments
how_used: Iterating f(x,y)=(f(x-1,y)+f(x,y-1))/2 to depth n gives f(x,y)=2^{-n} sum_i C(n,i) f(x-i, y-(n-i)), a binomial average of values along an anti-diagonal.

technique: Bound the difference of two expanded values by the total variation of the shifted weight sequence, exploiting that the entries are uniformly bounded
how_used: |f(x,y)-f(x-1,y+1)| = 2^{-n}|sum f(P_i)(C(n,i)-C(n,i-1))| <= 2^{-n} sum|C(n,i)-C(n,i-1)|; the consecutive differences change sign once at the center so the total variation telescopes to 2C(n,floor(n/2)), which is o(2^n), forcing the difference to 0 and f constant.

technique: Realize the averaging value as a bounded martingale along a coordinate-decreasing random walk and couple two such walks so their almost-sure collision forces equal values
how_used: f(Z_n) is a bounded martingale for a down/left walk; run walks from (x,y),(x',y') with x+y=x'+y' independently until they meet. The coordinate difference is a recurrent 1D walk so they collide a.s.; E|f(Z_n)-f(Z'_n)| <= P(not yet collided) -> 0, giving f(x,y)=f(x',y') on each anti-diagonal, hence f constant.

technique: Feed a factored polynomial p-p(n)=(x-n)*q into the divisibility hypothesis to transfer a difference of theta-values into a divisibility by theta(x-n)
how_used: Since x-n divides p(x)-p(n), the second axiom gives theta(x-n) | theta(p(x)-p(n)); with theta(x-n)=c-n and theta(p-p(n))=theta(p)-p(n) this yields c-n | theta(p(x))-p(n), converting the unknown functional equation into an arithmetic divisibility statement.

technique: Force an integer equality by showing a fixed integer is divisible by a divisor that can be driven arbitrarily large
how_used: Combining c-n | theta(p(x))-p(n) with c-n | p(c)-p(n) gives c-n | theta(p(x))-p(c); since theta(p)-p(c) is a fixed integer independent of n, letting n grow makes |c-n| exceed it, forcing theta(p(x))-p(c)=0, i.e. theta(p)=p(c).

technique: Negate the target property to assume every triple is non-acute, turning the goal into a growth constraint on the sorted values
how_used: Assume NO three of the sorted a_1<=...<=a_n form an acute triangle; for any triple the largest side c satisfies c^2 >= a^2+b^2, which for consecutive sorted terms gives a_{i+1}^2 >= a_i^2 + a_{i-1}^2, converting 'no acute triangle' into a recurrence lower bound.

technique: Recognize a two-term additive lower-bound recurrence as bounded below by the Fibonacci sequence and unfold it by induction
how_used: From a_{i+1}^2 >= a_i^2 + a_{i-1}^2 with a_1^2, a_2^2 >= a_1^2, unfold to a_i^2 >= F_i * a_1^2 (F_i Fibonacci), so in particular a_n^2 >= F_n a_1^2.

technique: Collide the derived exponential lower bound against the given linear-ratio hypothesis to pin the threshold via a crossover comparison
how_used: Combine a_n^2 >= F_n a_1^2 with max<=n*min (a_n <= n a_1) to force F_n <= n^2; since F_m <= m^2 exactly for m<=12 (proved by induction that F_m>m^2 for m>=15 via F_m=F_{m-1}+F_{m-2}>(m-1)^2+(m-2)^2), no acute-free config exists once n>=13, giving the answer n>=13.

technique: Interpret a sum over all subsets as 2^n times an expectation, modeling membership by independent 0/1 (coin-flip) indicator variables.
how_used: Wrote S_A = sum epsilon_i x_i with epsilon_i independent Bernoulli(1/2), so sum over all A of S_A^2 = 2^n E[S_A^2], turning the subset-sum-of-squares into a probabilistic expectation over the 2^n subsets.

technique: Expand the square of a sum of indicator-weighted terms and evaluate cross-term expectations, then substitute the elementary-symmetric constraint obtained from squaring the given linear relation.
how_used: E[(sum epsilon_i x_i)^2] = (1/2)sum x_i^2 + (1/2)sum_{i<j} x_i x_j; used (sum x_i)^2=0 with sum x_i^2=1 to get sum_{i<j} x_i x_j = -1/2, giving E=1/4 and sum_A S_A^2 = 2^{n-2}.

technique: Halve a symmetric total by pairing each object with its sign-flipped complement.
how_used: Paired each A with its complement (S_A = -S_{A^c}), so the positive-S_A subsets carry exactly half the total: sum over S_A>0 of S_A^2 = 2^{n-3}.

technique: Bound a count by dividing a total sum of squares by the per-item threshold squared (Markov/Chebyshev tail bound).
how_used: Each A with S_A >= lambda contributes at least lambda^2 to the sum 2^{n-3}, so the number of such A is at most 2^{n-3}/lambda^2, with equality iff every S_A is in {+/-lambda, 0}.

technique: Absorb a fixed multiplicative constant into a factored product by rewriting each factor's contribution so the global inequality splits into one inequality per factor.
how_used: Wrote M=a_1...a_n and (x+1)^k=(x+1)^{sum 1/a_i}=prod (x+1)^{1/a_i}, turning M(x+1)^k < prod(x+a_i) into prod a_i(x+1)^{1/a_i} < prod(x+a_i), reducing to proving a_i(x+1)^{1/a_i} <= x+a_i for each i.

technique: Bound a root-power expression by applying AM-GM to a multiset padded with copies of 1 so the geometric mean becomes the desired radical.
how_used: Applied AM-GM to the a_i numbers (x+1, 1, 1, ..., 1) with a_i-1 ones, giving (x+a_i)/a_i >= (x+1)^{1/a_i}, i.e. a_i(x+1)^{1/a_i} <= x+a_i, the per-factor inequality.

technique: Upgrade a product of non-strict inequalities to a strict one by identifying that the equality case cannot hold for every factor under the hypothesis.
how_used: Equality in AM-GM holds iff a_i=1; if all a_i=1 then M=1, contradicting M>1, so strict inequality a_i(x+1)^{1/a_i} < x+a_i holds for at least one i, making the product strict and P(x)<0 for all x>0.

technique: Bound the max-minus-min spread of a rearrangement objective by computing its mean and variance under a uniformly random permutation.
how_used: Define S_sigma = sum_i x_i y_{sigma(i)}. By rearrangement (both sequences sorted descending), sum x_i y_i = max_sigma S_sigma and sum x_i y_{n+1-i} = min_sigma S_sigma, so the target LHS equals max_sigma S_sigma - min_sigma S_sigma. Drawing sigma uniformly, sum x = sum y = 0 gives E[S_sigma] = 0; combined with the variance 1/(n-1) (crux 1) and the variance-to-range bound (crux 2), the spread is at least 2/sqrt(n-1).

technique: Compute the expectation of a bilinear form under a random permutation by splitting into diagonal and off-diagonal index pairs and evaluating each via the power-sum identity 2*sum_{i<j} a_i a_j = (sum a)^2 - sum a^2.
how_used: For E[S_sigma^2] = sum_{i,j} x_i x_j E[y_{sigma(i)} y_{sigma(j)}], the diagonal gives E[y_{sigma(i)}^2] = (1/n) sum y_k^2 = 1/n contributing (1/n) sum x_i^2 = 1/n; the off-diagonal gives E[y_{sigma(i)} y_{sigma(j)}] = (1/(n(n-1))) sum_{k!=l} y_k y_l = (1/(n(n-1)))((sum y)^2 - sum y^2) = -1/(n(n-1)), and sum_{i!=j} x_i x_j = -1 similarly, so the off-diagonal contributes 1/(n(n-1)); total E[S_sigma^2] = 1/(n-1).

technique: Turn a variance lower bound into a range lower bound: a variable of variance v confined to [m,M] forces M-m >= 2*sqrt(v).
how_used: Rescale S_sigma to B = (S_sigma - m)/(M-m) in [0,1]; since B^2 <= B pointwise, Var(B) <= E[B] - E[B]^2 <= 1/4, so Var(S_sigma) = (M-m)^2 Var(B) <= (M-m)^2/4. With Var(S_sigma) = 1/(n-1) this gives (M-m)^2 >= 4/(n-1), i.e. max_sigma S_sigma - min_sigma S_sigma >= 2/sqrt(n-1).

technique: Recognize the symmetric relation as a quadratic in the value at the summed argument, so its two roots become the only candidates for that value
how_used: Rewrote f(a)^2+f(b)^2+f(c)^2=2(ff sums) with c=-(a+b) as f(a+b)^2-2(f(a)+f(b))f(a+b)+(f(a)-f(b))^2=0, giving f(a+b) equal to one of the two roots (sqrt f(a) plus/minus sqrt f(b)) squared, discriminant 16 f(a)f(b); this seeds f(2) in {0,4k} from a=b=1 and forces f even / f>=0

technique: Pin a single unknown value by intersecting the two candidate sets produced by two different argument-pair substitutions
how_used: Got f(3) in {k,9k} from (a,b)=(1,2) and f(3) in {9k,25k} from (a,b)=(1,-4); the common element forces f(3)=9k, and the same intersection trick at (n,1) vs (n-1,2) forces f(n+1)=k(n+1)^2 since k(n-1)^2 != k(n-3)^2

technique: Turn a vanishing value into a period, forcing the whole solution onto a finite residue-class pattern
how_used: From f(r)=0 with r>=1, substituting b=r,c=-a-r gives (f(a+r)-f(a))^2=0 so period r; the branch points f(2)=0, f(4)=0 then generate the constant-0, mod-2, and mod-4 solutions before the k x^2 branch

technique: When disjointness of translated sumsets is given, test where a symmetric combination of one element from each part must land by ruling out the other parts.
how_used: For a in A, b in B, c in C: a+b-c cannot be in A (else a+b=a'+c puts an element in both A+B and A+C, which are disjoint) nor in B, so a+b-c in C; by symmetry b+c-a in A and c+a-b in B. These three relations are the engine, and immediately give the inclusions A+B subset C+C, B+C subset A+A, C+A subset B+B.

technique: Turn a closure lemma into a contradiction over a divisible ground set by taking a scaled preimage that the lemma forbids from its home part.
how_used: The lemma says 3r in A for every r in Q. This is harmless over Z (3r only hits multiples of 3, all in A, matching the mod-3 construction of part a). But over Q, pick any b in B (nonempty) and set r=b/3 in Q; then 3r=b must be in A, contradicting b in B and the disjointness of the partition. Hence no such partition of Q exists. Answers: a) Yes; b) No.

technique: To get the reverse of a derived sumset inclusion, apply the same forcing relation twice, inserting an auxiliary element from a third part and cancelling it.
how_used: To show A+A subset B+C: take a,a' in A, b in B, c in C. First relation (1) gives a'+c-b in B; then apply (1) again to a in A, (a'+c-b) in B, c in C to get a+a'-b = a+(a'+c-b)-c in C. Hence A+A subset B+C, and symmetrically B+B subset C+A, C+C subset A+B. Combined with the forward inclusions this upgrades them to exact equalities B+C=A+A, C+A=B+B, A+B=C+C.

technique: After a sumset identity, normalize a chosen element to 0 in one part so that part absorbs the others' sumset, collapsing the identity into a closure (idempotence) statement.
how_used: With B+C=A+A established, put 0 in A (WLOG). Then B={0}+B subset A+B and C subset A+C; since B+C is disjoint from A+B and A+C, it is disjoint from B and C, so B+C subset A. Thus A+A=B+C subset A, and A={0}+A subset A+A give A=A+A=B+C. Then A+B+C=A, and B+B=C+A, C+C=A+B give B+B+B=A+B+C=A and C+C+C=A. Consequently 3r in A for every r in A union B union C = Q; with 3Q=Q this forces A=Q, contradicting non-empty B,C.

technique: To make a power (1+t)^k tractable by AM-GM, split the constant 1 into k-1 equal pieces so the bound becomes a single monomial in t with a self-cancelling constant chain.
how_used: Each factor is written (1+a_k)^k = ((k-1)*(1/(k-1)) + a_k)^k and weighted AM-GM gives (1+a_k)^k >= k^k/(k-1)^{k-1} * a_k; multiplying, the constants telescope as prod_{k=2}^n k^k/(k-1)^{k-1} = n^n and the a_k product equals the given constraint a_2...a_n = 1, yielding LHS >= n^n.

technique: Upgrade a proven >= to a strict > by showing the AM-GM equality conditions across all factors form an inconsistent system with no positive solution.
how_used: Equality in each factor needs 1/(k-1) = a_k, forcing a_k = 1/(k-1) for all k, hence prod_{k=2}^n a_k = 1/(n-1)! which is < 1 for n>=3 and contradicts a_2...a_n = 1; equivalently in the substituted form x_1=x_2, x_2=2x_3, ..., forces x_1 = (n-1)! x_1, impossible for x_1>0, so the product inequality is strict, giving > n^n.

technique: Uniformly bound the roots of a one-parameter polynomial family by making the fixed perturbing term dominated by the scaled main term outside a fixed radius
how_used: Since deg f > deg g, there is R with |g(x)/f(x)| < 1 for |x| > R; then |pf(x)+g(x)| >= |f(x)|(p - |g/f|) > 0 for every prime p, so every (real or complex) root of pf+g lies in [-R,R] regardless of p, giving the prime-uniform bound that all later pigeonhole/finiteness arguments run against.

technique: After normalizing to a monic model, use the rational root theorem so a prime leading coefficient forces the denominator of any rational root to be 1 or that prime
how_used: Replace f(x), g(x) by a_n^{n-1} f(x/a_n), a_n^{n-1} g(x/a_n) to make f monic; then pf+g has leading coefficient p, so a reduced rational root u/v has v | p, i.e. v=1 or v=p. The v=1 branch is closed immediately: |u|<=R gives finitely many integers u, so one u recurs for two primes p,q, and (p-q)f(u)=0 gives f(u)=0. The v=p branch is the hard case handled separately.

technique: Reduce a cleared-denominator integer equation modulo the prime to pin the numerator's residue, turning it into a linear congruence you can solve for the numerator
how_used: In the monic v=p branch, the integer equation (u^n + a_{n-1}p u^{n-1} + ...) + (b_{n-1}u^{n-1} + b_{n-2}p u^{n-2} + ...) = 0 reduced mod p keeps only the two p-free terms: u^n + b_{n-1}u^{n-1} ≡ 0 (mod p). Since gcd(u,p)=1 divide by u^{n-1} to get u + b_{n-1} ≡ 0 (mod p), i.e. u + b_{n-1} = pk for some integer k. This linear form for u is exactly what the next step (pigeonhole on k) needs.

technique: When a bounded integer parameter selects a root-shape that holds for infinitely many primes, pigeonhole to a single value, then read the surviving polynomial identity at the boundary point p→∞ (variable set to 0)
how_used: From u + b_{n-1} = pk the root is u/p = k - b_{n-1}/p; the uniform bound |u|/p < R forces |k| < R + |b_{n-1}|, so k ranges over a fixed finite set and some k recurs for infinitely many primes p. For those p, f(k - b_{n-1}(1/p)) + (1/p) g(k - b_{n-1}(1/p)) = 0, so the fixed polynomial F(x) = f(k - b_{n-1}x) + x g(k - b_{n-1}x) has the infinitely many roots x = 1/p, hence F ≡ 0; setting x = 0 gives F(0) = f(k) = 0. So the monic f has integer root k, and undoing the monic reduction gives a rational root of the original f.

technique: When a whole family of polynomials shares a fixed high-degree part with only its leading coefficient scaled by a growing parameter, confine all their roots to one parameter-independent bounded region by dominating the fixed remainder with the scaled leading term
how_used: Because deg f > deg g there is a fixed R with |g(x)/f(x)| < 1 for all |x| > R; then for every prime p and every |x| > R, |p f(x)+g(x)| >= |f(x)|(p - |g(x)/f(x)|) > 0, so EVERY root of pf+g (real, or complex with the disk version) lies in [-R,R] with R independent of p. This p-uniform confinement is what later makes both the v=1 case (finitely many bounded integers u) and the v=p case (finitely many bounded k) collapse to a value that recurs for infinitely many primes; without it neither finiteness holds.

technique: To pin the relative degree of two polynomials whose scaled sum has a rational root of prime denominator, substitute the root and compare the exact power of that prime in the denominator of each side's leading term, forcing the unique degree that lets the top powers cancel
how_used: After monic reduction (replace f(x),g(x) by a_n^{n-1}f(x/a_n), a_n^{n-1}g(x/a_n) so a_n=1), the leading coefficient of pf+g is p, so a reduced root u/v has v=1 or v=p. In the v=p branch (gcd(u,p)=1): the top term of p·f(u/p) is u^n/p^{n-1} (denominator exactly p^{n-1}, since gcd(u,p)=1), while the top term of g(u/p) is b_m u^m/p^m (denominator p^m). For the sum to vanish the maximal p-denominator must be matched, forcing m = n-1 = deg f - 1 (if m < n-1 the u^n/p^{n-1} term has strictly the largest p-denominator and is unmatched, so the sum cannot be 0). Clearing p^{n-1} gives (u^n + a_{n-1}p u^{n-1} + ...) + (b_{n-1}u^{n-1} + b_{n-2}p u^{n-2} + ...) = 0; reducing mod p and using gcd(u,p)=1 yields u + b_{n-1} = pk for some integer k.

technique: When a polynomial's roots must be controlled uniformly across a family, exploit a strict degree gap between a dominant and a subordinate term to trap all roots in a fixed compact region independent of the family parameter
how_used: Because deg f > deg g, |g(x)/f(x)| < 1 for all |x| > R (some fixed R). Then for every prime p and every |x| > R, |pf(x)+g(x)| >= |f(x)|(p - |g(x)|/|f(x)|) > 0, so every real (and, via the analogous complex estimate, every complex) root of pf+g lies in [-R,R] with R independent of p. This single uniform bound is what later turns each 'infinitely many primes' pigeonhole into a finite-set argument.

technique: Rescale a non-monic polynomial to monic by the substitution x -> x/(leading coefficient) with a compensating power factor, so the leading coefficient of a scalar-multiple-plus-perturbation becomes exactly that scalar and the rational-root denominator is pinned to divide it
how_used: Replace f(x), g(x) by a_n^{n-1} f(x/a_n), a_n^{n-1} g(x/a_n) to reduce to a_n = 1 (monic f); a rational root of the rescaled family corresponds to one of the original, so it suffices to find a rational root of the monic f. Now the leading coefficient of pf+g is exactly p, so for a rational root u/v in lowest terms v | p, forcing the clean dichotomy v = 1 or v = p that splits the argument into its two cases.

technique: When a value depending on a growing parameter is confined to finitely many possibilities so one value recurs for infinitely many parameter values, feed the resulting infinitely many roots of a one-variable polynomial in the parameter's reciprocal back as an identity and evaluate at reciprocal zero to extract the sought root
how_used: In the v=p branch, root u/p = k - b_{n-1}/p with u+b_{n-1}=pk; boundedness of the root (|u|/p < R) forces |k| < R + |b_{n-1}|, so k ranges over a finite set. Hence some fixed integer k gives a root k - b_{n-1}/p of pf+g for infinitely many primes p, i.e. f(k - b_{n-1}/p) + (1/p)g(k - b_{n-1}/p) = 0 for infinitely many p. Viewing F(x) = f(k - b_{n-1}x) + x*g(k - b_{n-1}x) as a polynomial with infinitely many roots x = 1/p, F is identically zero; substituting x = 0 gives f(k) = 0, so the monic-reduced f has the integer root k and the original f has a rational root.

technique: Feed a functional equation an input pair and its image under an already-proven point symmetry so the two right-hand sides coincide, and subtract to force a fixed-shift difference of the unknown function.
how_used: With the reflection g(x)+g(2-x)=2 in hand, apply the FE to (u,v) and to the reflected pair (2-u,2-v) under the constraint u+v=1. The RHS products (g(u)-1)(g(v)-1) and (g(2-u)-1)(g(2-v)-1) are equal by the reflection identity, so subtracting the two FE instances cancels the RHS and yields g(uv+3)-g(uv+1)=g(3)-g(1): a constant shift value independent of u,v.

technique: Extend a relation proven only on the range of a two-variable parametrizing map by computing that range as a half-line (via a discriminant condition) and reflecting the missing half back into it through a known symmetry.
how_used: The point x=uv+1 with u+v=1 attains exactly x<=5/4, since t^2-t+(x-1) has real roots iff its discriminant 1-4(x-1)>=0; this proves the shift g(x+2)-g(x)=2 for x<=5/4. For x>5/4, note 2-x<5/4 lies in the proven region, and the reflection g(x)=2-g(2-x), g(x+2)=2-g(-x) transfers the shift, giving g(x+2)-g(x)=g(2-x)-g(-x)=2 everywhere.

technique: Pin a Cauchy-additive function to linear by exhibiting one-sided boundedness on a ray, obtained from a square identity.
how_used: From additivity plus multiplicativity, g(x^2)=g(x)^2>=0, so g>=0 on [0,infinity). An additive (Cauchy) function bounded below on a half-line is linear, hence g(x)=g(1)x; multiplicativity forces g(1)=1, giving g(x)=x and f(x)=x-1.

technique: Collapse a functional equation into Cauchy's additive equation by applying it to a variable and its negation as two paired substitutions and adding the results to cancel the cross terms.
how_used: Once g is odd (g(-x)=-g(x)), apply the FE g(1+xy)-g(x+y)=(g(x)-1)(g(y)-1) to the pairs (-x,y) and (x,-y). Using oddness the two instances become g(1-xy)-g(-x+y)=(g(x)+1)(1-g(y)) and g(1-xy)-g(x-y)=(1-g(x))(g(y)+1). Adding cancels the g(x-y)/g(y-x) terms and gives g(1-xy)=1-g(x)g(y); with g(1+xy)=1+g(x)g(y) (from the reflection g(x)+g(2-x)=2), the original FE reduces to g(x+y)=g(x)+g(y). Additivity plus g(1+xy)=1+g(x)g(y) then gives multiplicativity g(xy)=g(x)g(y), so g(x^2)=g(x)^2>=0 forces g nonnegative on [0,inf); an additive function bounded below is linear, giving g(x)=x, f(x)=x-1.

technique: To prove a fixed shift identity g(x+c)-g(x)=const for all x, parametrize the argument as a symmetric-function value (a product of two numbers with fixed sum) so a reflection symmetry equates two evaluations of the relation, establishing the identity on the range that parametrization covers.
how_used: Goal: g(x+2)-g(x)=2 for all x, where g=f+1. With the reflection g(x)+g(2-x)=2 in hand (from y=-1 in the FE plus C=g(-1)-1!=0), take u+v=1 and apply the FE to (u,v) and to (2-u,2-v). Since (2-u)+(2-v)=3 and (2-u)(2-v)=uv+2, and the reflection gives f(2-u)f(2-v)=f(u)f(v), the two right-hand sides coincide, yielding g(uv+3)-g(uv+1)=g(3)-g(1)=2. As u ranges over R with v=1-u, x=uv+1 covers all x<=5/4 (t^2-t+(x-1) has real roots iff x<=5/4), so the shift holds for x<=5/4; for x>5/4 use -x<5/4 with the reflection to transfer it. Replacing x by -x in the reflection and combining with the shift then forces oddness g(-x)=-g(x), the prerequisite for the paired-substitution collapse to additivity/multiplicativity.

technique: Force a set to be infinite by contradicting a distinct-count against the linear upper bound the structure imposes on its values
how_used: If only finitely many chains C_{t_1},...,C_{t_r} (starts t_1<...<t_r), then every f^n(1) with 1<=n<=N satisfies f^n(1)=t+(n-n_t)/2 <= t_r+N/2. But 1,f(1),...,f^N(1) are N+1 distinct naturals all below t_r+N/2, forcing N+1<=t_r+N/2, false for large N. Hence T is infinite.

technique: Pigeonhole more disjoint chain-starts than a fixed-width window has slots to force one chain to skip the window entirely, producing an oversized single step
how_used: Given T infinite, pick the first k+1 numbers of T and let t be the greatest, so all k+1 chain-starts are <=t. If every one of these disjoint chains had a member in {t+1,...,t+k}, that would be k+1 distinct values in a size-k window (chains disjoint by g-injectivity), impossible; so some chain has a member <=t and no member in the window, meaning its g-step jumps over it: n with g(n)-n>k, i.e. k_n>k. As k was arbitrary, (k_n) is unbounded.

technique: Prove a shift-type map on an orbit is injective by turning a collision into a smaller admissible exponent that contradicts the minimality defining that exponent
how_used: On S={1,f(1),f^2(1),...}, define g(n)=f^{2k_n}(n)=n+k_n where k_n is the SMALLEST k with f^{2k}(n)=n+k. If g(a)=g(b) with a<b then a+k_a=b+k_b forces k_a>k_b. Since f^{2k_a}(a)=a+k_a=b+k_b=f^{2k_b}(b), peel 2k_b copies of f off both sides using f-injectivity on S to get f^{2(k_a-k_b)}(a)=b=a+(k_a-k_b); as 0<k_a-k_b<k_a this is a smaller admissible exponent for a, contradicting minimality of k_a. (f is injective on S because a collision f^i(1)=f^j(1) would make the iterates eventually periodic and S finite, but S is unbounded since g(n)>n.)

technique: Telescope the iterated shift-map along a forward chain to express each orbit point's value as a closed linear function of its orbit index
how_used: S is the disjoint union of chains C_t={t,g(t),g^2(t),...} over the non-image starts t in T (each n in S\T is g(n') with n'<n, so tracing back lands on some t in T; disjointness from g-injectivity). For f^n(1) in C_t with t=f^{n_t}(1), write f^n(1)=g^j(f^{n_t}(1))=f^{2a_j}(...f^{2a_1}(f^{n_t}(1)))=f^{n_t}(1)+a_1+...+a_j while the orbit index advances by n-n_t=2(a_1+...+a_j) (each g-step adds 2k to the index but k to the value). Telescoping the two sums gives f^n(1)=t+(n-n_t)/2.

technique: Force a structural set to be infinite by contradiction: assume finitely many, derive a uniform upper bound on the values of the first N iterates, then collide it against the count of distinct iterates.
how_used: Show the set T of chain-starts is infinite. Assume instead only finitely many chains C_{t_1},...,C_{t_r} with largest start t_r. Using the affine law f^n(1)=t+(n-n_t)/2 with t<=t_r, every one of f^1(1),...,f^N(1) is at most t_r+N/2. But these N+1 numbers (including n=0) are DISTINCT (f injective on S), so N+1<=t_r+N/2, false for large N. Hence T is infinite.

technique: Extract a large gap of a shift map from an infinite family of chains by choosing enough chain-starts that one chain must skip a whole block of consecutive integers.
how_used: To show k_n unbounded, fix any k and take the k+1 smallest elements of T (the infinite set of chain-starts), with largest one t. Each of these k+1 disjoint chains contains a value <=t (its start). Among the k integers t+1,...,t+k there are only k slots and the chains are disjoint, so by pigeonhole at least one of the k+1 chains contains NO value in {t+1,...,t+k}. That chain has consecutive members n and g(n)=n+k_n straddling the whole block, so g(n)-n=k_n>k. As k was arbitrary, k_1,k_2,... is unbounded.

technique: When a minimally-chosen witness index is contested by an equal-value collision, subtract the two witness-exponents to build a strictly shorter witness satisfying the same defining relation, contradicting minimality.
how_used: Work inside the forward orbit S={1,f(1),f^2(1),...} (f is injective on S: a repeat f^i(1)=f^j(1) would make the orbit eventually periodic hence finite, but S is unbounded since each element n admits f^{2k}(n)=n+k>n in S). Define the shift g(n)=f^{2k_n}(n)=n+k_n where k_n is the SMALLEST k with f^{2k}(n)=n+k. To show g injective, suppose g(a)=g(b) with a<b; then a+k_a=b+k_b forces k_a>k_b, and f^{2k_a}(a)=f^{2k_b}(b). Cancelling the outer 2k_b applications of f (legal by injectivity on S) gives f^{2(k_a-k_b)}(a)=b=a+(k_a-k_b): a valid witness for a with exponent 0<k_a-k_b<k_a, contradicting minimality of k_a. So g is injective.

technique: To force a bounded-growth injective sequence to have infinitely many orbit-roots, assume finitely many roots, bound every one of the N+1 initial forward images by root-max plus half the index via the affine law, and let the pigeonhole count of distinct naturals below that bound fail for large N.
how_used: Suppose T were finite, T={t_1<...<t_r}. For 1<=n<=N, f^n(1) lies in some C_t and by the affine law f^n(1)=t+(n-n_t)/2<=t_r+N/2. But 1,f(1),...,f^N(1) are N+1 DISTINCT naturals (f injective on S) all <=t_r+N/2, so N+1<=t_r+N/2, impossible for large N. Hence T is infinite.

technique: To upgrade a self-map that shifts values by a variable amount into an injection, suppose two points share an image and use the injectivity of the underlying iteration to cancel a common prefix, producing a shorter shift that violates the minimality defining the variable amount.
how_used: On S={1,f(1),f^2(1),...} define g(n)=f^{2k_n}(n)=n+k_n. To prove g injective, suppose g(a)=g(b) with a<b. Then a+k_a=b+k_b forces k_a>k_b. Since f is injective on S (else the forward orbit of 1 would be eventually periodic and S finite), cancel 2k_b applications of f from f^{2k_a}(a)=f^{2k_b}(b) to get f^{2(k_a-k_b)}(a)=b=a+(k_a-k_b). But 0<k_a-k_b<k_a contradicts the minimality of k_a. Hence g is injective; this is what makes S split into disjoint forward g-chains.

technique: When an injective, strictly-increasing self-map partitions a set into disjoint forward orbits, express any element as an orbit iterate and telescope the per-step increments to get a closed affine formula relating its position along the base sequence to its value.
how_used: With g injective and g(n)=n+k_n>n, the roots T=S\g(S) start disjoint chains C_t={t,g(t),g^2(t),...} whose union is S. If f^n(1) lies in C_t with t=f^{n_t}(1), then f^n(1)=g^j(t) for some j, and each g gives f^{2a_i}(...)=(...)+a_i, so f^n(1)=t+(a_1+...+a_j) while the exponent bookkeeping gives n=n_t+2(a_1+...+a_j). Telescoping the increments yields a_1+...+a_j=(n-n_t)/2, hence the affine law f^n(1)=t+(n-n_t)/2. This is the uniform 'value grows at half the index rate' fact the counting argument needs; the intermediate f-iterates need not be monotone, but the telescoped orbit sum is exact.

technique: Given infinitely many disjoint infinite increasing orbits, select the first k+1 roots and pigeonhole their forced members through a length-k value window to make one orbit skip the whole window in a single step.
how_used: T infinite; list its first k+1 elements with largest t. Each C_{t_i} is an INFINITE chain (g is total on S and g(n)>n, so every chain climbs without bound) starting at t_i<=t, so each has a member <=t and members exceeding t+k. The window {t+1,...,t+k} has k slots; the chains are disjoint so at most k of the k+1 chains place a member there. Hence at least one chain C_{t_j} has NO member in {t+1,...,t+k}. That chain has a member n<=t and, climbing to infinity, a later member >=t+k+1; the g-step crossing the window goes from some n'<=t directly to g(n')>=t+k+1, so g(n')-n'=k_{n'}>k. Since k was arbitrary, {k_n} is unbounded.

technique: Split a sign-obstructed product identity into the nonnegative case by writing each function as positive-minus-negative part and expanding the product bilinearly
how_used: Because a<b, c<d fails to force ac<bd for negatives, write each metapolynomial f=f⁺−f⁻ with f⁺=max{f,0}, f⁻=max{0,−f} (both in M since M is closed under max/min with 0), then fg=f⁺g⁺−f⁺g⁻−f⁻g⁺+f⁻g⁻. Each of the four terms is a product of two NONNEGATIVE metapolynomials; combined with M's closure under sums and negation, this reduces the whole theorem to proving fg∈M only when f,g≥0.

technique: Realize the product of two independently-clamped nonnegative polynomials as one explicit max-of-min template, verified by casework on which factor is ≤1 or ≥1
how_used: The single-pair base case P⁺Q⁺∈M reduces to the closed identity u⁺v⁺ = max{0, min{uv,u,v}, min{uv,uv²,u²v}, min{uv,u,u²v}, min{uv,uv²,v}} (then substitute u=P(x), v=Q(x)). Verification: if u≤0 or v≤0 both sides are 0; if u,v≥0 the RHS is clearly ≤uv, and equality is hit by choosing the branch matching the region — min{uv,u,v} on 0≤u,v≤1; min{uv,uv²,u²v} on 1≤u,v; min{uv,u,u²v} on 0≤v≤1≤u; min{uv,uv²,v} on 0≤u≤1≤v — each region making its min-branch equal uv while no branch exceeds uv. This gives P⁺Q⁺ as an explicit max-min of the polynomials 0,u,v,uv,uv²,u²v, i.e. an element of M.

technique: To multiply two nonnegative max-min forms, clamp every branch polynomial to its nonnegative part so the whole array is pointwise ≥ 0, then push the product inside using that on [0,∞) the max (and min) of products equals the product of maxes (mins) over the paired index set
how_used: For f=max_i min_j P_{i,j} ≥ 0 and g=max_i min_j Q_{i,j} ≥ 0 one cannot multiply branchwise because a<b, c<d fails to give ac<bd unless all are ≥0. Since f≥0, replacing each P_{i,j} by P⁺_{i,j}=max{P_{i,j},0} leaves max_i min_j unchanged (a row with a negative entry has clamped-min 0 ≤ f, and the winning row is untouched), and likewise for Q; now every branch is pointwise nonnegative, so monotonicity of multiplication on [0,∞) gives fg = max_{(i1,i2)} min_{(j1,j2)} P⁺_{i1,j1}·Q⁺_{i2,j2} as a pointwise identity, collapsing the double max-min into one max-min over pair indices whose cells are the products P⁺_{i1,j1}·Q⁺_{i2,j2}. This isolates the sole remaining task: showing one such cell (a product of two clamped polynomials) is a metapolynomial.

technique: To realize the product of two clamped polynomials as a max-min of polynomials, write down an explicit max over min-blocks and verify it by casework on the unit-square regions of the two variables
how_used: The isolated cell u⁺v⁺ (u=P(x), v=Q(x)) must be exhibited as an honest max-min of polynomials, not of metapolynomials — otherwise the reduction is circular. The needed identity is u⁺v⁺ = max{ 0, min{uv,u,v}, min{uv,uv²,u²v}, min{uv,u,u²v}, min{uv,uv²,v} }. It is verified region by region: if u≤0 or v≤0 both sides are 0; if u,v≥0 the RHS is ≤ uv, and matching lower bounds come from splitting {u,v≥0} by whether each of u,v is ≤1 or ≥1, on each of the four subregions one of the four min-blocks equals uv (e.g. min{uv,u,v}=uv when 0≤u,v≤1; min{uv,uv²,u²v}=uv when u,v≥1). Substituting the polynomials P,Q for u,v gives a polynomial max-min representation, so P⁺Q⁺ ∈ M and the whole theorem closes.

technique: Pair a weighted sum of terms against the matching weighted sum of their reciprocals through the weighted AM-HM (equivalently Cauchy-Schwarz) inequality to collapse two constraints into one inequality in the free parameter.
how_used: Treat the multiset containing a_k with multiplicity k (k=1..n), total weight W=n(n+1)/2. Weighted AM-HM gives (sum k*a_k)/W >= W/(sum k/a_k); substituting the two given values 6n and 2+1/n yields 6n/(n(n+1)/2) >= (n(n+1)/2)/(2+1/n), i.e. 12/(n+1) >= n^2(n+1)/(2(2n+1)), a necessary condition purely in n.

technique: Replace each side of a messy rational inequality by a crude monomial bound (rounding denominators) to reduce it to a single polynomial inequality that caps the free parameter.
how_used: Bound 12/(n+1) < 12/n (drop the +1) and n^2(n+1)/(2(2n+1)) > n^2/4 (since 2(n+1) > 2n+1), turning 12/(n+1) >= n^2(n+1)/(2(2n+1)) into 12/n > n^2/4, i.e. 48 > n^3, so n <= 3; then n=1 and n=2 are ruled out by direct check and n=3 is realized by (a_1,a_2,a_3)=(6,3,2).

technique: Propagate a self-referential ratio bound by feeding the bound for the previous index back through the strict-inequality recurrence.
how_used: To bound the limit r from above, prove the inductive estimate b_n <= n(n+1)/2 (equivalently b_n/n^2 <= 1/2 + 1/(2n)): assuming b_{n-1} <= (n-1)n/2 (base b_1=1), the strict recurrence b_n < n^2 b_{n-1}/(n-1)^2 gives b_n < n^3/(2(n-1)) = n(n+1)/2 + (1/2)(1 + 1/(n-1)), whose correction term is <= 1 for n>=2, so b_n < n(n+1)/2 + 1.

technique: Sharpen a strict fractional upper bound on an integer quantity by flooring to the next lower integer.
how_used: From b_n < n(n+1)/2 + 1 with n(n+1)/2 an integer and b_n a positive integer, conclude b_n <= n(n+1)/2, hence b_n/n^2 <= (n+1)/(2n) -> 1/2, forcing r <= 1/2.

technique: To realize an arbitrary interior target as the limit of a rounded integer sequence while forcing strict monotonicity, add a lower-order linear offset inside the rounding so the manufactured slack outweighs the unit rounding jitter.
how_used: For fixed 0<r<1/2 set b_n = ceil(r n^2 + n) for n large enough that this stays below n(n+1)/2 (patching earlier terms to n(n+1)/2). The +n offset gives b_n/n^2 >= (r n^2 + n)/n^2 = r + 1/n, while b_{n+1}/(n+1)^2 <= (r(n+1)^2 + (n+1) + 1)/(n+1)^2; strict decrease reduces to 1/n > (n+2)/(n+1)^2, i.e. (n+1)^2 > n(n+2), true always. Then b_n/n^2 = r + O(1/n) -> r, so the infimum equals r.

technique: Hit the two extreme values of an inf-of-ratios range using the constant-numerator sequence for the low end and the size-bound-saturating sequence for the high end.
how_used: The range is r in [0,1/2]; its two endpoints need explicit sequences. Low end r=0: take b_n=1 for all n, so b_n/n^2=1/n^2 is strictly decreasing to 0, giving inf=0. High end r=1/2: take b_n=n(n+1)/2 (the sequence that meets the greedy bound b_n<=n(n+1)/2 with equality), so b_n/n^2=(n+1)/(2n)=1/2+1/(2n) is strictly decreasing with infimum exactly 1/2.

technique: Bound each ratio term by feeding the previous ratio's bound into the strict-inequality recurrence, then round the resulting non-integer bound down using integrality of the terms.
how_used: From b_n/n^2 < b_{n-1}/(n-1)^2 and the inductive hypothesis b_{n-1}/(n-1)^2 <= 1/2 + 1/(2(n-1)), get b_n < n^2(1/2 + 1/(2(n-1))) = n(n+1)/2 + (1/2)(1 + 1/(n-1)) <= n(n+1)/2 + 1. Since b_n is an integer, b_n <= n(n+1)/2, hence b_n/n^2 <= 1/2 + 1/(2n), so r = inf b_n/n^2 <= 1/2. This is the 'only if' direction ruling out any r above 1/2.

technique: To attain a prescribed interior limit value of an inf-of-ratios by a strictly monotone integer sequence, round up a linear-corrected copy of the target profile and verify strict monotonicity by rearranging the ratio inequality to an integer size comparison.
how_used: Fix 0<r<1/2. Set b_n=ceil(r n^2 + n) for n>=N and b_n=n(n+1)/2 for n<N, where N is chosen so ceil(r n^2+n)<n(n+1)/2 holds for all n>=N (possible since r<1/2 makes r n^2 grow slower than the greedy cap ~n^2/2); this splices the tail strictly under the triangular prefix and keeps b_1=1. Then b_n/n^2=(r n^2+n+O(1))/n^2 -> r, so the inf equals r. Strict decrease on the tail: b_n/n^2 >= (r n^2+n)/n^2 > ([r(n+1)^2+(n+1)]+1)/(n+1)^2 >= b_{n+1}/(n+1)^2, the middle step being exactly 1/n > (n+2)/(n+1)^2 (equivalently (n+1)^2 > n(n+2)). This fills the open interval (0,1/2).

technique: To cap a term of an integer sequence governed by a strict decrease of a normalized ratio, feed the previous term's cap through the strict inequality to get a real upper bound, then round that strict bound down to the nearest integer.
how_used: From the inductive cap b_{n-1} <= (n-1)n/2 (equivalently b_{n-1}/(n-1)^2 <= 1/2 + 1/(2(n-1))) and the strict decrease b_n/n^2 < b_{n-1}/(n-1)^2, get b_n < n^2(1/2 + 1/(2(n-1))) = n(n+1)/2 + (1/2)(1 + 1/(n-1)) <= n(n+1)/2 + 1. Since b_n is an integer strictly below the integer n(n+1)/2 + 1, conclude b_n <= n(n+1)/2, i.e. b_n/n^2 <= 1/2 + 1/(2n). Induction (base b_1 = 1) gives this cap for all n, so any admissible r = inf b_n/n^2 satisfies r <= 1/2. Combined with r >= 0 (positive integers) this is the upper-bound half of the answer 0 <= r <= 1/2.

technique: To realize an arbitrary target value of an infimum-type invariant that lies strictly between the extremal constructions, take the near-optimal formula (the ceiling of the target's leading part plus a lower-order pad), splice in the extremal sequence for the finitely many small indices where it would violate the ordering, and verify the strict monotonicity by a one-line rearrangement.
how_used: For fixed 0 < r < 1/2, set b_n = ceil(r n^2 + n) for n >= N and b_n = n(n+1)/2 for n < N, where N is chosen so ceil(r n^2 + n) < n(n+1)/2 for all n >= N (guaranteeing the splice never breaks the earlier triangular block's ordering). Then b_n/n^2 = (r n^2 + n + O(1))/n^2 -> r, so inf = r. Strict decrease for n >= N follows from b_n/n^2 >= (r n^2 + n)/n^2 > ([r(n+1)^2 + (n+1)] + 1)/(n+1)^2 > b_{n+1}/(n+1)^2, the middle inequality rearranging to 1/n > (n+2)/(n+1)^2. The endpoints use the pure extremal formulas: r = 1/2 via b_n = n(n+1)/2, r = 0 via b_n = 1. Together with the r <= 1/2 cap this shows every r in [0, 1/2] is attained.

technique: Substitute the approximate closed form back into the functional equation and drive one variable to infinity so the bounded error is dominated, forcing the coefficient it multiplies to vanish and pinning the function exactly
how_used: Plug f(x)=Kx+O(1) into f(xy+f(x))=xf(y)+2 to get K(xy+Kx+O(1))+O(1)=xf(y)+2, i.e. x*(Ky+K^2-f(y))=O(1); fixing y and letting x->infinity forces Ky+K^2-f(y)=0, so f is exactly affine; substituting f(t)=Kt+K^2 back gives K^3+K^2=2, so K=1 and f(x)=x+1, verified by f(xy+x+1)=xy+x+2=x(y+1)+2

technique: Sandwich a monotone unknown function between the floor and ceiling step-functions generated by an additive shift relation, converting exact lattice increments into a linear estimate with bounded error
how_used: From P(1,y) get the shift f(y+c)=f(y)+2 with c:=f(1), hence f(y+nc)=f(y)+2n for integers n>=0. With f weakly increasing (from the previous crux), interpolating any x between the lattice points nc traps f(x) between 2*floor(x/f(1))+C and 2*ceil(x/f(1))+C, where K:=2/f(1) and C:=f(f(1))-2, giving |f(x)-(Kx+C)|<=2, i.e. f(x)=Kx+O(1) for ALL positive reals. Feeding f(x)=Kx+O(1) back into the equation forces x*(Ky+K^2-f(y))=O(1); fixing y and sending x->infinity kills the O(1), so f(y)=Ky+K^2 is exactly linear, pinning f(x)=x+1.

technique: Subtract two instances of the equation at a common fixed variable so the unknown terms cancel into an identity that ties the sign of the target function's increment on the output side to its increment on the input side, then seed one concrete signed increment to propagate the sign globally
how_used: In f(xy+f(x))=xf(y)+2, subtract P(x,y1) from P(x,y2) to get f(xy2+f(x))-f(xy1+f(x))=x(f(y2)-f(y1)). Since x>0, the increment of f across the ordered inputs xy1+f(x)<xy2+f(x) has the SAME sign as f(y2)-f(y1). Seed a strictly positive increment from P(1,y): f(y+f(1))=f(y)+2>f(y). The increasing affine input-map t->xt+f(x), ranged over x>0, transfers this positivity to all pairs, so f is weakly increasing. (The claim 'RHS xf(y)+2 is increasing in y' is circular -- its y-monotonicity IS f's; the non-circular content is the cancellation identity plus a genuinely seeded increment.)

technique: When one substitution makes a fixed additive shift of the argument change the function by a constant, iterate that shift to pin the function exactly on an arithmetic progression, then use the function's monotonicity to trap every other point between consecutive progression values, yielding a leading-linear-plus-bounded-error estimate
how_used: P(1,y) gives f(y+f(1))=f(y)+2, so shifting the argument by a:=f(1) adds exactly 2 to f. Iterating: f(t+na)=f(t)+2n, so f is pinned on each progression t,t+a,t+2a,.... Feeding monotonicity (f weakly increasing, taken as a known/separately-established property here) in as the interpolation tool, any x is trapped between consecutive progression points, giving 2*floor(x/f(1))+C <= f(x) <= 2*ceil(x/f(1))+C with C=f(f(1))-2, i.e. |f(x)-(Kx+C)|<=2 with K=2/f(1), summarized as f(x)=Kx+O(1).

technique: Substitute an approximate closed form (exact leading term plus a bounded error) back into the original relation, then send a free variable to infinity so the bounded error is negligible and the coefficient it multiplies is forced to vanish, upgrading the approximation to an exact identity
how_used: Feed f(x)=Kx+O(1) into f(xy+f(x))=xf(y)+2: LHS = K(xy+Kx+O(1))+O(1) = Kxy+K^2 x+O(1), RHS = xf(y)+2, so x*(Ky+K^2-f(y))=O(1). Fixing y and letting x->infinity forces the coefficient Ky+K^2-f(y)=0, so f(y)=Ky+K^2 exactly. Plugging back pins K via K^3+K^2=2=(K-1)(K^2+2K+2)+... giving K=1 as the only positive root, hence f(x)=x+1, verified by f(xy+x+1)=xy+x+2=x(y+1)+2.

technique: Bound a squared sum-of-two-groups denominator by splitting it into two group-sums and applying AM-GM, turning it into a product that telescopes over a common denominator.
how_used: Write 2a+b+c=(a+b)+(a+c) and AM-GM gives (2a+b+c)^2 >= 4(a+b)(a+c), so 1/(2a+b+c)^2 <= 1/(4(a+b)(a+c)); summing the three cyclic terms over the common denominator 4(a+b)(b+c)(c+a) collapses to (a+b+c)/(2(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)), reducing the goal to 3(a+b)(b+c)(c+a) >= 8(a+b+c).
