technique: Clear a reciprocal-sum constraint into a polynomial relation among elementary symmetric functions by multiplying through by the product of the variables.
how_used: Multiply 1/a+1/b+1/c=a+b+c by abc to get ab+bc+ca=abc(a+b+c), i.e. q=rp with p=a+b+c, q=ab+bc+ca, r=abc; this relation is fed into the symmetric-function bounds so that q^2 >= 3rp collapses to q >= 3.

technique: Bound a product of pairwise sums below by summing over symmetric degree-3 monomials via AM-GM.
how_used: AM-GM a^2b+a^2c+...+c^2b >= 6abc gives 9(a+b)(b+c)(c+a) >= 8(a+b+c)(ab+bc+ca), and a^2b^2+b^2c^2+c^2a^2 >= a^2bc+ab^2c+abc^2 gives (ab+bc+ca)^2 >= 3abc(a+b+c); with the constraint ab+bc+ca=abc(a+b+c) these combine to 3(a+b)(b+c)(c+a) >= 8(a+b+c), closing crux 0's reduction with equality at a=b=c=1.

technique: Homogenize an inequality by inserting the constraint's ratio to make both sides the same degree, then normalize the symmetric sum to 1 to simplify each denominator.
how_used: Multiply the RHS 3/16 by (a+b+c)(1/a+1/b+1/c) (equal to (a+b+c)^2 by the constraint) to homogenize, then set a+b+c=1 so that 2a+b+c=1+a; the goal becomes sum 1/(1+a)^2 <= (3/16)(1/a+1/b+1/c) for a,b,c>0 with a+b+c=1.

technique: Apply weighted Jensen to a concave function with weights chosen so the weighted mean of the arguments becomes a harmonic mean controllable by AM-HM.
how_used: Write the normalized LHS sum 1/(1+a)^2 = sum (1/a)*f(a) with f(x)=x/(1+x)^2 (concave, increasing on [0,1]); weighted Jensen with weights 1/a,1/b,1/c gives sum(1/a)f(a) <= (sum 1/a) f(A) where A=3/(1/a+1/b+1/c) is the harmonic mean, and AM-HM bounds A <= (a+b+c)/3 = 1/3; since f is increasing, f(A) <= f(1/3)=3/16, yielding sum 1/(1+a)^2 <= (3/16)(1/a+1/b+1/c).

technique: Plug the smallest value of the free variable into a triangle/inequality constraint to force an integer-gap collapse into a periodicity relation, then kill the period via unboundedness
how_used: Setting x=1 turns the triangle condition on {1, f(y), f(y+f(1)-1)} into |f(y)-f(y+m)|<1 with m=f(1)-1; integrality forces f(y)=f(y+m), so f is m-periodic hence bounded by B; but the strict inequality x<f(y)+f(y+f(x)-1)<=2B fails for x>2B, forcing m=0 and f(1)=1.

technique: Specialize the free variables so the triangle/inequality constraint pins a composite value to the identity, yielding an involution identity
how_used: With f(1)=1, setting x=z and y=1 makes the sides z, f(1)=1, and f(f(z)); non-degeneracy forces |z-f(f(z))|<1, so f(f(z))=z for all z, giving an involution.

technique: Prove a linear (sub-slope-1) growth cap on f by minimal-counterexample descent: any violator of the cap forces a smaller violator via the functional relation
how_used: Assuming f(z)=w+1>z gives f(t)<=f(t-w)+(z-1) from the triangle inequality at x=z, y=t-w; if t is the smallest violator of f(t)<=((z-1)/w)t+M (M=max f on 1..w), then f(t-w) also violates it, contradicting minimality, so the cap with slope (z-1)/w<1 holds for all t.

technique: Iterate a contractive (slope<1) growth bound to make a composite grow slower than the identity, contradicting a fixed-point/involution identity for large arguments
how_used: Applying the cap f(t)<=((z-1)/w)t+M twice gives f(f(t))<=((z-1)/w)^2 t+((z-1)/w+1)M < t for large t, contradicting f(f(t))=t; hence f(z)<=z everywhere, and z=f(f(z))<=f(z)<=z forces f(z)=z.

technique: Factor a target term as a product so applying sqrt-concavity (QM-AM on square roots) to the second factor splits off exactly the opponent term you must dominate, leaving a controllable remainder.
how_used: Wrote each RHS term as √2·√(a+b) = 2√(ab/(a+b))·√(½(2+(a²+b²)/ab)) and used √(½(x+y)) ≥ ½(√x+√y) on the second factor to get √2·√(a+b) ≥ √(2ab/(a+b)) + √((a²+b²)/(a+b)), so the LHS term √((a²+b²)/(a+b)) is absorbed and only the harmonic remainder √(2ab/(a+b)) is left to handle.

technique: Bound a cyclic sum of terms below by the squared-harmonic mean (via power-mean AM ≥ sq-HM) so the reciprocals collapse into the given side-constraint expression.
how_used: Applied AM ≥ squared-harmonic-mean to √(2ab/(a+b))+√(2bc/(b+c))+√(2ca/(c+a)), turning it into 3√(3 / Σ(a+b)/(2ab)) = 3√(3abc/(ab+bc+ca)); the constraint ab+bc+ca ≤ 3abc then makes this ≥ 3, matching the +3 on the LHS.

technique: Substitute the argument so an inner nested term cancels to zero, collapsing the composite value to the fixed constant f(0)
how_used: In the assumed inequality f(x-f(y)) <= y f(x) + x, set x = f(y) so the left argument becomes f(y)-f(y)=0; this gives a = f(0) <= y f(f(y)) + f(y). (The ceiling f(y) <= y+a used here comes from the SEPARATE substitution y=0, which gives f(x-a) <= x, i.e. f(y) <= y+a.) Combining the two: for y>0, y f(f(y)) >= a - f(y) >= a-(y+a) = -y, so f(f(y)) >= -1 for all y>0.

technique: Assume a value has the forbidden sign, then choose the free variable below a threshold proportional to the reciprocal of that value so a fixed lower bound collides with the linear right-hand side
how_used: To prove f(x) <= 0, suppose f(x)>0 for some x. Choose y below both x-a and (-a-x-1)/f(x). The ceiling makes x-f(y) >= x-(y+a) > 0, so the positive-side lower bound f >= -a-1 applies to f(x-f(y)); then the assumed inequality gives y f(x)+x >= f(x-f(y)) >= -a-1, and dividing by f(x)>0 yields y >= (-a-x-1)/f(x), contradicting the choice of y. Hence f(x) <= 0 everywhere; setting x=0 gives a <= 0, and the ceiling then upgrades to f(x) <= x for all x.

technique: Drive a free variable to infinity against a linearly-decaying upper bound to force a controlled quantity below any level, contradicting its fixed value
how_used: With f(x) <= 0 and f(x) <= x established, pick y>0 with y > -f(-1)-1 and set x = f(y)-1, so x-f(y) = -1. The assumed inequality gives f(-1) <= y f(f(y)-1) + f(y)-1; using f(y) <= 0 and f(t) <= t we get f(f(y)-1) <= -1, so y f(f(y)-1) <= -y, hence f(-1) <= -y-1, i.e. y <= -f(-1)-1, contradicting the choice of y.

technique: After negating the target inequality into a universal upper bound, substitute the argument that makes the inner and outer variables coincide so the composite term appears with a coefficient of free sign.
how_used: Negate the goal: assume f(x-f(y)) <= y f(x) + x for all x,y. Setting y=0 gives f(x-a) <= x, i.e. the affine ceiling f(t) <= t+a for all t (a=f(0)). Put x = f(y): the inner argument is f(y)-f(y)=0, so the left side is f(0)=a, giving a <= y f(f(y)) + f(y). Feeding in the ceiling f(y) <= y+a turns this into a <= y f(f(y)) + y + a, i.e. 0 <= y(f(f(y))+1). Since y>0 makes the factor positive, this forces f(f(y)) >= -1 for all y>0 — a lower bound on the composite that the negation alone did not provide.

technique: To upgrade a one-sided pointwise bound to a global sign constraint, assume a value of the wrong sign and drive the negated inequality to a contradiction by sending a free variable to infinity, using the affine ceiling to keep the substituted argument in the range where the pointwise bound holds.
how_used: To show f(x) <= 0 for all x, suppose f(x)>0 for some x. Choose y very negative (y < x-a and y < (-a-x-1)/f(x)). The ceiling f(y) <= y+a keeps x-f(y) >= x-(y+a) > 0, so the positive-argument bound f(t) >= -a-1 (established in the previous crux) applies to f(x-f(y)); combined with the negated inequality y f(x)+x >= f(x-f(y)) >= -a-1. Since f(x)>0, solving for y yields y >= (-a-x-1)/f(x), contradicting the choice of y. Hence f(x) <= 0 everywhere; setting x=0 gives a=f(0) <= 0, and the ceiling sharpens to f(x) <= x for all x.

technique: Close the contradiction by substituting the argument that fixes the composite outer value to a constant target while collapsing the free-variable term into a linear function whose slope has been pinned negative, forcing the free variable to be bounded.
how_used: With f(x) <= x and f(x) <= 0 established, pick y > 0 with y > -f(-1)-1 and set x = f(y)-1, so x - f(y) = -1. The negated inequality gives f(-1) = f(x-f(y)) <= y f(f(y)-1) + f(y) - 1. Using f(f(y)-1) <= f(y)-1 <= -1 (from f(t)<=t and f(t)<=0) the right side is <= y(f(y)-1) - 1 <= -y-1. So f(-1) <= -y-1, i.e. y <= -f(-1)-1, contradicting y > -f(-1)-1. This final contradiction refutes the negation and proves the original existence claim.

technique: Combine a two-sided sandwich on a composite value f(f(t)) — a lower bound from one substitution and the affine ceiling as the upper bound — to descend to a pointwise lower bound on f itself over a half-line.
how_used: From the composite floor f(f(y)) >= -1 for all y>0, and from the affine ceiling applied at the point f(y): f(f(y)) <= f(y) + a. Chaining the two gives -1 <= f(f(y)) <= f(y) + a, so f(y) >= -a-1 for all y>0. This converts a bound on the composite (values only in the range of f) into a bound on f at every positive argument — the load-bearing lemma the later contradiction feeds on.

technique: To pin a lower bound on a composite f(f(·)) that an upper-bound-only inequality never states, substitute the argument so the OUTER application of f lands on the fixed point f(0), collapsing it to the constant f(0) and leaving the composite trapped on the other side.
how_used: In the assumed inequality f(x-f(y)) <= y f(x)+x, set x = f(y). The outer argument becomes f(y)-f(y)=0, so LHS = f(0)=a, a constant independent of y. This gives a <= y f(f(y))+f(y). Combined with the already-derived affine ceiling f(y) <= y+a (from y=0), one gets a <= y f(f(y))+y+a, i.e. 0 <= y(f(f(y))+1), so f(f(y)) >= -1 for all y>0. This is the delicate lower bound on the composite that the upper-bound-only inequality does not otherwise expose.

technique: To rule out any positive value of an unknown function, pick the free variable extreme enough (here very negative) that it simultaneously keeps a substituted argument in the region where a positivity lower bound already holds AND drives the linear right-hand side below that bound, producing a contradiction.
how_used: Having f(f(y)) >= -1 and the ceiling f(y) <= y+a yield f(y) >= -a-1 for all y>0. Now suppose f(x)>0 for some x. Choose y satisfying both y < x-a and y < (-a-x-1)/f(x). The first choice makes x-f(y) >= x-(y+a) > 0, so f(x-f(y)) lands where the lower bound -a-1 applies; the second choice makes the RHS y f(x)+x < -a-1. Since f(x-f(y)) <= y f(x)+x this forces f(x-f(y)) < -a-1, contradicting the lower bound. Hence f(x) <= 0 for all x, and then x=0 gives a=f(0) <= 0, upgrading the ceiling to f(x) <= x for all x.

technique: Close the argument by plugging the (now proven) global sublinear bound f(t) <= t back into the original inequality via a substitution that makes the right-hand side a large negative multiple of the free variable, contradicting the fixed value of f at one point.
how_used: With f(x) <= x for all x (from the previous step), choose y > 0 large, in particular y > -f(-1)-1, and set x = f(y)-1. Then x - f(y) = -1, so LHS = f(-1). The RHS is y f(f(y)-1)+f(y)-1; using f(f(y)-1) <= f(y)-1 and f(y) <= y this is <= y(f(y)-1)-1 <= -y-1 (since f(y) <= 0). So f(-1) <= -y-1, i.e. y <= -f(-1)-1, contradicting the choice of y. This completes the contradiction and proves some (x,y) with f(x-f(y)) > y f(x)+x must exist.

technique: Telescope a fixed arithmetic-difference of a composed subsequence across the underlying gaps to bound each gap by that fixed difference.
how_used: Writing d_n = s_{n+1}-s_n, the AP condition gives s_{s_{n+1}} - s_{s_n} = D constant; expanding it as the sum of the gaps d_{s_n},...,d_{s_{n+1}-1} (exactly d_n of them, each >= 1) yields d_n <= D, so the gaps are bounded and m=min d_n, M=max d_n are attained.

technique: Bound one fixed total both above (length x max) via the minimal block and below (length x min) via the maximal block; the two-sided pinch forces equality and pins every term of an extremal block to the opposite extreme.
how_used: A block with d_n=m gives D <= mM; a block with d_n=M gives D >= Mm; hence D=mM and equality forces every gap inside a minimal block to equal M (so d_n=m => d_{s_n}=M) and every gap inside a maximal block to equal m (so d_n=M => d_{s_n}=m).

technique: Iterate an equality-forced implication into a strictly increasing orbit along which a quantity must alternate between two values, then contradict that against an independently-known arithmetic-progression structure of the same quantity.
how_used: d_n=m => d_{s_n}=M and d_n=M => d_{s_n}=m with s_n>n let one build increasing indices n_{k+1}=s_{n_k} along which d_{s_{n_k}} alternates M,m,M,...; but d_{s_1},d_{s_2},... is the termwise difference of the two given APs, hence itself an AP, which is monotone on increasing indices and cannot alternate unless m=M.

technique: Plug the diagonal-type substitutions that make the argument of f collapse onto a single expression, yielding a clean formula for f on that expression's range.
how_used: Setting (x,y)=(t,0) gives f(tf(t))=t^2, and (x,y)=(t,-t) combined with f(0)=0 gives f(-tf(t))=-t^2; these two identities are the engine: they show f is surjective onto all reals and that f(t)=0 forces t=0 (since f(t)=0 makes t^2=f(tf(t))=f(0)=0).

technique: To prove a value relation like oddness, engineer a substitution whose right side equals zero, then invoke the already-proven fact that f vanishes only at 0 to pin the argument.
how_used: For f(s)<0 write f(s)=-t^2, pick a with af(t)=s; substituting (x,y)=(t,a) gives f(tf(t+a))=f(s)+t^2=0, so tf(t+a)=0 forces t+a=0, whence s=-tf(t) and f(-s)=f(tf(t))=t^2=-f(s). A parallel construction with (x,y)=(t,a-t) handles f(s)>0, establishing f(-x)=-f(x).

technique: Sum a cyclic triple of substitutions of the same shifted-argument triple so the unwanted mixed terms cancel and leave a bilinear formula for f.
how_used: Substituting (s,t),(t,-s-t),(-s-t,s), rewriting the last two with oddness, gives three equations in f(tf(s)), f(sf(s+t)), f((s+t)f(t)); adding them cancels those three unknowns pairwise to leave 2f(tf(s))=2ts, so f(tf(s))=ts. Fixing s with f(s)=1 gives f(x)=sx, and the original equation forces s=+/-1.

technique: Replace a constant term in a fraction's numerator by a homogeneous expression that the constraint bounds it below by, turning a mixed inequality into a scale-invariant homogeneous one
how_used: The constraint a^2+b^2+c^2+(a+b+c)^2<=4 is rewritten as a^2+b^2+c^2+ab+bc+ca<=2, so each '+1' in the numerator (doubled to '+2') is bounded below by that quadratic form Q, making every term homogeneous of degree 0

technique: Recognize a symmetric quadratic combination as a product of two sums of shifted variables to collapse the numerator into a perfect factorization
how_used: The homogenized numerator 2ab + (a^2+b^2+c^2+ab+bc+ca) is regrouped as (a+b)^2 + (c+a)(c+b), which after dividing by (a+b)^2 gives 1 + (c+a)(c+b)/(a+b)^2

technique: Bound a cyclic sum of ratios below by AM-GM, exploiting that the product of the ratios collapses to 1
how_used: Sum of (c+a)(c+b)/(a+b)^2 over cyclic terms is bounded by 3 times the cube root of their product; the product equals prod(c+a)(c+b) over prod(a+b)^2 = [(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)]^2 over the same, hence 1, giving bound 3 and total 6 (so >=3 after halving)

technique: Equate two substitutions that hit the same f(f(...)) argument to cancel the outer application and get a relation among inner values
how_used: Set (a=0,b=n+1) and (a=1,b=n): both give f(f(n+1)), so f(0)+2f(n+1)=f(2)+2f(n), yielding f(n+1)-f(n)=(f(2)-f(0))/2 constant, which over Z forces f linear f(n)=Mn+K.

technique: Plug the proven linear form back into the original equation and factor the resulting polynomial identity in the leading coefficient
how_used: Substitute f(n)=Mn+K into f(2a)+2f(b)=f(f(a+b)) to get (M-2)(M(a+b)+K)=0 for all a,b, forcing M=2 (any K) or M=K=0, giving f(n)=2n+K and f(n)=0.

technique: Write each variable as a convex combination of the two extreme values and bound its square by the same convex combination of the squares of the extremes
how_used: Each u_i = x_i a + y_i b with x_i,y_i>=0, x_i+y_i=1. Convexity of t^2 gives x_i a^2 + y_i b^2 - u_i^2 = x_i y_i (a-b)^2 >= 0, so u_i^2 <= x_i a^2 + y_i b^2. Summing, 1 <= X a^2 + Y b^2 with X=sum x_i, Y=sum y_i. The two linear constraints X+Y=2019 and (from sum u_i=0) |a|X = bY pin X=2019 b/(|a|+b), Y=2019|a|/(|a|+b), giving X a^2 + Y b^2 = 2019|a|b = -2019ab.

technique: Bound each squared term by the term times the extreme value on its side, then use a sum-balance identity to re-express one side's linear sum as the other's and re-bound it by count times the opposite extreme
how_used: Split indices into P={u_i>0} (size p) and N={u_i<=0} (size n), p+n=2019. On P, 0<u_i<=b gives u_i^2<=b*u_i; on N, |u_i|<=|a|=-a gives u_i^2<=|a|*|u_i|. The vanishing sum condition gives the balance sum_P u_i = sum_N |u_i|. Then sum_P u_i^2 <= b*sum_P u_i = b*sum_N|u_i| <= b*n|a| = -nab, and symmetrically sum_N u_i^2 <= |a|*sum_N|u_i| = |a|*sum_P u_i <= |a|*pb = -pab; adding gives 1 <= -(p+n)ab = -2019ab, i.e. ab <= -1/2019.

technique: When a distinguished subset is optimal, test a single boundary exchange (drop one element, add an adjacent one) and force the exchange not to improve the objective, reading off an inequality on the two swapped terms
how_used: With X minimising |Δ| where Δ=Σ_{X^c}a−Σ_X a≥0, if there is an adjacent straddling pair j∈X, j+1∈X^c, then swapping to X∪{j+1}∖{j} changes Δ by −2(a_{j+1}−a_j); minimality forbids this from strictly shrinking |Δ|, forcing a_{j+1}−a_j ≥ Δ, the gap inequality that lets a purely local perturbation absorb the whole imbalance. The SAME swap trick with the singleton exchange X∪{1} (adding index 1 when X=[k,n]) forces a_1 ≥ Δ.

technique: Reduce an exact-target constraint to a homogeneous balance/equality constraint by allowing a free positive global rescaling, so only the ratio of the two sides need be arranged, not the absolute total
how_used: Instead of directly building b_i with Σb=2 and Σ_X b=1, build any strictly increasing positive c_i with Σ_X c=Σ_{X^c}c, then set b_i=2c_i/Σ_j c_j; rescaling preserves strict increase, positivity and the equal-halves property while forcing total 2 and Σ_X b=1. Every later construction can then ignore the total and only equalize the two halves.

technique: Equalize two group-sums by a monotonicity-preserving local perturbation that pushes exactly the two boundary coordinates toward each other by half the surplus, using an ordering slack to keep strict increase and positivity
how_used: Given the straddling pair with a_{j+1}−a_j≥Δ, set b_j=a_j+Δ/2, b_{j+1}=a_{j+1}−Δ/2 (rest fixed): Σ_X gains Δ/2, Σ_{X^c} loses Δ/2, so the halves equalize with no scaling needed. Strictness b_j<b_{j+1} holds when the gap strictly exceeds Δ; the boundary gap=Δ is repaired by shifting a tiny ε into/out of a third index (available since n≥3) on the correct side (in X or X^c) to break the tie while keeping the equality.

technique: Rule out a dominance relation between an optimal set and its complement by exhibiting an intermediate set strictly between them in a suffix-count (majorization) order, then convert incomparability into prefix-count threshold constraints on the set
how_used: Order sets by X⪯Y iff |X∩[i,n]|≤|Y∩[i,n]| for all i (equivalently a value-dominating injection, so X⪯Y ⇒ Σ_X a≤Σ_Y a). If X≺X^c, insert Y=(largest of X^c)∪(X minus its largest): then Σ_X a<Σ_Y a<Σ_{X^c}a gives |1−Σ_Y|<|1−Σ_X|, contradicting minimality; symmetrically not X^c≺X. Incomparability yields thresholds |X∩[k,n]|>(n−k+1)/2 and |X∩[ℓ,n]|<(n−ℓ+1)/2, a purely combinatorial characterisation of minimising X from which an explicit strictly-increasing (b_i) with equal halves can be solved directly.

technique: Dispose of the exceptional configuration where the optimal set has no interior boundary — it is a top suffix — by perturbing only its two extreme coordinates symmetrically, using a minimality-exchange bound to license the downward move of the smallest one
how_used: When no adjacent straddling pair exists (no j with j in X, j+1 in X^c), X must be a top suffix [k,n], with 1 in X^c and n in X, and WLOG Delta = Sum_{X^c} - Sum_X > 0. The one-element exchange bound applied to X and X∪{1}: adding 1 to X changes Delta to Delta - 2a_1, and minimality of |Delta| forces |Delta - 2a_1| >= Delta, hence a_1 >= Delta. Then set b_1 = a_1 - Delta/2, b_n = a_n + Delta/2, all others fixed: Sum_X gains Delta/2 (n in X) and Sum_{X^c} loses Delta/2 (1 in X^c), equalizing the halves so Sum_X b = Sum_{X^c} b = 1. Positivity of b_1 holds because a_1 >= Delta > Delta/2; monotonicity survives since b_1 only moves down below b_2 and b_n only moves up above b_{n-1}, and n>=3 keeps positions 1 and n distinct. This covers exactly the top-heavy case (e.g. X={n}) that the interior-pair perturbation cannot reach.

technique: Recast a sum over a hard-to-control subset of pairs as minus the sum over the complementary subset, using that the full ordered double-sum of products vanishes
how_used: Since Σ_{1≤i,j≤n} a_i a_j = (Σ a_i)^2 = 0, split all ordered pairs into the 'far' set B (|a_i−a_j|≥1, no sign control on a_i a_j) and the 'near' set C (|a_i−a_j|<1, includes all diagonals). Then Σ_B = −Σ_C, and the target Σ_A = (1/2)Σ_B, so proving Σ_A<0 is equivalent to proving the near-pairs sum Σ_C>0.

technique: Lower-bound a sum of pairwise products by discarding cross-terms whose sign is unfavorable and completing the surviving inner block into a perfect square
how_used: Split indices into P (a_i≤−1), Q (−1<a_i≤0), R (0<a_i<1), S (a_i≥1). All pairs within Q∪R are near (both lie in (−1,1)); each diagonal contributes a_i^2 to Σ_C. Keep the diagonal squares of P∪S and the full ordered block over Q∪R, drop the remaining near cross-terms: Σ_C ≥ Σ_{P∪S} a_i^2 + Σ_{i,j∈Q∪R} a_i a_j = Σ_{P∪S} a_i^2 + (Σ_{Q∪R} a_i)^2 ≥ 0. (Dropping is valid because any opposite-sign straddling pair across the |a|=1 boundary automatically has |a_i−a_j|≥1, hence is far and never in Σ_C, so every near cross-term dropped is nonnegative.)

technique: Upgrade a chained ≥0 bound to strict by reading off BOTH equality conditions of the two bounding steps and showing they jointly force the hypothesis you assumed false
how_used: Equality in the discard step forces no far pair WITHIN Q∪R (all pairs there near); equality in the square step forces Σ_{P∪S} a_i^2=0, i.e. P=S=∅ (any a_i≤−1 or ≥1 gives a_i^2≥1>0). Combined: all indices lie in Q∪R AND every pair within Q∪R is near ⟹ every pair is near ⟹ A=∅, contradicting A≠∅. Hence Σ_C>0 strictly and Σ_A<0. (P=S=∅ alone does NOT force all pairs near — e.g. 0.6,−0.6 both in Q∪R differ by 1.2 — so the first step's equality condition is essential.)

technique: Lower-bound a sum restricted to a threshold-defined pair set by a sum of squares, justifying the discard by a term-by-term sign domination rather than by claiming set membership of every kept term
how_used: After reducing the goal to Σ_C > 0 (Σ_C over ALL ordered pairs (i,j), diagonals included, with |a_i−a_j|<1, using ½Σ_B = Σ_A and Σ_B = 0 − Σ_C since Σ over all pairs = (Σa_i)^2 = 0), partition indices by P={a_i≤−1}, Q={−1<a_i≤0}, R={0<a_i<1}, S={a_i≥1}. Lower-bound Σ_C ≥ Σ_{i∈P∪S} a_i^2 + Σ_{i,j∈Q∪R} a_i a_j = Σ_{P∪S} a_i^2 + (Σ_{Q∪R} a_i)^2 ≥ 0. The discard is NOT validated by claiming every Q∪R pair lies in C (false: a_i=0.6, a_j=−0.6 gives |diff|=1.2), but term-by-term: every positive product on the RHS also appears in Σ_C (the diagonals a_i^2 for i∈P∪S are always in C; same-sign Q∪R products, being both within a unit band on one side of 0, automatically have |diff|<1 so lie in C), and every negative product on the RHS (opposite-sign Q∪R pairs) also appears on the LHS Σ_C. So Σ_C − RHS is a nonnegative remainder.

technique: Upgrade a non-strict chained bound to strict by intersecting the equality conditions of BOTH discard steps and showing their conjunction forces the excluded hypothesis (contrapositive).
how_used: The chain Σ_C ≥ Σ_{P∪S} a_i² + (Σ_{Q∪R} a_i)² ≥ 0 gives only Σ_C ≥ 0, while A nonempty demands Σ_C > 0. Record BOTH equality conditions and use them TOGETHER: (i) equality in the SECOND inequality (SOS block = 0) forces Σ_{P∪S} a_i² = 0, i.e. P=S=∅, so every index lies in Q∪R; (ii) equality in the FIRST (term-domination) inequality forces every retained Q∪R pair to actually lie in C, i.e. |a_i−a_j|<1 for all i,j∈Q∪R. Conjoin: with P=S=∅ every index is in Q∪R, and by (ii) every pair then has |a_i−a_j|<1, so no pair meets the |diff|≥1 threshold, i.e. A=∅. Contrapositive: A nonempty ⟹ at least one inequality is strict ⟹ Σ_C>0. The single-condition shortcut 'P=S=∅ ⟹ A=∅' is FALSE (a=(0.6,−0.6) has P=S=∅ yet A nonempty); condition (i) alone does not close it — condition (ii) supplies the |diff|<1 on every remaining pair.

technique: Convert a sum of pairwise products over an index subset into (minus) the sum over the complementary subset by invoking the vanishing of the total square.
how_used: Set B = {(i,j): 1≤i,j≤n (ordered), |a_i−a_j|≥1} and C its ordered-pair complement, so Σ_A a_ia_j = ½Σ_B a_ia_j. Since Σa_i=0, the full ordered square vanishes: (Σa_i)² = Σ_{1≤i,j≤n} a_ia_j = 0. Splitting that full square as Σ_B + Σ_C gives Σ_B a_ia_j = 0 − Σ_C a_ia_j. Hence Σ_A a_ia_j = −½ Σ_C a_ia_j, and proving Σ_A < 0 is EXACTLY equivalent to proving the complementary sum Σ_C a_ia_j > 0 (where Σ_C runs over ALL ordered pairs including i=j, i.e. it contains the diagonal Σa_i²). This reframing is what turns a mixed-sign sum over the 'far' pairs A into a positivity statement about the 'near' pairs C plus diagonal, which is then amenable to a sum-of-squares bound.

technique: Choose a sign/threshold partition of the indices so a lower bound follows by term-domination: retain every same-class pair (whose contribution has a controlled sign and is guaranteed to survive), discard the out-of-class pairs (which only drop nonnegative contributions), and group one super-class into a single perfect square.
how_used: Partition the indices by the unit-threshold sign classes P={a_i≤−1}, Q={−1<a_i≤0}, R={0<a_i<1}, S={1≤a_i}. Claim Σ_C a_ia_j ≥ Σ_{i∈P∪S} a_i² + Σ_{i,j∈Q∪R} a_ia_j. Justification is pure term-domination: every product on the RHS that is POSITIVE (the diagonal squares a_i² for i∈P∪S, and Q·R-type products that are actually negative appear on the LHS too) is also present on the LHS, and every NEGATIVE product on the LHS is also present on the RHS — because any two indices both in Q∪R differ by <1 (all lie in (−1,1)) so their pair is in C and its (possibly negative) product is genuinely in Σ_C. Then collapse the Q∪R block: Σ_{i,j∈Q∪R} a_ia_j = (Σ_{i∈Q∪R} a_i)² (routine completing-the-square over the full ordered block). This yields Σ_C ≥ Σ_{P∪S} a_i² + (Σ_{Q∪R} a_i)² ≥ 0. The load-bearing design choice is the threshold at ±1 and 0: it makes same-class = within-distance-1 (so in C) and isolates the ≥1-magnitude indices (P,S) whose squares are the only large positive reservoir.

technique: Shift a variable to move the fixed point of an involution to the origin, converting an awkward reflection symmetry into evenness in the shifted variable.
how_used: Weak symmetry P(x,y,z)=P(x,y,xy-z) is a reflection fixing z=xy/2; setting P_1(x,y,z)=P(x,y,z+xy/2) makes P_1 even in z, hence a polynomial in x,y,z^2, which back-substitutes to show P is a polynomial in x,y and the invariant z(xy-z).

technique: Re-expand a polynomial in a nonlinear generating invariant and read off the top-degree part from the leading terms of each summand to constrain highest-degree monomial exponents.
how_used: Writing P=sum mu_{ijk} x^i y^j (z(xy-z))^k, each summand of maximal weight i+j+3k=m contributes an uncancellable leading term x^{i+k}y^{j+k}z^k, so every top-total-degree monomial mu x^a y^b z^c of a weakly symmetric P satisfies a,b>=c.

technique: Peel off the leading term with a known invariant raised to the matching power, dropping the total degree so induction on degree closes the representability claim.
how_used: Intersecting a,b>=c with the cyclic variants a,c>=b and b,c>=a forces a unique leading monomial mu(xyz)^c; subtracting mu(xyz-x^2-y^2-z^2)^c gives a lower-degree symmetric P_0, and induction on deg P expresses P as a polynomial in xyz-x^2-y^2-z^2.

technique: Build the existence witness as a 2-adic-valuation function so the functional equation reduces to a parity/valuation case-split with a single small fibre
how_used: Take f(0)=0 and f(x)=largest power of 2 dividing 2x (so f(2x)=2f(x) and every nonzero value is a positive even power of 2). Then X_0={0} is finite nonempty, making 0 f-rare; the FE f(f(x+y)+y)=f(f(x)+y) need only be checked when x or y is odd, where all values are even and both sides equal 2.

technique: After iterating the relation into an arithmetic-progression family, substitute the free variable to hit an extremal element of a finite fibre and read off one-sided monotonicity from that extremum
how_used: Iterating gives f(f(x+ky)+y)=f(f(x)+y). With a=min X_v, set y=a-f(x): the RHS lands in X_v, forcing f(x+k(a-f(x)))+a-f(x) in X_v, and since a is the minimum this yields f(x+k(a-f(x)))>=f(x) for all k. Using b=max X_v symmetrically gives f(x+k(b-f(x)))<=f(x).

technique: Multiply the two opposing progression step-sizes into a common difference on which both one-sided inequalities apply, forcing equality and an infinite constant progression inside a fibre
how_used: With common difference (a-f(x))(b-f(x)) both the min-inequality and max-inequality hold, giving f(x+k(a-f(x))(b-f(x)))=f(x). When f(x) is neither a nor b this step is nonzero, so X_{f(x)} contains a nondegenerate AP and is infinite; hence the only values whose fibre can be finite are a and b.

technique: Force a function to be constant on a nondegenerate arithmetic progression by squeezing between a matched pair of one-sided inequalities, each obtained by substituting so that a value lands in an extremal (min/max) fibre element.
how_used: Iterating the FE gives f(f(x+ky)+y)=f(f(x)+y) for all x,y,k. Fix an f-rare v with X_v finite; let a=min X_v, b=max X_v. Substituting y=a-f(x) makes the RHS f(a)=v, so f(x+k(a-f(x)))-f(x)+a in X_v; minimality of a forces f(x+k(a-f(x)))>=f(x) for all x,k. Symmetrically b=max X_v gives f(x+k(b-f(x)))<=f(x). Since these one-sided bounds telescope along multiples of their steps, taking common difference (a-f(x))(b-f(x)) (a multiple of both) makes both hold, so f(x+k(a-f(x))(b-f(x)))=f(x). If f(x) is neither a nor b the AP is nondegenerate, so X_{f(x)} is infinite. Hence only a,b (the two extremes of X_v) can be f-rare.

technique: In a functional equation, choose the free variable so a forced membership in a finite fibre becomes a one-sided inequality: set the shift equal to (extreme fibre element) minus (current value), so the argument that must land in the fibre is bounded on one side by that extreme element.
how_used: From the iterated relation f(f(x+ky)+y)=f(f(x)+y) (valid for all k, by substituting x+ky for x), pick an f-rare value v with finite fibre X_v and let a=min X_v. Substituting y=a-f(x) makes f(x)+y=a, so the inner argument f(x+k(a-f(x)))-f(x)+a must lie in X_v for all k; since a is the LEAST element of X_v this forces f(x+k(a-f(x))) >= f(x) for every k. Doing the same with b=max X_v gives the reverse inequality f(x+k(b-f(x))) <= f(x). So along the AP through x with common difference a-f(x), f is minimized at x; along the AP with common difference b-f(x), maximized at x.

technique: When two extremal choices give opposite one-sided bounds along two arithmetic progressions through the same point, step by a common multiple of both common differences so both bounds apply simultaneously and collapse into exact invariance of the function along that progression.
how_used: The inequalities f(x+k(a-f(x)))>=f(x) and f(x+k(b-f(x)))<=f(x) are combined by using the common difference (a-f(x))(b-f(x)), a multiple of both a-f(x) and b-f(x); along that progression both bounds apply, forcing f(x+k(a-f(x))(b-f(x)))=f(x) for all k. If f(x) is neither a nor b, both factors are nonzero, so this is a nondegenerate AP on which f is constant equal to f(x); hence X_{f(x)} is infinite. Contrapositive: an integer x can have finite fibre X_{f(x)} only if f(x) is a or b, so the only possible f-rare values are a and b.

technique: To force a set of candidate extremal witnesses to collapse to a single object, use that each witness is itself a preimage of the target value: it maps to the target, so any candidate that must equal a witness inherits the fixed-point relation and is pinned to the one value.
how_used: The two candidate f-rare values are a=min X_v and b=max X_v, and both lie in X_v, so f(a)=f(b)=v. The starting f-rare v is one of a,b, hence f(v)=v. Now any second f-rare integer v' is also forced (by the collapse crux) to lie in {a,b}, so f(v')=v (as a,b map to v under f); but the fixed-point relation forces f(v')=v', giving v'=v. Thus the f-rare integer is unique, proving (b). Note: the resolution of the solver's worry — 'why don't a and b give two distinct rare values' — is exactly that a and b are preimages of the SAME value v, so any rare value pinned to {a,b} equals v.

technique: Substitute a special argument into a two-term functional equation to force a reflection symmetry that merges the two terms into one
how_used: Setting y=1 (after deriving f(1)=1 from x=a,y=1) turns f(x)f(1)+f(a/x)f(a/1)=2f(x) into f(x)+f(a/x)=2f(x), giving the symmetry f(x)=f(a/x); this collapses f(x)f(y)+f(a/x)f(a/y)=2f(xy) into the multiplicative equation f(x)f(y)=f(xy)

technique: Pair the reflection symmetry with multiplicativity at complementary arguments whose product is fixed to pin the squared value
how_used: Using f(x)=f(a/x) and f(x)f(y)=f(xy) at y=a/x gives f(x)^2=f(x)f(a/x)=f(x·a/x)=f(a)=1, so f(x)=±1 pointwise

technique: Evaluate a multiplicative function on a square root to force a nonnegative value and eliminate the negative sign branch
how_used: Writing x=√x·√x and applying f(x)f(y)=f(xy) gives f(x)=f(√x)^2=(±1)^2=1, ruling out f(x)=-1 and forcing the constant solution f≡1

technique: Substitute the argument that zeroes the floor coefficient on one side, collapsing the functional equation into a scalar constraint on the floor of the output
how_used: Set x=0 so [x]=0, giving f(0)=f(0)[f(y)] for all y; when f(0) != 0 this forces [f(y)]=1 for all y, the equation degenerates to f([x]y)=f(x), and y=0 then gives f constant =C with [C]=1, i.e. 1<=C<2.

technique: Use a hypothesized nonzero value inside the interval where the floor of the argument vanishes to force the floor of every output to zero, then a floor-stripping substitution collapses the function to zero for a contradiction
how_used: In the f(0)=0 case, if some f(alpha) != 0 with 0<alpha<1 then [alpha]=0, so x=alpha gives 0=f(0)=f(alpha)[f(y)], forcing [f(y)]=0 for all y; then x=1 turns f(y)=f(1)[f(y)] into f(y)=0 for all y, contradicting f(alpha) != 0.

technique: Rescale an arbitrary real by an integer multiplier into the interval where the function is already known to vanish, then invert through the floor identity to propagate the zero value everywhere
how_used: In the complementary subcase f=0 on [0,1), for any real z pick integer N (=[z]+1 if z>=0, else [z]-1) so alpha=z/N in [0,1); since [N]=N, f(z)=f([N]alpha)=f(N)[f(alpha)]=0, extending f identically 0 to all of R.

technique: Complete a mixed cubic-quartic power-sum expression into a shifted single fourth-power sum plus lower-degree symmetric sums, then substitute the shift as new variables so the constraints collapse the lower-degree terms to constants
how_used: Use 4x^3 - x^4 = -(x-1)^4 + 6x^2 - 4x + 1 (check by expanding -(x-1)^4 = -x^4+4x^3-6x^2+4x-1). Summing over a,b,c,d and plugging sum a^2=12, sum a=6 gives 4(sum a^3)-(sum a^4) = -sum(a-1)^4 + 52. Setting x=a-1 etc., the constraint becomes sum x^2 = sum a^2 - 2 sum a + 4 = 4, and the target 36 <= 52 - sum x^4 <= 48 is exactly 4 <= sum x^4 <= 16.

technique: Lower-bound a sum of fourth powers by the square of the sum of squares over the count, via the power-mean (or Cauchy-Schwarz) inequality on the constrained second-power sum
how_used: With sum x^2=4 fixed over 4 variables, power mean gives sum x^4 >= (sum x^2)^2 / 4 = 16/4 = 4, i.e. expr <= 48 (tight at x=(1,1,1,-1), a=(2,2,2,0)).

technique: Upper-bound a sum of fourth powers by the square of the sum of squares, by expanding that square and discarding the nonnegative sum of cross products of squares.
how_used: After the shift x_i = a_i - 1 (so sum x^2 = 4 and the target equals 52 - sum x^4), write (sum x^2)^2 = sum x^4 + sum_{i!=j} x_i^2 x_j^2. The cross-term sum is nonnegative, so sum x^4 <= (sum x^2)^2 = 16, giving 4(sum a^3) - sum a^4 = 52 - sum x^4 >= 36. Equality when all cross products vanish (at most one x_i nonzero): x=(2,0,0,0), a=(3,1,1,1).

technique: Recenter a symmetric power-sum inequality by shifting every variable by the common mean, turning the constraints into a single centered second-moment condition.
how_used: Substitute x=a-1, y=b-1, z=c-1, t=d-1. Then 4(sum a^3)-sum a^4 = 52 - (x^4+y^4+z^4+t^4), and the two given constraints collapse to the single usable one x^2+y^2+z^2+t^2 = (sum a^2)-2(sum a)+4 = 12-12+4 = 4. The whole double inequality becomes 4 <= sum x^4 <= 16, a clean problem in the shifted variables governed by their fixed sum of squares.

technique: Lower-bound a sum of fourth powers by (sum of squares)^2 over the count, via the power-mean / Cauchy-Schwarz inequality on the squared terms.
how_used: For the upper endpoint 4(sum a^3)-sum a^4 <= 48, i.e. 52 - sum x^4 <= 48, one needs sum x^4 >= 4. Apply power mean (or Cauchy-Schwarz) to the four numbers x_i^2: sum (x_i^2)^2 >= (sum x_i^2)^2 / 4 = 16/4 = 4. Equality when all x_i^2 are equal (|x_i|=1), corresponding to a=(0,2,2,2). This delivers ONLY the 48 side.

technique: Upper-bound a sum of fourth powers by the square of the sum of squares, discarding the nonnegative cross-term of the expanded square.
how_used: After the shift x_i = a_i - 1 turns the target into E = 52 - sum x^4 (using the identity 4a^3 - a^4 = -(a-1)^4 + 6a^2 - 4a + 4 summed over the four variables, with the constraints giving sum x^2 = 4), the lower endpoint E >= 36 reduces to sum x^4 <= 16. Expand (x^2+y^2+z^2+t^2)^2 = (sum x^4) + q with q = 2 sum_{i<j} x_i^2 x_j^2 >= 0; dropping q gives sum x^4 <= (sum x^2)^2 = 4^2 = 16, hence E >= 52 - 16 = 36. Equality forces q = 0, i.e. exactly one x_i nonzero (= 2), corresponding to a = (3,1,1,1). No interval bound on the variables is needed for this direction.

technique: Partition a cyclic sum of products into consecutive blocks aligned to a parity pattern so each block can be bounded independently.
how_used: The 100-term cyclic sum was regrouped into 50 blocks each of the form x_{2i-1}x_{2i+1}+x_{2i}x_{2i+2} (odd-indexed cross-term plus even-indexed cross-term), matching the alternating extremal configuration x_{odd}=1/2, x_{even}=0.

technique: Use two separate constraint instances to replace two different factors in a block by the same slack expression, collapsing it to a single-variable product.
how_used: Within a block, x_{2i-1}\le 1-x_{2i}-x_{2i+1} (from constraint at 2i-1) and x_{2i+2}\le 1-x_{2i}-x_{2i+1} (from constraint at 2i) were both substituted, turning x_{2i-1}x_{2i+1}+x_{2i}x_{2i+2} into (x_{2i}+x_{2i+1})(1-x_{2i}-x_{2i+1}), a product of a quantity and its complement bounded by AM-GM at 1/4.

technique: After a termwise constraint substitution, rewrite the leftover cross-term-plus-square combination as a global sum of squares to expose a single scalar aggregate.
how_used: Bounding x_{i+2}\le 1-x_i-x_{i+1} gave \sum x_i-\sum x_i^2-\sum x_i x_{i+1}, which was recognized as \sum x_i-\tfrac12\sum(x_i+x_{i+1})^2; power-mean on \sum(x_i+x_{i+1})^2 reduced everything to a function of the single quantity \sum x_i, then maximized by AM-GM.

technique: Group the partial-sum terms into blocks of the recursion's branching factor and collapse each block back to a scaled copy of the sum at the halved index
how_used: Bundling four consecutive terms x_{4k-3..4k} using the derived pairings x_{4k-3}=-x_{4k-2} and x_{4k-1}=x_{4k}=x_k, so each block contributes 2x_k and S_{4k}=2S_k (and S_{4k+2}=S_{4k}); this self-similar recursion on S is what drives the whole induction and reduces the residue-0/2 cases immediately.

technique: Track a parity invariant of the partial sum to promote a weak nonneg bound into a strict lower bound of at least the parity value
how_used: Using S_n ≡ n (mod 2): when k is odd, S_{4k}=2S_k is even but S_k is odd hence ≥1, so S_{4k}≥2, and S_{4k+1}=S_{4k}+x_{4k+1}≥2-1=1 clears the otherwise-troublesome x_{4k+1}=-1 case.

technique: In an induction on partial sums, re-express a stubborn term via the sequence's own defining relations to fold it into a symmetric sum of two smaller partial sums
how_used: For the k-even sub-case, rewriting x_{4k+1}=x_{2k+1}=x_{k+1} so S_{4k+1}=2S_k+x_{k+1}=S_k+S_{k+1}, expressing the target as a sum of two already-nonnegative partial sums with no parity or slack needed.

technique: Evaluate one target quantity two ways through different substitution paths, then cancel via injectivity to force a structural identity
how_used: Compute f(f(xy)^2) both as (xy)^3 f(xy) using the y=1 relation f(f(x)^2)=x^3 f(x) with x->xy, and as f(f(x)^2 f(y)^2) by substituting x->xy in the equation and reapplying the y=1 relation to the pair (y, f(x)^2); first establish injectivity of f from x^3 = f(f(x)^2)/f(x). Injectivity then strips the outer f to give f(xy)^2 = f(x)^2 f(y)^2, i.e. f is multiplicative.

technique: Feed a newly proven regularity property back into the original equation to split a composite argument and solve for the iterate f(f(x))
how_used: Using multiplicativity, rewrite the original f(f(x)^2 y)=x^3 f(xy) as f(f(x))^2 f(y) = x^3 f(x) f(y); cancel the common positive f(y) to get f(f(x))^2 = x^3 f(x), hence f(f(x)) = sqrt(x^3 f(x)). Multiplicativity is exactly what lets f(f(x)^2) become f(f(x))^2 (the square pulled out of the argument), producing the square-root iterate relation that feeds the g-substitution.

technique: Introduce an auxiliary product g(x)=x f(x) so the equation's iterate becomes a clean self-map power law
how_used: Set g(x)=x f(x). Using multiplicativity and f(f(x))=sqrt(x^3 f(x)), compute g(g(x)) = g(x f(x)) = x f(x) * f(x f(x)) = x f(x)^2 f(f(x)) = x f(x)^2 * sqrt(x^3 f(x)) = (x f(x))^{5/2} = g(x)^{5/2}; by induction the (n+1)-fold iterate g^{(n+1)}(x) equals g(x)^{(5/2)^n}.

technique: Force a rational value to 1 by requiring an irrational-base power of it to stay rational for all n via integrality of prime exponents
how_used: Since g^{(n+1)}(x) = g(x)^{(5/2)^n} must be rational (g maps Q^+ to Q^+) for every n, writing g(x) = prod p_i^{alpha_i} forces each (5/2)^n * alpha_i to be an integer; for large n, 2^n does not divide alpha_i unless alpha_i = 0, so g(x) = 1, i.e. x f(x) = 1, giving f(x) = 1/x. Verify f(x)=1/x satisfies the original equation.

technique: Derive injectivity of an unknown function by writing the value at one substitution as a strictly monotone (here strictly-power) function of the argument, so equal outputs force equal inputs
how_used: Substitute y=1 into f(f(x)^2 y)=x^3 f(xy) to get f(f(x)^2)=x^3 f(x). Then for any x,y with f(x)=f(y): f(x)^2=f(y)^2 so f(f(x)^2)=f(f(y)^2), and by the y=1 relation these equal x^3 f(x) and y^3 f(y). Cancelling the equal factor f(x)=f(y) gives x^3=y^3, hence x=y over Q+. So f is injective, the lever that later turns f(A)=f(B) into A=B.

technique: Prove multiplicativity by producing two substitutions that make f agree on two arguments, then invoke injectivity to equate the arguments
how_used: Replace x by xy in f(f(x)^2)=x^3 f(x) to get f(f(xy)^2)=(xy)^3 f(xy). Rewrite (xy)^3 f(xy)=y^3(x^3 f(xy))=y^3 f(f(x)^2 y) via the original equation, then apply the original again with (a,b)=(y,f(x)^2): f(f(y)^2 f(x)^2)=y^3 f(f(x)^2 y). Chaining gives f(f(xy)^2)=f(f(x)^2 f(y)^2); injectivity yields f(xy)^2=f(x)^2 f(y)^2, and positivity gives f(xy)=f(x)f(y). Also f(1)=1 and f(x^n)=f(x)^n.

technique: Absorb the argument together with its factor into a single new function so a relation of the form f(f(x))=(known expression) becomes a clean self-composition of that new function.
how_used: After multiplicativity gives f(f(x))=sqrt(x^3 f(x)), set g(x)=x f(x) (also multiplicative). Then g(g(x))=g(x)*f(g(x))=x f(x)*f(x)f(f(x))=x f(x)^2*sqrt(x^3 f(x))=(x f(x))^{5/2}=g(x)^{5/2}. So g satisfies the pure self-iteration g(g(x))=g(x)^{5/2}, and by induction the (n+1)-fold iterate of g equals g(x)^{(5/2)^n}.

technique: When every iterate of a rational-valued map is forced to be a fixed base raised to a geometrically growing rational exponent, compare prime-factorization exponents: an exponent whose denominator's prime power grows without bound can never stay integral, forcing the base to 1.
how_used: The (n+1)-fold iterate of g equals g(x)^{(5/2)^n}, and every iterate is a value of g, hence in Q+. Writing g(x)=prod p_i^{alpha_i}, the exponent (5/2)^n * alpha_i = 5^n alpha_i / 2^n must be an integer for all n; since 2^n cannot divide the fixed integer alpha_i for large n, every alpha_i=0. Thus g(x)=1, giving f(x)=1/x; verify f(x)=1/x satisfies f(f(x)^2 y)=x^3 f(xy).

technique: Iterate a +1 functional relation along the other map's orbit to turn single steps into a +k jump, then use a minimal attained value to force surjectivity onto a tail
how_used: From f(g(n))=f(n)+1, induction gives f(g^k(x))=f(x)+k, and symmetrically g(f^k(x))=g(x)+k. Taking a=min f attained at n_f and b=min g attained at n_g, the values f(g^k(n_f))=a+k show f attains every integer in N_f={a,a+1,...}, and likewise g attains every integer in N_g={b,b+1,...}. This tail-surjectivity is what later lets any target value be written as a shifted image.

technique: Cross-substitute the paired functional equations to make the two fibers coincide, giving an equivalence of level sets, then feed the images back in to get injectivity on the value-set
how_used: Since g(f(x))=g(x)+1, f(x)=f(y) forces g(f(x))=g(f(y)) hence g(x)=g(y), and conversely; define x~y iff f(x)=f(y) (equiv. g(x)=g(y)). Applying this at the points f(x),f(y): if f(x)~f(y) then g(f(x))=g(f(y)) so g(x)=g(y), i.e. x~y (Claim 1). Consequently each ~class meets the value-set N_f (and N_g) in at most one element.

technique: Express a target functional value as a shifted image f(g(...)) of a smaller value, then collapse via the value-set injectivity to force two arguments equal
how_used: WLOG a<=b. Since f(a)>=a+1, pick x with f(a)=f(x)+1=f(g(x)), so a~g(x); as g(x)>=b>=a and both a,g(x) would be elements of N_f in one ~class, Claim 1 forces a=g(x)>=b, giving a=b. The same move written twice deep (f(a)=f(x)+2=f(g^2(x)) with g^2(x)=g(f(y))=1+g(y)) pins f(a)=g(a)=a+1, since a>=2 would put two large elements in one class.

technique: In a pair of mutually-composed functional equations, unwind one equation a single step to show that the two functions induce the SAME equivalence on the domain and that composing with either function respects that equivalence.
how_used: From g(f(x))=g(x)+1 read off g(x)=g(f(x))-1, so f(x)=f(y) forces g(x)=g(f(x))-1=g(f(y))-1=g(y), and symmetrically via f(g(x))=f(x)+1; hence f(x)=f(y) iff g(x)=g(y), giving one relation x~y. The same one-line unwind applied to f(x)~f(y) gives g(x)=g(f(x))-1=g(f(y))-1=g(y), i.e. x~y: applying f (or g) to two ~-equivalent points keeps them ~-equivalent. Separately, iterating f(g^k(x))=f(x)+k shows f attains every value >=a=min f and g every value >=b=min g. Combining the class-injectivity with this tail-surjectivity: each ~-class contains at most one value of f (one element >=a) and at most one value of g. This 'one tail-representative per class' is the engine every later step invokes.

technique: Once an identity is forced at the minimal argument, run a JOINT induction up the tail (each function's step consuming the other's just-proved value inside its argument), then push the identity to every argument by noting an arbitrary point's image already lands in the solved tail.
how_used: Base: f(a)=g(a)=a+1 with a=b. Joint induction on x>=a, hypothesis f(x)=g(x)=x+1: f(x+1)=f(g(x)) (using g(x)=x+1) =f(x)+1=(x+1)+1, and g(x+1)=g(f(x)) (using f(x)=x+1) =g(x)+1=(x+1)+1 — the two advance together because each uses the other's value inside the argument. Thus f(x)=g(x)=x+1 for all x>=a. For arbitrary n, g(n)>=min g=b=a sits in the solved tail, so f(g(n))=g(n)+1; but the equation gives f(g(n))=f(n)+1, hence f(n)=g(n).

technique: To pin the extremal value f(min), realize an assumed strict excess above the target as a tail-preimage: solve f(w)=(target)-k, rewrite the excess as an iterated composition f(g^k(w)) so the extremal argument becomes similar to a point provably >= the minimum, then collapse via the tail-meets-class-once lemma to an equality that contradicts the excess.
how_used: Let a=min f, b=min g, WLOG a<=b. (i) a=b: f(a)>a (else f(a)=a gives g(a)=g(f(a))=g(a)+1, false), so pick x with f(a)=f(x)+1=f(g(x)); then a~g(x) with g(x)>=b>=a, and tail-once forces a=g(x)>=b, so a=b. (ii) f(a)=a+1: if f(a)>=a+2, pick x,y with f(x)=f(a)-2 and f(y)=g(x) (legal since g(x)>=a=b), so f(a)=f(x)+2=f(g^2(x)) and a~g^2(x)>=a; tail-once gives a=g^2(x)=g(f(y))=g(y)+1>=a+1, contradiction. Each use turns an assumed excess into an argument sitting above a in class [a], whose unique tail-representative is a itself; from f(x)=g(x)=x+1 for x>=a the full f=g follows since g(n)>=a always.

technique: When two functional equations are cross-linked (each function shifts the other's value along its orbit), define the level relation x~y by equal image under one function and show the SAME relation is induced by the other function, so a single equivalence class carries one value of each function at once.
how_used: From g(f(n))=g(n)+1: if f(x)=f(y) then g(x)=g(f(x))-1=g(f(y))-1=g(y), and symmetrically from f(g(n))=f(n)+1 the converse holds; so 'f(x)=f(y)' and 'g(x)=g(y)' define one relation ~. Iterating f(g^k(x))=f(x)+k shows f attains every integer >=a (a=min f) and g every integer >=b (b=min g). This ~ is the scaffold on which all later collapses run: a class has a single f-value and a single g-value, and the value-tails {a,a+1,...}, {b,b+1,...} are exactly the ranges of f,g.

technique: To upgrade equal-image (x~y) to equal-argument (x=y) for arguments lying in a function's value-range, write each such argument as an image f(w) and pull the relation back through the invariance x~y => (any preimage of x)~(any preimage of y), forcing the two preimages similar and hence the two images equal.
how_used: Every integer c>=a is a value of f, so if u,v are in the same class and both >=a, write u=f(w1), v=f(w2); then f(w1)~f(w2), and the key invariance 'f(x)~f(y) implies x~y' (proved: f(x)~f(y) gives g(x)=g(f(x))-1=g(f(y))-1=g(y), so x~y) yields w1~w2, whence f(w1)=f(w2), i.e. u=v. So a class meets the tail {a,a+1,...} at most once; likewise it meets {b,b+1,...} at most once. This is precisely the license, missing before, to turn 'a~g(x)' into 'a=g(x)' whenever both a and g(x) sit above a.

technique: Unfold a max-plus superadditive recurrence into a maximum of a linear functional over compositions of the index into bounded base blocks
how_used: Repeatedly split a_n = max_k(a_k+a_{n-k}) until every summand has index <= r, giving a_n = max over compositions (i_1,...,i_k) of n with each i_j<=r (and the refinement i_1+i_2>r) of a_{i_1}+...+a_{i_k}. The reverse (>=) inequality: for any such composition set partial sums s_j=i_1+...+i_j and apply the defining recurrence at each s_j to telescope a_n = a_{s_k} >= a_{s_{k-1}}+a_{i_k} >= ... >= sum a_{i_j}.

technique: Normalize by the extremal per-index density ratio and designate its maximizer as a privileged zero-cost block
how_used: Set s = max_{1<=i<=r} a_i/i and fix ell<=r attaining it. Either subtract to form b_n=a_n-sn (sol 2: b_ell=0, b_i<=0, b inherits the same max-recurrence, so target a_n=a_{n-ell}+a_ell becomes b_n=b_{n-ell}), or keep ratios and use that a_ell/ell=s is the maximum density (sol 1). ell is the block that can be split off for free.

technique: Force a designated block into an optimal decomposition by an exchange argument swapping a pigeonhole-repeated block for copies of the designated one
how_used: For n large (n >= r^2*ell+2r) an optimal composition has k>=r*ell+2 parts, so some value j!=ell repeats at least ell times among i_3,...,i_k by pigeonhole. Delete ell copies of j and insert j copies of ell (sum preserved, still valid); optimality of the original gives ell*a_j >= j*a_ell, i.e. a_j/j >= a_ell/ell, which by maximality of s forces equality. The swapped composition is then also optimal and contains an ell-block, so a_n = a_{n-ell}+a_ell.

technique: Encode a symmetric inequality among two triples as a single polynomial by forming a weighted sum of the two monic cubics rooted at each triple, cross-weighting each product by the other triple's sum.
how_used: Set P(x)=T(x-a)(x-c)(x-e)+S(x-b)(x-d)(x-f) with S=a+c+e, T=b+d+f, so leading coeff is S+T, the x^2 coeff is -2ST, and the x^1 coeff is T*sigma+S*tau (sigma=ac+ce+ae, tau=bd+bf+df) -- exactly the quantities in the squared target 4S^2T^2>3(S+T)(S*tau+T*sigma).

technique: Locate a cubic's real roots by evaluating it at interlaced data points and reading off sign changes to force one root in each gap.
how_used: Evaluate P at a,c,e,f using a<b<c<d<e<f: P(a)=S(a-b)(a-d)(a-f)<0, P(c)>0, P(e)<0, P(f)=T(f-a)(f-c)(f-e)>0. The pattern -,+,-,+ forces a root in each of (a,c),(c,e),(e,f); a cubic has at most three, so exactly one distinct real root per interval, giving P=(S+T)(x-alpha)(x-beta)(x-gamma) with alpha,beta,gamma distinct.

technique: Turn distinctness of a cubic's roots into a strict inequality on its coefficients via the identity that the sum of squared pairwise differences equals 2(p1^2-3p2).
how_used: With Vieta p1=alpha+beta+gamma=2ST/(S+T) and p2=alpha*beta+beta*gamma+gamma*alpha=(S*tau+T*sigma)/(S+T), distinctness of alpha,beta,gamma makes the sum of squared differences positive, so p1^2>3p2, i.e. 4S^2T^2>3(S+T)(S*tau+T*sigma), which is the squared target.

technique: When every root of a polynomial identity lies on the unit circle, conjugate the whole identity and use root-bar = 1/root to obtain a second identity in the reciprocal roots
how_used: From (x+alpha_1)...(x+alpha_n) = (x+beta_1)...(x+beta_n) + 1/c_n (where alpha_i are roots of P and beta_i of P-1, all of modulus 1), conjugating and replacing each conjugated root by its reciprocal gives (x+1/alpha_1)...(x+1/alpha_n) = (x+1/beta_1)...(x+1/beta_n) + 1/conj(c_n), a genuine second relation to compare against the first

technique: Compare matching coefficients across two versions of an identity where one version scales each elementary-symmetric coefficient by a common reciprocal-product factor, forcing the shared coefficients to vanish
how_used: In the original identity the middle coefficients agree: e_k(alpha)=e_k(beta)=:s_k for k=1..n-1. In the reciprocal identity the z^{n-k} coefficient equals s_k/prod(alpha) on one side and s_k/prod(beta) on the other; since prod(alpha)-prod(beta)=1/c_n != 0 the factor 1/prod(alpha)-1/prod(beta) is nonzero, so s_k=0 for k=1..n-1, giving P(x)=lambda x^n - mu

technique: Read the argument of a product of chord-ratios between points on a common circle as a sum of INSCRIBED ANGLES IN THE DIRECTED-ANGLES-MOD-π CONVENTION, so each term equals the same half-arc independent of the third point, turning a product-equals-1 condition into a single directed-arc equation
how_used: Since A=P and B=P-1 share degree n and B(a_i)=P(a_i)-1=-1 is the same value at every root a_i of A, the product ∏_k (a_i-b_k)/(a_j-b_k)=B(a_i)/B(a_j)=(-1)/(-1)=1 for any two roots a_i,a_j. All a_i,a_j,b_k lie on the unit circle, so arg of each factor (a_i-b_k)/(a_j-b_k) is the directed inscribed angle ∠A_iB_kA_j. CRUCIAL: work with directed angles MOD 180° (mod π), NOT the raw complex argument mod 2π — the raw arg jumps by exactly π as b_k crosses from one arc A_iA_j to the other (an uncontrolled parity term), but mod π the inscribed angle is the SAME for every b_k on the circle, equal to half the directed arc A_iA_j (mod 360°). Hence ∑_k ∠A_iB_kA_j = n·(half-arc A_iA_j) ≡ 0 (mod 180°), i.e. n·arc(A_iA_j) ≡ 0 (mod 360°), so a_i/a_j is a power of ω=e^{2πi/n}; the distinct a_i are then a_1ω^0,...,a_1ω^{n-1} and A is a multiple of x^n - a_1^n (and symmetrically for B), forcing P=λx^n-μ.

technique: Normalize the extremal (min/max) variable to 1 using the joint homogeneity of constraint and target inequality
how_used: Both the constraint a+b+c=4(abc)^{1/3} and the target are homogeneous of matching degree, so scale to set c=min(a,b,c)=1; the target reduces to 4ab+2a+2b+3 >= (a+b)^2 under a+b=4(ab)^{1/3}-1.

technique: Introduce a single new variable for the constrained symmetric product and use the constraint to eliminate the remaining symmetric sum, collapsing to one variable
how_used: Set t=(ab)^{1/3} so ab=t^3, then use a+b=4t-1 from the constraint to replace every a+b in 4ab+2a+2b+3 >= (a+b)^2, yielding the pure one-variable inequality 4t^3+2(4t-1)+3 >= (4t-1)^2.

technique: Rearrange the reduced polynomial inequality to one side and factor out a perfect square to certify nonnegativity
how_used: The one-variable inequality rearranges to 0 <= 4t^3-16t^2+16t = 4t(t-2)^2, whose t(t-2)^2 form is manifestly nonnegative for t>0 and pinpoints equality at t=2 (giving ab=8, a+b=7).

technique: Parametrize a product-one constraint by the cyclic ratios of three free positive reals to make it hold identically
how_used: Setting x=b/c, y=c/a, z=a/b makes xyz=1 automatic and rewrites each argument: x+1/y=(a+b)/c, y+1/z=(b+c)/a, z+1/x=(a+c)/b, turning the constrained equation into f((a+b)/c)+f((b+c)/a)+f((a+c)/b)=1 for all a,b,c>0.

technique: Conjugate the unknown function by a Mobius change of variable to normalize its arguments onto a simplex coordinate
how_used: Setting f(t)=g(1/(t+1)) sends (b+c)/a to a/(a+b+c); with u=a/(a+b+c) etc. the equation becomes g(u)+g(v)+g(w)=1 for all u+v+w=1, u,v,w in (0,1), and g:(0,1)->(0,1).

technique: Extract a midpoint (Jensen) equation from a symmetric three-term sum by comparing an ordered pair against its average with the third term held fixed
how_used: On g(u)+g(v)+g(w)=1 (u+v+w=1), for a+b<=1 both g(a)+g(b)+g(1-a-b)=1 and 2g((a+b)/2)+g(1-a-b)=1 hold; subtracting cancels g(1-a-b) and yields g(a)+g(b)=2g((a+b)/2), Jensen's midpoint equation on (0,1/2).

technique: To force a Jensen/Cauchy-type solution to be affine, subtract the affine interpolant through two anchor points to zero out the endpoints, then exploit the resulting periodicity to extend the correction to a bounded additive function on R (hence linear), making the correction vanish
how_used: After reducing to g(a)+g(b)+g(c)=1 for a+b+c=1 (via x=b/c,y=c/a,z=a/b and f(t)=g(1/(t+1))), g obeys Jensen on (0,1/2). Set h(t)=g((2t+1)/8)-(1-t)g(1/8)-t g(3/8) so h obeys Jensen with h(0)=h(1)=0, forcing h(1/2)=0; Jensen then gives h(t)=h(t+1/2), so h extends periodically to an additive R->R map. Since g>0, this additive map is bounded below, hence linear, so h=0 and g is AFFINE on [1/8,3/8], then everywhere. The slope k is NOT pinned: g(u)+g(v)+g(w)=1 only gives k+3l=1, a one-parameter family. Transporting back, f(x)=k/(x+1)+(1-k)/3, and strict positivity constrains k to [-1/2,1]; it does NOT force a unique solution.

technique: When a sum of terms each bounded below by the same value equals that many copies of the bound, force every term to equal the bound (equality in a term-by-term lower bound).
how_used: With f(f(f(n)))+f(f(n))+f(n)=3n, once each of the three iterates is shown to be at least n, their sum being exactly 3n forces f(n)=f(f(n))=f(f(f(n)))=n; applied at n=1 (each iterate ≥1, sum=3) and at each induction step (each iterate ≥k, sum=3k).

technique: Use injectivity plus the strong induction hypothesis that small values are already fixed to bound the image of any larger argument below by the induction threshold.
how_used: Injectivity follows since f(m)=f(n) gives 3m=3n; assuming f(n)=n for all n<k, the values 1,...,k-1 are used up, so f(m)≥k for all m≥k, giving f(k)≥k, f(f(k))≥k, f(f(f(k)))≥k to feed the equality-forcing step.

technique: Replace positive-integer weights on terms by cloning each term as many times as its weight, turning a weighted sum condition into an unweighted sum over a longer sequence
how_used: With m = sum of the b_i, append b_i - 1 extra copies of each a_i so the original weighted relation sum a_i b_i = 0 becomes a plain equal-terms sum a_0 + ... + a_{m-1} = 0 over m values, each still drawn from A. This supplies the base m and a length-m block summing to zero for the digit-sum construction.

technique: Color the naturals by their base-m digit sum mod m (Prouhet/Thue-Morse coloring) so the extended sequence is constant on each digit-sum class
how_used: Define a_k = a_{s_m(k)} where s_m(k) is the base-m digit sum of k reduced mod m; this extends the seed sequence a_0,...,a_{m-1} validly, and makes every full block of m^{d+1} consecutive indices contain each residue class in a structured way so that the target sum decomposes block by block. It only sets up the block decomposition; the r-independence of each class's degree-d contribution is a separate move.

technique: Show a weighted class-indexed sum is independent of the class by multinomial-expanding a power whose exponent is below the number of free coordinates, so no monomial uses every coordinate and each partial sum is class-symmetric
how_used: For a block k = cm^{d+1} + sum_{j=0}^d e_j m^j, the digit sum is s_m(c) + (e_0+...+e_d), so class i fixes e_0+...+e_d congruent to i - s_m(c) mod m; expand (cm^{d+1}+1+ sum e_j m^j)^d. Since the exponent d is less than the d+1 coordinates e_0..e_d, every monomial omits at least one e_{j0}, and summing the omitted free coordinate over its complete residue system makes the value independent of i, so sum a_i = 0 kills each block.

technique: Fold two coupled parity-split inequalities into one monotone sequence via an alternating-sign difference substitution
how_used: Set d_n=(-1)^{n-1}(a_{n+2}-a_n). Then hypothesis a_{2n-1}+a_{2n}>a_{2n+1}+a_{2n+2} rewrites as (a_{2n+1}-a_{2n-1})+(a_{2n+2}-a_{2n})<0, i.e. d_{2n-1}<d_{2n}, and hypothesis a_{2n}+a_{2n+1}<a_{2n+2}+a_{2n+3} rewrites as (a_{2n+2}-a_{2n})+(a_{2n+3}-a_{2n+1})>0, i.e. d_{2n}<d_{2n+1}. Chaining gives d_1<d_2<d_3<..., so the two coupled parity-split hypotheses collapse to the single statement that (d_n) is strictly increasing.

technique: Recover subsequence terms as telescoping partial sums of the difference sequence to read off divergence from a single positive term
how_used: Telescope d_n=(-1)^{n-1}(a_{n+2}-a_n) into a_{2n+1}=a_1+(d_1+d_3+...+d_{2n-1}) and a_{2n}=a_2-(d_2+d_4+...+d_{2n-2}). Since (d_n) is strictly increasing, if any single d_k>0 then all d_m>0 for m>=k and are eventually bounded below by a positive constant; hence the odd partial sums diverge to +infinity (a_{2n+1}->+infty) and the even ones to -infinity (a_{2n}->-infty).

technique: To bound all consecutive products, reduce to large indices and show one factor is eventually positive and the other eventually negative
how_used: Standing reduction: it suffices to bound a_n a_{n+1} for all large n, since finitely many small-index products are absorbed by enlarging C. When the odd-index subsequence -> +infinity and even-index -> -infinity (or vice versa), for all large n one of a_n, a_{n+1} is positive and the other negative regardless of parity of n, so a_n a_{n+1} < 0. Hence C = 0 bounds the tail, and some finite C bounds all n. This closes every divergent branch (the d_k>0 case and both sandwich-forced divergences in the d_k<=0 case).

technique: Encode two alternating-direction inequalities on consecutive-pair sums as the statement that a single sign-alternated second-difference sequence is monotone
how_used: Define d_n = (-1)^{n-1}(a_{n+2} - a_n). The first hypothesis a_{2n-1}+a_{2n} > a_{2n+1}+a_{2n+2} rearranges to (a_{2n+1}-a_{2n-1}) + (a_{2n+2}-a_{2n}) < 0, i.e. d_{2n-1} < d_{2n} (checking signs: (-1)^{2n-2}=+1 gives d_{2n-1}=a_{2n+1}-a_{2n-1}, (-1)^{2n-1}=-1 gives d_{2n}=-(a_{2n+2}-a_{2n})); the second hypothesis gives d_{2n} < d_{2n+1}. Together the two families of hypotheses say precisely that (d_n)_{n>=1} is strictly increasing. This single reindexing is the setup that unlocks both the divergence and the bounded cases; without it the alternating inequalities are unusable.

technique: When a term equals its base plus a partial sum of a strictly increasing difference sequence, a single positive difference forces that partial sum, hence the term, to diverge
how_used: In the case some d_k > 0: because (d_n) is strictly increasing (from the setup), every d_m with m > k also exceeds a fixed positive value, so the partial sums grow without bound. Telescoping along the odd indices, a_{2n+1} = a_1 + (d_1 + d_3 + ... + d_{2n-1}) -> +infinity, and along the even indices a_{2n} = a_2 - (d_2 + d_4 + ... + d_{2n-2}) -> -infinity. This produces the opposite-sign divergence that the finishing move consumes.

technique: Sandwich a paired sum between fixed constants so each monotone interleaved subsequence must either converge or diverge, with divergence of one forcing opposite-infinity divergence of the other
how_used: In the case d_k <= 0 for all k, (a_{2n+1}) is weakly decreasing and (a_{2n}) weakly increasing (immediate from d_n<=0 telescoped). Adding the telescoped expressions for a_{2n+1} and a_{2n} bounds their sum: d_1 + a_1 + a_2 < a_{2n} + a_{2n+1} < a_1 + a_2. Each monotone subsequence thus either diverges to its monotone limit (-infinity for the odd, +infinity for the even) or converges. If a_{2n+1} -> -infinity the lower bound forces a_{2n} -> +infinity; if a_{2n} -> +infinity the upper bound forces a_{2n+1} -> -infinity -- opposite-sign divergence, handed to the finishing move. Otherwise both are bounded-and-monotone hence convergent, so a_{2n}a_{2n+1} -> L exists and any C>L works.

technique: Reduce the given additive relation modulo the range-bounding parameter to pin the number of summands to a single value, collapsing an existential over configurations into one design goal.
how_used: If a monic P of degree at most n satisfies P(x)≡1 (mod n) for every integer x, then reading P(x_1)+...+P(x_k)=P(x_{k+1}) mod n gives k≡1 (mod n); with 1≤k≤n this forces k=1, so the only surviving equation is P(x_1)=P(x_2) with x_1≠x_2. Hence the property FAILS for n exactly when one can build a single monic deg≤n polynomial that is both ≡1 (mod n) everywhere and injective on the integers. This converts 'no k, no tuple exists' into 'construct one polynomial with two properties'. (Answer: only n=2 works; n≥1, n≥3 fail via such a construction.)

technique: Force a monic integer polynomial to a constant residue mod m by adding a product of m consecutive shifted linear factors, which vanishes mod m at every integer.
how_used: Take f_n=(X-1)(X-2)...(X-n): at any integer x this is a product of n consecutive integers, divisible by n! hence by n, so f_n(x)==0 (mod n) for all x. Then P=f_n+nX+1 is monic of degree exactly n with P(x)==1 (mod n) for every integer x. Reading the target relation P(x_1)+...+P(x_k)=P(x_{k+1}) mod n gives k==1 (mod n); since 1<=k<=n this forces k=1, collapsing the whole condition to whether P(x_1)=P(x_2) can hold for distinct integers, i.e. to injectivity of P on Z. This uniform +nX+1 tweak keeps monicity and residue 1 for every excluded n. (For n=4 the official main text instead uses the ad hoc quartic P=X^4+7X^2+4X+1, which also has P(x)==1 mod 4.)

technique: Prove a polynomial is injective on the integers by factoring the difference P(x)-P(y)=(x-y)Q(x,y) and showing the cofactor Q can never vanish at integer points via an absolute-value size bound.
how_used: For the n=4 quartic P=X^4+7X^2+4X+1, P(x)-P(y)=(x-y)((x+y)(x^2+y^2+7)+4); the cofactor Q=(x+y)(x^2+y^2+7)+4 is nonzero because |(x+y)(x^2+y^2+7)| is either 0 (when x+y=0, giving Q=4) or at least 7 (since x^2+y^2+7>=7 and |x+y|>=1), so Q is never 0. Hence P(x)=P(y) forces x=y. Combined with the mod-n crux forcing k=1, an injective P with P(x)==1 mod n is a 'bad' polynomial, so that n fails the condition. For general n the official main text sidesteps the hard even case by choosing P=f_n+nX+1 for odd n and P=f_{n-1}+nX+1 for even n, both strictly increasing hence injective by an adjacent-difference check; only the Remark treats the symmetric even f_n via this same difference-bounding idea across the two monotone branches. The excluded set is everything except n=2 (n=1,3 and all n>=4), so the unique answer to the problem is n=2 — the positive side (P quadratic gives P(X)=P(-X-q); linear and constant handled directly) is routine and not a critical step.

technique: Feed an equation's own output (e.g. an involution image) back into a distinguished slot where a solved special value acts as identity, collapsing that side to expose the operation's normal form
how_used: Injectivity of y↦x◇y (from P(1,x,y)) plus P(1,x,1) gives x◇1=x, and P(1,1,y) gives 1◇(1◇y)=y so 1◇· is involutive. The key substitution is P(x,1,1◇y): the FE a◇(b◇c)=(a◇b)c with b=1 makes the left side x◇(1◇(1◇y))=x◇y (involution) and the right side (x◇1)·y=x·y... rather, feeding c=1◇y and using x◇1=x collapses one side to x·(1◇y), yielding x◇y=x·(1◇y). Setting f(y)=1◇y gives the normal form x◇y=x·f(y); reinserting into the FE gives f(b·f(c))=f(b)c, and involutivity of f then makes f completely multiplicative.

technique: Conjugate a completely multiplicative function on the positive reals by log/exp to convert it into an additive (Cauchy) function on the reals
how_used: Set g(t)=log f(e^t); complete multiplicativity f(e^s e^t)=f(e^s)f(e^t) becomes additivity g(s+t)=g(s)+g(t), involutivity f(f(x))=x becomes g(g(t))=t, and the constraint f(x)≥1/x for x≥1 becomes the one-sided lower bound g(t)≥−t for t≥0, reducing the problem to rigidity of an additive function bounded below on a half-line.

technique: Kill pathological additive solutions by invoking that a non-linear additive function has graph dense in the plane, so any one-sided bound forces linearity
how_used: The lemma that a non-linear additive g has graph dense in R^2 is incompatible with g(t)≥−t on t≥0 (density would put points below the line), forcing g linear: g(t)=rt, hence f(x)=x^r. Involutivity f(f(x))=x gives r^2=1, so r=±1; r=1 gives ◇=multiplication, r=−1 gives ◇=division, both passing the a◇a≥1 check.

technique: Kill a nested unknown-function term by substituting to make its inner argument reproduce a known evaluation of the same function
how_used: Setting y=-2x makes the argument of g(f(x+y)) become g(f(-x)); combined with the equation this gives the clean relation g(f(-x))=f(x), then feeding -x-y in place of x collapses the nested g∘f into f(-x-y)=f(x)+(2x+y)g(y), removing g's inner f entirely.

technique: Write the derived relation for three cyclically permuted argument choices and add to cancel the unknown into a single linear identity
how_used: From f(-a)=f(-b)+(a-b)g(a+b) and its two cyclic rotations in (a,b,c), summing eliminates all f-values and yields (y-x)g(z)+(z-y)g(x)+(x-z)g(y)=0 after the change of variables x=b+c etc.

technique: Read a vanishing three-argument determinant-type relation as forcing collinearity of the graph points, hence affinity of the function
how_used: The identity (y-x)g(z)+(z-y)g(x)+(x-z)g(y)=0 for all x,y,z is the area-zero condition for (x,g(x)),(y,g(y)),(z,g(z)), so g's graph is a line, giving g(x)=Ax+B.

technique: Pin an unknown linear coefficient by matching the leading-power coefficient on both sides of the recovered polynomial identity
how_used: With g(x)=Ax+B forcing f(y)=Ay^2-By+C, substituting back and comparing the x^2 coefficients in the original equation gives A^2=A, so A∈{0,1}, splitting into the vanishing and the x^2+C solutions.

technique: Discard the nonnegative terms of a functional equation to replace the equality by a strict inequality between a nested iterate and a neighbor value.
how_used: In f^{g(n)+1}(n)+g^{f(n)}(n)=f(n+1)-g(n+1)+1, the codomain is positive integers, so g^{f(n)}(n)>=1 and g(n+1)>=1. Dropping them from the equality leaves f^{g(n)+1}(n) <= f(n+1)-1, i.e. writing f^{g(n)+1}(n)=f(f^{g(n)}(n)) gives the strict inequality f(f^{g(n)}(n)) < f(n+1) for all n. This single inequality is the lever the whole determination of f rides on.

technique: Rule out a strict-excess case by propagating a pointwise inequality into a strictly increasing iterate chain, then squeezing that chain against an upper bound to force a forbidden value strictly between two consecutive images.
how_used: Alternate finisher to f(n)=n, taking as GIVEN (supplied by the interleaved-induction crux, or an equivalent lemma) that the n smallest values of f are exactly f(1)<...<f(n) — so f(n)>=n and the image is an initial segment with no integer strictly between consecutive images. Suppose f(n)>n for some n. Strict monotonicity propagates f(x)>x to all x>=n, so the iterates form a strictly increasing chain f(n)<f^2(n)<...<f^{g(n)+1}(n), giving f^{g(n)+1}(n)>f(n). But the inequality * (f(f^{g(n)}(n))<f(n+1), i.e. f^{g(n)+1}(n)<f(n+1)) gives an upper bound. Together f(n)<f^{g(n)+1}(n)<f(n+1): an attained value squeezed strictly between consecutive images, impossible for an initial-segment image. Contradiction, so f(n)=n for all n, and the same plug-in n+g^n(n)=(n+1)-g(n+1)+1 gives g^n(n)+g(n+1)=2, so g==1.

technique: When an iterated-function equation forces a sum of positive-integer terms to equal one side, discard the other positive terms to collapse the equation into a single strict inequality between function values.
how_used: Every term in f^{g(n)+1}(n)+g^{f(n)}(n)=f(n+1)-g(n+1)+1 is a positive integer. Dropping g^{f(n)}(n)>=1 on the left and noting -g(n+1)+1<=0 on the right, the equation yields the clean inequality (*): f(f^{g(n)}(n)) < f(n+1) for every n. This single inequality is what actually pins down f; g never re-enters until the very end.

technique: To force a function on the positive integers to be the identity, list its attained values in increasing order and run an interleaved induction that alternately pins each value's unique preimage and pins the value to its index, using the fact that any iterate landing below the current cutoff must have started exactly at that index.
how_used: Let y_1<y_2<... be the attained values of f. Prove in the order (i)_1,(ii)_1,(i)_2,(ii)_2,... the pair (i)_n: f(x)=y_n iff x=n, and (ii)_n: y_n=n. Base (i)_1: if f(x)=y_1 with x>1, then (*) at x-1 gives f(f^{g(x-1)}(x-1))<y_1, below the minimum value — impossible. The established (i)_1..(i)_n give the collapse fact: for a<n and any k>=1, f^k(x)=a forces x=a. Step: pick x with f(x)=y_{n+1} (prior (i)'s force x>n); (*) at x-1 gives b:=f^{g(x-1)}(x-1) with f(b) in {y_1..y_n}, so b in {1..n}; the collapse fact excludes b<n (would give x-1=b<n contra x>n), so b=n, which yields y_n=n (i.e. (ii)_n) and, unwinding the iterates via (i)_n, x-1=n so (i)_{n+1}. Hence f(n)=n for all n; substituting back gives g^n(n)+g(n+1)=2 in positive integers, forcing g(n)=1.

technique: Reparametrize a two-variable functional inequality by substituting the shift variable so the free argument becomes an affine function of a fixed parameter
how_used: Set y=t-x in f(x+y)<=y f(x)+f(f(x)) to get f(t)<= t f(x) - x f(x) + f(f(x)), making the RHS linear in t with slope f(x); this affine bound is the workhorse for every later step.

technique: Apply the derived bound twice with the two roles interchanged and add the copies to cancel the awkward composite term
how_used: Use f(t)<= t f(x)-x f(x)+f(f(x)) with (t=f(a),x=b) and with (t=f(b),x=a); the f(f(a)),f(f(b)) terms cancel on adding, yielding the symmetric inequality 2 f(a)f(b) >= a f(a)+b f(b).

technique: Substitute a parameter equal to a multiple of an unknown value into a symmetric inequality to make matching terms cancel and isolate a one-variable sign condition
how_used: Put b=2 f(a) into 2 f(a)f(b) >= a f(a)+b f(b) so the 2 f(a)f(b) terms cancel, leaving a f(a)<=0, hence f(a)>=0 for all a<0.

technique: Force a global sign by noting an affine upper bound with nonzero slope drives values below zero on a half-line, contradicting an already-proved sign
how_used: If f(x)>0 somewhere, the affine bound f(t)<= t f(x)+const has positive slope f(x), so f(t)<0 for all sufficiently negative t, contradicting f(t)>=0 for t<0; therefore f(x)<=0 everywhere, and with f(a)>=0 for a<0 this gives f(a)=0 for all a<0.

technique: Close a boundary point by choosing the free parameter equal to the fixed argument so the slope-carrying terms cancel and the bound collapses to a bare inequality on the boundary value
how_used: In the affine bound f(t) <= t f(x) - x f(x) + f(f(x)), set t=x with x<0. Since f(x)=0 there, f(f(x))=f(0), and t f(x)-x f(x)=0, so the bound reads f(x) <= f(0), i.e. 0 <= f(0). With f(0)<=0 from the global sign, this forces f(0)=0, completing f(x)=0 for all x<=0.

technique: Feed the function's own outputs into the linearized inequality as the free argument for two different anchor points, then add the two resulting inequalities so the double-nested terms cancel and leave a symmetric relation between the two anchors
how_used: In the affine form f(t) <= t f(x) - x f(x) + f(f(x)), take (t=f(a), x=b) and (t=f(b), x=a). Both produce f(f(a))-f(f(b)) terms; adding the two inequalities cancels f(f(a)) and f(f(b)) and yields 2 f(a) f(b) >= a f(a) + b f(b), a clean symmetric relation with no nested f left.

technique: Kill a quadratic-type product term in a symmetric inequality by setting the free variable equal to a multiple of the other side's factor, collapsing the relation to a one-sided sign condition
how_used: In 2 f(a) f(b) >= a f(a) + b f(b), substitute b = 2 f(a). Then b f(b) = 2 f(a) f(b) equals the whole left side, which cancels, leaving a f(a) <= 0 for all a. For a < 0, dividing by a<0 forces f(a) >= 0, establishing nonnegativity of f on the negative reals.

technique: Rule out any positive value of the function by exploiting that a positive value makes the linear bound have positive slope in the anchor, forcing the function strictly negative on a whole ray and contradicting an established sign on that ray
how_used: If f(x)>0 for some x, the affine bound f(t) <= f(x) t + (f(f(x)) - x f(x)) has slope f(x)>0, so as t -> -infinity the right side -> -infinity and f(t)<0 for arbitrarily negative t. But those t include negatives where f>=0 was already proved. Contradiction forces f(x)<=0 for all x; with f>=0 on negatives this yields f(x)=0 for all x<0.

technique: To settle a domain boundary point the sign argument left open, substitute the free argument equal to the anchor in the linearized inequality so the anchor-dependent linear terms cancel, leaving a nested-value comparison that pins the boundary value
how_used: The other moves give f(x)=0 for x<0 and f<=0 everywhere, but the a=0 division step is vacuous so x=0 is unresolved. In f(t) <= t f(x) - x f(x) + f(f(x)) set t=x with x<0: since f(x)=0 both t f(x) and x f(x) vanish, giving 0 = f(x) <= f(f(x)) = f(0). Hence f(0)>=0, and with f(0)<=0 this yields f(0)=0, completing f=0 on all x<=0.

technique: Rewrite each fraction so its numerator becomes a perfect cube of a chosen quantity, then apply the power-mean form of Holder to collapse the sum into a single fraction of aggregated numerator over aggregated denominator
how_used: Wrote a/(b+c-a)^2 = (a^2)^3 / (a^5(b+c-a)^2) so the Holder variant with p=2 gives lower bound (a^2+b^2+c^2)^3 / (sum a^{5/2}(b+c-a))^2 = 27/(sum a^{5/2}(b+c-a))^2

technique: Bound a cyclic sum of the form sum x^k(y+z-x) from above by invoking a weighted Schur inequality sum x^m(x-y)(x-z) >= 0 and re-expanding it into the desired sum-versus-product bound
how_used: Used Schur's sum a^{3/2}(a-b)(a-c) >= 0, rewritten as sum a^{5/2}(b+c-a) <= abc(sqrt a+sqrt b+sqrt c), to control the Holder denominator
