technique: Convert the constraint on the sum of squares into a bound on the sum of square roots via the power-mean (fourth-power-mean vs arithmetic-mean) inequality
how_used: From a^2+b^2+c^2=3 deduced ((sqrt a+sqrt b+sqrt c)/3)^4 <= (a^2+b^2+c^2)/3 = 1, so sqrt a+sqrt b+sqrt c <= 3, finishing the chain to 3/(abc)^2

technique: Recast a commutation constraint 'only the identity commutes with the given maps' as a preservation property: call a set invariant if it is mapped into itself by EVERY commuting f, and reduce proving f=id to shrinking invariant sets down to singletons.
how_used: For the candidate pair g=max(x-α,0), h=min(x+β,1) on [0,1], a set S is invariant if f(S)⊆S for all f commuting with both g,h. Since f({δ})⊆{δ} forces f(δ)=δ, exhibiting enough invariant sets whose intersections are singletons {δ} for every δ forces f=identity, replacing pointwise reasoning about f with set-level reasoning.

technique: Close a family of invariant sets under preimage: show that if S is invariant then g^{-1}(S) is invariant, via the commutativity chain g(f(g^{-1}S))=f(g(g^{-1}S))⊆f(S)⊆S.
how_used: Starting from {0} invariant (f(0) is a fixed point of g, forcing f(0)=0), each interval [0,nα-mβ] with 0≤nα-mβ≤1 is obtained as g^{-1} or h^{-1} of a previously-established invariant interval (g^{-1}[0,c]=[0,c+α], h^{-1}[0,c]=[0,c+β]), giving induction on m+n that all [0,nα-mβ] in [0,1] are invariant.

technique: Use the dense orbit of an irrational rotation to upgrade a discrete family of thresholds into all thresholds, then take intersections to isolate individual points.
how_used: With α irrational, {nα mod 1} is dense in [0,1], so [0,δ]=∩_{nα mod 1>δ}[0,nα mod 1] is invariant for every δ; symmetrically [δ,1] is invariant, so {δ}=[0,δ]∩[δ,1] is invariant for every δ, forcing f=identity.

technique: Encode a pair of self-maps as a two-colored directed graph on the domain (one color per map) so that a function commuting with both maps is exactly a color-preserving graph endomorphism, reducing 'only the identity commutes' to 'the colored graph is rigid'.
how_used: Solution 3 draws a red edge x→g(x) and a blue edge x→h(x); f(g x)=g(f x) and f(h x)=h(f x) say precisely that f sends each red edge to a red edge and each blue edge to a blue edge, i.e. f is an endomorphism of the 2-colored graph. So (g,h) is a tester pair iff this graph admits no nontrivial endomorphism, and since endomorphisms map components to components it suffices to build a continuum of pairwise-rigid components.

technique: Recast a 'functions commuting with a fixed family' problem as endomorphisms of a colored directed graph: put one colored edge x -> t(x) per generating map t, so a function commutes with all the maps iff it is a color-preserving graph endomorphism, and the extremal question becomes: does a graph exist with no nontrivial endomorphism?
how_used: For g,h: R->R, build G on vertex set R with a red edge x->g(x) and a blue edge x->h(x). Then f commutes with both g and h iff every edge x->y forces an edge f(x)->f(y) of the same color, i.e. f is an endomorphism of G. So a tester pair (g,h) exists iff there is such a graph whose only endomorphism is the identity; since endomorphisms map components to components, it suffices to build a continuum of components admitting no nontrivial endomorphism and no homomorphism between distinct ones.

technique: Pin down an endomorphism's freedom on a translation-homogeneous component by planting a fixed asymmetric 'marker' motif near a basepoint: use one generator's orbit structure to reduce the map to a single shift parameter, then a local sub-configuration that occurs uniquely forces the shift to a specific value, killing the residual symmetry.
how_used: Take g(x)=x+1, so its red edges make each component a coset S_x=x+Z and any homomorphism f: S_x->S_y is a shift f(x+n)=x+n+k. Then plant a marker of blue edges h(x-3)=x, h(x)=x-2, h(x-2)=x-1, h(x-1)=x+1 (and h(x-n)=x-n+1 for n>3). The edge (x-3)->x is the unique blue edge whose color/pattern has that local shape, so it must map to the unique corresponding edge (y-3)->y, forcing f(x)=y and k=0. This nails the basepoint and removes all translation freedom left by g.

technique: Realize a continuum of pairwise-rigid components by injectively encoding each component's identity into its local edge-pattern at successive positions: use a two-way distinguishable local motif per index and let one bit choose which motif appears, so matching an endomorphism edge-by-edge forces the target's bit-string to equal the source's.
how_used: For x=0.x_1 x_2... in [0,1), at block i put blue edges realizing pattern (1) [h(x+3i-2)=x+3i-1 etc.] if x_i=0, or the distinct pattern (2) [h(x+3i-2)=x+3i etc.] if x_i=1. With the basepoint already pinned (k=0), the existence of edge (x+3i-2)->(x+3i-1) versus (x+3i-2)->(x+3i) forces y_i=x_i for every i, so any homomorphism S_x->S_y forces x=y and is the identity. Distinct binary strings thus give a continuum of pairwise non-isomorphic rigid components.

technique: Evaluate a real polynomial at a complex conjugate pair of points to turn a symmetric product over its roots into a squared modulus of one value.
how_used: Recognize prod(x_j^2+1)=prod(x_j-i)(x_j+i)=P(i)P(-i)=|P(i)|^2, converting the four-root product into the modulus-squared of P evaluated at i.

technique: Read the real and imaginary parts of P(i) off the coefficients to express the target as a sum of two squares in the coefficients, then minimize each square against its constraint.
how_used: With P(i)=(-1+b-d)+(c-a)i, get |P(i)|^2=(b-d-1)^2+(a-c)^2; using b-d>=5 gives b-d-1>=4, so the minimum is 4^2+0^2=16, attained at x_1=...=x_4=1.

technique: Complete the square on a candidate relation to force a negative square, ruling that branch out over the integers
how_used: Assuming f(x)+f(-x)=-x^2 (the non-even branch obtained by subtracting x^2 f(-x)=f(x)^2 and its x->-x image and factoring), substituting back into x^2 f(-x)=f(x)^2 yields [f(x)+x^2/2]^2 = -(3/4)x^4 < 0 for x!=0, impossible; this forces f even and hence f(x)^2 = x^2 f(x).

technique: Read a per-input two-value dichotomy off a pointwise quadratic constraint
how_used: From x^2 f(-x)=f(x)^2 combined with evenness one gets f(x)^2 = x^2 f(x), i.e. f(x)(f(x)-x^2)=0, so for each x individually f(x) in {0, x^2}; this is only a pointwise dichotomy and does not yet fix a single global solution.

technique: Plug a hypothetical zero of f as a variable to propagate vanishing across an arithmetic-progression sublattice
how_used: Setting y=t with f(t)=0 makes the FE give t^2 f(2x)=0 for all x!=0, so f vanishes on all even integers; restricting x to even values then forces the remaining odd-argument candidate f(m)=m^2 to collapse (m^2 f(4k-m^2)=f(m^3) for arbitrary k is absurd unless everything vanishes), leaving only f=0, so f=x^2 is the only alternative.

technique: Recognize a bilinear cross-difference condition as every 2x2 minor of an array being unimodular, and lay the given boundary data out as adjacent quadrants of one infinite grid sharing a corner.
how_used: The relation f(m+1,n+1)f(m,n)-f(m+1,n)f(m,n+1)=1 is read as 'every 2x2 sub-grid has determinant +/-1'; the sequences A,B,C,D are placed as four arms/quadrants around the common corner k=a_0=b_0=c_0=d_0, turning D~A into the task of filling the one empty quadrant so all minors stay +/-1.

technique: Reduce filling a global unimodular array to a purely local extension: given a 3x3 grid with 8 entries fixed and all 2x2 minors +/-1, show the 9th entry can be chosen integral.
how_used: Filling the missing quadrant is reduced to the lemma on a corner 3x3 block [[a,b,c],[x,y,z],[p,q,?]]; solving the local case propagates to fill the entire quadrant one cell at a time.

technique: Force integrality of a proposed quotient by chaining congruences mod the central entry: from several products each congruent to -1 mod y, deduce the target product is also -1 mod y so the division is exact.
how_used: With center y (nonzero), the minor conditions give bx==xq==bz==-1 (mod y); multiplying/combining these yields qz==-1 (mod y), so the ninth entry (qz+1)/y is an integer (the y=0 case gives qz=-1 directly).

technique: Add two consecutive unimodular determinant relations along a strip and cancel the shared variable via a coprimality it forces, extracting a three-term divisibility recurrence.
how_used: From v*a_{n-1}-u*a_n=1 and w*a_n-v*a_{n+1}=1 one gets u+w=v(a_{n-1}+a_{n+1})/a_n; since gcd(v,a_n)=1 (forced by the first relation), this proves a_n | a_{n-1}+a_{n+1}, the divisibility law classifying great sequences.

technique: Substitute the same pair of values in two swapped orders and equate the two resulting expressions to force a symmetric quantity to be constant.
how_used: Plugging (x=f(a), y=b) and (x=f(b), y=a) both give f(f(a)^2 f(b)^2); equating yields f(f(a))^2 f(b) = f(f(b))^2 f(a), so f(f(a))^2/f(a) is independent of a, giving a constant C with f(f(a))^2 = C f(a).

technique: Iterate a squaring relation to express a value as a 2^n-th power for every n, then use that a rational cannot be an arbitrarily high perfect power unless it is 1.
how_used: From (f(f(a))/C)^2 = f(a)/C, iterating gives f(a)/C = (f^{n+1}(a)/C)^{2^n} for all n; since every prime exponent in f(a)/C would need divisibility by all 2^n, it forces f(a)/C = 1, hence f is constant C, and (*) gives C = C^3 so C = 1.

technique: Multiply two shifted copies of a recurrence together to expose a common product and eliminate it into a two-term-shifted identity
how_used: Writing the recurrence at index i as a_i·a_{i+1} = a_{i+2}-1 and at index i+1 as a_{i+1}·a_{i+2} = a_{i+3}-1, then forming the common triple product a_i·a_{i+1}·a_{i+2} two ways gives (a_{i+2}-1)a_{i+2} = a_i(a_{i+3}-1), rearranged to a_{i+2}^2 - a_i·a_{i+3} = a_{i+2} - a_i.

technique: Sum a per-index identity around the full cycle so the linear part telescopes to zero and the quadratic remainder assembles into a sum of squares that must vanish
how_used: Summing a_{i+2}^2 - a_i·a_{i+3} = a_{i+2} - a_i over i=1..n with indices mod n: the right side telescopes to 0 by periodicity, and the left side reorganizes into ∑(a_i - a_{i+3})^2 = 0, forcing a_i = a_{i+3} for all i, hence period 3 and 3 | n.

technique: Negate both dichotomy alternatives at once to promote 'a subset with this sum' into a well-defined value-indexed map: failing the collision option makes each attainable target hit by at most one subset, failing the omission option makes each target hit by at least one.
how_used: Assuming S satisfies neither (1) nor (2), define F_r as the unique finite subset of S with sum-of-reciprocals equal to r for every rational r in [0,1) (empty set giving 0), turning the problem into a study of the map r -> F_r.

technique: Track how a fixed element's membership in the uniquely-indexed set toggles when you shift the target by exactly that element's own contribution, then climb the resulting ladder from a base case to get a floor-parity law.
how_used: Show x in F_q iff x not in F_r whenever q - r = 1/x (uniqueness forces F_r = F_q minus {x} or F_q = F_r union {x}); climb r, r-1/x, ..., r-n/x with n=floor(rx) from the base F_{r-n/x} not containing x, yielding x in F_r iff floor(rx) is odd.

technique: Derive a contradiction from a floor-parity membership criterion by nudging the target down by a tiny rational epsilon chosen to preserve every relevant floor, forcing the finite indexed set to sit inside a strictly-smaller-target set.
how_used: For F_{2/3}, floor(2x/3) odd for each x in F means 2x/3 non-integral, so a small rational epsilon keeps floor((2/3-eps)x)=floor(2x/3) for all x in F_{2/3}, forcing F_{2/3} subset of F_{2/3-eps}, which is impossible since the sub-target 2/3-eps < 2/3 cannot uniquely represent a set already summing to 2/3.

technique: Manufacture two distinct subsets with equal reciprocal sum by realizing a small gap-valued target with a finite set and adjoining the single element whose reciprocal completes it to a one-term sum.
how_used: On the slow branch pick n with x_{n+1}<2x_n and set the target r = 1/x_n - 1/x_{n+1}, which satisfies 0<r<1/x_{n+1}<1. If no finite subset realizes r, then r is the required unhit rational and (2) holds. Otherwise r = sum over some finite F_0; since r<1/x_{n+1}, x_{n+1} cannot lie in F_0 (any subset containing it already exceeds r), so F_0 union {x_{n+1}} has reciprocal sum r+1/x_{n+1}=1/x_n = the sum over {x_n}. These two distinct finite subsets give a collision, so (1) holds.

technique: Bound a positive term-series by a geometric series with the branch's growth ratio; if the total falls strictly below the target level, any rational in the open gap between total and level is unattainable as a partial sum.
how_used: In the branch x_{n+1}>=2x_n (after: finite S trivially gives (2); drop the element 1; order x_1<x_2<... with x_1>=2), one has x_n>=2^{n-1}x_1, so the full reciprocal series is dominated by a geometric series: s=sum 1/x_n <= sum 1/(2^{n-1}x_1)=2/x_1. Reading the witness for (2) off the size of s: if x_1>=3 then s<=2/3<1; if x_1=2 with x_{n+1}>2x_n for some n the domination is strict so s<2/x_1=1; in both cases every finite subset sum is < s < 1, hence any rational r in [s,1) (nonempty) is never a subset sum and (2) holds. The lone remaining case x_1=2 with equality throughout (x_n=2^n) gives s=1, but every finite subset sum is dyadic k/2^m, so the non-dyadic r=1/3 is unattained and (2) holds. The complementary branch x_{n+1}<2x_n (some n), which forces a collision giving (1), is a separate crux.

technique: Bound a difference of two consecutive terms by the spread of the common set of admissible values both terms are forced to lie in
how_used: Both a_n and a_{n-1}=S(n,1)/1 lie in [m_n,M_n], the min/max of the averages S(n,k)/k over 1<=k<=n; hence a_2018-a_2017 <= M_2018-m_2018 = Delta_2018, converting the single-difference extremal problem into an upper bound on the spread Delta_n.

technique: Establish a per-step geometric contraction of a monovariant by peeling the newest term off the extremal average and bounding the remaining sub-average by the previous stage's extremum
how_used: Writing S(n,k)=a_{n-1}+S(n-1,k-1) and using S(n-1,k-1)<=(k-1)M_{n-1} gives M_n-a_{n-1} <= ((k-1)/k)(M_{n-1}-a_{n-1}) <= ((n-1)/n)(M_{n-1}-a_{n-1}); the symmetric bound for m_n uses S(n-1,k-1)>=(k-1)m_{n-1}. Adding yields Delta_n <= ((n-1)/n)Delta_{n-1}. The sign facts m_{n-1}<=a_{n-1}<=M_{n-1} hold since a_{n-1} is itself an admissible average at step n-1.

technique: Telescope the per-step contraction ratios from the base stage to the target, then maximize the resulting bound over the free base index
how_used: Multiplying Delta_{q+1}=(q-1)/q^2 by the ratios ((n-1)/n) for n=q+2,...,N+1 (N=2017) telescopes to Delta_{N+1} <= (1/(N+1))(1-1/q^2); this increases in q, so the worst case q=N=2017 gives the bound (N-1)/N^2 = 2016/2017^2.

technique: Attain an extremal-bound by holding the sequence constant until forced, then selecting the extreme (min then max) admissible average at each endpoint
how_used: Set a_1=...=a_2016=1 (each via k=1), then a_2017 via k=2017: (a_2016+...+a_0)/2017=1-1/2017 (pulling in a_0=0 minimizes), then a_2018 via k=2017: (a_2017+...+a_1)/2017=1-1/2017^2 (dropping a_0 and re-including a_1..a_2016=1 maximizes). Direct arithmetic gives a_2018-a_2017=2016/2017^2, matching the bound.

technique: Bound a target difference of two specified terms by the spread (max minus min) of a family of averages that both terms provably belong to, converting the extremal quantity into a monovariant over that spread.
how_used: Each a_n equals some window average S(n,k)/k with 1<=k<=n, and a_{n-1}=S(n,1)/1 is itself the k=1 window average at index n; so both a_n and a_{n-1} lie in [m_n,M_n] where M_n=max_k S(n,k)/k, m_n=min_k S(n,k)/k. Hence a_2018-a_2017 <= M_2018-m_2018 = Delta_2018, reducing the problem to upper-bounding the spread Delta_n.

technique: Show a spread-type monovariant contracts by a fixed factor per step by peeling the newest term off the extremal window and bounding the remaining shorter window with the previous step's extreme.
how_used: Pick k,l with M_n=S(n,k)/k, m_n=S(n,l)/l. Using S(n,k)=a_{n-1}+S(n-1,k-1): k(M_n-a_{n-1})=S(n-1,k-1)-(k-1)a_{n-1}<=(k-1)(M_{n-1}-a_{n-1}) since S(n-1,k-1)<=(k-1)M_{n-1}; symmetrically a_{n-1}-m_n<=((l-1)/l)(a_{n-1}-m_{n-1}). As k,l<=n the factors are <=(n-1)/n, so Delta_n<=((n-1)/n)Delta_{n-1}. Telescoping this from the base spread Delta_{q+1} up to n=2018 gives Delta_2018<=(1/2018)(1-1/q^2), maximized at q=2017 to give 2016/2017^2.

technique: Pin the starting value of the monovariant by locating the first index where a forced constant run must break and reading off the unique admissible value there.
how_used: While a_n=1 all window averages are 1 and Delta_n=0. Let q be minimal with a_q<1. For i<q, S(q,i)=i (all 1's) gives average 1; only the full window S(q,q)=q-1 (reaching a_0=0) drops below 1, forcing a_q=S(q,q)/q=1-1/q uniquely. Then S(q+1,i)=i-1/q for i<=q and S(q+1,q+1)=q-1/q give m_{q+1}=(q-1)/q, M_{q+1}=(q^2-1)/q^2, so the base spread is Delta_{q+1}=(q-1)/q^2 - the starting value for the telescoping contraction.

technique: Isolate one unknown function-value by choosing a small family of substitutions whose outputs share the SAME two intermediate values, then take pairwise differences to cancel those shared values
how_used: Chose x=y=t, x=t/a,y=at, x=a^2 t,y=t, x=y=at so that the first pair both produce f(t^2) and the second pair both produce f(a^2 t^2) (the remaining terms are the constants f(1),f(a^2),f(a^{-2}) and the wanted f(t),f(at)). Differencing (2a)-(2b) kills f(t^2); (2c)-(2d) kills f(a^2 t^2); combining the two differences kills f(at), leaving f(t) alone.

technique: Confirm an isolated variable's coefficient is a nonzero CONSTANT (free of the remaining free variable) by expanding the difference of two products and watching the free-variable terms cancel, so a single division gives the closed form
how_used: Expanded (at+1/(at))(t+1/t) - (t/a+a/t)(a^2 t+1/(a^2 t)); all t-dependent terms cancel, leaving a+1/a-(a^3+1/a^3) = -(a-1)^2(a+1)^2(a^2+1)/a^3, which is <0 for a!=1 and independent of t. Dividing the difference-equation by it makes the RHS a linear combination of 1 and t^2 over t, i.e. f(t)=C_1 t + C_2/t.

technique: Restrict a two-variable functional equation to a geometric progression in one variable to turn it into a constant-coefficient second-order linear recurrence, then read the solution shape off the characteristic roots
how_used: Set x=a (fixed, !=1), y=a^n, giving f(a^{n+1})-(a+1/a)f(a^n)+f(a^{n-1})=0, characteristic poly r^2-(a+1/a)r+1=(r-a)(r-1/a) with distinct roots a,1/a, so f(a^n)=C_1(a)a^n+C_2(a)/a^n along each ladder {a^n}. Coefficients C_1,C_2 depend on the base a; this only fixes f on discrete ladders, not globally.

technique: Derive a cross-ladder consistency relation among the per-ladder coefficients by substituting so the FE's two output arguments each land on a DIFFERENT ladder while the input rides a third
how_used: Normalize to f_0(x)=f(x)-f(1)x so f_0(1)=0, forcing the per-ladder form f_0(a^n)=K(a)(a^n-1/a^n). Substitute x=(a/b)^n, y=(ab)^n into (1): the input (ab)^n rides the {ab} ladder while the outputs a^{2n} and b^{2n} land on the {a} and {b} ladders. This yields K(ab)(a^{2n}-a^{-2n}+b^{2n}-b^{-2n}) = K(a)(a^{2n}-a^{-2n})+K(b)(b^{2n}-b^{-2n}).

technique: Collapse a parameter-dependent coefficient to a constant by dividing an identity by its dominant exponential term and letting the index tend to infinity so all subordinate terms vanish
how_used: In K(ab)(a^{2n}-a^{-2n}+b^{2n}-b^{-2n}) = K(a)(a^{2n}-a^{-2n})+K(b)(b^{2n}-b^{-2n}), order a>b>1 so a^{2n} strictly dominates the other three terms; divide by a^{2n} and let n->+infty, giving K(ab)=K(a); the surviving relation then forces K(a)=K(b), so K is constant and f_0(x)=K(x-1/x), i.e. f(x)=C_1 x+C_2/x.

technique: Replace a multivariate polynomial agreeing with a single-variable target on a box grid by the equivalent one-variable problem, transferring a degree bound between them
how_used: A lemma reduces the n-variable f (agreeing with floor((x_1+...+x_n)/m) on {0,...,m-1}^n) to a single-variable g(x) matching floor(x/m) on {0,...,n(m-1)}, showing deg f >= deg g so it suffices to lower-bound deg g.

technique: Apply the forward-difference operator in one variable to strip a degree while preserving the grid identity, then induct on target degree
how_used: Prove the lemma by induction on deg G: applying Delta_1 to F and Delta to G shrinks both grid and degrees by one (F_1(x)=G_1(x_1+...+x_n) on the reduced box), so the induction hypothesis gives deg F_1 >= deg G_1, hence deg F >= deg F_1 + 1 >= deg G.

technique: Bound a polynomial's degree from below by exhibiting a nonzero auxiliary combination whose vanishing set is a large explicit forced root count
how_used: Set h(x)=g(x+m)-g(x)-1; the constraints g(0)=g(1)=0, g(m)=1 force deg g >= 2 so deg(g(x+m)-g(x))=deg g -1 >=1, making h nonzero of degree deg g -1, yet h vanishes at 0,...,n(m-1)-m, giving (n-1)(m-1) roots, so deg g >= (n-1)(m-1)+1 >= n.

technique: To bound a cyclic sum of two-variable terms, sort the variables and use the rearrangement inequality to re-pair them into the extreme (smallest-with-largest) pairing.
how_used: With x<=y<=z<=t a sorted permutation of a,b,c,d, the cyclic sum S of cube-root terms is bounded by the paired sum (cbrt(x/(t+7))+cbrt(t/(x+7)))+(cbrt(y/(z+7))+cbrt(z/(y+7))), turning a 4-term cyclic quantity into two independent 2-variable brackets.

technique: To bound a sum of two cube roots u+v by a third cube root w, use the factorization (X+Y-Z)=... showing X^3+Y^3+3XYZ<=Z^3 iff X+Y<=Z, converting the cube-root inequality into a polynomial one in the radicands.
how_used: Setting X,Y,Z as the cube roots, the claim cbrt(x/(t+7))+cbrt(t/(x+7))<=cbrt((x+t+14)/7) becomes x/(t+7)+t/(x+7)+3*cbrt(xt(x+t+14)/(7(x+7)(t+7)))<=(x+t+14)/7 via the identity X^3+Y^3+3XYZ-Z^3=(1/2)(X+Y-Z)((X-Y)^2+(X+Z)^2+(Y+Z)^2).

technique: Split a cyclic sum of quotients into a product of separated sums by writing each numerator as a product of equal fractional powers and applying Holder's inequality.
how_used: S^3 is written as (sum a^{1/6} a^{1/6}/(b+7)^{1/3})^3 and Holder gives S^3<=(sum sqrt a)^2 * sum 1/(b+7), decoupling the numerators (sqrt a) from the denominators (1/(b+7)).

technique: Bound a reciprocal term 1/(b+7) by a linear-in-sqrt expression using a manifestly nonnegative squared-factor certificate over the term.
how_used: From (x-1)^2(x-7)^2/(x^2+7)>=0 (with x=sqrt b) one gets 1/(b+7)<=(b-16 sqrt b+71)/448, so sum 1/(b+7)<=(48-2 sum sqrt b)/56, reducing S^3 to a single-variable function of sum sqrt a bounded by AM-GM to 512/7.

technique: Collapse a multi-variable constrained functional equation to a single-variable one by choosing the free variables to make both sides depend on only one argument.
how_used: With constraint pq=rs, set p=x, q=1, r=s=sqrt(x) so r^2=s^2=x, turning the equation into (f(x)^2+1)/(2f(x)) = (x^2+1)/(2x), an equation in x alone.

technique: Clear denominators and factor the resulting pointwise polynomial relation into a product of two linear factors to force a dichotomy of values.
how_used: The relation xf(x)^2+x = x^2 f(x)+f(x) factors as (xf(x)-1)(f(x)-x)=0, so for each x either f(x)=x or f(x)=1/x.

technique: Rule out mixing the two pointwise branches by feeding a value from each branch into the original equation and deriving a contradiction with the same dichotomy.
how_used: Assuming f(a)=1/a (a not on x-branch) and f(b)=b (b not on 1/x-branch), plug p=a,q=b,r=s=sqrt(ab) to get f(ab)=ab(a^{-2}+b^2)/(a^2+b^2); matching against the forced f(ab) in {ab,1/ab} forces a=1 or b=1, contradicting the choices.

technique: Substitute the recurring fractional block by a fresh variable and rewrite the constraint in the new variables
how_used: Set a=x/(x-1), b=y/(y-1), c=z/(z-1) (so x=a/(a-1) etc.), turning the LHS into a^2+b^2+c^2 and turning xyz=1 into (a-1)(b-1)(c-1)=abc, which simplifies to a+b+c-1=ab+bc+ca.

technique: Manipulate the symmetric-function constraint into a perfect-square identity that makes the target inequality trivial
how_used: From a+b+c-1=ab+bc+ca, using a^2+b^2+c^2=(a+b+c)^2-2(ab+bc+ca), derive a^2+b^2+c^2-1=(a+b+c-1)^2, so the sum of squares is >=1 with equality exactly when a+b+c=1 and ab+bc+ca=0.

technique: Force a discriminant to be a rational square by parametrizing so each factor separately becomes a square
how_used: Equality needs a^2+ab+b^2=a+b; treating it as a quadratic in b gives discriminant (1-a)(1+3a). Writing a=k/m and choosing m=k^2-k+1 makes m-k=(k-1)^2 and m+3k=(k+1)^2 both perfect squares, yielding rational b (and c=(1-k)/m) for infinitely many integers k.

technique: Bound an iterated composition uniformly in the iteration count by inducting on that count, feeding the inductive hypothesis a shifted argument so the given relation collapses the extra iterate
how_used: Proved g_k(x) <= f(x) for ALL k by induction on k (base k=0 is x<=f(x)): at step k->k+1 apply the hypothesis to g_2(x) to get g_k(g_2(x)) <= f(g_2(x)), rewrite g_k(g_2(x))=g(g_{k+1}(x)), use condition (ii) f(g(g(x)))<g(f(x)) to get g(g_{k+1}(x))<g(f(x)), then strip the outer g by strict monotonicity, yielding g_{k+1}(x) < f(x)

technique: Derive a contradiction on a discrete/integer set by exhibiting a strictly increasing orbit that is trapped below a fixed upper bound
how_used: Since g is not the identity (else (ii) gives f(x)<f(x)), pick x_0 with x_0<g(x_0); the orbit x_k=g_k(x_0) is strictly increasing by monotonicity of g, but the uniform bound gives x_k<f(x_0) for all k, an impossible infinite strictly increasing sequence of positive integers bounded above

technique: Realize the functions on a set order-isomorphic to lexicographic pairs, letting the integer part carry an unbounded shift while a strictly increasing denominator gap absorbs the required strict inequality
how_used: On S={a-1/b}, set f(a-1/b)=a+1-1/b (shift integer part) and g(a-1/b)=a-1/(b+3^a); the super-increasing 3^a makes 2·3^a<3^{a+1}, so f(g(g(x)))=(a+1)-1/(b+2·3^a) < (a+1)-1/(b+3^{a+1})=g(f(x))

technique: Unfold a recurrence keyed to the top set bit of the argument by peeling off the highest power of 2, reducing any value to boundary values of the form f(2^n - t(...)).
how_used: Write N with 2^n <= N < 2^{n+1} as N = 2^n + m and apply f(2^n+m)=f(2^n-t(m))-f(m); recursing on m (peel its top bit each step) collapses f(N) into an alternating combination of anchor values f(2^{a_j} - t(n_{j+1})). Since t in {1,2,3}, every anchor is one of f(2^a-1), f(2^a-2), f(2^a-3), so the whole computation is governed by these six residue-classified boundary quantities.

technique: Conjecture closed forms for a family of boundary values indexed by parity of an exponent and prove them all at once by a single induction in which each new value is computed from previously established ones.
how_used: Guess (by parity of the exponent) f(2^{2k+1}-3)=0, f(2^{2k+1}-2)=3^k, f(2^{2k+1}-1)=-3^k, f(2^{2k+2}-3)=-3^k, f(2^{2k+2}-2)=-3^k, f(2^{2k+2}-1)=2*3^k. Base k=0 from f(-1),f(0),f(1) plus f(2)=-1, f(3)=2. Inductive step: each f(2^{n+1}-j)=f(2^n - t(2^n-j)) - f(2^n-j) with the six fixed t-values, so the six formulas at k follow from the six at k-1, closing the simultaneous induction.

technique: Bootstrap a global geometric magnitude bound by inducting on the bit-length of the argument, feeding the triangle inequality with a per-anchor magnitude bound as the base ingredient.
how_used: From the closed forms read off |f(2^n - t(m))| <= (2/3)*3^{n/2}, plus the dichotomy f(2^n-t(m)) >= 3^{(n-1)/2} when 3 | 2^n+m and <= 0 otherwise. Then prove |f(m)| <= 3^{n/2} for m < 2^n by induction on n: split m = 2^{n-1} + k, bound the anchor by (2/3)*3^{(n-1)/2} and f(k) by 3^{(n-1)/2} (IH); triangle inequality gives |f(m)| <= (2/3+1)*3^{(n-1)/2} < 3^{n/2}.

technique: Prove a target sign by expanding one recurrence step and dominating the negative error term with the positive anchor term via the previously established size bound.
how_used: Since 3p is not a power of 2, write 3p = 2^a + 2^b + c with a>b, 2^b>c>=0, and apply the recurrence twice: f(3p)=f(2^a - t(2^b+c)) - f(2^b - t(c)) + f(c). As 3 | 3p the first anchor is the divisible/positive branch >= 3^{(a-1)/2}; as 2^b+c is not divisible by 3 the middle anchor is <= 0 (so -f >= 0); and f(c) >= -3^{b/2} by the size bound. Hence f(3p) >= 3^{(a-1)/2} - 3^{b/2} >= 0 since a>b. The degenerate two-top-bits case 3p=2^a+1 (b=0, c=0, a odd) is settled by the same expansion using f(-2)=0<=0 (which satisfies the <=0 anchor bound at n=0), a routine boundary check rather than a distinct move.

technique: Use the product constraint to write a single variable as the fourth root of a product of four target-expression terms, hand-picking the multiplicands so the extraneous factors cancel, then bound the variable above by their AM-GM mean.
how_used: Since abcd=1, a = ((a^4)/(abcd))^{1/4} = ((a/b)(a/b)(b/c)(a/d))^{1/4}, chosen so b,c,d cancel; AM-GM gives a <= (1/4)(a/b + a/b + b/c + a/d), and cyclically b,c,d, each using three terms of S1 = a/b+b/c+c/d+d/a and one of S2 = b/a+c/b+d/c+a/d.

technique: Sum the per-variable bounds so the two target expressions appear as a fixed weighted combination, then feed the strict hypothesis inequality into that combination to flip it into the desired strict inequality.
how_used: Adding the four AM-GM bounds gives a+b+c+d <= (3/4)S1 + (1/4)S2; substituting the hypothesis S1 < a+b+c+d into the S1 term and rearranging yields a+b+c+d < S2 = b/a+c/b+d/c+a/d, with strictness carried by the hypothesis.

technique: Normalize a translation-invariant functional equation by shifting the argument so a chosen value lands at 0
how_used: Assume for contradiction f is surjective onto N. Pick a with f(a)=1 and set g(x)=f(x+a). Substituting x+a,y+a into the equation shows g satisfies the SAME equation (the relation is invariant under simultaneously shifting x and y), and g has the same value-set as f, with g(0)=1. So WLOG f(0)=1.

technique: Feed a surjective value-set through the equation to compress full surjectivity onto a countable family of arguments
how_used: Since f(R)=N, for any fixed c write f(R)={f(x+1/f(c)):x}={f(c+1/f(x)):x}. As f(x) ranges over N, the arguments c+1/f(x) lie in {c+1/n:n in N}, so {f(c+1/n):n in N} is sandwiched between two copies of f(R)=N. Hence {f(c+1/n):n in N}=N for EVERY c; used at c=0 and c=1/3.

technique: Use a Bezout combination of numerator and denominator to slide a value-1 point onto a unit-fraction argument and force a contradiction
how_used: By Claim-1 surjectivity at c=1/3 there is n with f(1/3+1/n)=1; write 1/3+1/n=s/t in lowest terms, t>1 (not an integer). Pick k,l with ks-lt=1. The scaling corollary gives f(ks/t)=1, and ks/t=1/t+l, so by +1 periodicity f(1/t)=1. But f(1/n)=n forces f(1/t)=t>1, a contradiction, so f cannot be surjective.

technique: Promote a single value-coincidence to a rational-translation congruence: substitute to strip one side, then range the freed variable over the whole value-set
how_used: Suppose f(u)=f(v). Plug x=u and x=v into the FE: the right sides f(x+1/f(u)) and f(x+1/f(v)) coincide, so f(u+1/f(x))=f(v+1/f(x)) for all x. As f(x) ranges over all of N (contradiction hypothesis), this gives f(u+1/n)=f(v+1/n) for every n. Since (u+1/n, v+1/n) is again a value-coincidence, re-feed it: k iterations of the +1/n step give f(u+k/n)=f(v+k/n), i.e. f(u+q)=f(v+q) for every nonnegative rational q. STOP here: this delivers only the congruence.

technique: Collapse the two-variable equation into a self-map fixed-point identity by setting one variable to the normalized zero-point, then invert it on a surjective argument-family
how_used: Set y=0 (f(0)=1) and x=q rational in the FE: f(1/f(q))=f(q+1)=f(q), using unit periodicity. This fixed-point identity f(1/f(q))=f(q) becomes an inversion once combined with unit-fraction surjectivity: for each n pick k with f(1/k)=n (from {f(1/k)}=N), then n=f(1/k)=f(1/f(1/k))=f(1/n). So f(1/n)=n for all n. STOP here: the endgame (pick n with f(1/3+1/n)=1, write 1/3+1/n=s/t coprime with t>1, use Bezout ks-lt=1 so f(ks/t)=1=f(1/t+l)=f(1/t)=t, forcing t=1) is the routine contradiction that follows.

technique: Sandwich a surjective value-set between two copies of itself using the two-argument symmetry, forcing a restricted argument-family to remain surjective
how_used: Under the contradiction hypothesis f(R)=N, fix any real c. The argument-shift x -> x+1/f(c) is a bijection of R, so {f(x+1/f(c)):x in R}=f(R)=N. By the FE this set equals {f(c+1/f(x)):x in R}. Since f(x) ranges over all of N (surjectivity), that set is contained in {f(c+1/n):n in N}, which is itself contained in f(R)=N. The chain N = {f(x+1/f(c)):x} subset {f(c+1/f(x)):x} subset {f(c+1/n):n in N} subset N pinches to {f(c+1/n):n in N}=N for EVERY real c. Instantiating c=0 and c=1/3 gives {f(1/n):n}=N and {f(1/3+1/n):n}=N. This unit-fraction surjectivity is the fact every later step consumes.

technique: Upgrade an equal-value pair into a shift-congruence: feed the pair through the functional equation against a free variable, then use surjectivity of the inner term to realize every unit-fraction shift and iterate it to every rational shift
how_used: Show: if f(u)=f(v) then f(u+q)=f(v+q) for every nonnegative rational q. Feed the pair into the FE f(x+1/f(y))=f(y+1/f(x)) against an arbitrary x: f(u+1/f(x))=f(x+1/f(u))=f(x+1/f(v))=f(v+1/f(x)) since f(u)=f(v). Because f attains every value in N (the surjectivity we are refuting), 1/f(x) ranges over all unit fractions 1/n, so f(u+1/n)=f(v+1/n) for all n in N -- a shift of the equal-value pair by any single unit fraction. For q=k/n, iterate the unit-fraction shift k times (each step reapplies to the freshly produced equal-value pair) to get f(u+k/n)=f(v+k/n). The per-application step is 1/n chained k times; this holds for every nonnegative rational q.

technique: Manufacture an integer period by locating an argument value whose function value equals a base value (via surjectivity of the unit-fraction fibre) and applying the shift-congruence to that same-value pair of anchor points
how_used: After normalizing f(0)=1 (replace f by g(x)=f(x+a) with f(a)=1; the FE and the value-set are invariant), promote a value-1 unit fraction to f(1)=1. From x=0 in the FE, {f(1/n):n in N}=N (Claim 1 with c=0), so some m has f(1/m)=1. The shift-congruence's telescoping corollary (from f(0)=f(1/m) shift by 1/m repeatedly) gives f(k/m)=1 whenever f(1/m)=1; at k=m this yields f(1)=1. Now f(0)=f(1)=1, so the shift-congruence on the pair (0,1) gives f(q)=f(q+1) for every nonnegative rational q -- unit periodicity on the nonnegative rationals.

technique: Force a whole reciprocal fibre to cover the full range by feeding the range back through one substituted slot of the symmetric functional equation
how_used: Assuming for contradiction f(R)=N, fix any real c. Substitute so both sides of f(x+1/f(y))=f(y+1/f(x)) are read with one argument centered at c: {f(x+1/f(c)) : x in R} = f(R) = N on the left, while the RHS equals {f(c+1/f(x)) : x in R}. Since f(x) ranges over all of N, this set is contained in {f(c+1/n) : n in N}, which is itself contained in f(R)=N. Squeezing gives {f(c+1/n) : n in N}=N for every c. Applied at c=0 and c=1/3 this yields {f(1/n)}={f(1/3+1/n)}=N -- every positive integer is attained on a reciprocal shift of any chosen base point, the surjectivity refinement that later fibre-picking arguments rely on.

technique: Propagate an equality of two function values along rational shifts by iterating the functional equation over the full integer fibre of the free variable, then chain the base case to climb a rational lattice
how_used: Show first: if f(u)=f(v) then f(u+q)=f(v+q) for all nonnegative rational q. From f(u+1/f(x))=f(x+1/f(u))=f(x+1/f(v))=f(v+1/f(x)) (using f(u)=f(v)) and the fact that f(x) hits every n in N, get f(u+1/n)=f(v+1/n) for all n; repeating k times gives f(u+k/n)=f(v+k/n), i.e. the shift by any positive rational q=k/n. Then the special consequence: from f(0)=1 (normalize by replacing f with x->f(x+a) where f(a)=1, which preserves the FE and the range), if f(q)=1 for rational q>=0 then chaining f(0)=f(q) => f(q)=f(2q) => ... => f(kq)=1. This telescoping lemma is the engine: it is what later turns f(0)=f(s/t)=1 into f(ks/t)=1.

technique: Read off exact values on a special sequence by turning the functional equation into a self-map fixed-point relation, then invert it using a surjective fibre
how_used: With f(0)=1 and unit-shift invariance f(q)=f(q+1) for rational q>=0 (from f(0)=f(1)=1: pick m with f(1/m)=1 by the fibre-surjectivity crux, then f(1)=f(m*(1/m))=1 by the telescoping lemma, then equality-propagation gives f(q)=f(q+1)), set x=q, y=0 in the FE: f(1/f(q))=f(q+1/f(0))=f(q+1)=f(q). So the relation f(1/f(q))=f(q) holds for all rational q>=0. Now invert: for each n pick k with f(1/k)=n (fibre surjectivity at c=0), and apply the relation at q=1/k to get n=f(1/k)=f(1/f(1/k))=f(1/n). Hence f(1/n)=n for every n in N.

technique: Manufacture a contradiction from an assumed unit-value on a non-integer point by using Bezout to convert it into an integer-plus-unit-fraction, then collapsing via the propagation lemma and the known exact values
how_used: By fibre surjectivity at c=1/3, pick n with f(1/3+1/n)=1; write 1/3+1/n=s/t in lowest terms, so t>1 since the value is non-integer. Choose k,l in N with ks-lt=1 (Bezout, gcd(s,t)=1). Since f(0)=f(s/t)=1, the telescoping lemma gives f(ks/t)=1. But ks/t=(lt+1)/t=1/t+l, and l applications of unit-shift invariance strip the integer l: f(1/t+l)=f(1/t). Combined with the exact-value law f(1/t)=t, this forces 1=f(ks/t)=f(1/t)=t, contradicting t>1. This closes the assumption f(R)=N.

technique: Split each fractional term with a mixed numerator into a perfect-square-over-denominator piece plus a signed cross piece by adding and subtracting inside the numerator
how_used: Double each term and write 2A = (a-c)^2/(a+b+c) + (a-c)(a-2b+c)/(a+b+c), isolating a manifestly nonnegative square part A' from a sign-indefinite cross part A''; done for all four cyclic terms so the two families can be bounded separately

technique: Bound a sum of squared-differences over denominators from below by the Cauchy-Schwarz (Engel/Titu) form, pairing each denominator with its complement so the weights sum cleanly
how_used: Apply Cauchy-Schwarz to A'+B'+C'+D' with weights sqrt(s-d),... whose squares sum to 3s, yielding A'+B'+C'+D' >= (2|a-c|+2|b-d|)^2/(3s) >= 16|a-c||b-d|/(3s). The tightness case of this same Cauchy-Schwarz step is later re-used to upgrade the equality condition from 'a=c or b=d' to 'a=c and b=d'

technique: Pair the two diametrically-opposite cross terms and combine over a common denominator so the mixed numerator collapses to a single product of two differences
how_used: Coupling A''+C'' collapses to 3(a-c)(d-b)(a+c)/M with M=s(a+c)+bd, and B''+D'' to 3(b-d)(a-c)(b+d)/N; their difference factors as 3(a-c)(b-d)W/(MN) with W=bd(b+d)-ac(a+c)

technique: Dominate a sign-indefinite cross term's magnitude by crudely lower-bounding its denominator product against its numerator so it is out-competed by the square lower bound
how_used: Show MN > (ac(a+c)+bd(b+d))s >= |W|s, giving |cross-sum| <= 3|a-c||b-d|/s; since 16/3 > 3, the square lower bound dominates and 2(A+B+C+D) >= 7|a-c||b-d|/(3s) >= 0

technique: Interpolate between two extreme configurations by flipping one entry at a time and invoke the discrete intermediate-value principle with a bounded per-step increment to catch a value in a target window
how_used: Order the terms and define c_k = sum_{i<=k} 1/floor(a_i) + sum_{i>k} 1/(floor(a_i)+1): each c_k is an admissible b-choice sum, c_0 (all ceilings) < sum 1/a_i = 1 < c_n (all floors), and the chain is strictly increasing. So a unique k has c_{k-1} < 1 < c_k, and the single flip that produced c_k raised the sum by only 1/(floor(a_k)(floor(a_k)+1)) <= 1/2 (since floor(a_k) >= 1), forcing 1 < c_k <= 3/2. This exhibits, for every sequence, an admissible choice in (1,3/2], proving C <= 3/2.

technique: To force a universal constant to its supremum, build a one-parameter family with a single 'lever' term plus many equal bulk terms tuned to saturate the constraint, then push the count to infinity
how_used: Build the tight instance: one lever term a_1 -> 2^- (so floor(a_1)=1, b_1 in {1,2}) and n-1 equal bulk terms a_i -> (2(n-1))^- (so floor=2n-2, b_i in {2n-2,2n-1}), scaled so sum 1/a_i = 1. The only choice with sum <= 1 is b_1=2, b_i=2n-2, which gives exactly 1 and so is NOT admissible (need strict >1); the cheapest admissible choice is b_1=1, b_i=2n-1, giving 1 + (n-1)/(2n-1) = (3n-2)/(2n-1). Letting n -> infinity drives this to 3/2, so C >= 3/2 (matching the upper bound to pin C = 3/2). NOTE: the official write-up has a typo ('a_i = (4n-3)/(2n-1) for i>1') which is infeasible since all terms near 2 make sum 1/a_i ~ n/2 != 1; the correct family is ONE term near 2 and n-1 terms near 2(n-1).

technique: To land a rounded sum inside a target window, walk a monotone chain of intermediate configurations from an all-low to an all-high rounding and bound each single-step increment, so the first crossing of the threshold lands within one step-size of it
how_used: For 0 <= k <= n define c_k = sum_{i<=k} 1/floor(a_i) + sum_{i>k} 1/(floor(a_i)+1): the first k terms rounded DOWN, the rest rounded UP. This chain is strictly increasing (c_0 < c_1 < ... < c_n) because moving one term from ceiling to floor raises its reciprocal. Since 1/(floor(a_i)+1) < 1/a_i < 1/floor(a_i), summing gives c_0 < 1 < c_n, so some k has c_{k-1} <= 1 < c_k. The single-step jump is c_k - c_{k-1} = 1/floor(a_k) - 1/(floor(a_k)+1) = 1/(floor(a_k)(floor(a_k)+1)) <= 1/(1*2) = 1/2. Hence 1 < c_k <= c_{k-1} + 1/2 <= 1 + 1/2 = 3/2, and choosing b_i = floor(a_i) for i <= k, b_i = floor(a_i)+1 for i > k gives a valid rounding with sum in (1, 3/2]. This establishes C <= 3/2.

technique: To show a proposed extremal constant is best possible, build a one-parameter family that pins every term to just two admissible rounding choices, so the only choice keeping the constrained sum above its strict threshold forces the objective toward the constant, then let the parameter run to the limit
how_used: Match the upper bound of 3/2 with a construction forcing the rounded sum arbitrarily close to 3/2 from below, proving no C < 3/2 works. Take a_1 just under 2 and a_2 = ... = a_n all equal, chosen so 1/a_1 + (n-1)/a_i = 1; concretely a_1 = a_i = (4n-3)/(2n-1) works (so 1/a_1 = (2n-1)/(4n-3) and the a_i>2 for i>1). Then b_1 in {1,2} and b_i in {2n-2, 2n-1} for i>1 are the only choices. If b_1 = 2, the best (largest) achievable sum is 1/2 + (n-1)/(2n-2) = 1, which is NOT > 1, so b_1 = 2 is inadmissible (violates the strict lower bound in (ii)). Hence b_1 = 1 is forced, giving sum >= 1 + (n-1)/(2n-1) = (3n-2)/(2n-1). This shows C >= (3n-2)/(2n-1) for every n, and n -> infinity gives C >= 3/2. Combined with the upper bound, C = 3/2.

technique: To show an admissible per-term rounding lands the total in a target window, order the roundings into a monotone chain from all-floors to all-ceilings and bound the jump of each single flip, so the first partial value to cross the lower endpoint cannot overshoot the upper endpoint
how_used: Establishes the achievability (upper-bound) half C <= 3/2. For 0 <= k <= n set c_k = sum_{i<=k} 1/floor(a_i) + sum_{i>k} 1/(floor(a_i)+1): start with all ceilings (c_0) and flip terms to floors one at a time up to all floors (c_n). Since 1/floor(a_i) > 1/(floor(a_i)+1), the chain is strictly increasing c_0 < c_1 < ... < c_n. Non-integrality gives floor(a_i) < a_i < floor(a_i)+1, so c_0 < sum 1/a_i = 1 < c_n. Hence a unique k has c_{k-1} <= 1 < c_k. The single flip from k-1 to k increases the sum by 1/floor(a_k) - 1/(floor(a_k)+1) = 1/(floor(a_k)(floor(a_k)+1)) <= 1/(1*2) = 1/2 (maximized at floor(a_k)=1). So c_k = c_{k-1} + increment < 1 + 1/2 = 3/2, giving 1 < c_k <= 3/2. Choosing b_i = floor(a_i) for i <= k and b_i = floor(a_i)+1 for i > k realizes the window.

technique: To prove a guaranteeing constant cannot be lowered, engineer an n-dependent extremal family in which one distinguished term straddles a value where the two admissible roundings differ maximally, so the forced choice makes the total tend to the claimed constant as n grows
how_used: Establishes the tightness (lower-bound) half C >= 3/2, which crux 0 does NOT deliver. Take a_1 = a_i = (4n-3)/(2n-1) for all i (a valid sequence: n copies with reciprocal sum 1). Then floor(a_1) = 1 forces b_1 in {1,2}, and floor(a_i) = 2n-2 forces b_i in {2n-2, 2n-1} for i>1. Only two admissible totals arise: taking b_1 = 2 gives sum <= 1/2 + (n-1)/(2n-2) = 1, which violates the strict lower bound sum > 1, so it is inadmissible; hence b_1 = 1 is forced, giving sum >= 1 + (n-1)/(2n-1) = (3n-2)/(2n-1). Thus any valid C must satisfy C >= (3n-2)/(2n-1) for every n; letting n -> infinity yields C >= 3/2. Combined with crux 0 this pins C = 3/2 (and for fixed n the optimal constant is (3n-2)/(2n-1)). The design idea: put one term just above 1 so its rounding gap 1/(1*2) = 1/2 is maximal, and set the remaining terms so that the 'safe' rounding of the special term is exactly barred by the strict inequality.

technique: To rule out periodicity, substitute a period shift into one argument and cancel every already-periodic term, isolating the one remaining term whose invariance forces the function constant.
how_used: Apply P(x,y+d) with d a nonzero period; f(y+d)=f(y), f(xf(y+d))=f(xf(y)), f(x+y+d)=f(x+y) all cancel against P(x,y), leaving only f(x(y+d))=f(xy). Setting y=0 gives f(dx)=f(0) for all x, and d≠0 makes x↦dx surjective, so f is constant. This 'nonzero period ⇒ constant' lemma is the engine that discharges every later defect quantity.

technique: To upgrade a symmetry relation to an additive (Cauchy-type) identity, form the defect between the two sides and show, by repeatedly chaining the symmetry inside a free outer shift, that the defect is a period of f; then the periodic-forces-constant lemma sends it to zero.
how_used: Set d:=f(f(x)+y)-f(x)-f(y). For arbitrary z, iterate Claim 2.2's f(f(a)+b)=f(f(b)+a) to walk f(z+f(f(x)+y)) through f(f(z)+f(x)+y)=f(f(x)+f(z)+y)=f(x+f(f(z)+y))=f(x+f(f(y)+z))=f(f(x)+f(y)+z)=f(z+f(x)+f(y)). So f(z+f(f(x)+y))=f(z+f(x)+f(y)) for all z, i.e. d is a period. Nonconstancy plus Crux 0 forces d=0, giving f(f(x)+y)=f(x)+f(y). The same defect-is-period tactic later pins f(0)=1 and f(x)≡x+1.

technique: After substituting one variable by an f-image to make the equation acquire a symmetric nested term, eliminate the residual asymmetric term by re-expressing it through the ORIGINAL equation at the swapped argument pair, then swap the two variables to read off a symmetry relation.
how_used: P(x,y): f(xf(y))+f(y)=f(x+y)+f(xy). Apply P(f(x),y): f(f(x)f(y))+f(y)=f(f(x)+y)+f(f(x)y). The term f(f(x)y) is not symmetric in x,y, so rewrite it via P(y,x): f(yf(x))+f(x)=f(y+x)+f(yx) gives f(f(x)y)=f(x+y)+f(xy)-f(x). Substituting back: f(f(x)f(y))=f(f(x)+y)+[f(x+y)+f(xy)-f(x)-f(y)]. The LHS f(f(x)f(y)) and the bracket are both symmetric under x<->y, so f(f(x)+y)=f(f(y)+x) — the master symmetry relation driving everything downstream.

technique: Upgrade a symmetry relation among nested f-evaluations to an additive-type identity by chaining that relation to rewrite one fixed nested evaluation two ways, exhibiting the additive defect as a period, then killing it with the rigidity lemma.
how_used: Given S(a,b): f(f(a)+b)=f(f(b)+a), fix x,y and set d:=f(f(x)+y)-f(x)-f(y). For arbitrary z, slide the outer argument through S repeatedly: f(z+f(f(x)+y))=f(f(z)+f(x)+y)=f(f(x)+f(z)+y)=f(x+f(f(z)+y))=f(x+f(f(y)+z))=f(f(x)+f(y)+z)=f(z+f(x)+f(y)). Hence f(z+f(f(x)+y))=f(z+f(x)+f(y)) for all z, so d is a period; the rigidity lemma (nonzero period => constant) forces d=0 for nonconstant f, giving f(f(x)+y)=f(x)+f(y). This additive identity (with y=0, f(0)=1) is the springboard toward f(x)=x+1.

technique: To kill periodicity in a functional equation, shift the free variable by the alleged period, subtract the unshifted assertion to collapse every shifted term, yielding a derived identity in which the argument scales with the remaining free variable; then specialize that variable to make the argument sweep all reals and force the function constant.
how_used: Rigidity lemma (a nonconstant solution admits no nonzero period). The equation is P(x,y): f(xf(y)) + f(y) = f(x+y) + f(xy). Suppose f has period d != 0. Write P(x, y+d): f(x(y+d)) = f(x+y+d) - f(y+d) - f(xf(y+d)). Apply the period d termwise: f(y+d)=f(y) (hence f(xf(y+d))=f(xf(y))) and f(x+y+d)=f(x+y), so the right side becomes f(x+y) - f(y) - f(xf(y)), which by P(x,y) equals f(xy). Thus f(x(y+d)) = f(xy) for ALL x,y — a DERIVED identity, not periodicity of the argument, since x(y+d)-xy = xd depends on x. Now SET y=0: f(dx)=f(0) for all x, and since d != 0 the map x -> dx is onto R, so f is constant. Contrapositive: a nonconstant solution has no nonzero period. This lemma is invoked each time a later step manufactures a candidate nonzero period for f (a shift under which f is invariant), immediately forcing that shift to be zero for the nonconstant branch.

technique: Substitute one interleaved sub-sequence's equations into the other's to eliminate that half of the variables and close the system on the remaining half
how_used: The even-indexed equations a_{2k}=a_{2k-1}+a_{2k+1} express each even term via its two odd neighbors; the odd-indexed equations a_{2k-1}=1/a_{2k-2}+1/a_{2k} and a_{2k+1}=1/a_{2k}+1/a_{2k+2} give those neighbors. Substituting eliminates every odd variable and yields the self-contained cyclic relation a_{2k}=1/a_{2k-2}+2/a_{2k}+1/a_{2k+2} (indices mod n) on the even terms alone.

technique: Evaluate a cyclic self-referential relation at the argmin and the argmax, bounding each term's neighbors by the global extremes, to squeeze min and max together
how_used: With m=min a_{2k} at index i and M=max at index j in a_{2k}=1/a_{2k-2}+2/a_{2k}+1/a_{2k+2}: at i the neighbors are <=M so their reciprocals >=1/M, giving m>=2/m+2/M; at j the neighbors are >=m so their reciprocals <=1/m, giving M<=2/m+2/M. Both sides meet at 2/m+2/M, forcing m>=M, hence m=M and the even sequence is constant.

technique: Bound one cyclic sum from both sides by two different inequalities to trap it at a single value and force equality throughout
how_used: For a_{2k}=1/a_{2k-2}+2/a_{2k}+1/a_{2k+2} with S=sum a_{2k}, T=sum 1/a_{2k}: summing gives S=4T, and Cauchy-Schwarz S*T>=n^2 yields T>=n/2. Multiplying the relation by 1/a_{2k} and summing gives n=sum(1/a_{2k}+1/a_{2k+2})^2, which QM-AM bounds below by (2T)^2/n, yielding T<=n/2. The two bounds pin T=n/2, forcing equality in Cauchy-Schwarz, so a_{2k} is constant.

technique: Refute a forced global linearity by constructing a function whose effective per-denominator slope is unbounded while the additive (Cauchy) defect stays integral
how_used: Define f(p/q) = (p/q)(1! + 2! + ... + q!) with p/q in lowest terms. Combining two fractions changes the factorial-sum only by integer multiples, so f(x+y)-f(x)-f(y) is always an integer; but the coefficient S(q)=1!+...+q! makes the slope on denominator-q rationals grow without bound. Since f(1)=S(1)=1 forces any working c to be an integer, and then f(1/q)-c/q = (S(q)-c)/q must be integral for every q, one needs c ≡ S(q) (mod q) for all q; because S(q) mod q wanders (e.g. 3 at q=5, 5 at q=7), no single c exists.

technique: Evaluate a claimed rational-function identity at a special point where the nonnegative-coefficient side is forced nonnegative, to eliminate target values that make the other side negative there
how_used: Setting x=1 gives f(1)/g(1)=1-c+1=2-c; since f,g have nonnegative coefficients and are nonzero, f(1)>=0 and g(1)>0 so the ratio is >=0, forcing 2-c>=0, i.e. c<=2. At c=2 the factor is (x-1)^2 forcing f(1)=0, but a nonneg-coefficient nonzero poly has f(1)>0, so the whole regime c>=2 is impossible.

technique: Turn a nonnegative-coefficient constraint into evaluation at a root on the unit circle and read off a forced strict sign of the imaginary part as the contradiction
how_used: With alpha=cos(theta)+i sin(theta) a root of x^2-2cos(theta)x+1 (c=2cos(theta)), f(alpha)=0 is required; but Im(f(alpha))=sum a_k sin(k theta) is strictly positive whenever all indices k<=deg f satisfy sin(k theta)>0, forcing deg f up to an index with sin(k theta)<=0, i.e. deg f>=ceil(pi/theta).

technique: Weight a chain of consecutive three-term coefficient inequalities by a sine-of-index sequence so the sine addition identity telescopes the sum to a single boundary condition
how_used: The nonneg-coefficient constraints give a_{k-1}+a_{k+1}>=2cos(theta)a_k for each k; multiplying the k-th by sin(k theta) and summing, the identity sin(k theta)+sin((k+2)theta)=2sin((k+1)theta)cos(theta) cancels interior terms leaving sin((n-2)theta)a_{n-2}>=2cos(theta)sin((n-1)theta)a_{n-2}, which after dividing by a_{n-2} and reapplying the identity is exactly sin(n theta)<=0, pinning n=ceil(pi/arccos(c/2)).

technique: Prove a degree bound is tight by choosing the coefficient sequence that turns every inequality in the derived chain into an equality
how_used: Setting a_k=sin((k+1)theta) makes each three-term inequality a_{k-1}+a_{k+1}>=2cos(theta)a_k sharp via the same sine addition identity, and stays nonnegative up to degree n=ceil(pi/theta), exhibiting a working nonneg-coefficient pair (f,g) at the minimal degree.

technique: Combine two homogeneous lower bounds on the same quantity by raising each to complementary fractional powers (summing to 1) and multiplying, choosing the exponents so the mismatched degrees on the other side average to the target.
how_used: From S:=a^2+b^2+c^2 \ge 3(abc)^{2/3} and S \ge \tfrac13(abc)^2, raise the first to power 3/4 and the second to power 1/4; the LHS collapses to S^{3/4+1/4}=S, and on the RHS the p:=abc exponents average (3/4)(2/3)+(1/4)(2)=1 while the constants give 3^{3/4}\cdot3^{-1/4}=\sqrt3, yielding S \ge \sqrt3\,abc.

technique: Feed each of the two available constraints into a common majorant of the target quantity to produce two independent homogeneous lower bounds on it.
how_used: Using S=a^2+b^2+c^2 \ge \tfrac13(a+b+c)^2, bound (a+b+c)^2 two ways: via AM-GM a+b+c\ge3(abc)^{1/3} giving S\ge3(abc)^{2/3}, and via the hypothesis a+b+c\ge abc giving S\ge\tfrac13(abc)^2 — the two seeds for the finishing move.

technique: Substitute the neutral value of one variable so the two-variable identity collapses to a linear relation in f(n) whose coefficient is a constant, then force that coefficient to zero by ruling out the constant-function solution.
how_used: Setting m=0 in f(m+n)+f(mn-1)=f(m)f(n)+2 gives f(n)+f(-1)=f(n)f(0)+2, i.e. f(n)(1-f(0))=2-f(-1) is independent of n; since a constant f=c would need c^2-2c+2=0 (discriminant -4, no integer/real root), f is non-constant, so 1-f(0)=0, pinning f(0)=1 and then f(-1)=2.

technique: Pin an undetermined function value by plugging in a few concrete argument pairs and chaining the resulting equations, forcing the value and eliminating a spurious alternative that a single specialization would leave open.
how_used: With f(0)=1, f(-1)=2 established, m=n=-1 gives f(-2)+f(0)=f(-1)^2+2, so f(-2)=5; then m=1,n=-1 gives f(0)+f(-2)=f(1)f(-1)+2, i.e. 1+5=2f(1)+2, forcing f(1)=2. This is essential because the m=1 specialization alone only yields f(1) in {0,2} (the branch f(1)=0 gives a spurious periodic sequence ...,2,1,0,1,2,... consistent with the m=1 recurrence); these specific substitutions eliminate f(1)=0.

technique: Specialize one variable to a fixed argument so the two-variable identity becomes a single-variable three-term linear recurrence, then induct both forward and backward from the base values to close the function on all integers.
how_used: Setting m=1 turns f(m+n)+f(mn-1)=f(m)f(n)+2 into f(n+1)+f(n-1)=f(1)f(n)+2; with f(1)=2 (pinned separately) this is f(n+1)=2f(n)+2-f(n-1). From seeds f(0)=1, f(1)=2, forward induction gives f(n)=n^2+1 for n>=0, and the rearrangement f(n-1)=2f(n)+2-f(n+1) inducts backward to n<=0, so f(n)=n^2+1 for all integers; verify this f satisfies the original equation (LHS=(m+n)^2+1+(mn-1)^2+1=m^2n^2+m^2+n^2+3=(m^2+1)(n^2+1)+2=RHS).

technique: In an integer/real functional equation, substitute a value that makes one variable collapse so the relation becomes (variable function value)·(constant coefficient) = constant; since the function is non-constant, force the coefficient to zero, which simultaneously pins two base values.
how_used: First rule out constants: f=c gives 2c=c^2+2, i.e. c^2-2c+2=0, no real root, so f is non-constant. Then m=0 turns f(m+n)+f(mn-1)=f(m)f(n)+2 into f(n)+f(-1)=f(0)f(n)+2, i.e. f(n)(1-f(0))=2-f(-1) for all n. The right side is constant while f(n) is non-constant, so 1-f(0)=0, giving f(0)=1, and then 2-f(-1)=0 gives f(-1)=2. These two anchors seed the rest of the solve.

technique: Shift each variable by the lower boundary of its domain so every square-root of a difference becomes a square-root of a single nonnegative variable
how_used: Set x=1+a, y=1+b, z=1+c so the constraint x,y,z>=1 becomes a,b,c>=0 and the right side sqrt(x-1)+sqrt(y-1)+sqrt(z-1) becomes sqrt(a)+sqrt(b)+sqrt(c). Under this shift each inner term x+xyz factors as (1+a)(1+(1+b)(1+c)), exposing the '(variable+1)' factors that the later Cauchy-Schwarz step consumes.

technique: When a min (or max) is taken over expressions that share a common additive term and differ only in one increasing argument, impose a WLOG ordering to identify which single argument attains the extremum and drop the min
how_used: The three inner expressions sqrt(x+xyz), sqrt(y+xyz), sqrt(z+xyz) share the common summand xyz under an increasing sqrt, so the minimum is at the smallest of x,y,z. Order a<=b<=c (i.e. x<=y<=z); then the equation collapses to the single equation sqrt((1+a)(1+(1+b)(1+c)))=sqrt(a)+sqrt(b)+sqrt(c).

technique: Rewrite each (variable+1) factor as ((sqrt of variable)^2 + 1) and apply the Cauchy-Schwarz product lower bound (p^2+1)(q^2+1) >= (pq+1)^2 to collapse a nested product of such factors into a single squared sum of the roots
how_used: See above.

technique: To prove the image of a functional equation is closed under a group operation, engineer substitutions that first hit a target output by cancelling a factor, then reuse that argument as a fresh input to combine outputs.
how_used: For f(x^2 f(y)^2)=f(x^2)f(y): y=1, x=1/f(1) forces f(z^2)=1 with z=1/f(1), so 1 is in W_f. For inverses, given w=f(u), take y=u, x=z/w so the LHS becomes f(z^2)=1 while the RHS is f(x^2)w, giving f(x^2)=1/w. For products, first realize any w as f(k^2) via x=z,y=u (k=z f(u)), then feed x=k,y=t to get f(k^2 f(t)^2)=w f(t)=wv. Hence W_f is a subgroup of Q+.

technique: To classify all solutions once the value-set is pinned to a subgroup U, define the function only on the arguments the equation actually constrains (here the squares) via the unique coset factorization, leave every unconstrained argument free in U, and verify the equation using that the image lands in U so factors commute.
how_used: With W_f forced to be a subgroup U and fixed coset reps a_i of Q+/U, DEFINE f on SQUARES only: each square t=x^2 factors uniquely as a_i^2 r^2 with r in U, and set f(t)=r*u_i where u_i:=f(a_i^2) in U is chosen freely per coset; f on NON-squares is any value in U (these arguments never appear as x^2 f(y)^2). Verification uses that f(y)=u lies in U: f(x^2 f(y)^2)=f(a_i^2 (r u)^2)=(r u) u_i, while f(x^2) f(y)=(r u_i) u, equal by commutativity in U. Reconstruction pitfall: do NOT define f(x)=r*u_i by decomposing x itself (that ignores f(y) and collapses to f=1); f is defined on the square t=x^2, and the u-factor from f(y) is what makes both sides agree.

technique: To prove the value-set of a functional equation is closed under the group operations, manufacture an argument whose value is the identity, then route any target value (an inverse or a product) through that identity point by choosing the free substitution variable to cancel or reproduce the desired factor.
how_used: For f(x^2 f(y)^2)=f(x^2)f(y), show W_f (the value set) is a subgroup of Q+ by three tailored substitutions built on one engine point. (i) Identity in W_f: put y=1, x=1/f(1); then x^2 f(1)^2=1, so f(1)=f(x^2)f(1) forces f(x^2)=1, i.e. 1 in W_f, and fix z=1/f(1) with f(z^2)=1. (ii) Inverse: given w=f(u) in W_f, put y=u, x=z/f(y); then x^2 f(y)^2=z^2, so 1=f(z^2)=f(x^2)*w, giving f(x^2)=1/w, so 1/w in W_f. (iii) Product: given v=f(t), w=f(u), put x=z, y=u and let k=z*f(u); since f(z^2)=1 the equation gives f(k^2)=w, then substituting x=k, y=t gives f(k^2 f(t)^2)=f(k^2)*v=w*v, so vw in W_f. The engine is the point z with f(z^2)=1: multiplying inside f by any value and dividing x to compensate moves you between arguments while tracking the product of values.

technique: To pin down the image (value set) of a solution to a multiplicative functional equation, prove it is a subgroup by hitting the equation with substitutions engineered to land the two sides on 1, an inverse, and a product of two arbitrary image elements.
how_used: For (*) f(x^2 f(y)^2)=f(x^2) f(y) on Q+, let W_f be the value set. (i) 1 in W_f: put y=1, x=1/f(1); the LHS argument becomes f(1)^2/f(1)^2, so f(1)=f(x^2)f(1), forcing f(x^2)=1, i.e. 1 in W_f, and fixing z:=1/f(1) with f(z^2)=1. (ii) closure under inverse: for w=f(u) in W_f, put y=u, x=z/f(y); then x^2 f(y)^2=z^2 so LHS=f(z^2)=1=f(x^2)*w, giving f(x^2)=1/w in W_f. (iii) closure under product: for v=f(t), w=f(u), first put x=z, y=u and set k=x f(y): f(k^2)=f(z^2) f(u)=w; then put x=k, y=t: f(k^2 f(t)^2)=f(k^2) f(t)=w*v, so vw in W_f. Hence W_f=:U is a subgroup of (Q+,*). This subgroup structure is the fact the whole classification rests on; it is NOT automatic and must be extracted by these targeted substitutions, not by a generic 'set x=1' that would wrongly suggest f is constant.

technique: Once the value set of a functional equation is known to be a multiplicative subgroup, coordinatize the domain by the cosets of that subgroup and evaluate the equation at a fixed representative of each coset to read the function's value off each coset.
how_used: Given W_f=U is a subgroup of (Q+,*), fix representatives a_1,a_2,... of the cosets of Q+/U. Every square t=x^2 in Q+ has a UNIQUE factorization t=a_i^2 * r^2 with r in U (this uniqueness makes the read-off well-defined). For r=f(u) in U, substitute x=a_i, y=u into (*): f(a_i^2 f(u)^2)=f(a_i^2 r^2)=f(a_i^2) f(u)=u_i * r, where u_i:=f(a_i^2). So on the coset indexed by a_i the value on squares is forced to r*u_i. CRITICAL and counterintuitive: this is the ONLY constraint the equation imposes. Because W_f is a subset of U, for ANY y (square or non-square) f(y)=u in U, and the LHS argument x^2 f(y)^2 is always a square-times-U, so (*) is verified for every x,y regardless of what value in U is assigned at a non-square. Hence f(x^2)=r*u_i on squares, while on each non-square f may take ANY value in U freely; check directly: LHS=f(a_i^2 (ru)^2)=(ru)u_i and RHS=(r u_i)u are equal for all u in U. The answer is a FAMILY parametrized by (i) the subgroup U, (ii) a choice u_i in U per coset rep, (iii) an arbitrary value in U at each non-square. f identical to 1 (U={1}) and f(x)=a*sqrt(x) on squares with free non-square values (U=Q+) are just two members. Do NOT collapse to uniqueness or to f==1: there is no minimality/valuation argument; the family is the genuine full solution set, and the free non-square assignments ARE compatible with (*) precisely because they still land in U.

technique: Split each fraction by dividing its numerator by its denominator to peel off the polynomial quotient plus a remainder term carrying a common linear factor.
how_used: Each term (i+1)^2/(x+i) is written as i+1 + (i+1)(1-x)/(x+i); the peeled constants 2+3+...+(n+1)=n(n+3)/2 cancel the RHS constant, and every remainder carries the factor (1-x), so with nx^2 moved over (nx^2-nx = -nx(1-x)) the equation becomes (1-x)(sum of (i+1)/(x+i) - nx) = 0.

technique: After factoring out the shared linear factor and reading off its obvious root, bound each residual term against its value at that root to show the residual equation holds nowhere else.
how_used: x=1 is the root of the (1-x) factor; for the residual sum(i+1)/(x+i)=nx, each fraction (i+1)/(x+i) exceeds (i+1)/(i+1)=1 when 0<x<1 (making the sum > n > nx) and is less than 1 when x>1 (making the sum < n < nx), so no x!=1 works and x=1 is the unique solution.

technique: Rewrite an inequality by completing it into a product of shifted factors around a critical value
how_used: The given (a_{n+1})^2 + a_n a_{n+2} <= a_n + a_{n+2} is recast as (a_{n+1})^2 - 1 <= (1 - a_n)(a_{n+2} - 1), isolating each term's deviation from 1 so that the sign of a factor (a term above or below 1) becomes usable; in particular if the middle term exceeds 1 the left side is positive, forcing the two factors to share a sign.

technique: Replace a factor by a larger bound of the same sign so a product collapses into a difference of squares
how_used: From the hypothesis rewrite (a_{n+1})^2-1 <= (1-a_n)(a_{n+2}-1). Assuming a_{n+1},a_{n+2}>1: since a_n>0 gives 0<1-a_n<1<a_{n+2}+1 and a_{n+2}-1>0, replace the factor (1-a_n) by the larger (a_{n+2}+1) to get (a_{n+1})^2-1 < (a_{n+2}+1)(a_{n+2}-1) = (a_{n+2})^2-1. The same replacement on the index-(n+1) bound gives (a_{n+2})^2-1 < (a_{n+1})^2-1; the two opposite strict inequalities contradict, so no two consecutive terms past a_1,a_2 both exceed 1. Then a_2022>1 forces a_2021,a_2023<=1, and the index-2021 bound gives 0<(a_2022)^2-1<=(1-a_2021)(a_2023-1)<=0, a contradiction, so a_2022<=1.

technique: Bound the extreme element of an ordered set by summing the k smallest/largest others available to represent it
how_used: Sorting a1<...<an, expressing a1 forces a1 >= a2+...+a_{k+1} (its k smallest possible summands) and expressing an forces a_{n-k}+...+a_{n-1} >= an, giving the two edge inequalities that seed every contradiction.

technique: Add two aligned extremal inequalities so shared terms cancel and leave a contradiction against the ordering
how_used: For n=k+3, add a1 >= a2+...+a_{k+1} and a3+...+a_{k+2} >= a_{k+3}; overlapping middle terms cancel to give a1+a_{k+2} >= a2+a_{k+3}, contradicting a1<a2 and a_{k+2}<a_{k+3}.

technique: Build the extremal example from symmetric ±i pairs so a representation of i yields the one for -i by negation
how_used: Take A_i={-i,i} for i=1..l+2 (k=2l), giving k+4 elements; each i<l+2 is written using l-1 full pairs plus {i+1,-1}, halving the verification since -i is handled by negating i's sum; the odd case k=2l+1 adds 0 to every expression and represents 0 via {1,2,-3} plus remaining pairs.

technique: Turn a 'unique solution' hypothesis into a strict inequality by feeding a candidate back into itself and using uniqueness to exclude a competing (diagonal) witness
how_used: Since y is the unique z with (x,z) good and y != x, the diagonal pair (x,x) is NOT good, forcing xf(x)+xf(x)>2, i.e. xf(x)>1; the symmetric argument (goodness is symmetric, so (y,x) good and by uniqueness x is y's partner) gives yf(y)>1.

technique: Apply AM-GM to a symmetric two-term sum so the product under the root regroups into terms already bounded
how_used: xf(y)+yf(x) >= 2*sqrt(xf(y)*yf(x)) = 2*sqrt(xf(x)*yf(y)) > 2 (regrouping xf(y)*yf(x)=xf(x)*yf(y) and using xf(x),yf(y)>1), contradicting that (x,y) is good and forcing every good pair to be diagonal, hence f(x)<=1/x.

technique: Substitute a self-referential argument built from the function's own value to manufacture a specific witness satisfying the property, then invoke the diagonal/uniqueness constraint on it
how_used: With x=1/f(t): (1/f(t))f(1/f(t))<=1 gives t*f(1/f(t))<=tf(t)<=1, so t*f(1/f(t))+1<=2 and (t,1/f(t)) is good; the diagonal-only conclusion forces t=1/f(t), i.e. f(t)=1/t.

technique: Pick the pair maximizing the target quantity and read off local domination inequalities from maximality
how_used: Choose 1<=a<b<=n maximizing 2^{b-a}x_a x_b; comparing (a,b) against (a+t,b) forces x_{a+t} <= 2^t x_a, and symmetrically x_{b-t} <= 2^t x_b, controlling every term by a geometric profile centered at the two endpoints a,b.

technique: Bound a tail of a sequence by a geometric series from a per-term ratio inequality to prove it stays below a constant
how_used: Using x_{a+t}<=2^t x_a, the head sum sum_{i=1}^{a+u-1} x_i is dominated by 2^u x_a(1/2+1/4+...) < 2^u x_a <= 1 (with x_a in (2^{-(u+1)},2^{-u}]); symmetrically the tail past b-v is < 1, so the mass outside the middle block [a+u, b-v] is strictly below 2, forcing (via s>=3, terms <=1) that block to contain >=2 integers, i.e. a+u<b-v.

technique: Linearize a convex exponential term via Bernoulli's inequality to close a chain of inequalities
how_used: After bounding s < b-a + (2^{u+1-alpha}+2^{v+1-beta}-(u+v+1)) with x_a=2^{-alpha}, x_b=2^{-beta} and alpha in (u,u+1], beta in (v,v+1], apply 2^x<=1+x on [0,1] so 2^{u+1-alpha}+2^{v+1-beta}-u-v-1 <= 3-alpha-beta, yielding s-3 < b-a-alpha-beta and hence 2^{s-3} < 2^{b-a-alpha-beta} = 2^{b-a}x_a x_b.

technique: Build the target set as consecutive partial sums of the sought terms so each gap is one term and the full span becomes the top term via a defining root
how_used: For n=3,4 set a_k = sum of r^1..r^{k-1} (so consecutive gaps are r,r^2,...) and pick r the real root of x^{n-1}-x-1=0, making the longest difference a_n-a_1 = r+...+r^{n-1} collapse to the required top power r^{b}; e.g. r root of x^3-x-1 gives the six differences r^1..r^6.

technique: Bound a growth rate by writing one value as a sum of two others each exceeding a common floor
how_used: Since only n-1 adjacent differences exist among differences with exponent <= n, some r^e (e<=n) splits as (a_j-a_{j-1})+(a_{j-1}-a_i) > r+r, giving r^n>2r hence r^{n-1}>2, the floor that later limits how many differences can be 'large'.

technique: Force each split of the maximum into a large part drawn from a short forced list by counting how many available values can exceed half the maximum
how_used: In the n-2 splits of a_n-a_1=r^b as (a_n-a_i)+(a_i-a_1), each has a part >= half; the lemma gives r^{b-(n-1)}<half so only r^{b-1},...,r^{b-(n-2)} qualify, pinning the 'large' exponents to L={b-1,...,b-(n-2)}.

technique: Transfer a convex function's strictly decreasing consecutive value-differences into strict inequalities on the arguments' consecutive gaps
how_used: From r^{b-1}-r^{b-2}>...>r^{b-(n-3)}-r^{b-(n-2)} (convexity of x->r^x, r>1) deduce r^{a2}-r^{a1}>...>r^{a_{n-2}}-r^{a_{n-3}} on the matched small parts, then again by convexity a2-a1>a3-a2>...>a_{n-2}-a_{n-3} on the small exponents.

technique: Squeeze a chain of strictly decreasing integer gaps between a minimal-staircase lower bound and a range upper bound to force every gap to its extreme
how_used: Strictly decreasing integer gaps with last >=2 force a_{n-2}-a_1 >= 2+3+...+(n-2)=n(n-3)/2, while a_{n-2}<=b-(n-1), a_1>=1 give <= b-n = n(n-3)/2; equality pins the small exponents exactly to S, yielding r^{n-1}=r+1 and r^{n+1}=r^4+1 which eliminate to r^3=r+1 hence n=4.

technique: Iterate a functional equation on its anchor output value, feeding each newly computed output back in as the next argument to grow an arithmetic-progression orbit.
how_used: With c=f(0): P(0,0) gives f(c)=2c; then repeatedly apply P(0,kc) (using that any image value t satisfies f(x+t)=f(x)+t) to get f(kc)=(k+1)c for all integers k (both signs, using P(-c,0) to seed f(-c)=0). Then z=kc realizes slope f(z)/z=(k+1)/k, so every (n+1)/n lies in Z. When c=0 the orbit is just z=0, which trivially solves f(z)=qz for any q, so sufficiency still holds.

technique: Realize a functional equation with an integer-valued additive term by decomposing the argument into fractional and integer parts, so an integer output shifts only the integer part and leaves the fractional part untouched.
how_used: Define f(x)=g({x})+floor(x) with g:[0,1)->Z arbitrary. Because f(y) is an integer, {x+f(y)}={x} and floor(x+f(y))=floor(x)+f(y), hence f(x+f(y))=g({x})+floor(x)+f(y)=f(x)+f(y) for ANY choice of g. This gives a large tunable family inside F, the reservoir from which one later picks g to exclude a target slope.

technique: To show a per-class integer value can be assigned to dodge an entire integer-indexed arithmetic progression, argue by contradiction on two consecutive candidate values: if every candidate failed, two consecutive ones would both hit the forbidden set, and subtracting forces the progression's step to be an integer.
how_used: Given fractional part alpha, need an integer m=g(alpha) with m+n != p(alpha+n) for all integers n, i.e. (m-p*alpha)/(p-1) never an integer (for p != 1; p=1 is trivial). Treat m as the free choice and n as the universal quantifier. If no such m existed, then for two consecutive integers m and m+1 each value (m-p*alpha)/(p-1) and ((m+1)-p*alpha)/(p-1) lands in Z, so does their difference 1/(p-1). But p not of the form (n+1)/n means 1/(p-1) is not an integer, a contradiction. Hence a valid m exists for every alpha, and the resulting g dodges the line y=px everywhere.

technique: To defeat a 'for every f, some z has f(z)=qz' claim, build one concrete counterexample f from a fractional-part template: fix f on integer translates by an additive rule and leave one free integer parameter per unit-interval class to be chosen adversarially.
how_used: For the excluding direction (p not of the form (n+1)/n is not forced), rather than classifying all f in F, directly construct one member: pick any g:[0,1)->Z and set f(x)=g({x})+floor(x). One checks f in F because g is integer-valued, so f(x+f(y))=g({x})+floor(x)+g({y})+floor(y)=f(x)+f(y) (the integer f(y) shifts floor but not the fractional class). This reduces 'f(z) != pz for all z' to a per-class condition on g({z}): namely g(alpha)+n != p(alpha+n) for all integers n, for each fractional part alpha, turning a global functional constraint into an independent integer-dodging problem on each class alpha. The per-class dodge succeeds because the target values solve for m along an arithmetic progression of stride 1/(p-1); that stride is a non-integer exactly when p is not of the form (n+1)/n, so consecutive targets never both land on integers and an integer m avoiding all targets exists.

technique: To realize a fixed target ratio q=f(z)/z for EVERY solution of a functional equation, anchor at c=f(0) and iterate the FE along the orbit c,2c,3c,... to force a linear relation f(kc)=(k+1)c, so z=kc is the witness.
how_used: For the inclusion S⊆Z one must handle EVERY f∈F, so work intrinsically. Set c=f(0). P(0,0) gives f(f(0))=2f(0), i.e. f(c)=2c. Induct with P(0,kf(0)): f((k+1)f(0))=f(0)+f(kf(0))=(k+2)f(0), giving f(kf(0))=(k+1)f(0) for all k≥1. Symmetrically P(-f(0),0) gives f(-f(0))=0 and downward induction gives f(-kf(0))=(-k+1)f(0). Reading off z=kf(0): f(z)=((k+1)/k)z (and negative k reproduce the same set), so every q=(n+1)/n is realized — for any f, when f(0)=0 take z=0 to cover all q. Hence S⊆Z.

technique: To exhibit a rich family of solutions of an additive-type functional equation (for a non-existence / counterexample direction), build candidates from the floor and fractional-part decomposition f(x)=g({x})+⌊x⌋ with g an arbitrary integer-valued function on [0,1).
how_used: For the exclusion Z⊆S one must, for each p∉S, produce an f∈F with f(z)≠pz for all z. The device is f(x)=g({x})+⌊x⌋ where g:[0,1)→ℤ is arbitrary. Because g takes only integer values, {x+f(y)}={x} and ⌊x+f(y)⌋=⌊x⌋+f(y), so f(x+f(y))=g({x})+⌊x⌋+g({y})+⌊y⌋=f(x)+f(y); thus any such f lies in F. This freedom in choosing g per fractional-part class is what lets one dodge the line y=pz.

technique: To choose a free integer parameter so a target linear relation is missed on a whole arithmetic orbit at once, translate 'no hit' into requiring a single fixed difference-quotient to be a non-integer, then get that freedom from an integrality obstruction stated on the target value.
how_used: With f(x)=g({x})+⌊x⌋, avoiding f(z)=pz on the class {z}=α means choosing m=g(α)∈ℤ with m+n≠p(α+n) for every n∈ℤ (here n=⌊z⌋). For p≠1 this is exactly the demand that (m-pα)/(p-1) never be an integer as n varies; if it were an integer for two consecutive values of m their difference 1/(p-1) would be an integer. But p∉S={(n+1)/n} is precisely the statement that 1/(p-1) is not an integer, so a suitable m exists for each α. Defining g(α)=m gives f(z)≠pz for all z, so p∉Z.

technique: To force the OTHER inclusion (every f must hit a prescribed slope), feed the functional equation its own output as an argument and iterate: plug the fixed base value f(0) back into the equation repeatedly to generate an orbit of points on which f is pinned exactly.
how_used: For S⊆Z one shows each q=(k+1)/k lies in Z, i.e. EVERY f∈F hits the line f(z)=qz. Using P(x,y): f(x+f(y))=f(x)+f(y), specialize to x=0 and iterate on the base value f(0). P(0,0) gives f(f(0))=2f(0); then P(0,kf(0)) with the inductive hypothesis f(kf(0))=(k+1)f(0) gives f((k+1)f(0))=f(0)+f(kf(0))=(k+2)f(0). So at z=kf(0) one has f(z)=(k+1)/k·z, hitting slope (k+1)/k; P(-f(0),0) gives f(-f(0))=0 and the same induction downward covers negative k. Since this holds for arbitrary f∈F, every (n+1)/n∈Z. This move is the missing half neither of the other two cruxes supplies.

technique: Propagate value-equalities one index forward by feeding equal terms through a self-referential functional relation
how_used: From a_{a_r+a_1}=a_{r+1} and a_{a_s+a_1}=a_{s+1}, the relation a_{a_i+a_j}=a_{i+j} gives a_r=a_s (r,s<n) implies a_{r+1}=a_{s+1}; iterating turns a single collision into full eventual periodicity of the tail (a_r,...,a_n) with minimal period d and offset r, and forces a_i=i below r.

technique: Encode the free choices left after imposing per-residue-class congruence and range bounds as a max-product-of-a-fixed-sum function
how_used: For small sequences each period entry a_j must satisfy r<=a_j<=k and d | a_j-j, so within each of the d residue classes the choices multiply; the count equals g(x,d), the maximum product of d positive integers summing to x=k+1-r, given explicitly by (p+1)^q p^{d-q} with p=floor(x/d), q=x-dp.

technique: Bound a max-product function against 3^{x/3} by padding its arguments to a ratio where the product is an exact power, using its multiplicativity g(kx,kd)=g(x,d)^k
how_used: Using g(kx,kd)=g(x,d)^k and the exact forms g=2^{3d-x}3^{x-2d} (for 2d<=x<=3d) and g=3^{4d-x}4^{x-3d} (for 3d<=x<=4d), one cubes and pads (3x,3d) to (15x-36d,4x-9d) landing in the 3:1..4:1 band, giving g(x,d)<=3^{x/3}(64/81)^{x/3-d} and symmetrically (8/9)^{d-x/3}, whose sum over d is a geometric series bounding f(n) by c_2*3^{n/6}.

technique: Encode a two-sided inequality as the sign of a single auxiliary integer sequence, choosing the quantity so that both bounds become sign conditions on consecutive terms.
how_used: Set d_n = (z_0+...+z_n) - n z_n; the first inequality z_n < (z_0+...+z_n)/n holds iff d_n > 0, and an algebraic rewrite of n z_{n+1} - (z_0+...+z_n) shows the second inequality (z_0+...+z_n)/n <= z_{n+1} is equivalent to d_{n+1} <= 0, reducing the goal to finding a unique n with d_n > 0 >= d_{n+1}.

technique: Prove a strictly monotone crossing of an integer sequence by computing its first difference and evaluating the initial term.
how_used: Compute d_{n+1} - d_n = n(z_n - z_{n+1}) < 0, so d_1 > d_2 > ... strictly decreases; with d_1 = z_0 > 0 and all d_n integers, the sequence must eventually go non-positive, forcing exactly one index (the last positive term) with d_n > 0 >= d_{n+1}.
