technique: Reframe the target inequality as a statement about which piece of a piecewise map the two iterates land in, by reading off the sign of f(x)-x on each branch
how_used: Since f(x)-x = 1/2 > 0 on (0,1/2) and f(x)-x = x^2-x < 0 on [1/2,1), the product (a_n - a_{n-1})(b_n - b_{n-1}) is negative exactly when a_{n-1} and b_{n-1} sit in different subintervals; so the goal becomes showing the two orbits cannot forever stay in the same branch.

technique: Track the gap between the two orbits as a monovariant and lower-bound its per-step growth on each branch to get a contradiction from boundedness
how_used: Assuming both iterates always share a branch, d_k=|a_k-b_k| is invariant on I_1 (both shift by 1/2) but on I_2 satisfies d_{k+1}=|a_k-b_k|(a_k+b_k) >= d_k(1+d_k) since both exceed 1/2; combining the two cases over two steps gives d_{k+2} >= d_k(1+d_0), hence d_{2m} >= d_0(1+d_0)^m, which eventually exceeds 1 while all iterates stay in (0,1) forcing d<1.

technique: Bound a single sequence entry by the extremal prefix sum by writing it as the difference of two consecutive prefix sums and applying the triangle inequality
how_used: To get D >= M/2: with M = max_k |x_k| the largest absolute value, pick in Dave's optimal ordering the index i with |d_i| = M, write d_i = (d_1+...+d_i) - (d_1+...+d_{i-1}), so M <= |prefix_i| + |prefix_{i-1}| <= D + D = 2D, forcing D >= M/2. (Paired with D >= S = |total|, this gives N = max{M,S} <= 2D.)

technique: Bound a greedy-minimizing running total by comparing its actual choice against a hypothetical opposite-sign candidate from the remaining pool, whose addition keeps the total inside the max-magnitude interval
how_used: In the induction |h_i| <= N = max{M,S} (h_i = George's i-th prefix sum): in the case where remaining terms g_i,...,g_n contain both signs, pick j>=i with h_{i-1}*g_j <= 0; George's minimality gives |h_i| = |h_{i-1}+g_i| <= |h_{i-1}+g_j| <= max{|h_{i-1}|,|g_j|} <= max{N,M} = N.

technique: Certify a ratio lower bound is tight by exhibiting a small explicit multiset on which the optimal actor and every greedy run realize the extreme values simultaneously
how_used: To show c >= 2: use the multiset {1,-1,2,-2}. Dave orders 1,-2,2,-1 with prefix sums 1,-1,1,0 so D=1. Any George run is forced to G=2, because once a +/-2 is placed the only cancelling term is the other +/-2, so some prefix hits magnitude 2 no matter how ties are broken (e.g. George may run 1,-1,2,-2 with prefix sums 1,0,2,0). Hence G/D >= 2 for a valid George sequence.

technique: When one greedy comparison move cannot reach a case, close it by noting the running partial sums are monotone there, so each is trapped between an already-bounded earlier partial sum and the (bounded) total
how_used: Case 1 of the |h_i| <= N induction (N = max{M,S}, M = max|x_k|, S = |sum of all x_k|). If all remaining chosen numbers g_i,...,g_n share a sign (WLOG >= 0), the future prefix sums are monotone nondecreasing h_{i-1} <= h_i <= ... <= h_n = (signed total), so |h_i| <= max{|h_{i-1}|, |h_n|}; since |h_{i-1}| <= N by induction and |h_n| = S <= N, get |h_i| <= N. This is the endgame the opposite-sign greedy comparison cannot reach.

technique: To bound a greedy locally-minimizing partial sum, compare George's actual pick against a still-available term whose sign opposes the current running sum; adding an opposite-sign number keeps the magnitude below the larger of the two magnitudes
how_used: Case 2 of the |h_i| <= N induction (h_i = g_1+...+g_i the greedy prefix sums, N = max{M,S}): when the remaining numbers g_i,...,g_n contain both signs, pick a remaining g_j with h_{i-1}*g_j <= 0. Since George minimizes |h_{i-1}+g_i| over all remaining numbers, |h_i| = |h_{i-1}+g_i| <= |h_{i-1}+g_j|; and because g_j opposes the sign of h_{i-1}, |h_{i-1}+g_j| <= max{|h_{i-1}|, |g_j|} <= max{N, M} = N. The comparison term g_j is the tool, not the pick George actually made. (The all-one-sign case and base case |h_1| <= M are routine and outside this crux.)

technique: Bound an individual term of an arrangement by the price by writing it as the difference of two consecutive prefix sums, each of which is at most the price in the optimal arrangement
how_used: Establishing D >= M/2, the lower bound that supplies the factor 2. Take an index i with |d_i| = M = max|x_k| in Dave's OPTIMAL arrangement d_1,...,d_n (price D). Then M = |d_i| = |(d_1+...+d_i) - (d_1+...+d_{i-1})| <= |d_1+...+d_i| + |d_1+...+d_{i-1}| <= D + D = 2D. Combined with the trivial D >= S (the full sum is one prefix sum), this gives N = max{M,S} <= 2D, closing G <= N <= 2D.

technique: To force a min-vs-greedy ratio to its worst value, hand-craft a small collection with two magnitude scales so that a legal greedy tie-break commits to the large-scale term before its cancel while the optimum interleaves the scales to cancel early
how_used: Proving c >= 2 (the lower half of 'find the least c'). Take the collection {1, -1, 2, -2}. George: pick 1 (prefix 1), then -1 (prefix 0), then at sum 0 both +2 and -2 give |2| — a genuine tie, so a random tie-break may pick +2 (prefix 2), then -2 (prefix 0); prefix sums 1,0,2,0 give G = 2. Dave arranges 1,-2,2,-1 giving prefix sums 1,-1,1,0, so D = 1. Hence G/D = 2, forcing c >= 2. For n > 4 pad with zeroes (they never change a prefix sum), so the ratio persists for all n >= 4.

technique: To bound the largest single term of an ordering by the price, write that term as the difference of two consecutive prefix sums and apply the triangle inequality
how_used: Proving D >= M/2, where M = max|x_i| and D is Dave's optimal price. In Dave's optimal sequence d_1,...,d_n pick index i with |d_i| = M. Then M = |d_i| = |(d_1+...+d_i) - (d_1+...+d_{i-1})| <= |d_1+...+d_i| + |d_1+...+d_{i-1}| <= D + D = 2D, since every prefix sum has absolute value at most the price D. Hence D >= M/2. Combined with the trivial D >= S = |x_1+...+x_n| (the full sum is a prefix of every arrangement), this supplies the two lower bounds on D needed to turn G <= max{M,S} into G <= 2D.

technique: To bound a greedy prefix sum by induction, dominate the greedily chosen increment by a hypothetical remaining term of sign opposite to the running sum
how_used: Proving G <= N := max{M, S}, where M = max|x_i|, S = |x_1+...+x_n|. Let h_i = g_1+...+g_i be George's prefix sums; show |h_i| <= N by induction. Base: |h_1| = |g_1| <= M <= N. Step (assume |h_{i-1}| <= N): if all remaining terms g_i,...,g_n share a sign, the h's are monotone from h_{i-1} to h_n = (signed) S, so |h_i| <= max{|h_{i-1}|, |h_n|} <= N; otherwise some remaining g_j has sign opposite to h_{i-1} (h_{i-1} g_j <= 0), and since George minimizes |h_{i-1}+g_i| over remaining terms, |h_i| <= |h_{i-1}+g_j| <= max{|h_{i-1}|, |g_j|} <= N. This bounds G <= N; with D >= M/2 and D >= S it gives G <= max{M,S} <= 2D.

technique: Absorb the inhomogeneous term into an auxiliary function of the free variable to turn a Cauchy-like FE into a shift-plus-additive form, then iterate the shift
how_used: Setting g(m)=f(3m)-f(m)+2C (C=1007) rewrites f(f(m)+n)+f(m)=f(n)+f(3m)+2014 as f(f(m)+n)=g(m)+f(n); induction in both directions on the number of copies of the step f(m) then gives f(tf(m)+n)=tg(m)+f(n) for all integers t.

technique: Evaluate one composite value two ways by feeding two different argument-triples into the iterated identity, then equate to force a proportionality between two derived functions
how_used: Applying f(tf(m)+n)=tg(m)+f(n) to (r,0,f(0)) and (0,0,f(r)) both compute f(f(r)f(0)), yielding f(0)g(r)=f(r)g(0); after ruling out f(0)=0 (which would make f identically 0, contradicting the FE), this gives g(r)=αf(r) with α=g(0)/f(0), hence the dilation law f(3m)-β=(1+α)(f(m)-β) with β=2C/α.

technique: Reconcile a multiplicative dilation law with an additive shift law by choosing an exponent making the dilation base's argument congruent to 1 modulo an attained coprime period
how_used: From 3 not dividing 2014 an attained value d=f(a) with gcd(d,3)=1 exists, giving the additive shift f(n+td)=f(n)+α·td; choosing k=φ(|d|) so d|3^k-1 makes f(3^k m)=f(m)+α(3^k-1)m, which set equal to the k-fold dilation f(3^k m)-β=(1+α)^k(f(m)-β) forces ((1+α)^k-1)(f(m)-β)=α(3^k-1)m, proving f linear; substituting f(m)=Am+β into the FE pins A=2, β=C, so f(m)=2m+1007.

technique: Design one side of an iff-condition to be identically false by writing the target quantity as a sum of squares plus the threshold whose two equality conditions are mutually exclusive
how_used: For the negative case P(0)=-C, take P(x)=-(2x^2/C + C) and rewrite |y^2-P(x)| = y^2 + x^2/C + (|x|-C)^2/C + 2|x|, then observe the two equality cases (|x|=C from the square term and x=0 from the second bound) cannot both hold, so |y^2-P(x)|>2|x| always; the iff then holds vacuously as an equivalence of two false statements by symmetry

technique: Verify a candidate satisfies a symmetric iff by squaring the absolute-value inequality and factoring the resulting difference into a manifestly symmetric product
how_used: For P(x)=x^2+1, |y^2-P(x)|<=2|x| squares to (y^2-x^2-1)^2<=4x^2, which factors as 0<=((x+y)^2-1)(1-(x-y)^2); this expression is symmetric in x,y so the condition is unchanged under swapping x and y

technique: Bound the degree by substituting a value that nests the polynomial inside itself and comparing the two sides' growth orders
how_used: Plug y=sqrt(P(x)) into (1) to get P(sqrt(P(x)))<=x^2+2sqrt(P(x)); with a x^n<P(x)<b x^n for large x, the left side grows like x^{n^2/2} while the right grows like x^{n/2}, forcing x^{(n^2-n)/2} bounded, absurd for n>=4, so P is quadratic

technique: Transport a symmetry across an iff by re-running the equivalence at a sign-changed argument that leaves the OTHER side invariant, then equate the two resulting one-variable conditions
how_used: The property gives |y^2-P(x)|<=2|x| iff |x^2-P(y)|<=2|y|; the right side involves x only through x^2, so it is unchanged under x->-x. Running the equivalence at x and at -x (same |x|) chains to |y^2-P(x)|<=2|x| iff |y^2-P(-x)|<=2|x|. As y^2 sweeps R_{>=0}, this forces [P(x)-2|x|,P(x)+2|x|] cap R_{>=0} = [P(-x)-2|x|,P(-x)+2|x|] cap R_{>=0}; on the infinitely many x with P(x)+2|x|>=0 the equal-length bands share their upper endpoint, giving P(x)=P(-x). Then P(x)-P(-x) has infinitely many roots, so P is even.

technique: Realize an entire interval of a target quantity by a one-parameter polynomial family for which BOTH sides of the iff are always false, verified by rewriting the discriminating quantity as a sum of squares above the threshold
how_used: To attain every negative P(0)=-C (C>0), take P(x) = -(2x^2/C + C). By the symmetry of the construction it suffices to show |y^2-P(x)| > 2|x| always, so the iff relates two always-false statements. Rewrite |y^2-P(x)| = y^2 + x^2/C + (|x|-C)^2/C + 2|x| >= 2|x|, where the two equality conditions require |x|=C and x=0 simultaneously -- impossible -- so the inequality is strict. This sweeps the whole ray (-infty,0). The isolated value P(0)=1 is realized separately by P(x)=x^2+1.

technique: Substitute a radical of the polynomial for one variable of the constraint to make the polynomial act on itself, then force the degree down by comparing the composition's growth order against the constraint's
how_used: After P>0 everywhere is known, set y=sqrt(P(x)) (well-defined since P>0). The left side |y^2-P(x)|=0<=2|x| holds automatically, so the iff forces |x^2-P(sqrt(P(x)))|<=2*sqrt(P(x)), i.e. P(sqrt(P(x))) <= x^2 + 2*sqrt(P(x)) for all real x. Writing deg P=n with leading coefficient d>0, sandwich a*x^n < P(x) < b*x^n for large x (e.g. a=d/2, b=2d). Then the LHS is a composition growing like x^{n^2/2}, while the RHS grows like max(x^2, x^{n/2}); the surviving power x^{(n^2-n)/2} must stay bounded as x->infinity, which is impossible unless n<=2. Combined with evenness this pins deg P=2.

technique: Turn a symmetric functional iff into an equality of two truncated intervals over the free variable, then read off a matched endpoint at infinitely many points to force a polynomial identity
how_used: Chain the given equivalence with the substitution x->-x: |y^2-P(x)|<=2|x| iff |x^2-P(y)|<=2|y| iff |y^2-P(-x)|<=2|x|. As y^2 ranges over R_{>=0}, the first-vs-third equivalence says [P(x)-2|x|,P(x)+2|x|] cap R_{>=0} = [P(-x)-2|x|,P(-x)+2|x|] cap R_{>=0} for every x. To extract a value equality, one needs x where both truncated intervals are nonempty with their true right endpoints P(x)+2|x| and P(-x)+2|x|: this requires P(x)+2|x|>=0, which holds for infinitely many x whenever P(0)>=0 (WLOG the coefficient of x in P is >=0, so P(x)+2|x|>=0 for all sufficiently small x>0). On that range the right endpoints coincide, giving P(x)=P(-x) at infinitely many points, so the polynomial P(x)-P(-x) vanishes identically and P is even.

technique: Trap a perfect square strictly between two consecutive squares of the correct parity to force an exact equality.
how_used: From 4|f(a)| = |f(f(a))^2 - a^2| >= a^2 - (|a|-2)^2 and same-parity, |f(a)| is squeezed into the window [|a|-1, |a|+3]; then c^2 = a^2 + 4f(a) = (a±2)^2 + d with d in {-16,...,8} and |a±2|>=8 forces c^2 = (a±2)^2 exactly, yielding f(a) = 1±a for all sufficiently large |a|.

technique: Pick the maximum-modulus element of a bounded forward-invariant orbit and apply the relation there so the extremal inequality collapses the possibilities.
how_used: For c in the exceptional set Z_0 (shown finite and f-invariant), the orbit c_i = f^i(c) is bounded; choosing k with |c_k| maximal gives |c_{k+2}| <= |c_k|, and (|c_k|-2)^2 - 4 <= c_{k+2}^2 with matching parity leaves only |c_k| in {0,4}, ultimately forcing Z_0 = {0} with f(0)=0.

technique: Feed the function's own iterates back into the functional equation to turn it into a recurrence along the orbit of a single seed point.
how_used: Setting n = a_k with a_k = f^k(1) in n^2 + 4 f(n) = f(f(n))^2 converts the equation into the orbit recurrence a_k^2 + 4 a_{k+1} = a_{k+2}^2 with a_0 = 1. This is the engine for the positive side: once the seed is pinned to a_1 = 2, a_2 = 3, induction on a_{k+1}^2 = a_{k-1}^2 + 4 a_k gives a_k = k+1 for all k, so the orbit {a_k} is exactly {1,2,3,...} and f(n) = f(a_{n-1}) = a_n reads f(n) = n+1 for EVERY positive integer n (not just isolated values). Because a_2^2 = 1 + 4 a_1 is odd, one writes a_2 = 2r+1, a_1 = r^2 + r, feeding the seed-elimination move.

technique: Eliminate spurious seed values of an integer orbit by bounding a nonzero square-difference between the two consecutive same-parity squares it must lie between, then finite-checking the survivors.
how_used: The orbit recurrence gives a_3^2 = (r^2+r)^2 + 8r + 4, a perfect square differing from (r^2+r)^2 by 8r+4 != 0. Because both 8r+4 and r^2+r are even, a_3^2 must differ from (r^2+r)^2 by at least the gap to the nearest even square, so |8r+4| >= (r^2+r)^2 - (r^2+r-2)^2 = 4(r^2+r-1). This quadratic-vs-linear inequality forces |r| < 4; checking r in {-3,...,3} shows (r^2+r)^2+8r+4 is square only for r = -3, 0, 1, and running the recurrence forward on r=-3 and r=0 produces two different values for f(1) (contradiction), leaving r=1, i.e. a_1=2, a_2=3.

technique: Classify a self-referential value at a new argument by strong induction that routes its inner iterates into the already-classified regime, so the double/triple iterate becomes an explicit affine form and the equation collapses to a perfect-square identity.
how_used: For n >= 1 the value f(-n) is unknown, so induct on n: whenever an inner iterate f(-n) or f(f(-n)) lands where f is already known (nonnegatives, where f(m)=m+1, or smaller-magnitude negatives via the induction hypothesis), it satisfies f(known) = +/- known + 1. The sign-tracking is the real work: when f(-n) <= -n one bounds |f(f(-n))| <= n-3 and derives a numeric contradiction n^2 <= n^2 - 8, ruling that branch out; in the surviving branch f(-n) > -n one substitutes f(f(-n)) = +/- f(-n) + 1 into (-n)^2 + 4 f(-n) = f(f(-n))^2, and the '+1' branch gives n^2 = (f(-n)-1)^2, i.e. the pointwise dichotomy f(-n) in {-n+1, n+1}. (The '-' branch n^2 = (f(-n)-3)^2 - 8 needs two squares 8 apart, forcing n=1, already handled.) This yields ONLY the per-value dichotomy; assembling the values into the listed families is a separate move.

technique: Turn a pointwise two-value dichotomy into a single monotone threshold by proving the 'switched' value at one argument forces the switched value at the adjacent argument, so once the switch happens it propagates one way and the switched set is an interval.
how_used: Granting the pointwise dichotomy f(m) in {m+1, -m+1}, show the negative part is not an arbitrary mix but a single wall. At argument -n (n>=2) suppose the switched value f(-n) = -n+1. Then the functional equation at -n gives f(f(-n))^2 = f(-n+1)^2 = (-n)^2 + 4f(-n) = (n-2)^2, so f(-n+1) = +/-(n-2). The two dichotomy values at -n+1 are n (switched) and -n+2 = -(n-2) (unswitched); since +/-(n-2) never equals n, f(-n+1) = -n+2, the switched value again. Hence 'switched at -n' forces 'switched at -n+1', i.e. the set of arguments where f is switched is downward-closed, so there is a largest integer m below which f(n) = -n+1. Assembling the three families is then routine bookkeeping.

technique: To force a value everywhere on a ray, run the forward orbit of a base point as a second-order integer recurrence, then bound each next term into a unique square using the gap between a fixed square and its nearest same-parity neighbor, killing all but the linear branch.
how_used: To prove f(n)=n+1 for n>0, iterate the orbit a_k = f^k(1); substituting n=a_k gives a_k^2 + 4a_{k+1} = a_{k+2}^2. With a_0=1 and a_2 odd, write a_2=2r+1 so a_1=r^2+r and a_3^2 = (r^2+r)^2 + 8r+4. Because 8r+4 != 0, a_3^2 differs from (r^2+r)^2 by at least the gap to the nearest even square, forcing |8r+4| >= (r^2+r)^2-(r^2+r-2)^2 = 4(r^2+r-1); this bounds |r|<4, and a finite check leaves only r in {-3,0,1}. The two bad values are killed because their orbits assign f(1) two different values (r=-3 gives f(1)=6 and later f(1)=2; r=0 gives f(1)=0 and f(1)=+/-2); r=1 gives a_k=k+1, extended by induction (the alternative sign a_{k+1}=-(k+2) is excluded because it later needs (k-1)^2-8 to be a square, impossible except k=4, which is then ruled out by continuing the orbit).

technique: Establish a pointwise two-value dichotomy on a ray by strong induction: substitute f(-n) into the equation, use a same-parity square-difference identity so the only escape from the two linear values is a difference-of-two-squares equal to a fixed constant, which has finitely many solutions.
how_used: For n>=1 prove f(-n) in {-n+1, n+1} by strong induction on n. Given f(-n) (composing with the already-known nonnegative-argument behavior f(f(-n)) = +/- f(-n)+1 via the induction hypothesis and Steps 1-2), the equation (-n)^2 + 4f(-n) = (+/- f(-n)+1)^2 splits into two: either n^2 = (f(-n)-1)^2, giving f(-n) = +/- n+1 (the dichotomy), or n^2 = (f(-n)-3)^2 - 8. The second forces two perfect squares differing by 8, and since 1 and 9 are the only such pair, n=1 (already handled in the base case). The case f(-n) <= -n is separately excluded by a bounding chain n^2 <= f(-n)^2 <= n^2-8. The base case f(-1) in {0,2} comes from 1+4f(-1) being a square with f(-1)>=0.

technique: Differentiate an identity asserting a family member is a perfect square, then eliminate the family parameter by combining the differentiated relation with the original so the square root divides a parameter-free polynomial
how_used: From P+lambda_i Q = R_i^2 differentiate to P'+lambda_i Q' = 2 R_i R_i', so R_i | P'+lambda_i Q'; combine Q'(P+lambda_i Q) - Q(P'+lambda_i Q') to cancel the lambda_i Q'Q terms, giving R_i | Q'P - QP', the Wronskian, which no longer contains lambda_i (and is nonzero since P,Q coprime nonconstant means P/Q nonconstant)

technique: Normalize a projective (linear-pencil) family by a Mobius transformation of the pencil coordinates to send the special parameter values to convenient standard ratios before factoring
how_used: Working over C, the four ratios [alpha:beta] for which alpha P + beta Q is a square are sent by a Mobius automorphism of P^1 to [1:0],[0:1],[1:-1],[1:-k]; the generators at [1:0],[0:1] are themselves the squares A^2=P+lambda_1 Q, B^2=P+lambda_2 Q (Mobius preserves coprimality and nonconstancy), turning the remaining two conditions into A^2-B^2=C^2 and A^2-kB^2=D^2 with gcd(A,B)=1

technique: Bound how many members of a linear pencil can be perfect squares by making the square roots pairwise-coprime divisors of one fixed polynomial (the Wronskian) and comparing degrees
how_used: Reformulate as: at most three ratios [alpha:beta] make alpha*P+beta*Q a square. Suppose four values lambda_i give P+lambda_i*Q=R_i^2. Differentiate: P'+lambda_i*Q'=2*R_i*R_i', so R_i divides Q'(P+lambda_i*Q)-Q(P'+lambda_i*Q')=Q'P-QP' =: W, the Wronskian. The R_i are pairwise coprime (a common prime factor divides R_i^2-R_j^2=(lambda_i-lambda_j)Q hence Q, then divides R_i^2=P+lambda_i*Q hence P, contradicting gcd(P,Q)=1). So R_1R_2R_3R_4 | W. Normalize deg P != deg Q first (replace (P,Q) by (P+cQ,Q)), so every P+lambda_i*Q has degree m=max(deg P,deg Q) and each deg R_i=m/2; then sum deg R_i=2m > deg P+deg Q-1 >= deg W, forcing W=0, i.e. (P/Q)'=0, impossible for nonconstant P/Q.

technique: Normalize a projective one-parameter family by a Mobius change of parameter that sends three distinguished parameter values to standard positions, leaving a single free invariant
how_used: Phrase over C: gcd(P,Q)=1 with alpha*P+beta*Q a square for four ratios [alpha:beta] forces P,Q constant (a 'bad pair'). Use the GL_2 action on the pencil <P,Q>, which is sharply 3-transitive on the ratios [alpha:beta] in P^1, to carry three of the four square-giving ratios to [1:0],[0:1],[1:-1]; the fourth becomes a free invariant [1:-k] with k not 0,1. In the new basis (A,B): [1:0] gives A^2, [0:1] gives B^2, [1:-1] gives A^2-B^2=C^2, [1:-k] gives A^2-kB^2=D^2, with gcd(A,B)=1 inherited. These symmetric relations are what the descent step factors.

technique: Factor a coprime relation so its square-conditions reconstitute the SAME predicate on a strictly-smaller object, then close by infinite descent
how_used: From A^2-B^2=C^2 and A^2-kB^2=D^2 with gcd(A,B)=1: set mu with mu^2=k, so C^2=(A+B)(A-B) and D^2=(A+muB)(A-muB). Since gcd(A,B)=1 the factors A+B,A-B,A+muB,A-muB are pairwise coprime, and a product of pairwise-coprime polynomials being a square forces each factor to be a square (units absorbed over C). Hence the four ratios [1:1],[1:-1],[1:mu],[1:-mu] (distinct since k not 0,1) all make alpha*A+beta*B a square, so (A,B) is ITSELF a bad pair -- the identical predicate -- with deg A+deg B < deg P+deg Q. Taking the original bad pair of minimal total degree gives a contradiction, so no nonconstant bad pair exists.

technique: Bound a target variable by splitting one power into a fractional piece to feed a pairing AM-GM, then recognize the leftover cross-term bundle as a positive-definite quadratic form and discard it as nonnegative.
how_used: To get x<=2, write 5 = (3x^4/4) + (x^4/4 + y^4) + (z^4+1) + xyz and AM-GM the split pieces to x^2y^2 and 2z^2, leaving x^2y^2 + 2z^2 + xyz; this equals a^2+ab+2b^2 with a=xy, b=z, a positive-definite form (discriminant 1-8<0), hence >=0, giving 3x^4/4 <= 5 so x^4 <= 20/3 and x <= 2.

technique: After assuming the negation, use one-shot AM-GM to linearize squared/linear terms into a top-degree polynomial, then substitute the equality constraint to eliminate the highest-degree term, collapsing onto a single cross-term relation.
how_used: Assuming 4x + y^2 + 2yz + z^2 > 8, apply x^4+3>=4x and (y^4+1)/2>=y^2, (z^4+1)/2>=z^2 to get x^4 + (y^4+z^4)/2 + 2yz + 4 > 8; replacing x^4 = 4-(y^4+z^4+xyz) from the constraint yields (2-x)yz > (y^4+z^4)/2, forcing yz>0.

technique: Chain two opposing bounds on the same quantity to eliminate it and land a pure homogeneous polynomial inequality that AM-GM refutes.
how_used: Combine (y^4+z^4)/(2yz) < 2-x with 2-x < ((y+z)/2)^2 to get 2y^4+2z^4 < yz(y+z)^2 = y^3z + 2y^2z^2 + yz^3, which is false by AM-GM (y^3z<=(3y^4+z^4)/4, yz^3<=(y^4+3z^4)/4, 2y^2z^2<=y^4+z^4), completing the contradiction.

technique: To bound a polynomial with interval-constrained coefficients below, replace each coefficient by the endpoint that minimizes its term given the sign of the corresponding power
how_used: For x<0, since x^k>0 for even k and x^k<0 for odd k, a_k x^k >= 2014 x^k (even k) and a_k x^k >= 2015 x^k (odd k); this reduces the arbitrary P(x) to the single extremal polynomial Q_n with alternating coefficients 2014 (even), 2015 (odd), so it suffices to show Q_m(x)>0 for m<=2013.

technique: Certify positivity of a fixed real polynomial by exhibiting an explicit decomposition into a weighted sum of squares plus manifestly-signed products plus a positive remainder term
how_used: Q_m(x) is rewritten as 1007*sum (x^nu + x^{nu+1})^2 + (1/2) sum (x^{2nu+1}+1)(x^{2m-2nu-1}+1) + (1007 - m/2)(x^{2m}+1); the squares are nonnegative, each factor x^{2k+1}+1 has the same sign so their products are nonnegative, and for m<=2013 the coefficient 1007-m/2>0 leaves a strictly positive remainder.

technique: Attain a target extremum with a boundary/alternating construction and verify it hits the critical value at a symmetric evaluation point
how_used: Take Q_{2014} with coefficients alternating 2014 (even powers) and 2015 (odd powers); evaluating at x=-1 gives Q_{2014}(-1)=0 (the 2015 terms cancel and the 2014 terms give 2014-2014=0), proving n=2014 is achievable so the answer is at most 2014.

technique: Argue a polynomial's zero-set is too sparse to separate its sign-regions, forcing a single sign
how_used: The zero-set (configurations forming a regular 2n-gon or all-equal) is a thin set, so any config with positive value can be continuously moved to any config with negative value without ever hitting the zero-set; hence f cannot take both signs and is everywhere nonnegative or everywhere nonpositive.

technique: Restrict a multivariate polynomial to a line so its total degree bounds the resulting univariate degree
how_used: Animate the 2n points linearly in a real parameter t (each coordinate degree 1 in t); then g(t)=f(A_1(t),...,A_{2n}(t)) is univariate with deg g <= deg f, so any lower bound on deg g transfers to deg f.

technique: Upgrade a root of a sign-definite univariate polynomial to a root of even multiplicity
how_used: Since g(t) never changes sign, each parameter value where the animated points form a regular 2n-gon is a zero of even (>=2) multiplicity; n such instants therefore contribute >= 2n roots with multiplicity, giving deg g >= 2n and hence deg f >= 2n.

technique: Realize a target configuration a controlled number of times by moving a point through a family of reflections whose target condition is a linear locus
how_used: Place n mirrors through the origin at angles pi/n apart; the 2n reflections of a point P form a regular 2n-gon exactly when P lies on one of the n angle bisectors, so animating P along a line meeting all n bisectors (off the origin) makes the 2n images form a regular 2n-gon at exactly n distinct parameter values.

technique: Encode a geometric vanishing condition as a sum of squares to cap the degree at twice the maximum constituent degree
how_used: Write f = sum of g_i^2 where each g_i (a real or imaginary part of a power-sum / equal-modulus constraint) has degree <= n; then f = 0 iff every constraint vanishes iff the config is a regular 2n-gon or all-equal, while deg f <= 2 max deg g_i <= 2n.

technique: Characterize a regular polygon by vanishing power sums and use conjugate symmetry to force the complementary symmetric functions to vanish
how_used: For equal-modulus complex a_1..a_{2n}, imposing p_k = sum a_i^k = 0 for k=1..n makes elementary symmetric sums e_1..e_n vanish (Newton); conjugating (a_i -> 1/conj(a_i) for equal modulus) sends these to the top e_{n+1}..e_{2n-1}, forcing them to vanish too, so the a_i are the roots of z^{2n}-const, a regular 2n-gon.

technique: Feed the constraint two degenerate inputs (a repeated pair on each end) and intersect the two forced medians to trap a symmetric pair of unknowns at opposite extremes
how_used: For a<c, plugging the degenerate triples (a,a,c) and (a,c,c) into the median condition gives median(a,f(a,c),f(c,a))=a and median(f(a,c),c,f(c,a))=c. The first forces one of f(a,c),f(c,a) to be <=a, the second forces one to be >=c; intersecting, exactly one of the ordered pair f(a,c),f(c,a) is >=c and the other is <=a.

technique: When a median (middle-value) constraint must hit a target and one of the three slots is already known to be extreme (too big or too small to be the middle), the target must be supplied exactly by one of the two remaining slots
how_used: For a<b<c the triple (a,b,c) forces median(f(a,b),f(b,c),f(c,a))=b. By the prior extremeness lemma f(c,a) is extreme (either >=c or <=a), so f(c,a) can never be the middle value; hence the middle value b must be delivered by one of the other two slots, forcing f(a,b)=b OR f(b,c)=b exactly. Reading (c,b,a) the same way forces f(b,a)=b OR f(c,b)=b.

technique: Pick a WLOG branch on one of two symmetric forced-equalities, then feed a fresh degenerate triple to convert the disjunction on the paired cell into an inequality that kills one alternative
how_used: Take WLOG f(b,a)=b (of the disjunction f(b,a)=b OR f(c,b)=b). Feeding (a,a,b) gives median(a,f(a,b),b)=median(a,a,b)=a, forcing f(a,b)<=a; this kills the alternative f(a,b)=b in the (a,b)/(b,c) disjunction, so f(b,c)=b, and then f(c,b)>=c. Combined with the extremeness lemma on (a,c), reading (c,b,a) forces f(a,c)<=a and f(c,a)>=c, assembling the rigid 3-point table (f(b,a)=b, f(a,b)<=a, f(b,c)=b, f(c,b)>=c, f(a,c)<=a, f(c,a)>=c).

technique: To upgrade an inequality on an off-diagonal cell into an exact equality, introduce a fresh point outside the current range and pick the triple whose two other cells are already forced to opposite extremes, so the median constraint pins the middle cell exactly
how_used: The 3-point table only gives f(c,a)>=c (an inequality). Adding a fourth point d>c and applying the median condition to (d,c,a) gives median(f(d,c),f(c,a),f(a,d))=median(d,c,a)=c; since f(d,c)>=d>c (top) and f(a,d)<=a<c (bottom) are the extremes (from the same crux-3-type facts for the new point), the middle slot f(c,a) must equal c exactly. A point d<a symmetrically pins f(a,c)=a. Iterating over all points collapses every off-diagonal inequality to equality, giving f(x,y)=x globally (and by the mirror branch f(x,y)=y).

technique: Feed the functional equation a degenerate input with two coordinates equal, so the target median collapses to a boundary value and forces a pair of symmetric off-diagonal cells to opposite extremes
how_used: For a<c evaluate the median condition on the triples (a,a,c) and (a,c,c). On (a,a,c) the cells are f(a,a),f(a,c),f(c,a); since the diagonal f(a,a)=a (from (a,a,a)) the median of the three real medians is median(a,a,c)=a, which forces the pair {f(a,c),f(c,a)} to contain a value <=a. On (a,c,c) the same collapse to median(a,c,c)=c forces the pair to contain a value >=c. Combining, one of f(a,c),f(c,a) is >=c and the other is <=a: each off-diagonal cell is pushed to an extreme (beyond the pair's range). This is the foundational lemma all later steps ride on.

technique: Feed the functional equation a fully-distinct input triple so the required output median is the strict middle value, forcing an unconstrained off-diagonal cell to equal that middle value exactly (turning an earlier one-sided bound into an equality)
how_used: With a<b<c, apply the median condition to the triple (a,b,c). Its median is b, so median(f(a,b),f(b,c),f(c,a)) must equal b. A previous 'extreme' lemma (from triples (a,a,c),(a,c,c)) has already sent the cross cell z=f(c,a) to an extreme: either z>=c or z<=a. If z>=c>b, then the median of {f(a,b),f(b,c),z} equals the max of the two interior cells, forcing max(f(a,b),f(b,c))=b; if z<=a<b, the median equals the min, forcing min(f(a,b),f(b,c))=b. Either way one of f(a,b),f(b,c) is pinned to exactly b (not merely bounded). Running the symmetric distinct triple (c,b,a) likewise pins one of f(b,a),f(c,b) to exactly b. These exact-equality pins are what upgrade the extreme lemma's inequalities into a rigid table.

technique: Replace an isolated additive constant by a free variable to homogenize an inhomogeneous inequality once the constraint is scale-invariant
how_used: The bare constant 1 on the left is generalized to k in k^2 \le (k-a)^2+(k-b)^2+(k-c)^2 + 2\sqrt2\,abc/\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}, valid for any k when (a,b,c) are (possibly degenerate) triangle sides; the original follows at k=1, and the condition a+b,b+c,c+a\ge1 with a,b,c\in[0,1] is recognized as exactly the triangle inequality on (a,b,c) since the extra abc/\sqrt{S} term is k-independent

technique: Ravi substitution: replace triangle sides by their half-differences to absorb the triangle condition into positivity of new variables
how_used: Setting x=\tfrac12(b+c-a), y=\tfrac12(c+a-b), z=\tfrac12(a+b-c) gives a=y+z, b=z+x, c=x+y, converting the inequality into the symmetric form (x+y+z)^2 \le x^2+y^2+z^2 + 2(x+y)(y+z)(z+x)/\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2+xy+yz+zx}, equivalently x^2+y^2+z^2+xy+yz+zx \le ((x+y)(y+z)(z+x)/(xy+yz+zx))^2

technique: Name the elementary symmetric sum as one letter and use the pairing identity (x+y)(x+z)=x^2+(xy+yz+zx) to collapse a product of sums into a factored form
how_used: Letting t=xy+yz+zx and using (x+y)(x+z)=x^2+t recasts the target as t^2(x^2+y^2+z^2+t) \le (x^2+t)(y^2+t)(z^2+t), whose difference RHS-LHS = x^2y^2z^2 + t(x^2y^2+y^2z^2+z^2x^2) \ge 0 is obvious upon expansion

technique: Show an order statistic (max/min) of the terms is preserved by the recurrence to confine the sequence to a bounded interval, forcing eventual periodicity of an integer sequence
how_used: Since each x_n is a floor-average of a fixed window of predecessors, it lies between their min and max; so an interval [A,B] containing the initial block traps all terms. A bounded integer sequence whose next term is a deterministic function of the last d_1 terms takes finitely many state-vectors, hence is eventually periodic with some period T.

technique: Exploit the equality case of a floor-of-average (a floored mean equalling its own maximum) to force every argument to equal the extreme value
how_used: On the periodic part let M be the maximum term. If x_n = floor((x_{n-d_1}+...+x_{n-d_k})/k) = M, then the sum of the k predecessors is at least kM while each predecessor is at most M, so every x_{n-d_i} must equal M.

technique: Use a Bezout combination of the step sizes modulo the period to convert index-shifts by the d_i into a shift by 1, propagating a property to every index
how_used: The 'x=M' property jumps backward by any d_i (indices read mod T). Choosing integers c_i with sum c_i d_i ≡ 1 (mod T) via gcd(d_i)=1 composes these jumps into a shift by 1 (negative coefficients padded by multiples of T using periodicity), so x_n=M implies x_{n-1}=M, forcing M everywhere; the sequence is constant.

technique: Exploit that a polynomial in even powers is symmetric under x to -x, so its real roots come in +-pairs and the smallest real root is non-positive
how_used: P_n(x) has only even-degree terms, so if alpha is a root so is -alpha; hence the smallest real root a_{n+1} is never positive, giving a_n <= 0 for all n>2020 (the sign fact the ordering argument later relies on)

technique: Write the next member of a polynomial family as a monomial multiple of the previous one plus a constant, then evaluate at a known root of the previous member to collapse the product term
how_used: P_{n+1}(x) = x^2 * P_n(x) + a_{n+1}; applying this at index n-1 and substituting x = a_n (a root of P_{n-1}) collapses the product to zero, yielding P_n(a_n) = a_n, which is <= 0 by the sign fact

technique: Dominate the lower-degree tail by the leading term for |x| beyond a threshold set to the sum of the lower coefficients, forcing the polynomial positive far out
how_used: For x < -max(2, sum|a_i|) the leading x^{2n} exceeds the tail (each |a_k x^{2n-2k}| <= |a_k| x^{2n-2} and the sum of |a_k| <= |x|), so P_n(x) > 0 there; against P_n(a_n) <= 0 the intermediate value theorem gives a root <= a_n, and since a_{n+1} is the smallest root, a_{n+1} <= a_n

technique: Rearrange a rational recurrence into a difference of a shifted quantity so summing collapses telescopically.
how_used: Invert the bound to get k/a_{k+1} <= a_k + (k-1)/a_k, hence a_k >= k/a_{k+1} - (k-1)/a_k; the -(k-1)/a_k term at index k cancels the +k'/a_{k'+1} term at k'=k-1, so summing k=1..m collapses to a_1+...+a_m >= m/a_{m+1}.

technique: Close an induction by case-splitting the new term against a threshold, using the induction hypothesis on one side and the auxiliary bound on the other.
how_used: For the step a_1+...+a_{n+1} >= n+1: if a_{n+1} >= 1 use the hypothesis a_1+...+a_n >= n directly; if a_{n+1} < 1 discard the hypothesis and use a_1+...+a_n >= n/a_{n+1}, then bound n/a_{n+1} + a_{n+1} = (n-1)/a_{n+1} + (1/a_{n+1} + a_{n+1}) > (n-1) + 2 (the second bracket by AM-GM).

technique: In a functional equation, manufacture an input where the unknown function takes a pinned value by substituting a self-referential expression built from the equation's own outputs, then plug that pinned-value input back in to collapse a composite term.
how_used: Put x=0, y=f(0) in f(x-f(y))=f(f(x))-f(y)-1 to learn z=-f(f(0)) satisfies f(z)=-1. Plugging y=z (so f(y)=-1) turns f(x-f(y)) into f(x+1) and makes -f(y)-1=0, giving the reduction f(x+1)=f(f(x)) (call it (2)); substituting (2) back simplifies the equation to f(x-f(y))=f(x+1)-f(y)-1 (call it (3)). These are the shared springboard for every route.

technique: In the non-injective branch of a functional equation, use a value collision to propagate a shift-equality by induction into a periodic (hence bounded) tail, then bound the min and max of the tail's value-set by evaluating the equation at the extreme-attaining argument.
how_used: Route B. If f injective, (2) gives f=successor. Else f(a)=f(b) with a>b; induction with (2) gives f(a+n)=f(b+n) for all n>=0, so f is periodic (period a-b) and bounded on the tail t>=a. Let phi=min, psi=max of tail values. Pick y with f(y)=phi and x>=a with f(x-f(y))=phi; (3) gives phi<=f(x+1)=f(x-f(y))+f(y)+1=2phi+1, so phi>=-1. Symmetrically psi<=-1; with phi<=psi this forces phi=psi=-1, so f(t)=-1 for t>=a, and (3) with large x extends f=-1 to all of Z.

technique: To show a function's first difference is constant, write that difference via the equation, then rewrite the awkward variable-dependent term as an outer composite so a previously derived pinned-value identity forces its inner argument to a constant.
how_used: Route A. From (3) with y=x: f(x+1)-f(x)=f(x-f(x))+1. Rewrite f(x-f(x)) using (2) read backwards (f(w+1)=f(f(w)) at w=x-1-f(x)) as f(f(x-1-f(x))). Then (3) at argument x-1 evaluates the inner term: f((x-1)-f(x))=f(x)-f(x)-1=-1, so f(x-f(x))=f(-1) and f(x+1)-f(x)=f(-1)+1=:A, a constant independent of x. Two-directional induction then gives f(x)=Ax+B; substituting into (2) forces A^2=A and, for A=1, B=1 (successor), while A=0 forces the constant -1.

technique: Turn a functional equation into a self-map identity of the form f(argument)=argument+const by substituting an input that makes the inner term a difference of two outputs, using an auxiliary iterate-collapse to simplify the resulting triple composite.
how_used: Route C seed. Set d=f(0). Plug x=f(y) into (1): LHS f(0)=d, RHS f^3(y)-f(y)-1, giving (4) f^3(y)=f(y)+d+1. Replace x by f(x) in (1): f(f(x)-f(y))=f^3(x)-f(y)-1, and (4) collapses f^3(x) to f(x)+d+1, giving the clean self-map identity (5) f(f(x)-f(y))=f(x)-f(y)+d. This (5) is the engine for the subgroup argument.

technique: From a self-map identity showing a shifted value-set is closed under differences, conclude that value-set is a full coset of kZ, so the function acts with slope 1 on it.
how_used: Route C finish, given (5). Let E={f(x)-d}. For a,b in E, (5) shows a-b=f(f(x)-f(y))-d is again of the form f(z)-d, so E is closed under differences: E={0} (then f is constant -1) or E=kZ. In the E=kZ case {f(x)}=kZ+d and (5) gives f(kt)=kt+d, so f has slope 1 on kZ. This coset structure is what later lets one compare y=0 vs y=k in (1) to extend slope 1 to every residue class and pin the constants.

technique: To pin a specific output value of an unknown function, choose a substitution that makes both sides collapse so the equation directly exhibits an integer whose image is a known constant.
how_used: In f(x-f(y))=f(f(x))-f(y)-1 (1), substitute x=0, y=f(0): this exhibits z=-f(f(0)) with f(z)=-1. Feeding this preimage back as y=z in (1) kills the -f(y)-1 term and yields the load-bearing reduction (2) f(x+1)=f(f(x)), which in turn simplifies (1) to (3) f(x-f(y))=f(x+1)-f(y)-1. Every route-A step downstream (the difference f(x+1)-f(x) computation forcing linearity) rests on this (2)/(3) pair.

technique: For a form linear in each variable over a box, push the optimum to the corner values of every coordinate
how_used: Z is affine in each x_i on [-1,1], so the maximum occurs with every x_i in {-1,1}; this is what makes the later y_i integer-valued and lets x_r^2=1 collapse the squared sum.

technique: Encode a weighted quadratic form as a sum of squares of signed partial sums, chosen so the target weights fall out as the pairwise coefficients
how_used: Set y_i = (x_1+...+x_i) - (x_{i+1}+...+x_{2n}); squaring and summing over i makes the coefficient of x_r x_s equal 4(n-s+r), giving sum y_i^2 = 4n^2 - 4Z, so maximizing Z becomes minimizing sum y_i^2.

technique: Bound a sum of integer squares from below by pairing consecutive terms that must differ by a fixed step
how_used: Each y_i is even and y_i - y_{i-1} = 2x_i = +-2, so y_{2j-1}, y_{2j} are consecutive even integers forcing y_{2j-1}^2 + y_{2j}^2 >= 4; summing the n pairs gives sum y_i^2 >= 4n, hence Z <= n(n-1), attained by alternating signs.

technique: Substitute a value that makes the outer argument reappear on the right, turning the equation into the statement that a whole x-indexed expression is a fixed point of f
how_used: Setting y=1 in f(x+f(x+y))+f(xy)=x+f(x+y)+yf(x) cancels the f(x)/f(xy) terms and gives f(x+f(x+1))=x+f(x+1), so x+f(x+1) is a fixed point of f for every real x, an x-indexed supply of fixed points to feed later substitutions.

technique: Feed a known fixed point into a specialized instance of the equation to force every fixed point to a single numerical value
how_used: In the case f(0)!=0, x=0 gives f(f(y))+f(0)=f(y)+yf(0); substituting a fixed point y0 (so f(f(y0))=y0) gives f(0)=y0 f(0), forcing y0=1. Hence the only fixed point is 1, so x+f(x+1)=1 identically and f(x)=2-x.

technique: Add a sign-substituted copy of the equation to the original so the nonlinear/opaque term cancels and the map collapses to the identity
how_used: Substitute (x,y)->(-1,-y) and use f(-1)=-1 with oddness (f(-y-1)=-f(y+1), f(-1+f(-y-1))=-f(1+f(y+1))) to get -f(1+f(y+1))+f(y)=-1-f(y+1)+y; adding this to the reduced x=1 equation f(1+f(y+1))+f(y)=1+f(y+1)+y cancels the f(1+f(y+1)) terms and yields 2f(y)=2y, i.e. f(y)=y.

technique: From a fixed-point-producing substitution, extract an additive closure rule for consecutive fixed points, then re-index the certified expression to the target argument
how_used: In the case f(0)=0: y=1 gives f(x+f(x+1))=x+f(x+1), so x+f(x+1) is a fixed point (2); y=0 with x->x+1 gives x+f(x+1)+1 is also a fixed point (3), so these are two consecutive fixed points. The x=1 instance, after pinning f(-1)=-1 (from (2) at x=-1) and f(1)=1 (from that instance at y=-1), reduces to f(1+f(y+1))+f(y)=1+f(y+1)+y, which yields the closure rule: if y0 and y0+1 are both fixed points then so is y0+2. Applying this to the consecutive pair x+f(x+1), x+f(x+1)+1 certifies x+f(x+1)+2 as a fixed point; re-indexing x->x-2 gives f(x+f(x-1))=x+f(x-1).

technique: Equate two independently-derived expressions for the same left-hand side to force a symmetry (oddness) relation
how_used: In the case f(0)=0, the y=-1 substitution gives f(x+f(x-1))=x+f(x-1)-f(x)-f(-x), while the separately established identity gives f(x+f(x-1))=x+f(x-1) for the same left side; equating cancels x+f(x-1) and forces f(x)+f(-x)=0, i.e. f is odd.

technique: Reflect the equation through a symmetric argument substitution and add the result to a prior identity so the unknown nonlinear terms cancel
how_used: In the case f(0)=0 with f odd and f(-1)=-1: substitute (x,y)->(-1,-y) into the original equation to get f(-1+f(-y-1))+f(y)=-1+f(-y-1)+y; using oddness this becomes -f(1+f(y+1))+f(y)=-1-f(y+1)+y. Adding this to the reduced x=1 identity f(1+f(y+1))+f(y)=1+f(y+1)+y makes the f(1+f(y+1)) and f(y+1) terms cancel, leaving 2f(y)=2y, i.e. f(y)=y, closing the case.

technique: Recast a functional equation as an identity about the finite-difference operator Δ_t g(x)=g(x+t)-g(x), so that the equation becomes a symmetry/vanishing statement about Δ rather than about pointwise values.
how_used: Setting a=x+y turns the odd-valued FE f(x+f(x)+y)+f(x-f(x)-y)=f(x+y)+f(x-y) into Δ_{f(x)}f(a)=Δ_{f(x)}f(2x-a-f(x)), a reflection symmetry of the step-f(x) difference of f about center x; all subsequent work is phrased via Δ, with 'quasi-period t' meaning Δ_1Δ_t f=0.

technique: Telescope a step-t relation by summing its shifted copies over an arithmetic progression of the base point, collapsing the interior terms so the relation upgrades from step t to step kt (any integer multiple of t).
how_used: Summing Δ_{f(x)}f(a)=Δ_{f(x)}f(2x-a-f(x)) over a=b,b+f(x),...,b+(k-1)f(x) telescopes both sides to Δ_{kf(x)}f(b)=Δ_{kf(x)}f(2x-b-kf(x)); allowing negative k gives Δ_M f(b)=Δ_M f(2x-b-M) for every M divisible by f(x).

technique: Compose two reflection-symmetries about different centers to produce a genuine translation-periodicity, the translation being twice the distance between the centers.
how_used: With L=lcm(f(x),f(y)), the relation Δ_L f(b)=Δ_L f(2c-b-L) holds at both centers c=x and c=y; chaining the two reflections gives Δ_L f(b)=Δ_L f(b+2(y-x)), so Δ_L f is 2(y-x)-periodic (Lemma 1).

technique: Descend a coarse period to a finer one via a second-difference averaging lemma: if Δ_{ts}g=0 and Δ_tΔ_t g=0, then the s equal copies of Δ_t g sum to the vanishing Δ_{ts}g, forcing Δ_t g=0.
how_used: Applied to g=Δ_1 f with t=T/p, s=p: from Δ_TΔ_1 f=0 and Δ_{T/p}Δ_{T/p}Δ_1 f=0 (Lemma 2) one gets Δ_{T/p}Δ_1 f=0, so T/p is a smaller quasi-period, contradicting minimality of T and proving T∣f(x) for all x.

technique: To descend a minimal (quasi-)period by a prime factor, produce a witness where the period fails to divide a structural quantity, then read one vanishing second-difference two ways so intersecting periods lands the step strictly below the prime power, contradicting minimality.
how_used: T is the minimal quasi-period (Δ_T f = const). Suppose an odd prime power p^α||T with p^α∤f(u) for some u. From 2f(u)=f(u+f(u))+f(u-f(u)) pick v∈{u±f(u)} with p^α∤f(v); set L=lcm(f(u),f(v)), so p^α∤L. Lemma 1 with |u−v|=f(u) gives Δ_L f is 2f(u)-periodic; it is also T-periodic (since Δ_T(Δ_L f)=Δ_L(Δ_T f)=Δ_L(const)=0), so Δ_{gcd(T,2f(u))}Δ_L f=0. Re-read the SAME equation as: g:=Δ_{gcd(T,2f(u))}f is L-periodic; and g is T-periodic because Δ_T g=Δ_{gcd(T,2f(u))}(Δ_T f)=Δ_{gcd(T,2f(u))}(const)=0 — the quasi-period hands T-periodicity to any single difference free. Hence Δ_{gcd(T,L)}g=0. Since p^α∤f(u),L, both gcd(T,2f(u)) and gcd(T,L) divide T/p, coarsening to Δ_{T/p}Δ_{T/p}f=0, whence Δ_{T/p}Δ_{T/p}Δ_1 f=0. Combined with Δ_T Δ_1 f=0, Lemma 2 gives Δ_{T/p}Δ_1 f=0, so T/p is a quasi-period — contradiction.

technique: When an iterated functional equation forces a fixed-step difference of f to be invariant under a point-reflection whose center moves with the argument, compose two such reflections about different centers to turn that difference into a genuinely periodic function (period = twice the center-shift).
how_used: Rewriting the FE (a=x+y) gives Delta_{f(x)}f(a)=Delta_{f(x)}f(2x-a-f(x)): the f(x)-difference is invariant under reflecting the argument about x-f(x)/2. Summing shifted copies extends this to any M with f(x)|M: Delta_M f(b)=Delta_M f(2x-b-M). For distinct x,y with L=lcm(f(x),f(y)) (so both f(x)|L and f(y)|L), apply this reflection first about x, then about y: Delta_L f(b)=Delta_L f(2x-b-L)=Delta_L f(2y-(b+2(y-x))-L)=Delta_L f(b+2(y-x)). So Delta_L f is 2(y-x)-periodic. This is Lemma 1, the fact the descent engine consumes (with y-x=f(u), giving the 2f(u)-period).

technique: To promote a coarse-step vanishing to a fine-step vanishing, use that a constant fine-step difference summed over one coarse period splits into equal fine-step pieces whose total is zero, forcing each to vanish (averaging descent).
how_used: Lemma 2: for g and nonzero t,s, if Delta_{ts}g=0 and Delta_t Delta_t g=0 then Delta_t g=0. Delta_t Delta_t g=0 means Delta_t g is t-periodic, so Delta_t g(a)=Delta_t g(a+t)=...=Delta_t g(a+(s-1)t); these s equal numbers sum to Delta_{ts}g(a)=0, so each is 0. In Step 2 this is applied to g=Delta_1 f with t=T/p, s=p: from Delta_{T/p}Delta_{T/p}Delta_1 f=0 and Delta_T Delta_1 f=0 it yields Delta_{T/p}Delta_1 f=0, i.e. T/p is a quasi-period -- the contradiction (T not minimal) that finishes the descent.

technique: To upgrade a difference that is only known to be periodic (constant on residue classes) to a genuinely constant function, use an independent instance of the underlying symmetry that equates two of its values lying in DIFFERENT residue classes.
how_used: Step 1: set Q=lcm(f(0),f(1)). Lemma 1 (with x=0,y=1) gives that g=Delta_Q f is 2-periodic, i.e. constant on evens and on odds separately -- but a priori the even-value and odd-value may differ, so Q is not yet shown to be a quasi-period. Close the gap with a second, independent use of the reflection identity Delta_M f(b)=Delta_M f(2x-b-M): take M=Q, x=0, b=0 to get g(0)=Delta_Q f(0)=Delta_Q f(-Q)=g(-Q). Since 0 and -Q have opposite parity (Q is odd), this equates the even-class value to the odd-class value, so g is fully constant. Hence Delta_1 g=Delta_1 Delta_Q f=0, i.e. Q is a genuine quasi-period of f -- f is quasi-periodic, so its minimal positive quasi-period T exists (and is odd). This supplies the finite T that the whole descent then shrinks.

technique: When a difference of f is simultaneously periodic with two commuting moduli, collapse the pair to a single gcd-period, then use a prime-power that divides one modulus but not a controlling lcm to force every emerging gcd below that prime factor, producing a vanishing second difference at the reduced step.
how_used: Step 2, proof by contradiction: suppose an odd prime power p^alpha | T but p^alpha does not divide f(u). From 2f(u)=f(u+f(u))+f(u-f(u)) pick v in {u+f(u),u-f(u)} with p^alpha not dividing f(v); set L=lcm(f(u),f(v)), so p^alpha does not divide L. Lemma 1 (|u-v|=f(u)) makes Delta_L f both 2f(u)-periodic and T-periodic, hence gcd(T,2f(u))-periodic: Delta_{gcd(T,2f(u))}Delta_L f=0. Reading the same vanishing the other way, Delta_{gcd(T,2f(u))} f is both L-periodic and T-periodic, hence Delta_{gcd(T,L)}Delta_{gcd(T,2f(u))} f=0. Because p^alpha does not divide L, both gcd(T,2f(u)) and gcd(T,L) divide T/p, so Delta_{T/p}Delta_{T/p} f=0, i.e. Delta_{T/p}Delta_{T/p}Delta_1 f=0. Together with Delta_T Delta_1 f=0 this is exactly the pair of inputs the quasi-period-shrink lemma consumes to produce a strictly smaller quasi-period, contradicting minimality of T.

technique: To pass from a doubly-differenced vanishing back down to a singly-differenced one, average a block of equal difference-values whose telescoping sum is already known to vanish, forcing each equal term to zero.
how_used: This is Lemma 2, the final shrink step of the Step 2 descent: given Delta_{T/p}Delta_{T/p}(Delta_1 f)=0 (write t=T/p) and Delta_T(Delta_1 f)=0 (T is a quasi-period, so Delta_1 f is T-periodic), conclude Delta_{T/p}(Delta_1 f)=0. Set g=Delta_1 f and s=p, so ts=T. Since Delta_t Delta_t g=0, the values Delta_t g(a), Delta_t g(a+t), ..., Delta_t g(a+(s-1)t) are all EQUAL. Their sum telescopes to Delta_{ts} g(a)=Delta_T g(a)=0. A block of s equal numbers summing to 0 forces each to be 0, so Delta_t g(a)=Delta_{T/p}(Delta_1 f)(a)=0. This means T/p is a quasi-period of f, contradicting minimality of T -- completing the contradiction that yields T | f(x) for all x. Without this averaging move the earlier gcd/prime-power argument only produces the two inputs but cannot execute the actual shrink from T to T/p.

technique: Realize a within-block value-permutation by unit-shifting a polynomial that is constant across all block-boundary points
how_used: For part (a), take P(x)=prod_{i=0}^n (x-ik) with k=2015 and Q(x)=P(x-1). Since P(0)=P(k)=...=P(nk)=0, on block i the shift moves the argument set {ik-(k-1),...,ik} to {(i-1)k,...,ik-1}: the two sets differ only by swapping ik for (i-1)k, both of which are roots giving value 0, so the value-multisets of P and Q on each block coincide. This yields distinct block-similar polynomials of degree n+1.

technique: Convert a per-block multiset-equality condition into root conditions by summing the first two power sums of the difference and building the discrete partial-sum polynomial
how_used: Block-similarity means {P}={Q} as multisets on each block, so sum_{block i} (P-Q)=0 and sum_{block i} (P^2-Q^2)=0. Using Sigma_F(m)=sum_{j=1}^m F(j) (a polynomial of degree deg F+1), each block sum is Sigma_F(ik)-Sigma_F((i-1)k); together with Sigma_F(0)=0 this forces Sigma_{P-Q} and Sigma_{P^2-Q^2} to vanish at 0,k,2k,...,nk, converting the combinatorial condition into n+1 roots for each partial-sum polynomial.

technique: Invert a prescribed-root partial-sum polynomial by writing the summand as the backward difference of the factored partial sum
how_used: From Sigma_F(x)=T(x)G(x) with T(x)=prod_{i=0}^n(x-ik) carrying the roots 0,k,...,nk (deg G=deg F-n), recover F itself via F(m)=Sigma_F(m)-Sigma_F(m-1)=T(x)G(x)-T(x-1)G(x-1); this identity holds at all integers hence as polynomials, giving deg F>=n and the exact difference form F(x)=T(x)G(x)-T(x-1)G(x-1). Applied to P-Q (deg <= n) this forces deg=n and G constant, so R_1=alpha(T(x)-T(x-1)).

technique: Strip a coprime product factor from a divisibility relation to reduce it to a difference-operator divisibility that fails on degree
how_used: To force S=P+Q constant: R_2=R_1 S has difference form T(x)G-T(x-1)G(x-1)=T(x)(G(x)-G(x-1))+G(x-1)(T(x)-T(x-1)); since R_1=alpha(T(x)-T(x-1)) divides R_2, it divides T(x)(G(x)-G(x-1)); because gcd(T(x),T(x-1))=1 (T and its unit shift have disjoint simple roots) gives gcd(T,R_1)=1, hence R_1 | G(x)-G(x-1), impossible since deg(G(x)-G(x-1))<n=deg R_1 unless G constant, so R_2 is a scalar multiple of R_1 and S is constant.

technique: Refute an equality of two evaluations of a product polynomial by a termwise absolute-value comparison, pairing the crossover factors and bounding the rest
how_used: To contradict T(ell+1)=T(ell) with T(m)=prod_{i=0}^n(m-ik), k=2ell+1: the i=0 and i=1 factors pair up (|ell+1||ell| on the left equals |ell||ell+1| on the right, since ell+1-k=-ell and ell-k=-ell-1), and for every i>=2 the point ell+1 lies strictly closer to ik than ell does, so |ell+1-ik|<|ell-ik|. Hence |T(ell+1)|<|T(ell)| strictly (using n>=2), contradicting T(ell+1)=T(ell).

technique: Turn a hypothesis of block-wise permuted values into vanishing of a discrete antiderivative at block endpoints, using that a permutation preserves each power sum
how_used: Block-similarity of P,Q means each length-k block of P-values is a permutation of the corresponding Q-block. A permutation preserves EVERY power sum, so both the first moments (block sums) and the second moments (block sums of squares) agree across each block. Encode a moment as a discrete antiderivative: Sigma_F(m)=sum_{i=1}^m F(i), which is a polynomial of degree deg F+1 (Faulhaber). Block-sum agreement makes Sigma_{P-Q} vanish at m=0,k,2k,...,nk; block-sum-of-squares agreement makes Sigma_{P^2-Q^2} vanish at the same n+1 points. This produces the n+1 forced roots that drive part (b). (The sum-of-squares/second-moment preservation is the extra load-bearing input, easy to miss: it is what lets P^2-Q^2 enter alongside P-Q.)

technique: Normalize a difference polynomial by factoring its vanishing discrete antiderivative through a fixed root-polynomial and telescoping back
how_used: Lemma: if F is nonzero and Sigma_F vanishes at 0,k,...,nk (n+1 points), then deg F>=n, and F(x)=T(x)G(x)-T(x-1)G(x-1) with T(x)=prod_{i=0}^n(x-ik) and deg G=deg F-n. Proof: the n+1 roots force Sigma_F=T*G (degree count); then F_1:=T(x)G(x)-T(x-1)G(x-1) telescopes to Sigma_{F_1}(m)=T(m)G(m)=Sigma_F(m) on all integers, so F=F_1. Apply to R_1=P-Q, which has degree <=n: the lemma forces deg R_1=n exactly (so G is a constant alpha) and R_1(x)=alpha(T(x)-T(x-1)) with alpha!=0 (else P=Q).

technique: Force a companion sum-polynomial to be constant by feeding its product with the known difference into the same factorization and killing it via coprimality plus a degree-drop
how_used: With R_1=P-Q=alpha(T(x)-T(x-1)), set S=P+Q and suppose S nonconstant. Then R_2=P^2-Q^2=R_1*S is nonzero and its second-moment vanishing gives the lemma form R_2=T(x)G(x)-T(x-1)G(x-1) with 0<deg G. Rewrite R_2=T(x)(G(x)-G(x-1))+G(x-1)(T(x)-T(x-1)); R_1 divides the second summand, so R_1 | T(x)(G(x)-G(x-1)). Coprimality gcd(T,R_1)=gcd(T(x),T(x-1))=1 (roots ik vs ik+1 all distinct) forces R_1 | G(x)-G(x-1). But deg(G(x)-G(x-1))=deg G-1<n=deg R_1 (using deg G=deg S<=n, since in part (b) deg P=deg Q=n so deg S<=n) and G(x)-G(x-1) is nonzero, contradiction. Hence S=beta is constant; affine rescaling (2P-beta)/alpha, (2Q-beta)/alpha (block-similarity is affine-invariant) reduces to the normalized pair P=-Q=T(x)-T(x-1).

technique: Pin a fixed central term of an odd-length sign-constrained sequence to zero by combining its exact-value negation symmetry with a one-sign-change count
how_used: For the normalized pair P=-Q=T(x)-T(x-1): first establish the integer sequence P(1),...,P(k) changes sign exactly once. On block i, T(ik-k+1) and T(ik-1) share a sign, so P(ik-k+1)=T(ik-k+1) and P(ik)=-T(ik-1) have opposite signs, giving a root of P in each segment [ik-k+1,ik]; as deg P=n there is exactly one root per block, so the sequence over one block changes sign exactly once. Separately, P block-similar to -P forces the block's value-multiset to be negation-symmetric, hence equally many positive and negative entries. Equal +/- counts among an odd number k=2ell+1 of entries is impossible unless one entry is zero, and the single sign change places that zero at the center: P(ell+1)=0, i.e. T(ell+1)=T(ell).

technique: Refute a forced equality between two values of a product-of-linear-factors polynomial by comparing the two products factor-by-factor in absolute value
how_used: The previous move yields the forced equality T(ell+1)=T(ell) with T(x)=prod_{i=0}^n(x-ik), k=2ell+1. Compare the two products term by term in absolute value: |T(ell+1)|=|ell+1|*|ell|*prod_{i=2}^n|ell+1-ik| and |T(ell)|=|ell|*|ell+1|*prod_{i=2}^n|ell-ik|. The i=0,1 factors match after pairing; for each i>=2, |ell+1-ik|<|ell-ik| since ik>ell+1 (as k=2ell+1). With n>=2 there is at least one such factor, so |T(ell+1)|<|T(ell)| strictly, contradicting T(ell+1)=T(ell). This is the final contradiction that completes part (b), and it is exactly where n>=2 and k>2 are used.

technique: Resolve the boundary case of a '>= threshold' bound by invoking injectivity: when the arithmetic stops exactly at an integer threshold, use that the threshold value is already occupied elsewhere to upgrade to strict '>'.
how_used: In the boundary case a_i = i+1, the bound a_{i+1} >= (i+1)^2/(i+2) = i+1 - 1/(i+2) only forces the integer a_{i+1} >= i+1. But the sequence is a permutation, and the value i+1 is already used by a_i, so a_{i+1} != i+1, hence a_{i+1} >= i+2 = (i+1)+1. This supplies the strict step a_i = i+1 implies a_{i+1} > i+1 that the coarse numeric estimate left open, completing the propagation.

technique: Turn a chained one-step constraint into a self-propagating strict inequality: assume the desired violation at index i, feed it through the constraint to force the same (or stronger) violation at index i+1, closing the boundary case with the ambient structural constraint.
how_used: Assume a_i > i (i.e. a_i >= i+1) for some i <= n-1. The constraint a_i^2/a_{i+1} <= i+2 gives a_{i+1} >= a_i^2/(i+2) >= (i+1)^2/(i+2) = i + 1 - 1/(i+2) > i, so a_{i+1} > i. Push to strict at i+1: if a_i >= i+2 then a_{i+1} >= (i+2)^2/(i+2) = i+2 > i+1; if a_i = i+1 then the value i+1 is already used, so by permutation distinctness a_{i+1} != i+1, and since a_{i+1} >= i+1 as an integer, a_{i+1} >= i+2 > i+1. Either way a_i > i implies a_{i+1} > i+1. Chaining from any violating index i up to n forces a_n > n, contradicting a_n <= n. Hence a_i <= i for all i, and a_1 <= 1, a_2 <= 2, ... force the identity a_i = i, which satisfies the constraint since k^2/(k+1) < k+2.

technique: Rotate a two-variable inequality by the sum/difference substitution to make the constraint symmetric in its two arguments
how_used: Set s=x+y, t=x-y (so x=(s+t)/2, y=(s-t)/2) so the given f(x+y)f(x-y) >= f(x)^2 - f(y)^2 becomes f(s)f(t) >= f((s+t)/2)^2 - f((s-t)/2)^2, isolating the product f(s)f(t) on the left and an antisymmetric squared-difference A(s,t)=f((s+t)/2)^2 - f((s-t)/2)^2 (with A(s,-t)=-A(s,t)) on the right.

technique: Add a sign-flipped copy of an inequality to itself so the antisymmetric right-hand side cancels, leaving a one-signed product
how_used: Replacing t by -t swaps the two squared terms on the right (A(s,-t)=-A(s,t)); summing that copy with the original gives f(s)(f(t)+f(-t)) >= 0 for all s,t. Taking t0=x0-y0 from the strict pair makes the sum strict, so c:=f(t0)+f(-t0) != 0; then f(s)c >= 0 for all s forces f to keep the fixed sign of c.

technique: After appending a block of terms to a product of partial sums, expand and lower-bound the two cross-term products by AM-GM so the result completes to a perfect square in the previous value
how_used: Writing a_{n+2}^2 = (S+u)(T+v) with S=sum_1^n x_i, T=sum_1^n 1/x_i, u=x_{n+1}+x_{n+2}, v=1/x_{n+1}+1/x_{n+2}, the expansion is ST + uv + (Sv+uT); AM-GM gives Sv+uT >= 2 sqrt(Sv*uT) = 2 sqrt(ST)*sqrt(uv) = 2 a_n sqrt(uv), so a_{n+2}^2 >= (a_n + sqrt(uv))^2, i.e. a_{n+2} >= a_n + sqrt((x_{n+1}+x_{n+2})(1/x_{n+1}+1/x_{n+2}))

technique: When distinctness makes a Cauchy-Schwarz/AM-GM bound strict, push the perfect-square lower bound strictly past the next integer square and use integrality of both sides to round the gap up
how_used: Since x_{n+1} != x_{n+2}, (x_{n+1}+x_{n+2})(1/x_{n+1}+1/x_{n+2}) = 2 + x_{n+1}/x_{n+2} + x_{n+2}/x_{n+1} > 4 strictly, so a_{n+2}^2 > (a_n+2)^2; as a_{n+2}, a_n are integers this forces a_{n+2} >= a_n + 3. With a_1 = 1, telescoping over odd indices gives a_{2k+1} >= 3k+1, so a_2023 = a_{2*1011+1} >= 3034

technique: Iterate a one-step substitution along the orbit of the unknown function so a single inequality becomes a shift-invariant relation between consecutive iterate-gaps
how_used: Two setup substitutions first: y=x gives x >= f^2(x) (so the base gap y-f^2(y) >= 0), and x=f(y) gives f(y)+f^2(y) >= y+f^3(y), i.e. f(y)-f^3(y) >= y-f^2(y). Then replace y by f^{n-1}(y) in the latter to get f^n(y)-f^{n+2}(y) >= f^{n-1}(y)-f^{n+1}(y); iterating down to the base, every gap f^n(y)-f^{n+2}(y) >= y-f^2(y) >= 0

technique: Telescope a chain of iterate-gaps into a bound linear in the step count, then pit it against a fixed bound to force the base gap to vanish
how_used: Summing over even indices, y-f^{2m}(y)=sum_{i=0}^{m-1}(f^{2i}(y)-f^{2i+2}(y)) >= m(y-f^2(y)). Positivity of f gives y-f^{2m}(y)<y, so m(y-f^2(y))<y for all m; combined with y-f^2(y)>=0 (from the y=x substitution), the only possibility is y-f^2(y)=0, i.e. f is an involution f^2(y)=y

technique: Feed the derived involution back into the original inequality to collapse it into a symmetric two-variable inequality, then swap the variables to force a product to be constant
how_used: With f^2(y)=y, the original x(f(x)+f(y)) >= (f(f(x))+y)f(y) = (x+y)f(y) becomes xf(x)+xf(y) >= xf(y)+yf(y), i.e. xf(x) >= yf(y). Swapping x and y gives yf(y) >= xf(x), so xf(x)=yf(y) is constant =c>0, giving f(x)=c/x; verify c/x satisfies the original with equality

technique: When a fixed monic degree-k polynomial equals a sliding product of k sequence terms, expand each factor around the base term and compare the subleading coefficient of the two sides to pin the sum of the shifts
how_used: Writing P(a_n)=prod_{i=1}^k (a_n+(a_{n+i}-a_n)) and forming Q_n(x)=P(x)-prod(x+c_i) with c_i=a_{n+i}-a_n, the difference has degree <=k-1 with leading coefficient (b-sum c_i) where b is the x^{k-1} coefficient of P; since Q_n(a_n)=0 and a_n is large, the sign of that leading term forces sum_{i=1}^k (a_{n+i}-a_n)=b for all n beyond some N. Requires knowing a_n is eventually large and the shifts stay controlled (finitely many shift-tuples of each fixed sum), which comes from a separate monotonicity/unboundedness step.

technique: Difference a per-index relation at n and n+1 to cancel the shared overlapping window and expose a clean linear recurrence in the consecutive gaps
how_used: Subtracting the shift-sum equation sum_{i=1}^k (a_{n+i}-a_n)=b (i.e. (a_{n+1}+...+a_{n+k})-k a_n=b) from the same equation at n+1 cancels the overlap a_{n+2},...,a_{n+k}, leaving a_{n+k+1}-a_{n+1}=k(a_{n+1}-a_n); in gap notation g_{n+1}+...+g_{n+k}=k g_n, so each gap is the mean of the next k gaps.

technique: Apply the extremal principle to the minimum of an integer quantity that equals an average of copies of itself, forcing every term in the averaging window down to the minimum and propagating it
how_used: With d=min over n>=N of the gap a_{n+1}-a_n (attained by well-ordering on non-negative integers), the relation kd=a_{n+k+1}-a_{n+1}=sum_{i=1}^k (a_{n+i+1}-a_{n+i}) has each summand >=d, so all k gaps in the window equal d; propagating gives every gap equal to d for large n, so P(x)=(x+d)(x+2d)...(x+kd) holds at infinitely many x=a_{n'} hence identically. The eventual-AP-to-full-AP backward induction is the routine finish.

technique: Turn a single local strict drop in an integer sequence into self-propagating infinite descent: compare two consecutive shifted copies of the defining relation to get a sign-equivalence forcing another strict drop within a bounded window.
how_used: Comparing P(a_n)=a_{n+1}...a_{n+k} with the shifted P(a_{n+1})=a_{n+2}...a_{n+k+1}, dividing cancels the common block a_{n+2}...a_{n+k} and, using that P (monic, non-negative integer coefficients) is strictly increasing on positive reals, yields a_n>a_{n+1} <=> a_{n+1}>a_{n+k+1} (and equality<->equality). So a strict drop a_{n(i)}>a_{n(i)+1} forces a_{n(i)}>a_{n(i)+k}, hence some strict adjacent drop at an index within [n(i)+1, n(i)+k]; picking the minimal such index repeatedly builds an infinite strictly decreasing sequence of positive integers, contradicting well-ordering. Hence (a_n) is non-decreasing (and, since an eventually-constant block would force P(x)=x^k and full constancy, strictly increasing under the not-eventually-constant assumption).

technique: When a fixed monic degree-k polynomial equals a sliding product of k shifted sequence terms, pin the sum of the shifts by comparing the subleading coefficient of the two sides for all large arguments.
how_used: Write a_{n+i}=a_n+(a_{n+i}-a_n) so P(a_n)=prod_{i=1}^k (a_n+c_i^{(n)}) with c_i^{(n)}=a_{n+i}-a_n. Since P(x)-prod(x+c_i)=(b-sum c_i)x^{k-1}+(lower), where b is the coefficient of x^{k-1} in P, a nonzero sum-defect makes the difference eventually one-signed; a uniform threshold A (obtained by covering the finitely many tuples with sum b+1 and monotonicity in each c_i) forces, for all a_n>=A, the exact relation (a_{n+1}-a_n)+...+(a_{n+k}-a_n)=b. Because monotonicity makes a_n unbounded, this holds for all large n.

technique: Force a family of integer gaps to be constant by an extremal (minimum) argument: show the minimal gap must recur at every subsequent index, then upgrade a relation holding on the resulting subsequence to a polynomial identity.
how_used: Differencing the pinned relation sum_i(a_{n+i}-a_n)=b at n and n+1 gives a_{n+k+1}-a_{n+1}=k(a_{n+1}-a_n) for all large n. Let d=min{a_{n+1}-a_n} over large n, attained at some n0; then kd=a_{n0+k+1}-a_{n0+1}=sum of k consecutive gaps each >=d, forcing every one of them to equal d, hence d recurs at n0+1,...,n0+k and inductively at all n>=n0. So a_{n+i}=a_n+id on this tail, meaning P(x)=(x+d)(x+2d)...(x+kd) holds at the infinitely many values x=a_n, hence identically; backward induction then extends the common difference d to the whole sequence.

technique: Round an analytic quantity to its nearest integer so an approximate balancing target becomes an exact integer target, absorbing the rounding error into a large permitted slack.
how_used: Round each sqrt(k) to the nearest integer: k in [j^2-j+1, j^2+j] rounds to j, so {sqrt1,...,sqrtN} becomes (up to error <0.5 each) the multiset with j appearing exactly 2j times. The generous bound 2023 (versus the ~3 actually achieved) is what makes this crude rounding legal: it reduces the real inequality on triple sqrt-sums to the exact integer problem of making three permutations of the rounded multiset have constant column-sum.

technique: Reduce a target multiset whose every multiplicity is even to two independent copies of the half-multiset, solving the constant-sum problem once on the half.
how_used: The rounded multiset {1x2,2x4,...,mx2m} has each value j with even multiplicity 2j, so it is two disjoint copies of T_m={1x1,2x2,...,mxm} (of size m(m+1)/2). It therefore suffices to find three permutations of a single T_m with constant column-sum 2m+1, then juxtapose two independent such solutions to fill all N=m(m+1) columns.

technique: For an inductive construction on a self-similar object, exploit two different decompositions of the enlarged object simultaneously: shift the old solution into one decomposition and fill the fresh block via the other.
how_used: Use T_m = (T_{m-1}+1) sqcup {1,...,m}. Keep the first row's old permutation, add +1 to the other two rows on the old columns (raising the column-sum from 2m-1 to 2m+1 and realizing T_{m-1}+1), then append m fresh columns (m, r, m+1-r) for r=1..m, each summing to 2m+1 and together supplying the new {1,...,m} block. Base m=1 is (1,1,1).

technique: Extend a construction from a special size to an arbitrary size by inserting a small block of new values just above a chosen threshold, pushing every larger existing entry up to make room, and charging the perturbation to the large permitted slack.
how_used: For general N with m(m+1)<=N<(m+1)(m+2), write N=m(m+1)+t (t<=2m+1) and take L=floor(4N/9). Start from the constant-column-sum permutations for m(m+1). Relabel each old entry a_k -> a_k if a_k<=L, else a_k+t; this frees exactly the t slots L+1,...,L+t, into which t brand-new columns are appended (for r=1..t the new column takes value L+r in all three rows). The relabel is a bijection of {1..m(m+1)} onto {1..N}\{L+1..L+t}, so each row stays a permutation of {1..N}. Bound the disturbance per shifted entry via sqrt(A_k)-sqrt(a_k)=(A_k-a_k)/(sqrt A_k+sqrt a_k) <= t/(2 sqrt(L+1)) <= (2m+1)/((4/3)m) <= 2, and check the t new all-equal columns directly: 3 sqrt(L+1) > 2 sqrt(N) and 3 sqrt(L+t) < 2 sqrt(N)+8.5 by L~4N/9. Total deviation stays a bounded constant, crushed by the 2023 slack.

technique: Replace an approximate real-valued target by an exact integer target by rounding each term to its nearest integer and absorbing the accumulated rounding error into the problem's slack.
how_used: Round each sqrt(k) to the nearest integer: since sqrt(k^2-k+1),...,sqrt(k^2+k) (exactly 2k values) all round to k with error <1/2, the multiset {sqrt(1),...,sqrt(N)} becomes the integer multiset {1_x2,2_x4,...,m_x2m} for N=m(m+1). The real constraint |sqrt(a_k)+sqrt(b_k)+sqrt(c_k)-2sqrt(N)|<2023 is thereby replaced by the exact combinatorial constraint 'three permutations of that integer multiset with a fixed per-column sum 2m+1' (note 2sqrt(m^2+m) is within 1 of 2m+1). Three roundings cost <1.5, plus <1 from the 2m+1 vs 2sqrt(N) gap, all trivially absorbed by the 2023 slack. KEY HANDOFF the crux must name: the rounded multiset {1_x2,...,m_x2m} is exactly TWO disjoint copies of T_m={1_x1,...,m_xm} (each value j appears 2j=j+j times), so it suffices to solve the constant-column-sum problem on the single multiset T_m and then place that arrangement twice side by side; and general N is padded up to the nearest m(m+1) with the extra indices inserted so the slack still absorbs them (Sol 1 Step 2). The next move (crux 1) builds the T_m arrangement.

technique: Build a constant-column-sum arrangement of a self-similar multiset by induction, exploiting that the multiset admits two different decompositions at once: append-the-new-block, and previous-multiset-shifted-by-one plus a fresh consecutive block.
how_used: Target: three permutations (u_k),(v_k),(w_k) of T_m={1_x1,2_x2,...,m_xm} with u_k+v_k+w_k=2m+1 constant, over its m(m+1)/2 columns. Use the two identities T_m = T_{m-1} sqcup {m_xm} AND T_m = (T_{m-1}+1) sqcup {1,2,...,m} simultaneously. Inductive step from an arrangement of T_{m-1} with sum 2m-1: on the old m(m-1)/2 columns keep u_k but set v_k -> v_k+1, w_k -> w_k+1 (this reads rows v,w as the shifted copy T_{m-1}+1 and lifts the column-sum 2m-1 to 2m+1); then add m new columns (u,v,w)=(m, r, m+1-r) for r=1..m, each summing to 2m+1 (this consumes the fresh block {1..m} in rows v,w and the m-th copy of m in row u). Because one decomposition governs row u and the other governs rows v,w, every element of T_m appears exactly once in each row, so all three remain permutations while the column-sum jumps in lockstep. Base m=1: (1,1,1). This T_m arrangement is what crux 0's reduction hands off to; N=m(m+1) uses it twice (two copies of T_m).

technique: Encode three simultaneous constant-sum orderings as one point set read from three symmetric frames, using an invariant that makes the three frame-coordinates of every point sum to a constant.
how_used: For a triangular number N=m(m+1)/2, arrange N points as an equilateral triangular lattice whose l-th row (counted from a vertex tip) has l points. Label points 1..N rows-then-left-to-right from vertex A to get permutation W_a; the same labeling read from vertices B and C (the whole procedure rotated 120 and 240 degrees) gives W_b, W_c, each a genuine permutation of 1..N by symmetry. The single invariant doing the work: in an equilateral triangle the distances from any interior point to the three sides sum to a constant, equivalently the barycentric coordinates sum to a constant; hence the three row-indices-from-the-tips satisfy l_a+l_b+l_c = 2m+1, independent of the point. A point in row l from a vertex has label W with l(l-1)/2 < W <= l(l+1)/2, so sqrt(2W) lies within 1/2 of l; summing over the three frames gives |sqrt(W_a)+sqrt(W_b)+sqrt(W_c) - (2m+1)/sqrt2| < 3/2 * 1/sqrt2, and (2m+1)/sqrt2 tracks 2sqrt(N). This is a self-contained solution for triangular N (independent of cruxes 0 and 1), extended to general N by deleting points from the bottom row.

technique: Bootstrap a parametrized family of facts by feeding several structured tuples with a common invariant into the equation and chaining iterate-compositions to extend the parameter range
how_used: Call k 'good' if f^{t^k-t}(t^k)=t. Chaining f^{t^9-t^3}(t^9)=t^3 with f^{t^3-t}(t^3)=t gives f^{t^9-t}(t^9)=t (k=1,3 good); feeding the fixed-product triples (a,b,c)=(t,t^4,t^4) and (t^2,t^3,t^4) into the equation then forces k=4 and k=2 good, and k=2 is the target lemma f^{t^2-t}(t^2)=t for all t.

technique: Instantiate an additive divisor relation at a product of distinct large-prime powers so each variable gets a distinct prime coefficient, then combine a coprimality/divisibility constraint with a one-sided size bound to force each coefficient's value to zero
how_used: For arbitrary a,b>=2 pick primes p>q>max(a,b), set s=a^p b^q and t=s^2. Multiplicativity of the additive relation gives p*g_t(a)+q*g_t(b)=g_t(a^p b^q)=g_t(s), and g_t(s)=f^{s^2-s}(s^2)-s=0 by the base lemma. So p*g_t(a)=-q*g_t(b). Since f maps into N, g_t(n)=f^{t-n}(t)-n>-n, so |g_t(a)|<q and |g_t(b)|<p; gcd(p,q)=1 then forces q|g_t(a) and p|g_t(b), hence both are 0. Thus f^{t-n}(t)=n for all n>=2; taking a=n, b=n+1 yields f(n+1)=n, i.e. f(n)=n-1 for n>=3.

technique: Combine two instances of the identity whose argument tuples share a product relation (one tuple's product is the square of the other's), rewrite the higher iterates as lower ones through an intermediate fixed value, then subtract so the common term cancels and a two-variable relation survives.
how_used: The equation for a triple with product t reads f^{t-a}(t)+f^{t-b}(t)+f^{t-c}(t)=a+b+c; define g_t(n)=f^{t-n}(t)-n so it says g_t(a)+g_t(b)+g_t(c)=0 whenever abc=t. Take the base instance at (a,b,c) with abc=t, and the instance at (ab, t, c) whose product is (ab)(t)(c)=(abc)^2=t^2, giving f^{t^2-ab}(t^2)+f^{t^2-t}(t^2)+f^{t^2-c}(t^2)=ab+t+c. Route each t^2-iterate down through the fixed value t by composition, f^{t^2-n}(t^2)=f^{t-n}(f^{t^2-t}(t^2))=f^{t-n}(t) using the descent lemma f^{t^2-t}(t^2)=t (also the middle term becomes exactly t). Subtracting the base instance, the c-term f^{t-c}(t)-c cancels, leaving [f^{t-a}(t)-a]+[f^{t-b}(t)-b]=[f^{t-ab}(t)-ab], i.e. g_t(a)+g_t(b)=g_t(ab) for a,b>=2, ab|t, ab<t.

technique: Bootstrap a set of 'good' parameter values for an iteration identity by feeding argument tuples whose entries are powers of a base back into the functional equation, using already-known instances to peel off terms and promote new values into the set.
how_used: Prove the descent lemma f^{t^2-t}(t^2)=t. Call exponent k 'good' if f^{t^k-t}(t^k)=t. Setting a=b=c=r gives k=3 good; taking the base r=t^3 and composing f^{t^9-t^3}(t^9)=t^3 with f^{t^3-t}(t^3)=t gives k=9 good (and k=1 trivially). Then plug (a,b,c)=(t,t^4,t^4) (product t^9) into the equation: the known f^{t^9-t}(t^9)=t peels off, leaving f^{t^9-t^4}(t^9)=t^4, which composes to k=4 good; plug (t^2,t^3,t^4) (product t^9) and use the k=3,k=4 instances to peel off, leaving f^{t^9-t^2}(t^9)=t^2, composing to k=2 good. k=1 and k=2 good give the lemma f^{t^2-t}(t^2)=t, the load-bearing input to the subtraction that yields the additive relation g_t(a)+g_t(b)=g_t(ab).

technique: To force an additive-over-factorizations function to vanish, evaluate it at an argument built from high prime powers of the two targets, so the additive relation becomes a linear combination with distinct prime coefficients equal to a known value; coprimality of each prime to the boundedly-negative individual values forces every term to zero.
how_used: With g_t(a)+g_t(b)=g_t(ab) for a,b dividing t (obtained by subtracting two instances of the equation and applying the descent lemma), and g_t(n)=f^{t-n}(t)-n, fix arbitrary a,b>=2 and pick primes p>q>max{a,b}. Set s=a^p b^q and t=s^2. Additivity gives p g_t(a)+q g_t(b)=g_t(a^p b^q)=g_t(s)=f^{s^2-s}(s)-s=0 by the descent lemma. So p g_t(a)+q g_t(b)=0, whence q|g_t(a) and p|g_t(b); but g_t(a)=f^{t-a}(t)-a>-a>-q and g_t(b)>-b>-p (since f>=1) bound them below, forcing g_t(a)=g_t(b)=0. Thus f^{t-n}(t)=n for all n>=2; taking a=n,b=n+1 yields f(n+1)=n, i.e. f(n)=n-1 for n>=3 (f(1),f(2) free), which checks.
