technique: After a pointwise dichotomy leaves a rescaled zero-set undetermined, plug a substitution that ties the zero-status of two dilated arguments into one equation, forcing zeros to propagate along a scaling orbit
how_used: Substitute (x,y)=(3t,t): then x-3y=0 kills the first term (f(0)=0), while 3x-y=8t and x+y=4t, giving (f(t)+3t^2)f(8t)=f(4t)^2. Since f>=0, the coefficient f(t)+3t^2>=0, so f(4t)!=0 forces f(8t)!=0, i.e. the reverse implication f(2z)=0 => f(z)=0. Combined with (star)'s forward doubling f(z)=0 => f(2z)=0 this yields the equivalence f(z)=0 <=> f(2z)=0, so 'f=0' is invariant up and down each scaling orbit; nowhere-zero orbits fall on the f(x)=x^2 branch, killing the mixed pathological solutions allowed by f(x)=x^2 or f(4x)=0 and leaving f(x)=x^2 or f(x)=0 pointwise

technique: To force a target value to vanish, choose the two free variables so one composed argument hits the target and another lands on a known zero, collapsing the identity to a one-signed inequality that pins the target
how_used: By the global dichotomy f is everywhere >=0 (each value is x^2 or 0). Suppose some nonzero zero a exists; the scale-linking relation gives zeros c=2^n a of arbitrarily large size, so for any target b>0 pick a zero c>b. Set (x,y)=((3c+b)/4,(c-b)/4), so x-3y=b, x+y=c, 3x-y=b+2c, and c>b>0 gives x,y>0 hence xy>0. Since f(x+y)=f(c)=0 the RHS is 0, so 0=(f(x)+xy)f(b)+(f(y)+xy)f(b+2c). Both summands are >=0 (f>=0), and f(x)+xy>0 strictly, so f(b)=0. Thus a single nonzero zero propagates to make f identically 0; otherwise f(x)=x^2, giving the two solutions.

technique: Specialize the free variables so two of the composed arguments collapse to one expression, turning the identity into a factored product-equals-square relation that forces a pointwise dichotomy
how_used: After deriving f(0)=0 and (via x=0 giving f(y)f(-y)=f(y)^2) that f is even, set y=-x in the FE. The inner arguments x-3y and 3x-y both collapse to 4x, and x+y=0. Using f(0)=0 and evenness the equation reduces to (f(x)-x^2)f(4x)=0, giving the pointwise dichotomy (star): for every real x, f(x)=x^2 or f(4x)=0. This is the entry point for the classification.

technique: To upgrade a dichotomy stated only at a scaled argument into one holding at every point, find a substitution producing a scale-linking relation controlling the value at a doubled scale, so vanishing transfers between dyadic scales
how_used: The pointwise dichotomy (star) mixes scales (f(x)=x^2 or f(4x)=0). Substituting x=t, y=3t yields (R): (f(t)+3t^2)f(8t)=f(4t)^2. If f(4t)!=0 then (star) gives f(t)=t^2, so f(t)+3t^2=4t^2>0 and (R) forces f(8t)!=0; running (star) and (R) both ways yields f(z)=0 <=> f(2z)=0, hence f(4x)=0 <=> f(x)=0. Feeding this back into (star) removes the scale mismatch and gives the global dichotomy: for every x, f(x)=x^2 or f(x)=0.

technique: Bound each factor of a product by a fractional power of a common base via AM-GM on one big copy plus (weight-1) unit copies, so the product collapses to that base raised to the sum of reciprocal weights
how_used: Applied AM-GM to one copy of (x+1) and a_i-1 copies of 1 to get a_i(x+1)^{1/a_i} <= x+a_i; multiplying over i turns the product prod(x+a_i) into M(x+1)^{sum 1/a_i}=M(x+1)^k, giving P(x)<=0 for x>0

technique: Force strict inequality in a product bound by observing the equality case of each factor is incompatible with a global hypothesis
how_used: Equality in each AM-GM step needs a_i=1 for all i, which forces M=prod a_i=1, contradicting M>1; hence the product inequality is strict and P(x)<0, so no positive root

technique: Realize a scalar multiple of a product (a-b)(c-d) as a signed sum of squares by pairing the four variables crosswise
how_used: For the sufficiency direction: each first-line number is a difference of napkin values, so write the two chosen first-line factors as a=x-y and b=u-v. The crosswise-pairing identity 2(x-y)(u-v)=(x-v)^2+(y-u)^2-(x-u)^2-(y-v)^2 shows 2ab is a signed sum of four squares of first-line numbers, i.e. of the required a^2+b^2-c^2-d^2 form, so q=2 works; negating both sides gives q=-2, and q=0 is trivial (0=c^2+d^2-c^2-d^2).

technique: Pin an unknown real parameter to a finite integer set by choosing consecutive-integer inputs (forcing integrality via a unit-valued instance) and reading a magnitude cap off the extremal achievable output
how_used: Necessity, bounding step. Take the napkin to be {1,...,10}, so the first line is {-9,...,9} (all integers). The second line contains q (=q*1*1) and 81q (=q*9*9), both of which must appear in the third line. Every third-line value a^2+b^2-c^2-d^2 with a,b,c,d in {-9,...,9} is an integer, forcing q to be an integer, and lies in [-162,162] (extreme 162=9^2+9^2-0^2-0^2); so 81q in [-162,162] gives |q|<=2. Thus q is an integer with |q|<=2. Since q in {-2,0,2} is already known good, the only remaining bad-candidate values are q=+-1.

technique: Eliminate a residual candidate value by choosing inputs so every relevant square lands in a restricted residue class mod a small power of 2, excluding the residue the sought value would have to occupy
how_used: Necessity, killing q=+-1. Choose the napkin {0,1,4,8,12,16,20,24,28,32}, whose entries and all pairwise first-line differences are never 2 mod 4, so every first-line number a has a^2 in {0,1} mod 8. Then every third-line value a^2+b^2-c^2-d^2 lies in {-2,-1,0,1,2} mod 8. But 1 and 4 are first-line numbers, so for q=+-1 the second line contains q*1*4=+-4, which is 4 mod 8 - excluded from the third line, a contradiction.

technique: Convert an 'exists a witness for every input' constraint into a single polynomial identity by taking the product over all finitely many witness choices, forcing the whole product to vanish everywhere hence identically, then use that the polynomial ring is an integral domain to pick one factor that vanishes identically
how_used: Alternative unified necessity. Treat the napkin as variables x1..x10 and form P = (prod_{i<j}(xi-xj)) times the product, over all index-choices a_i in {x1..x10}, of the factor q(x1-x2)(x3-x4) - (a1-a2)^2-(a3-a4)^2+(a5-a6)^2+(a7-a8)^2. For any real napkin, goodness makes at least one factor zero, so P vanishes on all of R^10 (Vandermonde kills the coincidence locus), hence P is the zero polynomial; since R[x1..x10] is an integral domain, one specific factor F (a fixed choice of the a_i) is identically zero.

technique: Extract a linear constraint on an unknown parameter from a polynomial identity by comparing the coefficient of a single well-chosen monomial on both sides
how_used: Given F(x1..x10) = q(x1-x2)(x3-x4) - (a1-a2)^2-(a3-a4)^2+(a5-a6)^2+(a7-a8)^2 identically zero, compute the coefficient of x1 x3. The q-term contributes q. Each squared block contributes +-2 exactly when {a_i,a_{i+1}}={x1,x3} (indicator u_i, i in {1,3,5,7}); the four blocks realize {x1,x3} at most once, so at least three u_i are zero. Vanishing gives q+2(u1+u3-u5-u7)=0 with at least three u_i=0, forcing q in {-2,0,2}.

technique: Track two running-extreme quantities of the sequence and sandwich each new term between them using both directions of the defining max-relation
how_used: Define M_n=max_{k<n}a_k and m_n=-min_{k<n}a_k. From a_n=-(a_p+a_q) with a_p,a_q<=M_n get a_n>=-2M_n; choosing the index k achieving a_k=M_n gives a_n<=-a_{n-k}-M_n<=m_n-M_n. This yields -2M_n<=a_n<=m_n-M_n, feeding recursions m_{n+1}<=max{m_n,2M_n} and M_{n+1}<=max{M_n,m_n-M_n}.

technique: Split on a threshold comparing the two monovariants so that in each case one of them is forced to stall, collapsing the growth
how_used: Call n lucky if m_n<=2M_n. If some lucky index exists, luckiness self-propagates and M_n freezes, bounding both by 2M_n; if no index is ever lucky then 2M_n<m_n forces m_n constant, bounding both by m_{D+1}. Either way both running extremes are bounded.

technique: When an extremal index is chosen as the argmax over a FLAT range of all smaller indices, and its complement is itself governed by the same relation, expand that complement to exhibit a strictly larger competitor lying in the very same range, contradicting the argmax
how_used: Alternative route (contradiction). Assuming unboundedness above, first note bounded-above implies bounded-below via a_n>=-2Q, so it suffices to bound above; pick a 'good' index n with a_n>a_i for all i<n, a_n>-2l (l=min of first D terms), n>D. The KEY point: let u be the index maximizing a_u over the FLAT set 1<=u<=n-1 (not over pairs summing to n), and v=n-u; then a_u>=a_v. From a_n+a_u+a_v<=0: if v<=D then a_u,a_v>=l gives a_n<=-2l, contradiction. If v>D, expand a_v=-(a_{w1}+a_{w2}) with w1+w2=v; since v<n we have w1,w2<v<n, so w1,w2 lie in the SAME flat range 1..n-1. Then a_n+a_u<=a_{w1}+a_{w2}, and a_n>a_u forces max(a_{w1},a_{w2})>a_u — a competitor in the maximization range beating the maximum, contradiction.

technique: To show a candidate extremal constant is sharp for a symmetric-sum bound, build a one-parameter near-degenerate family where one variable scales inversely to a common value so the finitely many distinct products stay pinned to the constraint threshold.
how_used: Set x_2=...=x_n=t>0 and x_1=-1/(2t): every pairwise product is t^2 (i,j>=2) or -1/2 (with x_1). Any Hamiltonian-path sum touches x_1 in at most two edges, so it is >= 2(-1/2)+(n-3)t^2 = (n-3)t^2-1 >= -1, making the tuple Shiny for all t. Then sum_{i<j} x_i x_j = -(n-1)/2 + (n-1)(n-2)/2 t^2 -> -(n-1)/2 as t->0+, so K cannot exceed -(n-1)/2.

technique: Decompose a full pairwise-product sum into a fixed number of edge-disjoint Hamiltonian-path sums plus a leftover edge set, so each path becomes one instance of the given per-permutation constraint.
how_used: Group the products z_i z_j by the pair of residue classes {2p-1,2p} of i+j mod n; each group is realizable as a path y_1y_2+...+y_{n-1}y_n via y_{2i-1}=z_{i+p-1}, y_{2i}=z_{p-i} (indices mod n). This writes sum_{i<j} z_i z_j as floor((n-1)/2) path-sums (each >= -1 by Shiny) plus a leftover L, giving sum >= -floor((n-1)/2) + L. The permutation z of the x_i is left free, to be chosen later so L is controllable.

technique: When a leftover sum after a graph decomposition is a pairing of a sorted sequence, relabel so each pair joins two sorted-adjacent entries of the same sign, forcing every product nonnegative.
how_used: For n odd, sort x_1<=...<=x_n and let k be the count of nonpositive entries; if k is odd negate all x_i (this preserves Shiny and preserves the target sum, and flips k to n-k with n odd, so WLOG k is even). With k even the sign boundary at 0 falls between consecutive sorted pairs, so x_1x_2, x_3x_4, ..., x_{n-2}x_{n-1} are each products of same-sign factors, all >= 0; set L = x_1x_2+x_3x_4+...+x_{n-2}x_{n-1} >= 0. Choose the z_i relabeling (from the decomposition crux, with z_n=x_n) so that {z_1,z_{n-1}},...,{z_{(n-1)/2},z_{(n+1)/2}} realize the pairs {x_1,x_2},...,{x_{n-2},x_{n-1}}; then this L equals the decomposition's odd-n leftover. Combined with sum >= -(n-1)/2 + L this gives sum >= -(n-1)/2.

technique: To lower-bound a leftover chain-sum whose only negative term is a single sign-crossing product, double the sum and in one copy drop a nonnegative term and replace the crossing product by the extreme-endpoint product, yielding a genuine constrained path.
how_used: For n even, take the leftover L = x_1x_2 + x_2x_3 + ... + x_{n-1}x_n (sorted chain); its unique negative term is the 0-crossing x_k x_{k+1} where x_k<=0<=x_{k+1}. Write 2L = L + L; in one copy drop the nonnegative x_1x_2, and replace x_k x_{k+1} by x_n x_1, valid because x_1<=x_k<=0<=x_{k+1}<=x_n gives |x_1||x_n| >= |x_k||x_{k+1}| so x_n x_1 <= x_k x_{k+1} (the swap only decreases the copy). The result x_2x_3+...+x_{n-1}x_n + x_n x_1 is a Hamiltonian-path sum, hence >= -1 by Shiny, while the other copy's remaining terms are all same-sign hence >= 0; so 2L >= -1, i.e. L >= -1/2. Then -floor((n-1)/2)+L = -(n-2)/2 + L >= -(n-1)/2. Relabel x_{2i-1}=z_{-i}, x_{2i}=z_i so L is the decomposition's even-n leftover.

technique: To turn a per-permutation constraint into a linear inequality among grouped product-sums, average the constraint over only those permutations that pin one index-class to a fixed alternating set of positions, so each product-type is selected with a fixed, computable frequency.
how_used: Split indices by sign: S negatives (|S|=k), T nonnegatives (|T|=l), WLOG k>=l, k<n; let K,L be the within-S, within-T product sums (>=0) and M the cross sum (<=0); target K+L+M >= -(n-1)/2. Average f(phi)=sum of path-edge products over all phi with phi^{-1}(T)={2,4,...,2l}, so T occupies only even positions and no path edge is T-T. By symmetry each cross product appears with frequency 2l/(kl) and each within-S product with frequency (k-l-1)/C(k,2), giving -1 <= (2l/(kl))M + (2(k-l-1)/(k(k-1)))K for k>l (yielding K+L+M >= -k/2 + (l/(k-1))K + L >= -k/2 >= -(n-1)/2), and for k=l=n/2 each phi selects 2l-1 of the kl cross products (no within-class edges), giving -1 <= ((2l-1)/(kl))M, so M >= -n^2/(4(n-1)) >= -(n-1)/2 for n>=4.

technique: To reduce a full pairwise-product sum to a bounded number of copies of a per-permutation path constraint, decompose the complete graph's edges into edge-disjoint Hamiltonian paths (plus an explicit leftover) by grouping edges according to the residue class of their endpoint-index sum modulo n.
how_used: Relabel the x_i as z_i with indices read mod n, so sum_{i<j} x_i x_j = sum over edges {i,j} of K_n of z_i z_j. Group the C(n,2) edges by (i+j) mod n. For each p=1..floor((n-1)/2), the union of residue classes 2p-1 and 2p is a set of n-1 edges forming a Hamiltonian path, realized explicitly by y_{2i-1}=z_{i+p-1}, y_{2i}=z_{p-i}; hence each such block equals y_1 y_2+...+y_{n-1} y_n for a genuine permutation y of the z, so is >= -1 by the Shiny hypothesis. This accounts for floor((n-1)/2) paths and leaves a leftover L: for n odd, L is the residue-0 class, a perfect matching z_1 z_{-1}+...+z_{(n-1)/2} z_{-(n-1)/2}; for n even, L is residues 0 and -1 together, z_1 z_{-1}+z_1 z_{-2}+z_2 z_{-2}+.... Thus sum_{i<j} z_i z_j >= -floor((n-1)/2) + L. The permutation z of the x is left free, to be fixed afterward so L has a controlled sign.

technique: When a residual perfect-matching term has uncontrolled sign but the underlying relabeling is still free, first normalize the count of nonpositive entries to be even by a global sign flip (which preserves the degree-2 objective and the hypothesis), then relabel so every matched pair is same-sign, making the residual a sum of nonnegative products.
how_used: For n odd the leftover from the decomposition is the residue-0 perfect matching L = z_1 z_{-1}+...+z_{(n-1)/2} z_{(n+1)/2}. Sort x_1<=...<=x_k<=0<=x_{k+1}<=...<=x_n where k = count of nonpositive entries; if k is odd, negate ALL x_i (leaves sum_{i<j} x_i x_j unchanged since degree-2 homogeneous, preserves Shininess) so k is EVEN. Then consecutive pairs {x_1,x_2},{x_3,x_4},...,{x_{n-2},x_{n-1}} are each two same-sign numbers, so each product >= 0. Relabel z so the matched pairs {z_1,z_{n-1}},...,{z_{(n-1)/2},z_{(n+1)/2}} are exactly these pairs and z_n=x_n. Then L equals this sum of nonnegative products, so L >= 0, giving sum_{i<j} x_i x_j >= -(n-1)/2 in the odd case.

technique: Split the full pairwise-product sum by pairing indices via their residue class on a cyclic labeling, so each residue class becomes a Hamiltonian path (a genuine permutation the given per-permutation bound controls), leaving one structured residual class.
how_used: Place the values z_1..z_n on the cycle Z/n and group the pair {i,j} by r = i+j mod n. Reading 2*sum_{i<j} z_i z_j as a sum over residue classes, each class {i+j == 2p-1, 2p mod n} is a Hamiltonian path y_1..y_n via y_{2i-1}=z_{i+p-1}, y_{2i}=z_{p-i}, so its edge-sum equals a permutation path-sum sum_k y_k y_{k+1} >= -1 by Shiny. This packs floor((n-1)/2) such paths, giving sum_{i<j} z_i z_j >= -floor((n-1)/2) + L, where the single leftover class L is a residue-0 perfect matching z_1 z_{-1}+...+z_{(n-1)/2} z_{-(n-1)/2} when n is odd, and a residue-{0,-1} zigzag path z_1 z_{-1}+z_1 z_{-2}+z_2 z_{-2}+... when n is even. The still-free choice of the permutation z is what later forces L to the needed sign.

technique: To lower-bound a sorted-value path-sum whose sole negative term is the single zero-straddle product, double the sum, discard a nonnegative endpoint term from one copy and all-but-the-straddle from the other, then replace the straddle by the extreme-endpoints product to reassemble a genuine permutation path the per-permutation bound controls.
how_used: For n even the leftover is the sorted path L = x_1 x_2 + x_2 x_3 + ... + x_{n-1} x_n; its only negative consecutive product is the straddle x_k x_{k+1} (with x_1<=..<=x_k<=0<=x_{k+1}<=..<=x_n). Assume k != 1 so the leading x_1 x_2 >= 0. Write 2L = (x_1 x_2+...+x_{n-1}x_n)+(x_1 x_2+...+x_{n-1}x_n) >= (x_2 x_3+...+x_{n-1}x_n) + x_k x_{k+1} (drop leading nonnegative x_1 x_2 from copy 1, keep only the lone negative straddle from copy 2). Since x_1 <= x_k <= 0 <= x_{k+1} <= x_n, x_k x_{k+1} >= x_n x_1, so 2L >= x_2 x_3+...+x_{n-1}x_n + x_n x_1, which is the permutation path (x_2,x_3,...,x_n,x_1) hence >= -1 by Shiny. Thus L >= -1/2. Relabel x_{2i-1}=z_{-i}, x_{2i}=z_i (mod n) so this L matches the residue-{0,-1} leftover, closing sum_{i<j} x_i x_j >= -(n-1)/2.

technique: Substitute to make two of the equation's argument-expressions coincide, so their terms cancel and force a value to zero
how_used: For fixed x != 1, pick y = x/(x-1) so that x+y = x^2/(x-1) = xy; then the f(x+y) and f(xy) terms cancel in f(f(x)f(y))+f(x+y)=f(xy), giving f(f(x)f(x/(x-1)))=0 and hence a zero of f. Taking x=0 yields the concrete root f((f(0))^2)=0 that seeds the classification.

technique: Exploit a sign symmetry of the equation to normalize the value at a base point without loss of generality
how_used: Since g = -f satisfies g(g(x)g(y))+g(x+y) = -[f(f(x)f(y))+f(x+y)] = -f(xy) = g(xy), f is a solution iff -f is; so one may assume f(0) <= 0. This halves the casework, reducing to recovering f===0 and f(x)=x-1, with f(x)=1-x obtained as the negation.

technique: Bound an unknown positive-integer coefficient below by its smallest admissible value to turn a bilinear recurrence step into a linear inequality.
how_used: Each b_m is a positive integer, so on any step where b_m>=2 the recurrence a_{m+1}=a_m b_m - a_{m-1} (the minus branch) is bounded below by replacing b_m with 2: a_{m+1} >= 2a_m - a_{m-1}. This discards the unknown multiplier and yields a clean linear lower bound that both the positivity argument and the growth induction are built on.

technique: Rewrite a two-term linear lower bound as current-term-plus-gap so a single strict increase self-propagates along the sequence.
how_used: Write 2a_m - a_{m-1} = a_m + (a_m - a_{m-1}); then on any block where b_m>=2 for all m, a_m>a_{m-1} forces a_{m+1}>a_m, so one strict rise propagates a_n>a_{n-1}>...>a_{r+1}. Since the terms are integers, a strictly increasing chain from a seed a_{r+1}>=r+1 telescopes to a_n>=n (>=2017 near n=2017).

technique: To prove a global positivity/monotonicity property, take a minimal counterexample and shrink it to the minimal descending run bordering it, so the run's left neighbor is strictly smaller and turns the recurrence's lower bound into a strict ascent that contradicts the descent.
how_used: To show a_n>=1: take the smallest n with a_n<=0 (n>=2, so a_{n-1}>=1, a_{n-2}>=0); the plus branch would give a_n>0, so the minus branch holds and a_{n-2}>=a_{n-1}>=a_n, a descending triple. Let r be the SMALLEST index with a_r>=a_{r+1}>=a_{r+2}; minimality forces a_{r-1}<a_r, and 2<=r<=n-2 keeps a_{r-1},a_r,a_{r+1}>0. The descent a_{r+1}>=a_{r+2} forces the minus branch there, whence the coefficient governing index r satisfies b_r>=2. Then a_{r+1}=a_r*b_r +/- a_{r-1} >= 2a_r-a_{r-1} = a_r+(a_r-a_{r-1}) > a_r, contradicting a_r>=a_{r+1}.

technique: To trigger the additive (plus) branch of a two-branch recurrence at the base of a block of large coefficients, backtrack to the last index where the governing coefficient equals its minimum value, using a normalization convention on the free initial coefficient as the guaranteed floor of the backtrack.
how_used: In the main induction for max{a_n,a_{n+1}}>=n, hard case b_{n-1}>1: normalize b_0=1 (legal since a_0=0 makes b_0 irrelevant), then there is r with 1<=r<=n-1 and b_{n-1},...,b_r>=2 but b_{r-1}=1; the b_0=1 convention guarantees such r exists (the backtrack cannot fall past index where b_{r-1}=b_0=1). At index r the governing coefficient b_{r-1}=1 activates the PLUS branch: a_{r+1}=a_r*b_r+a_{r-1}>=2a_r+a_{r-1}, so a_{r+1}-a_r>=a_r+a_{r-1}. By the induction hypothesis one of a_r,a_{r-1} is >=r-1 and the other >=1 (positivity lemma), so a_r+a_{r-1}>=r, giving a_{r+1}-a_r>=r, hence a_{r+1}>=r+1 and a_{r+1}>a_r: the seed value plus strict ascent.

technique: To carry a single strict inequality forward across a whole block, show the recurrence's step map is strictness-preserving on that block (a strict gap at one index forces a strict gap at the next), then telescope the seeded bound to the block's far end.
how_used: After seeding a_{r+1}>=r+1 and a_{r+1}>a_r at the base r of the block where b_r,...,b_{n-1}>=2, the minus branch on the block is strictness-preserving: for m=r+1,...,n-1, a_m>a_{m-1} implies a_{m+1}=a_m*b_m-a_{m-1}>=2a_m-a_{m-1}=a_m+(a_m-a_{m-1})>a_m. So a_n>a_{n-1}>...>a_{r+1}>=r+1; since these are integers strictly increasing over n-(r+1) steps from a value >=r+1, a_n>=r+1+(n-1-r)=n, giving max{a_n,a_{n+1}}>=n and, at n=2017, the required bound.

technique: Seed a growth bound at the entry point of a favorable regime by evaluating the recurrence one step past the last unfavorable index, where the sign flips to additive and the induction hypothesis lower-bounds the two feeding terms.
how_used: At the block base r (smallest index with b_{n-1},...,b_r>=2, so b_{r-1}=1), the PLUS branch applies: a_{r+1}=a_r*b_r+a_{r-1}>=2a_r+a_{r-1}, hence a_{r+1}-a_r>=a_r+a_{r-1}. By the outer induction (max{a_k,a_{k-1}}>=k-1) one of a_r,a_{r-1} is >=r-1 and the other is >=1 by the positivity lemma, so a_r+a_{r-1}>=r. With a_r>=1 this yields both a_{r+1}>=r+1 and a_{r+1}>a_r -- the seed the carry-forward step needs.

technique: Prove a global positivity bound for a sign-branching recurrence by taking the minimal counterexample and then the minimal index where the sequence first stops strictly increasing, so the additive/multiplicative structure at that index yields a contradiction.
how_used: To show a_n>=1 for all n>=1: suppose n is the smallest index with a_n<=0; then n>=2, a_{n-1}>=1, a_{n-2}>=0, forcing the minus branch and a_{n-2}>=a_{n-1}>=a_n. Let r be the smallest index with a_r>=a_{r+1}>=a_{r+2} (exists, r<=n-2, and r>=2 by checking b_1). Minimality gives a_{r-1}<a_r and (by minimal n) a_{r-1},a_r,a_{r+1}>0; the drop a_{r+1}>=a_{r+2} forces b_r>=2, so a_{r+1}=a_r*b_r±a_{r-1}>=2a_r-a_{r-1}=a_r+(a_r-a_{r-1})>a_r, contradicting a_r>=a_{r+1}. Hence a_n>=1 always; this positivity is the prerequisite used silently in the seeding step.

technique: To prove every term of an integer recurrence with a sign-flipping branch stays positive, take a minimal counterexample and then locate the smallest index at which the sequence first fails to strictly increase across two consecutive steps; use that minimality to force the offending step onto the subtractive branch and derive a contradiction.
how_used: Assume a_n <= 0 for some n and take n minimal; then n>=2, a_{n-1}>=1, a_{n-2}>=0, so the PLUS branch a_{n-1}b_{n-1}+a_{n-2} cannot give a_n<=0 — the MINUS branch holds, yielding a_{n-2} >= a_{n-1} >= a_n. Now let r be the SMALLEST index with a_r >= a_{r+1} >= a_{r+2} (exists since r <= n-2; and r>=2 by checking b_1=1 vs b_1>1). Minimality of r gives a_{r-1} < a_r, and n-minimality gives a_{r-1},a_r,a_{r+1} > 0. The non-increase a_{r+1} >= a_{r+2} forces the MINUS branch at r+1, hence b_r >= 2, so a_{r+1} = a_r b_r ± a_{r-1} >= 2a_r - a_{r-1} = a_r + (a_r - a_{r-1}) > a_r, contradicting a_r >= a_{r+1}. Thus a_n >= 1 for all n >= 1.

technique: To seed a growth induction inside a maximal terminal run of the 'strong' (multiplier b>=2, subtractive) branch, drop to the last index before the run where the additive branch still applies and use that single additive step to manufacture a surplus (a_{base+1} minus a_base bounded below by a size quantity already controlled by induction).
how_used: When b_{n-1} > 1, let r be the largest index with b_{r-1}=1 and b_{n-1},...,b_r all >= 2 (exists because b_0 is taken = 1). At the base, b_{r-1}=1 gives the PLUS branch a_{r+1} = a_r b_r + a_{r-1} >= 2a_r + a_{r-1}, so a_{r+1} - a_r >= a_r + a_{r-1}. By the induction hypothesis one of a_r, a_{r-1} is >= r-1 and (by the positivity lemma) the other >= 1, so a_r + a_{r-1} >= r; hence a_{r+1} - a_r >= r. With a_r >= 1 this delivers the seed a_{r+1} >= r+1 and a_{r+1} > a_r that the block-propagation step needs.

technique: Propagate a single strict increase through a whole run of the subtractive branch by observing the branch is self-reinforcing: with multiplier at least 2, one term exceeding its predecessor forces the next to exceed it too, so the strict inequality telescopes across the run.
how_used: Throughout the terminal run b_m >= 2 (m = r+1,...,n-1) the MINUS branch holds: a_{m+1} = a_m b_m - a_{m-1} >= 2a_m - a_{m-1} = a_m + (a_m - a_{m-1}). Hence a_m > a_{m-1} implies a_{m+1} > a_m. Starting from the seed a_{r+1} > a_r with a_{r+1} >= r+1, chaining gives a_n > a_{n-1} > ... > a_{r+1} >= r+1; since each strict step between integers adds at least 1, a_n >= (r+1) + (n-1-r) = n. This settles the b_{n-1} > 1 case of max{a_n, a_{n+1}} >= n (the b_{n-1} = 1 case is the routine one-line PLUS-branch bound).

technique: Substitute a difference variable g(x)=x-f(x) to convert a product-sign functional constraint into a symmetric statement about g and the sum x+y
how_used: Setting g(x)=x-f(x) gives f(x)+y=(x+y)-g(x) and f(y)+x=(x+y)-g(y). The hypothesis '(f(x)+y)(f(y)+x)>0 forces f(x)+y=f(y)+x' becomes '((x+y)-g(x))((x+y)-g(y))>0 forces g(x)=g(y)', and the target f(x)+y<=f(y)+x for x>y becomes g nondecreasing: g(x)<=g(y) whenever x<y.

technique: Read a 'product positive implies equal' hypothesis contrapositively as a betweenness (order) condition on a linear expression
how_used: Contrapositive of '((x+y)-g(x))((x+y)-g(y))>0 forces g(x)=g(y)': if g(x)!=g(y) then that product is <=0, i.e. x+y lies non-strictly between g(x) and g(y). So g(x)<g(y) implies g(x)<=x+y<=g(y). This single betweenness inequality is the quantitative engine used everywhere later.

technique: Chain the betweenness inequality across a sandwiched triple of values to convert a value-ordering into an argument-ordering
how_used: From g(x)<g(y)<g(z), betweenness on (x,y) and (y,z) gives g(x)<=x+y<=g(y)<=z+y<=g(z), so x+y<=z+y, hence x<z (Claim 2). This order-preservation lemma is the tool that later forces the two-valued 'Dirichlet interval' structure on any interval where monotonicity would fail.

technique: To show a level set of a constructed function is bounded, pair each of its points against one fixed off-level witness and read the two-sided bound straight off the standing betweenness inequality; recover the missing sign case by passing to the reflection-symmetric copy of the function.
how_used: For g(x)=x-f(x), the hypothesis becomes: g(x)!=g(y) implies x+y lies between g(x) and g(y). To bound S_c={x:g(x)=c} (Claim 1): fix y with g(y)>c; for any x in S_c betweenness gives c<=x+y<=g(y), so c-y<=x<=g(y)-y, a fixed bounded range. The opposite witness case g(y)<c is handled by the reflected function g1(x)=-g(-x), which satisfies the same betweenness condition. Consequence: each level set is bounded, so g takes infinitely many values, guaranteeing a third distinct value for the triple-chaining ordering used later.

technique: To kill a bad two-valued structure that would violate the target monotonicity, take the inf/sup of the maximal intervals carrying that structure and apply the pairwise inequality to two crossing pairs straddling the boundary, forcing the interval to be narrower than its own half-width.
how_used: Assuming monotonicity fails for some x<y, the Dirichlet property (Claim 3, a quick consequence of the betweenness ordering) makes g take only X=g(x),Y=g(y) on [x,y]. Set r=inf{a:(a,y] Dirichlet}, s=sup{b:[x,b) Dirichlet}, finite by level-set boundedness, and Delta=(y-x)/2. Just left of r pick r' with g(r') not in {X,Y} (exists since (r-Delta,y] is not Dirichlet, and Claim 3 forces g(r')<Y), and t just right of r with g(t)=X; applying betweenness to the crossing pairs (r',y) and (t,x) gives r-Delta+y<r'+y<=Y<=t+x<r+Delta+x, i.e. y-x<2Delta, contradicting Delta=(y-x)/2. A symmetric application at s (using two interior points s1<s2) finishes.

technique: To lower-bound a max of absolute errors, pick the two extremal witness indices realizing the target gap and add their signed errors so the monotonicity constraint drops out.
how_used: Chose p<=r with d=a_p-a_r where a_p is the prefix-max at q and a_r the suffix-min at q; summed (a_p-x_p)+(x_r-a_r) = d+(x_r-x_p) >= d using x_r>=x_p, forcing one of the two errors to be at least d/2.

technique: To build the optimal monotone approximant, take the running midpoint of the prefix-max and suffix-min sequences, which are each monotone so their average is automatically monotone.
how_used: Set x_i=(M_i+m_i)/2 with M_i=max prefix and m_i=min suffix; both nondecreasing so x_i is nondecreasing, and m_i<=a_i<=M_i sandwiches |x_i-a_i|<=(M_i-m_i)/2=d_i/2<=d/2, attaining equality.

technique: To bound an over-large output, feed the output value itself back through the inequality's self-composition slot so the nested term appears on both sides and cancels.
how_used: Assuming f(n)>n, write f(f(n))=f((f(n)-n)+n) and apply (1) to get f(f(n)) >= f(f(n)-n)+f(f(n))-1; canceling f(f(n)) forces f(f(n)-n) <= 1, hence f(n)-n < a where a is the least argument with f(a)>1. This makes the excess f(n)-n finite, so a maximal excess exists.

technique: Evaluate the inequality at the argument that maximizes a chosen gap functional so the same maximum reappears amplified, forcing the gap to collapse.
how_used: Let c=max(f(n)-n), attained at k with f(k)=k+c. Monotonicity gives f(2k) <= 2k+c, while (1) with m=n=k plus f(f(k)) >= f(k) gives f(2k) >= 2f(k)-1 = 2(k+c)-1. Chaining: 2k+c >= 2k+2c-1, so c <= 1, hence f(n) <= n+1 and f(2007) <= 2008.

technique: For a find-all-values problem, exhibit an explicit parametrized family of admissible functions, one per target value, verifying the constraint by casework.
how_used: For j <= 2007 use f_j(n)=max{1, n+j-2007}, which is nondecreasing with f_j(n) <= n so f_j(f_j(n)) <= f_j(n), giving f_j(2007)=j and verifying (1) by casing on whether f_j(m)=1; for the endpoint j=2008 use f(n)=n except f(n)=n+1 when 2007 | n, verifying (1) by casing on whether 2007 divides m+n.

technique: Bound a term by peeling off an explicitly nonnegative remainder written as a factored product
how_used: Wrote (1+t^2)/(1+t^4) = 1/t - (1-t)(1-t^3)/(t(1+t^4)) so the subtracted piece is a product of factors each positive on (0,1), giving the clean strict bound (1+t^2)/(1+t^4) < 1/t for each term with t=x^k and t=y^k

technique: Replace each summand by a geometric term so the whole sum collapses via the geometric-series formula
how_used: After bounding each term by 1/x^k, summed sum_{k=1}^n 1/x^k = (1-x^n)/(x^n(1-x)) as a finite geometric series with ratio 1/x, converting the awkward sum into a closed form in x^n (and likewise in y^n)

technique: Use the constraint to rewrite one side's numerator as the other variable's power, so the paired product cancels
how_used: Used x^n+y^n=1 to substitute 1-x^n=y^n and 1-y^n=x^n into the two closed forms, making the product (y^n/(x^n(1-x)))(x^n/(y^n(1-y))) cancel to 1/((1-x)(1-y))

technique: Solve for the argument that makes one side collapse by choosing the free variable to cancel a term inside f
how_used: To rule out f(y)<y, set x = y-f(y) (positive under the assumption) so that x+f(y)=y, turning f(x+f(y)) into f(y) and forcing f(y)=f(y-f(y)+y)+f(y)>f(y), a contradiction; this establishes f(y)>y everywhere.

technique: Substitute f(x)=g(x)+x to convert an f-inside-f equation into a shift-additivity relation for the excess g
how_used: Writing g(x)=f(x)-x>0 and setting t=x+y turns the equation into g(t+g(y))=g(t)+y for all t>y>0, the workhorse relation from which injectivity, Cauchy-additivity, and the involution all follow.

technique: Derive Cauchy additivity by expanding a nested application two ways and cancelling via injectivity
how_used: From g(t+g(y))=g(t)+y, injectivity is shown by equating g(t)+y1=g(t)+y2; then g(t+g(u)+g(v)) computed two ways gives g(t+g(u)+g(v))=g(t+g(u+v)), and injectivity yields g(u)+g(v)=g(u+v), plus positivity forces g increasing.

technique: Pin a monotone involution to the identity by playing g(g(x))=x against monotonicity
how_used: Combining g(t+g(y))=g(t)+y with additivity gives g(g(y))=y; then if x>g(x) monotonicity forces g(x)>g(g(x))=x and vice versa, both contradictions, so g(x)=x and f(x)=2x.

technique: Iterate a two-term subadditive-type inequality into a weighted many-term bound whose weights obey a Kraft-style budget constraint
how_used: From a(m+n) ≤ 2a(m)+2a(n) prove Lemma 2: whenever positive integers s_i satisfy Σ 2^{-s_i} ≤ 1, then a(Σ n_i) ≤ Σ 2^{s_i} a(n_i); the induction sorts s_1≤…≤s_k, pairs the two largest indices, merges n_{k-1}+n_k into one term with weight index s_{k-1}−1, and uses Σ_{i<k}2^{-s_i}≤1−2^{-s_{k-1}} to verify the merged weights still satisfy the ≤1 budget before applying the two-term inequality

technique: Tune the free per-term weights so the Kraft budget is saturated to order 1, turning the weighted bound into a convergent p-series in the given data
how_used: For n = Σ 2^{u_i} pick s_i = ⌊log2((u_i+1)^q)⌋ + d with q = c/2 > 1 and choose the integer d so that 1/2 < Σ 2^{-s_i} ≤ 1; the upper half licenses Lemma 2 while the lower half forces 2^d < 4Σ(u_i+1)^{-q}. Substituting a(2^{u_i}) ≤ (u_i+1)^{-2q} yields a(n) ≤ 2^d Σ(u_i+1)^{-q} < 4(Σ (u_i+1)^{-q})^2, bounded because q > 1

technique: Group binary-digit positions into geometrically spaced blocks so a per-block max-and-count bound telescopes to a geometric series
how_used: In solution 1, split the binary support of n into intervals [M_{k-1}, M_k) with M_k = 4^{k/(c-2)}−1; the block factor 2^k·2(M_k−M_{k-1}+1)^2·max a(2^i) becomes ((M_k+1)/(M_{k-1}+1))^2 · 2^{k+1}/(M_{k-1}+1)^{c-2}, which the geometric spacing collapses to 8·4^{2/(c-2)} Σ (1/2)^k

technique: Repackage a cyclic sum as an inner product of one sequence against a tailored second sequence, then Cauchy-Schwarz so the given normalization constraint becomes one whole factor and vanishes
how_used: Write 3S = sum_k a_{k+1}(a_k^2 + 2 a_{k+1} a_{k+2}) (the factor 3 collects S from a_{k+1}a_k^2 plus 2S from a_{k+1}^2 a_{k+2}). Cauchy-Schwarz splitting off the a_{k+1} factor gives (3S)^2 <= (sum a_{k+1}^2)(sum (a_k^2 + 2 a_{k+1} a_{k+2})^2); since sum a_{k+1}^2 = 1 this collapses to (3S)^2 <= T := sum (a_k^2 + 2 a_{k+1} a_{k+2})^2.

technique: Bound a cyclic sum of squared adjacent-product terms by an alternating even/odd residue-class split, majorizing by the product of the two class sums, then AM-GM the two factors whose total is fixed
how_used: With n = 100 even, each term a_k^2 a_{k+1}^2 pairs an odd-index square with an even-index square, so sum a_k^2 a_{k+1}^2 <= (sum_i a_{2i-1}^2)(sum_j a_{2j}^2) =: p q with p + q = sum a_k^2 = 1. AM-GM gives 4 p q <= (p+q)^2 = 1, i.e. sum a_k^2 a_{k+1}^2 <= 1/4. Feeding this into (3S)^2 <= 1 + 4 sum a_k^2 a_{k+1}^2 <= 1 + 1 = 2, so S <= sqrt(2)/3 ~ 0.4714 < 12/25.

technique: Linearize an odd-degree triple-product monomial inside a cyclic sum by applying AM-GM to its two outer factors, replacing it with a symmetric sum of pair-square monomials
how_used: In the expanded Cauchy-Schwarz bound (3S)^2 <= sum(a_k^4 + 4 a_k^2 a_{k+1} a_{k+2} + 4 a_{k+1}^2 a_{k+2}^2), the term 4 a_k^2 a_{k+1} a_{k+2} is not a product of two squares. AM-GM 2 a_{k+1} a_{k+2} <= a_{k+1}^2 + a_{k+2}^2 gives 4 a_k^2 a_{k+1} a_{k+2} <= 2 a_k^2(a_{k+1}^2 + a_{k+2}^2); re-indexing the 4 a_{k+1}^2 a_{k+2}^2 term (k -> k-1) turns the whole bound into sum(a_k^4 + 6 a_k^2 a_{k+1}^2 + 2 a_k^2 a_{k+2}^2), built only from products of two squares.

technique: Bound a cyclic sum of pair-square monomials by recognizing a chosen subgroup of its terms as a subset of the (necessarily nonnegative) terms of a squared power-sum, which the constraint pins to 1, leaving only a small explicit remainder to bound
how_used: Split sum(a_k^4 + 6 a_k^2 a_{k+1}^2 + 2 a_k^2 a_{k+2}^2) = sum(a_k^4 + 2 a_k^2 a_{k+1}^2 + 2 a_k^2 a_{k+2}^2) + 4 sum a_k^2 a_{k+1}^2. With x_k = a_k^2, the first group's monomials (x_k^2, and x_k x_{k+1}, x_k x_{k+2} each with coefficient 2 for the two orderings) are all distinct index-pairs occurring inside (sum_k x_k)^2 = sum_{i,j} x_i x_j (distinct because n=100 >= 5), so the group is <= (sum a_k^2)^2 = 1. This yields (3S)^2 <= 1 + 4 sum a_k^2 a_{k+1}^2, isolating the single remainder sum a_k^2 a_{k+1}^2.

technique: To bound a weighted cyclic sum, first scale it to absorb the cyclic symmetry, then rewrite the scaled sum as a single cyclic dot product of two sequences, choosing the split so one factor's square-sum equals the constraint; apply Cauchy-Schwarz so that factor collapses.
how_used: Write 3S = sum_k a_{k+1}(a_k^2 + 2 a_{k+1} a_{k+2}), where the factor 3 and the doubled cross term come from re-indexing the cyclic sum so each degree-3 monomial is counted correctly. View this as the dot product of (a_{k+1}) with (a_k^2 + 2 a_{k+1} a_{k+2}). Cauchy-Schwarz gives (3S)^2 <= (sum a_{k+1}^2)(sum (a_k^2 + 2 a_{k+1} a_{k+2})^2), and the first factor is sum a_{k+1}^2 = sum a_k^2 = 1 by cyclic shift, leaving (3S)^2 <= sum (a_k^2 + 2 a_{k+1} a_{k+2})^2. This turns the degree-3 target S into a manageable degree-4 sum.

technique: When bounding a cyclic sum of squared products of consecutive terms under a fixed total square-sum, and the cycle length is even, split indices by parity so every consecutive pair straddles the two blocks, then dominate the cyclic sum by the product of the two block square-sums.
how_used: After Cauchy-Schwarz leaves (3S)^2 <= sum (a_k^2 + 2 a_{k+1} a_{k+2})^2, expand and apply AM-GM 2 a_{k+1} a_{k+2} <= a_{k+1}^2 + a_{k+2}^2 to the cross term, then regroup into sum(a_k^4 + 2 a_k^2 a_{k+1}^2 + 2 a_k^2 a_{k+2}^2) + 4 sum a_k^2 a_{k+1}^2. Bound the first group by (sum a_k^2)^2 = 1 (it is a sub-sum of the expansion of (sum a_k^2)^2). For the second: since 100 is even, each consecutive pair has one odd and one even index, so sum a_k^2 a_{k+1}^2 <= (sum_i a_{2i-1}^2)(sum_j a_{2j}^2); then 4(sum_odd)(sum_even) <= (sum_odd + sum_even)^2 = 1 by AM-GM. Hence (3S)^2 <= 2, giving S <= sqrt(2)/3 < 12/25.

technique: Pair each reciprocal with a permuted numerator so a Cauchy-Schwarz lower bound isolates a single extremal ratio and its inverse against a block of ones
how_used: Rewriting the sum-times-sum as (a_2+a_1+a_3+...+a_n)(1/a_1+1/a_2+...+1/a_n) — swapping a_1 and a_2 in the first factor — Cauchy-Schwarz gives (sqrt(a_2/a_1)+sqrt(a_1/a_2)+1+...+1)^2, so only the largest/smallest pair produces the nontrivial terms sqrt(M)+sqrt(1/M) plus (n-2) ones, with M = a_max/a_min

technique: Reduce a bound on the extremal ratio to a quadratic in its square root and solve the resulting inequality
how_used: From (n+1/2)^2 >= (sqrt(M)+sqrt(1/M)+(n-2))^2, taking square roots gives sqrt(M)+1/sqrt(M) <= 5/2; setting t=sqrt(M) yields t^2 - (5/2)t + 1 <= 0, whose roots 1/2 and 2 force 1/4 <= M <= 4, hence max <= 4 min

technique: Substitute cosine to turn a radical-shifted functional equation into an angle-shift invariance
how_used: Setting Q(x)=P(x√2) and x=cosθ rewrites P(x√2)=P(x+√(1−x²)) as Q(cosθ)=Q(cos(θ−45°)): the (cosθ+sinθ)/√2 becomes cos(θ−45°), converting the equation into invariance of Q under a 45° shift of the argument angle over θ∈[0°,180°].

technique: Peel off the minimal solution by polynomial division and recurse on the remainder to show every solution is a composition
how_used: Dividing any good Q by the minimal good polynomial U forces the remainder r (deg<8) to also be good — since U(cosθ)=U(cos(θ−45°)), r(cosθ)−r(cos(θ−45°))=−U(cosθ)·[Q̃(cosθ)−Q̃(cos(θ−45°))] and U(cosθ)≠0 generically — hence by minimality r is a constant c and Q̃ is good too; iterating gives Q(x)=f(U(x)), so P(x)=f(U(x/√2)).

technique: Force a degree lower bound by exhibiting many distinct arguments where the function is pinned to one common value
how_used: After rewriting the equation as Q(cos θ)=Q(cos(θ−45°)) with Q(x)=P(x√2), iterate θ↦θ−45° from the seed 136°, folding cos(−44°)=cos44° when the angle leaves [0°,180°], to reach 8 DISTINCT arguments cos1°,cos46°,cos91°,cos136°,cos44°,cos89°,cos134°,cos179° at all of which the invariance chains Q to a single common value v. Then Q(x)−v has these 8 distinct roots, so a nonconstant good Q has deg≥8 — matching deg U where U(cosθ)=cos8θ.

technique: Classify every solution of an invariance functional equation as a polynomial in the minimal nonconstant solution, by peeling it off through Euclidean division and forcing the remainder to be constant via a degree lower bound.
how_used: Put Q(x)=P(x√2); the equation becomes Q(cosθ)=Q(cos(θ−45°)) (call such Q good). The engine that pins the minimal good nonconstant polynomial is a degree lower bound: chaining the invariance θ↦θ−45° from a seed angle produces EIGHT distinct cosine values at which Q takes one common value (e.g. cos136°,cos91°,…,cos44°,…,cos179°, the ninth coinciding with an earlier one), so any nonconstant good Q has deg≥8; and U with U(cosθ)=cos8θ (Chebyshev T_8, minimal because 8·45°=360°) is good and attains degree 8. Then for any good Q write Q=Q̃·U+r by division; deg r<8 together with r being good forces r constant, and iterating on Q̃ peels off powers of U to give Q=f(U), i.e. P(x)=f(U(x/√2)).

technique: Recast a divisibility/existence claim as the nontriviality of a linear map's kernel, then force a nonzero solution by comparing domain and codomain dimension.
how_used: Take V = real polynomials of degree at most d/2 and the linear map V⊕V → R[x]/(P), (A,B) ↦ A+QB mod P. The domain has dimension 2(⌊d/2⌋+1) > d = dim of the codomain R[x]/(P), so the map has a nontrivial kernel, yielding (A,B) not both zero with P | A+QB and max{deg A, deg B} ≤ d/2.

technique: Instantiate the constraint at several small partitions that differ by moving one element between blocks, then take a fixed linear combination of those instances so all the many-term sums cancel and only a single low-order term survives.
how_used: Apply the triple-sum condition to A={1},B={2},C={3..n}; A={1},B={3},C={2,4..n}; and A={1},B={2,3},C={4..n}; then (first)+(second)-(third) cancels every c>=4 term and leaves X_{123}+X_{132}=2, i.e. W(1,2)W(2,3)+W(1,3)W(3,2)=2, generalizing to all distinct triples.

technique: Produce two instances of the same two-term relation that share one of their two product terms, subtract to force the other two products equal, then cancel the common nonzero factor to turn the product equality into a linear equality of the leftover factors.
how_used: The combination move yields both W(1,2)W(2,3)+W(1,3)W(3,2)=2 (i.e. X_{123}+X_{132}=2, from refining/merging the B-block) and, re-running the identical combination with the outer roles swapped, W(1,2)W(2,3)+W(2,1)W(3,2)=2 (X_{123}+X_{321}=2). These share the term X_{123}=W(1,2)W(2,3); subtracting gives X_{132}=X_{321}, i.e. W(1,3)W(3,2)=W(2,1)W(3,2). Cancelling W(3,2) (nonzero: a zero off-diagonal would make some two-term instance read 0=2) gives W(1,3)=W(2,1). Relabeling shows all off-diagonals equal one constant w, and w^2+w^2=2 forces w=+/-1 (diagonal entries W(k,k) never enter the sums, so are arbitrary).

technique: Evaluate a set-additive identity on two singleton-refined instances and one merged instance of the same index block, then add the singletons and subtract the merged copy so the common bulk/tail terms cancel and only a short fixed-length combination of terms survives.
how_used: The identity is additive in the middle block B: with A={1} fixed, take B={2},C={3,..,n}; B={3},C={2,4,..,n}; and the merged B={2,3},C={4,..,n}. The first two give X_{123}+(X_{124}+..+X_{12n})=n-2 and X_{132}+(X_{134}+..+X_{13n})=n-2; the merged one gives (X_{124}+..+X_{12n})+(X_{134}+..+X_{13n})=2(n-3). Adding the first two and subtracting the third annihilates every tail term X_{12k},X_{13k} (k>=4) and leaves exactly X_{123}+X_{132}=2, isolating a clean two-term relation among the products W(a,b)W(b,c).

technique: When a symmetry of the setup yields two instances of the same short relation that share a common product term, subtract them to equate the two non-shared terms, then cancel the shared nonzero factor to force equality of two individual unknowns.
how_used: From X_{123}+X_{132}=2 and its companion X_{123}+X_{321}=2 (both anchored at the shared term X_{123}), subtracting gives X_{132}=X_{321}, i.e. W(1,3)W(3,2)=W(3,2)W(2,1). The factor W(3,2) is common and nonzero (any W(a,b)=0 would let a partition sum vanish against |A||B||C|>0), so dividing it out yields W(2,1)=W(1,3). Chaining this 'any two W-entries sharing an index are equal' across all distinct triples (n>=4 supplies the needed third indices) forces W(a,b) to be one constant on off-diagonal pairs; substituting back into the two-term relation pins that constant to +/-1 with a globally fixed sign, while diagonal entries W(k,k) never appear and stay arbitrary.

technique: To extract a short clean relation from a summed identity whose blocks range over a large index set, evaluate it on a few near-singleton partitions differing by which single element sits in each small block, then take a fixed linear combination of those evaluations so every long tail-sum cancels and only a couple of individual terms survive.
how_used: The partition identity sums W(a,b)W(b,c)=X_{abc} over A x B x C. Evaluate it on three partitions with singleton small blocks so the long C-sums are identical tails: A={1},B={2},C={3,...,n} gives X_{123}+X_{124}+...+X_{12n}=n-2; A={1},B={3},C={2,4,...,n} gives X_{132}+X_{134}+...+X_{13n}=n-2; A={1},B={2,3},C={4,...,n} gives (X_{124}+...+X_{12n})+(X_{134}+...+X_{13n})=2(n-3). Adding the first two and subtracting the third annihilates every X_{12k} and X_{13k} with k>=4, leaving the two-term relation X_{123}+X_{132}=2. The same construction under a relabel that keeps X_{123} as the surviving anchor produces the companion X_{123}+X_{321}=2.

technique: When two extracted relations share a common anchor term, subtract them so the anchor drops out and the remainder is an equality of two products that share one factor; cancel that provably-nonzero shared factor to descend from a quadratic constraint to a linear one, then propagate the resulting equality across all index tuples by symmetry.
how_used: The two two-term relations X_{123}+X_{132}=2 and X_{123}+X_{321}=2 share the anchor X_{123}. Subtracting gives X_{132}=X_{321}, i.e. W(1,3)W(3,2)=W(3,2)W(2,1). The factor W(3,2) is nonzero (a zero off-diagonal value would make the corresponding partition sum fall short, so no entry vanishes), so cancel it to get the LINEAR relation W(2,1)=W(1,3). Relabeling the ground set gives W(a,b)=W(b,c) for every distinct triple a,b,c. Chaining this transitively (n>=4 supplies enough distinct triples) forces all off-diagonal W(a,b) to a single common value t with t=W(a,b)=W(b,a); plugging any single partition back in pins t^2=1, so t=+1 or t=-1 with the sign fixed globally, while W(k,k) stays free. This is what kills the spurious sqrt(2)- and 0-valued solutions that solving the two-term quadratic relations in isolation would admit.

technique: Realize a prescribed difference of values at two fixed points by noting the shifted difference of the polynomial has odd degree, hence is surjective onto R
how_used: Lemma 1, base case n=2, EVEN-degree S: T(x)=S(x+a2)-S(x+a1) has degree deg(S)-1 which is odd (leading terms cancel, next term survives), so it is surjective; pick x0 with T(x0)=b2-b1. Then G(x)=S(x+x0) satisfies G(a2)-G(a1)=b2-b1, and F(x)=G(x)+(b1-G(a1)) gives F(a1)=b1, F(a2)=b2. All moves are board-legal (P(C+x) then C+P).

technique: Find a real quantity that grows monotonically under every allowed generating operation, then pick a target pair violating it to prove unreachability
how_used: For odd-degree S with POSITIVE leading coefficient, S is eventually increasing with slope >3 off a bounded segment, so there is a constant T (fixed once, from S) with S(b)-S(a) >= b-a whenever b-a >= T. This inequality (*) is inherited with the SAME T by every board move: shift P(C+x), add-constant C+P(x), sum P+Q (gap difference at least doubles), and composition P(Q(x)) (inner move already expands the gap past T so the outer hypothesis reapplies). So no board polynomial can send A={0,T} onto B={0,T/2}, since that needs the gap T to shrink to T/2. This rules out the odd-degree positive-leading case; linear S is excluded separately since the board stays affine and an affine map is pinned by 2 points.

technique: When a difference polynomial has even degree and only covers one sign, add a composed copy of the polynomial whose iterate has the opposite-sign leading coefficient, so the sum of the two shifted differences covers all of R
how_used: Lemma 1 base case for A={a1,a2}, odd-degree S with NEGATIVE leading coefficient. Here S(x+a2)-S(x+a1) has even degree and reaches only large negatives, but S2(x):=S(S(x)) is odd with POSITIVE leading coefficient, so S2(x+a2)-S2(x+a1) reaches large positives. Because one summand covers +infinity and the other -infinity, fixed constants x0,y0 exist with S2(x0+a2)-S2(x0+a1)+S(y0+a2)-S(y0+a1)=b2-b1; bundle into the SINGLE board polynomial G(x)=S2(x+x0)+S(x+y0) (a sum move), giving G(a2)-G(a1)=b2-b1, then an add-constant shift pins F(a1)=b1,F(a2)=b2. (Even-degree S is simpler: the single difference already has odd degree, so it hits b2-b1 directly.)

technique: Collapse two of the input points to a common value using a sum of two far-shifted copies made convex on the interval, reducing the number of distinct values by one
how_used: Lemma 2: build a board polynomial F, convex on [a1,an], with F(a1)=F(a2). For even positive-leading S, S(x+c) is convex on the interval for |c| large, and S(a2+c)-S(a1+c) sweeps all large negatives as c->-infinity and all large positives as c->+infinity; pick large c1<0<c2 so F(x)=S(x+c1)+S(x+c2) is convex AND has F(a1)=F(a2). For odd negative-leading S use F(x)=S(x+c1)+S2(x+c2), the iterate supplying the convex/positive branch. Convexity is exactly what caps the value list at n-1 distinct numbers (a convex function takes each value at most twice, and only the pair a1,a2 is forced to coincide), so no separate distinctness argument is needed.

technique: Glue a base-case two-point fit to an inductive many-point fit by writing the answer as a composition-plus-additive-correction so each part handles a disjoint set of points
how_used: Inductive step (n-1 => n). After shifting S so all S(a_i) are distinct, Lemma 2 gives f with c_i=f(a_i) all distinct EXCEPT c1=c2. Lemma 1 gives g with g(a1)=b1, g(a2)=b2. The inductive hypothesis (on the n-1 distinct values c2,...,cn) gives h with h(c_i)=b_i-g(a_i) for i=2..n. Then F(x)=h(f(x))+g(x) works: for i>=2 it is h(c_i)+g(a_i)=b_i, and at a1 it is h(c1)+g(a1)=h(c2)+g(a1)=(b2-g(a2))+g(a1), which with g(a2)-g(a1)=b2-b1 equals b1. The additive g(x) is what recovers two distinct target values at the collapsed pair a1,a2.

technique: Divide two bivariate polynomials with respect to one variable by treating the coefficients as living in the rational-function field of the other variable, so the ordinary single-variable division algorithm applies.
how_used: View A and B as polynomials in x over the field R(y); the division algorithm gives A = Q*B + R with Q, R in (R(y))[x] and deg_x R < deg_x B, reducing the divisibility question to showing the remainder R vanishes.

technique: Force a remainder polynomial to be identically zero by specializing the free variable to infinitely many values where a degree inequality makes each specialized remainder vanish, then use that each coefficient has infinitely many roots.
how_used: For infinitely many y0, B(x,y0) | R(x,y0) while deg_x B(x,y0) > deg_x R(x,y0) holds for all but finitely many y0, forcing R(x,y0) identically 0 for infinitely many y0; hence every coefficient (in R(y)) of R has infinitely many roots and is the zero polynomial, so R = 0.

technique: Combine two coprime denominator representations of the same rational function via cross-multiplication and unique factorization to force one denominator to be a unit.
how_used: Having written A/B = F(x,y)/M(y) = G(x,y)/N(x) in lowest terms, coprimeness of M and N (one depends only on y, the other only on x) plus F*N = G*M gives M | F*N; since gcd(F,M)=1 and gcd(M,N)=1, M is constant, so A/B is a genuine polynomial and B | A.

technique: Split each coefficient as a fixed baseline plus a small deviation to isolate a positive main part from a controllably-small perturbation
how_used: Wrote c_i = 1 - d_i so the constraint sum|c_i-1|<1 becomes sum|d_i|<1; the c_i=1 baseline collapses the alternating-sign polynomial into a clean positive form (x^n+1 plus the geometric sum, packaged as x^n+1+(x^{n+1}+1)/(x+1) for x>0), leaving the d_i part as the perturbation sum d_i x^i to be dominated.

technique: Dominate a whole weighted sum of intermediate terms by a single uniform per-term bound times a total weight below 1
how_used: Bounded x^n+1 > x^i for every 1<=i<=n-1 and x>0, so since sum|d_i|<1 we get x^n+1 > sum|d_i|x^i >= sum d_i x^i, forcing the baseline to exceed the perturbation and the polynomial to stay positive.

technique: Differentiate the polynomial identity to turn each additive lower-order term into a multiplicative factor.
how_used: Differentiating P^10+P^9 = Q^21+Q^20 gives P'P^8(10P+9) = Q'Q^19(21Q+20); the '+9' and '+20' shifts become the factors 10P+9 and 21Q+20, surfacing 10P+9 as a degree-(deg P) factor sitting on the left that must divide the right-hand product.

technique: Show a large-degree factor of one side must divide a smaller-degree factor of the other, then compare degrees for a contradiction.
how_used: With deg P = 21n and deg Q = 10n (from leading-term comparison), gcd(10P+9,P)=gcd(10P+9,P+1)=1 gives gcd(10P+9, P^9(P+1))=1, so by the original equation gcd(10P+9,Q)=1 (and 10P+9 shares no root with Q'). The differentiated identity then forces 10P+9 | Q'(21Q+20). But deg(10P+9)=21n exceeds deg(Q'(21Q+20))=20n-1, impossible for a nonzero divisor.

technique: Force a polynomial to be constant by exhibiting more points where it takes a fixed value than its degree.
how_used: At each of the >= m+1 distinct roots of P(P+1) the original equation P^9(P+1)=Q^20(Q+1) forces Q in {0,-1}. Since m >= 2n (from the degrees), m+1 >= 2n+1 such points split between two values, so by pigeonhole one value is attained at >= n+1 = deg Q + 1 points, forcing Q constant — contradicting non-constancy.

technique: For a product of two coprime polynomials whose difference is a constant, apply Mason-Stothers to bound below the number of distinct roots of the product.
how_used: P and P+1 are coprime and differ by the constant 1, so viewing this as the coprime additive relation A=P, B=1 (constant), C=P+1 with A+B=C, Mason-Stothers forces the number of distinct roots of the radical of P(P+1) to exceed deg P = m; hence P(P+1) has at least m+1 distinct complex roots.

technique: Count root incidences: evaluate a low-degree factor at the many common roots of the other side and force it constant by exceeding its degree.
how_used: At each of the >= m+1 >= 2n+1 distinct roots of P(P+1) the LHS P^9(P+1) vanishes, so Q^20(Q+1) vanishes there, meaning Q takes a value in {0,-1} at each such root. Since there are more than n = deg Q such points, one of Q or Q+1 has more than deg Q roots, forcing Q (hence Q+1) to be identically zero — impossible for non-constant Q, so Q must be constant.

technique: Represent a non-polynomial atom as a convergent parameter integral of a fixed kernel evaluated at the atom's argument, choosing the kernel's homogeneity so the integral reproduces the atom up to a positive constant.
how_used: Write sqrt|p| = (1/I(1)) integral_0^infty (1-cos(px))/x^{3/2} dx, where I(1)=integral_0^infty (1-cos u)/u^{3/2} du is finite and positive; the substitution y=|p|x gives I(p)=sqrt|p| I(1), so each root term sqrt|x_i +/- x_j| becomes an integral of the SAME kernel, letting the whole two-index sum be handled inside one integral.

technique: Use a product-to-difference trig identity to collapse the difference of the two atom-values into a single bilinear product term, so that summing over the index makes the integrand a perfect square.
how_used: cos((a-b)x)-cos((a+b)x)=2 sin(ax) sin(bx) turns sqrt|a+b|-sqrt|a-b| into an integral of 2 sin(ax)sin(bx)/x^{3/2}; summing over i,j gives integrand 2(sum_i sin(x_i x))^2, a nonnegative perfect square, so the integral (hence the difference RHS-LHS) is >=0.

technique: Shift all variables by a common parameter to make one side of a symmetric two-sided inequality invariant, turning the other side into a one-parameter piecewise-concave function; then use that concavity to reduce proving the inequality everywhere to proving it only at the function's kink points.
how_used: Adding t to every x_i leaves LHS=sum sqrt|x_i-x_j| fixed (differences unchanged) and turns RHS into H(t)=sum sqrt|x_i+x_j+2t|. Each summand sqrt|x_i+x_j+2t| is concave in t off its single kink at t=-(x_i+x_j)/2, so H is concave on every interval between consecutive breakpoints p_ij=-(x_i+x_j)/2 (and on the two outer rays). Choosing T large with H(-T),H(T)>L, on the segment [a,b] containing 0 concavity gives H(0)>=min(H(a),H(b)); walking outward, the minimum of H over [-T,T] is attained at some breakpoint (endpoints are ruled out since H(+-T)>L). At a breakpoint the shifted configuration has some x_i+x_j=0, so it suffices to prove the original inequality under the extra assumption that two variables sum to zero.

technique: Given a forced coincidence among the variables, delete the coincident index (or the canceling pair) and check that both sides of the inequality decrease by the identical amount, so the inequality descends to a smaller instance and closes by induction.
how_used: Assuming (from the reduction) some coincidence: if x_i=0, deleting index i drops each side by 2 sum_k sqrt|x_k| (LHS row+column sqrt|x_i-x_k|=sqrt|x_k| and RHS sqrt|x_i+x_k|=sqrt|x_k| match, RHS diagonal sqrt|2x_i|=0). If x_j=-x_i with i!=j, deleting the pair {i,j} drops both sides by 2 sqrt(2|x_i|) + 2 sum_{k!=i,j}(sqrt|x_k+x_i|+sqrt|x_k+x_j|): the third-index cross-terms match as multisets (LHS sqrt|x_k-x_i|+sqrt|x_k+x_i| equals RHS sqrt|x_k+x_i|+sqrt|x_k-x_i|), and the intra-pair contributions coincide because LHS loses the two off-diagonal sqrt|x_i-x_j|=sqrt(2|x_i|) while RHS loses the two diagonal sqrt|2x_i|=sqrt(2|x_i|) each (its off-diagonal sqrt|x_i+x_j|=0 vanishes). Base cases n=0,1 are trivial.

technique: Bound each summand of a partial-sum sum by a consecutive difference of a cubed prefix sum so the total telescopes to a boundary value
how_used: Each term b_k = a_k s_{k-1}^2/(1-a_k) (with s_k the prefix sum a_1+...+a_k, s_0=0, s_n=1) is bounded by (s_k^3 - s_{k-1}^3)/3; summing over k=1..n telescopes to (s_n^3 - s_0^3)/3 = 1/3, and strictness of the per-term bound gives the required strict inequality < 1/3.

technique: Prove the per-term difference inequality by clearing denominators, expanding the cube, and factoring the remainder into manifestly nonnegative pieces using the constraint
how_used: The inequality b_k < (s_k^3 - s_{k-1}^3)/3 (with a=a_k, s=s_{k-1}) reduces after multiplying by 3(1-a)>0 and expanding (s+a)^3 to 0 < a[3(1-a-s)s a + (1-a)a^2]; the outer factor a>0, and each bracketed piece is nonnegative/positive since a+s = s_k <= 1 (so 1-a-s >= 0) and a in (0,1) (so (1-a)a^2 > 0), giving the strict per-term bound.

technique: Introduce a weighted linear combination of consecutive terms as a new variable so the given quadratic constraint becomes a clean monotone step bound on that variable's square.
how_used: Set y_i = 2x_i + x_{i+1}; the constraint x_i x_{i+1} - x_{i-1}^2 >= 1 then yields y_i^2 - y_{i-1}^2 >= 6, from which induction gives y_i >= sqrt(6i), and summing 3(x_0+...+x_{n+1}) >= y_1+...+y_n.

technique: Prove a difference of two squares dominates a target constant by rewriting it as an explicit sum of squares plus the given constraint quantity.
how_used: Show (a+2b)^2 - (b+2c)^2 = (a-b)^2 + 2(b-c)^2 + 6(ab-c^2) >= 6, giving the step increment for y_i^2 from the hypothesis ab - c^2 >= 1.

technique: Lower-bound a sum of square roots by comparing each term's difference of 3/2-powers to (3/2)sqrt(k) via Bernoulli's inequality, then telescoping.
how_used: Use (k-1)^{3/2} > k^{3/2} - (3/2)sqrt(k) to sum and get sqrt(1)+...+sqrt(n) > (2/3)n^{3/2}, converting the y_i >= sqrt(6i) bound into the final (2n/3)^{3/2} threshold.

technique: When a functional equation's RHS is f(P)-f(Q) with P,Q built symmetrically from the variables, factor P-Q; if it splits into the same difference-product that the LHS is a product over, a single equal-value coincidence f(a)=f(b) zeroes the whole LHS and transports to a new coincidence, giving an orbit map on the equal-value set.
how_used: Here P-Q = (ab^2+bx^2+xa^2)-(a^2b+b^2x+x^2a) = (a-b)(b-x)(x-a), and E(a,b,x) has LHS (f(a)-f(b))(f(b)-f(x))(f(x)-f(a)). So if (a,b) is in Theta (f(a)=f(b)) the first factor vanishes, killing the entire product, forcing f(P)=f(Q), i.e. H_{a,b}(x)=(ab^2+bx^2+xa^2, a^2b+b^2x+x^2a) is in Theta for ALL x. This is the engine that propagates one coincidence into an orbit.

technique: To pin the exponent of a power-function solution, divide the equation by the factor that equals the argument-difference and take the confluent limit (all variables to a common point) so each difference quotient becomes a derivative, yielding a transcendental equation in the exponent whose roots are bounded by a convexity argument.
how_used: Divide E(a,b,c) by (a-b)(b-c)(c-a) — which equals P-Q by the crux-0 identity, so the RHS reduces to (P^tau-Q^tau)/(P-Q). Let a,b,c->1: LHS difference quotients (a^tau-b^tau)/(a-b)->tau each, giving tau^3; RHS ->tau*3^{tau-1} (P,Q->3, since each of the three monomials ab^2 etc ->1). So tau^3=tau*3^{tau-1}, i.e. tau^2=3^{tau-1}, i.e. F(tau):=3^{(tau-1)/2}-tau=0; F strictly convex gives at most two roots, and tau in {1,3}.

technique: To upgrade a lemma of the form 'either f is degenerate or f is injective', push the equal-value set through the equation's induced orbit map to a maximally structured witness where one coordinate is forced to zero, so that at that witness the orbit map degenerates and the coincidence spreads to a full symmetry of f, which then re-collides with the orbit to collapse f to the degenerate case.
how_used: From (a,b) in Theta* one squares coordinates (via comparing E(alpha,1,0) and E(beta,1,0), which gives (alpha^2,beta^2) in Theta*) until delta>5*gamma>=0; then solves the quadratic delta*gamma^2+gamma*x^2+x*delta^2=0 (real since discriminant delta^4-4*delta*gamma^3>0) to land H_{delta,gamma}(x)=(0,r) in Theta* with r nonzero. From (0,r): H_{0,r}(x)=(r x^2, r^2 x) gives f(r x^2)=f(r^2 x)=f(-r^2 x), so f is even; then H_{a,-a}(x) with x=(1+sqrt5)/2 * a lands (0,(1+sqrt5)a^3) in Theta, forcing f identically 0. Hence non-constant f is injective.

technique: Once a near-multiplicative relation kappa*f(a)(f(a)-kappa)=f(a^2)-f(a) is in hand, pair it with its negated-argument copy (a -> -a) and cancel the common factor f(a)-f(-a) (nonzero by injectivity) to extract that f(a)+f(-a) is a constant independent of a.
how_used: E(a,b,0) gives f(a)f(b)(f(a)-f(b))=f(a^2 b)-f(a b^2); with b=1 and kappa=f(1) this is kappa f(a)(f(a)-kappa)=f(a^2)-f(a). Subtracting the a->-a copy (same a^2) and dividing by f(a)-f(-a)!=0 yields f(a)+f(-a)=kappa-kappa^{-1}=:lambda. A second pairing: adding relation (a,b) to (-a,-b) forces f(a)f(b)=(lambda-f(a))(lambda-f(b)); lambda!=0 would give f(a)+f(b)=lambda contradicting injectivity, so lambda=0, f is odd, kappa=+/-1.

technique: For a multiplicative f on the positive reals, rule out pathological (non-power) solutions by the density dichotomy — a multiplicative map is either a pure power or has graph dense in the quarter-plane — and defeat the dense case by feeding one substitution into a quadratic-trinomial lower bound to make f bounded on a ray, contradicting density (and simultaneously killing negative exponents).
how_used: After deriving f(ax)=f(a)f(x), f(x^2)=f(x)^2 (so f>=0, and >0 for x>0 by injectivity): if f is not x^tau its graph is dense on (0,inf)^2, so pick 0<b<1/10 with f(b)>1 (same b exists if tau<0). Since x^2+xb^2+b>=0, E(1,b,x) gives f(b^2+bx^2+x)=f(x^2+xb^2+b)+(f(b)-1)(f(x)-f(b))(f(x)-1), and the trinomial bound (t-f(1))(t-f(b))>=-(f(b)-1)^2/4 with t=f(x) makes the RHS bounded below, so f is bounded below on a ray — contradicting density, and (via oddness) bounded above near 0, absurd for tau<0. Hence f=x^tau with tau>0.

technique: To force a continuous exponent of an already-established power-law solution to discrete values, coalesce all free variables to a common point so each difference quotient in the equation becomes a derivative, turning the identity into a transcendental equation in the exponent, then cap its root count by strict convexity.
how_used: With f(x)=x^tau on the positives (already reduced to this form, with tau>0 already known), divide E(a,b,c) by (a-b)(b-c)(c-a) = (ab^2+bc^2+ca^2)-(a^2b+b^2c+c^2a) and let a,b,c -> 1. Each ratio (a^tau-b^tau)/(a-b) -> (x^tau)'|_{x=1}=tau, so the LHS/denominator -> tau^3 and the RHS/denominator -> tau*3^{tau-1}. Hence tau^3 = tau*3^{tau-1}, i.e. tau^2 = 3^{tau-1}. Because tau>0 was already secured upstream (so the negative branch is irrelevant), take the positive square root: F(tau):=3^{(tau-1)/2}-tau=0. F is strictly convex, so it has at most two roots, giving tau in {1,3}. This pins the exponent only; assembling the final f=alpha x+beta / alpha x^3+beta is the separate structural work done earlier.

technique: When an equal-value pair of a function feeds a functional equation whose right side is an antisymmetric expression in the arguments, substitute the pair to make that right side vanish, turning the induced argument map into a self-map of the equal-value set that pumps out a new equal-value pair for every value of the remaining free variable.
how_used: Let Theta = {(a,b): f(a)=f(b)}. For (a,b) in Theta, in E(a,b,x) the LHS carries the factor (f(a)-f(b))=0, so the whole LHS vanishes; the RHS f(ab^2+bx^2+xa^2)-f(a^2b+b^2x+x^2a)=0 then says H_{a,b}(x):=(ab^2+bx^2+xa^2, a^2b+b^2x+x^2a) lies in Theta for EVERY real x. So one seed pair in Theta yields a whole x-parametrized family of new pairs in Theta -- the propagation engine that all subsequent structure (down to injectivity-or-constant) is built on. Crux 2 supplies the separate move that actually collapses this orbit to a contradiction.

technique: From a single equal-value pair of a symmetric functional equation, generate a whole one-parameter family of equal-value pairs by substituting the pair into two of the three slots and letting the third slot run free, so the vanishing of the symmetric product on the left turns the right-hand argument-pair into an orbit inside the equal-value set.
how_used: For (f(a)-f(b))(f(b)-f(c))(f(c)-f(a)) = f(ab^2+bc^2+ca^2) - f(a^2b+b^2c+c^2a), define Theta = {(a,b): f(a)=f(b)} and Theta* its off-diagonal part. If (a,b) in Theta, then f(a)=f(b) makes E(a,b,x) have LHS=0, so H_{a,b}(x) := (ab^2+bx^2+xa^2, a^2b+b^2x+x^2a) lies in Theta for ALL real x. This orbit map is the engine driving the whole injectivity lemma: every equal-value pair spawns a one-parameter family of equal-value pairs, and the two useful controls are arg1-arg2 = (a-b)(b-x)(x-a) and arg1+arg2 = (x^2+ab)(a+b)+x(a^2+b^2).

technique: To push an orbit onto a distinguished degenerate member, treat the still-free substitution variable as the unknown of a polynomial equation obtained by setting one coordinate of the orbit map to zero, and pick a real root (checking the discriminant sign is forced by an available inequality between the seed coordinates).
how_used: Having reached (gamma,delta) in Theta* with delta > 5*gamma >= 0, to obtain a pair with a zero coordinate choose x a real root of the quadratic delta*gamma^2 + gamma*x^2 + x*delta^2 = 0 (the first coordinate of H_{delta,gamma}(x)); its discriminant delta^4 - 4*delta*gamma^3 > 0 is guaranteed precisely by delta > 5*gamma, and the root is negative. This yields (0,r) in Theta* with r != 0 (since r = -(delta-gamma)(gamma-x)(x-delta) != 0). The same zeroing trick is reused twice: from (0,r), H_{0,r}(x)=(r*x^2, r^2*x) gives f(r*x^2)=f(r^2*x), and x -> -x forces f even so (a,-a) in Theta for all a; then for (a,-a), taking x = ((1+sqrt5)/2)*a zeroes the first coordinate of H_{a,-a}(x), giving (0,(1+sqrt5)*a^3) in Theta for all a, which forces f constant (=f(0)) and hence, contrapositively, f injective when f is non-constant.

technique: Split on a threshold value of the free variable so that in each regime a different one of the two summed terms is bounded away from the target
how_used: Split on whether x >= 1 - 1/(100*2016). Above the threshold x^2016 is large enough on its own; below it, 1-x is large enough that the constraint x+y^2016>=1 forces y large, so each regime controls a different term of x^2016+y.

technique: Bound a power (1+t)^n below by Bernoulli's inequality (1+t)^n >= 1+nt, choosing t as a small perturbation from 1
how_used: With x = 1 - 1/(100*2016) written as 1+t, t=-1/(100*2016), Bernoulli gives x^2016 > 1 - 2016/(100*2016) = 1 - 1/100, directly clearing the target in the high-x case.

technique: Regroup a large exponent into a product of a chosen inner exponent times an outer exponent so one Bernoulli pass on the inner factor exceeds the crossing point
Solve the constraint for one variable to parametrize the surface, then upgrade vanishing on a real region to a formal polynomial identity valid over the complex numbers
how_used: After clearing denominators, Q = xP(x)+yP(y)+zP(z) - xyz(P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x)) vanishes on the real surface 2xyz = x+y+z with xyz != 0. Substituting z = (x+y)/(2xy-1) makes R(x,y):=Q(x,y,z) a rational function vanishing on a two-parameter real region, so R is identically zero as a rational identity; the identity then holds for complex x,y,z as well, letting one feed complex substitutions into the functional equation.

technique: Choose a targeted complex substitution that collapses the relation into a second-order finite difference in one variable equal to a constant, forcing a degree bound
how_used: Substituting (x, y, z) = (x, i/sqrt2, -i/sqrt2) (which satisfies 2xyz = x+y+z) into the extended complex identity yields P(x + i/sqrt2) + P(x - i/sqrt2) - 2P(x) = P(sqrt2 i) identically in x. The left side is a second-order finite difference of P (whose degree is deg P - 2), and its being constant forces deg P <= 2; combined with P even (from (t,-t,0)), P(x)=cx^2+d, and checking gives P(x)=c(x^2+3).

technique: To find the smallest constant in an inequality tight at a known point, substitute a small perturbation there and match the lowest-order coefficient in the perturbation of the two sides.
how_used: With equality at x=1, set x=1+t and expand ((1+t+a_n t^2)^N - ((1+t)^{2N}+1)/2) as a power series in t; the leading t^2 coefficient is (N a_n - N^2/2), which must be nonnegative for small t>0, forcing a_n >= N/2.

technique: Prove a family of inequalities indexed by N=2^n by a doubling induction: square the target bound and algebraically rewrite the square to expose the next-level bound plus a nonnegative remainder.
how_used: To get I(2N) from I(N), square x+N(x-1)^2 and use the identity (x-1)^2((x+1)^2-(x-1)^2)/2 to rewrite it as x^2 + (N/2)(x^2-1)^2 + (N^2-N/2)(x-1)^4, dropping the last term and applying I(N, x^2) to bound x^2+(N/2)(x^2-1)^2 below by the (4N)-th-root LHS, then take square roots.

technique: Bound a monic-normalized polynomial that has all real negative-reciprocal roots above by AM-GM on its factored form, turning the product of linear factors into a power using the root-sum (subleading coefficient).
how_used: After substituting t=(x-1)^2/x so f_N=(x^N+x^{-N})/2 becomes a degree-N polynomial in t, locate its roots t_k=-(2-2cos((2k-1)pi/2N)) via x_k on the unit circle, factor f_N=prod(1-t/t_k), and apply AM-GM to get f_N(t) <= (1 + (t/N)sum 1/t_k)^N = (1+(N/2)t)^N since sum 1/t_k = f_N'(0)/1 = N^2/2.

technique: Feed a single variable into its own defining characteristic relation to rewrite its cube as a combination of the elementary symmetric functions, exhibiting a pure power inside the ideal.
how_used: With p=x+y+z, q=xy+yz+zx, r=xyz, the identity 0=(x-x)(x-y)(x-z)=x^3-px^2+qx-r gives x^3=p*x^2-q*x+r, so x^3 in B (and by symmetry y^3,z^3). This is the seed that, combined with x^2y^2 in B, covers all monomials of degree >=4 by divisibility.

technique: Hand-craft a target mixed-power monomial as an explicit small integer combination of the ideal generators to certify its membership.
how_used: Exhibit x^2y^2 = xy*q - (x+y)*r = xy(xy+yz+zx) - (x+y)xyz in B (and symmetrically y^2z^2, z^2x^2). Together with x^3,y^3,z^3 in B, every monomial of degree >=4 is divisible by some cube (an exponent >=3) or by x^2y^2 (two exponents equal to 2) or by r (all three exponents >=1), hence lies in B, giving n<=4.

technique: Prune the unknown cofactors in an ideal-membership ansatz by isolating a monomial that only ONE generator-times-cofactor product can create, so no cancellation is possible and the offending cofactor coefficient must vanish.
how_used: To rule out x^2y in B, suppose x^2y = pP+qQ+rR with p=x+y+z, q=xy+yz+zx, r=xyz. Truncate to degree 3 (deg-2 part of P, deg-1 of Q, deg-0 of R). The monomial x^3 can only be produced by x*(x^2-term of P): every term of q has two distinct variables and Q is linear so qQ has >=2 distinct variables, and r=xyz forces all three. Since x^2y has no x^3 term and nothing can cancel it, the x^2 coefficient of P is 0; by the x<->y<->z symmetry of p,q,r the y^2 and z^2 coefficients vanish too. This reduces P to axy+byz+czx.

technique: After truncating an ideal-membership identity to a single homogeneous degree, match coefficients of every monomial of that degree to over-determine the finitely many surviving cofactor unknowns and force a contradiction with the target coefficient.
how_used: With P reduced to axy+byz+czx, Q=dx+ey+fz, R=g, write x^2y=(x+y+z)(axy+byz+czx)+(xy+yz+zx)(dx+ey+fz)+g*xyz and match all 10 degree-3 monomials. The squared-type monomials give e=-a, e=-b, f=-b, f=-c, d=-c, forcing a=b=c and d=e=f=-a; then the coefficient of x^2y equals a+d=0, which cannot equal the required 1. Hence x^2y not in B, so n>=4; with the separately proved upper bound n<=4 this gives n=4.

technique: Pair the terms of a cyclic sum by their opposite (non-adjacent) positions before applying AM-GM, so each pair's geometric mean collapses to the single ratio the constraint controls
how_used: Regroup S = a/b+b/c+c/d+d/a as (a/b+c/d)+(b/c+d/a) rather than by adjacent terms; AM-GM on each pair gives 2√(ac/bd)+2√(bd/ac), so S depends only on ac/bd, which is exactly the quantity the constraint (a+c)(b+d)=ac+bd governs

technique: Feed the equality constraint through AM-GM on its own factors to bound the reduced single ratio away from 1, pinning where the monotone one-variable target attains its minimum
how_used: Set x=√(ac/bd)≥1; AM-GM gives (a+c)(b+d)≥4√(ac)√(bd), so the constraint forces ac+bd≥4√(ac·bd), i.e. x+1/x≥4, hence x≥2+√3; since S≥2(x+1/x) is increasing for x≥1, the minimum is at x=2+√3, giving S=8 (attained at a=c, b=d, a/b=2+√3)

technique: Apply weighted AM-GM with the weights taken equal to the quantities being weighted, so a product of powers x_i^{x_i} is bounded by a sum of squares
how_used: The four positive quantities a,b,c,d sum to 1, so they are valid weights for weighted AM-GM; feeding each quantity in as both its own weight and its own base gives a^a b^b c^c d^d = prod a_i^{a_i} <= sum a_i * a_i = a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2, replacing the transcendental factor by a polynomial and reducing the goal to (a+2b+3c+4d)(a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2) < 1.

technique: After reducing a bound to one variable, prove it stays below a constant by showing the log of the bounding function is strictly convex, so its supremum on the interval sits at the endpoints
how_used: In the branch 1/2 <= a < 1, the bound f(a)=(3-2a)a^a(1-a)^{1-a} has g=log f with g''(x)=-4/(3-2x)^2 + 1/x + 1/(1-x) = (1+8(1-x)^2)/(x(1-x)(3-2x)^2) > 0, so g is strictly convex; since g(1/2)=0 and g->0 as x->1, strict convexity forces g<=0 on [1/2,1), i.e. f(a)<=1, closing this branch.

technique: Bound a homogeneous polynomial inequality that fails termwise by routing through an intermediate expression that both sides compare against cleanly
how_used: After reducing to (a+2b+3c+4d)(a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2) < (a+b+c+d)^3, the naive difference (a+b+c+d)^3 - (a+2b+3c+4d)(a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2) is not termwise nonnegative (it carries -b^3,-2c^3,-3d^3). Insert M = a^2(a+3b+3c+3d)+b^2(3a+b+3c+3d)+c^2(3a+3b+c+3d)+d^2(3a+3b+3c+d). Then (a+b+c+d)^3 - M = 6abc+6abd+6acd+6bcd > 0 exactly, and M - (a+2b+3c+4d)(a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2) = a^2(b-d)+b^2(2a-b-d)+c^2(2a+b-2c-d)+d^2(2a+b-3d), each bracket nonnegative because a>=b>=c>=d>0; chaining gives the strict inequality.

technique: Uniformly weaken a weighted geometric mean of the small variables by replacing every base with the common upper bound implied by the normalization constraint
how_used: In Solution 2's branch 1/2 <= a < 1, since b,c,d are each strictly less than 1-a (as a+b+c+d=1), replace each base by 1-a to get b^b c^c d^d < (1-a)^b (1-a)^c (1-a)^d = (1-a)^{b+c+d} = (1-a)^{1-a}; combined with the linear bound a+2b+3c+4d <= 3-2a (from b>=d), this collapses the 4-variable LHS onto the single-variable envelope f(a)=(3-2a)a^a(1-a)^{1-a}, reducing the whole branch to proving f(a) <= 1.

technique: Bound a one-variable envelope on a closed sub-interval by showing its logarithm is strictly convex there and vanishes at both endpoints, forcing the log nonpositive between the two zeros.
how_used: After reducing (Solution 2) to the envelope f(a)=(3-2a)a^a(1-a)^{1-a} for the regime 1/2<=a<1, set g=log f=log(3-2x)+x log x+(1-x)log(1-x). Then g''(x) = -4/(3-2x)^2 + 1/x + 1/(1-x) = (1+8(1-x)^2)/(x(1-x)(3-2x)^2) > 0, so g is strictly convex on (0,1). Because g(1/2)=log2+2*(1/2)log(1/2)=0 and lim_{x->1-} g(x)=0, a strictly convex function that vanishes at both ends of [1/2,1) lies below the chord (which is the zero line) on the open interior, giving g<=0, i.e. f(a)<=1, on [1/2,1). This closes the a>=1/2 case only; the endpoints 1/2 and 1 are exactly the two zeros of g, which is why the interval of validity is [1/2,1) and not the full domain.

technique: In a weighted-geometric-mean product where every base is bounded by the largest term, replace each base by that maximum so the exponents (a probability weight summing to 1) collapse the whole product to a single power of the maximum.
how_used: For the case a<1/2, instead of bounding b^b c^c d^d by (1-a)^{1-a}, use the sharper a>=b,c,d: since each of b,c,d is <= a, a^a b^b c^c d^d <= a^a a^b a^c a^d = a^{a+b+c+d}=a^1=a. Combined with the linear bound a+2b+3c+4d <= 3-2a (from b>=d), the LHS <= (3-2a)a = 1-(1-a)(1-2a), which is <1 precisely because a<1/2 makes (1-a)(1-2a)>0.
