This disposes of the a<1/2 regime, which the convexity envelope f(a)=(3-2a)a^a(1-a)^{1-a} cannot handle (there f(a)>1, e.g. f(0.4)>1).

technique: To bound a product of a linear factor and a one-variable exponential envelope below its boundary value, take logs and prove the log is convex on the interval (second derivative positive), so its maximum is at the endpoints, where both boundary values hit the target bound.
how_used: This closes the regime 1/2 <= a < 1, which the max-variable collapse (companion crux) cannot cover there. First reduce the product to one variable: from b,c,d < 1-a, bound b^b c^c d^d < (1-a)^b (1-a)^c (1-a)^d = (1-a)^{b+c+d} = (1-a)^{1-a}, giving LHS < (3-2a) a^a (1-a)^{1-a} =: f(a). Then set g(x)=log f(x)=log(3-2x)+x log x+(1-x)log(1-x) and compute g''(x) = -4/(3-2x)^2 + 1/x + 1/(1-x) = (1+8(1-x)^2)/(x(1-x)(3-2x)^2) > 0, so g is strictly convex on (0,1). Since g(1/2)=log2 + 2*(1/2)log(1/2)=0 and g(x)->0 as x->1-, strict convexity forces g(x) <= 0 (i.e. f(x) <= 1) on [1/2,1), so LHS < f(a) <= 1.

technique: When every variable in a product of powers x_i^{x_i} is dominated by one distinguished variable, replace each base by that maximum to collapse the whole weighted geometric mean into a single power of it, then the outer factor times that single power telescopes to a form obviously below the target.
how_used: This closes the regime a < 1/2 (specifically 1/4 <= a < 1/2, the range left uncovered by the log-convexity crux, since a >= 1/4). Since a is the maximum, a^a b^b c^c d^d <= a^a a^b a^c a^d = a^{a+b+c+d} = a. Combined with the linear bound a+2b+3c+4d <= 3-2a, get LHS <= (3-2a)*a = 1-(1-a)(1-2a); for a<1/2 both (1-a)>0 and (1-2a)>0, so this is < 1. (The linear bound itself comes from b >= d, giving 2b+4d <= 3b+3d, hence a+2b+3c+4d <= a+3b+3c+3d = 3-2a.)

technique: Impose the desired structural conditions as a homogeneous linear system in the unknown coefficients and invoke that fewer equations than unknowns forces a nonzero solution
how_used: The n conditions P(x_{2i-1})+P(x_{2i})=0 become n homogeneous linear equations in the n+1 coefficients a_0,...,a_n; more unknowns than equations guarantees a nonzero polynomial P (of degree at most n) satisfying all pairing conditions

technique: Force a nonzero polynomial to reach its maximal possible degree by counting sign-change-guaranteed roots via the intermediate value theorem
how_used: Each pairing P(x_{2i-1})+P(x_{2i})=0 makes P take opposite-valued (opposite-sign or both-zero) endpoints, so the closed segment [x_{2i-1},x_{2i}] contains a root; the n segments are pairwise disjoint (x_{2i}<x_{2i+1}), giving n distinct roots, and with deg P<=n and P nonzero this forces deg P=n exactly

technique: Build an indistinguishable pair by applying a symmetry of the data that permutes the observed multiset while changing the object
how_used: Take Q=-P; the pairing condition P(x_{2i-1})=-P(x_{2i}) makes {Q(x_{2i-1}),Q(x_{2i})}={P(x_{2i}),P(x_{2i-1})} for every pair, so P and Q yield the identical sorted list of 2n values while P!=Q (both of degree n), defeating the magician

technique: Evaluate an iterated-map functional equation at two argument-shifted specializations so that the two forward orbits produced share a tail, then chain the shift across all inputs to force a global all-or-nothing property (here: orbit finiteness)
how_used: E(0,b) gives f^{b^2}(b)=b f(b), and b=-1 yields f(-1)=0. Then E(a,-1) reads f^{a^2+1}(a-1)=a f(a)=f^{a^2}(a), so the orbits O(a-1) and O(a) coincide after finitely many steps. Chaining over consecutive a, any two orbits differ by finitely many terms, so either every orbit is finite or every orbit is infinite, splitting into the f=0 and f(x)=x+1 branches.

technique: Bound the minimal period of a periodic sequence by showing the period divides each of two parameter expressions, then take their gcd to pin it
how_used: In the finite-orbit case O(0) is finite; E(a,-a) gives a(f(a)-f(-a))=f^{2a^2}(0)∈O(0), so for |a| exceeding max|O(0)| the value must be 0, forcing f(a)=f(-a) and making (f^k(0)) purely periodic with minimal period T dividing 2a^2. The same for a+1 gives T | 2(a+1)^2, so T | gcd(2a^2,2(a+1)^2)=2, i.e. f(f(0))=0 and a(f(a)-f(-a))=0 for all a.

technique: When two sequences eventually merge, package their index alignment as a single well-defined additive shift function between inputs, and pin it to a linear form from one seed value plus additivity
how_used: In the infinite-orbit case orbits share infinitely many terms, so for any a,b all (n,m) with f^n(a)=f^m(b) have the same n-m (else O(b) would be eventually periodic hence finite); call it X(a,b). From f^{a^2+1}(a-1)=f^{a^2}(a) we get X(a-1,a)=1, and X is additive, so X(a,b)=b-a. Applying f: X(f(a-1),f(a))=1 gives f(a)-f(a-1)=1, and with f(-1)=0 two-sided induction yields f(x)=x+1.

technique: Turn an iterate-shift relation into an orbit-comparison: from a substitution equating one iterate of an input with an iterate of a neighboring input, conclude their forward orbits agree from some point on, and propagate this across a generating family to force an all-or-nothing dichotomy on orbit finiteness
how_used: E(0,-1) gives f(-1)=0; then E(a,-1) reads f^{a^2+1}(a-1)=a f(a)=f^{a^2}(a). So a term of the forward orbit O(a-1) (step a^2+1) equals a term of O(a) (step a^2): the two orbits coincide from that point on, differing in only finitely many initial terms. Chaining over consecutive integers, EVERY pair of orbits differs by finitely many terms; since finiteness/infiniteness is shared by orbits that eventually coincide, either every orbit is finite or every orbit is infinite. This dichotomy is the top-level case split (Case 1 finite / Case 2 infinite).

technique: Close a functional equation by minimal counterexample with a folding symmetry: assume some nonzero input violates the target value, take one of least absolute size, and use a two-input specialization to produce a strictly smaller violator, folding a known even symmetry to keep the descent on the side where magnitude decreases
how_used: Finite-orbit case, given f(a)=f(-a) for all a≠0 and f(1)=f(-1)=0. E(n,1-n) has exponent 2n^2-2n+1≥1, and f(1)=0 forces f^k(1)=0 (k≥1), so 0=n f(n)+(1-n)f(1-n), i.e. n f(n)=(n-1)f(1-n). Suppose some m≠0 has f(m)≠0; pick minimal |m|, so |m|>1. Fold via f(m)=f(-m) to assume m≥2; then n=m gives f(1-m)≠0 with |1-m|=m-1<|m|, contradicting minimality. Hence f(n)=0 for n≠0, and f(0)=f^3(0)=f^4(2)=2f(2)=0, so f≡0.

technique: Build an additive integer index on orbits that eventually merge: define the iterate-count offset at any coincidence of two inputs, show it is well-defined (a differing offset would force eventual periodicity), verify additivity, and pin it from one base coincidence
how_used: Infinite-orbit case: any two orbits share infinitely many terms. Define X(a,b)=n-m for any coincidence f^n(a)=f^m(b); well-defined because two coincidences with different offsets make (f^k(b)) eventually periodic, forcing O(b) finite (impossible). X is additive: X(a,b)+X(b,c)=X(a,c). From E(a,-1)'s relation f^{a^2+1}(a-1)=f^{a^2}(a) read X(a-1,a)=1, so X(a,b)=b-a. Applying to f(a-1),f(a): f(a)-f(a-1)=X(f(a-1),f(a))=1; with f(-1)=0, two-sided induction gives f(x)=x+1.

technique: Pin an unknown period by intersecting divisibility constraints from two coprime instances: use a magnitude bound to force a bounded iterate-value to the base point so the orbit is purely periodic, deduce the period divides each of two coprime-derived expressions, and take their gcd
how_used: Finite-orbit case. E(a,-a) gives a(f(a)-f(-a))=f^{2a^2}(0)∈O(0), a finite set; let M=max|z| over O(0). For |a|>M the bounded RHS forces f^{2a^2}(0)=0, so (f^k(0)) is purely periodic with minimal period T | 2a^2. Running the same for a+1 gives T | 2(a+1)^2; since gcd(a,a+1)=1 => gcd(2a^2,2(a+1)^2)=2, hence T|2, i.e. f^2(0)=0. This crux stops at pinning the period to 2.

technique: Bootstrap a small forced period into a global relation: once an element's orbit has a known short period, evaluate the periodic iterate-count on the whole target family to see it always lands on the base point, collapsing a scaled difference to zero everywhere
how_used: Finite-orbit case, having f^2(0)=0 (period of O(0) divides 2). Since 2a^2 is even for every nonzero integer a, periodicity gives f^{2a^2}(0)=0 for ALL a, not just large |a|. Plugging back into E(a,-a): a(f(a)-f(-a))=0, so f(a)=f(-a) for every a≠0; with f(-1)=0 this yields f(1)=f(-1)=0. This earns the symmetry hypothesis (and f(1)=0) used by the descent.

technique: When two orbits provably merge (agree from some point on), define the common iterate-index offset between them as an invariant, prove it well-defined by showing a second offset would force eventual periodicity, then use its additivity along a chain of unit steps to pin it globally
how_used: Infinite-orbit case (Case 2). Setup from cheap substitutions: E(0,-1) forces f(-1)=0 outright, and E(0,a) gives f^{a^2}(a)=a f(a); substituting both into E(a,-1) yields the pure iterate identity f^{a^2+1}(a-1)=a f(a)=f^{a^2}(a). Because O(a-1) and O(a) differ by finitely many terms (chaining this across a finite index range, any two orbits share infinitely many terms), define X(a,b) as the common value of n-m over all pairs with f^n(a)=f^m(b). A second offset would give f^{l+d}(b)=f^l(b) for large l with d!=0, i.e. eventual periodicity, contradicting the infinite orbit — so X is well-defined. Read the offset directly off the iterate identity: f^{a^2+1}(a-1)=f^{a^2}(a) means (n,m)=(a^2+1,a^2), so X(a-1,a)=1 (no appeal to values, hence no circular use of f(-1)=0). Additivity X(a,b)+X(b,c)=X(a,c) plus X(a-1,a)=1 telescopes to X(a,b)=b-a. Apply to f(a-1),f(a) via f^{a^2+1}(f(a-1))=f^{a^2}(f(a)) to get X(f(a-1),f(a))=1=f(a)-f(a-1); with f(-1)=0, two-sided induction gives f(x)=x+1.

technique: Split the index set into dyadic bands by variable magnitude, then discard cross-band terms in each denominator so every term reduces to a scale-free ratio
how_used: Indices are partitioned into M_1,...,M_k with a_l in [2^{j-1},2^j] for l in M_j; keeping only same-band predecessors in the denominator each term is bounded by 2^j/(2^{j-1}√i)=2/√i where i counts the position within the band, making the per-band sum independent of the actual magnitudes

technique: Bound a running sum of 1/√i by telescoping with the difference of consecutive square roots
how_used: Using √i-√(i-1)=1/(√i+√(i-1))≥1/(2√i), the band sum 2Σ1/√i telescopes to 2·2(√p_j)=4√p_j, giving a clean √p_j bound per band

technique: Recombine per-block square-root bounds into a single bound over the whole set via QM-AM / Cauchy-Schwarz on the block sizes
how_used: Summing 4√p_j over the k bands and applying QM-AM to the p_j (which sum to n) yields 4Σ√|M_j| ≤ 4√(k·Σ|M_j|) = 4√(kn)

technique: Telescope a product of self-normalization complements and dominate it by exp(-sum) to convert a ratio floor into an upper bound on a block's sum of squares
how_used: With x_l=a_l/sqrt(a_1^2+...+a_l^2), note 1-x_l^2=(a_1^2+...+a_{l-1}^2)/(a_1^2+...+a_l^2), so over the block l=t+1..2t the product telescopes to (a_1^2+...+a_t^2)/(a_1^2+...+a_{2t}^2), which is >= 1/(1+4^k) because a_{t+i} <= 2^k a_i. Combined with 1-u <= e^{-u} (so prod(1-x_l^2) <= exp(-Sum x_l^2)) this gives Sum_{l=t+1}^{2t} x_l^2 <= log(4^k+1) <= 2k, a magnitude-free bound on the second half's squared ratios.

technique: Induct on sequence length by splitting at the midpoint, using that a truncated prefix leaves the earlier normalized terms unchanged so the inductive hypothesis applies verbatim to the head
how_used: Prove Sum x_i <= 4 sqrt(kn) by induction. For n=2t the prefix a_1..a_t has exactly the same x_1..x_t, so the IH bounds the head by 4 sqrt(kt); the tail is bounded by Cauchy-Schwarz on the block, Sum_{t+1}^{2t} x_l <= sqrt(t * Sum x_l^2) <= sqrt(2kt) using the per-block square-sum bound, and 4 sqrt(kt)+sqrt(2kt) <= 4 sqrt(2kt)=4 sqrt(kn). The odd case n=2t+1 splits as prefix of length t+1 plus tail of length t and the slack (4 sqrt(2t+1)-sqrt(2t) >= 4 sqrt(t+1)) closes it; base case n<=16 uses the trivial bound n <= 4 sqrt(kn).

technique: Isolate the free variable on one side of a functional equation so the equation reads as an explicit inverse formula, forcing injectivity of the inner argument.
how_used: Setting x=1 in f(x+f(xy))+y=f(x)f(y)+1 rearranges to y = f(1)f(y)+1-f(1+f(y)), expressing y as a function of f(y) alone; hence f(y1)=f(y2) implies y1=y2, so f is injective.

technique: Turn injectivity of a fixed-parameter slice of the equation into a sign constraint on the difference quotient of f, pinning its sign because a free parameter sweeps all reciprocals.
how_used: Since g(x)=f(x+f(xy)) is injective for fixed y, x1+f(x1 y) != x2+f(x2 y); substituting z_i=x_i y gives 1/y != (f(z2)-f(z1))/(z1-z2) for all positive y, and since -1/y ranges over all negatives the quotient is never negative, so f is non-decreasing (strictly, with injectivity).

technique: Take a one-sided limit of a functional equation at the boundary of the domain, using monotonicity to make the nested f-term converge to a constant and collapse the equation into an explicit formula for f.
how_used: Monotone f has right-limits; setting p=lim_{x->0+}f(x), q=lim_{t->p+}f(t) and letting x->0+ in (*) gives q+y=p f(y)+1, so f(y)=(q+y-1)/p is affine (p!=0 else q+y=1 is absurd). Plugging f=ax+b back and matching coefficients then forces a=b=1, i.e. f(x)=x+1.

technique: Multiply a single-variable expression by the symmetric completion of the remaining variables' factors so the constraint substitutes in and collapses it into a product of pair-sums.
how_used: To simplify (x^2+1)/(x+1), multiply numerator and denominator by (y+1)(z+1); expanding the numerator and substituting the constraint xyz+xy+yz+zx = x+y+z+1 turns (x^2+1)(y+1)(z+1) into 2(x+y)(x+z), giving (x^2+1)/(x+1) = (x+y)(x+z)/(1+x+y+z).

technique: Apply Cauchy-Schwarz to a cyclic sum of square roots of a two-factor product, splitting the two factors so the bound becomes a product of two independent cyclic sums.
how_used: Writing each term as sqrt(x+y)*sqrt(x+z)/sqrt(1+s), Cauchy-Schwarz gives (sum)^2 <= (sum(x+y))(sum(x+z))/(1+s) = 4s^2/(1+s), where s = x+y+z, reducing the three-variable inequality to one in s.

technique: Prove a rational-versus-fractional-power inequality by raising both sides to the common integer power that clears the fractional exponent, then exhibit the resulting polynomial difference as a manifestly nonnegative factored form.
how_used: To show 4s^2/(1+s) <= 9(s/3)^{5/4} for the reduced single variable s=x+y+z, raise both sides to the 4th power (turning the 5/4 exponent into the integer power (s/3)^5) and clear the (1+s) denominator, forming 9^4*(s/3)^5*(1+s)^4 - (4s^2)^4; this equals s^5 (s-3)^2 (27s^2+14s+3) >= 0 for s>0 (the quadratic factor has discriminant 14^2-4*27*3 = -128 < 0 so it is positive), with equality at s=3.

technique: Clear a per-term radical whose radicand is a rational function under a symmetric constraint by multiplying numerator and denominator by the missing symmetric factors, then use the constraint to collapse the result into a product of pairwise sums.
how_used: To handle sqrt((x^2+1)/(x+1)) under xyz+xy+yz+zx = x+y+z+1, multiply top and bottom of (x^2+1)/(x+1) by (y+1)(z+1). The denominator becomes (x+1)(y+1)(z+1) = 2(1+x+y+z) (using the constraint). The numerator (x^2+1)(y+1)(z+1), rewriting the mixed terms via the constraint xyz+xy+xz = x+y+z+1-yz, collapses to 2(x+y)(x+z). Hence (x^2+1)/(x+1) = (x+y)(x+z)/(1+s) with s=x+y+z, so each radical is sqrt((x+y)(x+z))/sqrt(1+s). This is where the constraint is consumed.

technique: Bound a sum of square roots of pairwise products by Cauchy-Schwarz, splitting each product's two factors between the two Cauchy vectors so the two resulting sums telescope to symmetric-sum expressions.
how_used: Applied to sum_cyc sqrt((x+y)(x+z))/sqrt(1+s): pull out 1/sqrt(1+s) and Cauchy-Schwarz on sum sqrt((x+y)(x+z)) = sum sqrt(x+y)*sqrt(x+z), giving (sum sqrt((x+y)(x+z)))^2 <= (sum (x+y))(sum (x+z)) = (2s)(2s) = 4s^2. Thus (sum of the three radicals)^2 <= 4s^2/(1+s), reducing the whole three-variable inequality to a single-variable claim in s.

technique: Prove a single-variable inequality carrying a fractional exponent by raising both sides to the integer power that clears the exponent, then certify the resulting polynomial difference nonnegative via an exact factorization with a perfect-square factor pinning equality.
how_used: Once the LHS is reduced to 4s^2/(1+s), it remains to show 4s^2/(1+s) <= 9*(s/3)^{5/4} for s>0. Raise both sides to the 4th power to clear the quarter-power, reducing to (s/3)^5 * 9^4 * (1+s)^4 - (4s^2)^4 >= 0. Certify this by the exact identity (s/3)^5*9^4*(1+s)^4 - (4s^2)^4 = s^5*(s-3)^2*(27s^2+14s+3), whose factors are all >= 0 for s>0; the (s-3)^2 factor forces equality at s=3, i.e. x=y=z=1. This closes the single-variable step; a numerical monotonicity check does NOT count as the intended proof.

technique: To collapse a stubborn single-variable rational term under a symmetric multivariate constraint, multiply it by the missing symmetric factors and reduce the numerator against the constraint until it factors as a product of pairwise sums.
how_used: Each summand carries a factor (x^2+1)/(x+1). Multiply numerator and denominator by (y+1)(z+1). The denominator (x+1)(y+1)(z+1) equals 2(1+x+y+z) on the constraint xyz+xy+yz+zx=x+y+z+1, and the numerator (x^2+1)(y+1)(z+1) reduces, using that same constraint, to 2(x+y)(x+z) (checkable via the identity (x^2+1)(y+1)(z+1) - 2(x+y)(x+z) = (x-1)*(xyz+xy+yz+zx-x-y-z-1), which vanishes on the constraint). Hence on the constraint (x^2+1)/(x+1) = (x+y)(x+z)/(1+s) with s=x+y+z, so each radical term becomes sqrt((x+y)(x+z))/sqrt(1+s). This factorization is the whole engine of the problem; from it, Cauchy-Schwarz ((sum sqrt((x+y)(x+z)))^2 <= (sum(x+y))(sum(x+z)) = 4s^2) collapses the LHS to a single-variable expression in s, and the final bound reduces to checking 4s^2/(1+s) <= 9(s/3)^{5/4}, equivalent to s^5(s-3)^2(27s^2+14s+3) >= 0.

technique: Partition a scale-space into parity-indexed dyadic blocks so a fixed dilation swaps the two blocks while negation fixes each
how_used: Split R\{0} into annuli S_n containing all x with |x| in (2^n,2^{n+1}], namely [-2^{n+1},-2^n)∪(2^n,2^{n+1}], and collect the even-n annuli into A and odd-n into B; multiplying by 2 shifts S_n to S_{n+1} flipping parity so A=2B and B=2A, and negation stays inside each annulus so A=-A, B=-B, with A∩B=∅ and A∪B∪{0}=R

technique: Define the sought map as +identity on one block and -identity on the other and take the second map as a scaling of the first, so each composition's sign is decided by which block the doubling lands in
how_used: Set f=x on A, -x on B, f(0)=0, and g=2f; using A=2B, B=2A, A=-A, B=-B, for x in A: g(x)=2x∈B so f(g(x))=-2x while g(f(x))=2x, and for x in B the doubling lands in the opposite parity block so the negation attaches to the other composition, giving f∘g=-2x (strictly decreasing) and g∘f=2x (strictly increasing) everywhere — f,g themselves need not be monotone

technique: Approximate a monic polynomial of degree mn by a perfect m-th power of a monic degree-n polynomial, solving the root's coefficients top-down so the error drops below degree (m-1)n.
how_used: Lemma: for monic f of degree mn there is monic g of degree n with deg(f-g^m)<(m-1)n. Write g=x^n+β_{n-1}x^{n-1}+…; the coeff of x^{mn-k} in g^m is mβ_{n-k}+φ_k(β_n,…,β_{n-k+1}), so set β_{n-k}=(α_{mn-k}-φ_k)/m (m≠0 in char 0) for k=1..n, killing the top n error coefficients. Applied to P (degree bc) and R (degree ac) with m=c to get monic U (degree b), V (degree a) with deg(P-U^c)<(c-1)b and deg(R-V^c)<(c-1)a.

technique: Reduce a composition identity P(Q)=R(S) to showing the outer argument of one side is itself a composition through the inner polynomial of the other, then verify the reduced identity holds as polynomials via infinitely-many values.
how_used: To get P=R(T) it suffices to show S(x)=T(Q(x)) for some T: then P(Q)=R(S)=R(T(Q)), so P(t)-R(T(t)) vanishes at t=S(x) for infinitely many t (S non-constant), hence identically, giving P=R(T). This reframes the entire problem as the single target S=T(Q).

technique: Define a 'composition remainder' by subtracting the best available multiple-of-the-inner-polynomial from a target, chosen to minimize the remainder's degree over the whole family, then derive a contradiction from a divisibility the minimal remainder's degree must satisfy.
how_used: Write S(x)=T(Q(x))+M(x) with deg M minimized over all T. If M!=0, minimality forces q=deg Q does NOT divide m=deg M (else M=beta*Q^{m/q}+M_1 with deg M_1<deg M could be folded into T). Substitute into R(S)-P(Q)=0 and expand: terms that are pure polynomials in Q collect into N(Q(x)), while the unique highest-degree M-carrying term is alpha*r*M*T(Q)^{r-1} (r=deg R, alpha=lead R, and 0<m<s forces deg T(Q)=s so this term dominates). Then N(Q(x))=alpha*r*M*T(Q)^{r-1}+lower: the left side's degree is a multiple of q, the right side's is m+(r-1)s which is not a multiple of q since q does not divide m. Contradiction, so M=0.

technique: Take an instance of the whole configuration whose overall degree is minimal, so any strictly-smaller-degree instance produced later contradicts the extremal choice; reduce the goal to trivializing a single scaling parameter.
how_used: Among all (P,R) with P(Q)=R(S) and deg R | deg P, pick one making deg F=deg P(Q) minimal. Set d=gcd(deg Q,deg S), deg Q=ad, deg S=bd, gcd(a,b)=1; then deg P=bc, deg R=ac, deg F=abcd for some c>=1. The target becomes c=1: then deg R=a divides deg P=b with gcd(a,b)=1 forces a=1, R linear, so S=T(Q) and P=R(T). This crux only builds the extremal instance and the c=1 target; the descent forcing c=1 is a separate move.

technique: Approximate a monic polynomial of degree mn by a perfect m-th power of a monic degree-n polynomial, solving for the base's coefficients recursively so the discrepancy has degree below the naive (m-1)n threshold.
how_used: Lemma: for monic f of degree mn there is a monic g of degree n with deg(f - g^c) < (c-1)n, where c=m. Proof: writing g=sum beta_k x^k with beta_n=1, the x^{mn-k} coefficient of g^c is c*beta_{n-k}+phi_k(beta_n,...,beta_{n-k+1}); solve beta_{n-k} recursively (c!=0 in char 0) to kill the top (c-1)n-1 coefficients below x^{mn}. Applied to P (degree bc) and R (degree ac) this yields monic U (deg b), V (deg a) with deg(P-U^c)<(c-1)b and deg(R-V^c)<(c-1)a. This SHARP approximation is the load-bearing fact the next crux needs; without it one only gets the trivial bound < c*b.

technique: When two monic polynomials of equal degree have equal c-th powers up to a remainder of degree below (c-1)*deg, factor the difference of their c-th powers and compare its degree to that of the always-full-degree cofactor to force the bases equal.
how_used: Setup (context, established before this move): among all valid pairs (P,R) with P(Q)=R(S), pick one minimizing deg F=deg(P(Q)); write deg Q=ad, deg S=bd with gcd(a,b)=1, so deg P=bc, deg R=ac, deg F=abcd, and a | b forcing a=1. Assume for contradiction c>1. By the truncated-c-th-root lemma there exist monic U (deg b) and V (deg a) with deg(P-U^c)<(c-1)b and deg(R-V^c)<(c-1)a. THE MOVE: composing, deg(F-U(Q)^c)<(c-1)abd and deg(F-V(S)^c)<(c-1)abd, whence deg(U(Q)^c - V(S)^c) < (c-1)abd. Factor U(Q)^c - V(S)^c = (U(Q)-V(S))*W with W = sum_{i=0}^{c-1} U(Q)^i V(S)^{c-1-i}; since U(Q),V(S) are monic of degree abd, every term of W is monic of degree (c-1)abd and the c leading coefficients sum to c != 0, so deg W = (c-1)abd EXACTLY. The product's degree being strictly below deg W forces deg(U(Q)-V(S)) < 0, i.e. U(Q)=V(S) EXACTLY. PAYOFF (routine finish): U(Q)=V(S) is itself a valid instance of the SAME problem but of degree abd < abcd = deg F -- contradicting the minimality of deg F. Hence c=1.

technique: Bound a full product by partitioning its factors into disjoint index-pairs and applying the given pairwise constraint to each pair, then multiply the pair-bounds.
how_used: Split a_1...a_2010 into 1005 disjoint consecutive pairs (a_1a_2)(a_3a_4)...(a_2009a_2010); apply a_ia_j <= i+j to the k-th pair (i=2k-1, j=2k) to get a_{2k-1}a_{2k} <= 4k-1; multiplying gives a_1...a_2010 <= prod_{k=1}^{1005}(4k-1) = 3*7*11*...*4019. Using disjoint pairs is what makes the product of the right-hand sides valid; this consecutive pairing yields the smallest such product (a rearrangement-type observation).

technique: To prove an extremal bound is attained, build the equality case by forcing the tightest family of constraints to hold with equality, parametrizing the sequence by a free variable so the remaining slack constraints follow automatically.
how_used: The bound prod_{k=1}^{1005}(4k-1) needs each pair-constraint a_{2k-1}a_{2k} <= (2k-1)+2k to be tight. Force these by choosing a free scale on each even index: a_{2k}=sqrt(4k) and a_{2k-1}=(4k-1)/sqrt(4k), so every adjacent pair product hits its bound exactly and the total product equals prod(4k-1). Equivalently the solution writes a_n=sqrt(2n) for even n, a_{n-1}=sqrt(2n)-1/sqrt(2n). The remaining (non-adjacent and even-index-adjacency) constraints a_i a_j <= i+j then hold with slack; they can be discharged by telescoping ratios of the tight equalities, e.g. a_1 a_4 = (a_1 a_2)(a_3 a_4)/(a_2 a_3) = 3*7/5 < 5.

technique: Track the integer floor of the iterates as a monotone integer monovariant to force the sequence into a constant-floor regime
how_used: For a_i >= 1: a_{i+1}=floor(a_i)*<a_i> lies in [0,floor(a_i)) so floor strictly decreases among nonnegative integers until a term enters [0,1) and all subsequent terms are 0. For a_i <= -1: a_{i+1} lies in (floor(a_i),0], so 1+floor(a_{i+1})>a_{i+1}>floor(a_i) makes floor nondecreasing among integers <= -1, hence eventually constant equal to a negative integer c for all i>=i_0.

technique: Subtract the fixed point of an affine map to linearize the recurrence into a pure geometric sequence
how_used: With floor(a_i)=c the rule becomes a_{i+1}=c*<a_i>=c*a_i - c^2, an affine map with fixed point c^2/(c-1); setting b_i=a_i - c^2/(c-1) gives b_{i+1}=c*b_i, so b_i=c^{i-i_0} b_{i_0}.

technique: Use boundedness of the iterates to kill a geometric factor, forcing either zero amplitude or unit ratio
how_used: Since all a_i lie in [c,c+1) the b_i are bounded, but b_i=c^{i-i_0} b_{i_0} with |c|>=1; this forces b_{i_0}=0 (constant a_i) or c=-1 (ratio -1 giving the two-value alternation a_i, 1-a_i), yielding a_i=a_{i+2}.

technique: Take a weighted difference of two consecutive instances of a summation recurrence to isolate the newest term
how_used: Wrote the relation for n and n+1 as sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k/(n-k+1)=0 and sum_{k=0}^{n+1} a_k/(n-k+2)=0, then formed (n+2)*[second] - (n+1)*[first] so the isolated a_{n+1} term appears cleanly, choosing the multipliers (n+2) and (n+1) to clear the leading denominators.

technique: Combine the two coefficient fractions over a common denominator to expose a manifestly positive factor
how_used: Simplified (n+1)/(n-k+1) - (n+2)/(n-k+2) into k/((n-k+1)(n-k+2)); the numerator k and both denominator factors are positive for 1<=k<=n, and the a_0 coefficient vanishes, so the sign of a_{n+1} follows from the inductive positivity of a_1,...,a_n.

technique: Force a free parameter by demanding a Binet/closed-form linear combination stay bounded, killing the coefficient of the root of modulus greater than one
how_used: Since every (c_n,c_{n-1}) lies in S, the target expression alpha*c_n+beta*c_{n-1} must stay in a bounded window; writing it in Binet form gives (1/sqrt5)[(alpha*phi+beta)phi^{n-2}-(alpha*psi+beta)psi^{n-2}], and because phi>1 while |psi|<1 boundedness forces alpha*phi+beta=0, so one may take alpha=psi, beta=1

technique: Collapse a linear form on set-sums into a single sum of powers of a root by substituting the per-term closed-form identity, then bound it by the two extremal geometric series
how_used: The identity c_j*psi+c_{j-1}=psi^{j-1} makes psi*a_J+b_J = sum_{j in J} psi^{j-1}; since -1<psi<0 this sum lies strictly between the all-odd-index series sum psi^{2j+1}=-1 and the all-even-index series sum psi^{2j}=phi, yielding the window -1<psi*x+y<phi

technique: Recover integer coordinates from a single irrational linear equation by matching rational and irrational parts
how_used: From psi*x+y = psi*a_J+b_J with x,y,a_J,b_J integers and psi irrational, rearranging to psi*(x-a_J)=b_J-y forces x=a_J and y=b_J (else psi would be rational), so the constructed J realizes (x,y) as an element of S

technique: Among minimum-length representations pick the lexicographically minimal exponent multiset, then kill any repeated exponent by a local length-preserving rewrite that lowers the multiset in the ordering, contradicting minimality
how_used: Represent psi*x+y = sum_r psi^{j_r} with minimum number of terms and, among those, lexicographically smallest sorted exponent list (the crude x-copies-of-psi + y-copies-of-1 representation shows one exists). A repeated exponent j_r=j_{r+1}=e>=2 is replaced by {e-2, e+1} using 2*psi^e = psi^{e-2}+psi^{e+1} (from 2*psi^2=1+psi^3): same length, same value, but strictly smaller in lex order (introduces e-2>=0), contradicting the choice. Hence every exponent value >=2 occurs at most once.

technique: Rule out the last low-index duplicates that the local rewrite cannot reach by bounding the whole power-sum past the allowed window, using the sparsest legal completion (alternate-parity tail) as the extremal packing
how_used: The rewrite needs exponent>=2, so duplicates at 0 or 1 remain. Minimality forbids consecutive exponents (since psi^0+psi^1=psi^2 shortens the sum), so a double-0 sits among exponents >=3 and the sparsest legal completion is the odd tail: psi*x+y > 2 + psi^3+psi^5+... = 2-psi^2 = phi, exceeding M=phi; symmetrically a double-1 forces psi*x+y < 2*psi + psi^4+psi^6+... = 2*psi-psi^3 = -1, below m=-1. Both contradict -1<psi*x+y<phi, so no low-index duplicate survives and the representation uses distinct nonneg powers.

technique: Collapse a two-coordinate linear form over an index set into a single-variable power-sum by choosing the coefficient vector to be the eigen-direction that kills the growing root of the underlying linear recurrence
how_used: The pairs are (a_J,b_J)=(sum_{j in J} c_j, sum_{j in J} c_{j-1}) for the Fibonacci-type c. Testing (c_n,c_{n-1}) in S: alpha*c_n+beta*c_{n-1} = (1/sqrt5)[(alpha*phi+beta)phi^{n-2} - (alpha*psi+beta)psi^{n-2}], which stays bounded as n grows only if the phi^{n-2} coefficient vanishes, i.e. alpha*phi+beta=0; take alpha=psi, beta=1. Then the same recurrence identity read the other way gives psi*c_j+c_{j-1}=psi^{j-1} for each j (since psi solves t^2-t-1=0 so 1+psi=psi^2), so termwise psi*a_J+b_J = sum_{j in J} psi^{j-1}. Membership in S becomes: psi*x+y is a subset-sum of distinct powers psi^{i}, i>=0. Bounding this subset-sum by its two extreme geometric series (all-even vs all-odd exponents, using -1<psi<0) gives sum_{odd}psi^i = psi/(1-psi^2) = -1 < psi*x+y < 1/(1-psi^2) = 1-psi = phi, so m=-1, M=phi.

technique: To show a target admits a representation as a sum of DISTINCT terms from a prescribed family, take a minimal-length representation with repeats allowed (made lexicographically-least in its sorted exponents) and use a local exchange identity to rewrite any repeated term into smaller-exponent terms, contradicting minimality.
how_used: Converse direction of the ISL problem: given nonnegative integers (x,y) with -1<psi*x+y<phi (psi=(1-sqrt5)/2, phi=(1+sqrt5)/2), exhibit a finite J with psi*x+y=sum_{j in J} psi^{j-1} and DISTINCT exponents. Start from the crude representation using x copies of psi^1 and y copies of psi^0; take one of minimum length k and among those the lexicographically-least sorted exponent list j_1<=...<=j_k. If a repeat j_r=j_{r+1}>=2, the identity 2*psi^2=1+psi^3 (scaled: 2*psi^{j_r}=psi^{j_r-2}+psi^{j_r+1}) keeps the length but strictly lowers the sorted tuple, contradicting lex-minimality. The two boundary repeats are killed by the value bound instead: minimal length forbids consecutive exponents (since psi^e+psi^{e+1}=psi^{e+2}), so two copies of psi^0 force the sum > 2+psi^3+psi^5+...=phi, and two copies of psi^1 force it < 2psi+psi^4+psi^6+...=-1, both violating the hypothesis. Hence exponents are distinct. (Setup identity psi*c_j+c_{j-1}=psi^{j-1}, the forward geometric-series bounds, and the psi-irrational injectivity x=a_J, y=b_J are the routine surrounding steps.)

technique: Rewrite a harmonic-mean term ab/(a+b) via the identity (1/4)[(a+b) - (a-b)^2/(a+b)] to split it into a linear part plus a subtracted square-difference remainder.
how_used: Applied to each L-term a_i a_j/(a_i+a_j) so L = (n-1)S/4 - (1/4)∑(a_i-a_j)^2/(a_i+a_j); the analogous square-difference form is then produced for R (via n∑a_ia_j = (n-1)S^2/2 - (1/2)∑(a_i-a_j)^2), giving R = (n-1)S/4 - (1/4)∑(a_i-a_j)^2/S, so L and R share the linear term and differ only in the denominator of the subtracted error.

technique: When two expressions match a common form differing only in a positive denominator inside a subtracted error term, weaken that denominator up to a larger dominating quantity so the subtracted amount only grows.
how_used: Since S = ∑a_k ≥ a_i+a_j for every pair, replacing a_i+a_j by S in the subtracted term (a_i-a_j)^2/(a_i+a_j) makes L's subtracted error at least R's error (a_i-a_j)^2/S term by term, yielding L ≤ R.

technique: Substitute the positive denominators as new variables and re-express the numerator radicand in terms of them
how_used: Set x=√b+√c−√a, y=√c+√a−√b, z=√a+√b−√c (positive since √a+√b>√(a+b)>√c), invertible with √a=(y+z)/2 etc.; this turns b+c−a into x²−½(x−y)(x−z), so each ratio √(b+c−a)/x becomes √(1−(x−y)(x−z)/(2x²)).

technique: Bound a square root above by its tangent line to linearize each term
how_used: Apply √(1+2u) ≤ 1+u (valid since (1+u)²−(1+2u)=u²≥0) with u = −(x−y)(x−z)/(4x²), giving √(b+c−a)/x ≤ 1 − (x−y)(x−z)/(4x²); summing the three cyclic terms reduces the target LHS≤3 to Σ(x−y)(x−z)/x² ≥ 0.

technique: Prove a Schur-type cyclic sum by ordering the variables and dominating the lone negative term by an adjacent positive one
how_used: For Σ(x−y)(x−z)/x² ≥ 0 (Schur exponent t=−2), WLOG x≤y≤z; the middle term is the only negative one, and (y−x)(z−x)/x² ≥ (y−x)(z−y)/y² cancels it (using 1/x²≥1/y² and z−x≥z−y≥0) while (z−x)(z−y)/z² ≥ 0.

technique: Treat a cyclic expression as a polynomial in one variable, locate its roots by inspection, and factor it fully using the leading coefficient
how_used: View the LHS with a replaced by t as the cubic P(t)=tb(t^2-b^2)+bc(b^2-c^2)+ct(c^2-t^2); check P(b)=P(c)=P(-b-c)=0 and read the t^3 coefficient b-c to conclude P(t)=(b-c)(t-b)(t-c)(t+b+c), so the LHS equals |(b-c)(a-b)(a-c)(a+b+c)|

technique: After ordering the variables, bound a product of two consecutive gaps by the square of half their sum via AM-GM
how_used: Assuming a<=b<=c, bound |(a-b)(b-c)|=(b-a)(c-b) <= ((b-a)+(c-b))^2/4 = (c-a)^2/4, with equality iff 2b=a+c, collapsing the two-factor product into (c-a)^2/4 and reducing the target to bounding (c-a)^3|a+b+c|

technique: Bound the square of a spread by a sum of squared pairwise gaps via QM-AM to prepare a symmetric power-mean estimate
how_used: With S=(b-a)^2+(c-b)^2+(c-a)^2, apply QM-AM to ((c-b)+(b-a))/2 to get 3(c-a)^2 <= 2S, i.e. (c-a)^2 <= (2/3)S, equality iff b-a=c-b; combined with AM-GM (b-a)(c-b) <= ((c-a)/2)^2 this rewrites |(b-c)(a-b)(a-c)(a+b+c)| <= (1/4)|(c-a)^3(a+b+c)| <= (1/4)(2S/3)^{3/2}|a+b+c|, a clean root of a product of S-blocks and (a+b+c)^2

technique: Turn a product of unequally-many factors into a fourth power of an arithmetic mean by splitting one factor into equal-weight copies and applying weighted AM-GM across the blocks
how_used: Write the target as a fourth root of (S/3)^3 * (a+b+c)^2 (three equal blocks S/3 plus one block (a+b+c)^2) and apply AM-GM to the four blocks: (S/3)^3(a+b+c)^2 <= ((S+(a+b+c)^2)/4)^4; using the identity S+(a+b+c)^2 = 3(a^2+b^2+c^2), the whole chain gives |(b-c)(a-b)(a-c)(a+b+c)| <= (9sqrt2/32)(a^2+b^2+c^2)^2, so M=9sqrt2/32, attained at (a,b,c) proportional to (1-3sqrt2/2, 1, 1+3sqrt2/2)

technique: Recognize a cyclic cubic expression as a polynomial in one variable and factor it by locating its roots
how_used: Freeze b,c and view the LHS as the cubic P(t)=tb(t^2-b^2)+bc(b^2-c^2)+ct(c^2-t^2) in t=a; check P(b)=P(c)=P(-b-c)=0 and read the leading coefficient b-c to get P(a)=(b-c)(a-b)(a-c)(a+b+c), turning the opaque cyclic expression into a product of linear forms so the inequality becomes |(b-c)(a-b)(a-c)(a+b+c)| <= M(a^2+b^2+c^2)^2

technique: To bound a homogeneous product by a power of a quadratic form, split it into equal-weight factors whose sum is a fixed multiple of that form, then apply AM-GM
how_used: After factoring the LHS as |(b-c)(a-b)(a-c)(a+b+c)| and bounding (WLOG a<=b<=c) |(a-b)(b-c)| <= (c-a)^2/4 and 3(c-a)^2 <= 2[(b-a)^2+(c-b)^2+(c-a)^2]=2S, the target reduces to bounding [ (S/3)^3 * (a+b+c)^2 ]^{1/4}. The non-obvious move: the four numbers S/3, S/3, S/3, (a+b+c)^2 have sum S+(a+b+c)^2 = 3(a^2+b^2+c^2) (from sum of pairwise (x-y)^2 = 2 sum x^2 - 2 sum xy and (a+b+c)^2 = sum x^2 + 2 sum xy), so equal-weight AM-GM on these four terms turns the fourth-root of their product into (3/4)(a^2+b^2+c^2), giving the sharp M=9*sqrt2/32, with equality when all four terms are equal (2b=a+c and (c-a)^2=18b^2)

technique: Rewrite a product of two "square-plus-one" factors via the Brahmagupta-Fibonacci identity into a sum of two squares
how_used: Wrote (x^2+1)(y^2+1)=(xy-1)^2+(x+y)^2, isolating the cross term xy-1 (the only place the constraint xy>=1 acts) from the sum term (x+y)^2, turning the two-variable Claim into a comparison of squares.

technique: Bound one summand of a sum-of-squares while holding the other fixed, using the constraint to compare the varying squares monotonically
how_used: Held (x+y)^2 fixed and used xy>=1 => ((x+y)/2)^2-1 >= xy-1 >= 0 (AM-GM gives ((x+y)/2)^2>=xy) to replace (xy-1)^2 by (((x+y)/2)^2-1)^2, proving the Claim (x^2+1)(y^2+1) <= (((x+y)/2)^2+1)^2 for xy>=1.

technique: Introduce the target arithmetic mean as an auxiliary variable and pair terms so a two-variable lemma, applied twice then once to the pair-averages, telescopes every entry to that mean
how_used: Set d=(a+b+c)/3; applied the Claim to (a,d) and to (b,c), then to ((a+d)/2,(b+c)/2) whose average is again d, collapsing the fourfold product to (d^2+1)^4; divided out the extra (d^2+1) and took a cube root.

technique: When a two-variable lemma with a product-hypothesis is applied repeatedly, verify the hypothesis at each application by ordering the variables WLOG and pushing the extremal one through, using AM-GM to certify the averaged pairs
how_used: Each use of the Claim needs xy>=1. WLOG a>=b>=c, so a^2>=ab>=1 forces a>=1; then ad=(a^2+ab+ac)/3 >= (1+1+1)/3 = 1 certifies pair (a,d), and bc>=1 is given for pair (b,c). For the outer pair, AM-GM gives (a+d)/2 >= sqrt(ad) and (b+c)/2 >= sqrt(bc), so their product is >= sqrt(ad)*sqrt(bc) >= 1, certifying the final application.

technique: Prove a two-variable smoothing inequality by rewriting the product of shifted squares as a sum of two squares, then bounding one square via the constrained AM-GM gap
how_used: The Claim: for xy>=1, (x^2+1)(y^2+1) <= (((x+y)/2)^2+1)^2. Rewrite (x^2+1)(y^2+1) = (xy-1)^2 + (x+y)^2 and likewise (((x+y)/2)^2+1)^2 = (((x+y)/2)^2-1)^2 + (x+y)^2. The shared (x+y)^2 cancels, reducing the claim to (xy-1)^2 <= (((x+y)/2)^2-1)^2. Since AM-GM gives ((x+y)/2)^2 >= xy >= 1, both bases satisfy ((x+y)/2)^2-1 >= xy-1 >= 0, so squaring preserves the inequality. (Equivalently the difference factors as (x-y)^2(x^2+6xy+y^2-8)/16 >= 0 when xy>=1.)

technique: Reduce a mean-of-n inequality to iterated two-variable smoothing by adjoining the target mean itself as an extra variable, so the augmented multiset shares that mean and a balanced pairwise tournament telescopes to it
how_used: Set d=(a+b+c)/3, so the four numbers a,b,c,d have mean (3d+d)/4 = d. Apply the two-variable Claim ((x^2+1)(y^2+1) <= (((x+y)/2)^2+1)^2 when xy>=1) in a two-round tournament: first to pairs (a,d) and (b,c), then to the outer pair ((a+d)/2,(b+c)/2). Because averaging pairs preserves the overall mean, round 2 lands on d, telescoping (a^2+1)(d^2+1)(b^2+1)(c^2+1) up to (((a+b+c+d)/4)^2+1)^4 = (d^2+1)^4. Cancel one (d^2+1) to get (a^2+1)(b^2+1)(c^2+1) <= (d^2+1)^3, i.e. the target after cube root.

technique: Before applying a constrained smoothing lemma along a fixed pairing schedule, fix a WLOG ordering of the variables and use it to verify the lemma's product-constraint holds at every step of the schedule
how_used: The Claim needs xy>=1 for each pair used. Assume WLOG a>=b>=c; combined with ab,bc,ca>=1 this forces a>=1 (since a^2>=ab>=1). Then the round-1 pairs are legal: ad = a(a+b+c)/3 = (a^2+ab+ac)/3 >= (1+1+1)/3 = 1, and bc>=1 by hypothesis. The round-2 outer pair is legal because (a+d)/2 * (b+c)/2 >= sqrt(ad)*sqrt(bc) >= 1 by AM-GM. Thus all three applications of the Claim satisfy its hypothesis.

technique: Pick a cyclic list of the sorted-ratio quantities so that every cyclically-adjacent pair automatically uses four distinct indices, turning any pigeonhole-forced close neighbor into a legal choice
how_used: From a_1<=...<=a_5 list the five ratios a1/a2, a3/a4, a1/a5, a2/a3, a4/a5, all in (0,1], on a 5-cycle where each adjacent pair (including the wrap a4/a5 with a1/a2) draws four distinct subscripts; since a color class of size >=3 on C5 contains an adjacent pair, the pigeonholed close pair is automatically realizable as a_i/a_j and a_k/a_l with i,j,k,l distinct, giving C<=1/2

technique: Build the extremal example with a repeated value plus one diverging parameter so the two would-be-close small ratios both use the diverging index and thus cannot be picked with distinct subscripts
how_used: Take 1,2,2,2,n with n large; the only ratios in (0,1/2) are 1/n and 2/n, both having n as an index, so distinct-subscript choices cannot use both; the smallest achievable distinct-index gap is 1/2 - 2/n (e.g. 1/2 versus 2/n), forcing C>=1/2 as n->infinity

technique: Rule out a residue class by exhibiting an extremal instance where every signed choice forces the target sums into a lattice bounded away from 0
how_used: For even n, set a_1=...=a_{n-1}=0, b_1=...=b_{n-1}=1 and a_n=1, b_n=0 (all satisfy |a_k|+|b_k|=1). Then for any x_k in {-1,1}, sum(x_k a_k)=x_n is an odd integer and sum(x_k b_k)=x_1+...+x_{n-1} is a sum of an odd count (n-1) of odd terms hence an odd integer, so each absolute value is >=1 and the total is >=2>1, so even n fail.

technique: After sorting the coefficients monotonically, pick the alternating-sign choice so the signed sum collapses into consecutive nonnegative brackets, bounding it between 0 and the largest term
how_used: First WLOG b_k>=0 (flip (a_k,b_k)->(-a_k,-b_k) with x_k->-x_k, which leaves both target sums invariant). Sort a_1>=...>=a_m>=0>a_{m+1}>=...>=a_n and take x_k=(-1)^{k+1}. Then s=sum_{k<=m}x_k a_k=(a_1-a_2)+(a_3-a_4)+... is a sum of nonnegative brackets so 0<=s, and s=a_1-(a_2-a_3)-... <= a_1 <=1; symmetrically t=-sum_{k>m}x_k a_k satisfies 0<=t<=-a_n<=1. The odd count just leaves a single nonnegative leftover term at the end of each block.

technique: Reparametrize both target expressions through the same two bounded auxiliary variables so the goal collapses to a fixed low-dimensional absolute-value inequality settled by sign casework
how_used: Using a_k+b_k=1 for k<=m and -a_k+b_k=1 for k>m, rewrite sum(x_k a_k)=s-t and sum(x_k b_k)=1-s-t with s,t in [0,1] from the bracket bound. The goal becomes |s-t|+|1-s-t|<=1 on the unit square: assume s>=t; if 1-s-t>=0 the sum is 1-2t<=1, if 1-s-t<=0 it is 2s-1<=1.

technique: Symmetrize a functional equation by swapping the two variables and subtracting the two copies to cancel the symmetric terms, then specialize the difference at a unit argument to extract a one-variable relation
how_used: Swapping x and y in (1) leaves the f(xy)(f(f(x^2))+f(f(y^2))) term unchanged; subtracting gives (2) x f(x^2) f(f(y)) + f(yf(x)) = y f(y^2) f(f(x)) + f(xf(y)). Setting y=1 (with f(1)=1) collapses (2) to x f(x^2)+f(f(x)) = f(f(x))+f(x); the f(f(x)) cancels, yielding the workhorse relation f(x^2)=f(x)/x, i.e. x f(x^2)=f(x).

technique: Prove injectivity by feeding the hypothesis f(x)=f(y) into a symmetric substitution to equate two mixed-argument values, then substitute a separately derived closed form for that value and cancel the common factor to force x=y
how_used: Assuming f(x)=f(y), the symmetrized relation (8) f(x)f(f(y))+f(yf(x))=f(y)f(f(x))+f(xf(y)) collapses (equal outer products) to f(yf(y))=f(xf(x)). Substituting the diagonal identity (7) f(xf(x))=f(f(x))(2/x-f(x)) on both sides and cancelling the equal factor f(f(x))=f(f(y)) leaves 2/y-f(y)=2/x-f(x), which with f(x)=f(y) gives x=y.

technique: Substitute the reciprocal of one distinguished variable into the equation and reduce it against the already-derived workhorse identities so a multiplicative reciprocal symmetry f(x)f(1/x)=1 drops out.
how_used: Working from the identities f(1)=1, (9) f(f(y))=f(y)f(f(y^2)), and (10) x f(x^2)=f(x), replace y by 1/x in the original equation (1). The term x f(x^2) becomes f(x) via (10); the term f(f(x^2)) matches f(f(x)/x)=f(x)f(1/x)... more precisely (10) gives f(f(x)/x)=f(f(x^2)) so two terms cancel, and (9)/(10) applied at 1/x collapse the remainder to f(x)=1/f(1/x). This yields (11) f(x)f(1/x)=1, the reciprocal symmetry the whole reciprocal-division route depends on.

technique: When a functional equation carries an inversive symmetry f(x)f(1/x)=1, substitute the reciprocal of every variable to obtain a copy of the equation with each factor inverted, then use that symmetry to convert every inverted factor back and re-substitute the original equation into the cleared numerators.
how_used: This is the non-injectivity route. First DERIVE the inversive symmetry (11) f(x)f(1/x)=1: put y=1/x in (1), then use the already-established (9) f(f(y))=f(y)f(f(y^2)) and (10) x f(x^2)=f(x) (equivalently f(x^2)=f(x)/x) to collapse it to f(x)f(1/x)=1 (this is a legitimately derived intermediate, not circular). Then replace x by 1/x and y by 1/y in (1) and apply (11) to each of the six factors; every factor becomes the reciprocal of the corresponding factor in the original (1). Clearing all denominators produces a relation whose numerators are exactly the two sides of (1), so re-substituting (1) into those numerators simplifies them, giving f(xy)^2 f(f(x^2)) f(f(y^2)) = x f(x^2) f(f(y)) f(y f(x)). Rewriting with (9) and (10) yields the workhorse identity (12): f(xy)^2 f(f(x)) = f(x)^2 f(y) f(y f(x)).

technique: Manufacture a closed-form monomial power law for a nested composition f(f(x)) by specializing the workhorse identity at self-referential arguments (setting the free variable equal to the input or to f of the input) and squaring to eliminate the leftover nested term.
how_used: From the workhorse (12) f(xy)^2 f(f(x)) = f(x)^2 f(y) f(y f(x)): first set y=f(x) and apply (10) at argument f(x) to get the auxiliary (13) f(x f(x))^2 = f(x) f(f(x)). Then set y=x in (12), square both sides, and substitute (10) and (13) to cancel the f(x f(x)) and f(x^2) terms; what survives is the power law (14) f(f(x)) = x^4 f(x)^3, a purely monomial expression for the double composition. This is the object the final telescoping step consumes.

technique: Close a functional equation by writing one nested-composition quantity two different ways along a chain of already-proven identities, equating the two monomial expressions so the resulting equation collapses to pin the function pointwise.
how_used: With the power law (14) f(f(x))=x^4 f(x)^3, relation (9) f(f(y))=f(y) f(f(y^2)), and (10) f(y^2)=f(y)/y in hand, evaluate f(f(y)) along two routes: directly (14) gives y^4 f(y)^3; via (9) then (14) then (10) gives f(y) * f(f(y^2)) = f(y) * y^8 f(y^2)^3 = f(y) * y^8 (f(y)/y)^3 = y^5 f(y)^4. Equating the two expressions y^4 f(y)^3 = y^5 f(y)^4 cancels to 1 = y f(y), i.e. f(y)=1/y. Finish by verifying 1/x satisfies (1): LHS = x(1/x^2)y + x/y = y/x + x/y, RHS = (1/(xy))(x^2+y^2) = x/y + y/x.

technique: Build the extremal construction by partitioning the shared roots into interlacing blocks via a residue class, assigning each block's roots between the two sides so the sides' root sets nest
how_used: From the 4032 pooled factors keep on the left the (x-k) with k≡0,1 (mod 4) and on the right those with k≡2,3 (mod 4), giving ∏_{j=0}^{503}(x-4j-1)(x-4j-4)=∏_{j=0}^{503}(x-4j-2)(x-4j-3): 504 quadratic blocks per side where the right pair {4j+2,4j+3} nests inside the left pair {4j+1,4j+4}, so the blocks interlace on every unit interval and each is sign-controllable there; this erases exactly 2016 factors, matching the target count.

technique: To show a product-of-quadratic-ratios never equals 1, rewrite each ratio as 1 plus a controlled rational correction and bound its denominator on each root-delimited region so every factor lands strictly on one side of 1
how_used: Using (x-4j-1)(x-4j-4)=(x-4j-2)(x-4j-3)-2, each ratio becomes 1-2/((x-4j-2)(x-4j-3)); on x<1, x>2016, or 4k<x<4k+1 every denominator exceeds 2 so each factor is in (0,1) and the product is <1; on 4k+2<x<4k+3 an alternate regrouping pulls out (x-1)/(x-2)·(x-2016)/(x-2015) and factors 1+2/((x-4j+1)(x-4j-2)) all >1, forcing the product >1; the interlacing (4k+1<x<4k+2 etc.) and integer cases give an immediate sign mismatch — so equation (1) has no real root.

technique: For a counting lower bound, note any value that zeroes a factor kept on BOTH sides is a shared root, so every commonly-shared factor must be removed from at least one side.
how_used: The two sides start identical, so all 2016 factors (x-1),...,(x-2016) are common. If any (x-k) is left on BOTH sides then x=k makes both sides zero, hence is a real root. To have no real root, for each k=1,...,2016 the factor (x-k) must be erased from the left or the right (at least one), forcing at least 2016 erasures. Combined with the 2016-erasure construction, the minimum is exactly 2016.

technique: To build the extremal configuration, split the index set by residue class modulo a small period so the two sides' roots end up interleaved on the number line rather than separated into disjoint blocks.
how_used: Achieving exactly 2016 erasures means each factor (x-k) is kept on exactly one side. The winning partition (valid when the count is divisible by 4) keeps (x-k) on the LEFT when k is congruent to 2 or 3 mod 4 and on the RIGHT when k is congruent to 0 or 1 mod 4. This yields L(x)=prod_{j=0}^{503}(x-4j-2)(x-4j-3) and R(x)=prod_{j=0}^{503}(x-4j-1)(x-4j-4), i.e. the two sides interleave their roots in a periodic ...LRRL... pattern, which is exactly what makes the ensuing sign comparison work.

technique: To show a product equation L(x)=R(x) has no real solution, partition the real line at the shared integer roots and on each interval either read off a sign mismatch or rewrite the ratio R/L as a product of factors all forced simultaneously above or below 1.
how_used: With L and R the interleaved products from the mod-4 partition, one checks each x-region. Integer roots x=1,...,2016 kill one side but not the other. On an interval where exactly one pairwise product (x-a)(x-b) is negative while all others are positive, the two sides differ in sign. On the remaining intervals write R/L = prod (x-4j-1)(x-4j-4)/((x-4j-2)(x-4j-3)) = prod(1 - 2/((x-4j-2)(x-4j-3))): where each (x-4j-2)(x-4j-3)>2 every factor lies in (0,1) so the product is <1; and by regrouping as (x-1)/(x-2)*(x-2016)/(x-2015)*prod(1 + 2/((x-4j+1)(x-4j-2))) each factor exceeds 1 so the product is >1. Either way the equation fails, so there is no real root.

technique: For a 'least deletions/changes' lower bound when both sides start from an identical multiset of factors, observe that any factor surviving on BOTH sides forces a shared common root, which the goal forbids; hence each common factor must be removed from at least one side, and counting those forced removals gives the bound.
how_used: Both sides begin as the full product (x-1)(x-2)...(x-2016), so all 2016 factors (x-k) are common. If a factor (x-k) survives on both the left and the right, then x=k zeroes both sides, making x=k a real root of the equation, which is forbidden. So for each k in {1,...,2016} the factor (x-k) must be erased from at least one side; these are 2016 distinct factors, forcing at least 2016 erasures. (This is only the lower bound; achievability that exactly 2016 suffices is a separate construction, see the partition crux.)

technique: To force a factored equation prod A_i(x) = prod B_j(x) to have no real root, deal the shared linear factors into the two sides so that neighboring survivors pair into quadratics whose paired difference is a constant, letting a global sign/magnitude comparison of the two products rule out equality on every interval.
how_used: Erase, on the left, every (x-k) with k congruent to 2,3 mod 4 and, on the right, every (x-m) with m congruent to 0,1 mod 4 (1008 per side, 2016 total). This leaves prod_{j=0}^{503}(x-4j-1)(x-4j-4) = prod_{j=0}^{503}(x-4j-2)(x-4j-3). The staggering makes each left pair equal its matching right pair minus 2: (x-4j-1)(x-4j-4) = (x-4j-2)(x-4j-3) - 2. No real x satisfies it, shown by cases on x: (i) x an integer 1..2016 zeros exactly one side; (ii) on (4k+1,4k+2) or (4k+3,4k+4) the left is negative (one pair negative, rest positive) while the right is positive; (iii) for x<1, x>2016, or (4k,4k+1), write L/R = prod(1 - 2/((x-4j-2)(x-4j-3))) with each denominator >2, so 0<L/R<1; (iv) on (4k+2,4k+3), regroup as (x-1)/(x-2) . (x-2016)/(x-2015) . prod(1 + 2/((x-4j+1)(x-4j-2))), each factor >1, so L/R>1.

technique: For a 'least number of deletions' problem, get the lower bound by counting the objects that are common to both sides and must all be destroyed: each common root survives as a solution unless at least one of its two occurrences is erased, forcing a deletion count at least the number of common objects.
how_used: Both sides start as the identical product (x-1)...(x-2016), so all 2016 factors are common. For each k in 1..2016, x=k is a root of both sides; as long as (x-k) survives on both sides x=k remains a root, and even keeping it on one side alone still lets x=k zero that side (both sides must be nonzero there to avoid a root, since the equation reads 'nonzero = nonzero' only if neither side vanishes). To kill the root x=k one must erase (x-k) from at least one side; doing so for all k=1..2016 requires at least 2016 erasures. Hence the answer is at least 2016, matching the construction's 2016, so the minimum is exactly 2016.

technique: Absorb an additive constant by shifting the unknown function so a quadratic self-relation becomes a clean squaring identity
how_used: After x=y=0 forces f(0)=-1 and y=0 gives f(x)^2=-2f(x)+f(x^2), i.e. (f(x)+1)^2=f(x^2)+1, set g(x)=f(x)+1 to get the pure multiplicative relation g(x^2)=g(x)^2 (hence g(y)>=0 for y>=0), which drives the entire analysis

technique: Discard the max by keeping only the branch that yields an inequality of one fixed sign
how_used: Replace max{f(x^2)+f(y^2), f(x^2+y^2)} by its first argument f(x^2)+f(y^2) to turn the equality into f(x+y)^2 >= 2f(x)f(y)+f(x^2)+f(y^2), which in g becomes (g(x+y)-1)^2 >= (g(x)+g(y)-1)^2 - 1, a tractable one-sided quadratic inequality (3)

technique: Iterate the squaring relation and take 2^n-th roots so a bounded target squeezes the value at a single point
how_used: Using g(x^{2^n})=g(x)^{2^n}, feed the bound at x^{2^n} (e.g. g(2^{2^n}-x)>=0 giving g(x)^{2^n} bounded, or the g(2k)>=k+1 growth giving g(a)^{2^n} > (a^{2^n}-2)/2) and let n go to infinity to force |g(x)|<=1 in Case 1 and g(a)=a in Case 2

technique: Split a single reciprocal term via Cauchy-Schwarz against a two-term weighted sum whose weights are tuned so the resulting bound is a difference of consecutive index-shifted quantities that telescope on summation
how_used: Applied CS as (x_{k-1}+(x_k-x_{k-1}))((k-1)^2/x_{k-1}+3^2/(x_k-x_{k-1})) >= (k-1+3)^2=(k+2)^2, chosen so it rearranges to 9/(x_k-x_{k-1}) >= (k+2)^2/x_k - (k-1)^2/x_{k-1}; summing over k telescopes the RHS into 4*sum (k+1)/x_k plus a leftover n^2/x_n>0, yielding a=4/9

technique: Attain the extremal constant by choosing the sequence gaps that force equality in each Cauchy-Schwarz step, then let n grow so both telescoping sides reach their limits
how_used: Chose x_k - x_{k-1} = k(k+1), i.e. x_k = k(k+1)(k+2)/3, the equality case of the CS split; then LHS = sum 1/(k(k+1)) -> 1 and RHS-bracket = sum (k+1)/x_k = 3 sum 1/(k(k+2)) -> 9/4, forcing a <= 4/9 and matching the admissible bound

technique: To prove an order-implication about a function, negate the conclusion to produce a strictly positive quantity, then feed exactly that quantity as the free variable of the functional equation so one term's argument collapses to a chosen value and the remaining strictly-positive terms contradict the assumed inequality.
how_used: From P(x,y): f(x)=f(f²(x)+y)+f(x·f(y))·f(x+y) with all terms in R_{>0}, define Q(a,b): f(a)≥f(b) ⟹ f²(b)≥a. To prove Q, suppose f(a)≥f(b) but a>f²(b); then a−f²(b)>0 is a legal input. Plug P(b, a−f²(b)): the first term's argument becomes f²(b)+(a−f²(b))=a, giving f(b)=f(a)+f(b·f(a−f²(b)))·f(b+a−f²(b)). The extra product term is strictly positive, so f(b)>f(a), contradicting f(a)≥f(b). Hence a≤f²(b). Q is the engine for all later monotonicity deductions.

technique: Apply an order-implication to itself at iterated arguments so the resulting chain of inequalities sandwiches a high iterate between a lower one from both sides, forcing an iterate identity.
how_used: From Q(a,a) (trivial premise f(a)≥f(a)) get f²(t)≥t for all t. Setting t=f²(x) gives f⁴(x)≥f²(x); setting t=f(x),f³(x) gives f(x)≤f³(x)≤f⁵(x). The last chain makes the premise of Q(f⁴(x),x) hold (need f⁵(x)≥f(x)), so Q yields f²(x)≥f⁴(x). Combined with f⁴(x)≥f²(x) this forces f⁴(x)=f²(x).

technique: Prove injectivity by evaluating the equation at two inputs assumed to share an output, cancelling the common factor to get a shift-invariance, then rule out the resulting nonzero period by feeding it into an order-implication that would force an unbounded chain.
how_used: P(f²(x),u) and P(f²(x),v) both equal f³(x); each factors as f³(x)=(1+f(x·f(·)))·f(x+·). If f(u)=f(v) the bracket factors match, so f(x+u)=f(x+v) for all x, i.e. f has period T=u−v>0. But then f(1+nT)=f(1) makes Q(1+nT,1) valid, forcing f²(1)≥1+nT for all n — absurd. So u=v and f is injective; with f⁴=f² and injectivity of f²=f∘f, f²(x)=x (f is an involution).

technique: Once an involution collapses the equation to a product form, pin the function on a half-line by a normalizing substitution, then propagate to the full domain by varying the remaining free arguments.
how_used: With f^2(x)=x, the first term f(f(f(x))+y)=f(x+y) (since f(f(x))=x), so the FE becomes f(x)=f(x+y)[1+f(xf(y))]. P(1,y) gives f(1+y)=f(1)/(1+y), fixing f on inputs >1. Then for a,b>1, P(a,b) reads 1/a = (1/(a+b))[1+f((a/b)f(1))]; varying (a,b) determines f everywhere, yielding f(x)=c/x with c=f(1)>0. Direct substitution confirms f(x)=c/x solves the original FE, so it is the unique solution.

technique: To extract an order-reversing implication from an inequality-free functional equation, assume the desired implication fails, turn the resulting positive gap into a legal fresh argument, and substitute it so one term becomes the value you want to bound while a manifestly positive term remains, yielding a contradiction.
how_used: Introduce Q(a,b): f(a) >= f(b) => f(f(b)) >= a. To prove it, assume for contradiction a > f(f(b)), so a - f(f(b)) > 0 is a legal positive input; substitute P(b, a - f(f(b))) into f(x) = f(f(f(x))+y) + f(xf(y))f(x+y). The outer argument f(f(b)) + (a - f(f(b))) = a, so the first term is f(a), and since f maps R+ to R+ the product term f(bf(y))f(b+y) is strictly positive; the equation reads f(b) = f(a) + (positive) > f(a), contradicting f(a) >= f(b). So Q holds. Q is the sole tool by which the order structure of f is later exploited.

technique: Chain a derived order-implication against iterated values of the function to sandwich an iterate between two of its own further iterates, collapsing the tower of iterates to a fixed small period.
how_used: From Q take a=b=t: f(t) >= f(t) gives f(f(t)) >= t for all t (call it L). Apply L at t=f^2(x) to get f^4(x) >= f^2(x). Apply L at t=f(x), f^3(x) to get f(x) <= f^3(x) <= f^5(x), so f^5(x) >= f(x), i.e. f(f^4(x)) >= f(x). That validates the hypothesis of Q(f^4(x), x), whose conclusion is f(f(x)) >= f^4(x), i.e. f^2(x) >= f^4(x). Combined with f^4(x) >= f^2(x) this forces f^2(x) = f^4(x) for all x: the iterate tower stabilizes with period dividing 2.

technique: Prove injectivity by showing that two arguments sharing a value would force a nonzero period, then discard periodicity because it contradicts the previously derived order-implication at arbitrarily large arguments.
how_used: Suppose f(u) = f(v) with u != v, T = u - v > 0. Substitute P(f^2(x), u) and P(f^2(x), v). The LHS is f^3(x) both times; using f^4 = f^2 the outer term is f(f^2(x)+y) and the middle factor is f(f^2(x)f(y)); since f(u) = f(v) the bracket [1 + f(f^2(x)f(y))] is equal for y=u and y=v, so the equality of the two right-hand sides forces f(f^2(x)+u) = f(f^2(x)+v). As x varies this makes f periodic with period T on all sufficiently large arguments. But periodicity contradicts Q, since Q(1+nT, 1) would have to hold for all n, absurd for large n. Hence u = v and f is injective; applying injectivity to f^2(x) = f^4(x) gives f^2(x) = x (an involution), after which P reduces to f(x) = f(x+y)[1 + f(xf(y))] and pins f(x) = c/x.
